verdict.summary: RepeatedAttrDefEqual writes attacker-influenced AttrDef names into a LOG(ERROR) stream without neutralizing control characters (newlines/CR), enabling log injection/forgery when a caller supplies duplicate names containing embedded separators.

evidence.snippet:
LOG(ERROR) << "AttrDef names must be unique, but '" << def.name()
                 << "' appears more than once";
evidence.reason: def.name() originates from attacker-controlled parameter a1 (accessed at line 5 and passed through unmodified at line 7). The duplicate-name guard at line 6 merely detects repetition; it does not restrict the name's byte content. A witness value such as name = "ok\n[spoofed log line]" appearing twice in a1 passes the guard and reaches the log sink at lines 7-8 with the newline intact, allowing the attacker to inject forged or malformed log records (CWE-117).

assumptions: def.name() and a1/a2 are supplied by callers outside the shown code; per task rules, parameter provenance is sufficient to establish taint.
The LOG macro is assumed to append raw bytes of the streamed value to a log line without escaping control characters, as no sanitization is shown.
limitations: Actual severity depends on the log consumer (plain text files vs. structured/parsed logs); if an upstream caller sanitizes AttrDef names or the build's log backend strips control characters, the injection is not exploitable, but no such mechanism is shown.
Many attacker-controlled duplicate names could inflate log volume (log-flood DoS); this is a separate algorithmic/resource concern and is not confirmed as an additional CWE.
The overwrite of duplicate map entries at line 10 is a data-integrity quirk with no security sink in the shown code.

verdict.summary: GetInitOp dereferences the iterator returned by outputs().find(kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey) without checking it against outputs().end(), so a crafted MetaGraphDef whose __saved_model_init_op signature entry lacks that output key triggers an end-iterator (NULL-class) dereference at the assignment, causing undefined behavior / a crash when loading a malicious SavedModel (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: Line 6 only verifies that the outer signature_def map contains kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey; the nested find on line 8 is dereferenced on line 9 without checking against outputs().end(). The attacker-controlled MetaGraphDef provides a SignatureDef under that key whose outputs map is empty or lacks the key, so find returns end() and ->second is undefined behavior — a reachable null/end-iterator dereference (CWE-476) on loading a crafted SavedModel.

assumptions: meta_graph_def is deserialized from a SavedModel bundle file, so its map contents are attacker-controlled when loading an untrusted model.
kSavedModelInitOpSignatureKey is a fixed constant; its exact value does not affect the analysis.
The caller passes a valid non-null init_op_name output pointer.
limitations: export_dir is concatenated into an errors::FailedPrecondition message (line 26); if the caller logs that status, embedded newlines could inject log lines, but no log write exists in the shown code, so log injection is not confirmed.
A NULL init_op_name parameter would crash at lines 7/28, but producing it requires an out-of-scope caller fault, not a path constructed by the shown code.
If neither the signature nor a collection defines an init op, the function returns OK without setting *init_op_name; this is a correctness concern, not a security finding.
The confirmed dereference is demonstrated as a crash/denial of service; no arbitrary memory read or write was proven.

verdict.summary: The shown function is a thin orchestration wrapper: it ensures the repo exists (lines 24-25), loads the bundle via flatpak_bundle_load (lines 27-33), and then either reuses an existing deployment's remote with optional GPG-data config import (lines 46-62) or creates an origin remote from parsed fields (lines 63-80). Every security-relevant operation (bundle parsing/validation, remote-name construction, config writes, GPG import) is delegated to unseen callees; the shown code contains no memory operations, no loops, no string/query/log/command construction, no crypto choices, and no file/access logic. All NULL-able values are guarded before use (lines 24, 34-35, 38-42, 47, 52, 78-79), and both outcomes of every branch are fully handled, so no attacker-controlled value reaches a dangerous operation in the shown code.

assumptions: flatpak_dir_ensure_repo, flatpak_bundle_load, flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data, flatpak_dir_modify_remote, and flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote perform their own input validation; the shown code only delegates parsing, remote-name construction, config writes, and GPG import to them.

After flatpak_bundle_load returns non-NULL metadata (line 34), the out-parameter ref is treated as valid for flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data (line 46) and flatpak_decomposed_dup_id/flatpak_decomposed_get_ref (lines 65, 72); no shown path manufactures a NULL ref.
g_file_get_basename (line 67) yields a non-NULL basename for the supplied GFile.
limitations: Bundle contents are parsed inside flatpak_bundle_load (lines 27-33), which is not in the shown code; parser/decoder/checksum/compression flaws there are out of scope (pure delegated parse with failure handled at line 34).

Potential injection into remote names or OSTree config via basename/origin/id/collection_id/gpg_data reaches flatpak_dir_modify_remote (lines 58-59) and flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote (lines 68-77) only as opaque arguments; the actual string construction and writes occur in unseen callees, so this is a pass-through concern, not a shown-code finding.

A denial-of-service via a large or malformed bundle would depend on allocation inside the unseen flatpak_bundle_load and on a loop that is not present in the shown code; no volume-scaling loop exists here.
No loops, pointer arithmetic, casts, or explicit buffer operations exist in the shown code, so no memory-safety or ReDoS amplification can be demonstrated in it.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only indexed access, node_list().value(0) at line 33, is fully guarded by the value_size() != 1 check at line 29 which admits exactly size==1 (index 0 < size 1) and rejects empty or multi-element lists. The only other attacker-controlled data flow is export_dir embedded into a Status message at line 31; the shown code contains no logging/display sink, so log injection is out of scope.

assumptions: init_op_name is a non-null valid std::string* supplied by the caller.
meta_graph_def is a fully parsed, structurally valid protobuf message.
std::string assignment and strings::StrCat are memory-safe for any input length.
limitations: export_dir flows unvalidated into the error Status message at lines 30-32; if an unseen caller logs or displays the Status, newline/control characters in the path could cause log/terminal injection. Not a confirmed finding because the injection sink is absent from the shown code.

When neither the signature key nor the chosen collection key is present, GetInitOp returns Status::OK() without setting *init_op_name (line 35). This is a behavioral/robustness concern, not a security vulnerability in the shown code.
The attacker-controlled init op name returned via *init_op_name (lines 14, 33) is consumed by an unseen caller that may look up and execute the op; any abuse of that flow is outside the shown code.
An OOB read at line 33 would occur for an empty node_list, but the guard at line 29 (value_size() != 1) rejects that case, so no failing witness exists.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The key tensor is constrained to exactly one element (lines 14 and 17) before the copy at line 23; the loop at lines 26-28 indexes OpInputList only with i in [0, values_tensor.size()) under the strict-inequality guard i < values_tensor.size(), so no out-of-bounds access is reachable. The only unvalidated input, indices_tensor, is passed through to StagingMap<Ordered>::put at line 31, but all operations on it occur inside that unseen callee (pass-through), which is out of scope. No injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: On success of OP_REQUIRES_OK at lines 3, 11-13, map and the tensor pointers are non-null and valid.
values_tensor.size() and OpInputList::operator[] are consistent (indices 0..size()-1 valid).
The key tensor dtype (int64 scalar) is enforced by kernel/op registration, not by the shown code.
StagingMap<Ordered>::put enforces its own capacity and indices handling (unseen code).
limitations: indices_tensor (line 12) is forwarded unvalidated to map->put at line 31; any OOB, type-confusion, or logic flaw from malformed indices would occur inside StagingMap<Ordered>::put, whose body is not shown — a pure pass-through, so it is not confirmable from the given code.
Resource-exhaustion/DoS via unbounded staging growth is governed by the unseen capacity logic in put and by framework graph limits, not by a reachable unbounded loop in the shown code.
Missing validation of indices dtype/shape is a defensive-hardening concern only; no sink for it exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only memory-sensitive operations are fully guarded: node.input(0) is read only when node.input_size() > 0 (line 4, so index 0 is always in bounds), control edges are rejected before lookup (lines 6-8), and the NodeDef* returned by graph.GetNode is null-checked before dereference (lines 11-13). The shown code contains no injection, crypto, file-handling, or authz sinks.

assumptions: MutableGraphView::GetNode returns nullptr for names not present in the graph and does not mutate the graph.

ParseTensorName returns a node-name/port TensorId and signals control edges so IsTensorIdControlling and GetNode receive a valid lookup name; malformed inputs either become a plain name or cause a lookup miss that yields nullptr and is handled.
The graph and the node reference remain valid for the duration of the call (no mutation in the shown code; Grappler is single-threaded).
Protobuf field limits bound the length of node.input(0); no attacker-controlled length reaches an allocation in this function.
limitations: Without the null check at lines 11-13, a NULL dereference at line 14 would be reachable from an Identity node whose input names a non-existent node (attacker-crafted GraphDef); the shown code contains that check, so it is not a finding here.
Attacker provenance of node.input(0) from a serialized GraphDef is plausible, but no sink in the shown code consumes it unsafely.
Caller-side invariants outside the shown code (e.g., a dangling node/graph reference if the graph were mutated elsewhere during the optimization pass) are out of scope.

verdict.summary: mrb_ary_shift_m is safe as shown: the attacker-controlled count n is fully constrained before every memory operation. Line 13 rejects n<0 with an ArgumentError, and line 14 clamps n>len to exactly len, establishing the invariant 0 <= n <= len for all later uses. Consequently the shared-window bump (lines 18-19), the allocation at line 15, and the copy loop (lines 33-36) only touch indices in [0, len-1]: max read index = (size-1)+n = len-1, max write index = size-1 = len-n-1, both strictly below len. The loop terminates in exactly size = len-n iterations. No injection, crypto, file, or auth sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: mrb_get_args with '|i' either assigns n a valid mrb_int or raises (TypeError for non-integers, RangeError on Bignum overflow), so n is never used uninitialized and cannot exceed the mrb_int range.
ARY_LEN(a) accurately reflects the allocated capacity of a's buffer; this is a VM-maintained invariant for valid RArray objects.
ARY_PTR(a) and ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN semantics (threshold constant) are the standard mruby definitions; the threshold only affects which of two equally safe copy strategies runs.
limitations: The no-argument path (line 9) delegates to mrb_ary_shift, whose implementation is not shown; any concern there is a pure pass-through and out of scope.
Float-to-mrb_int conversion behavior inside mrb_get_args is not shown; even a pathological conversion result is neutralized by the line 13 rejection or the line 14 clamp before any sink.

When len == n on the shared path, line 18 leaves a->as.heap.ptr one-past-the-end with len 0; the shown code performs no dereference of that pointer, so this is a hardening/robustness note, not a finding.
For an empty array with a negative n, line 12 returns [] without raising (semantic quirk); no memory operation occurs, so there is no security impact.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled shift count n is fully constrained before every sink: line 15 raises on n < 0 and line 16 clamps n to len (invariant 1 <= n <= len). The allocation read at line 17, the shared-path pointer adjustment at lines 20-21, and the copy loop at lines 35-38 (max read offset n + size - 1 = len - 1, max write offset size - 1 = len - n - 1) all stay within [0, len), and the loop terminates because size strictly decreases. No OOB, injection, weak-crypto, or file/access-control sink is reachable.

assumptions: mrb_int is a signed integer type, and mrb_get_args(mrb, "|i", &n) either raises TypeError/RangeError or stores a representable mrb_int, so n is valid when consumed.
ARY_LEN(a) returns the live element count with 0 <= len <= allocated capacity, and ARY_PTR(a) is readable for len elements.
limitations: The early return at line 14 (len == 0 || n == 0) fires before the n < 0 check, so shifting an empty array with a negative argument returns an empty array instead of raising ArgumentError; behavioral discrepancy with no memory-safety impact.
Allocation failure in mrb_ary_new_from_values at line 17 is not attacker-scalable because n is clamped to the existing array length len, bounding the allocation by the array's own size.
n is never read uninitialized: it is only consumed when mrb_get_args returned nonzero, meaning the optional integer argument was actually supplied.
The shown code contains no printf-family, exec, SQL, log, header, crypto, or file-path sinks; the only formatted call (mrb_raise at line 15) uses a constant string.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad computes in_index and the depth index from attacker-controlled pooling sequences and shape dimensions without validating that row/col sequence values are non-negative and within input bounds, or that out_batch/out_depth do not exceed in_batch/in_depth, causing a heap out-of-bounds write at in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor values (lines 98, 103) and shape dims flow unvalidated into in_index (line 115) and d (line 117). The only guards are element-count checks (lines 38-49) and !=0 dim checks (lines 59-70); neither constrains sequence values to [0, in_rows), nor requires out_batch <= in_batch or out_depth <= in_depth. Witness: in_shape=(1,4,4,1), row_seq=[-1,0], col_seq=[0,1], overlapping_=false passes all guards; in_row_start=-1 reaches the in_r loop (line 113), giving in_index=-4, so coeffRef(0,-4) writes before the buffer. Equally, out_batch=2 with in_batch=1 yields in_index=16 (one past the 16-element buffer), and out_depth=8 with in_depth=1 indexes row d=1 of a 1-row map. All are heap out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787).

assumptions: TensorFlow op inputs (orig_input_tensor_shape, out_backprop, row_seq_tensor, col_seq_tensor) are attacker-controlled, e.g., via a crafted model or direct API invocation; overlapping_ is a trusted op attribute.
TensorFlow builds use NDEBUG where DCHECK-style validation in TensorShape/Tensor may be compiled out; the shown code contains no explicit shape-consistency or sequence-value validation regardless.
limitations: Attacker-controlled in_shape dims can also request extremely large allocations (lines 76, 81-83); this is a resource-consumption/DoS concern not separately confirmed and not needed for the OOB finding.

Negative in_shape dims (admitted by the !=0 checks, lines 59-70) may produce an invalid TensorShape and an op-level error instead of memory corruption; the confirmed witnesses above use a valid positive input shape.
Division by num_elements_in_pooling_cell == 0 is not reachable: when the factor is <= 0 the corresponding inner loop is empty, so the division at line 123 never executes with a zero divisor.
No separate CWE is assigned for integer overflow in the in_index arithmetic (line 115); it is subsumed by the same CWE-787 finding.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayCreate derives its malloc size from an attacker-controlled int through 32-bit signed arithmetic; a large positive size (e.g. size = 2^30) wraps alloc_size to a small positive value (4), bypassing the `alloc_size <= 0` guard and allocating far fewer bytes than the returned object advertises, causing out-of-bounds heap access when consumers index data[0..size-1].

evidence.reason: alloc_size is derived from the unvalidated parameter `size` via TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes (line 2) and only filtered by `alloc_size <= 0` (line 3), which rejects nothing above zero. With sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)=4 and 4-byte ints, size = 1,073,741,824 (2^30) wraps the computed 4 + 4*size to 4, a positive value that passes the guard, so malloc(4) at line 4 allocates 4 bytes while line 6 records ret->size = 2^30, and consumers writing data[0..size-1] overrun the heap allocation (CWE-190).

assumptions: TfLiteIntArray is the standard { int size; int data[]; } layout with sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)=4 on 32-bit-int platforms, and TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes computes sizeof(TfLiteIntArray) + size*sizeof(int), returning -1 for negative size; the witness still produces an undersized allocation even if sizeof(TfLiteIntArray)=8.
Callers of TfLiteIntArrayCreate write to or read data[0..size-1] according to the stored size, per standard TFLite usage.
limitations: The out-of-bounds read/write statement itself is performed by unseen callers; the shown code creates the undersized allocation and records the inflated capacity.
No injection, cryptographic, file-handling, or authz sinks exist in the shown code; the NULL-path on malloc failure is handled correctly.

verdict.summary: IsIdentityConsumingSwitch dereferences the result of graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) at line 11 without a null check. A crafted node whose non-control input names a node absent from the graph makes GetNode return nullptr, causing a NULL pointer dereference and process crash (DoS).

evidence.reason: input_node is assigned the unchecked return of graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()) at line 10. tensor_id.node() derives from the attacker-influenced node.input(0) parsed at line 5 and is not constrained to an existing node name (only control inputs are excluded at line 6). For an Identity node with node.input(0) = "no_such_node", GetNode returns nullptr and IsSwitch(*input_node) dereferences it, crashing the process.

assumptions: MutableGraphView::GetNode returns nullptr when the requested node name is not present in the graph (standard lookup semantics for the graph-view API).
The NodeDef input strings are derived from caller-supplied graph/model data; the shown code performs no validation that a regular input name references an existing node.
limitations: If the unseen enclosing pipeline validates that every non-control input name references an existing node before this function runs, the NULL path would be unreachable in that pipeline; such validation is not present in the shown code.
No other security-relevant sinks (format strings, command execution, SQL/XPath, log/header injection, crypto, file handling, authz) exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: recalc_intercepts performs bounded intercept recombination: both array loops use strict i < MAX_INTERCEPT against fixed-size intercepts[] arrays, guest-controlled values are only OR-ed (enable) or bit-tested, and the only guest-triggered clears (CR8/VINTR under V_INTR_MASKING_MASK) are documented as unnecessary in that mode; SMI/VMMCALL clears are fixed or trusted-global gated. No reachable memory-safety, injection, or isolation-bypass flaw is present.

assumptions: The intercepts[] arrays have exactly MAX_INTERCEPT entries and INTERCEPT_* constants are less than MAX_INTERCEPT (struct/enum invariants defined outside the shown code).
svm->vmcb, svm->vmcb01.ptr, and svm->nested.ctl are valid kernel-maintained state whenever the function runs.
svm->nested.ctl faithfully reflects the L1-supplied nested VMCB control area, and is_guest_mode() correctly reflects whether the active vmcb is the L2 vmcb.
intercept_smi is a trusted module-global configuration value.
limitations: Because the V_INTR_MASKING branch clears occur before the OR loop at line 35, an L1 guest can re-enable the CR8/VINTR/VMMCALL intercept bits it set; this is a behavioral/performance quirk only, since re-enabling intercepts merely increases vmexits and cannot remove an intercept L0 relies on.

A hypothetical DoS via reserved bits in g->intercepts[] is not substantiated: reserved intercept bits have no defined effect demonstrated in the shown code, and any effect would be confined to L2 execution.
Cross-function invariants (e.g., that c aliases the vmcb02 control area exactly when is_guest_mode() is true) are assumed from unseen callers and are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Both intercept-merge loops are bounded by the strict condition `i < MAX_INTERCEPT`, admitting indices 0..MAX_INTERCEPT-1 against MAX_INTERCEPT-element arrays, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable. The only guest-influenced data, `svm->nested.ctl`, reaches fixed-index bit operations (copy/OR/clear of compile-time intercept bits) and never an index, length, pointer, or injection sink; the OR can only add interception relative to L1's set.

assumptions: `MAX_INTERCEPT` equals the element count of the `intercepts[]` arrays in `struct vmcb_control_area` (32 u32s in the kernel definition), so `i < MAX_INTERCEPT` keeps every loop access in bounds.

`c`, `h`, and `g` point to control areas of identical layout; `svm->vmcb`, `svm->vmcb01.ptr`, and `svm->nested.ctl` are valid under KVM invariants, with the `is_guest_mode()` check gating subsequent use.

`svm->nested.ctl` is the kernel's copy of the L1-supplied L2 VMCB control area, validated during nested-VMCB load before this function runs; even absent that validation, the shown code derives no index or length from it.
`vmcb_clr_intercept`/`vmcb_set_intercept` use compile-time intercept indices within array bounds (defined outside the shown code).
limitations: The L1-supplied intercept bits are OR-ed into the active L2 intercepts (`c->intercepts[i] |= g->intercepts[i]`); as shown this can only expand interception relative to L1's own set and never lets L2 reduce it, so no virtualization-confinement break is demonstrable from the shown code.
No candidate reached the 0.5 confidence threshold required for a finding; the completeness of the unshown nested-VMCB validation and of the `vmcb_*` helpers is outside the scope of the shown code.

verdict.summary: vidioc_querycap is not vulnerable: every output write is bounded — labellen is the ternary minimum of sizeof(cap->card) and sizeof(dev->card_label) so it never exceeds the card buffer, snprintf/strlcpy cap all writes at the destination sizes (including the %03d expansion of device_nr), reserved is zeroed, and no attacker-controlled input reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink in the shown code.

assumptions: cap is a kernel-side copy of the user's struct v4l2_capability supplied by the V4L2 core, and ioctl/open access control is enforced by core VFS/file-permission checks before this handler runs.
Per the V4L2 UAPI, sizeof(cap->card) == 32 and sizeof(cap->bus_info) == 32; in this driver sizeof(dev->card_label) == 32, so labellen resolves to 32 in both ternary branches.
dev->card_label is NUL-terminated within its declared size by its producer (set outside the shown code via a bounded copy); this is the invariant that makes the '%s' read on line 14 in-bounds.
limitations: If dev->card_label were not NUL-terminated within its 32 bytes (a property established only by producers outside the shown code), the '%s' read at line 14 could read past the array; not confirmed because no shown code writes card_label unsafely.

Bytes of cap->card/cap->bus_info after the terminating NUL are not re-zeroed; because the V4L2 core copies the user's own struct into cap, the residue is the caller's own data rather than uninitialized kernel memory, so no confirmed disclosure.

A NULL dereference of dev, dev->vdev, or video_get_drvdata(dev->vdev) is not reachable from the shown code; those pointers are guaranteed non-NULL by core device registration invariants, so any NULL would have to be produced by an unseen caller.
Truncation of card_label/bus_info to 31 chars plus NUL is silent but has no security impact since both snprintf sizes are strictly respected.

verdict.summary: GetHintFormat dereferences trak->Media->information->sampleTable->SampleDescription->child_boxes without NULL checks on sampleTable/SampleDescription (line 8). A crafted hint track with an HMHD box whose subType is 0 and a missing sample-description box passes the line 4 and line 7 guards and crashes the process (NULL-pointer dereference, DoS).

evidence.reason: The chain trak->Media->information->sampleTable->SampleDescription->child_boxes is dereferenced with no NULL check. The taint source is trak (line 1), built by the parser from an attacker-controlled media file, so sampleTable or SampleDescription may be NULL on malformed input. The only guards on the path are line 4 (validates hmhd non-NULL and type == HMHD) and line 7 (requires !hmhd || !hmhd->subType, which after line 4 means subType == 0); neither constrains sampleTable or SampleDescription. Concrete failing witness: an HMHD box with subType == 0 and SampleDescription == NULL passes both guards and dereferences NULL at this sink.

assumptions: trak is produced by the GPAC parser from an untrusted media file, so the nested pointers (Media, information, sampleTable, SampleDescription) are attacker-influenced and may be NULL on malformed input.
gf_list_get returns NULL for an empty/absent list; that NULL return (a) is checked by the 'if (a)' guard at line 10, so an empty child_boxes list alone is not a crash.
limitations: The same NULL-deref class also applies to the line 3 chain trak->Media->information->InfoHeader if trak/Media/information are NULL; grouped under the same CWE-476 finding but not evidenced separately.
The 'if (!hmhd)' at line 9 is dead code (line 4 already returns for NULL hmhd); robustness redundancy, not a separate vulnerability.
Impact is limited to denial of service (crash); no memory-corruption, injection, or weak-crypto sink exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in BiasAndClamp: array_data is written at offsets array_offset+i that can exceed array_size-1 whenever array_size is not a multiple of bias_size (e.g., array_size=10, bias_size=4 writes indices 10-11). The only guard, TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ at line 10, is a debug-only assertion compiled out in NDEBUG/release builds and also admits negative bias_size, so caller-supplied sizes reach the write unvalidated in the loops at lines 58-64 (and the NEON loops at 16, 39-42, 50, 53, which additionally never terminate when the divisibility invariant fails).

evidence.snippet:
array_data[array_offset + i] = ActivationFunctionWithMinMax(
          array_data[array_offset + i] + bias_data[i], clamp_min, clamp_max);
evidence.reason: Caller-supplied sizes bias_size and array_size (parameters, lines 1-2) are not runtime-validated: line 10's TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ is compiled out in release builds (and admits negative bias_size even in debug). With array_size=10, bias_size=4 the outer loop (line 58) admits offsets 0,4,8 with 8<10, and the inner loop (line 60) writes indices 10 and 11 via array_data[array_offset+i], past the 10-float array_data buffer - an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787). The same pair makes the NEON loop at line 16 skip past array_end_ptr forever, writing OOB at lines 39-42/50/53.

assumptions: TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ follows standard DCHECK semantics: active (aborting) in debug builds, a no-op under NDEBUG/release.
bias_size and array_size are caller-supplied length values; in the surrounding TFLite context they derive from tensor/shape metadata that can originate in a possibly untrusted model file.
array_data and bias_data are real allocations of at least array_size and bias_size floats respectively, so the demonstrated overflow is a true heap OOB rather than a logical-only error.
limitations: If every upstream caller always enforces array_size % bias_size == 0 before calling, the non-divisible pair cannot occur through that caller; the shown function itself provides no such enforcement, which is the defect.

Negative bias_size (e.g., -2 with even array_size passes line 10 even in debug) causes backward-walking, non-terminating loops and OOB writes before array_data; not counted as a finding because negative sizes are not produced by the known callers (robustness concern only).

NEON vld1q/vst1q require 16-byte alignment; bias_size not a multiple of 4 can misalign later blocks and fault. This is a DoS/robustness concern depending on unshown buffer alignment guarantees, not a memory-safety write, and is not scored.
No injection, crypto, or authz sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: gitn_box_del is a box destructor that frees each entry name, the entries array, and the box. The loop bound i < ptr->nb_entries admits exactly indices 0..nb_entries-1, which is correct for an array of nb_entries elements, and the pointer NULL check at line 5 is exact. The only weakness is the absence of an 'entries != NULL' guard before the line 7 dereference, but a NULL or undersized entries array can only be produced by code outside this function, so no attacker-triggerable failure is reachable within the shown code.

assumptions: ptr->entries is allocated by the unseen construction/parse code with at least ptr->nb_entries elements
nb_entries is an unsigned integer field so the loop cannot go negative
gf_free is NULL-safe per the codebase convention
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference at ptr->entries[i] (line 7) if ptr->entries == NULL while nb_entries > 0; the NULL-producing state can only be supplied by an unseen caller, so it is out of scope per the NULL-dereference reachability rule
Out-of-bounds read if ptr->entries is allocated with fewer than nb_entries elements; the mismatch would be an unseen-allocation invariant violation, not a flaw in the shown loop
Potential double-free if two entries alias the same name pointer; no shown code path establishes such aliasing
These items are defensive hardening concerns only and carry no CWE

verdict.summary: ReadPSDChannelPixels reads channel data from the caller-supplied `pixels` buffer for `image->columns` iterations with no length parameter or bounds check, so a crafted PSD whose header sets a large `image->columns` (with `packet_size` from image depth) drives the loop at line 32 to read beyond the end of `pixels` at lines 35/39/47, causing a heap-buffer over-read (crash / potential memory disclosure).

evidence.reason: The loop at line 32 iterates `x` while `x < (ssize_t) image->columns`; `image->columns` comes from the attacker-controlled PSD header and is never validated in the shown code. Each iteration consumes one byte (`*p++`, line 35), two bytes (`PushShortPixel`, line 39), or four bytes (`PushFloatPixel`, line 47) from `pixels`, whose length is not passed to this function and is never checked. The only guard on the read is the loop bound itself, which admits every value of `image->columns`, so a header value such that `columns * packet_size` exceeds the caller's buffer (e.g., `columns=1000000` with a 4-byte packet at line 47) reads out of bounds. The missing protecting check is a comparison of the consumed offset against the buffer length before lines 35/39/47; no such check exists between lines 26 and 74.

assumptions: `image->columns`, `image->depth`, and the cache/storage-class state are derived from the untrusted PSD file header/metadata by the caller and are not validated inside the shown function.
`GetPSDPacketSize` (line 31) returns the per-pixel byte size (1, 2, or 4) derived from image depth, and the reads at lines 35/39/47 consume exactly that many bytes.
The caller supplies decompressed channel data via `pixels` but does not pass its length to `ReadPSDChannelPixels`.
limitations: Actual occurrence of the overflow depends on the unseen caller allocating `pixels` smaller than `image->columns * packet_size`; a caller that always allocates exactly that many bytes would keep the read in-bounds, though the shown code contains no check enforcing it.

`GetAuthenticIndexQueue` (line 30) may return NULL but is dereferenced only inside `SetPSDPixel` for `PseudoClass` images, where the pixel cache provides the queue; no NULL-dereference is confirmed in the shown path.
If `image->columns` exceeds `SSIZE_MAX`, the cast at line 32 makes the loop condition false and no read occurs, so the signedness cast is not itself an exploitable overflow.

The 1-bit decoding branch (lines 55-72) consumes at most `ceil(image->columns/8)` bytes, which does not exceed a `columns`-byte allocation, and its nested loop terminates; it adds no separate finding.
Algorithmic-complexity / decompression-bomb denial of service is not assessed beyond the shown function.

verdict.summary: TfLiteIntArrayCreate derives the malloc size from the caller-supplied `size` through an int-returning helper; an attacker-chosen value such as 536870912 makes the helper's 64-bit byte count wrap in the int return to 4, which passes the only guard (`alloc_size <= 0` on an unsigned size_t admits every value except 0). malloc(4) returns a header-only buffer while `ret->size` records 536870912 elements, so any downstream indexed access of `data[]` is out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled parameter `size` (line 1) flows into `alloc_size` via the helper's int return (line 2); for `size = 536870912` the helper's 64-bit sum 4 + size*4 = 2147483652 truncates to int 4, so `alloc_size = 4` passes the line 3 guard (unsigned `alloc_size <= 0` excludes only the value 0). Line 6 then records `ret->size = 536870912`, producing a 4-byte allocation that claims ~134M int elements; consumers indexing `data[0..size-1]` read/write past the heap allocation (CWE-190 overflow into CWE-131 incorrect buffer size, yielding heap OOB).

assumptions: TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes is the standard TFLite implementation: returns -1 when size < 0, otherwise returns (int)(sizeof(TfLiteIntArray) + size * sizeof(int)), with sizeof(TfLiteIntArray) == 4 for the flexible-array struct { int size; int data[]; }.
The `size` parameter is attacker-influenced through model/tensor-derived caller data; the shown code places no constraint on it.
limitations: The negative-size path (-1 sentinel sign-extending to SIZE_MAX and bypassing the line 3 guard) is not exploitable in the shown code: malloc(SIZE_MAX) necessarily fails and line 5 returns NULL.
Values whose wrap lands exactly on 0 (e.g., size = 1073741822) are rejected by the line 3 guard, so only positive wrapped values trigger the undersized allocation.
The actual out-of-bounds read/write occurs in unseen TFLite consumers of the returned array; the shown code is the confirmed undersized allocation plus the inconsistent `ret->size` field.

verdict.summary: In the shown code, no attacker-controlled value reaches a dangerous operation. Tensor::FromProto only validates the shape (L4) and dtype (L5, L25-L27), branches on N=shape.num_elements() (L8), and delegates all parsing/memory work to unseen helpers Helper<T>::Decode (L12) and FromProtoField<T> (L15). The remaining operations (L29-L39) are pointer/refcount bookkeeping and a null-guarded log write of a constant string. Any content-size-vs-N, N*sizeof(T) overflow, or buffer-access issue would live in those unseen helper bodies, which are outside the analyzed snippet.

assumptions: The workspace is empty, so line numbers L1-L40 are a 1-based map of the provided snippet (L1 = 'bool Tensor::FromProto(...)', L40 = closing brace).

CASES_WITH_DEFAULT dispatches recognized DT_* enum values to the typed helper and executes its default arms (dtype_error = true) for any unrecognized value, so only known dtypes reach the decode/field calls.
TensorShape::IsValid at L4 admits only shapes whose num_elements() is -1 (incomplete), 0, or a positive product, so N takes no other negative values.
The bodies of Helper<T>::Decode and FromProtoField<T> are not shown and are treated as unseen callers/helpers.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read if a caller-supplied tensor_content() is shorter than N * sizeof(T): the size-consuming read occurs inside the unseen Helper<T>::Decode invoked at L12; the shown code merely passes (content, N) through (pure delegation), so it is out of scope for this snippet.

Potential integer overflow of N * sizeof(T) or oversized allocation for a very large N (L7, L8) would occur inside the unseen helpers; the shown code performs no allocation and no arithmetic on N, and the impact would be single-shot DoS.
CHECK_NOTNULL(a) at L2 aborts on a null Allocator*; a null value can only be supplied by an unseen caller and is not produced by any shown path.
For N == -1 or N == 0 the shown code commits a tensor with a null buffer (L29-L32); any subsequent dereference would occur in unseen consumers, not in the shown code.
No loops exist in the snippet, so no iteration-bound, hang, or ReDoS concern applies to the shown code.
No format-string, command, SQL, HTTP/header, crypto, file, or authz sinks exist in the shown lines; the only log call (L36-L37) writes a constant literal.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown function. It contains no memory-safety, injection, crypto/entropy, or file/access-control sink of its own: attacker-influenced values (bundle-derived origin, id, basename, gpg data, collection_id) are only selected, copied, or forwarded to unshown helpers (flatpak_bundle_load, flatpak_dir_modify_remote, flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote), which is a pass-through per the reachability rules. The shown control flow propagates NULL failures (lines 24-25, 34-35, 53, 71-72) and NULL-guards all optional outputs (lines 75-85).

assumptions: flatpak_bundle_load returning non-NULL metadata (checked at line 34) implies its derived out-values (ref, origin, to_checksum, included_gpg_data, collection_id) are valid per the helper contract.
g_file_get_basename (line 60) strips all directory components and cannot return a basename containing '/' per GLib's contract.
flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data, flatpak_dir_modify_remote, flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote, and ostree_repo_copy_config internals are not part of the shown code.
limitations: Attacker-controlled bundle bytes flow to GPG-key import and remote creation via lines 37, 51-52, and 61-70, but those sinks (keyring import, remote gpg-verify policy, remote-name sanitization) are in unshown helpers; any flaw there is out of scope and no concrete failing witness reaches a sink shown here.
remote (line 42) can be NULL if deploy-data origin is NULL and is passed to flatpak_dir_modify_remote (line 51); the potential dereference would occur inside the unshown helper.
No authn/authz check appears in the shown code; any permission enforcement for installing bundles lives in unseen callers.

Installing a flatpak bundle inherently executes its content, so importing the bundle's own GPG keys does not by itself cross an additional trust boundary; a stronger claim would require the unshown helpers' behavior.

verdict.summary: Duplicate AttrDef names in a1 are not validated by the shown code; they reach a debug-only DCHECK (line 6) that aborts the process, enabling denial of service against debug builds, while the DCHECK message streams the unsanitized attacker-controlled name into the log. In release builds the same input silently overwrites the map entry, degrading comparison correctness.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled names from parameter a1 (unvalidated in the shown code) flow into the DCHECK sink: an a1 containing two AttrDefs with the same name, e.g. "x", makes the condition false, aborting the process in debug builds and writing the raw name to the log without neutralization. The only guard is the debug-only DCHECK itself; it does not protect the release-build overwrite at line 9 and provides no filtering of log-breaking characters.

assumptions: a1/a2 are deserialized from untrusted protobuf input (e.g., loaded graph/model data) in the calling context, making their element names attacker-controlled.
The analyzed build configuration compiles DCHECK as an active assertion (debug/dbg build); in NDEBUG builds the check is removed.
def.name() is treated as an ordinary string returned by the protobuf accessor.
limitations: Duplicate names in a1 also cause a release-build correctness flaw: with a1 = [{x,f1},{x,f2}] and a2 = [{x,f2}], the last-wins overwrite at line 9 makes the function return true despite differing element counts; no security impact is demonstrable from the shown code, so it carries no CWE.
The newline/CRLF injection into the DCHECK log message shares the same trigger and statement as the CWE-617 abort and is not counted as an independent CWE.

unordered_map worst-case hash-collision complexity and key-copy allocation growth scale with attacker-controlled input but show no concrete amplification beyond ordinary input-size behavior; kept as a robustness note.
The dereference at line 14 is safe on all reachable paths: line 9 always stores &def, and line 13 checks iter != end() before dereference.

verdict.summary: Tensor::FromProto computes N = shape.num_elements() from attacker-controlled tensor_shape dims without an overflow check; a wrapped positive N passes the N > 0 guard and is passed to Helper<T>::Decode/FromProtoField, which size allocation and copies from N, producing a Tensor whose buffer is far smaller than its recorded shape and enabling heap out-of-bounds access in downstream consumers.

evidence.reason: N is the unchecked int64 product of attacker-controlled proto.tensor_shape() dims; e.g., dims {16, 2^60+1} multiply to 2^64+16 which wraps modulo 2^64 to N=16. TensorShape::IsValid (line 4) admits these dims, so the guard at line 4 does not protect the subsequent use.

N from line 7 reaches this allocation/copy sink. For the witness dims {16, 2^60+1}, N wraps to 16, passes N > 0 on line 8, and Decode allocates/copies from a 16-element buffer while line 20 records shape_ with 2^61+16 elements, breaking the element-count invariant and enabling out-of-bounds access downstream. The N > 0 guard admits this wrapped value and excludes only N <= 0.

Same overflowed N from line 7 reaches this size-derived decoder when tensor_content is empty; the wrapped N=16 witness also triggers this sink, with the same buffer/shape inconsistency and downstream OOB consequence.

assumptions: shape.num_elements() multiplies dims as plain int64 arithmetic that wraps on overflow, and IsValid does not bound the product.
Helper<T>::Decode and FromProtoField allocate and copy based on the N argument passed from this function.
proto is untrusted because it is deserialized from attacker-influenced input (network/file/model graph).
limitations: The wrapped-negative-N variant (e.g., dims {2, 2^62, 3}) makes N <= 0, skips the decoder branches, and returns a tensor with shape_ set and buf_ == nullptr; no NULL dereference occurs in the shown code, so only downstream effects would be a separate finding.
The actual OOB read/write occurs in consumers of the returned inconsistent Tensor, which are outside this function; the shown code creates the inconsistent state.
No format-string, command, SQL, header, path, crypto, ReDoS, or authz sink exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: vidioc_querycap passes dev->card_label as the format string to snprintf (line 14) without sanitization. A label containing '%' directives (e.g., "%n", "%s") is interpreted as format specifiers against nonexistent arguments, enabling arbitrary kernel-memory reads/writes and kernel Oops (CWE-134). The labellen bound only caps the output text size and does not prevent format-directive processing.

evidence.reason: Taint: dev->card_label is the per-device label string (device/global configuration data) with no filtering in the shown path; it reaches the format-string argument of snprintf verbatim. Guard/sufficiency: labellen (lines 5-7) bounds only the number of output characters written into cap->card (at most sizeof(cap->card)-1) and does not constrain the label's bytes, so a label such as "%n" or "%s" passes the guard untouched and is parsed as printf directives against absent arguments. Failure: '%n' writes the chars-written count to an address formed from a popped stack word and '%s' dereferences arbitrary stack words, yielding arbitrary kernel writes/reads and kernel Oops in ring 0, confirmed on every VIDIOC_QUERYCAP call.

assumptions: vidioc_querycap is the VIDIOC_QUERYCAP ioctl handler for v4l2loopback device nodes, so the shown path executes on each QUERYCAP call.
cap->card is the fixed 32-byte field of struct v4l2_capability.
dev->card_label is the per-device label string and the shown code imposes no constraint on its contents.
limitations: Whether dev->card_label can be influenced by an unprivileged user is not visible inside this snippet; its origin in the shown code is device/global configuration data, which per the task's rules is a sufficient taint source, and the format-string side effect at line 14 is confirmed regardless.
No out-of-bounds write into cap->card is confirmed: labellen caps the produced text at sizeof(cap->card)-1 characters, so CWE-787 is not an independent finding.
The code contains no loops, no other memory/injection sinks, and no weak-crypto or authz logic; driver and bus_info writes use literal formats with matching argument types.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled RTCP XR report blocks are parsed without validating that the declared block length (rb_len, a 16-bit packet field read at line 25) fits within the remaining packet. The loop guard (line 23) only bounds the block-header position; after the loop, saved block pointers (lines 31/34/37/40) are dereferenced with no per-block bounds check (e.g., line 211), causing an out-of-bounds read. A 12-byte packet with common.length=2 and one BT_VOIP_METRICS block (length=1) passes all guards yet reads fields through byte ~35.

evidence.reason: rb_voip_mtc is tainted: its origin is the raw network packet (pkt) and it is saved whenever rb_len != 0 and rb_hdr->bt == BT_VOIP_METRICS (lines 25, 28, 39-40); rb_len is the attacker-controlled 16-bit block length read at line 25. The only guards before this dereference are the packet-type check (lines 14-15), the whole-packet fit check (lines 19-20, bounding pkt_len+1 <= size/4), and the loop header bound (line 23, rb_hdr < pkt + pkt_len); none validates that the declared block (rb_len+1 32-bit words) lies inside the buffer, and no per-block length check exists between the pointer save (line 40) and this read. Concrete witness: size=12 bytes, common.length=2 (pkt_len=2, guard line 19 passes since 3 <= 12/4), one block at rtcp_xr->buf with bt=BT_VOIP_METRICS and length=1 — loop iteration 1 saves rb_voip_mtc = pkt+4, the advance (lines 46-47) moves past the packet end so the loop exits, and this line then reads jb_abs_max at roughly pkt+34..35 while the buffer is only 12 bytes, i.e., an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: size reflects the true usable length of the pkt buffer supplied by the caller.
sess (and sess->name / sess->rtcp_session) is a valid, trusted internal object.
Line numbers refer to the code exactly as provided; no file path was supplied.
limitations: The function reads rtcp_xr->common.pt (line 14) and common.length (line 17) before any size >= 4 check; this is only exploitable if an unseen caller passes a buffer smaller than 4 bytes, which is out of scope here.

The same missing per-block bounds validation also makes the rb_rr_time (lines 53-54), rb_dlrr (lines 73, 76), and rb_stats (lines 139-175) dereferences out-of-bounds; these are the same root cause, not separate findings.
The division by sess->rtcp_session->ts_freq (line 61) appears only inside the TRACE_ macro (normally compiled out) and is not treated as a finding.
No format-string, command/shell, SQL, crypto, or file/access-control sinks exist in the shown code; TRACE_/PJ_LOG calls use constant format strings with numeric arguments.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad's Compute writes into a temporary in_backprop buffer indexed by (b * in_rows + in_r) * in_cols + in_c and by depth d without ever checking that out_batch <= in_batch or out_depth <= in_depth. An attacker supplying an out_backprop whose batch or depth exceeds the declared input shape drives in_index (or d) past the allocated in_depth * in_cols * in_rows * in_batch doubles, causing a heap out-of-bounds write via Eigen coeffRef at line 132.

evidence.reason: in_index is computed at line 126 as (b * in_rows + in_r) * in_cols + in_c with b looping up to out_batch-1 (line 96) and d looping up to out_depth-1 (line 128), while in_batch/in_depth come from attacker-controlled orig_input_tensor_shape (lines 55-58) and out_batch/out_depth from attacker-controlled out_backprop (lines 33-36). The guards at lines 38-49, 59-70, 102-106, and 112-118 constrain only sequence lengths, non-zero dims, and non-negative capped ends; none requires out_batch <= in_batch or out_depth <= in_depth. Witness: in_shape=[1,2,1,1], out_backprop shape [2,1,1,1], row_seq=col_seq=[0,1] passes all guards, then at b=1 in_index=2 with matrix cols=2 and rows=1, so coeffRef(0,2) writes data()[2] past the 2-element double buffer -- a reachable heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: overlapping_ is a trusted, framework-validated bool attribute and is not attacker-controlled in the shown code.
Eigen Maps are column-major, so coeffRef(d, in_index) accesses data()[d + in_index * in_depth] of the temporary buffer.
context->input(0..3) are validated by the framework as tensors of the declared dtypes; any allocation failure aborts via OP_REQUIRES_OK at lines 81-83 and 144-145 rather than continuing.
Out-of-range dim_size calls on a rank<4 out_backprop are not the demonstrated failure; rank validation is assumed by the op contract.
limitations: A shape mismatch with in_batch > out_batch or in_depth > out_depth is in-bounds and only leaves output elements at zero -- a correctness issue, not a memory-safety finding.
Non-monotonic row/col sequences merely produce empty or repeated pooling regions; the inner loops are empty and no memory operation is reached, so it is a correctness concern with no CWE.

num_elements_in_pooling_cell is never used as a divisor unless both inner loops execute (factors >= 1), so division-by-zero and negative divisor are unreachable; int64 overflow of the product is bounded by the already-succeeded allocation of the temporary tensor.
Out-of-bounds reads and injection sinks (printf/system/SQL/HTML/log, crypto, file/auth) are absent from the shown code.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in gf_avc_parse_nalu: avc->s_info.sps (and n_state.sps) are dereferenced at the poc_type comparison after slice parsing, guarded only by assert(), which is a no-op in release builds and an abort in debug. A crafted stream of two consecutive slice NALs with no preceding SPS leaves avc->s_info.sps NULL (propagated by the memcpy at the end of each NAL), so the comparison at the sink dereferences NULL and crashes the parser.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled NAL stream: a slice NAL (type 1/5/DP_*) is parsed via avc_parse_slice (line 54, only guarded by ret<0 at line 55) while avc->s_info.sps is NULL because no SPS NAL preceded it; the NULL value is preserved by the memcpy at line 13 and recirculated into avc->s_info by line 159. The only guard before this sink is assert(avc->s_info.sps) at line 77, which admits NULL under NDEBUG (release) and aborts the process in debug, so it protects nothing. Witness: two byte-identical non-IDR slice NALs with no SPS — first slice breaks at line 61 and leaves s_info.sps NULL; second slice passes the guards at lines 55, 57-62 and 63-76 and dereferences NULL at line 79, crashing the parser (CWE-476).

assumptions: AVCState/avc->s_info are zero-initialized at stream start (sps == NULL), the standard GPAC usage; the shown code never otherwise initializes avc->s_info.sps.
Line numbers assume the snippet starts at line 1 with the function signature.
limitations: A NULL n_state.sps independent of avc->s_info.sps depends on unshown avc_parse_slice internals; it hits the same line 79 but is not independently confirmed.

If the unshown avc_parse_slice itself crashes on a NULL sps before returning, the shown-code deref at line 79 would not be the first fault; the finding holds for the helper behavior the shown code permits (return >= 0 with n_state.sps unchanged/NULL).
svc_parse_slice's return value is discarded (line 29) and idr_flag is fixed at 0 (line 17): robustness/logic concerns without a security sink in the shown code.
(s32) gf_bs_read_ue at line 127: values that stay positive are not consumed by the shown branch, so no OOB is reachable here.

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read trusts the attacker-controlled extent_count without tying it to the remaining box size. When offset_size, length_size, and index_size are all zero, each of up to 65535 inner-loop iterations allocates a GF_ItemExtentEntry while consuming zero bytes, and the outer item_count loop multiplies this, so a tiny crafted iloc box forces millions to billions of heap allocations, causing memory/CPU exhaustion (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: extent_count is read from the attacker-controlled bitstream at line 50 with no cap. With version=0 and offset_size=length_size=index_size=0, lines 58 and 64 consume zero bytes per iteration, so the loop bound is the full untrusted u16 value and every iteration performs a heap allocation at line 53; a 6-byte payload (item_ID 2 + data_reference_index 2 + extent_count 2) forces 65535 allocations, and version>=2 with item_count=65535 multiplies this to ~4.3 billion allocations.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is the standard GPAC macro that verifies ptr->size is not below the requested byte count and then decrements it.
The iloc box is parsed from untrusted media, so ptr->version and every gf_bs_read_* return value are attacker-controlled.
Host integers are 32/64-bit as usual, so u32 counts and fixed-size struct allocations are as described.
limitations: Any out-of-bounds behavior inside gf_bs_read_int for the up-to-120-bit reads (lines 44, 59, 66-67) is not analyzable because the helper implementation is not shown; only the pass-through call is visible.
A NULL dereference at line 56 would require gf_list_new() at line 51 to fail on a fixed-size allocation; that is an out-of-scope allocation-failure concern, not an attacker-controlled path.
Ignored gf_list_add return values and cleanup of partially parsed entries on error returns are robustness concerns in code not shown.
The outer item_count loop can also allocate entries before its per-item size check fails, but that linear amplification is dominated by the extent_count amplification and is not reported separately.

verdict.summary: The batch index read from the attacker-controlled `indices` tensor (line 63) is only upper-bounded by the guard at line 64 (`batch < num_batches`); negative values pass the guard and are used at lines 75/77/79 to index `per_batch_counts` (sized `num_batches` at line 48), causing an out-of-bounds heap write.

assumptions: `T` is a numeric type so attacker values such as 1 pass the line 73 filter for any `maxlength_`; `BatchedMap` is a per-batch container whose outer size is `num_batches` (line 48), so indexing with a negative/huge batch is out of bounds.

`GetOutputSize` (line 87) and `OutputSparse` (line 88) are not in the shown code, so any huge dense-allocation driven by attacker `max_value` is out of scope.
With `maxlength_ <= 0`, large `value` keys grow the per-batch maps only in proportion to input volume; no compounding DoS or memory-safety issue is confirmed in the shown code.
`num_values` narrowing (line 29) with `NumElements() > INT_MAX` would just skip the loop; no reachable failure is confirmed.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read at line 36 when maxRank == 0: if every input shape is rank-0 (empty SymbolicExpr array) or the operand list is empty, shape_and_rank_for_dim is an empty SmallVector, llvm::is_splat(empty) is vacuously true, and shape_and_rank_for_dim[0] dereferences the empty vector, yielding UB reachable from attacker-supplied IR. evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced shape operands flow through found_shape->size() (line 11) into maxRank; when all shapes are rank-0 (or the operand list is empty), maxRank == 0 so shape_and_rank_for_dim (line 16) has zero elements. is_splat on the empty container is vacuously true, so the guard admits the failing value and line 36 indexes element [0] of the empty SmallVector, an out-of-bounds read (UB); no maxRank > 0 or empty() check exists anywhere in the shown code before this access.

assumptions: llvm::is_splat returns true for an empty range (vacuous truth per LLVM STLExtras semantics).
A rank-0 (scalar) shape operand is representable and GetValueInfo returns a non-null Optional with size() == 0 for it, so line 9's nullopt check does not reject the rank-0 path.

limitations: If the enclosing op verifier or caller rejects rank-0 or empty shape operand lists before this canonicalization runs, the maxRank == 0 path is unreachable from valid IR; that check is outside the shown code, which itself imposes none.
Release-build consequences of the indeterminate Value read (line 36) are unspecified; if non-null it is returned at line 37, but the confirmed fault is the OOB read/UB itself.
shapes[0] at line 45 is not a separate finding: the elements loop (line 41) requires maxRank > 0, which implies shapes non-empty.
The tensor::ExtractOp index at lines 51-52 is provably within [0, rank-1] via the reverse-index identity (i - maxRank + r = r - 1 - d) and is not a finding.
NULL builder or non-RankedTensorType shape operand type at lines 44-45 are caller/verifier invariants not established by the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in gitn_box_del: the loop at line 7 iterates i < ptr->nb_entries and reads ptr->entries[i].name at line 8, but the shown code never validates nb_entries against the number of elements actually allocated for ptr->entries. If the parser-produced box has nb_entries larger than the entries allocation, the destructor reads (and possibly frees) an out-of-bounds entry pointer, causing OOB read and potentially an invalid free/crash.

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced nb_entries (u32, parsed from box/file contents, unvalidated in the shown code) is the loop bound at line 7 and indexes into ptr->entries here. The only guard is i < ptr->nb_entries, which bounds i by the same unvalidated count and never by the actual allocation size of ptr->entries, so nb_entries > number of allocated entries reaches an OOB element (e.g., nb_entries=2 with a 1-element allocation reads entries[1]) and may pass a garbage non-NULL name to gf_free at this same line.

assumptions: ptr->nb_entries and ptr->entries are populated by the unseen box parser from untrusted file/box content, so nb_entries is attacker-controlled and is not guaranteed to match the allocated entry count.
ptr->entries is an array of GroupIdToNameEntry structs (indexed with '.', not '->'), with the parser owning the allocation whose element count is not visible in this snippet.
limitations: If the unseen parser always allocates exactly (or more than) nb_entries elements, the destructor is safe; the allocation invariant is not present in the shown code, which is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.
A double-free or use-after-free would require two entries to alias the same name allocation or a prior free elsewhere; the shown code contains no evidence of such aliasing.
NULL-dereference candidates for ptr, entries, and name are all guarded by the shown checks at lines 5, 6, and 8 and were not treated as findings.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates the rank and lengths of the sparse tensor inputs but never validates the numeric entries of dense_shape (zero or negative dimensions) or the bounds of sparse indices against dense_shape. An attacker-controlled dense_shape such as [2, 0] or [0] passes every OP_REQUIRES check (lines 10-36, 47-56) and is copied verbatim into TensorShape at line 51 and into the SparseTensor stored in the returned Dataset, producing an internally inconsistent SparseTensor whose iteration later triggers a CHECK failure or out-of-bounds access (the vulnerability class documented for SparseTensorSliceDatasetOp, CVE-2020-15212).

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled int64 entries of dense_shape (input tensor, lines 8-9) reach this sink with no domain check: the only guards are IsVector (line 16), length equality with indices' column count (lines 26-32), and dense_shape->NumElements() > 0 (lines 34-36), all of which test the vector's rank/length, not whether each entry is positive. A witness such as dense_shape = [2, 0] (or [0], or a vector with a negative entry) with indices confined to column 0 passes every guard including the batch-monotonicity loop (lines 47-56), so TensorShape is constructed with a zero/negative dimension and SparseTensor::Create plus the Dataset on line 55 carry the inconsistent shape out of this function; consuming the dataset triggers a CHECK failure or out-of-bounds access in SparseTensor iteration (CWE-125, the CVE-2020-15212 class for SparseTensorSliceDatasetOp).

assumptions: indices/values/dense_shape are framework-supplied tensors whose contents (especially dense_shape entries) are user/attacker-controllable when the dataset is constructed, matching TensorFlow's threat model for Dataset ops.

sparse::SparseTensor::Create may reject some malformed inputs via its own status checks, but such rejection is not guaranteed by anything in the shown code, so the shown validation must enforce the full domain itself; in release builds non-negative checks of entries flow through.
limitations: The exact byte-level failing access (CHECK failure or OOB read) occurs in the downstream SparseTensor iterator/slicing code that consumes the Dataset emitted on line 55, which is not shown here; the shown code is the confirmed producer of the invalid SparseTensor state.
A negative dense_shape entry may be caught by a debugging-only check in SparseTensor::Create or downstream; zero-volume dimension entries like [2, 0] are the strongest witness.
No log injection, command injection, weak-crypto, or authz issues exist in this snippet; none were reported.
No out-of-bounds issue exists in the batch-ordering loop at line 47: the strict bound i < indices->dim_size(0) keeps the (i, 0) read within the matrix.

verdict.summary: The AV1 config parser subtracts 4 from the caller-supplied u32 `size` (line 40) without first requiring `size >= 4`. For size values 1-3 the subtraction wraps to ~0xFFFFFFFF, so the `while (size)` OBU loop (line 42) is no longer bounded by the declared config size: it parses and allocates over the entire remaining bitstream using input-derived `obu_size` (lines 61, 67), enabling memory exhaustion and out-of-config data consumption. Primary CWE-191.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled `size` (line 1) is only guarded by `if (!size)` at lines 8-9, which admits 1, 2, and 3 but never enforces `size >= 4`. A witness of `size=3` with a valid 4-byte AV1C-style header passing line 28 makes `size -= 4` wrap u32 to 0xFFFFFFFF, so `while (size)` at line 42 no longer bounds OBU processing; the loop then repeatedly executes `gf_malloc((size_t)obu_size)` (line 61) and `gf_bs_read_data(..., (u32)obu_size)` (line 67) on input-derived lengths for the whole remaining bitstream, and the only later guard `if (size<obu_size)` (line 72) can never fire against the wrapped budget, yielding memory-exhaustion DoS and consumption of data beyond the declared config size.

assumptions: `size` is treated as attacker-controllable per the task rules for function parameters supplied by an unseen caller (typical GPAC use: a container/file size field).
`gf_bs_read_int`, `gf_bs_available`, `gf_bs_read_data`, and `gf_av1_parse_obu` keep bitstream accesses within the underlying buffer; their own past-end behavior is not evaluated here.
limitations: Whether `gf_av1_parse_obu` caps `obu_size` to remaining bitstream bytes is not shown; if it does, the underflow impact is over-parsing and per-OBU allocation roughly linear in input size rather than amplification.

`gf_bs_read_data` at line 67 writes `(u32)obu_size` bytes into a buffer allocated at line 61 with `(size_t)obu_size`; buffer and length are internally consistent, so an OOB write/read at that sink would depend on unseen `gf_bs_read_data` internals and is not confirmed.

Line 57 passes `pos` as the only argument for a format with `%u` plus two `LLU` conversions, and line 73 prints `obu_size - size` (u64) with `%d`; these are varargs/type mismatches causing log corruption/UB, but the format strings are literal so no attacker-controlled format-string injection.

The oversized-OBU fit check at line 72 runs after the allocation (line 61) and read (line 67), so an OBU larger than the remaining budget is read and buffered before rejection; this is a parsing-correctness/over-read-of-logical-extent issue, not a confirmed memory-safety violation.
`cfg` is dereferenced without a NULL check if `gf_odf_av1_cfg_new` fails; this is a fixed-size allocation failure not controlled by the attacker.
The `assert` at line 53 can only abort debug builds if `gf_av1_parse_obu`'s returned size disagrees with consumed byte count, which depends on unseen parser internals.

verdict.summary: The grouped-conv functor divides by attacker-controlled tensor dims with no guard (filter dim 2 of 0, or filter depth exceeding input depth, feeds SIGFPE at line 12 or at lines 20/26 via the first post_shuffle call on line 37), and it reads explicit_paddings[2..5] under only a mode check, so a short EXPLICIT-padding vector yields an out-of-bounds read at lines 75-78. Both are reachable from crafted op inputs and enable process crash (DoS); the OOB read additionally risks corrupting the convolution's padding values.

evidence.reason: patch_depth is filter.dim_size(2) (line 11), an attacker-controlled tensor-shape value with no check in the shown code. patch_depth == 0 makes this line divide by zero (SIGFPE); with in_depth < patch_depth, num_groups becomes 0, so lines 20/26 evaluate tensor.dim_size(3) / 0 at the first post_shuffle call (line 37). Concrete witnesses: filter shape [1,1,0,1], or input depth 3 with filter dim 2 == 6. No guard exists between the taint source and either sink, so the crash is directly reachable (CWE-369, denial of service).

explicit_paddings (line 4) is an attacker-controlled op attribute; the only guard is `if (padding == EXPLICIT)` (line 71), which admits any vector length and does not enforce size() >= 6. A witness such as explicit_paddings = {0,0,0,0} passes that guard yet reads indices 4 and 5 past the 4-element vector at lines 77-78, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose values are consumed as convolution padding.

assumptions: TensorShape dims are non-negative int64 per TF invariants, so patch_depth == 0 is representable and in_depth < patch_depth is legal.
input/filter/output are 4-D NHWC tensors as implied by the dim_size(3) reads; the data_format DCHECK is debug-only.
explicit_paddings' contents are trusted only as op-attribute input, not length-validated inside the shown code.
limitations: Reachability of the explicit_paddings OOB read depends on the unseen caller not enforcing explicit_paddings.size() >= 6 before this functor; if the Conv2D OpKernel validates that bound, CWE-125 is not reachable in practice.
Consequences of in_depth % patch_depth != 0 inside Eigen's SpatialConvolution (depth mismatch) are outside the shown code and were not assessed.
The DCHECK for FORMAT_NHWC (line 6) is inactive in release builds and provides no runtime protection.
The truncated out_depth / num_groups element count for the final back-shuffle (lines 88-90) is a correctness issue, not a memory-safety finding.

verdict.summary: simplifyBroadcast indexes shapes[0] without any non-emptiness check on the caller-supplied ValueRange. An empty shapes range makes maxRank == 0, so the early-return branch executes shapes[0].getType() on a zero-element range: an out-of-bounds read / assertion failure, enabling a compiler crash on crafted input.

evidence.reason: Taint: the ValueRange parameter `shapes` (lines 2-3) reaches `shapes[0]` at line 15 with no emptiness validation in the shown code. Reachability: an empty range makes the loop at lines 7-12 execute zero times so maxRank remains 0, the guard at line 13 (maxRank == 0) admits the empty range, and lines 14-15 then read index 0 of a zero-element range; the protective check that would exclude this (`shapes.empty()`) is absent. Impact: out-of-bounds read / assertion failure inside ValueRange::operator[] (CWE-125), attacker-triggerable crash when the caller passes an empty range.

assumptions: ArrayRefs returned by analysis.GetValueInfo remain valid for the function's lifetime; they are held in shapes_found (lines 5-11).
shapes is treated as caller-supplied/unvalidated input; the shown code imposes no non-emptiness invariant.
limitations: The shown code does not demonstrate a real caller that passes an empty ValueRange; if all callers guarantee at least one operand, the OOB is unreachable and the practical impact is nil.

When all shapes exist but have rank 0, the branch at lines 14-15 builds a tensor::FromElementsOp with zero elements against shapes[0].getType(), which may fail operation verification; robustness concern with no confirmed memory-safety impact.
Loop at line 45 compares int i against size_t maxRank; non-termination would require maxRank > INT_MAX, which is not feasibly representable in IR, so it is not a finding.

The unsigned-wrapping extraction-index computation at lines 55-56 is mathematically correct for the recorded invariants (the source dim exists, so R >= maxRank - i) and was verified in bounds for every recorded position; not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read trusts attacker-controlled item_count/extent_count and the box-declared remaining size as loop bounds: a crafted MP4 declaring a large iloc box with zero-size offset/length/index fields drives billions of per-item and per-extent allocations (lines 25-28, 55-58) and loop iterations (lines 23, 53) from a tiny file, causing memory exhaustion and CPU DoS (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: item_count is read from the file (u32, up to 0xFFFFFFFF) at line 20 and is attacker-controlled with no cap independent of the declared box size. The loop at line 23 iterates floor(size/min_per_item) times because the only guard, ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE (min 8 declared bytes per item for version>=2), checks the attacker-supplied remaining box size (up to u64 max), not the actual file bytes; reads past EOF return 0 without terminating the loop. Each iteration allocates and appends an entry (lines 25-28), so a 4-8 byte header field can force ~5.4e8 or more heap allocations and CPU burn from a near-empty file (CWE-770).

extent_count is read from the file at line 51 (attacker-controlled u16 up to 0xFFFF). For each extent, the guard at line 66 (ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, offset_size+length_size)) decrements 0 declared bytes when the attacker sets offset_size=length_size=index_size=0 (nibbles from lines 7-11), so the inner loop at line 53 is not bounded by remaining box size at all; each of up to 65535 iterations allocates and appends an entry (lines 55-58). Combined with the outer loop, total allocations reach ~(declared_size/8) * 65536 from a few bytes of data, amplifying the CWE-770 memory-exhaustion DoS.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is the standard GPAC macro that compares/decrements the box-declared remaining payload size (ptr->size) and does not consult the actual bytes left in bs.
gf_bs_read_u16/u32/int return 0 past end-of-stream and do not abort the parse, so loop termination depends on the declared size, not on available file data.
ptr->location_entries is guaranteed non-NULL by the unseen box constructor; ptr->version is constrained to values 0-2 by the shown branches.
Line numbers are relative to the code snippet exactly as provided (line 1 = 'GF_Err iloc_box_read(...)').
limitations: location_entry->extent_entries = gf_list_new() (line 52) is unchecked; a NULL result would be dereferenced by gf_list_add at line 58, but the NULL path only occurs under allocation failure, which is the same OOM condition as the confirmed finding, so it is not reported as a separate CWE.

gf_bs_read_int is called with up to 120 bits (lines 45, 61, 68-69) because the 4-bit size nibbles allow 15; the resulting behavior is defined by the unseen bitstream implementation and involves no memory operation on a buffer in the shown code, so it is out of scope for a memory-safety finding.
All actual file-buffer reads are performed by the bounds-checked bitstream layer; the shown code contains no raw memory copy or indexing that could itself over-read the input buffer.
The item_count/extent_count loops always terminate (bounded by declared size or count), so this is reported as resource exhaustion (CWE-770), not as a hang/non-termination defect.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability. Every seccomp rule, socket-family range, and loop is constructed from compile-time constant tables and trusted framework parameters; all table loops are bounded by strict '<' against G_N_ELEMENTS, the socket gap logic admits no unblocked family for any CAN/BLUETOOTH flag combination, and no attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or file sink. The only weaknesses are non-attacker-triggerable robustness gaps (silently ignored libseccomp/lseek return values), recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: seccomp_x86_64_extra_arches and seccomp_aarch64_extra_arches (lines 163, 173) are static, zero-terminated arrays, guaranteeing termination of the sentinel loop at line 192.
arch (line 2) is a valid NUL-terminated C string supplied by framework-internal callers; its only uses are the strcmp chain at lines 156-170.
glnx_open_anonymous_tmpfile_full (line 264) creates a private anonymous O_TMPFILE-style file with O_CLOEXEC, so no predictable /tmp pathname is exposed.
flatpak_bwrap_add_args_data_fd (lines 272-273) takes ownership of the fd stolen by glnx_steal_fd.
limitations: Lines 218 and 236: `if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT)` is logically `r == -EFAULT`, so any other negative seccomp_rule_add result (e.g. -EDOM/-EINVAL) would silently omit a blocklist rule. Not a confirmed finding because no attacker-controlled value reaches `r` and no concrete in-scope trigger exists; it is a hardening gap for libseccomp-internal failures.
Lines 257 and 262: seccomp_rule_add_exact results are unchecked; the comment at lines 241-243 states this is intentional because socket filtering does not work on some architectures (e.g. i386).
Line 270: the lseek result is unchecked; with the private anonymous tmpfile this has no security consequence.
Socket-family coverage relies on the allowlist entries remaining in ascending numerical order (line 134); current values {0,1,2,10,16,29,31} satisfy it.

The filter intentionally keeps the native architecture allowed alongside a requested arch (lines 181-185) and leaves the native-only default for unrecognized arch strings (line 179); both are design choices, not vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference of n_state.sps in gf_avc_parse_nalu: for a slice NALU, avc_parse_slice (line 54) may leave n_state.sps NULL based on attacker-controlled pic_param_id, and the guard at lines 77-78 checks only avc->s_info.sps, so line 80 dereferences n_state.sps->poc_type on NULL, crashing the parser on crafted input (DoS).

evidence.reason: n_state.sps is tainted from the attacker-controlled bitstream: it is copied from avc->s_info.sps at line 13 and then may be overwritten by avc_parse_slice at line 54 based on the attacker-chosen pic_param_id read from bs. The guard at lines 77-78 checks only avc->s_info.sps, so a state with avc->s_info.sps != NULL and n_state.sps == NULL passes it; the unchecked dereference n_state.sps->poc_type at line 80 then dereferences NULL. Reachable when a prior NALU established avc->s_info.sps and the current slice references a PPS with no SPS while returning >= 0 from avc_parse_slice (line 55 only rejects negatives). Impact: NULL-pointer crash (CWE-476) on crafted media input.

assumptions: bs is an attacker-controlled bitstream (media file or network payload), as in GPAC demux/parse entry points.
AVCSliceInfo.sps is NULL whenever no matching SPS is associated with the parsed slice/PPS.
avc->s_info and the SPS/PPS tables are populated by earlier NALU parses of the same attacker-controlled stream.
limitations: The NULL-producing path depends on avc_parse_slice returning >= 0 while leaving n_state.sps NULL; that helper is not shown, so the concrete helper-internal branch is not demonstrated, only the shown code's failure to constrain n_state.sps before the line-80 dereference.

The SVC_SLICE path (lines 26-41) ignores the svc_parse_slice return and then calls avc_compute_poc(&n_state) (line 34); any NULL dereference would occur inside that unseen helper, so it is not a confirmed finding in the shown code.
The post-switch avc_compute_poc call at lines 158-159 would also dereference n_state.sps inside unseen code; same out-of-scope reason.
(s32) gf_bs_read_ue(bs) at line 128 may wrap values >= 2^31 to negative, but it only results in an early -1 return at line 129 with no memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: bias_size and array_size reach in-place array writes with no effective validation: the sole guard TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ((array_size % bias_size), 0) is a debug-only divisibility assertion that is compiled out in release builds and never checks 0 < bias_size <= array_size or the real buffer sizes. An attacker-controlled pair such as bias_size=8, array_size=4 (e.g., from a crafted TFLite model) makes the inner loop write/read array_data[0..7] against a 4-element allocation, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) at lines 60-61 (scalar) and lines 38-41/49/52 (NEON).

evidence.snippet:
array_data[array_offset + i] = ActivationFunctionWithMinMax(
          array_data[array_offset + i] + bias_data[i], clamp_min, clamp_max);
evidence.reason: The index array_offset + i is bounded only by the inner loop i < bias_size (line 59), and bias_size is an attacker-controlled parameter derived from tensor shapes. The sole guard, line 9 (TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ((array_size % bias_size), 0)), is a debug-only divisibility check that is absent in release builds and, even when active, never verifies bias_size <= array_size or 0 < bias_size. Concrete witness: array_size=4 with a 4-float array_data and bias_size=8 reach this store with i up to 7, writing/reading array_data[4..7] out of bounds (CWE-787; the same-index read is the same failure).
