A sparse index of -1 with positive strides (strides built at lines 65-68) yields loc = -1, which passes the guard; output_t(loc) then indexes the flat output buffer of size output_elements (line 62) at offset -1, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The identical guard-sink pattern repeats at lines 106-112, 120-126, 136-142, and 154-160.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES_OK causes Compute to return when the unseen helpers (ValidateShapes, TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape, SparseTensor::Create) fail, and the shown code itself imposes no constraint on the values inside hypothesis_indices/truth_indices.
output_elements is positive (lines 55-58) and the output tensor holds exactly output_elements floats (lines 61-63), so the valid index range is [0, output_elements-1].
limitations: If the unseen ValidateShapes/SparseTensor::Create implementations reject negative indices, the confirmed trigger would be blocked; this uncertainty is reflected in the confidence value.

Integer overflow in the inner_product could also wrap loc to an unexpected nonnegative value, but for in-range indices loc cannot exceed output_elements-1, so the primary confirmed trigger is the missing lower-bound (loc >= 0) check.

If dense ranks 0 or 1 pass the unseen validation, line 46 (dims()-1 underflow to size_t) and line 66 (output_strides[-1] write) are additional memory-safety issues; reachability depends on validation code not shown here, so they are not part of the verdict.
The O(n*m) LevenshteinDistance computation and attacker-sized output allocation are algorithmic-complexity/DoS concerns without a demonstrated memory-safety failure in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only direct memory access with attacker-influenced state is the 4-byte read c[0..3] (line 399), which is exactly guarded by 'box->dataSize==4'; all list accesses use strict k < gf_list_count(...) bounds over lists that are not mutated in the loop bodies; the tfhd/trex dereferences (333, 345) and MOOV mvhd check (77) cover their later uses. Injection sinks are absent (GF_LOG uses only static formats; the u64->%d mismatch at line 27 is a non-security log bug). NULL-dereference hypotheses at lines 101-102 and 366 depend on an unseen parser accepting trak-without-mdia or moof-without-mfhd, so they are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: gf_isom_parse_root_box (line 30) returns a fully constructed box whose data pointer holds exactly dataSize bytes (GF_UnknownBox invariant), which makes the 'box->dataSize==4' guard at line 399 sufficient for c[0..3].

current_top_box_start is always set to gf_bs_get_position(bs) + bytes_removed (lines 26, 446), so the restart seek target 'totSize = current_top_box_start - bytes_removed' (lines 13-18) structurally equals the bitstream position and cannot underflow.

gf_list_count/gf_list_get/gf_list_enum semantics: strict '<' loop bounds admit only indices 0..count-1, and none of the shown loop bodies (senc_Parse, convert_compact_sample_groups, gf_list_enum, GetTrackbyID) mutate the enumerated list, so there is no count-change TOCTOU.
limitations: Unchecked dereference of trak->Media->information->sampleTable->sampleGroups (lines 101-102) is a potential NULL-deref DoS, but the NULL-producing state (parser accepting a trak without mdia) is only reachable inside the unseen gf_isom_parse_root_box, so it is not confirmable from the shown code.
Unchecked dereference of mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number (line 366) is a potential NULL-deref only if the unseen parser accepts a moof without the mandatory mfhd box; not confirmable here.

u64 accumulations totSize += a->size (lines 59, 112, 118, 136, 190, 231, 259, 263, 308, 408, 433, 438) and main_sidx_end_pos = current_top_box_start + a->size (line 287) could in principle wrap, but no memory operation consumes these values in the shown code and a->size bounds are enforced by the unseen parser.
Forward progress / termination of the main loop (line 23) depends on gf_isom_parse_root_box advancing the bitstream; a zero-advance infinite loop cannot be demonstrated from the shown code.
The '%d' format used with u64 current_top_box_start at line 27 is a format/type mismatch that corrupts log output only; the value is numeric and cannot carry log-injection content.

Ignored return values of gf_list_add at lines 154 and 328 can leak boxes on OOM, but this requires an allocation failure without attacker-controlled size and does not compound into memory unsafety here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The token accumulator in ReadPCLImage looks like a classic post-increment off-by-one, but the guard `(size_t)(p-command) < (MagickPathExtent-1)` (L117) combined with the terminator write (L119) and reset (L120) caps every write at index MagickPathExtent-1; index MagickPathExtent is unreachable regardless of input length or the position of '/' and '\n' separators. Candidates for log injection, delegate command injection, and huge-geometry denial of service depend on unshown logger/delegate internals or operator-controlled flags and fail the required three-part confirmation.

assumptions: MagickPathExtent is the declared size of command/filename/geometry/input_filename; the bound argument holds for any N = MagickPathExtent.
The tokenizer is active only when image_info->page == NULL (the default); with a page override the parser loop stores no file bytes.
ReadBlobByte eventually returns EOF, so the parsing loop is finite.
image->resolution and image_info->page are framework-parsed numeric/geometry values, not raw attacker strings after ParseGeometry/ParseAbsoluteGeometry.
limitations: Log injection via image_info->filename at L56-57 is unconfirmed: it is gated on the operator-controlled image_info->debug flag and depends on unshown LogMagickEvent sink behavior/sanitization; no CWE attached.

Delegate command injection at L214-218/L221 is not confirmable from the shown code: only numeric %g/%.20g strings and generated unique filenames are substituted, and template quoting plus ExternalDelegateCommand's shell invocation are unshown.

Crafted CropBox/MediaBox values (huge or NaN) can make the CastDoubleToLong/size_t conversions at L153-154 and L192-193 produce implementation-defined page sizes passed to GhostPCL; potential impact is delegate-side resource exhaustion, not a memory-safety failure in the shown code.
Unchecked CloneImageInfo/AcquireString results (L197-198, L186-187) could only NULL-dereference on allocation failure with no attacker-controlled size, which is out of scope.
The stale `count` value across tokens (L102, L148) can re-run the geometry update with prior bounds; this is a non-security logic quirk.

verdict.summary: Log injection: when debug is enabled, image_info->filename is written to LogMagickEvent with %s (lines 56-57) without any newline sanitization, so a caller-supplied filename containing '\n' can split the record and forge trace-log lines. Memory-safety candidates were verified safe: the PCL token loop's post-increment guard (p-command < MaxTextExtent-1) plus the terminating NUL caps writes at command[MaxTextExtent-1]; the density/options FormatLocaleString writes are within AcquireString's >= MagickPathExtent allocation; and the delegate command embeds regenerated unique names rather than the raw caller path.

evidence.reason: image_info->filename is a caller-supplied (argv/user-controlled) path that undergoes no validation or escaping in the shown code. Guarded only by image_info->debug at line 55, it is emitted with %s into the trace log at lines 56-57; a filename containing '\n' (legal path bytes) passes the guard, splits the log record, and injects forged lines — an unneutralized log-injection sink (CWE-117). All memory-safety candidates are protected: the tokenizer at lines 115-119 admits writes only up to command[MaxTextExtent-2] (data) and command[MaxTextExtent-1] (NUL) because the continuation guard at line 117 is evaluated post-increment and offset MaxTextExtent is unreachable; density/options writes at lines 188-197 rely on AcquireString allocating >= MagickPathExtent bytes; and the delegate command at lines 216-220 receives AcquireUniqueFilename/AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink-generated names, not the raw caller path.

assumptions: MaxTextExtent and MagickPathExtent are both 4096 in ImageMagick.
ImageMagick's AcquireString allocates at least MagickPathExtent bytes regardless of source length, keeping FormatLocaleString(density/options, MaxTextExtent, ...) in-bounds.
AcquireUniqueFilename and AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink write names bounded by MagickPathExtent into the provided buffers.
limitations: The PCL token loop (lines 108-159) is not an OOB write: the continuation guard admits writes only while the post-increment offset is < MaxTextExtent-1, so max written indices are MaxTextExtent-2 (data) and MaxTextExtent-1 (NUL); guard-time offset MaxTextExtent is unreachable.

OS command injection via the caller filename into the GhostPCL delegate is not confirmable from the shown code: read_info->filename is regenerated by AcquireUniqueFilename (line 215) before use in command (line 220), and input_filename is produced by the unseen AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink; whether attacker path components survive in those generated names and whether the delegate template quotes them is outside the shown code.
File-controlled doubles can produce huge/wrapped size_t page sizes, but in the shown code they reach only numeric format strings and delegate arguments, no memory operation.
Unchecked AcquireImage/CloneImageInfo results can fail only on allocation failure (no attacker-controlled size); a NULL dereference from attacker data is not reachable in the shown code.

The log-injection finding requires image_info->debug to be enabled (line 55) and a deployment where the processed filename is attacker-influenced; where the application generates filenames itself, the taint is absent.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node's PI, comment, and CDATA handlers loop without any end-of-buffer guard, so truncated attacker-controlled XML (e.g. `<?`, `<!`, or CDATA ending in a lone `]` such as `<a><![CDATA[a]`) makes the parser spin forever while dereferencing scanner->curptr at/after scanner->end (lines 17, 21, 33, 37, 98-100), yielding a remote denial of service via hang or crash.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled XML reaches this loop after the `<![CDATA[` guard at lines 93-94 and line 97 parks curptr on a ']'. With witness `<a><![CDATA[a]` (lone trailing ']', `]]>` truncated), line 98 re-tests the same bytes, line 100 cannot advance (get_until_ch stops at the ']'/EOF without moving and its PJ_EEOF return is ignored), so the loop never terminates and pj_scan_strcmp at line 98 repeatedly probes past scanner->end - no EOF/progress guard exists.

For attacker-controlled input `<?` (no `?>` before end), line 13 leaves curptr==end, line 16 returns PJ_EEOF without moving, line 17 dereferences *curptr and *(curptr+1) at/after scanner->end (out-of-bounds read), and line 21 advances curptr past end; iterations repeat indefinitely. The identical structure at lines 30-39 does the same for `<!` without `>`. The pj_scan_get_until_ch EOF result is ignored, so the loops have no terminating guard.

assumptions: pj_scan_get_until_ch advances curptr to end and returns PJ_EEOF when the terminator character is absent; these return values are ignored in the shown code (lines 16, 32, 97, 100).
The scanner buffer has no guaranteed slack, so reads at curptr==end or (curptr+1) when curptr==end-1 are treated as out-of-bounds.
XML bytes in the scanner are attacker-controlled (SIP message body / XCAP / config consumed by pj_xml_parse); the shown function is the parser.
Line numbers are assigned to the code listing as provided (121 lines).
limitations: Unbounded recursion via the sub-node loop (lines 80-85) and tail recursion (lines 24, 40) can exhaust the stack on deeply nested documents (no depth cap in the shown code); not used as the confirmed primary finding.
attr->value.slen -= 2 (line 62) would underflow if pj_scan_get_quotes returned a value shorter than 2 bytes (e.g., truncated quote); reachability depends on pj_scan_get_quotes internals not shown.
One-byte OOB peeks at *(scanner->curptr+1) when input ends with '<' or '?' (lines 12, 80-81, 93) are subsumed by the same missing-EOF-guard family as the confirmed findings.

The CDATA loop with an interior lone ']' (e.g., `<![CDATA[a]b]]>`) is definitely stuck only if pj_scan_strcmp is non-consuming; the trailing-']' witness `<a><![CDATA[a]` is stuck regardless, which is the one used.
No format-string/exec/SQL/log-injection, weak-crypto, or authz sinks exist in this code, so none were reported.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The afra box parser guards every bitstream read: the local-entry loop is bounded by the line-14 size/entry-size check, and every read in both loops is preceded by ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE whose byte counts exactly match the read widths (8/4/16 bytes). malloc results are NULL-checked before use, and no injection, crypto, path, or authz sinks exist in the shown code. The only concerns are large-count resource consumption and a slightly over-strict 9-byte header accounting, neither of which is a confirmed security flaw.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, n) enforces ptr->size >= n and then subtracts n; the parenthetical byte counts passed at lines 6, 22, 25, 28, 34, 41, 44, 48, 53, 57 are consumed as declared.
ptr->size is an unsigned 64-bit remaining box size as is conventional for GF_Box; comparisons at line 14 promote entry_count to u64 without truncation.
gf_bs_read_u32/u16/u64/u32 and gf_bs_read_int consume exactly the byte counts matching their names (4, 2, 8, and bits respectively).
unsigned int is at least 32 bits, so the loop counter can represent every admitted u32 entry_count.
limitations: The global_entries section (lines 33-62) has no upfront global_entry_count-vs-size check analogous to line 14, but every per-field ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE prevents an out-of-bounds read; the worst outcome is an early GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE return, not corruption.

A maliciously huge declared box size together with huge entry_count/global_entry_count could force many fixed-size gf_malloc calls (lines 18, 37); this is bounded by the declared size, the loops terminate, and allocation failure returns cleanly, so it is only a resource-consumption/robustness concern, not a confirmed memory-safety or DoS finding in the shown code.

Line 6 subtracts 9 bytes for a header that actually consumes 9 bits plus 4 bytes (about 5 bytes); this is over-conservative and can only cause spurious rejection of valid boxes, with no security impact.

Return values of gf_list_insert (lines 20, 39) are unchecked; a failure would leak the just-allocated entry on the error path, with no attacker-visible memory-safety consequence demonstrated in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In yank_copy_line, the trailing-whitespace trim loop reads one byte before bd->textstart: the guard `s > 0` is the right operand of `&&`, so when s reaches 0 (e.g., yanking an empty line or a whitespace-only line with exclude_trailing_space), `VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1))` is evaluated before the guard and dereferences `bd->textstart - 1`, a one-byte out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Taint: bd->textlen (unvalidated in the shown code) initializes `int s = bd->textlen + bd->endspaces` at line 19 (endspaces is 0 because line 6 ran), and bd->textstart/textlen are the yanked line's buffer/length pair. The sink line 21 dereferences `bd->textstart + s - 1` as the left operand of `&&`, before the `s > 0` guard (right operand) is evaluated. Concrete failing witness: exclude_trailing_space set, textlen == 1, textstart[0] == ' ' — iteration 1 executes the body, line 23 sets `s = 1 - mb_head_off(...) - 1 = 0`, and the next test of line 21 reads `*(bd->textstart - 1)`; equivalently textlen == 0 and s == 0 trigger the under-read on the very first test. The guard admits s >= 1 for the body but does not cover the dereference at s == 0, so the shown code performs an out-of-bounds read one byte before the text region (CWE-125).

assumptions: bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces, and bd->textlen are non-negative and textstart/textlen describe a valid region per the caller contract.
mb_head_off() returns a value >= 0 on the executed path, so s never goes negative and the loop terminates.
exclude_trailing_space is a frame-internal flag enabled on the block-yank path that calls this function.
limitations: y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew at line 10 has no bounds check on y_idx, but y_idx is not shown to be attacker-controlled (caller contract), so it is not a confirmed finding.
Integer overflow in alloc(bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1) would require a line/block size near INT_MAX; no reachable path is demonstrated in the shown code.
Negative bd fields would be cast to huge size_t values in the memset/memmove calls at lines 11/13/15, but negative values cannot be produced inside the shown code (caller contract).

The under-read is a single byte before bd->textstart; whether it crosses an allocation boundary depends on the unseen caller's memory layout, so realistic impact is a one-byte OOB read with limited disclosure/crash potential, and the yanked output itself is not corrupted.
No injection (format string, command, SQL, log, HTTP/HTML), crypto, file-handling, or authz sinks exist in this function.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the SVDF size validation: `memory_size * num_filters` (line 50) is computed in 32-bit signed `int` from attacker-controlled tensor dims with no upper bound. E.g., 65536 * 65536 wraps to 0 and `SizeOfDimension(state, 1) == 0` passes the check even though the true product is 2^32, so the guard that is supposed to guarantee the state buffer can hold `memory_size * num_filters` elements per batch is bypassed, enabling out-of-bounds access on the op's state buffer.

evidence.reason: memory_size (line 30, weights_time->dims->data[1]) and num_filters (line 26, weights_feature->dims->data[0]) are attacker-controlled int32 dims; the only checks applied before this are rank != 0 and num_filters % rank == 0, which impose no magnitude bound. The 32-bit signed product overflows: with memory_size = 65536 and num_filters = 65536 the product wraps to 0, so the equality check passes when state dims[1] == 0 while the true product is 2^32. The guard therefore admits values it is meant to reject, leaving state access unbounded by the real product and allowing out-of-bounds access on the state buffer.

assumptions: Tensor dims are 32-bit int as per TfLiteIntArray, so 65536 and 65536 are representable dim values.
GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe enforce index bounds and return errors on invalid indices, making the temporaries accesses (indices 0-5 vs. allocated sizes 1/2/6) safe as analyzed.

IsHybridOp distinguishes float-input/int8-weights (hybrid) from int8-input (full-integer); combined with the input type restriction (lines 19-20), the hybrid and full-integer branches are mutually exclusive.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds read/write would occur in the op's Eval step, which is not part of the shown code; only the flawed overflow validation is confirmed here, so no CWE-787 is asserted.

batch_size * num_filters and batch_size * num_units products feed ResizeTensor (lines 56-57, 90-91) but the multiplication/indexing occurs in unseen interpreter code; a wrap there is not independently confirmable.

The full-integer branch dereferences quantization params without validating quantization.type or scale non-null (lines 184-199); a NULL/absent scale would have to be supplied by the model-file parser outside this function, so it is treated as a robustness concern, not a confirmed NULL-deref finding.

Negative dims (no positivity checks on batch_size, num_filters, memory_size, rank) and NULL from a failed fixed-size temporaries allocation are not confirmed as attacker-reachable security failures in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in GetEXIFProperty: in the all==1 ('exif:*') path, key=AcquireString(property) (line 763) allocates only strlen(property)+1 bytes (7 bytes for 'exif:*'), but FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,"%s",description) (lines 785-786) writes the full EXIF tag description selected from the static table by the attacker-chosen tag_value (up to 35 chars + NUL). MaxTextExtent is unrelated to the key's actual capacity and no check ties the write to strlen(property)+1, so a short wildcard property plus any valid entry in an attacker-supplied EXIF profile overwrites the heap allocation by 4-29 bytes.

evidence.reason: Taint: the caller-supplied property parameter (e.g. "exif:*", which passes the strlen>5 check at line 447 and sets all=1 at lines 458-459) is copied by AcquireString(property) at line 763 into a heap key of exactly strlen(property)+1 = 7 bytes; description is set from EXIFTag[] at lines 774-784 using tag_value read from the attacker-controlled profile (line 615). Reachability: with any validly parsed entry (format check 617-620, value!=NULL at line 755), the all==1 branch executes this sink; witness property="exif:*" and tag_value=0x301 gives description="exif:Gamma" (10 chars), so FormatLocaleString writes 11 bytes into the 7-byte allocation (4-byte overflow; up to 29 bytes for the longest description). The format-size argument MaxTextExtent (4096) does not bound the write to the actual key capacity and no guard compares the write length to strlen(property)+1, so the guard coverage at line 447 (a lower bound on strlen) is insufficient. Impact: heap corruption of adjacent chunk metadata/objects, i.e. heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122).

assumptions: MaxTextExtent is ImageMagick's 4096-byte constant, so FormatLocaleString writes the entire description string plus NUL.
AcquireString(property) allocates exactly strlen(property)+1 bytes.
ReadPropertyByte/ReadPropertyUnsignedShort/ReadPropertySignedLong decode the values from the profile buffer with correct endianness as selected at lines 551-557.

The 'exif' profile (line 440) is decoded from the image file and is therefore attacker-controlled; the property parameter itself is caller-supplied and its length is not constrained by the shown code beyond strlen > 5.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read in the 'Exif\0\0' magic scan (lines 533-548): if the profile ends with matching 'Ex' bytes, ReadPropertyByte can be invoked with length==0 within the same iteration; whether that reads memory depends on the unshown ReadPropertyByte implementation (which may internally guard length<1), so it is not a confirmed finding in the shown code.

NewSplayTree at line 576 is unchecked; a NULL exif_resources would be dereferenced at line 612, but this requires an allocation failure with no attacker-controlled size (DoS-only, single-shot), so it is recorded as a robustness concern rather than a finding.

The components*tag_bytes product at line 624 is computed in size_t; on a 32-bit build the wrap-around could pass the line 625 guard for very large components, but such entries are then rejected by the dir_offset+number_bytes bounds checks (lines 640-643), so no out-of-bounds access was demonstrated.

In common deployments (e.g. CLI identify) the property string is a fixed constant such as 'exif:*' rather than freely attacker-chosen; the overflow is nevertheless deterministically triggered by the shown code whenever a short wildcard property is used against an image containing any valid EXIF entry.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice is not vulnerable in the shown code: start is clamped to [0,length] (line 26), deleteCount to [0,length-start] (lines 32, 42), final length is capped at NJS_MAX_LENGTH (line 47), and every raw buffer operation (deleted fill at line 62, item memcpy at lines 116-117) is bounded algebraically (start+items = start+delete+delta <= length+delta) with capacity ensured by njs_array_expand for growth. No injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks exist. All remaining concerns depend on unseen helper contracts or bounded single-shot DoS loops and are not confirmed findings.

assumptions: args has exactly nargs elements and nargs >= 1 (njs VM call convention), so args[3 .. 3+items-1] is valid for items = nargs-3.
Fast arrays preserve size >= length, so indexing array->start up to length-1 (via start+delete-1 <= length-1) is in bounds.
njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta) guarantees capacity >= length + delta when delta > 0.
njs_array_alloc(vm, 0, delete, 0) returns a fast array with capacity >= delete whenever deleted->object.fast_array is set; for fast 'this', delete <= length <= 2^32-1 so no narrowing occurs.
NJS_MAX_LENGTH fits in int64 and bounds the final array length.
limitations: No concrete failing value exists for any memory-safety candidate; OOB via deleted->start (line 62) or memcpy (lines 116-117) is blocked by the clamps at lines 26/42, the max-length check at line 47, and the expand call at line 98.

With a plain array-like object carrying a huge length property (e.g., 2^40), splice.call(obj, 0) drives bounded-but-astronomical property loops at lines 68-81 and 129-134 (algorithmic DoS); these loops are finite-state and terminate, so they are not confirmed hang findings per scope.
A huge deleteCount can force a large njs_array_alloc attempt at line 54, but failure is checked (NULL -> NJS_ERROR) and the effect is single-shot.
The fast-array copy_within relocation (lines 104-105) and expand (line 98) delegate actual memmove/allocation to unseen helpers; any flaw inside those helpers is outside the shown code.
njs_value_to_integer and njs_object_length bounds are assumed per framework semantics; if they returned out-of-range values, the shown clamps still confine start/delete to [0,length].

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node reads past the end of the scanner buffer when parsing unterminated PI/comment/CDATA constructs. The for(;;) loops (lines 14-23, 30-39) and the CDATA loop (98-103) advance scanner->curptr to end-of-input and then dereference *(scanner->curptr+1) / run pj_scan_strcmp over 3 bytes at the end, with no pj_scan_is_eof or remaining-length guard; crafted input such as "<?x?" or "<a><![CDATA[abc]" triggers an out-of-bounds read that repeats past the buffer (crash / adjacent-memory disclosure). Other in-function checks (line 88) guard only the content scan and do not bound these reads.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled XML determines the scanner position: for input "<?x?", pj_scan_get_until_ch (line 16) stops scanner->curptr at the trailing '?', and line 17 dereferences *(scanner->curptr+1), reading one byte past the last input byte (curptr+1 == end). If the byte is not '>', the else branch (line 21) advances curptr past end with PJ_FALSE (no clamping) and the loop (14-23) subsequently reads further out of bounds. No pj_scan_is_eof or curptr+1 < end guard exists on this path, so the attacker-controlled termination of the PI (missing ?>) reaches the OOB read (CWE-125).

For input "<a><![CDATA[abc]", pj_scan_get_until_ch (line 97) stops at the final ']' with curptr pointing at/beyond end; the loop condition calls pj_scan_strcmp(scanner, "]]>", 3), which dereferences curptr[0..2] even though fewer than 3 input bytes remain (fully out of bounds when no ']' exists). On mismatch, the body advances curptr past end (line 101) and re-scans (line 102), repeating the OOB read until it collides with arbitrary memory or crashes. The loop has no pj_scan_is_eof break, so the attacker's choice of unterminated CDATA content reaches repeated out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125).

assumptions: The scanner wraps an input buffer whose contents and length are attacker-controlled (e.g., an XML document delivered in a network message) and which is not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated, so a read at curptr == end is an out-of-bounds access.

Helper semantics relied on: pj_scan_get_until_ch leaves curptr at end-of-input when the delimiter is absent; pj_scan_strcmp compares len bytes at curptr without an EOF short-circuit; pj_scan_advance_n with PJ_FALSE advances curptr by N without clamping.
Per the task's scope rule, scanner is a parameter that may be supplied by an unseen caller; no caller code is required to establish the taint of the buffer it points to.
limitations: If the buffer happens to be NUL-terminated with spare capacity, the very first one-past read (lines 12/17) may touch only the terminator byte (logical OOB); the walk past end after line 21 still performs physical OOB reads on subsequent iterations.

attr->value.slen -= 2 (line 62) can underflow to a negative length for unterminated values (e.g., input "<a x="), but the shown code only stores that value and passes it to unseen callers; the consuming memory operation lies outside the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding here (no CWE).

Unbounded recursion on deeply nested input via line 83 (e.g., "<a><a><a>...") can exhaust the stack (DoS, CWE-674 class); it is reachable from attacker input but is treated as a robustness concern because the shown code performs no out-of-bounds write and PJ_CHECK_STACK only inspects.
The EOF/comment/attribute-loop OOB reads (lines 12, 33, 53, 80-81, 93) share the same root cause as the confirmed finding and are not listed as separate CWEs.
No injection, crypto, or file-system sinks exist in the shown function; line 109's double pj_scan_get_char correctly enforces '</' and is not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: lsquic_qeh_settings forwards attacker-controlled QPACK SETTINGS sizes (SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY via max_table_size and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS via max_risked_streams, each valid up to 2^32-1) unvalidated into lsqpack_enc_init at lines 19-21. The only local check (lines 17-18) floors dyn_table_size to 0 and never constrains the other two parameters, so a remote peer can drive oversized encoder-internal structures (e.g., risked/blocked-stream tracking sized by max_risked_streams), causing memory exhaustion and denial of service.

evidence.reason: Sink receives attacker-controlled sizes: max_table_size and max_risked_streams originate in the peer's HTTP/3 SETTINGS frame (SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS, valid range [0, 2^32-1]) and are forwarded verbatim into lsqpack_enc_init, which sizes encoder-internal dynamic-table and blocked/risked-stream state from them. The only guard on the shown path, `if (QENC_MIN_DYN_TABLE_SIZE > dyn_table_size) dyn_table_size = 0;` (lines 17-18), tests only dyn_table_size and imposes only a floor, so the witness max_risked_streams = 4294967295 (or max_table_size = 4294967295) passes every shown check and reaches line 20, letting a remote peer trigger unbounded per-connection allocations (memory exhaustion / denial of service, CWE-770).

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based relative to the code snippet exactly as provided; no enclosing source file was supplied.

Parameter provenance follows HTTP/3 (RFC 9114): SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS are sent by the remote peer, so max_table_size and max_risked_streams are attacker-controlled when the settings handler calls this function.
lsqpack_enc_init allocates/sizes encoder-internal state from the supplied max_table_size and max_risked_streams arguments; the call that carries them is in the shown code at lines 19-21.
QENC_MIN_DYN_TABLE_SIZE and the LSQPACK_ENC_OPT_* constants are treated as compile-time constants; their exact values do not change the analysis.
limitations: The allocation itself and any internal caps reside inside lsqpack_enc_init (not shown), so the exact callee-side allocation size is inferred rather than anchored to a shown line; the oversized-allocation failure mode for values up to 2^32-1 is consistent with the shown control flow and is not contradicted by it.

dyn_table_size is not capped against max_table_size in the shown code; dyn_table_size > max_table_size passes through — the same uncontrolled-resource family as the confirmed finding, so it is not counted as a separate CWE.

No OOB access, NULL dereference, or injection flaw is fully contained in the shown code: all LSQ_* log calls use constant format strings with only numeric arguments (lines 10, 23, 26, 30-31), and the only pointer dereferences target the caller-supplied qeh whose QEH_INITIALIZED precondition is asserted at line 6.
Both outcomes of the lsqpack_enc_init error branch (lines 22-25) are handled; there is no use-after-failure path in the shown code.

verdict.summary: On the executed val==TRUE path, every pair-derived stack pop (pop_n(len*2) at lines 11/37, pop_n(len*2+1) at line 52) exactly matches the 2 slots per pair pushed at lines 31-32 and reset by lines 28/47, and the spill guard at line 36 (cursp() >= slimit, with slimit <= INT16_MAX) bounds every len operand consumed by genop_2 to <= 16384, preventing 16-bit operand truncation and stack underflow. The only gap is an internal inconsistency: the kw-rest flush at lines 10-20 runs unconditionally while the loop-end flush is gated by 'val &&' (line 36), so a val==FALSE caller compiling a hash containing '**' would call pop_n(len*2) against slots never pushed for the pairs; however, the security impact (clean compile error vs. memory corruption) depends on the unseen pop_n implementation and reachability on an unseen val==FALSE caller path, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

assumptions: mruby codegen invariant: each codegen(expr, val) call leaves exactly 1 modeled stack slot when val is truthy and 0 when falsy; this is what makes lines 31-32 contribute exactly 2 slots per pair on the val==TRUE path.
tree is a finite, acyclic, NULL-terminated cons list built by the parser, so the while at line 8 terminates and line 9's car/car/car dereference is shape-safe for syntactically valid ruby.
GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX are framework constants with GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX <= INT16_MAX; the spill keeps cursp() bounded to slimit + 2.

pop_n/push/genop_* bodies are outside the shown code; current mruby's pop_n checks cursp() < n before decrementing, which would convert any residual mismatch into a clean codegen error rather than memory corruption.
limitations: Candidate 2 (unconfirmed): with val==FALSE and a hash containing a '**' element, pop_n(len*2) at line 11 pops 2 slots per pair that lines 31-32 never pushed (24*2*... 2*len pops against 0 pushed slots). Example syntax that would reach line 11 with len>=1 under such a caller: {f() => g(), **h()}. Not promoted because (a) no shown code path invokes gen_hash with val==FALSE on a hash containing NODE_KW_REST_ARGS, and (b) whether the resulting stack underflow is a clean 'stack pointer underflow' error (checked mruby pop_n) or an out-of-bounds stack write (unchecked/older pop_n) is decided by the unseen pop_n implementation, so impact is not confirmable from the shown code alone.

Candidate 3 (limitation): the chain nint(tree->car->car->car) at line 9 trusts the parser's node layout for every hash element; a NULL or non-node key would fault here, but no syntax admitted by the parser produces that shape in the shown code path.

Candidate 4 (limitation): int overflow of len*2/len*2+1 would require >1e9 hash pairs in one literal and is already bounded to <=16384 on the val==TRUE path by the line-36 spill, so it is not attacker-reachable.
Candidate 5 (limitation): no ReDoS or hang is present; the loop is an O(1)-per-element walk over a finite parser-built list.

The 'limit' parameter is never used in the shown code; any recursion-depth protection it was intended to provide is absent, but no recursion occurs inside this function, so there is no depth-based failure here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-reachable vulnerability in the shown code. Every EVP_DigestUpdate call is fed by a server-side configuration object whose pointer is valid for the supplied length (byte-vector and CRL string sizes match their containers), the X509_digest write is bounded by the EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE buffer and the SHA-256 length assertion, and no injection, weak-crypto, or access-control sink receives attacker-controlled data.

assumptions: The caller passes hash_buffer with at least EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE writable bytes, as the declared parameter type states.
verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ are standard byte containers for which data() is valid for size() bytes and value_type has size 1.
md wraps a valid, initialized EVP_MD_CTX.
ca_cert_ and config_ are immutable, framework-owned validator state not directly controlled by the remote client.
limitations: If an unseen caller passed a hash_buffer smaller than EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE, X509_digest could overflow that caller-provided buffer, but the shown signature declares the 64-byte capacity and no attacker-controlled length reaches the write.

A theoretical session-resumption bypass would require an unhashed validation-affecting config field outside the fields enumerated in the shown code, or a MessageUtil::hash collision; neither is demonstrated here and the resumption logic is unseen.
RELEASE_ASSERT aborts on crypto failure could be a DoS only if an attacker could force X509_digest or EVP_DigestUpdate to fail, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: afra_box_read reads attacker-controlled global_entry_count from the bitstream and uses it as an unbounded loop counter: unlike entry_count (guarded at line 14), global_entry_count is never validated against the box's declared size. With global_entries=1 and global_entry_count up to 0xFFFFFFFF, each iteration allocates a GF_GlobalAfraEntry and links it into the list; the loop only stops when the declared size is exhausted (~size/8 iterations, up to ~536M for a u32 size), so a tiny crafted file with a large declared box size drives massive heap allocation and list growth, exhausting memory/CPU (DoS).

evidence.reason: global_entry_count is read directly from the attacker-controlled bitstream at line 36 (gf_bs_read_u32) with no bound tied to ptr->size, unlike the guard at line 14 that caps entry_count to size/12 or size/16. The loop at line 37 iterates up to global_entry_count (max 0xFFFFFFFF) and each iteration unconditionally allocates a heap object at line 38 and inserts a list node at line 61; the only stop condition is ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, 8) failing after ~size/8 increments. A crafted box header declaring size 0xFFFFFFFF (with only a few real payload bytes, since EOF on the reads is not surfaced as an error in the shown code) yields up to ~536M allocations from a tiny file, exhausting memory/CPU before GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE is returned. This is the same per-entry accounting the line-14 guard protects for local entries but is absent here (CWE-400).

assumptions: ptr->size is set by the ISO-BMFF box-header parser from attacker-controlled file data, as the shown code itself treats it as the consumption bound.

The bitstream read functions (gf_bs_read_u64/u32/u16) do not surface a read-past-EOF error to the shown code, so the loop continues while the declared size permits; the loop bound derives from the declared size, not the actual file length.
local_access_entries and global_access_entries are initialized by the unseen box constructor, so gf_list_insert is not passed NULL.
limitations: No out-of-bounds write/read is confirmed in the shown code: the local-entry loop is fully bounded by the line-14 guard and per-read ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE checks; impact of the confirmed finding is resource exhaustion only.
gf_list_insert internals are not shown; a position-clamping or memory-safety issue there would be out of scope for this finding.

The exact read behavior of gf_bs_read_* past EOF is not shown; even without relying on it, the iteration count and allocations scale with the attacker-controlled declared box size rather than with real file bytes.

verdict.summary: ParseEquation reads (*input_label_counts)[0] and [1] at lines 51-52 without verifying that num_inputs is at least 2 (or 1). num_inputs is the attacker-influenced number of parsed input subscripts derived from the equation string at line 16; the 'num_inputs == 1' short-circuit covers exactly one input, but for num_inputs == 0 with a non-empty output (e.g., an equation whose input side parses to zero subscripts) the loop at line 48 reaches line 51 and performs an out-of-bounds heap read on the empty input_label_counts vector (heap OOB read, CWE-125).

evidence.reason: num_inputs originates from ParseEinsumEquation on the attacker-controlled equation (line 11, line 16) and the shown code never constrains it before this sink; input_label_counts is resized to exactly num_inputs at line 27. The only guard, 'num_inputs == 1', short-circuits solely for one input. With num_inputs == 0 and num_labels >= 1 (a parsed equation with an empty input side and a non-empty output side), the line-48 loop executes line 51, which reads row 0 (and 1) of the empty vector — an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) that can crash or disclose adjacent memory.

assumptions: MapToLabels assigns non-ellipsis labels consecutively in [0, label_mapping.size()), so label-indexed accesses at lines 33, 41, 50, and 53 are in-bounds for non-ellipsis labels.
kEllipsisLabel is a negative sentinel distinct from mapped labels, so the 'label != kEllipsisLabel' guards at lines 32 and 40 prevent negative indices.
Caller-provided pointer out-parameters are non-null and ParseEinsumEquation returns OK only for syntactically parsed equations.
limitations: The num_inputs == 0 trigger depends on the unshown ParseEinsumEquation accepting an equation whose input side yields zero subscripts (e.g., an empty left-hand side); if that parser always yields at least one subscript, the OOB read is unreachable and this becomes non-exploitable.

For num_inputs > 2 the 'unique' computation consults only the first two inputs, producing incorrect DimensionType classification; this is a correctness logic error with no memory-safety or security impact, so no CWE is attached.
A label-indexed OOB would require MapToLabels to break the consecutive-label invariant assumed at lines 13-14; no evidence in the shown code supports that, so it is not a finding.
No other memory, injection, crypto, file, or auth sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every attacker-influenced label index is bounded: MapToLabels assigns consecutive integers in [0, num_labels-1] (documented at lines 13-14), num_labels equals label_mapping.size() (line 26), all count/type vectors are resized to exactly num_labels (lines 30, 39, 49), kEllipsisLabel is excluded by guards (lines 33, 42, 51) before any indexing, and all loops use strict i < bound. The only unguarded risky access, (*input_label_counts)[0][label] at line 53 when num_inputs == 0, is unreachable because ParseEinsumEquation (line 11) rejects equations with an empty operand list, so num_inputs >= 1 at that point.

assumptions: MapToLabels assigns new labels as consecutive integers starting at 0, per the in-code comment at lines 13-14, and kEllipsisLabel is a sentinel distinct from every mapped label, which the guards at lines 33/42 are designed to exclude.
ParseEinsumEquation (line 11) rejects malformed equations and any equation with an empty operand list, so num_inputs >= 1 whenever line 53 executes.
limitations: If MapToLabels were changed to emit non-consecutive or oversized labels, lines 34/43/52-55 would become out-of-bounds; under the invariant stated in the shown code this is not a confirmed finding and no CWE is assigned.

A num_inputs == 0 path reaching the (*input_label_counts)[0][label] read at line 53 would be an OOB read on the empty outer vector, but it is unreachable given the einsum grammar enforced at line 11; no CWE is assigned.
The kEllipsisLabel check at line 51 can never fire when the sentinel is negative because the loop counter is non-negative; it is dead code, not a vulnerability.
The size_t-to-int conversions at lines 16 and 26 are value-preserving because operand count and distinct-label count are grammar-bounded; no truncation risk.

verdict.summary: ReadPCLImage's tokenizer and geometry path are bounded: the write-before-check at lines 115-119 cannot overrun command[MaxTextExtent] because line 117 caps the post-write cursor at MaxTextExtent-1 and lines 119-120 then terminate at index <= MaxTextExtent-1 and reset (max payload index N-2, NUL index N-1; a 4095-character token is the boundary witness). Values reaching the delegate exec at lines 216-224 are systematically neutralized by the shown code: attacker-influenced geometry/density/page values are re-formatted with %g/%.20g (digit charset only), and the two filename arguments are regenerated unique names from AcquireUniqueFilename/AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink, so no shell metacharacters are constructible from file content or options in the shown data flow. Remaining concerns (trace-level log injection of the raw filename, double-to-size_t conversion UB producing huge -g delegate arguments, ignored AcquireUniqueFilename return, and the generic external delegate template dependency) are documented in notes.limitations and do not rise to confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: Line numbers are per the single-function listing provided, counting from line 1 (function signature) through line 259 (closing brace).
MaxTextExtent is 4096; the tokenizer bound argument only requires MaxTextExtent >= 2.

PSPageGeometry, PSDensityGeometry, and DefaultResolution are compile-time constants; ParseAbsoluteGeometry, AcquireUniqueSymbolicLink, AcquireUniqueFilename, CloneImageInfo, SyncNextImageInList, GetDelegateInfo, and GetDelegateCommands are trusted framework helpers whose internal bounds/quoting are outside the shown code.
ReadBlobByte returns 0..255 or EOF, so (char) c at line 115 never receives the EOF sentinel.
The delegate command template returned by GetDelegateCommands is trusted framework configuration (its quoting is not part of the shown code).
limitations: Log injection (CWE-117) at lines 56-57: image_info->filename is written raw to LogMagickEvent with a %s format; a newline in an attacker-chosen filename would forge log lines, but this requires image_info->debug (trace logging) to be enabled and treats the operator-supplied filename as untrusted; assessed as a hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Double-to-size_t conversion UB at lines 153-154 and 192-195: crafted values such as MediaBox [-1e308 0 1e308 1e308] or -page 1e300x1e300 produce out-of-range casts yielding huge page.width/page.height; the values only reach %g-formatted delegate options and image->page, never an allocation/index in the shown code, so impact (huge -g arguments to GhostPCL, potential external DoS) is outside the shown code and unconfirmed.

The delegate exec sink (lines 216-224) is the generic ImageMagick pattern; exploitation would require a metacharacter to survive the shown numeric re-encoding or the regenerated filenames, or unquoted placeholders in the unseen delegates.xml template; none is constructible from the shown data flow, so it is not a confirmed finding.

The return of AcquireUniqueFilename at line 215 is ignored; if it failed, read_info->filename would remain the user-supplied string and be passed at line 220, but such failure is not attacker-controllable in the shown path and impact depends on the unseen command template.

read_info->scene + read_info->number_scenes (ssize_t addition, lines 205/209) could overflow only for caller-supplied extremes; the result is immediately cast to double and digit-formatted, with no memory impact in the shown code.
Termination of the do/while list walk at lines 243-257 depends on the trusted SyncNextImageInList helper returning NULL at list end; the shown loop itself is finite-state given that helper.

verdict.summary: yank_copy_line computes the heap allocation size as bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1 (line 7) with no overflow check. startspaces/endspaces/textlen are attacker-influenced column/length counts derived from a crafted file's line; when their sum wraps (e.g., each equal to 0x55555555, sum+1 wraps to 0), alloc returns an undersized buffer and the subsequent vim_memset (lines 11, 15) and mch_memmove (line 13) write the unwrapped byte counts past the heap block, causing an out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced bd->startspaces/endspaces/textlen (derived from a crafted file's line length during blockwise yank) are summed in 32-bit colnr_T arithmetic with no overflow guard. With each value equal to 0x55555555 the expression wraps to 0, so alloc returns a far smaller buffer than the bytes later written; the only guards are the NULL check on this line and the s>0 loop guard, neither of which validates the size sum.

Sink of the confirmed write: textlen (attacker-influenced, unvalidated) is cast to size_t and copied into the heap block whose size came from the wrapped value at line 7, so this memmove writes textlen bytes past the end of the undersized allocation (same applies to the vim_memset calls at lines 11 and 15).

assumptions: struct block_def column fields (startspaces, endspaces, textlen) are 32-bit colnr_T and alloc takes a 32-bit size, as in classic Vim builds, so the three-term sum can wrap.
The trigger requires a crafted file with a line of roughly 2^31-2^32 columns and a user-initiated blockwise yank.
Caller invariants assumed: y_idx < y_current->y_size and textlen <= actual line length (both unshown).
limitations: Any OOB write via y_current->y_array[y_idx] at line 10 or OOB read of textstart at line 13 depends on unshown caller invariants, so it is not a confirmed finding.
The int truncation at line 19 (s = bd->textlen + bd->endspaces) stays in-bounds because of the s > 0 guard; it can only produce malformed register content, not memory corruption.
Allocation-failure denial of service (huge size passed to alloc) is out of scope; the confirmed finding requires wrap-to-small, not mere failure.
The trailing-space trimming loop (lines 21-25) is verified safe: s decreases by at least 1 per iteration, reads stay in [0, textlen-1], and pnew-- cannot precede the start of the allocation.

verdict.summary: ComputeAsync reads input.dim_size(ndims-1) and rhs.dim_size(ndims-1) before any rank validation, so attacker-chosen shapes (scalar input giving index -1, or rhs with rank < input rank giving index == rhs.dims()) trigger out-of-bounds reads of TensorShape storage (CWE-125), causing UB/process crash (DoS). The ndims >= 2 and rank-equality OP_REQUIRES checks run only after these reads and cannot protect them.

evidence.snippet:
const int64 n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1);
    const int64 nrhs = rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1);
evidence.reason: ndims is attacker-controlled via the tensor rank (line 4) and is used unvalidated here: a scalar input (ndims == 0) makes line 5 index TensorShape storage with -1, and an rhs of rank ndims-1 makes line 6 index with ndims-1 == rhs.dims() (out of range). The only guards, OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(ndims >= 2) (lines 8-11) and rhs.dims() == ndims (lines 12-16), execute after these reads, so they cannot protect the uses on lines 5-6; both cases are therefore out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) reachable before the kernel aborts.

assumptions: Tensor ranks/sizes are attacker-controlled in the kernel-validity sense: raw-op/eager dispatch reaches this kernel without a rank pre-filter, and the kernel's own checks are the runtime backstop.
Release TensorFlow builds compile out the DCHECK bounds checks inside TensorShape::dim_size, so indices -1 or == dims() perform an actual out-of-bounds access rather than a clean abort.
limitations: The garbage values read at lines 5-6 are not consumed downstream because the subsequent OP_REQUIRES rank checks abort the kernel, so the impact is UB/crash (DoS) rather than memory corruption or information disclosure; crash reproducibility depends on memory layout/allocator, though ASAN/DCHECK builds fail deterministically.

Integer-overflow candidates (128 * batch_size at line 99; input.NumElements() * sizeof(Scalar) at lines 76, 145, 202) are not triggerable within TensorFlow tensor-size and allocatable-memory constraints and are not findings.
No injection (format-string/command/SQL/log/header), weak-crypto, file-handling, or authorization sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All attacker-controlled indices are clamped before use (start to [0,length] at line 26; delete to [0,length-start] at lines 31-42), final length is capped by NJS_MAX_LENGTH at line 47, items = nargs-3 is bounded by the caller's args buffer, the fast-path buffer is extended via the error-checked njs_array_expand before the memcpy, and every copy loop bound (lines 61, 68, 134, 144) stays within [0, new_length). No OOB, injection, crypto, or access-control sink is reachable with a violating value in the shown code.

assumptions: njs_object_length returns the true array length for fast arrays (equal to array->length), so length == array->length in the fast path.
njs_array_alloc(vm, 0, delete, 0) guarantees deleted->size >= delete (and its failure is checked at lines 55-57).
njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta) guarantees capacity >= array->length + delta and its failure is checked at lines 104-106.
The JS engine always allocates args with exactly nargs entries, so args[0..nargs-1] are valid.
NJS_MAX_LENGTH is at most 2^32-1, so all int64 arithmetic (length+start, length+delta, start+items, items*sizeof(njs_value_t)) cannot overflow.
limitations: For a generic object whose length property is negative (e.g. {length: -5}), start and delete can become negative; however, only generic property get/set/delete operations are reached (lines 69, 76, 135, 145, 151), and no memory-indexing sink in the shown code is accessed with an out-of-range index, so no OOB is demonstrated.

delete can be as large as the pre-existing array length, making njs_array_alloc attempt a large allocation (line 54); this is error-checked, requires an attacker to already hold an array of that size, and does not compound beyond the attacker's own volume, so it is a robustness/DoS concern only.

The direction/semantics of njs_array_copy_within's last argument (neg) is not visible in the shown code; if misused it could cause a correctness (value-clobbering) bug, but bounds remain within the array and no memory-safety impact is demonstrated from the shown code.
No input in the shown code reaches printf/system/SQL/XPath/HTTP-header/file/crypto sinks, so injection, weak-crypto, and access-control classes are not applicable.

verdict.summary: Matrix dimensions from attacker-controlled input tensor shapes are narrowed from int64 to int (lines 9-12) without any magnitude or sign check. A dimension of 2^31 truncates to -2147483648, passes the truncated k==k2 guard, and reaches TensorShape({m,n}) at line 19, causing a CHECK abort / invalid Eigen sizing; wraps for dims >= 2^32 (e.g. 2^32+3 -> 3) let a mismatched inner product pass the guard, yielding inconsistent Eigen contraction dimensions. The guard k==k2 runs on already-truncated values, so it cannot protect the allocation/contraction sinks.

evidence.reason: m and n are produced by narrowing int64 dim_size() results to int at lines 9-12 (taint: attacker-controlled tensor shapes from ctx->input(0)/ctx->input(1), lines 2-3). A dim of 2^31 truncates to -2147483648; the guard k==k2 at line 14 passes because it compares the already-truncated k/k2 values and never checks sign or int-range of m/n, so the negative dimension reaches TensorShape({-2147483648, 1}) here, causing a CHECK abort or invalid Eigen sizing (similarly, k_true=2^32+3 and k2_true=3 both truncate to 3, passing the guard while the true contract dims at line 54 mismatch). The result is CWE-190 integer overflow/truncation with availability (abort) and incorrect output rather than graceful error handling.

assumptions: TensorShape::dim_size returns int64 (TensorFlow API), so the assignments at lines 9-12 are genuine int64-to-int narrowing.
Framework guarantees tensor dims are non-negative, so the only harmful transformation is the int narrowing; dims >= 0 are otherwise attacker-chosen.
Eigen contract/shuffle and DoMatMul internals are out of scope; the analysis covers sizes passed to them.
limitations: Exploitation requires an input tensor axis with at least 2^31 elements (about 4 GiB for bfloat16 or 8 GiB for float32) already resident in memory; on memory-constrained deployments input allocation itself fails first.

For dims >= 2^32 the wrap produces smaller positive ints, leading to wrong output dimensions/results or Eigen dimension-mismatch asserts, but no demonstrated out-of-bounds write, since the output buffer is never allocated larger than the true product.
The exact post-truncation failure mode (CHECK abort vs. Eigen assert) depends on framework debug/release settings.
Single-shot allocation-failure DoS from new Tensor(DT_FLOAT, a.shape()) at line 38 is not compounded by attacker-controlled volume in a reachable loop, so it is not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: The shown Gather wrapper contains no security-relevant operation of its own: it copies params.axis and params.batch_dims (lines 4-5) and forwards tensor shapes and raw data pointers to optimized_ops::Gather (lines 6-9). The actual indexing of input_data by positions values, the writes to output_data, and any use of axis/batch_dims all occur inside the unseen callee, so this is a pure pass-through and no dangerous operation is provably present in the shown code. Out-of-range positions or invalid axis values could cause out-of-bounds access only in the callee, which is out of scope for this analysis; no format/injection, crypto, or file/authz sink exists here.

assumptions: The TFLite framework guarantees input, positions, and output are non-null, allocated tensors before this template helper runs, which is the invariant GetTensorShape/GetTensorData rely on.
params is decoded by the interpreter from the model's builtin_data, and positions contents may be attacker-controlled model input (indices).
limitations: Potential heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): positions values (GetTensorData<PositionsT> at line 8) are forwarded without any bounds check in the shown code; if optimized_ops::Gather lacks a release-mode runtime check, an index outside [0, input_shape.Dims(axis)) or a negative index would read out of bounds of input. This is not confirmable here because the indexing sink is inside the unseen callee (explicit pass-through, out of scope).

params.axis and params.batch_dims (lines 4-5) are passed unvalidated; any misuse (e.g., negative axis, axis >= rank, invalid batch_dims) is decided inside optimized_ops::Gather or the unseen caller's validation, so no failure can be demonstrated from the shown code.
The shown code provides no validation to protect the callee; this is a defense-in-depth gap, not an independently confirmed vulnerability in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The per-slice loop bounds index i by num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) (line 8) but the shown code never verifies that input_min_range/input_max_range (or the minmax_shape-sized outputs) contain at least num_slices elements. With input shape [4,2,3], axis_=0, and scalar (1-element) min/max range tensors, iteration i=1 reads min_ranges(1) (line 51) out of bounds and forms OOB output min/max pointers (lines 53-54) that QuantizeSlice stores through, giving attacker-controlled heap OOB read/write.

evidence.snippet:
QuantizeSlice(ctx->eigen_device<Device>(), ctx,
                    input_tensor.template chip<1>(i), min_ranges(i),
                    max_ranges(i), output_tensor.template chip<1>(i),
                    &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i),
                    &output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i));
evidence.reason: Index i comes from the loop at line 49 with bound i < num_slices, where num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) (line 8) is attacker-controlled via the input tensor shape and the axis_ attribute. input_min_range/input_max_range are attacker-controlled tensors (lines 3-4) and no shown code checks that their element counts (or the minmax_shape-sized outputs allocated at lines 31-34) are >= num_slices. Witness: input shape [4,2,3], axis_=0 gives num_slices=4; scalar ranges give vec<float>() size 1, so at i=1 min_ranges(1) (line 51) reads one float past the 1-element vector and &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(1) (line 53) forms a pointer one element past the 1-element output_min_tensor passed to QuantizeSlice for storage. All guards on the path (axis_ > -1 at line 7, num_slices == 1 at line 18, mode at line 28) are passed by this witness; the missing check is input_min_range.NumElements() == num_slices (and symmetric checks for max range and outputs).

assumptions: axis_ and mode_ are op attributes taken from the graph/model definition and are attacker-influenceable when a hostile model/graph is executed.
TensorShape::dim_size, Eigen vec/operator(), and the flat/chip views impose no bounds checks in release builds; the shown code contains no compensating verifications.
The witness uses the default MIN_COMBINED mode so the MIN_FIRST guard at line 28 is passed.
limitations: axis_ >= input.dims() makes line 8 (num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_)) read past the shape's dims array because only the axis_ > -1 check (line 7) exists; downstream impact depends on the garbage value, so it is not the primary CWE.
The scalar branch reads input_min_range.flat<float>()(0) at lines 21-22 without verifying the range tensors are non-empty, which is OOB for empty range tensors.
num_slices narrows the int64 dim_size result to int (line 8), which can wrap for axis dims above INT_MAX.

The store through the OOB pointers at lines 53-54 occurs inside QuantizeSlice, whose body is not shown; the fully in-code memory fault is the read at line 51 (CWE-125), with the write path as the same root cause.
Any framework-level shape inference that might reject these witnesses is outside the shown code and is not relied upon for the verdict.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes the tstring vector inputs with the unvalidated restore_index parameter (line 16 for input(1), line 53 for input(2)) with no bounds check against NumElements(), so an out-of-range or negative restore_index performs a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: restore_index is an int parameter with no NumElements() bound check in the shown code; tensor_name_t is a tstring vector whose size is fixed by the caller. A value restore_index >= tensor_name_t.NumElements() (e.g., 1 with a 1-element input) or restore_index < 0 makes the unchecked Eigen flat<T>()(i) accessor read past the heap buffer, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Same unvalidated restore_index taint reaches input(2) (tensor_shape_and_slices) when restore_slice is true; the shown code never compares restore_index with input(2).NumElements(), so a spec vector shorter than restore_index+1 triggers the same out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: restore_index and the element counts of inputs 0-2 are determined by the graph/checkpoint supplied by the model author (attacker-controlled inputs per the checkpoint-restore threat model).
Eigen's flat<T>() operator() performs no bounds checking in release builds (asserts are compiled out), so an out-of-range index reads adjacent heap memory.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK abort the kernel (return) on failure, so paths after a failing check are not executed.
limitations: The real TensorFlow caller (RestoreV2Op/RestoreOp::Compute) may enforce tensor_names_t.NumElements() == num_outputs and loop restore_index in [0, num_outputs); that invariant is not present in the shown code, so it cannot be credited here.

Newlines/control characters in tensor_name or file_pattern are embedded unescaped into errors::NotFound/InvalidArgument messages (lines 39-40, 46); this is a CWE-117 log/message-injection candidate but the shown code has no concrete log sink and impact is limited, so it is demoted.

An attacker-crafted checkpoint can set saved_shape so allocate_output (line 71) requests a huge allocation; the failure path is a graceful Status error rather than memory corruption, and slice bounds are validated inside unseen ParseShapeAndSlice/CopySliceData, so this is a DoS-only robustness concern.
The type-mismatch message reads context->expected_output_dtype(0) instead of expected_output_dtype(restore_index) (line 44) - cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads the MF field count (nbFields) directly from the attacker-controlled bitstream with no upper-bound check and passes it straight into gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc, allowing a single small crafted stream to request up to ~2^31 field entries (multi-GiB allocation), causing resource exhaustion.

evidence.reason: nbFields is obtained at line 20 from attacker-controlled bitstream reads (line 19 sets NbBits up to 31, so nbFields is unbounded up to 0x7FFFFFFF) and reaches this allocation sink with no cap or validation; the only check (line 30) runs after the oversized allocation is attempted, so a 31-bit field count forcing a ~8 GiB request for 4-byte element types is admitted and enables memory-exhaustion DoS (CWE-400).

assumptions: bs carries attacker-controlled media bitstream data, so gf_bs_read_int values at lines 19-20 are attacker-controlled.
gf_bs_read_int honors its bit count (0..31) and returns values within 2^NbBits - 1.
gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc dimensions storage for nbFields elements; its internals are not shown.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds or integer-overflow inside gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc/gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item depends on unseen helper implementations; the shown loop index i < nbFields is consistent with the requested count, so no memory-safety finding is confirmed from the shown code.
Memory leak when node == NULL and codec->pCurrentProto is NULL (lines 46, 49, 75) requires caller-side state not shown here, so it is not confirmed.
Behavior of gf_bs_read_int(bs, 0) when NbBits == 0, and the later consumption of the QP14 length set at line 25, are in unseen code and are not confirmed.
The MFNODE loop bound (line 43) is huge but effectively constrained by bitstream length; without an allocation-size sink for that path it is only noted, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The record payload is validated before the copy: SliceTensorShape rejects invalid slice extents (lines 42-43), and the equality guard (lines 48-49) admits only a payload whose element count exactly equals shp_s.num_elements(), so any mismatch aborts with false (line 54) before the copy at lines 56-58. The filename->index lookup (lines 24-25) is protected by the reader invariant that detail filenames are the registered shard filenames that key fname_to_index_ and index sss_. Unseen helpers (CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice, sstable Get, ParseProtoUnlimited) are outside review scope.

assumptions: details entries are produced by FindTensorSlice from TensorSliceSet registries whose filenames are the reader's own opened shard names — the same set keyed by fname_to_index_ and indexed by sss_ — so idx at line 24 is always in [0, sss_.size()) and CHECK_GE (line 25) holds; no attacker-chosen string inside a record is used as fname.

CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice (lines 56-58) copies only the intersection of slice_s and slice within tss->shape(), and TensorProtoDataSize<T> returns the element count of the byte payload for T; both helpers are unseen and assumed faithful.
The caller allocates data with enough space for the requested slice (function contract); the shown code does not re-check this.
tss is guaranteed non-null past the early return at lines 14-17, so all tss->shape() uses (lines 42, 57) are guarded.
limitations: A memory-corruption bug inside the unseen CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice can be neither confirmed nor refuted from this snippet; the shown source-size guard (lines 48-49, backed by shp_s from lines 41-42) is the protective check binding the record payload to the expected element count, and any mismatch returns false (line 54).

If FindTensorSlice could ever yield a filename outside the reader's registered shard set, CHECK_GE (line 25) would abort on idx == -1; this contradicts the registration invariant and is treated as a robustness/hardening concern rather than a confirmed finding.
Parsing behavior inside ParseProtoUnlimited and sstable Get is unseen; resource exhaustion is bounded by record length and does not scale in a reachable hot loop in the shown code.
Potential int64 overflow in shp_s.num_elements() on crafted shapes fails the equality check (lines 48-49) — fail-closed — and no concrete witness exploit is demonstrated.
VLOG statements (lines 9-10, 29-31, 36-37, 44-45, 50-53) interpolate name/filename/DebugString into local logs; no security boundary impact is demonstrated, so no log-injection finding.

verdict.summary: SVDF Prepare validates params->rank only with rank != 0, so a negative rank from a crafted model (e.g., rank=-1 with num_filters=1) produces num_units=-1, which is written into the output tensor's dimension array and passed to context->ResizeTensor. Negative/overflowed signed dims are later converted to unsigned sizes or used as indexing metadata, enabling huge allocations or out-of-bounds access.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled params->rank (line 24, from node->builtin_data/model SVDFOptions) is guarded only by rank != 0 (line 27), which admits negative values. Witness rank=-1 with num_filters=1 passes line 28 (1 % -1 == 0) and yields num_units = 1 / -1 = -1 (line 29); all shape equality checks (lines 31-33, 47-50) pass with matching crafted dims. num_units=-1 is stored at output_size_array->data[1] (line 55) and reaches this ResizeTensor call for the output tensor with no num_units > 0 (or rank > 0) check. The signed negative dimension flows into interpreter size computation (NumElements * element size converted to unsigned), producing a huge allocation/CHECK failure and inconsistent shape metadata used for indexing, i.e., an invalid attacker-controlled size reaching a memory operation (out-of-bounds write class, CWE-787).

assumptions: TFLite node builtin_data, tensor dims, and quantization fields are derived from the model flatbuffer and are attacker-controlled (standard untrusted-.tflite threat model).
scratch_tensor_index is bounded by the framework's tensor-count invariant via Init/GetTensorIndex, so scratch_tensor_index + 1..5 cannot overflow.
context->ResizeTensor/GetTemporarySafe honor node->temporaries size, so temporaries writes (indices 0..5, 0..1, 0) stay in bounds.
limitations: memory_size * num_filters (line 50) is a signed int32 product that can wrap (e.g., 65536*65536 -> 0) and defeat the state-shape check, but the resulting inconsistent state is only consumed in the unshown Eval path, so it is out of scope here (no dangerous operation in the shown code).
Positive but huge dims (e.g., batch_size near INT_MAX) yield attacker-sized scratch allocations; treated as resource-exhaustion robustness, not an independently confirmed finding.

input->dims->data[1] and weights_feature->dims->data[1] are read without an input/weights rank>=2 check; rank-0/1 tensors read allocated-but-uninitialized slots (TfLiteIntArray covers data[0..size]), not an OOB past the allocation.

scale->data[0] reads (lines 201-206) assume affine quantization with non-empty scale vectors; absent scale maps to kTfLiteNoQuantization (caught by lines 184-198) and an empty vector reads an allocated-but-uninitialized slot, not a confirmed OOB.
Division by zero at lines 28-29 is prevented by the rank != 0 guard (line 27); the confirmed flaw is the guard's failure to exclude negative rank, not the absent zero check.

verdict.summary: TensorSliceReader::CopySliceData streams checkpoint-derived strings (shard filename fname, tensor name, computed key) into log sinks without newline/CR sanitization. A crafted checkpoint whose tensor metadata references a filename such as "shard0.data\n[EVENT] forged" reaches the CHECK_GE log stream at line 25 (unconditional), and crafted tensor names/slices reach the VLOG sinks at lines 29-31 and 36-37, splitting log lines and forging log entries (CWE-117).

evidence.snippet: CHECK_GE(idx, 0) << "Failed to find the index for filename " << fname;
evidence.reason: fname originates from details, which FindTensorSlice (lines 7/12) fills from attacker-controlled checkpoint file-slice metadata and is bound at line 23. A filename such as "shard0.data\n[EVENT] forged" produces idx == -1 for an unloaded shard at line 24, passes the index guard (which bounds only the index, not the logged string), and is written verbatim to the log at this sink, injecting a newline-terminated forged log line.

The caller/checkpoint-supplied parameter name (line 1) and key, derived at line 27 from name plus checkpoint slice metadata, are written to the log sink without any escaping when Get() fails. A tensor name containing newlines injects arbitrary log lines on this path; unlike the line-25 CHECK sink, this one requires VLOG level >= 1.

assumptions: Checkpoint files (tensor names, tensor metadata, shard filenames, and record bytes) are treated as attacker-controlled input, matching the standard untrusted-checkpoint loading threat model.
gtl::FindWithDefault returns the stored map value or the supplied default (-1).
std::string::data() does not return nullptr in C++11 and later, so an empty sts.data() does not produce a NULL dereference in the shown code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds indexing of sss_[idx] if idx >= sss_.size() is not excluded by line 25 (only idx >= 0 is checked), but no concrete attacker value can be constructed from the shown code because fname_to_index_ is built by unseen code; treated as a trust-invariant concern.

Slice-data size mismatch (SavedTensorSlices.data length vs slice geometry) could cause an out-of-bounds access in CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice (lines 40-42), but that memory operation is in an unseen helper and is out of scope for this snippet.
ParseProtoUnlimited (line 35) parses attacker-controlled record bytes with no shown size cap; parser internals and resource consumption are unseen, so amplification/ReDoS is not confirmable here.
idx == -1 causes an intentional CHECK abort (fail-fast DoS) with no memory-safety impact; single-shot, not compounding with attacker-controlled volume.
VLOG(1) sinks are disabled at default verbosity; the line-25 CHECK stream is the unconditional log sink.

verdict.summary: Integer sign/unsigned confusion in pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi: with an RTCP packet whose length field is 0 or 1, line 18 computes an int value of -8/-4 that widens to a huge pj_size_t, making the line 19 length check vacuous (rpsi_len+12 wraps to 4). A minimal 4-8 byte attacker packet with pt=RTCP_PSFB and count=3 then reaches out-of-bounds reads at lines 23 and 24, and lines 25-26 store an attacker-inflated RPSI length into the output string, which can overflow callers that copy rpsi->rpsi.

evidence.reason: Root integer overflow: pj_ntohs returns pj_uint16_t, which is promoted to signed int, so for attacker-set hdr->length==0/1 the expression yields -8/-4; assigning to unsigned pj_size_t rpsi_len wraps it to 2^64-8/2^64-4, and rpsi_len+12 on line 19 then wraps to 4/8, making the guard admit all length>=4 and never rejecting the truncated packet.

Out-of-bounds read: with a minimum-size attacker packet (length == sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common), hdr->length=0, pt=206, count=3), line 12 passes, line 15 passes, and line 19's vacuous check (rpsi_len+12 == 4) admits it; p points at offset sizeof(*hdr), so *p++ reads one byte past the buffer. The guard admits length >= 4 but the read requires length >= sizeof(*hdr)+1.

Second out-of-bounds read in the same walk: for the same 4-8 byte witness packet admitted by the wrapped guard on line 19, *p++ dereferences offset sizeof(*hdr)+1, which the guard never protects (it only requires length >= 4 while this read needs length >= sizeof(*hdr)+2).

Attacker-inflated output size: with the wrapped rpsi_len (line 18) or an unvalidated padlen byte, line 25 makes rpsi_bit_len = rpsi_len*8 - 16 - padlen wrap to a huge unsigned value, so this line stores a giant slen (~2^61 bytes) into rpsi->rpsi; no check ties it to remaining buffer length (length - sizeof(*hdr) - 2), so a caller copying or logging rpsi->rpsi performs an oversized read/alloc.

assumptions: sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common) is 4 bytes on this ABI (packed version/p/count/pt bitfield block plus 16-bit length field); the wrap makes the finding robust for any size 4-8 with the witness packet size adjusted to sizeof(*hdr).
pj_ntohs returns pj_uint16_t and is promoted to int in the line 18 expression; pj_size_t and rpsi->rpsi_bit_len are unsigned (standard pjlib declarations).
buf/length originate from the RTCP receive path where an attacker controls the datagram contents and (within transport limits) its size.
limitations: The heap overflow that results when an unseen caller copies the inflated rpsi->rpsi (e.g., pj_strdup or logging) is not in the shown code; the in-code confirmed failure is the OOB read plus the corruption of the output length.

A second trigger for the same root class: even with a genuine hdr->length >= 2, an oversized padlen (e.g., 255 with rpsi_len=4) underflows rpsi_bit_len on line 25 and inflates the line 26 slen; it produces no separate sink in the shown code and is folded into the CWE-190/CWE-125 finding.
No loop exists in the function, so no loop-bound or parser-read-position finding applies.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in IsConstantFoldable: out_shape.num_elements() * DataTypeSize(n->output_type(i)) is computed in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic and can wrap, so the max_constant_size_in_bytes guard is bypassed (e.g. a fully-defined shape with 2^62 float32 elements yields a product of 0 mod 2^64). The node is then treated as constant-foldable and the downstream fold materializes a tensor of ~16 EiB, causing memory exhaustion/DoS.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled shape entry (from shape_map, line 24, populated from graph shape data) supplies out_shape.num_elements(), promoted from int64 to size_t at line 29. A fully-defined shape with num_elements() == 2^62 and DataTypeSize == 4 wraps the product to 0 in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic; 0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes is false, so the oversized guard is bypassed and the function falls through to return true at line 70, marking an ~16 EiB constant as foldable and enabling memory exhaustion in the subsequent folding allocation.

assumptions: The constant-folding pass can process a model graph loaded from an untrusted source, so node shapes/attrs feeding shape_map are attacker-controlled.
max_constant_size_in_bytes is a positive framework-configured cap (e.g. default 10 MB).
64-bit platform where DatatypeSize returns size_t and PartialTensorShape::num_elements() returns int64; int64 * size_t is evaluated as unsigned 64-bit.
A fully-defined PartialTensorShape can represent dimensions up to int64 range, so num_elements() == 2^62 is representable.
limitations: The actual oversized allocation and resulting OOM occur in the constant-folding code outside this function; only the guard bypass is demonstrated in the shown code.

n->output_type(i) at line 29 would be an out-of-bounds access if a caller supplied a shape_map vector longer than the node's output count; this is not confirmed because the framework invariant (one PartialTensorShape per output) is enforced outside the shown code.
n->output_type(0) at line 11 assumes Const has at least one output (op-def invariant); not confirmed as reachable.
