VLOG at line 66 writes node-derived text to logs, but it is compile-gated and DebugString escapes content; not elevated to a finding.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable security vulnerability is confirmable in the shown code. All attacker-indexed loads are guarded (map lookups bounded to indices 0..31 by the 255 checks; UCD lookups bounded by valid codepoints; caseless-set reads are either dead code or backed by compile-time-validated offsets). The only concrete defect is the always-false guard `*cc == PT_CLIST && *cc == XCL_PROP`, which silently disables caseless-set min/max tightening — a performance/correctness-of-optimization issue with no security impact.

assumptions: `cc` points at an internally consistent XCLASS chunk produced by pcre2_compile (flags byte, optional 32-byte map iff XCL_MAP, self-delimiting items, XCL_END terminator, sorted items, validated property payloads/offsets).
`read_char` yields a valid codepoint <= READ_CHAR_MAX (0x10FFFF) for UTF modes; the 32-bit non-UTF case is explicitly capped in the shown code.
The ucd_* tables are static, correctly sized, and NOTACHAR-terminated; the caseless sets referenced by PT_CLIST entries contain >= 3 chars before the terminator.

XCL_* item markers and PT_* property codes come from disjoint enumerations (e.g., XCL_PROP is an item marker, PT_CLIST is a property code), so `*cc == XCL_PROP` where `*cc` is a property code is never true.
Line numbers are relative to the pasted snippet; no file path was provided for this function.
limitations: The always-false condition `if (*cc == PT_CLIST && *cc == XCL_PROP)` makes the scanning-loop caseless-set walk dead code and skips the min/max tightening for PT_CLIST items; impact is limited to wider read_char envelopes and lost optimization (no security impact demonstrated, no CWE attached).

Match-semantics correctness of generated code (e.g., the meaning of falling through past the class block for characters >255 in map-only classes) depends on unseen callers (compile_char1_matchingpath etc.) and was not assessed as a finding.
Any OOB possibility inside unseen helpers (GETCHARINCTEST target buffer sizing, read_char, optimize_class) is out of scope for this function.
Compile-time work is linear in class-item count; no quadratic or unwound attacker-driven loop was found.

verdict.summary: The output write at line 77 is fully guarded by OP_REQUIRES at lines 71-76 enforcing 0 <= idx < out_flat.size(), so every attacker-derived index is constrained to the output buffer before use; the group-size check at lines 63-69 similarly protects the coords/strides reads inside CoordinatesToFlatIndex. No confirmed OOB read/write, injection, crypto, or access-control vulnerability is reachable in the shown code; remaining concerns (unseen ValidateInputs/helper bounds, integer-overflow data-integrity, huge-allocation DoS) are not confirmed findings.

assumptions: ValidateInputs (line 8) and SparseTensor::Create/TensorShape enforce non-negative dimensions and valid reduction axes such that group_by_dims entries are within [0, rank) of shape_vec.
SparseTensor::Create and SparseTensorReduceHelper guarantee that coordinates returned by sp.group() respect the tensor shape, so coords[i] is bounded by the corresponding shape dimension.
allocate_output/allocate_temp failure paths are fully handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK and terminate Compute before the write loop.
limitations: The write-index guard at lines 71-76 was confirmed as the protecting check; without it, out_flat(idx) at line 77 would be an attacker-controlled OOB write, but that path is unreachable in the shown code.
A possible OOB read of shape_vec at line 41 via group_by_dims[d+1] cannot be confirmed because the bounds are enforced only in the unseen ValidateInputs/SparseTensorReduceHelper code.

int64 multiplication at lines 41 and 53 could theoretically wrap, but any out-of-range result is rejected by the index guard before the write, and products are bounded by the output element count when the allocation succeeds; the residual risk is in-bounds data corruption, not memory safety or an injection/access-control failure.
An attacker-chosen reduced_shape could cause large allocations; any allocation failure is handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK, so this remains a DoS-only robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
VLOG output (lines 78-80) contains only numeric values and a compile-time op name, so no log-injection path exists.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel validates only that indices are non-negative and never bounds-checks them against the input dimension size selected by params.axis. An attacker-controlled positions tensor containing an index >= input->dims->data[params.axis] (e.g., 100000 against an axis of size 10) passes the only guard at line 8 and reaches optimized_ops::Gather at lines 18-21, which reads GetTensorData<InputT>(input) past the end of the input buffer: a confirmed out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: positions is attacker-controlled: its contents (indexes) and size (num_indices = positions->bytes / sizeof(PositionsT), line 6) flow from model/tensor input with no magnitude constraint. The only validation, `if (indexes[i] < 0)` at line 8 plus TF_LITE_ENSURE at line 13, excludes only negative values and admits every index >= 0, including values >= input->dims->data[params.axis]. Concrete witness: an input with 10 elements on the gather axis and a positions value of 100000 passes the guard and reaches this call, so optimized_ops::Gather reads GetTensorData<InputT>(input) at offset 100000, past the 10-element allocation: an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by the guard checking sign but not magnitude.

assumptions: PositionsT is a signed integer type (int32_t/int64_t) and positions->bytes equals the underlying allocation size, so the scan loop reads index 0..num_indices-1 in-bounds and the non-negativity check is effective for negatives.
optimized_ops::Gather uses each index to read along input's axis given by params.axis with its documented gather semantics, i.e., the index selects a slice at offset index * inner_size.
params.axis, params.batch_dims, and the tensor shapes are framework-validated model-graph data, so the dimension/axis values themselves are not treated as attacker-controlled here.
limitations: The actual pointer arithmetic and indexed load execute inside the unseen optimized_ops::Gather; the shown code is the gatekeeper whose sole security check (non-negativity) is insufficient, so the confirmed defect is the missing upper-bound guard at the call site rather than a memory statement visible in this snippet.

Any write-side corruption would require the unseen Gather implementation to store based on index magnitude; the confirmed impact here is an out-of-bounds read (crash or information disclosure), and negative-index out-of-bounds is prevented by the existing check.

No integer overflow, null dereference, injection, weak-crypto, or authz issues were confirmed in the shown code; num_indices is floored from a framework-maintained size and GetTensorData results are framework-provided.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled ISO BMFF input reaches gf_isom_parse_movie_boxes_internal and can crash it: in the default non-debug MOOV branch, the expression trak->Media->information->sampleTable->sampleGroups at line 100 dereferences file-decoded pointers with no NULL checks. A crafted moov containing a trak that omits the mdia (or mdia/minf without the stbl) subtree leaves the member chain NULL, producing a NULL-pointer dereference and denial of service.

evidence.reason: trak is taken from mov->moov->trackList, populated from the attacker-controlled file by gf_isom_parse_root_box (line 30). No conditional constrains trak->Media, Media->information, or information->sampleTable before this dereference: the loop guard at line 98 (k < gf_list_count) bounds only the list index, and the mvhd check at line 76 constrains only the moov child, not trak internals. A trak whose mdia (or minf/stbl) subtree is absent leaves the decoded pointers NULL (box structs are zero-initialized), so the failing witness 'trak without mdia' passes every shown guard and triggers the NULL dereference at line 100, crashing the process (DoS, CWE-476).

assumptions: gf_isom_parse_root_box (line 30) is a lenient parser: it accepts a moov whose trak children omit mdia (or mdia/minf omit stbl), registers the trak in trackList, and leaves the corresponding member pointers NULL.
GF_Box structures and decoded member pointers are zero-initialized when boxes are created, so an absent child box yields NULL rather than an indeterminate pointer.
Line numbers are 1-based relative to the code listing as provided.
limitations: mov->NextMoofNumber = mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number+1 (line 365) is a second NULL-deref of file-decoded state, but the branch requires mov->openMode==GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS, a caller-chosen mode rather than attacker input; kept as a lower-confidence concern without a CWE.

u64 arithmetic on attacker-controlled a->size (totSize accumulation lines 74/125/135/189/230/307/432/437; main_sidx_end_pos at line 286) can in principle wrap, but no memory operation in the shown code consumes those wrapped values, so there is no confirmed sink.
Non-termination of the while loop at line 23 for a zero-advance box depends on the unseen advancement logic in gf_isom_parse_root_box and is not confirmable from the shown code.
The root_ssix cleanup deletes mov->seg_ssix instead of mov->root_ssix (lines 380-382); a logic defect with no attacker-reachable sink in the shown code.
Line 27 passes u64 mov->current_top_box_start to a %d format (varargs type mismatch); the format string is a compile-time literal, so this is not an injection, only a debug-log value-width concern.
The subtraction at lines 14-18 can underflow only when mov->bytes_removed exceeds current_top_box_start; bytes_removed is set by application/edit operations, not by the input file.

verdict.summary: All size-dependent operations are gated by exact shape guards: rank >= 2 (lines 8-11), equal ranks (lines 12-16), square input matrices (lines 17-21), matching RHS rows (lines 22-27), and a non-empty guard (line 38). These bound every later index and allocation (n x n input blocks, n x nrhs RHS blocks, batch_size-wide pivot/pointer arrays), so no attacker-controlled length or index reaches a memory operation out of bounds. Residual concerns (pre-guard dim_size reads for rank < 2, int64->int narrowing for batch_size > 2^31, size_t overflow beyond ~2^61 elements) are not attacker-reachable in deployment and do not meet the confirmed-finding bar.

assumptions: TensorFlow threat model: op inputs (input/rhs tensors) and their shapes are attacker-controlled.
OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC / OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC abort the kernel, so values flowing past a failing guard never reach later sinks.
Upstream shape inference for this op enforces rank >= 2 on both operands before ComputeAsync runs, so the pre-guard dim_size reads at lines 5-6 cannot see rank < 2 in deployed execution.
limitations: Lines 5-6 read dim_size(ndims - 1) before the rank guard at line 8: a hypothetical rank-0/rank-1 input would be an out-of-bounds read of TensorShape::dims_, but the value is discarded when the guard fires, it does not compound with attacker-controlled volume, and the op's shape function prevents such tensors from reaching the kernel.

int64 -> int narrowing of n/nrhs/batch_size into cuBLAS int arguments and the int batch loop counters at lines 98/112/164/184 require a single tensor with more than 2^31 batch elements (>= 8-16 GiB plus full copies) and depend on signed-overflow UB; no deterministic product-reachable failing witness exists.

size_t byte-size computations (NumElements()*sizeof(Scalar) at lines 69/140/203 and sizeof(Scalar*)*batch_size at lines 88/151/154) could only overflow beyond ~2^61 elements, which is unreachable given required host/device allocations.
The historical non-square-input OOB issue in this op family is closed in the shown code by the squareness check at lines 17-21 and the RHS row check at lines 22-27.

verdict.summary: No confirmation of an in-scope vulnerability. Every allocation and tensor-view shape in the shown code is fully constrained by exact-equality OP_REQUIRES guards (lines 31-61) before allocation (lines 64-110). The only validation gap is the complete absence of size checks for wci/wcf/wco (lines 14-21, consumed at lines 118-119); however, the actual indexing of those vectors occurs inside the unshown functor LSTMBlockCellFprop (lines 114-123), so the dangerous operation is not present in the shown code and the concern is out of scope by the stated reachability rule.

assumptions: Tensor shapes and values of the eight op inputs (x, cs_prev, h_prev, w, wci, wcf, wco, b) are attacker-controllable; dtype is fixed by template parameter T.
OP_REQUIRES_OK on ctx->input (lines 3-24) guarantees non-null tensors; failures abort Compute before any dereference.
functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop (lines 114-123) performs the actual tensor indexing; its body is not shown, so its memory operations cannot be verified here.
dim_size() values are non-negative int64_t; behavior of dim_size(d) for d >= rank is a property of the unseen TensorShape implementation.
limitations: wci, wcf, wco tensor sizes are never validated (unlike w at lines 49-56 and b at lines 58-61). If use_peephole_ is true and any of these vectors has fewer than cell_size elements, the unshown LSTMBlockCellFprop functor could read out of bounds (OOB read, CWE-125). This mirrors the known TensorFlow LSTMBlockCell missing-validation issue, but the failing memory operation is absent from the shown code (pure pass-through of tensor views at lines 117-119), so it fails the reachability requirement and carries no CWE here.

No rank validation exists for any input: calling dim_size(1) (lines 27, 28, 35, 44, 45, 49, 53) on a rank-0/rank-1 tensor depends on unseen TensorShape semantics and could abort the process; the crash behavior is in framework internals, not the shown code.

int64_t overflow of cell_size * 4 (lines 53, 58, 109) or input_size + cell_size (lines 49, 103) would require dimensions near 2^61 elements, unreachable for real tensor allocations, and no in-scope sink consumes the overflowed value.

forward_input_or_allocate_output with {"h_prev"}->"i" and {"cs_prev"}->"o" (lines 65-67, 80-82) can alias inputs with outputs; any resulting corruption would occur inside the unshown functor and is not confirmable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in IsConstantFoldable's oversized-output guard (lines 27-29): num_elements() * DataTypeSize(...) is evaluated in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, so a fully-defined attacker-controlled shape such as {2^31, 2^31} with an 8-byte dtype (2^62 elements * 8 bytes = 2^65 mod 2^64 == 0) bypasses the max_constant_size_in_bytes cap, admitting oversized nodes to constant folding and enabling memory-exhaustion DoS.

evidence.reason: The multiplication at line 28 is the security decision that caps the size of constant-folded outputs. num_elements() (int64_t, attacker-influenced via shape dims in shape_map from the graph's TensorShapeProto) is multiplied by DataTypeSize(...) (size_t) as unsigned 64-bit arithmetic mod 2^64. The guard IsFullyDefined() (line 27) only excludes unknown dims and imposes no magnitude bound, so the cap comparison at lines 28-29 is the sole protection. A concrete witness, dims {2^31,2^31} with DT_INT64, yields num_elements()=2^62 and product 2^62*8=2^65≡0 (mod 2^64); 0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes is false, so the guard admits a 2^65-byte output and the function returns true at line 69, allowing the oversized node to be constant-folded and exhausting memory (CWE-190).

assumptions: int64_t and size_t are 64-bit (LP64/LLP64), so the mixed-type multiplication is performed as unsigned 64-bit arithmetic modulo 2^64.
shape_map is populated by shape inference from the attacker-supplied GraphDef, making the shape dims (and thus num_elements()) attacker-influenced.
DataTypeSize(output_type) is a small per-dtype byte count (e.g., 8 for DT_INT64/DT_DOUBLE) and does not constrain the product.
limitations: n->output_type(i) could assert/CHECK if a shape_map entry contained more shapes than the node has outputs, but shape inference emits exactly one shape per output, so no reachable mismatch witness exists in the shown code; no CWE attached.
num_elements() itself (a callee outside the shown code) can also wrap for even larger dims; the shown defect is its unguarded use in the multiplied cap check.
The VLOG sink (lines 65-66) writes n->DebugString(), which is inherently multi-line and debug-gated, so no log-injection finding is confirmed.

The final oversized allocation is performed by the unseen folding pass; the confirmed defect is the removal of the cap protection inside this function, with the OOM impact following standard folding behavior.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer releases the just-decoded global-quantizer node twice (gf_node_unregister(node, NULL) at lines 32-33) without ever registering it for the two new owners (scenegraph->global_qp at line 29 and the command field inf->new_node at line 37). For a freshly created QuantizationParameter node, which the shown code itself identifies as having num_instances == 0 (lines 17-19), the first unregister frees the node and the second operates on freed memory, storing the dangling pointer into the command field - a use-after-free/double-release reachable from a crafted BIFS/MP4 stream.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled bitstream (bs, line 1) selects the GLOBAL_QUANTIZER command and a freshly parsed node with num_instances == 0 (the code's own convention at lines 17/19). The right-tag path then stores node into scenegraph->global_qp (line 29) and later into inf->new_node (line 37) without any gf_node_register and without any count guard; the first unregister at line 32 releases the 0-count object (free path, per the normalization demonstrated at lines 19-21), and the second unregister at line 33 operates on the freed node (use-after-free / double release). After line 33 the pointer stored at line 29 and line 37 is dangling.

assumptions: gf_node_unregister releases one reference and destroys the node when its instance count reaches the free threshold, consistent with the fragment's own convention that a fresh node (num_instances == 0) must be normalized to 1 before a single unregister destroys it (lines 19-21).
gf_bifs_dec_node returns newly created nodes with num_instances == 0 and USE nodes with a positive count, matching the code comment at lines 17-18.
The BIFS command dispatcher (not shown) routes a GLOBAL_QUANTIZER command to this function; the shown function is the parse path that contains the dangerous operation.
limitations: Unchecked return values of gf_sg_command_new/gf_sg_command_field_new (lines 35-36) and gf_list_add (line 40) could cause a NULL deref if an internal allocation fails; this is allocation-failure-only with no attacker-sized allocation in the shown code, so it is not a finding.

Whether the second unregister at line 33 manifests as a double-free rather than a use-after-free depends on whether the freed node memory is reused between lines 32 and 33; both are consequences of the same double release.

The USE-node variant (num_instances >= 1) is a slower-triggering refcount underflow (premature free at scene teardown) rather than an immediate UAF; the fresh-node witness is the deterministic trigger.
No injection, weak-crypto, or file/access-control sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor reads context->input(2) (shape_and_slices) at restore_index with no bounds check at all, unlike input(1) which is guarded at line 18; when shape_and_slices has fewer than restore_index+1 elements the indexed read at line 58 is out of bounds (CWE-125). Independently, the line 18 guard (size > restore_index) admits negative restore_index values, enabling a second out-of-bounds read of tensor_name_t at line 23.

evidence.reason: context->input(2) is an attacker-controlled op input (both contents and element count), and restore_index is a caller-supplied linear index. The only index guard in the function, line 18 (`size > restore_index`), validates input(1) (tensor_name_t) and imposes no constraint on input(2). Concrete witness: restore_slice=true, restore_index=0, tensor_name_t.NumElements()==1 (passes `1 > 0` at line 18), shape_and_slices has 0 elements — then flat<tstring>()(0) reads past the end of the empty tensor (sink line 58), and the resulting garbage tstring is used at lines 59/61. Out-of-bounds read, CWE-125.

restore_index is a caller-supplied int used as a linear index into tensor_name_t. The protecting guard at line 18 (`size > restore_index`, int64 size promoted from int) excludes only indices >= size and admits every negative index. Concrete witness: restore_index=-1 with size=0 — `0 > -1` passes the guard, then flat<tstring>()(-1) at line 23 dereferences before the tensor buffer. Out-of-bounds read, CWE-125.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based within the provided snippet.
Op registration guarantees context->input(2) exists when restore_slice is true.
Tensor flat accessors perform raw linear pointer indexing without bounds checks (standard release-build TensorFlow behavior).
limitations: The negative-index trigger at line 23 requires a caller to pass restore_index < 0; in the canonical TensorFlow caller (RestoreV2 loop) the index is a non-negative loop counter, so the attacker-reachable path for an out-of-bounds index is primarily the unvalidated input(2) length (Candidate A).

Bounds validation and parsing inside checkpoint::ParseShapeAndSlice, TensorSliceReader::CopySliceData, HasTensor, and the file open are outside the shown code; slice-based write overflows or spec-parser memory errors are not confirmable here.

A crafted checkpoint can declare a huge saved_shape making allocate_output (line 76) attempt a very large allocation; this is a single-allocation DoS concern with no reachable compounding loop in the shown code.
tensor_name/file_pattern embedded into errors::* status strings (lines 46-51, 66-70) reach no log sink shown in the code; log/status injection is not confirmed.
Uses of restore_index against framework vectors (expected_output_dtype at line 49, allocate_output at line 76) depend on unseen OpKernelContext validation.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled tensor dimensions are narrowed from int64 to int32 at lines 9-12 with only a non-negativity guard (line 18), which admits positive wraparound values from shapes with >= 2^32 elements. The truncated values size the output allocation (line 23), but the Eigen contraction (lines 62-63) writes the real-size result (e.g., 2^32+1 x 1) into the undersized buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence.reason: dim_size() returns int64 attacker-controlled tensor dimensions, implicitly narrowed to int32 without a magnitude check. The only later guard (line 18, 'm >= 0 && n >= 0 && k >= 0') admits positive wraparound values: a shape {2^32+1, 1} truncates to m=1 and passes every check, while the real dimension remains 2^32+1. This tainted, truncated value sizes the output allocation at line 23.

With the witness shapes a={2^32+1,1}, b={1,1}, output is allocated as {1,1} (4 bytes) at line 23 from the truncated m=1, but out's data buffer is written by a contraction whose result has the real dimensions (2^32+1 x 1 ~17 GiB), producing an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) caused by the unguarded int64-to-int32 truncation (CWE-681) at lines 9-12.

assumptions: TensorShape::dim_size returns int64, so the assignments at lines 9-12 are implicit narrowing conversions to int32 on this platform.
Input tensor shapes originate from attacker-controlled graph/model data as is standard for TensorFlow op inputs.
TL/TR scalar types are float/bfloat16, matching the SparseMatMul op contract.
limitations: The precise write behavior of the Eigen contraction expression (whether it writes its full result size or clamps to the destination dimensions) is not literal code in the shown snippet; if the runtime clamps to the lhs size, the failure degrades to an incorrect/truncated result. This drives confidence to 0.55.
The sparse path passes the same undersized out to DoMatMul (lines 106-109, 111-114), whose write loop is delegated to unseen code, so that sub-path is not used as independent evidence.

Exploitability requires an attacker-controlled tensor with at least 2^32 elements (~16 GiB for float32), and TF's k==k2 and sign guards only fail to protect values >= 2^32; with typical sizes the code is dimensionally correct in all four transpose/sparse combinations.

Potential one-shot allocation-failure/termination from the raw new Tensor calls (lines 47, 53, 90-92) with huge attacker shapes is a robustness/DoS concern, not a confirmed finding: failures at line 23 are handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK and no attacker-controlled loop amplifies volume.
No NULL dereference is reachable: allocate_output failure is handled via OP_REQUIRES_OK before output is used at lines 34 and 38.

verdict.summary: handle_PORT parses the attacker-controlled PORT argument with sscanf without checking the return value. If fewer than six integer fields match, the uninitialized locals a-f are read in snprintf (line 15) and in data_port computation (line 25), causing undefined behavior and potential stack-data disclosure into server logs and control state.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(addr, sizeof(addr), "%d.%d.%d.%d", a, b, c, d);
evidence.reason: The attacker-supplied PORT string 'str' is matched at line 14 with sscanf("%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d", ...) and its return value is discarded. A witness such as an empty argument or '1,2,3' assigns fewer than four fields, leaving a-d uninitialized; this snprintf then reads those indeterminate ints (and copies them into 'addr', which is later logged via ERR/DBG and stored into ctrl->data_address), i.e. CWE-457 with no guard between the parse and this sink.

Same root cause: when sscanf matches fewer than six fields at line 14, e and f remain uninitialized and are read here and stored into control state used for the data connection; the inet_aton branch at lines 18-22 does not guard this path (addr validation does not cover e/f or the port arithmetic).

assumptions: str is a NUL-terminated, network-derived command argument provided by the caller.
sizeof(ctrl->data_address) is a compile-time bound sufficient for strlcpy truncation.
INET_ADDRSTRLEN is the standard 16, making the snprintf write bounded.
limitations: FTP bounce / connecting to an attacker-chosen IP and port (lines 24-25): the actual connect happens outside the shown code, so the dangerous operation is absent from this snippet; out of scope.
Signed overflow in e * 256 + f for e >= 8388608 is UB but grants no extra capability because any 16-bit port is already reachable with e,f in 0..255.
Potential stack-bytes disclosure via ERR/DBG depends on the server's logging configuration; treated as part of the CWE-457 impact, not a separate finding.
inet_aton accepting abbreviated/octal forms is not exploitable here because addr is always rebuilt as canonical decimal from parsed ints.

verdict.summary: adts_decode_extradata trusts caller-supplied extradata (buf,size) without bounding the remaining bit count. Primary finding: with chan_config==0 (line 37), lines 38-42 copy an attacker-sized PCE through ff_copy_pce_data into the fixed 40-byte pce_data buffer, and put_bits/flush_put_bits write past the end when the PCE emits more than MAX_PCE_SIZE (320) bits, a heap OOB write with attacker-controlled bytes (CWE-787). Secondary finding: lines 25/29/33 call get_bits without any get_bits_left check after skip_bits_long (line 12), so the 32-bit bitstream cache fetch can read past buf when the config parse consumes all available bits, an OOB read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Taint: attacker-controlled buf/size (lines 8-9) feed gb, and the PCE element/comment count fields inside ff_copy_pce_data come from buf. Line 37 admits chan_config==0 with no check on the remaining bit count or on the number of bits to be emitted; line 38 sets only a nominal MAX_PCE_SIZE (320-bit) capacity for adts->pce_data, which is MAX_PCE_SIZE/8 = 40 bytes, and put_bits/flush_put_bits (lines 40-42) enforce no runtime bound in release builds. A witness is a >=50-byte extradata with chan_config==0 and comment_bytes>=31 (e.g., 40) so ff_copy_pce_data emits >320 bits and lines 40-42 write past pce_data[39] into adjacent heap memory; comment_bytes=255 with ~270 bytes of input yields ~287 bytes written. Sink line 41 alongside 40 and 42; heap OOB write, CWE-787.

Taint: off from line 9 sets gb.index via skip_bits_long at line 12; the only preceding guard is off<0 (lines 10-11), which admits off==size*8. get_bits fetches a 32-bit cache word from gb->buffer + (index>>3); with a 2-byte buffer (size==2) and off==13, the fetch at buf+1 reads 2 bytes past the buffer, and with off==16 it starts fully past the end. This read executes unconditionally at lines 25/29/33 before either branch outcome is known, with no get_bits_left(&gb) check present. Heap OOB read, CWE-125; identically repeated at lines 29 and 33.

assumptions: buf/size are AudioSpecificConfig extradata extracted by an outer demuxer from attacker-influenced file/network data; size is the caller-supplied byte length and is not further bounded in this function.

ADTSContext::pce_data is declared MAX_PCE_SIZE/8 = 40 bytes, and the PutBitContext writer (put_bits/flush_put_bits) performs no runtime bounds enforcement in release builds (av_assert2 is compiled out).
Default FFmpeg builds use the unchecked bitreader, so get_bits performs the 32-bit cache fetch even when fewer (or zero) valid bits remain beyond the current index.
limitations: The 1-4 byte overread at lines 25/29/33 would be masked in callers that guarantee at least AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE (64) zero bytes after extradata; the shown code does not establish that invariant, and the long PCE read/write path at line 41 exceeds any such padding.
size*8 at line 8 could overflow int only for size > 2^28, outside realistic container-extradata limits, so that integer-overflow path is not treated as a finding.
m4ac.object_type==0 would make adts->objecttype==-1 and fail the unsigned comparison at line 17 benignly (error return); it is not attacker-relevant on the success path.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in handle_PORT: attacker-controlled PORT arguments are parsed by sscanf (line 14) into unconstrained ints and written by sprintf into the 16-byte addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN] (line 15) before the inet_aton validation (line 18) runs, so a value such as "-2147483648,-2147483648,-2147483648,-2147483648,1,1" writes 48 bytes and overruns the buffer by 32 bytes.

evidence.reason: Tainted network input str is parsed at line 14 by sscanf into ints a-d with no range or return-value check, then formatted here into addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN] (16 bytes). Any %d can emit up to 11 characters (e.g., -2147483648), so the witness PORT argument "-2147483648,-2147483648,-2147483648,-2147483648,1,1" makes sprintf write 47 characters plus NUL (48 bytes), overflowing the 16-byte buffer by 32 bytes. The only nearby guard, inet_aton() at line 18, executes after this write and constrains only the later strlcpy at line 24; no check limits a-d to 0-255 before the sink, so the out-of-bounds stack write is reachable on the unconditional path.

assumptions: str is a NUL-terminated copy of the attacker-supplied FTP PORT command argument.
INET_ADDRSTRLEN is 16 (POSIX), so addr is a 16-byte buffer.
ctrl is initialized by the server before handle_PORT runs; its fields (data_address, sd) are trusted internal state.
limitations: sscanf's return value is unchecked: an input with fewer than 6 fields (e.g., "1,2") leaves some of a-f uninitialized, which are then read at lines 15 and 25 (CWE-457 class). The trigger is reachable but no concrete attacker-visible security impact is demonstrated, so it is not listed as a finding.
e * 256 + f (line 25) can overflow int or produce an out-of-range/negative data_port for large e/f; it has no memory-safety impact in the shown code.
The out-of-bounds read of addr inside inet_aton/ERR (lines 18-19) after the overflow is a consequence of the same write, not a separate finding.
Final exploitability (stack canaries, ASLR, etc.) depends on mitigations outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: The BIFS decoder reads an attacker-controlled field count (up to 0x7FFFFFFF) from the bitstream and passes it without validation into an MF allocation whose size is derived from that count; on 32-bit size arithmetic the element-count product wraps, producing an undersized buffer that the subsequent indexed access writes past, enabling heap corruption from a crafted bitstream.

evidence.reason: nbFields originates at line 20 from the attacker-controlled gf_bs_read_int(bs, NbBits) and reaches this allocation unvalidated; the only constraint is NbBits's 5-bit width, which still admits nbFields = 0x40000000. With a 4-byte element type, 4 * 0x40000000 wraps to 0 in 32-bit arithmetic, yielding an undersized allocation; the loop at line 32 with i < nbFields and the indexed access at line 33 then write past the allocated storage (e.g., at i >= 1). No check in the shown code bounds nbFields or nbFields * element_size before this use.

assumptions: bs is an attacker-controlled BIFS bitstream (file/network input).

gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc computes the MF storage size from nbFields and the field element size with 32-bit arithmetic, and gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item resolves the i-th element as a write destination inside that storage (the standard contiguous MF-array behavior).
field->fieldType selects an MF element type whose size (e.g., 4 bytes) makes the 31-bit count able to wrap the size product.
limitations: If a patched/64-bit callee validates nbFields * element_size or uses 64-bit arithmetic before allocation, the same trigger would degrade to an allocation failure / denial-of-service rather than an out-of-bounds write; that callee code is not shown here.

The MFNODE branch (lines 40-80) admits up to 0x7FFFFFFF node decode/registration iterations from a crafted stream; this attacker-scalable CPU/memory consumption is a separate DoS-class concern and is not counted as a second CWE.
No injection, crypto, authentication, or filesystem sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: QuantizeAndDequantize gradient Compute performs an out-of-bounds read: with axis_ != -1 it calls input_min_tensor.dim_size(0)/input_max_tensor.dim_size(0) on min/max tensors that were only validated to have dims()==0 or dims()==1. A rank-0 (scalar) min/max tensor passes the guard at lines 20-21/26-27 and then indexes dimension 0 of a 0-dim TensorShape at lines 33/37, reading past the dim array (CWE-125) and leaking the garbage value into the InvalidArgument error message.

evidence.reason: input_min_tensor is ctx->input(2) (line 19), attacker-controlled. The only shape guard (lines 20-21) admits dims()==0 || dims()==1, so a rank-0 tensor passes. With axis_ != -1 (line 31, axis_=0 passes lines 7-13 for any rank>=1 input), the condition at line 33 evaluates dim_size(0) on a shape with dims()==0. TensorShape::dim_size requires 0 <= d < dims(); index 0 on an empty dim array is an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read (CWE-125), and its value is re-read into the InvalidArgument message at line 35.

Same failure as line 33 for input_max_tensor (ctx->input(3), line 25): the guard at lines 26-27 admits rank-0, and with axis_ != -1 the condition evaluates dim_size(0) on a 0-dim shape, performing the same out-of-bounds read, re-read into the error message at line 39.

assumptions: axis_ is the op attribute recorded from the graph node; under TensorFlow's threat model (untrusted model/graph input), attributes and input tensors are both attacker-controlled.
OP_REQUIRES fully evaluates its condition expression before aborting, so the dim_size(0) calls at lines 33/37 (and 35/39) always execute.
TensorShape::dim_size(d) is only valid for 0 <= d < dims(); calling it with d=0 on a shape with dims()==0 reads out of bounds/uninitialized storage.
limitations: When axis_ == 0, flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1) (lines 67/68/70) receives -1; whether Eigen converts this into an out-of-bounds access cannot be confirmed from the shown code because the reshape internals are unseen.

depth is narrowed from int64 to int at line 18; truncation for dim sizes > INT_MAX could distort the equality checks, but depth is not used as a memory bound in the shown code, so no concrete impact is confirmed.
Allocation sizes driven by attacker-controlled shapes (lines 6, 45, 49) are allocator-bounded and are at most a DoS concern, not a confirmed vulnerability here.

If the garbage value read at line 33/37 happened to equal depth by chance, execution would continue into the per-channel functor with rank-0 min/max tensors; that path's behavior depends on unseen functor code and is unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer unconditionally overwrites node->sgprivate->num_instances with 2 after the node was decoded from the attacker-controlled bitstream. If the SFWorldNode field resolves to an already-instantiated node reference that holds pre-existing references, the true reference count is silently reduced; the two unregisters that later occur (global-QP reset at line 11 and the pending command-field cleanup of inf->new_node at line 31) reach zero and free the node while codec->ActiveQP, codec->scenegraph->global_qp, and outstanding holders still reference it, producing a use-after-free/double-free.

evidence.reason: Taint: the node is produced at line 6 by gf_bifs_dec_node(codec, bs, NDT_SFWorldNode) from the attacker-controlled bitstream, so the attacker selects both the node object and its pre-existing reference count (a BIFS node-reference encoding yields an already-registered node with num_instances >= 2). Sink: line 27 forcibly sets num_instances to 2 with no guard, discarding every pre-existing reference and assuming only the global pointer (line 24) and the pending command field (line 31) will ever unregister it. Failure: the global-QP reset at line 11 and the command-field cleanup unregister exactly twice, driving the forced count to 0 and freeing the node while codec->ActiveQP (line 22), codec->scenegraph->global_qp (line 24), and other references remain; any later use or unregister of the freed node is a use-after-free/double-free. The tag check at line 16 constrains only the node type, not its reference count, so no boundary value is excluded and no protecting check exists.

assumptions: gf_bifs_dec_node at line 6 can return a reference to an already-instantiated node whose sgprivate->num_instances already counts its existing holders.
Each retention point (the global pointer at line 24, the command field at line 31) is later balanced by exactly one gf_node_unregister call, and the count reaching 0 frees the node.
codec, codec->scenegraph, and codec->current_graph are non-NULL framework-provided state.
limitations: The NULL dereference of com (line 29) and inf (line 30) at line 31 requires an unchecked allocation failure, whose size is not attacker-controlled here; no CWE attached.
A pure memory-leak/refcount-inflation scenario for always-fresh nodes cannot be confirmed without the unseen command-application code; no CWE attached.
The precise refcount convention of the unseen framework helpers (node creation count and unregister-on-free semantics) is not visible in the shown code, which keeps confidence below 0.7.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The historically dangerous double-free/UAF path on parse failure is neutralized by the Unref() followed by release() at lines 15-16 for every failing input, and ownership is transferred once at line 25. The only remaining dangerous operations (proto parsing in InitFromSerialized and resource creation in CreateResource) are delegated to unseen code, and the shown code is a pure pass-through for those inputs.

assumptions: new BoostedTreesEnsembleResource() starts with refcount 1 and Unref() deletes the object at refcount 0 (standard TF ResourceBase semantics), which makes the L15 Unref + L16 release failure path perform exactly one destruction.

CreateResource/ResourceMgr::Create takes ownership of the released pointer and unrefs/destroys it on failure, including ALREADY_EXISTS, so the L25 release neither leaks nor double-frees within the shown control flow.

The kernel's op registration type-constrains the stamp_token (int64) and tree_ensemble_serialized (string) inputs, so scalar<int64>()() and scalar<tstring>()() cannot be driven to a dtype/shape CHECK failure by an attacker through the public op contract.
limitations: Serialized-proto parsing at lines 13-14 is delegated to BoostedTreesEnsembleResource::InitFromSerialized (unseen code); any parser memory-safety or complexity bugs there are out of scope for this snippet, though the shown code applies no length or format validation before the call.
Resource container/name handling at line 25 (HandleFromInput -> CreateResource) is delegated to unseen resource-manager code; no validation of the handle is performed in the shown code.

Missing explicit dtype/shape validation before the scalar reads at lines 5 and 14 would be a CHECK-fail process-abort only if the framework's type-constraint invariant is violated; not confirmed attacker-reachable here.
No loops, explicit memory operations over input-derived sizes, injection sinks, crypto, file, or log operations exist in the shown code; ReDoS/weak-crypto/injection classes were not applicable.

verdict.summary: elo_probe contains no attacker-controlled size, index, format string, or injection sink. All allocations use compile-time constant sizes with NULL checks, all log calls use constant format strings, USB refcounting is balanced between usb_get_dev (line 16) and usb_put_dev (line 39), and the delayed work is only queued on the success path, so kfree(priv) on the error path cannot race a scheduled callback. The line-15 dereference of hdev->dev.parent is guarded by the hid_is_usb check at line 7, and hid_parse/hid_hw_start failures are checked before cleanup.

assumptions: hdev and id are supplied by the HID core as trusted framework-internal probe arguments.
hid_is_usb(hdev) at line 7 establishes the USB invariant that hdev->dev.parent is a valid usb_interface, making to_usb_interface(...) at line 15 safe.
hid_parse and hid_hw_start are trusted framework APIs whose return codes are honored (error paths verified).
limitations: Parsing of potentially malicious HID report descriptors occurs inside hid_parse and the unseen elo_work callback; those sinks are outside the shown code, so their safety is out of scope here.
A physical USB attacker who presents a malicious Elo device controls data consumed downstream (e.g. by elo_work), but no such data is consumed anywhere in the shown probe function.
Lifetime of priv->usbdev on the success path (lines 32-37) is released by the unseen remove/cleanup path; not verifiable from the shown code.
The hdev->dev.parent dereference at line 15 has no explicit NULL check, but no NULL-producing path is reachable in the shown control flow after the line-7 guard.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in njs_function_frame_save: the argument-relayout loop stores function->args_count pointers starting at pointer-array index njs_function_frame_args_count(active) + function->args_offset (lines 29, 44) with no comparison against the destination capacity of value_count + function->u.lambda->temp (lines 22-24). A function whose args_offset + args_count exceeds that capacity (attacker-controlled via the executed/constructed function signature) writes past the frame arrays at line 51, corrupting adjacent memory (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenceable function-signature fields function->args_count and function->args_offset (from active->function, line 20) reach this pointer write unchecked: local is based at new + njs_function_frame_args_count(active) + function->args_offset (lines 29, 44), the loop bound at line 46 admits all args_count >= 0, and the destination pointer array holds only value_count + function->u.lambda->temp entries (lines 22-24). No guard compares args_count(active) + args_offset + args_count against value_count + temp, so a witness such as args_count = 2, args_offset = 1 against a frame with value_count = 1, temp = 0 writes indices 3 and 4 of a 1-entry array, an 8-byte-pointer out-of-bounds write on this line (CWE-787).

assumptions: njs_function_frame_value_count(active) and njs_function_frame_values(active, &end) are consistent helpers on the same active frame, so the while loop (lines 36-39) copies exactly value_count entries (end - start == value_count).
The unseen frame allocator sizes the destination pointer and value arrays as value_count + function->u.lambda->temp entries each, matching the layout implied by lines 22-24.
njs_value_t* is a multi-byte pointer, so each *local++ = p++ advances one entry past the last.
limitations: The exact numeric slack between the for-loop write extent (args_count(active) + args_offset + args_count) and the capacity (value_count + temp) may be guaranteed by an unseen allocator in some call paths; the shown code itself contains no such check, which is the confirmed flaw.

Line 28 (value + (function->args_offset - 1)) forms a pointer one slot before the value array when args_offset == 0, but the shown code never dereferences it, so no confirmed finding; only unseen consumers would turn it into a memory fault.

The while-loop safety depends on the helper invariant end - start == value_count; a mismatch (end - start > value_count) would also overflow, but the shown code gives no evidence such a mismatch occurs.
No injection, crypto, or file/access-control sinks exist in this function; the analysis is limited to memory safety.

verdict.summary: The sparse-reduce kernel writes reduced values via out_flat(idx) (line 64), where idx is the unchecked dot product of raw sparse indices coordinates (attacker-controlled input_indices, read verbatim by sp.group() at line 61) with output strides (lines 36-43, 51-54). No shown code verifies that each coordinate lies in [0, shape(dim)) or that 0 <= idx < numel(out_values) before the write, so an out-of-range coordinate (e.g., value 2 in a dimension of size 2, stride 1) produces idx >= numel and performs an out-of-bounds heap write; negative coordinates write before the buffer. The only nearby check, CHECK_EQ(coords.size(), strides.size()) at line 50, validates array sizes, not coordinate values.

evidence.reason: idx is computed at line 53 (idx += coords[i] * strides[i];) from g.group() coordinates that flow unvalidated from the attacker-controlled input_indices tensor (lines 3, 17-19, 61), and from strides built at lines 36-43 from the same shape input. The only guard on this path, CHECK_EQ(coords.size(), strides.size()) at line 50, checks that the coords and strides arrays have equal size but imposes no bound on coordinate values or on the final index relative to the output allocation (reduction.reduced_shape, line 25). A concrete failing witness: shape [2, 3] with reduction axis {1} gives group_by_dims {0}, output_strides {1}; an index row coordinate 2 in dim 0 yields idx = 2 >= numel(out_values) = 2, so out_flat(2) = reduced_val() writes out of bounds on the heap (CWE-787); a negative coordinate yields a write before the buffer start.

assumptions: For valid coordinates (0 <= coords[i] < shape_vec(group_by_dims[i])) idx stays within [0, numel(reduced_shape)) by construction of the stride products, so the OOB write requires at least one out-of-range coordinate.
In the reduce-all case (empty group_by_dims/strides) the lambda returns 0 at line 48 and the single write at line 64 is in-bounds.
limitations: A potential OOB read of shape_vec at line 41 via reduction.group_by_dims[d+1] depends on outputs of the unseen SparseTensorReduceHelper and the unseen ValidateInputs (line 8); not independently confirmable from the shown code.

The int64 multiplication/addition at lines 53 can overflow with extreme coordinates and strides, but its impact converges on the same line-64 misindex, so it is part of the same finding, not a separate CWE.

The signedness edge case at line 39 (output_strides.size() - 2 for size 1) relies on implementation-defined size_t-to-int conversion, and on typical two's-complement platforms the loop is skipped; not reported as a finding.
Whether SparseTensor::Create or the op's external validation rejects out-of-range coordinates lies outside the shown code; the shown path itself contains no such check.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every attacker-influenceable size used by the slice loop is validated before use: line 9 requires input.dims() > axis_ (axis_=dims is the first rejected witness), lines 21/34 require min/max ranges to be 1-D with dim_size(0) == num_slices exactly, and lines 42-51 require scalar ranges on the non-axis path. All loop indices satisfy i < num_slices (line 92) against containers of exactly num_slices elements (output 0 reshape at lines 88-89, per-slice outputs allocated with the validated minmax_shape at lines 74-77, min/max vectors at lines 90-91). The only unverifiable edge is axis_ == 0 passing rank -1 to the unseen flat_inner_outer_dims helper (lines 79-80); no failing witness can be established from the shown code, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based as displayed in the provided snippet.
axis_ and mode_ are op attributes; they are treated as attacker-influenceable graph configuration throughout, as required by the analysis rules.

Tensor::flat_inner_outer_dims(rank) yields the view {product of dims[0..rank], dims[rank+1], product of dims[rank+2..]} matching the pre_dim/num_slices/post_dim split used by the op (this is the standard contract of that helper).
min/max range tensors have the float dtype as implied by flat<float>()/vec<float>(), and the op registration enforces input/output dtypes.
QuantizeSlice and QuantizeTensor write only within the chip/scalar views and scalar outputs passed to them.
ctx->input()/allocate_output() enforce Tensor invariants (allocated buffer length equals NumElements * dtype size).
limitations: When axis_ == 0, line 9 admits the value and line 80 calls flat_inner_outer_dims(axis_ - 1) with rank -1. Whether this yields an in-bounds view (no outer dims, middle = dims[0] = num_slices) or an out-of-bounds read/indexing inside the unseen helper/Eigen chip implementation cannot be decided from the shown code; no concrete failing witness (value + sink) is derivable, so this potential memory-safety issue is unconfirmed.

int64 -> int narrowing of num_slices at line 14 could only change the value for axis dims >= 2^31, and such mismatches are rejected by the int64 equality comparisons at lines 21/34 before any indexed use.

Pre_dim/post_dim int64 multiplication (lines 82-87) could overflow only for shapes whose element-count product already overflows; allocating such an input tensor fails earlier in the framework, and the worst shown-code effect would be a reshape dimension-check failure, not an out-of-bounds access.
Failure modes of the unseen QuantizeSlice/QuantizeTensor callees are out of scope; the shown code passes only validated, in-bounds views and pointers.
No injection (format/system/SQL/log/header), weak-crypto, file/symlink, or authz/authn sinks exist anywhere in the shown code, so no findings are possible in those classes.

verdict.summary: selinux_ptrace_traceme performs a single SELinux authorization check: it computes the parent's subject SID and current's object SID and calls avc_has_perm with SECCLASS_PROCESS / PROCESS__PTRACE. No attacker-controlled input reaches any memory, injection, crypto, or file sink; there are no branches or loops, no arithmetic or casts, and the only security-relevant operation is the enforcement check itself, which is correctly oriented (parent as subject, current as object).

assumptions: parent is a valid task_struct supplied by the kernel ptrace subsystem (LSM ptrace_traceme hook) and is never NULL on this path; the shown code never produces NULL.
task_sid_subj and task_sid_obj return valid SIDs for the given tasks.
avc_has_perm is the intended enforcement point; its policy-decision internals are outside the shown code.
limitations: Enforcement quality ultimately depends on the SELinux policy granting/denying PROCESS__PTRACE; the shown code correctly delegates that decision.
This hook covers PTRACE_TRACEME only; other ptrace checks (e.g., TRACEBK/TRACEPERM, parent-relationship gating) live in other SELinux hooks not shown here.

verdict.summary: A crafted RTCP PSFB/RPSI packet whose 16-bit header length field is 1 (network byte order) underflows rpsi_len at line 24 ((L-2)*4 => -4 converted to pj_size_t), so the line-25 bounds check rpsi_len+12 wraps modulo to 8 and admits an 8-byte buffer; on little-endian hosts the line-18 raw comparison (no pj_ntohs) fails to reject wire length 1. Control then reaches the offset-8 read at line 29 (padlen = *p++) and offset-9 read at line 43, producing a heap out-of-bounds read, and line 45 binds rpsi->rpsi to an ~2^(N-3)-byte length, enabling large out-of-bounds reads in consumers of the returned pj_str.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled wire header length field (bytes 2-3) = 0x0001 passes the line-15 type check, passes the line-18 raw comparison on little-endian hosts (raw 0x0100=256 >= 3), and underflows in line 24: pj_ntohs=1 -> (1-2)*4 = -4 -> rpsi_len = 2^32-4 / 2^64-4. Line 25 then evaluates length < (rpsi_len+12), where rpsi_len+12 wraps modulo to 8, so a caller-supplied length of 8 (an 8-byte datagram matching the header claim) is admitted even though the read at this sink accesses byte offset 8 of an 8-byte buffer (p = hdr + sizeof(*hdr) at line 28) - a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), produced by the unsigned underflow (CWE-190).

With the same underflowed rpsi_len = 2^N-4 (wire length field 1), line 37 passes because rpsi_len*8 wraps to 2^N-32 and is never < 16+padlen, so rpsi_bit_len (line 44) becomes ~2^N-48-padlen and this sink binds rpsi->rpsi to (char*)hdr+10 with slen ~2^(N-3) bytes. For adversarially chosen datagrams of length 9-12 the in-function reads at offsets 8-9 stay in bounds, but this huge pointer/length pair extends far past the actual buffer, so any consumer of pjmedia_rtcp_fb_rpsi.rpsi (e.g., a strncpy/append of the bit string) performs an out-of-bounds read - the same CWE-125 consequence of the line-24 CWE-190 underflow defeating the line-25 guard.

assumptions: pj_size_t is an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit type, so the (L-2)*4 computation underflows and rpsi_len+12 wraps to 8 for wire length L=1.
hdr->rtcp_common.length is a 16-bit network-byte-order field per the RTCP wire format, and pj_ntohs at line 24 converts it; the line-18 comparison reads the raw (unconverted) field.
buf/length are supplied from the RTCP receive path over a network datagram (standard pjsip usage), so an 8-byte PSFB packet with length field 1 is attacker-controllable.
pj_strset only assigns the pointer and length; it performs no copy in the shown code.
Host is little-endian (x86-64/ARM64); on big-endian hosts line 18 rejects wire length 1 (raw 1 < 3) and the in-scope trigger does not fire.
limitations: The large out-of-bounds read/copy that would occur when an unseen caller consumes the oversized rpsi->rpsi (line 45 result) is outside the shown code; the in-function OOB reads at lines 29 and 43 are the confirmed in-scope memory-safety failures.
Wire length L=2 (rpsi_len=0) is neutralized by the line-37 guard, and L>=3 packets are correctly bounded by line 25, so the finding is specific to the L=1 underflow path.
No injection, crypto, file, authz, or loop-structure concerns exist in this function; PJ_PERROR calls use only static format strings.
If an unseen caller guarantees buffer length > 10 for all packets, the in-scope OOB reads disappear and only the oversized pj_str binding (line 45) remains, with impact realized only in the caller.

verdict.summary: LSTMBlockCellOp validates shapes for x/cs_prev/h_prev/w/b but only checks rank 1 for wci/wcf/wco; absent size validation lets attacker-supplied peephole vectors shorter than cell_size reach functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop, which indexes them up to cell_size, causing an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
h_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(), w_tensor->matrix<T>(), wci_tensor->vec<T>(),
        wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>(), b_tensor->vec<T>(),
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled wci/wcf/wco lengths (inputs at lines 15/18/21) are constrained only by the rank-1 checks at lines 129-140, which admit any length m, including m < cell_size; no dim_size(0) == cell_size guard exists (unlike w/b at lines 49-61). With cell_size=4 and wci=(1,), all shown checks pass and wci_tensor->vec<T>() (length 1) reaches the functor (line 173), which indexes the peephole vectors up to index 3 when use_peephole_ is true (attribute passed at line 175), reading 3 elements past the 1-element allocation: out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125).

assumptions: Tensor shapes and contents are attacker-controllable via graph construction/feeding (standard TF input model).
functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop indexes the peephole vectors wci/wcf/wco by cell_size when use_peephole_ is true, per the LSTMBlockCell op contract (the functor body is not shown).
TensorFlow dims are non-negative int64, so the arithmetic in input_size + cell_size and cell_size * 4 only wraps to negative values on overflow, which TensorShape rejects.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds byte access occurs inside functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop, whose body is not part of the shown code; the shown code's flaw is the absent length validation that allows the too-short vector to reach that consumer.

dim_size(1) reads at lines 27-28 precede the rank-2 checks at lines 115-128; reading past the dims array for rank<=1 inputs would require the framework's shape inference to be bypassed, and the impact of the single int64 read is unproven, so this is recorded as a robustness limitation without a CWE.

int64 overflow of input_size + cell_size / cell_size * 4 is not a confirmed finding: it needs dimensions near 2^62 (not reachable for real allocated tensors) and any overflow wraps negative and is rejected by TensorShape and the equality checks.
The wcf rank-1 error message at line 136 incorrectly prints wci_tensor->dims(); cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: crun_command_exec parses the attacker/invoker-controlled LISTEN_FDS environment variable with strtoll and adds it to crun_context.preserve_fds without any range, sign, or error check. Negative or out-of-int-range values (e.g., LISTEN_FDS=2147483647 with --preserve-fds 1, or LISTEN_FDS=3000000000) truncate or wrap the 32-bit fd-count fields that govern which host file descriptors are passed into the container, causing signed-overflow UB and corrupted fd-preservation counts (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: LISTEN_FDS is attacker/invoker-controlled environment data with no constraint in the shown path. strtoll returns an unbounded signed long long (up to LLONG_MAX/MIN, negatives allowed, ERANGE unchecked); it is narrowed into the 32-bit int field listen_fds and accumulated into preserve_fds. Concrete witnesses: LISTEN_FDS=2147483647 with --preserve-fds 1 wraps preserve_fds to INT_MIN (signed overflow) at line 31; LISTEN_FDS=3000000000 truncates to negative at line 30 and makes preserve_fds negative; LISTEN_FDS=-5 yields preserve_fds=-5. The only guard, line 28 (`if (getenv ("LISTEN_FDS"))`), checks presence, not value, so negative and oversized values reach the arithmetic sink unvalidated, corrupting the fd-count fields used to pass host descriptors into the container (CWE-190).

assumptions: argv is a standard C main argument vector with argv[argc] == NULL and argp_parse leaves first_arg in [0, argc].

crun_context.listen_fds and crun_context.preserve_fds are 32-bit int fields (as in crun's libcrun_context_t); if they were 64-bit, the addition at line 31 would still narrow back into an int and overflow on out-of-range sums.
exec_options is the global struct populated by argp_parse from argv.
limitations: The args-copy loop at lines 43-45 runs argc - first_arg iterations and reads argv[first_arg + i + 1] up to index argc (the NULL terminator), duplicating NULL one extra time; this is an off-by-one in counting but memory-safe under the standard argv invariant, and whether xstrdup(NULL) crashes depends on the unseen helper.
process->args_len = argc (line 41) overstates the number of copied process args; downstream consumers of args_len are outside the shown code.

The concrete downstream effect of a negative or overflowed preserve_fds/listen_fds (fd duplication loops, sync messages) lives in libcrun_container_exec_with_options, which is not shown; the overflow/truncation itself occurs in the shown code.

capabilities->effective aliases exec_options.cap while bounding/ambient/permitted are duplicates; a use-after-free would require exec_options to be freed while still referenced, and its lifetime is outside the shown code.
Repeated getenv("LISTEN_FDS") calls (lines 28 and 30) are not a vulnerability in a single-threaded process.

verdict.summary: Unsigned 64-bit wraparound in the two chunk-offset bounds guards (lines 94 and 184) lets a crafted EXR chunk-offset-table value such as 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 (scanline) or 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC (tiled) pass the check; DecodeChunk then builds head + offset and memcpy-reads out of bounds at lines 195 and 106, producing an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: offsets is attacker-controlled (file chunk-offset table), and no bound is placed on the offset value itself. The guard at line 184, `if (offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2 > size)`, is evaluated in unsigned 64-bit; for the witness offset 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 the sum wraps to 0, so `0 > size` is false and the guard admits the entry. data_ptr is then `head + offsets[y_idx]` (line 192), i.e. head - 8, and this 4-byte memcpy reads out of bounds (CWE-125).

Same wraparound flaw in the tiled path: the guard at line 94, `if (offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5 > size)`, wraps to 0 for the witness offset 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC and passes; data_ptr = head + offsets[tile_idx] (line 103) becomes head - 20, and this 16-byte memcpy reads out of bounds (CWE-125). No check constrains the offset value below 2^64 - 20 before this use.

assumptions: tinyexr_uint64 is an unsigned 64-bit integer, so offsets[t] + sizeof(int)*k is computed modulo 2^64.
head/size is a caller-supplied matched pair with exactly size readable bytes, and offsets entries denote byte positions relative to head.

offsets entries originate from the file's chunk-offset table (attacker-controlled); the analysis follows the rubric that a function may be vulnerable by trusting a caller-supplied value even when its producer is unshown.
Analysis assumes the common 64-bit build where size_t is 64-bit; the wrap also yields an OOB read (via different in-range/large values) on 32-bit targets.
limitations: Unchecked calloc at lines 82-83 leaves exr_image->tiles NULL on allocation failure with attacker-controlled num_tiles; the dereference at line 87 is a DoS-only, allocator-dependent NULL-deref candidate, not a confirmed memory-safety finding.
NULL images returned by AllocateImage (lines 87-89, 174-176) are dereferenced inside DecodeTiledPixelData/DecodePixelData, which are not in the shown code (pass-through rule); excluded.

The write at lines 269-270 to exr_header->pixel_types[c] relies on the unseen caller having sized pixel_types/requested_pixel_types to num_channels; no shown check or failure path demonstrates an OOB write.

The total_data_len overflow cap at line 162 applies only on 64-bit builds; the 32-bit wrap case cannot be tied to a memory error in the shown code (writes occur in unseen helpers).
Large attacker-controlled allocations (tile_size_x/y unbounded, up to 256 GiB pixel buffers) are DoS/robustness concerns where volume scales with attacker input, not confirmed vulnerabilities here.
No injection, cryptographic, or authorization/authn sinks exist in this function; the only confirmed issue is the OOB read via offset arithmetic wraparound.

verdict.summary: In the non-`--process` branch of `crun_command_exec`, the args-copy loop bound `i < argc - first_arg` is off by one: its final iteration reads `argv[first_arg + (argc - first_arg)] = argv[argc]`, the mandatory NULL terminator of `argv`, and passes NULL to `xstrdup` (strdup), producing a NULL-pointer dereference/crash. Any `crun exec CONTAINER CMD` invocation without `--process` reaches this (e.g. argc=4, first_arg=2, i=1 reads argv[4]=NULL), deterministically crashing the exec command (DoS, CWE-476). The loop should be bounded by `argc - first_arg - 1`, with `args_len` set to the same value; no such correction or protective check exists in the shown code.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)
        process->args[i] = xstrdup (argv[first_arg + i + 1]);
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled argc/argv flow into the loop bound (line 43) and the index expression (line 44). With `crun exec c1 cmd1`: argc=4, first_arg=2, n=argc-first_arg=2; the guard at line 17 (`crun_assert_n_args(argc - first_arg, ..., -1)`) admits n=2 but does not protect the loop. On the last iteration i=1, the index is first_arg+i+1 = argv[4] = argv[argc], which the C runtime guarantees is NULL, and the shown code passes it to xstrdup (strdup) at line 44, dereferencing NULL (UB/crash). The loop's max write index to `args` (allocated argc+1 at line 42) is n-1 <= argc-1, so the failure is the NULL dereference in the string-duplicating memory operation, not an out-of-bounds array write.

assumptions: C standard guarantees argv[argc] == NULL and that argv contains argc+1 pointer elements.
`crun_assert_n_args(argc - first_arg, ..., -1)` admits n >= 2 (or exactly 2 if max=-1 means exact); the off-by-one read of argv[argc] is confirmed in either interpretation.
`xmalloc0` zero-fills `process->args`, so entries beyond the filled count are NULL.
limitations: `crun_context.listen_fds = strtoll(getenv("LISTEN_FDS"), NULL, 10)` (line 30) and `preserve_fds += listen_fds` (line 31) allow narrowing/signed overflow from an attacker-set environment variable, but the impact is realized only in unseen consumers of `preserve_fds`.

`process->args_len = argc` (line 41) overcounts the real argument count by first_arg+1; its impact (e.g., on JSON marshalling/exec of NULL entries) sits in unseen libcrun/libocispec code, so it is not confirmed as a separate finding.
Container-id handling (`argv[first_arg]`, lines 19/92) and cgroup/exec wiring are delegated to unseen functions; no conclusion is drawn on them.

`offsets` holds per-chunk file offsets parsed from the input EXR (attacker-controlled), with at least one element, and `head` is a readable buffer of exactly `size` bytes.

No injection (printf/exec/query), crypto, or file/path sinks exist in the shown code.

TensorShape::num_elements() and the loop's product computation both multiply int64 dims in the same order, so an intermediate overflow can be consistent on both sides of the equality checks.

Attacker-controlled output_rank/nnz can drive large single-shot allocate_output calls, but allocation failure is handled (OP_REQUIRES_OK) and is not an attacker-volume-scaled loop, so only potential DoS, not a confirmed finding.
