limitations: An out-of-bounds read (e.g., at lines 15 or 28) would require the caller to hand this function a corrupted state — L->base outside [stack, top], a broken cframe chain, or forged frame links — i.e., a violation of the VM invariants that the shown code itself relies on; no concrete attacker-controlled value or path to such a state is present in the shown code, so it stays a robustness concern with no CWE.

Known LuaJIT upstream crash scenarios during deep stack overflow / error-handling reallocation involve calls to this function with state mutated by other components (lj_state, lj_err); those mutate the inputs this function trusts and are out of scope of the shown control flow.

The `default: lua_assert(0); return 0;` path (lines 45-47) reads type bits from slots that may be stale in a corrupted-state scenario, but in release builds it safely returns 0 without further dereferences; treated as no-op handling, not a vulnerability.

No reachable hang/unbounded iteration exists: frame strictly decreases on every iteration and is bounded below by bot, and cf strictly moves toward NULL in the inner loop; pathological runtime would require the same invariant violations noted above.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability. Every state-machine read is preceded by a p == pe or ++p == pe bound check, so reads never occur at buffer index >= len; all MARK/LEN pairs delivered to the callbacks lie inside [buffer, buffer+len) with non-negative lengths; the only in-bounds write (snake_upcase_char at tr21/tr23) fires only while p < pe; and the header-done path (tr22) is reachable only after reading the final LF, so p+1 <= pe and the body length pe-p-1 >= 0. off <= len is enforced only by an assert and is a caller invariant (off = prior nread), not attacker-controlled; mutation of the const input buffer is a contract/robustness concern, not an out-of-bounds condition.

assumptions: MARK(x,y), PTR_TO(x), LEN(x,y) are the standard puma macros (x=y, (x), (y)-(x)), so every callback length is the unsigned difference p - mark with mark <= p.

buffer points to at least len writable bytes, and off <= len is guaranteed by the caller (Puma passes off = parser->nread of the prior call); the asserts at lines 5 and 11 document this invariant but are compiled out under NDEBUG.
parser->cs and the callback pointers are initialized to valid values by the unseen caller; the content of buffer is the only attacker-controlled data.
char is signed on the target platform, so bytes >= 0x80 evaluate to negative values in (*p) range checks.
limitations: snake_upcase_char((char *)p) writes one byte at p (lines ~306, ~310) despite the const char* parameter; the write is strictly in-bounds because p < pe when the action fires, and the caller always passes a writable I/O buffer, so this is a const-contract/robustness concern, not an out-of-bounds or attacker-triggerable flaw in the shown code.

If a caller ever violated off <= len (only enforced by the NDEBUG-compiled assert at line 5), p = buffer+off could exceed pe and the case-1 read at line 21 would go out of bounds; the shown code provides no path by which attacker input controls off, so this is a caller-invariant limitation rather than a reachable finding.

In the fragment/query states (st20/st21/st25/st26) the control-byte rejection relies on 0 <= (*p) <= 31, which high-bit bytes (>= 0x80) evade due to signed char, so such bytes are accepted as token content; this is a parsing-robustness deviation with no memory-safety or injection impact in the shown code.
NULL or misbehaving parser callbacks (request_method/request_uri/http_field/header_done) are caller-supplied; any failure from them is outside the shown code.

Requests exceeding internal token limits (e.g., >20-char method names, st0 on mismatch) simply error out; the machine consumes exactly one byte per transition and terminates within len-off iterations, so there is no unbounded-loop or algorithmic-complexity concern.

verdict.summary: call_qftf_func() adopts the list returned by the user-configured 'quickfixtextfunc' callback after only a VAR_LIST type check and dereferences it without verifying vval.v_list is non-NULL. A callback that returns Vim's null_list yields rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST with vval.v_list == NULL, so qftf_list->lv_refcount++ dereferences NULL and crashes Vim (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Taint: rettv is the return typval of call_callback() (line 30) executing the user-supplied 'quickfixtextfunc' function, so rettv.vval.v_list (line 34) is user-influenced. Reachability: when that function returns null_list, line 32 admits it because null_list is typed VAR_LIST with a NULL v_list, so qftf_list is NULL at line 34 and line 35 dereferences NULL. The type-only guard at line 32 does not establish v_list != NULL, so the NULL value passes the guard and reaches the sink; impact is a NULL-pointer dereference crash (CWE-476).

assumptions: qfl, qf_winid, start_idx, start_idx and end_idx are framework-internal/trusted (non-NULL pointer, valid ids), and call_callback() may return a VAR_LIST typval whose vval.v_list is NULL, e.g. when the user function returns Vim's null_list (which is type v:t_list with a NULL pointer).
dict_alloc_lock() returns a dict with refcount 0 so that ++d->dv_refcount (25) paired with dict_unref(d) (39), and qftf_list->lv_refcount++ (35) paired with clear_tv(&rettv) (37), are balanced.
limitations: The NULL-dereference severity is limited to a local crash/DoS of the editor; no memory corruption or code execution is demonstrated in the shown code.
start_idx/end_idx are only passed into the argument dict (lines 23-24); no bounds/indexing sink consuming them exists in the shown code, so any related OOB concern is out of scope here.
Ignored FAIL returns from dict_add_number() (lines 20-24) are an allocation-failure robustness concern, not a security finding (no attacker-controlled size, single-shot).

verdict.summary: pcx_write_rle never validates the caller-supplied `step` before using it in pointer arithmetic (`from += step`, line 13) and dereference (`*from`, line 14/20). With `step = -1` the first dereference reads one byte before the caller's buffer and the outer loop (line 10) continues walking backward while `from < end` stays true, so every iteration performs an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); `step = 0` additionally causes a non-terminating loop at line 20 (CWE-835, DoS). The existing guard `from >= end` only prevents overshoot past `end`, not undershoot below the buffer start; the missing check is `step > 0`.

evidence.reason: Attacker-supplied parameter `step` (line 1) is used unvalidated in `from += step` (line 13). For `step = -1` with `from` = buffer base B and `end` = B+n, `from` becomes B-1 and the line-14 guard `from >= end` is false, so `*from` dereferences one byte before the caller's buffer. The outer loop (line 10) then continues while `from < end` (always true as `from` decreases), so every iteration performs an out-of-bounds read. The guard covers only the `from >= end` overshoot and imposes no lower bound; the missing check is `step > 0`.

assumptions: `from`/`end` delimit a valid byte buffer with `from < end` (the shown code performs no NULL check).
Per the analysis rules, the `step` parameter is treated as potentially attacker-influenced because the shown code imposes no constraint on it before using it in pointer arithmetic.
`gp_fputc` is assumed to write one byte and return normally.
limitations: `step = 0` is a separately confirmed non-terminating loop at lines 20-21 (`while ((from < end) && (*from == data))` never advances `from`; CWE-835, DoS); kept out of the `cwe` list to preserve a single primary CWE-125.

Signed overflow of `max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT` (line 8) requires |step| > INT_MAX/15 (~1.43e8); a wrapped-negative `max_run` turns the chunk loop (lines 23-27) into an infinite loop, but this is treated as hardening, not a separate finding.
Division by zero at line 29 for `step = 0` is unreachable because the inner loop at lines 20-21 never terminates first.
A NULL `from`/`end` dereference is not counted because the NULL-producing path is not in the shown code.
With `step < 0` the chunk loop and outer loop are also non-terminating, compounding the OOB reads into a DoS; this does not add a separate CWE.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in njs_function_frame_save()'s 'Move all arguments' loop: the loop writes function->args_count 8-byte pointers into the new frame's local-pointer array starting at index njs_function_frame_args_count(active) + function->args_offset with no bound check against the array capacity value_count + function->u.lambda->temp, overflowing into the copied value slots and potentially past the frame allocation.

evidence.reason: Sink of an unbounded pointer write. 'local' starts at 'native->local + function->args_offset' (line 40) and 'native->local' at 'new + njs_function_frame_args_count(active)' (line 25), while the 'new' array holds only 'value_count + function->u.lambda->temp' pointer slots (lines 19-20, 26) and 'p' walks the value slots. The loop bound at line 42, 'function->args_count', and the starting offset are both taken from script/lambda and call-arity data ('active->function' and 'njs_function_frame_args_count(active)') with no check that 'njs_function_frame_args_count(active) + function->args_offset + function->args_count <= value_count + function->u.lambda->temp'. Any violating combination (e.g., large declared args_count with large actual argc) writes new[] indices above the pointer-array end (up to 'active_args + args_offset + args_count - 1'), corrupting saved njs_value_t slots at indices >= value_count + temp and, for larger values, past the frame buffer — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). A secondary write of the same loop is njs_set_undefined(p) at line 44, which writes value slot n when args_count exceeds the V+T value-slot budget.

assumptions: Line numbers count from the function signature line ('njs_function_frame_save(...)') since the prompt provides no line numbers.
njs_function_frame_values(active, &end) returns a range of exactly value_count slots, consistent with njs_function_frame_value_count(active).
The caller-allocated 'frame' contains value_count + function->u.lambda->temp pointer slots followed by the same number of value slots, as implied by lines 19-20 and 26.
njs layout invariants keep function->args_offset >= 1 so the 'value + (args_offset - 1)' arithmetic at line 24 does not underflow.
limitations: Whether a violating combination (args_count/nargs exceeding capacity) is reachable in a given deployment depends on how the unseen helpers compute frame->size and frame->nargs, and on whether the executed scripts or call arities are attacker-controlled; in deployments where scripts are trusted configuration and arity is fixed, this is a robustness concern rather than an attacker-triggerable flaw.

When the violating write stays inside the frame's overall backing space (indices >= value_count + temp but < 2*(value_count + temp)), it corrupts saved njs_value_t argument slots with raw pointers, producing type confusion; only sufficiently large magnitudes escape the whole frame allocation into a true heap OOB write.
No injection, crypto, authentication, or file-handling sinks exist in this function, so no other vulnerability classes apply.

verdict.summary: In the uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN branch, p aliases the caller's signature buffer (2*curve->num_bytes bytes) and EccPoint_mult writes the affine point as 2*curve->num_words words (2*num_words*word_size bytes) with no bounds check. For supported curves whose bit width is not a multiple of the word size (secp521r1: 144 B written vs 132 B buffer = 12 B OOB; secp224r1/secp160r1 with 64-bit words: +8 B), every signing operation corrupts memory past the signature buffer.

evidence.reason: In the uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN branch p aliases the caller's signature buffer (line 12), whose API contract is 2*curve->num_bytes bytes. EccPoint_mult writes 2*num_words words (2*num_words*word_size bytes) into p with no check in the shown code that this fits 2*num_bytes: for secp521r1 with 64-bit words (num_words=9, num_bytes=66) it writes 144 bytes into a 132-byte buffer (+12 B), and secp224r1/secp160r1 overflow by 8 bytes on 64-bit builds. The only guards, line 22 (0<k<n) and line 64 (numBits(s)<=num_bytes*8), validate k and the final s value, not the line-27 point write, so the oversized write is unconstrained on the shown path.

assumptions: signature points to at least 2*curve->num_bytes bytes per the uECC API contract.
private_key has at least curve->num_bytes readable bytes per the uECC API contract.
EccPoint_mult writes the affine point as 2*num_words words (x then y) to its result pointer, as in uECC's implementation; the shown code never reconciles that write size with the aliased buffer.
uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN evaluates to 1 on mainstream little-endian builds where uECC_WORD_SIZE matches the native word size.
Unseen helpers (bits2int, uECC_vli_*, uECC_generate_random_int) behave as in uECC, e.g. bits2int clamps its input length to BITS_TO_BYTES(num_n_bits).
limitations: The OOB write is limited to the uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN branch and to curves whose bit width is not a multiple of the word size (secp160r1, secp224r1, secp521r1 with 64-bit words; secp521r1 with 32-bit words, +4 B). The non-native branch uses a local 2*uECC_MAX_WORDS buffer and is safe.

The overflow trigger depends on the caller-selected curve; if an integration never uses a misaligned curve, the overflow is unreachable in that build, and attacker control of the curve choice is not established from the shown code.
hash_size is passed to bits2int (line 61) unclamped in the shown code; safety rests on the unseen helper's clamp, so no separate OOB read is confirmed from this code.
When g_rng_function is NULL the blinding multiplier becomes 1 (lines 34-36), weakening side-channel resistance; this is a hardening concern, not a demonstrated exploit from the shown code.
Line 68 reads up to num_bytes from s (num_n_words words); it is safe for standard curves where num_n_bits == num_bits and only a concern for non-standard caller curves.
s[num_n_words - 1] = 0 (line 57) would underflow only if num_n_words == 0, unreachable with valid curves.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown Ragel-generated HTTP parser. Every byte read is guarded by `if (p == pe) goto _test_eof` (entry, ~lines 16-17) and `if (++p == pe) goto _test_eofN` before each `case N` dereference, so reads stay within `buffer+off .. buffer+len-1`. All callback lengths (`LEN(mark,p)`, `field_len`, `pe-p-1`) are non-negative and bounded by `len`; the only writes (`snake_upcase_char`) are in-bounds by design. Possibly dangerous operations such as dereferencing `p+1 == pe` would occur inside the unshown `header_done` callback, which is out of scope.

assumptions: MARK/PTR_TO store offsets relative to `buffer` and reconstruct pointers within the current buffer (consistent with the epilogue assertions comparing `parser->mark` and `parser->field_start` to `len`).
The caller maintains `off` equal to the previous cumulative `nread` and keeps the request buffer writable and stable for the lifetime of the parse.

Callbacks treat the passed lengths as authoritative bounds and do not dereference past them; the commented-out `assert(*pe == '\0')` means NUL termination past `len` is not guaranteed by the shown code.
limitations: `header_done` is invoked with `p+1` (which equals `pe` when the terminating LF is the last byte) and length `pe-p-1 == 0`; any OOB read or NUL-dependent behavior would occur inside that unseen callback, not in the shown code.
`snake_upcase_char((char *)p)` writes into the input buffer through a const cast (tr21/tr23); this is in-bounds and by design but requires the framework to pass a writable buffer.

The `off <= len`, `mark < len`, `field_len <= len`, and `nread <= len` checks are debug-only asserts and vanish under `NDEBUG`; however, these values are framework-internal counters, not attacker-controlled, so no attacker-reachable memory operation is left unguarded.
Parser-behavior edge cases (e.g., resuming with body bytes after headers complete routes through state 46 to an error state) were reviewed and are functional concerns, not confirmed security issues.

verdict.summary: OP_ARGARY (and OP_BLKPUSH) perform an out-of-bounds read of the lexical environment when the keyword-argument flag kd is set: the guard `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` admits an env of length exactly m1+r+m2+2, while the sink reads stack[m1+r+m2+1] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+2], i.e. index == len, one mrb_value past the allocated env. Operand bits and env size are derived from bytecode (untrusted .mrb input), so crafted bytecode triggers a one-element heap/stack OOB read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Bytecode operand b supplies kd=1 and m1/r/m2 (lines 620-623); with lv>=1 the guard at lines 639-640 admits an env length len == m1+r+m2+2 (it only rejects len <= m1+r+m2+1). Since stack = e->stack+1 (line 641), this read dereferences e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] == e->stack[len], one mrb_value past the env allocation — an out-of-bounds read reachable with crafted bytecode controlling both the operand bits and the enclosing frame that fixes MRB_ENV_LEN(e).

Same off-by-one: with kd==1 the guard at lines 1165-1166 admits len == m1+r+m2+2, and stack[m1+r+m2+kd] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+kd+1] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] reads index len, past the env end (the identical OOB is also probed by the nil check on line 1172). Operand bits come from instruction operand b (lines 1155-1159), attacker-controlled in untrusted bytecode.

assumptions: irep contents (iseq opcodes/operands, pool, syms, reps) are treated as attacker-controlled, as when a compiled .mrb binary is loaded from a file or network source; the shown code performs no validation of any operand against irep->nregs/plen/slen/rlen.
MRB_ENV_LEN(e) is the allocated element count of e->stack, so e->stack[len] is out of bounds.
limitations: Additional crafted-bytecode OOB candidates share the same premise but are pure missing-validation (no guard to contradict): OP_JMPUW pc = irep->iseq + a (line 322, only a debug mrb_assert at 308), OP_HASH signed-int overflow of lim (lines 1560-1563), OP_ARYPUSH regs reads (lines 1437-1438), OP_STRING/OP_SYMBOL len = pool[b].tt>>2 (lines 1525/1540), OP_LAMBDA/OP_EXEC irep->reps[b] (lines 1597/1678), OP_ERR pool[a] (line 1757).

The lv==0 paths of OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH and all regs writes rely on the compiler-guaranteed frame layout (nregs); violations there need the same untrusted-bytecode premise and were not used as the primary finding.
printf-family and mrb_format calls use only literal format strings (lines 823, 853, 1142, 1748); no format-string injection, and no crypto, SQL, file, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability: no attacker-controlled size, index, or pointer value reaches a memory operation; the only cast (to_usb_interface at line 15) is protected by the hid_is_usb() guard at line 7; all allocation and set-up calls are NULL/return-checked, and there are no injection, crypto, or file/access sinks. The missing usb_put_dev() on the error path is a refcount-leak limitation, not a security finding.

assumptions: hid_is_usb(hdev) at line 7 enforces that hdev->dev.parent is the parent type (USB interface) required by to_usb_interface()/interface_to_usbdev() at line 15; the helper body is not part of the shown code.
wq is a module-level workqueue created by the unshown driver init before driver registration, so it is non-NULL when queue_delayed_work() runs at line 34.
elo_broken_firmware(), elo_work, and ELO_PERIODIC_READ_INTERVAL are trusted module state; their internals are outside the shown code.
limitations: usb_get_dev() at line 16 is not paired with usb_put_dev() on the err_free path (lines 38-40), so each failed probe leaks one USB device reference; this is a resource leak without memory-corruption impact and with no attacker-controlled loop in the shown code to amplify it, so it is not a confirmed vulnerability.
hid_parse() and hid_hw_start() delegate report parsing and hardware bring-up to the HID core; any flaw in parsing attacker-crafted report descriptors would live in unshown code (a pass-through here).

If hid_is_usb() were implemented to admit a parent that is a usb_device rather than a usb_interface, the cast at line 15 would be type-confused; because the helper body is not shown, this remains an unconfirmed hypothesis, not a finding.
On a failed probe after line 18, hdev->driver_data points to the kfree'd priv, but the shown code never dereferences it and whether any unseen remove() path runs for a failed probe is out of scope.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse copies sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) (4) bytes from pnt+3 regardless of the attacker-chosen capability length hdr->length. The length guard at line 41 only ensures the declared payload fits in the message; it never requires hdr->length >= 4, so a final capability with hdr->length in 0..3 makes memcpy read up to 4 bytes past the end of the message buffer (heap out-of-bounds read, DoS and possible information disclosure).

evidence.reason: hdr->length is an attacker-chosen byte from the capability TLV; the only guard at line 41, (pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end, enforces an upper bound on the declared payload but no lower bound. With hdr->length = 0 and end == pnt + 3 (the 3-byte header at the message tail), line 17 and line 41 both pass, and memcpy reads 4 bytes starting at pnt+3, up to 4 bytes past end — a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) is 4 bytes (afi_t 2 + reserved 1 + safi_t 1, no extra padding).
bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices() correctly bounds afi/safi before the afc_recv/afc_nego array writes at lines 79/82/88/89.
limitations: The afi/safi array writes would be out-of-bounds only if bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices() is faulty; that function is not shown, so this is not a confirmed finding.

When hdr->length is 1-3 but enough whole-message bytes remain, line 49 reads indeterminate but in-bounds bytes; those values are discarded by bgp_afi_safi_valid_indices(), so no second CWE is confirmed.
peer->host in zlog calls is framework-supplied session data, not an attacker-controlled parameter in this function; no log-injection finding is confirmed.
A NULL peer or pnt supplied by an unseen caller is out of scope for this analysis.

verdict.summary: search_impl's found branch fabricates the post-match remainder string: op1->value.bytes is set to ptr + size (line 42) and its size to count + (backward ? size-1 : 0) (line 43), which can far exceed the bytes actually remaining after the match (count - pos). For a backward match at the first tested position (pos = count), this stores size len1 - 1 with the pointer at the end of the buffer, so any subsequent operator reading that returned string performs an out-of-bounds read; the forward case overestimates by pos as well. The only guard (line 14) bounds search start positions, not the remainder length.

evidence.reason: Sink for CWE-125: attacker-controlled haystack length r_size(op1) and pattern length size (lines 5, 14, 18) plus match offset pos = ptr - start (line 41) reach this size/pointer write. True remainder is count - pos, but the code stores count (forward) or count + size - 1 = len1 - 1 (backward). Witness: backward search, haystack "aXYb" (len1=4), pattern "XY" (size=2): line 14 passes (2<=4), the loop matches at the first tested position pos=2=count (lines 23, 27-28), then lines 42-43 set the remainder pointer to the buffer end with declared size 3 (true remainder 0), so any read of the returned string overruns the buffer by up to len1-1 bytes. The line-14 guard (size > r_size(op1)) admits this value (2<=4) and does not constrain the remainder length at all.

assumptions: search_impl is invoked only after the interpreter verified the operand stack has at least two string operands and that push(2) capacity exists (framework-internal invariants).
String operands satisfy the Ghostscript ref invariant: value.bytes points to at least r_size readable bytes.
uint is 32-bit unsigned and r_size exactly equals the string byte length.
limitations: The byte-level out-of-bounds read itself executes in later PostScript operators that consume the malformed remainder string returned on the operand stack; the shown code performs the incorrect size/pointer write that makes that read out-of-bounds.
The search loops (lines 26-31) themselves stay in bounds: both directions test exactly count+1 start positions, the last of which permits a full size-byte read ending at len1-1.
Small overreads may be masked by allocator chunk padding, weakening observed impact without changing the object-level defect; raw heap layout was not part of the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the tool-change stop-switch branch, `get_line(fd++)` (line 26) post-increments the local `fd` pointer by sizeof(gerb_file_t), so the `fd->filename` dereference at line 30 reads heap memory past the gerb_file_t object. A crafted drill file whose bytes after the leading 'T' are 'C','S','T' (e.g. "TCST\n") triggers the branch, producing an out-of-bounds read whose garbage pointer is then passed to %s in the error message, crashing the parser or disclosing heap contents.

evidence.reason: fd->filename is dereferenced after `tmps = get_line(fd++);` (line 26) has post-incremented the local gerb_file_t* by sizeof(gerb_file_t). The branch at lines 22-24 is reachable with purely attacker-chosen file bytes: with the caller having consumed the leading 'T' (entry fd->ptr == 1), the next bytes must be 'C','S','T' and (fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen (line 22) — witness file "TCST\n" (datalen 5) satisfies (2+2)<5 and all three byte tests. Neither the line-22 read-ahead guard nor any other check constrains the post-increment, so line 30 reads the filename field beyond the heap-allocated gerb_file_t object; the recovered garbage pointer is then dereferenced by %s in gerbv_stats_printf, causing a crash (DoS) or heap-content disclosure. Primary CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read).

assumptions: The caller consumed the leading 'T' before invoking the function, so fd->ptr >= 1 when the 'C','S','T' branch runs; under this invariant the `fd->ptr -= 4` rewind at line 25 lands at index >= 0.
TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX match the allocated size of image->aperture[], so the guard at line 63 fully bounds the indices used at lines 73, 127, and 185.
gerb_file_t is heap-allocated and get_line() is a function taking gerb_file_t*, so `fd++` advances the local pointer by sizeof(gerb_file_t).
image->drill_stats is non-NULL (created at image initialization), so stats->error_list and stats->drill_list dereferences do not fail.
limitations: If a caller could enter the function without consuming a preceding 'T' (entry fd->ptr == 0), line 25's `fd->ptr -= 4` could underflow to -1 before get_line; this contradicts the shown function's contract (name and line-18 diagnostic), so it is an unconfirmed hypothesis, not a finding.

Integer truncation at line 57 `(int) gerb_fgetint(fd, NULL)`: a large 64-bit tool value that truncates into [TOOL_MIN, TOOL_MAX) still indexes in-bounds because the truncated value is the one checked and used; no out-of-bounds results.
g_new0() NULL results are handled by GERB_FATAL_ERROR (lines 129-131, 186-187) and are not attacker-scalable, so they are not findings.
isdigit(temp) at line 40 can be called with a negative value (e.g. EOF); this is undefined behavior with no attacker-visible security impact here.
The internals of read_double, gerb_fgetint, gerb_fgetc, and drill_stats_add_to_drill_list are not shown and were not audited.

verdict.summary: rsi_send_beacon calls skb_pull() with length 64 - dword_align_bytes (1..63) on an skb whose len is still 0 (allocated by dev_alloc_skb and only memset, which does not set len). Whenever the allocator returns a non-64-byte-aligned data pointer, the guard at line 13 admits the value and the pull always exceeds skb->len, violating the skb_pull contract and triggering skb_under_panic/BUG (kernel crash) in enforcing kernels; the return value is unchecked. The missing check is a bound on the pull length relative to skb->len (the alignment adjustment should be an skb_reserve against headroom).

evidence.reason: skb->len is 0 at this point: dev_alloc_skb (line 6) returns a zero-length skb and memset (line 10) does not update len/tail. dword_align_bytes = (unsigned long)skb->data & 0x3f (line 12) is an allocator-chosen value in [1,63] whenever the data pointer is not 64-byte aligned; the guard at line 13 admits every such value, and the pull length 64 - dword_align_bytes always lies in [1,63], strictly exceeding skb->len (0). This violates the skb_pull len <= skb->len contract, causing skb_under_panic/BUG (kernel crash) in enforcing kernel implementations, while the unvalidated return means a NULL-return failure is also silently ignored. Concrete witness: dword_align_bytes = 1 pulls 63 bytes from a 0-length skb. No check bounds the pull length by skb->len.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based as laid out in the shown snippet.
dev_alloc_skb() returns an skb with len == 0 and a linear area of at least MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE bytes.
skb_pull() requires its length argument not to exceed skb->len; enforcing kernels invoke skb_under_panic()/BUG() on violation.
limitations: The exact failure mode (kernel BUG vs. silently ignored NULL return) depends on the kernel's skb_pull implementation; the shown code never checks the return value and never bounds the pull length by skb->len.

A possible heap out-of-bounds write inside rsi_prepare_beacon() after the pull shortens the usable linear area is not demonstrated because that helper's code is not shown; the write would occur outside the shown code.
The bounds of common->tx_queue[MGMT_BEACON_Q] cannot be verified from the shown code alone.
The triggering alignment value is determined by the allocator rather than directly chosen by an attacker; attacker influence is limited to reaching the beacon-send path.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans dereferences spans[1] without first establishing num_spans >= 2: with num_spans == 1 the do-while body still runs once and reads one cairo_half_open_span_t past a one-element spans array (CWE-125, line 15). That out-of-bounds value is then used as composite geometry and, in the partial-coverage branch, as the length for a memset into r->_buf with no capacity check, enabling a heap buffer overflow (CWE-787, line 85).

evidence.reason: num_spans==1 passes the only count guard (`if (num_spans == 0) return;` at line 9), and the loop condition `while (--num_spans > 1)` at line 90 executes the body exactly once (1->0, and 0 is not > 1), so this first statement reads spans[1] although the caller's array has exactly one element — an out-of-bounds read past the array. The value flows to the composite width (line 49), to x0 (lines 52/81), to the tail check (line 92), and to the memset length at line 85.

In the partial-coverage branch (coverage neither 0xff nor 0x0, lines 82-88) writes into the caller-allocated r->_buf are sized by len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x with no check that m plus len stays within the buffer's capacity: line 83 writes one byte and this line writes len-1 more. On the num_spans==1 path len is itself the out-of-bounds value from line 15, so a garbage spans[1].x = spans[0].x + M with M larger than the _buf allocation produces a heap buffer overflow.

assumptions: Standard cairo layout: r->_buf is a caller-allocated row buffer; u.composite.run_length is a small non-negative constant; pixman_image_composite32 clips geometry in the unseen callee.
spans points to exactly num_spans contiguous elements, so num_spans == 1 means a genuinely one-element array.
limitations: For num_spans >= 2, the memset writes are normally bounded by the caller-side invariant that spans partition a row no wider than _buf; that case is defense-in-depth only and is not separately confirmed.
The composite widths (e.g., lines 49, 100, 114) are passed to a trusted, clipping callee, so they are not an independent finding.
No NULL dereference, hang, injection, crypto, or file-handling issues were found in the shown code; a NULL r->_buf would require an unseen allocation failure.

verdict.summary: Stack out-of-bounds write in string_scan_range's per-string buffer tmp: the inner-loop bound `i < sizeof(tmp) - 4` assumes r_utf8_encode writes at most 4 bytes, but a crafted 5/6-byte UTF-8 sequence in the file (e.g. 251 ASCII 'A' bytes followed by FC 84 80 80 80 80 at line 142) decodes to a rune >= 0x4000000, passes r_isprint at line 156, and is re-encoded into tmp as 6 bytes; i then exceeds sizeof(tmp)-4, so `tmp[i++] = '\0'` at line 184 writes past the stack buffer and r_str_ndup at line 281 over-reads it.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled file bytes read at line 42 are decoded at line 142 by r_utf8_decode; a 6-byte sequence (e.g. FC 84 80 80 80 80) yields a rune >= 0x4000000 that passes r_isprint (line 156) and makes r_utf8_encode write 6 bytes at tmp+i. The only guard, the loop bound `i < sizeof (tmp) - 4` (line 129), admits i = sizeof(tmp)-5, so the write reaches tmp[sizeof(tmp)], one byte past the stack array.

After line 162 returns rc = 5 or 6 for the same crafted rune (bytes F8 88 80 80 80 => rune 0x200000, or FC 84 80 80 80 80 => 0x4000000), the loop's `i += rc` makes i = sizeof(tmp) or sizeof(tmp)+1, so this terminator write lands 1-2 bytes past tmp and line 281's r_str_ndup((const char*)tmp, i) performs the matching OOB read. No check limits the encode length; line 129's bound assumes rc <= 4.

assumptions: r_utf8_decode accepts 5/6-byte UTF-8 sequences (0xF8-0xFD prefixes) and produces runes up to 0x7FFFFFFF, and r_utf8_encode emits 5/6 bytes for runes >= 0x200000/0x4000000, per radare2's libr/util/utf.c.
r_isprint returns true for non-ASCII runes (radare2's unicode heuristic), so runes 0x200000/0x4000000 take the line 156 branch.
R_STRING_SCAN_BUFFER_SIZE >= 6; the failure is at index sizeof(tmp)-1 and beyond regardless of the exact value.
from=0 and to <= bf->size (full-file scan) makes the witness file-triggerable with a normal caller range.
limitations: OOB read at line 78 via ut64 wrap of `needle + 4 < to` (line 77) when from/to are within 4 of 2^64-1 is real but depends on a caller supplying near-max offsets; no concrete in-flow witness, so not a confirmed finding.
Allocation DoS only: calloc(len,1) at line 27 up to ~2 GiB and calloc(len,4) at line 48 up to ~8 GiB, plus int overflow of `outlen = len * 4` at line 47 for len > 2^30; impacts availability only.
tmp is uninitialized stack memory; r_str_ndup at line 281 can copy unwritten bytes and expose stale stack contents in scan output (info-disclosure hardening, not confirmed attacker impact).
Parallel-array reads block_list[j]/freq_list[j] (lines 219-224) assume r_utf_block_list returns equally-sized, -1-terminated arrays; helper internals are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO upload-status block, when the attacker-supplied STOR filename length sl equals the size of shm_data_cur->filename (S), the else branch computes the memcpy source as &name[sl - S - 1U], which wraps to &name[-1] and reads one byte before the name buffer (off-by-one OOB read). The guard at line 150 only excludes sl < S and does not protect this exact value.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled filename (FTP STOR argument, line 142 strlen) flows unvalidated into this memcpy. With sl == sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename), the unsigned expression sl - sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) - 1U wraps to SIZE_MAX, so &name[SIZE_MAX] dereferences one byte before name and memcpy reads S bytes there; the guard at line 150 (sl < sizeof(...)) admits this case because it only rejects sl <= S-1. The index should target the tail ending at the NUL (start sl - S + 1); as written it is two bytes too low, causing the OOB read for exactly that boundary length.

assumptions: FTPWHO is compiled in (#ifdef FTPWHO at line 140), so shm_data_cur->filename is a fixed-size char array whose sizeof is known at compile time.
name is a NUL-terminated C string of attacker-chosen length; nothing in the shown code (checknamesanity call at line 33 or elsewhere) caps its length below sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename).
The FTP/REST parser feeds restartat into byte position of the file, and append/autorename are framework-generated flags.
limitations: The else branch at lines 154-156 never NUL-terminates shm_data_cur->filename (the copied window name[sl-S-1..sl-2] excludes the terminator), but the resulting over-read would occur in an unseen ftpwho consumer, not in this shown code.

When ul_init fails (lines 171-173), ulhandler.total_uploaded is read uninitialized at lines 193 and 251; this is a use-of-uninitialized-value defect (CWE-457 class) but no security mechanism is demonstrably broken, so it is not scored as a finding.

Path-based operations (rename/open/unlink) on attacker-chosen names present only hardening-level TOCTOU concerns; O_NOFOLLOW at lines 58/60 mitigates final-symlink following and no concrete failing witness exists in the shown code.

A negative restartat could reach ftruncate (line 101) and fail with EINVAL, aborting the transfer; the REST parser is outside the shown code, and no memory-safety impact results, so it is not a finding.
Open mode 0777 & ~u_mask (line 61) yields permissive permissions only if the hosting umask is permissive; this is configuration-dependent, not a confirmed vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The element-dispatch loop in stroke() reads up to 6 qreals per CurveToElement, but the only bound is the total point budget lastPoint = points + 2*elementCount (line 88) enforced by `points < lastPoint` (line 111), which does not guarantee 6 remaining qreals or 3 remaining element slots. A caller-supplied QVectorPath with elementCount()==1, elements[0]==CurveToElement, and a 2-qreal points buffer passes the guard and causes an out-of-bounds heap read of points[2..5] at the cubicTo call (lines 124-126), with types += 3 (line 128) also overrunning the elements array; the cosmetic-pen loop (lines 184-187) has the identical flaw.

evidence.reason: points and types are taken unvalidated from the path parameter (lines 84-86). The only guard on this read is `while (points < lastPoint)` (line 111) with lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1) (line 88), which admits any state with at least one qreal remaining and does not check that a CurveToElement has 6 qreals or 3 element slots. Witness: elementCount()==1, elements[0]==QPainterPath::CurveToElement, points buffer of 2 qreals passes the guard and this cubicTo reads points[2..5] (indices 2-5) past the 2-qreal heap buffer (CWE-125); types += 3 on line 128 simultaneously walks past the 1-entry elements array.

assumptions: The QVectorPath API stores the caller-supplied points and elements arrays without cross-validating that points holds 2*elementCount qreals or that each CurveToElement is followed by two data elements; the shown code does not re-validate them.
path is attacker-influenced when an application strokes vector paths derived from untrusted content (e.g., parsed SVG/PDF/fonts) or when a QVectorPath is constructed directly from untrusted data.
elementCount is non-negative and far below 2^30, so int arithmetic on line 88 and line 13 does not overflow in practice.
limitations: A malformed elements array whose visited entry is CurveToElementData (3) hits the `default:` case (lines 131-132) which advances nothing, giving a non-terminating loop (CWE-835-style DoS); same malformed-input family but not independently confirmed, so no second CWE is assigned.

new StrokeHandler(path.elementCount()+4) (line 13) can only fail via int overflow at elementCount near 2^31 or an allocation failure; no attacker-controlled volume scaling, so treated as DoS-hardening only.
Well-formed QVectorPath inputs (each curve occupying exactly 3 elements and 6 points) stay within bounds and terminate; the flaw requires inconsistent caller-supplied arrays.
The cosmetic-pen branch (lines 167-196) contains the identical unguarded curve read at lines 184-187; covered by the same finding, not a second evidence item.
The QT_DEBUG_DRAW qDebug() at line 4 writes pen data only and is disabled in production builds.

verdict.summary: The shown function is a delegation loop over an OVS packet batch. Its only local memory operations are dp_packet_batch_refill(pb, pkt, pb_idx) at lines 18 and 24, which write at the current iteration index within the batch's fixed capacity, and dp_packet_delete(pkt) at line 20, after which pkt is not reused in the shown code. The classification guard at lines 10-14 covers both outcomes (handle-under-lock vs. plain refill), pb_idx is never derived from or incremented by attacker data, and no injection, crypto, or file/access sinks are present. All parsing of attacker-controlled fragment bytes takes place in unshown callees (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag), which is out of scope for this analysis.

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH maintains the batch count/refill invariants so that pb_idx always denotes a valid slot within the batch array capacity.
The batch count is bounded by the fixed OVS batch capacity, making the int/size_t comparison at the loop bound free of overflow.
ipf, pb, and the dp_packet objects are framework-allocated and valid when the function is invoked.
The ipf mutex is not already held by the caller and ipf_handle_frag does not re-enter this function.
limitations: Memory-safety analysis of fragment parsing itself (truncated headers, fragment offsets, sizes, reassembly allocation) is out of scope: those operations are inside the unshown callees ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, and ipf_handle_frag, and the shown code is a pure pass-through that delegates the parsing.

Releasing ipf->ipf_lock between packets permits interleaved fragment handling and expiration by other threads; no concrete failure (double-free, lost update, OOB) is demonstrable from the shown code, so it is a robustness/correctness concern, not a confirmed finding.
NULL handling of pkt relies on the unshown macro expansion; no dereference of pkt is present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: get_visual_text() computes the selection length *lenp from VIsual.col / curwin->w_cursor.col at lines 24/29 without bounding it by the current line length. The guards at lines 31 and 33 only handle a NUL start and a non-negative length; when a stored column exceeds the line length (line shortened after the visual position was recorded, or a past-end-of-line column), the index *lenp - 1 reads past the terminating NUL at line 38 ((*mb_ptr2len)(*pp + (*lenp - 1))) and line 39 ((*pp)[*lenp - 1]), a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that can crash the editor or leak heap memory.

evidence.reason: Taint: *lenp is derived at lines 24/29 as max(VIsual.col, curwin->w_cursor.col) - min(...) + 1 from user/file-influenced global columns that line 8 constrains only to the same lnum, never to the current line length, and line 33 (`*lenp > 0`) admits any positive value. Concrete failure: for a line of L=2 bytes with VIsual.col=3 and w_cursor.col=0, both admitted by lines 8 and 21, *lenp = 4, so *pp + (*lenp - 1) = line + 3 reads two bytes past the NUL at offset 2 — heap out-of-bounds read that can crash or disclose memory. No upper bound such as STRLEN(*pp) >= *lenp exists in the shown code; the non-mbyte sibling at line 39 uses the same unbounded index.

assumptions: Line numbers refer to the provided snippet starting at `get_visual_text(`; no source file exists in the workspace.
ml_get_curline()/ml_get_pos() return NUL-terminated line buffers: a line of L bytes owns indices 0..L, where index L is the terminator.
VIsual.col and curwin->w_cursor.col are byte offsets; after the line-8 guard both positions refer to the same buffer line.
has_mbyte selects between the two correction paths (lines 38 and 39); either may be active at runtime.
limitations: Triggering the failing witness requires VIsual/cursor columns to exceed the current line length (line shortened after the visual position was recorded, or a position stored beyond end-of-line); the shown code imposes no check preventing this state.
`**pp` at line 31 can also read out of bounds when the else-branch start pointer itself is past the terminator — same missing upper bound, subsumed by this finding.
Integer overflow of the column difference at lines 24/29 would require columns near INT_MAX; not confirmed as a separate finding.
NULL pp/lenp would fault, but non-NULL is a trusted caller contract; out of scope.
No loops, injection sinks, weak crypto, or file/access-control operations exist in the shown code; the linewise path (lines 14-18) is bounded by construction.

verdict.summary: parallels_open trusts ph.catalog_entries from the image file: the 32-bit value is narrowed into signed s->catalog_size, and the guard only rejects values > INT_MAX/4, admitting wrapped-negative values such as 0xFFFFFFFF (-1). The multiplication at g_malloc(s->catalog_size * 4) then overflows to a huge gsize (~2^64-4), so GLib aborts the process — an attacker-triggerable DoS on opening a crafted image.

evidence.reason: s->catalog_size comes from the attacker-controlled file field ph.catalog_entries (read at line 11, assigned at line 32). The only guard, line 33, tests 's->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4' on a signed int, which admits every value >= 0x80000000 after the uint32->int wrap (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFF becomes -1). For that witness, -1 > 536870911 is false, so the guard passes, and 's->catalog_size * 4' overflows to -4, converted to gsize 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC; GLib g_malloc aborts the process. The guard fails to exclude the negative class that breaks this exact size computation.

assumptions: s->catalog_size in BDRVParallelsState is a signed 32-bit int, as implied by the 'INT_MAX / 4' comparison and the 'int i' loop counter (struct definition not shown in the provided code).
s->opaque is zero-initialized by the block layer before parallels_open, making g_free(s->catalog_bitmap) on early fail paths safe.
GLib g_malloc aborts the process when the requested allocation cannot be satisfied.
limitations: A truncated file can make bdrv_pread return a short positive read, leaving parts of ph or catalog_bitmap uninitialized; accesses stay within allocated bounds, so no OOB or injection is confirmed.
ph.nb_sectors is stored into bs->total_sectors without validation (up to 0xFFFFFFFF), but no dangerous operation on this value appears in the shown code.
ph.tracks is only validated against zero and is not used in the shown code, so no divide-by-zero is reachable here.
The in-place catalog swap loop (lines 45-46) is in-bounds for all admitted positive catalog_size values and does not execute for negative values, so no out-of-bounds write is confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The size cap at line 7, the capacity check at line 11, and the free-space check at line 29 bound every arithmetic and memory-write operation; the u64-to-u32 conversion of size/len is lossless for every admitted value under the kernel's 16 MiB record cap. No injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks are present.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is the kernel constant 1<<24 (16 MiB); with that cap, size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ and round_up(...) fit exactly in u32 at line 10 and line 36. The macro is not defined in the shown excerpt.
rb and rb->data are valid for the map lifetime, and the ring is vmalloc-mapped twice so a record may safely straddle the physical page boundary.
BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT, bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off(), and the barrier helpers behave as in the kernel implementation.
limitations: If RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ were at least ~2^32-8, round_up(size + 8) could exceed U32_MAX and truncate u32 len, which would invalidate the safety conclusion; this contradicts the kernel constant and is not supported by the shown code.
A NULL dereference of rb->data or of the returned record would require the unseen map-allocator/caller to violate lifetime invariants; it is not produced by any path inside this function.

The consumer_pos snapshot taken at line 14 can only be stale in the conservative direction for the line 29 check, but this was reasoned from the shown control flow rather than proved by a concurrent-memory-model argument.
No loops exist in the shown code, so loop-bound and termination analysis does not apply.

verdict.summary: drill_parse_T_code indexes image->aperture[] with a file-derived tool_num. The only range check (lines 63-68) logs an error but does not return, clamp, or abort, so out-of-range values such as TOOL_MAX or a negative number reach line 72 (out-of-bounds read) and, when the read slot is NULL, lines 126-127 or 184 (out-of-bounds write of a heap pointer), enabling memory corruption.

evidence.reason: tool_num is the unvalidated `(int)` result of gerb_fgetint (line 57) fed by attacker-controlled file bytes. The guard at lines 63-68 admits every out-of-range value (it only prints and falls through), so e.g. tool_num == TOOL_MAX or tool_num == TOOL_MIN-1 reaches this array index and performs an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

The same unvalidated tool_num writes the address of a freshly allocated gerbv_aperture_t outside image->aperture[] (CWE-787) when the OOB-read slot at line 72 is NULL, e.g. for input 'T<TOOL_MAX>C<size>'; the identical OOB write occurs at line 184 in the fallback path, and a non-NULL garbage slot is instead dereferenced at lines 114-117.

assumptions: TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX define the valid index range and image->aperture[] is sized to it; the guard at line 63 exists precisely to bound tool_num.
gerb_fgetint can return values outside [TOOL_MIN, TOOL_MAX-1]; otherwise the guard at line 63 would be dead code.
The caller consumed the leading 'T' before invoking this function (see the comment at lines 15-16, 'after the T'), so fd->ptr -= 4 at line 25 stays non-negative.
limitations: The OOB write at lines 126-127/184 executes only if the out-of-bounds slot read at line 72 happens to be NULL; if non-NULL, the garbage pointer is dereferenced at lines 114-117/135-138, a different manifestation of the same index fault.
Whether a negative tool_num can be produced depends on gerb_fgetint's sign handling; the tool_num >= TOOL_MAX witness does not depend on it.
An out-of-range drill size at lines 103-107 is only reported, not rejected, and is stored into apert->parameter[0]; this has no memory-safety impact in the shown code.
The defensive dead-code branch at lines 173-175 (newline restore after EOF) and any get_line NULL-return behavior would be robustness concerns only.

verdict.summary: ex_copy performs no range validation on the line-number parameters line1/line2/n. An out-of-range source index (e.g., line1=0 with line2=0) passes the loop guard at line 29 and reaches the indexed read ml_get(line1) at line 33, causing an out-of-bounds read of the buffer's line array; the same missing validation lets n drive an invalid insert index into ml_append at line 36.

evidence.reason: line1 is an attacker-influenced parameter with no range check in the shown code; the sole guard, `while (line1 <= line2)` at line 29, admits the witness line1=0, line2=0 (u_save(1,2) at line 25 succeeds, so line 26 is not taken). Line 33 then indexes the 1-based buffer line array at 0, which is out of range for every buffer, producing an OOB read (CWE-125). The same unconstrained value flows through curwin->w_cursor.lnum into ml_append at line 36, making the destination index invalid as well.

assumptions: linenr_T is the signed Vim line type; valid buffer line indices are 1..linecount, so index 0 or any value above linecount is out of range.
ml_get(line1) reads the buffer's line storage at the given index, and ml_append(lnum, ...) inserts a line at the given destination index.
u_save(n, n + 1) returns FAIL only when the undo record cannot be created; n=1 passes it.
limitations: The unseen caller (ex-command address parser) is not part of this snippet; if it clamps line1/line2/n to the buffer range, the out-of-bounds path is unreachable and the concern reduces to defensive hardening with no CWE.

When vim_strsave returns NULL (line 34), the loop still advances line1/line2/cursor and lines 50/52 report count as if lines were appended; this is an accounting inconsistency, not a confirmed memory hazard.
Signed overflow in `count = line2 - line1 + 1` (line 6) would require values near LONG_MAX and is not reachable at real buffer sizes.
No format-string, command, SQL, header, or crypto sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled catalog_entries value (ph.catalog_entries, line 27) is capped by the guard at line 28 to catalog_size <= INT_MAX/4 = 536870911. Under that bound, catalog_size * 4 never wraps (max 2147483644 < 2^32 and < INT_MAX), the bdrv_pread length on line 35 equals the allocation size, and the loop on lines 40-41 reaches at most index 536870910 inside a 536870911-element buffer. The minimal overflowing witness (catalog_entries = 0x40000001 or any value >= 536870912) is rejected at lines 28-31, so no out-of-bounds access or integer overflow is reachable in the shown code. Remaining concerns (unvalidated tracks/nb_sectors with no sink in this function, a possible ~2 GiB allocation and read, and short-read semantics) are hardening/out-of-scope issues, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: bdrv_pread returns 0 on success and a negative errno on failure, performing a full read or returning an error (raw reads past EOF are converted to -EIO), which makes the `ret < 0` checks on lines 12 and 36 complete guards for the buffer contents.
s->catalog_size is uint32_t, so the comparison on line 28 and the multiplication on lines 33/35 are performed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic.
bs->opaque (s) is zero-initialized by the QEMU block layer, so s->catalog_bitmap is NULL on the line 12/16 failure paths and g_free(NULL) at line 47 is safe.
struct parallels_header is packed and 64 bytes, so the header read (line 11) and catalog read at offset 64 (line 35) do not overlap.
limitations: s->tracks = le32_to_cpu(ph.tracks) on line 25 is unvalidated (can be 0 or arbitrarily large) and bs->total_sectors = le32_to_cpu(ph.nb_sectors) on line 23 is unvalidated, but neither value reaches a dangerous operation (division, indexing, allocation) anywhere in the shown code; any downstream crash would be in an unseen function and is out of scope.

Accepting catalog_entries = 536870911 forces g_malloc of ~2 GiB (line 33) and a matching bdrv_pread (line 35); impact is transient large allocation/read and only a DoS if allocation aborts, which is a resource-consumption hardening concern without a confirmed failure in the shown code (no CWE attached).

The code checks only `ret < 0` after each bdrv_pread (lines 12, 36), not exact byte counts; if the linked QEMU version allowed short positive reads, partially uninitialized stack/heap data could be processed. This is not confirmed under the assumed bdrv_pread contract and is noted only for completeness.
No injection, weak-crypto, file-handling, or authentication sinks exist in the shown code; bs->read_only = 1 on line 9 is a policy statement, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: When axis_ != -1, input_min/input_max are admitted at rank 0, so dim_size(0) (lines 33/37) already reads out of bounds on scalar shapes, and if that value equals depth the per-channel gradient functor reached at lines 60-66 indexes these 1-element scalar tensors as depth-length vectors, producing an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.snippet:
f(ctx->eigen_device<Device>(),
        gradient.template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
        input.template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
        &input_min_tensor, &input_max_tensor,
        input_backprop->template flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(axis_ - 1),
        input_min_backprop->template flat<T>(),
        input_max_backprop->template flat<T>());
evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled scalar input_min/input_max tensors admitted by the rank-0||rank-1 check (lines 20-30) are passed by pointer to the per-channel gradient functor, which indexes them as depth-length vectors in a loop over num_channels == depth. With input shape [2] and axis_=0, the scalar buffers contain 1 element but are read at indices 0..1, so index 1 reads out of bounds; the missing rank-1 guard is the insufficiency that lets the scalar reach this sink.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(
          ctx, input_min_tensor.dim_size(0) == depth,
          errors::InvalidArgument("min has incorrect size, expected ", depth,
                                  " was ", input_min_tensor.dim_size(0)));
evidence.reason: On a rank-0 input_min_tensor, dim_size(0) violates TensorShape's documented contract (0 <= d < dims()) and reads uninitialized/out-of-bounds shape state. When that value coincidentally equals depth (e.g., depth=2), the guard passes and the per-channel functor call at lines 60-66 performs the out-of-bounds vector reads described in the first evidence item.

assumptions: TensorShape::dim_size(d) requires 0 <= d < dims(); calling it on a scalar is a contract violation and an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read.

The per-channel gradient functor reached at lines 60-66 iterates i from 0 to input.dimension(1)-1 (depth) and reads input_min_tensor->vec<T>()/input_max_tensor->vec<T>() at index i, per the TensorFlow kernel contract of this call site.
axis_ and the tensor shapes are supplied by the model/graph and are attacker-controllable in an untrusted SavedModel/graph scenario.
Line numbers are relative to the shown Compute method (line 1 = 'void Compute(...) override {').
limitations: The axis_ == -1 branch with rank-1 input_min/input_max calls scalar<T>() inside an unseen library function; whether this aborts or reads only the first element is not determinable from the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.

The dim_size(0)==depth equality on a scalar may reject the input on some builds before the per-channel functor executes; however, the dim_size(0) call itself is already an out-of-bounds read whenever a scalar reaches line 33/37, and the read materializes when the guard passes.

verdict.summary: The shown __bpf_ringbuf_reserve includes the protective size cap at line 7 (size <= RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ = 1<<24) and the space check at line 26 (new_prod_pos - cons_pos <= rb->mask). The cap keeps len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8) <= 2^24+8, so the u64->u32 narrowing at line 10 is lossless, size + header cannot overflow u64, and the line-26 check guarantees every header write (lines 33-34) and the returned size-bounded region (line 41) stay within the ring memory without overlapping unconsumed records. No attacker-controlled value admitted by the shown guards can reach the sinks with an out-of-bounds index, size, or truncated length.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is the kernel constant (1<<24), so the maximum admitted size is 2^24 and the maximum len = round_up(2^24+8, 8) = 2^24+8 fits u32; the constant itself is not defined in the shown snippet.

struct bpf_ringbuf is created with a power-of-two ring size and a data buffer of mask+1 bytes (mask = ring_size-1), and producer/consumer positions are monotonic counters guarded by the shown spinlock and acquire/release barriers.
bpf_ringbuf_rec_pg_off() returns a page offset derived from rb and hdr and is trusted (helper not shown).
limitations: If RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ were greater than 2^32-8, the u32 len assignment at line 10 could truncate attacker-controlled size and enable an out-of-bounds write via lines 31-34/41; this is excluded by the kernel constant and is outside the shown code.

The theoretical unsigned-long producer-position wraparound at line 21 is not attacker-reachable (it would require on the order of 2^40 maximum-size reservations), and the modular subtraction at line 26 remains exact for outstanding amounts far below 2^63, so it cannot admit an oversized reservation.
Line 7 would be a one-line missing check in older kernel versions, but it is present in the analyzed code; a version without it is not the program under analysis.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf passes the caller-supplied int len through rlen into memcpy without validating its sign; a negative len admitted by the remain >= len guard is converted to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t, causing an out-of-bounds read/write from dp->data and into buf.

evidence.reason: The unvalidated int parameter len flows into rlen at line 12; the guard at line 11 ('remain >= len') admits negative lengths whenever remain >= len (witness: len = -1, remain = 10), so rlen = -1 is converted to (size_t)-1 in this memcpy, copying ~SIZE_MAX bytes — an out-of-bounds read from dp->data and out-of-bounds write past buf (CWE-787). The only other check, 'remain <= 0' at line 14, does not constrain the sign of len.

assumptions: dp->data points to storage of at least dp->logicalSize bytes, and dp->pos / dp->logicalSize are consistent library-managed state.
buf is sized by the caller to hold at least len bytes per the getBuf contract.
limitations: The concrete caller that could supply an attacker-controlled negative len is outside the shown code; per scope, the parameter reaching the memcpy sink inside this function is sufficient for reachability.
If every real caller in a given build guarantees len >= 0, the flaw is latent (defense-in-depth gap), but nothing in the shown code enforces that bound.
Only the negative-length memcpy issue was confirmed; no injection, crypto, or authz vulnerabilities exist in this snippet.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled input reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or file sink in the shown code. The only sink, dp_packet_batch_refill() at lines 18 and 22, writes at index pb_idx, which is bounded by the strict loop condition pb_idx < pb_cnt and the batch capacity invariant (dp_packet_batch_size <= DP_PACKET_BATCH_SIZE); the maximum admitted index is pb_cnt - 1, below capacity. Fragment parsing and packet consumption occur inside unseen helpers, so helper-level bugs are out of scope.

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH iterates pb_idx from 0 while pb_idx < pb_cnt, incrementing by 1, as in OVS.
dp_packet_batch_size(pb) returns a count no larger than the compile-time batch capacity (DP_PACKET_BATCH_SIZE), and every slot in pb->packets is a valid, non-NULL dp_packet.
ipf_handle_frag() returns true only when pkt was consumed (stored, freed, or reassembled) and false only when pkt remains owned by the caller, so refilling at line 18 never writes a freed pointer.
limitations: The body of ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag/ipf_handle_frag is not shown; any parsing, freeing, or reassembly defect inside those helpers (e.g., OOB header reads or use-after-free of fragments) is out of scope for this verdict.

The exact definition of the DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH macro is not shown; if its condition or index accounting differed from the standard OVS definition, the loop-bound analysis would need revisiting.
A NULL or invalid pkt (C3), or a helper freeing pkt while returning false (C2), would only be triggerable by an out-of-scope caller or helper and cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
Concurrency/TOCTOU between the unlocked validity checks (lines 10-14) and the locked handle path (line 16) is not demonstrable as attacker-triggerable from the shown lines.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in _inplace_src_spans: the partial-coverage branch writes len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x bytes into the mask buffer at base with no bounds check against the mask row capacity. len (L15) is derived entirely from caller-supplied span coordinates; for any span with coverage other than 0x00/0xff (or 0xff with len < run_length) the else branch at L82-87 executes, so spans whose run extends past the mask width overflow the buffer (e.g., spans={{x:0,coverage:0x80},{x:W+K,coverage:0x0}} on a W-byte row writes W+K bytes).

evidence.reason: len is the unvalidated difference spans[1].x - spans[0].x (L15) of caller-supplied, attacker-controlled span coordinates and reaches the mask write at L83-86 with the write size equal to len. For a partial-coverage span (guards at L16 and L53 both fail; L84 only requires len > 1), spans = {{x:0, coverage:0x80}, {x:W+K, coverage:0x0}} with a W-byte mask row yields len = W+K, so memset writes W+K bytes at base and m advances W+K, overflowing the row by K bytes. No comparison of m/len against the mask width exists anywhere in the shown code, so the missing guard is a capacity check on the write; CWE-787.

assumptions: The mask buffer created by the unseen caller contains one row of W bytes (r->mask at L6), and spans/num_spans are supplied by the caller; in real cairo consumers span geometry derives from untrusted rendering input (document/canvas coordinates).
The pixman_image_composite32 calls (L19-49, L56-76, L94-114) are treated as pass-through sinks, not analyzed for their own memory behavior.
limitations: Separate, independently confirmed off-by-one: for num_spans == 1 the guard at L9 admits it, the loop body executes once and reads spans[1] one element past the array (L15), and the post-loop flush reads one element past the end after spans++ (L92). Kept out of the CWE array to preserve a single primary finding; the garbage len it yields can also feed the L83-86 write path.
Signed overflow of the int subtraction spans[1].x - spans[0].x (L15) with extreme coordinates is undefined behavior and compounds the write-size issue.

Whether a specific real-world caller can produce spans extending beyond the mask width is not shown in this snippet; per the analysis rules the caller-derived length reaching the shown memory operation is treated as attacker-controlled input.
The narrowing of int coverage to uint8_t at L83 is truncation only and has no memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in QPaintEngineEx::stroke: the type-driven point walk trusts the caller-supplied QVectorPath element-type buffer without validating per-element geometry. A types entry of QPainterPath::CurveToElement makes the CurveToElement case read points[0..5] (6 qreals) while the only guard, the while condition at line 111 with lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1), guarantees only that at least 2 qreals remain; e.g., elementCount()==1 with a single CurveToElement type and a 2-qreal points buffer reads 4 qreals past the buffer at lines 124-126 (and identically at lines 184-186 in the cosmetic branch), causing a heap/stack OOB read while painting attacker-controlled vector data.

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced QVectorPath supplies types/points/pointCount (lines 84-86) with no validation that a CurveToElement is backed by 6 qreals; the only guard, `points < lastPoint` with `lastPoint = points + (pointCount<<1)` (lines 88, 111), admits any state with at least 2 qreals remaining, so the witness elementCount()==1 + types[0]==CurveToElement + 2-qreal points buffer passes the guard and reads points[2..5] 4 qreals past the 2-entry buffer in the cubicTo call.

The cosmetic-pen branch repeats the same unguarded 3-point read: the while condition at line 167 (end pointer from line 88) guarantees only that >= 2 qreals remain, whereas `CurveToElement` dereferences points[0..2] (6 qreals); the identical witness (elementCount()==1, types[0]==CurveToElement, 2-qreal points buffer) reads 4 qreals out of bounds at lines 184-186.

assumptions: The caller of QPaintEngineEx::stroke can supply a QVectorPath whose elements()/points()/elementCount() buffers reach attacker-influenced data (e.g., vector data parsed from untrusted documents); the shown code itself performs no consistency validation between the type array and point array.

QVectorPath's well-formed contract is that points() holds 2*elementCount() qreals and each CurveToElement occupies 3 type slots with 6 qreals; the shown code relies on that invariant without verifying it.
limitations: The same unvalidated types input can also cause a non-terminating loop (CWE-835): a first type value of QPainterPath::CurveToDataElement or any unrecognized value hits `default: break;` (lines 131-132 / 193-194), advancing neither points nor types; recorded here rather than as a second CWE.

Integer overflow of `pointCount<<1` (line 88) or `path.elementCount()+4` (line 13) requires elementCount near INT_MAX and a multi-gigabyte allocation, not plausibly attacker-reachable; allocation-failure DoS is not attacker-volume-controlled.
qDebug() (line 4) is compiled out unless QT_DEBUG_DRAW and is not a security-relevant serialization sink.
Well-formed paths built through Qt's public path-building API (moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo) keep the walk in bounds; the OOB read requires a caller supplying an internally inconsistent type/point buffer.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor never verifies that input_indices_in has one column per input_shape dimension; the per-row read width passed to ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor is the attacker-controlled input rank, so indices with fewer columns than the rank cause a heap out-of-bounds read (e.g., 1-column indices with a rank-2 input shape).

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor<Device>()(
                                context, input_shape, output_shape,
                                input_indices_in.matrix<int64>(),
                                result_indices->matrix<int64>()));
evidence.reason: input_indices_in (shape [nnz,k], line 22) and input_shape_in (rank r, line 20) are attacker-controlled op inputs with no check that k == r: line 6 admits any matrix, and the total-count guard at line 67 compares dense elements, not per-row width. Sink: the functor reads input_indices(i,j) for j < input_shape.dims() = r, but the row buffer has only k columns. Concrete witness that passes every shown OP_REQUIRES (lines 6,10,14,41,57,67,95): indices shape {1,1} = [[0]], input_shape = [2,3] (dense_size 6, rank 2), target_shape = [6] (6 == 6). The functor then reads input_indices(0,1) — one int64 past the end of the 1-element heap buffer — a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: SparseReshape op inputs (input_indices_in, input_shape_in, target_shape_in) are user/attacker-supplied tensors, per the standard TensorFlow kernel threat model.

ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor follows its documented contract: per non-zero row i it reads input_shape.dims() entries of input_indices and writes output_shape.dims() entries of result_indices; the shown code therefore fixes the read width to the unvalidated input rank while the input buffer's column count is unvalidated.
TensorShape stores dims as given in release builds (set_dim validation is DCHECK-only), so negative dims from input_shape_in can reach downstream arithmetic.
limitations: Negative input_shape_in entries (e.g., [-1,4] with target [-1]) make dense_size = -1 and can pass lines 57 and 67, reaching the functor with negative dims; the standard helper's writes stay column-bounded (output_rank), so this produces corrupted values or a build-dependent CHECK/abort rather than a confirmed in-scope memory corruption - no CWE assigned.

Integer overflow in product *= size (line 45) cannot be shown to defeat a memory operation in this code: line 51 rejects non-positive products before the division, and line 67 compares via checked num_elements().

Over-long shape vectors (> TensorShape's dim limit) or huge nnz/output_rank can trigger framework CHECK-aborts or large allocations; DoS only, scaling with the attacker's input size, not a confirmed vulnerability here.
Line 30 and 86 use int loop counters against int64 bounds; any mismatch requires shape vectors with > 2^31 elements (~16 GB of tensor data), deemed unreachable attacker input.

The byte-level OOB access executes inside the functor invoked at lines 96-99; the shown code is the site that forwards the unvalidated rank/columns pair, which is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse validates only 3 bytes before memcpy(&cap, pnt+1, sizeof(struct capability)) copies 6 bytes (~4 bytes past the message end) — an attacker-controlled over-read (CWE-125). Independently, when PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is set, a MultiProtocol capability ('continue' at line 57-58) skips the only pointer advance (line 104), so 'while (pnt < end)' spins forever — an attacker-triggered non-terminating loop (CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled pnt/length bound the read region to end = pnt + length (line 11). The only prior guard, 'if (pnt + 3 > end)' (line 16), admits any remaining length >= 3, but sizeof(struct capability) is 6, so the copy reads pnt[1..6] and needs 7 valid bytes. Witness: a 3-byte capability (action + code + length=0) passes line 16 (pnt + 3 == end) and reads pnt[3..6], 4 bytes past end — a 4-byte out-of-bounds read consumed at lines 53-54 and mirrored into debug logs (lines 67-72).

Attacker sets cap.code == CAPABILITY_CODE_MP (line 51). If the operator configured PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY, this 'continue' jumps to 'while (pnt < end)' (line 13) without executing 'pnt += cap.length + 3' (line 104), leaving pnt/end unchanged; since line 16 already proved pnt + 3 <= end, pnt < end stays true forever — a non-terminating loop and BGP-processing hang (CWE-835).

assumptions: struct capability is the standard Quagga/FRR layout (u_char code; u_char length; u_char mpc[4]) with sizeof == 6 and no padding; the mpc member (afi/safi) used at lines 53-54 implies at least 4 bytes of payload after code/length.
pnt/length describe the attacker-supplied capability section of a received BGP OPEN or CAPABILITY message, bounded by the BGP maximum message size.
bounded constructs: cap.length is u_char so cap.length + 3 cannot overflow; bgp_size_t is unsigned.
limitations: PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is a non-default operator setting, so the CWE-835 hang is configuration-gated; without the flag the loop advances and terminates.

The shown code does not include the caller, so the allocation layout around the over-read is unknown; whether the 4-byte over-read stays inside a larger stream buffer (limited stale-data disclosure) or crosses an allocation/page boundary (crash) cannot be fully resolved here.
The afi/safi whitelist (lines 61-65) plus safi remap (75-76) fully constrains the afc_recv/afc/afc_nego indexing (lines 80-90), so no array-index OOB finding is reported.
Log writes use constant format strings with numeric/internal arguments; no format-string or log-injection finding.

verdict.summary: In stl_remove_degenerate, neighbor indices read from stl->neighbors_start[facet] at lines 45/46/56 are guarded only by an equality test against the -1 sentinel before being used as subscripts (lines 62-63, 66-67, 74). The guard admits any out-of-range value such as neighbor1 == L (with an L-element neighbors_start array), so line 62 performs a heap out-of-bounds write; the parameter `facet` is likewise used to index facet_start with no bounds check (e.g., line 14), giving an OOB read. Both indices are derived from attacker-controlled STL mesh data, making this heap memory corruption reachable in a file-parsing library.

evidence.reason: neighbor1 is read from stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge1] at line 45 (file-derived connectivity data) and is used as an array index here after only the sentinel test `if(neighbor1 != -1)` at line 61. That guard admits every value except exactly -1; with neighbors_start holding L elements, the concrete value neighbor1 = L passes the guard and writes beyond the allocation, a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). No range check against stl->stats.number_of_facets exists anywhere between line 45 and this sink.

The parameter `facet` is used to index the L-element facet_start array with no bounds validation in the shown code (only `if (stl->error) return;` precedes it at line 12). A caller-supplied value facet = L indexes facet_start[L] on this memcmp read, producing an out-of-bounds read of sizeof(stl_vertex) bytes (CWE-125); facet also reaches the same unchecked subscript at lines 45-46 and 56-59.

assumptions: facet_start and neighbors_start are dynamically allocated arrays of stl->stats.number_of_facets elements each.
Each stl_neighbors record contains int neighbor[3] and int which_vertex_not[3], and facet vertices are three separately addressable stl_vertex values.
The mesh contents (vertex coordinates, facet counts, connectivity) ultimately originate from an attacker-controlled STL file.
limitations: The pass-through calls stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, neighbor2/neighbor1/neighbor3) at lines 49/52/73 can transmit -1 (or another unchecked index) into the unseen callee; the dereference itself is not in the shown code, so any fault there is out of scope for this analysis.

The real caller of stl_remove_degenerate typically bounds `facet` to [0, L); the OOB-read finding (CWE-125) relies on the parameter-origin standard and on an uninstrumented caller path, so it is reported as the secondary finding.

Whether the library can actually materialize an out-of-range (non-sentinel) neighbor value depends on earlier unseen connectivity-building passes; the shown function itself never bounds neighbors, so the OOB-write finding holds within the shown control flow.
The printf at line 20 uses a fixed literal format string and is not an injection sink; no other injection, crypto, or access-control issues are present.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds read in dostor()'s FTPWHO block: when the attacker-supplied STOR filename has strlen(name) exactly equal to sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename), the else branch computes &name[sl - sizeof - 1U], which underflows to name[-1] and memcpy (lines 153-155) reads one byte before the name buffer.

evidence.reason: name is attacker-controlled (STOR argument); sl = strlen(name) at line 141 is the untrusted length. The guard at line 149 (sl < sizeof) admits sl >= sizeof into this branch, but the branch is only in-bounds for sl >= sizeof+1. Witness: a filename with strlen(name) == sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) makes sl - sizeof - 1U wrap to SIZE_MAX, so the source pointer is name-1 and the memcpy reads indices [-1, sl-2] — a 1-byte out-of-bounds read whose result is published into the ftpwho shared-memory record; the final name character is also dropped.

assumptions: FTPWHO is compiled in and shm_data_cur is non-NULL (the block starting at line 139-140); otherwise the memcpy is compiled out.
name is a standalone NUL-terminated buffer as used at lines 141-155; the shown code imposes no length cap before the guard at line 149.
Earlier guards (lines 19-74) constrain type/resume/guest/disk-sanity only and do not limit filename length.
limitations: Use-after-close: file descriptor f is closed at line 173 and reused by FSTATFS(f, ...) at line 179; exploitation requires fd-number reuse by a concurrent open within the window, so no concrete attacker-controlled trigger is demonstrable in the shown flow.

Possible uninitialized read of ulhandler.total_uploaded at lines 192 and 250 when ul_init fails (lines 170-172); whether ul_init left the field uninitialized is outside the shown code, so it cannot be confirmed.

The else branch at lines 153-155 also produces a non-NUL-terminated filename missing its last character; combined with the single-byte pre-buffer read this caps impact at low (stats corruption / small disclosure), or a crash only if name[-1] falls on an unmapped page.
