Path/symlink and TOCTOU considerations involving checknamesanity, get_atomic_file and rename depend on code outside this function and are not confirmed.
No loops exist in the shown code, so no loop-bound analysis applies.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate indexes stl->neighbors_start with neighbor values taken from the facet connectivity table after checking only that they differ from -1. A stale or file-influenced neighbor value outside [0, number_of_facets) passes the guard and causes an out-of-bounds heap write at lines 61-62, 65-66, and 73 (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: neighbor1 is read at line 45 from stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge1] (data derived from attacker-controlled STL content and mutated by this function's removals) and is used here as the index of stl->neighbors_start after only a '!= -1' check at line 60. That guard admits every value except -1, including neighbor1 = number_of_facets (one past the end) or -2, so the write lands outside the heap allocation (CWE-787).

neighbor3 is read at line 55 from the same connectivity table and guarded only by 'neighbor3 != -1' at line 71; a value >= number_of_facets or <= -2 passes that guard and indexes stl->neighbors_start out of bounds when writing -1 (CWE-787).

assumptions: stl is non-NULL and facet_start/neighbors_start are each allocated with number_of_facets entries (library invariant).
facet is assumed by the caller to be in [0, number_of_facets); it is not validated in the shown code.
which_vertex_not[*] is assumed to hold values in {0,1,2}, so (vnot + 1) % 3 stays in 0..2 without signed overflow.
vertex and neighbor arrays each have exactly 3 elements.
limitations: The shown code does not demonstrate the exact producer sequence that places an out-of-range neighbor value; it relies on file-derived connectivity data and on stale indices left by stl_remove_facet calls at lines 22 and 69, per the rubric's allowed provenance. This bounds confidence to 0.7.

Out-of-bounds access through the caller-supplied facet parameter (lines 14-17, 45-46, 69) depends on an unseen caller passing an invalid index; the caller-side invariant is assumed, so it is noted but not a finding.
stl_update_connects_remove_1 at lines 49, 52, and 72 receives the same unvalidated neighbor index, but its internal sinks are outside the shown code, so no independent CWE is attached.
printf at line 20 uses a constant format string; no format-string injection exists.

verdict.summary: OP_GETUPVAR forms the register pointer regs + a (line 249) from the bytecode operand a and writes through it unconditionally at lines 253/256 with no a < irep->nregs bound check; the guard at line 252 constrains only the upvalue index b and protects neither branch of the write. With nregs=4 (attacker-chosen, used by mrb_stack_extend at line 474) and operand a=255, the else-branch writes an 8-byte value ~2 KB past the 4-slot frame — an out-of-bounds heap write on the VM stack (CWE-787), reachable by executing a crafted irep. The same operand-trust defect recurs in OP_ENTER (800/804/811), OP_APOST (1491-1507), OP_HASH (1560/1573), and irep->reps[b] indexing (1597/1678).

evidence.reason: The register index a is decoded from the attacker-controlled irep bytecode (function parameter proc, line 4) and reaches the pointer arithmetic regs + a at line 249 unvalidated; the frame capacity is the equally attacker-chosen irep->nregs, extended at lines 474/515/933/1693, and no a < nregs check exists. The guard at line 252 (e && b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e)) admits every value of a — it only selects which value is written — and both branches write through *regs_a (lines 253 and 256). Concrete witness: irep with nregs=4 and OP_GETUPVAR operands a=255, b=0, c=0; the else-branch writes mrb_nil_value() (8 bytes) at regs+255*8, ~2 KB beyond the 4-slot frame, an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787).

assumptions: Untrusted bytecode can reach this function: mruby's documented mrb_load_irep/.mrb loading path executes serialized irep from files/network/user data, so proc->body.irep and all operands are attacker-controlled.
regs = mrb->c->ci->stack (line 40) is the heap-allocated fiber VM stack; the current frame provides on the order of irep->nregs slots, sized by mrb_stack_extend at lines 474/515/933/1693.
uvenv may return NULL for an out-of-range upvalue level, and MRB_ENV_LEN(e) is the environment stack length, so the else-branch at line 256 is reachable for the witness.
limitations: The same missing operand-vs-nregs validation affects other opcodes (OP_ENTER register writes at 800/804 and 811-813, OP_APOST else-loop writes at 1504-1507, OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD lim at 1560/1573, OP_ARRAY2 at 1417, irep->reps[b] at 1597/1678, pool[b]/syms[b] indexing); these are the same root-cause class and are not reported as separate CWEs.

If the embedding never executes bytecode other than compiler-generated irep, the compiler invariant (operands < nregs) makes these operands trusted; that invariant is not enforced anywhere in the shown code and cannot be verified here, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than a protecting check.
OP_DEBUG's printf (line 1748) uses a fixed format string with %d operands and is debug-only; no log/format-injection finding.
mrb_format calls at lines 823 and 853 use fixed '%v' formats; no attacker-controlled format string.
The mrb_assert at line 308 (OP_JMPUW) is a debug-only check and is not a security control in release builds.
OOB reads via pool/syms/reps indexing (CWE-125 class) are the same bytecode-trust root cause and are deliberately not added as a second CWE.

verdict.summary: Heap-buffer-overflow in ReadCINImage: the per-row read size `length` is derived from attacker-controlled `image->depth` (= channel[0].bits_per_pixel, 0-255) via GetBytesPerRow (line 379, up to ~95.6 bytes per pixel for 3 channels), while the `pixels` destination is sized only for the fixed 32-bit RGB quantum (~12 bytes per pixel; `extent` computed at line 377 is discarded at line 378). The only guard, line 348, bounds columns*rows against file size, not `length` against the buffer. A crafted file (bits_per_pixel=255, columns=100000, rows=1, >=9,562,504 bytes of raster data) passes all checks and makes ReadBlobStream at line 395 write ~9.56 MB into a ~1.2 MB heap buffer, corrupting memory (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Per-row read length is computed unboundedly from two attacker-controlled values: image->columns (channel[0].pixels_per_line, up to 2^32-1) and image->depth (channel[0].bits_per_pixel read from the file at line 134, assigned at line 340, 0-255). For depth=255 and 3 channels, GetBytesPerRow yields ~96 bytes per pixel, whereas the destination `pixels` buffer (AcquireQuantumInfo at line 371, 32-bit quantum set at line 374, RGB) is only ~12 bytes per pixel; the extent that would prove this mismatch is computed at line 377 and explicitly discarded at line 378 `(void) extent;`.

Sink write: ReadBlobStream writes `length` bytes read from the attacker file directly into `pixels`. Witness reaching it: bits_per_pixel=255, pixels_per_line=100000, lines_per_image=1, image_offset<=2048, and a file containing >=9,562,504 raster bytes. The only guard, line 348 `((MagickSizeType) image->columns*image->rows/8) > GetBlobSize(image)`, admits this witness (12500 <= ~9.6MB) because it bounds columns*rows against file size, not `length` against the ~1,200,000-byte pixel buffer, so the first loop iteration (y=0, line 387) writes ~8.36 MB past the end of `pixels`; the count==length break at line 396 is checked only after the corrupting write.

assumptions: Library contract of GetQuantumExtent (bytes = columns * channels * quantum/8) and GetBytesPerRow (pad8(columns*channels*depth/8)); the buffer returned by GetQuantumPixels is sized for the 32-bit RGB quantum (~4 bytes per pixel per channel).
64-bit build with size_t width covering columns*rows without wrap; the depth-vs-quantum overflow finding does not depend on this.
ReadBlobStream writes the bytes it reads into the caller buffer `data`.
limitations: User-data block (lines 330-337): user_length is compared only to total blob size, so a partial read can leave uninitialized bytes in the dpx:user.data profile; this is not counted as a confirmed finding because any file short enough to cause the partial read also triggers the skip-loop EOF throw (line 359-360) or UnexpectedEndOfFile (line 412-413) before the image/profile can be exported.

Pixel-cache amplification: line 348 permits allocations of up to ~128x the file size (columns*rows <= 8*blobsize, ~16 bytes/pixel); this is a bounded DoS-style concern handled by the ResourceLimitError path at lines 362-366, not a memory-safety finding.

On 32-bit builds the columns*rows product at line 348 can wrap (e.g., columns=rows=65536), but SetImageExtent at line 361 performs its own overflow/allocation failure checks, so no independent exploit is confirmed.
File-derived strings copied into image properties (lines 86-318) could embed control characters; no concrete injection sink (log/header/SQL/command) exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The array-index writes at lines 9, 19, and 40 are bounded by visible guards: line 7 restricts field overrides to stored field indices, lines 12-14 cap member growth at MEMBER_MAX_COUNT (each insertion adds exactly one entry, so stored indices remain < vector sizes), and line 18 restricts the metamethod index to a valid framework range. No concrete attacker-controlled value reaches a sink out of bounds in the shown code, so no confirmed vulnerability is established.

assumptions: MEMBER_MAX_COUNT is a compile-time constant with a value below 2^30 (0x40000000), so the INDEX_TYPE bit used by _make_method_idx/_isfield/_member_idx cannot collide with real indices; its value is not present in the shown code.
SS->GetMetaMethodIdxByName returns -1 for non-metamethod keys and an index in [0, MT_COUNT) for metamethod names (used at line 18-19).
_members stores only index values produced by this function (lines 36 and 47); SQObjectPtrMap::Get/NewSlot/CountUsed behave as a normal key-value map, and _defaultvalues/_methods are never shrunk.
limitations: If MEMBER_MAX_COUNT were >= 2^30, inserting that many members would flip the INDEX_TYPE bit on a stored field index, making _isfield return false and causing line 40 to index _methods with a masked value (potential OOB write, CWE-787); the trigger depends on an unshown constant, so it is not confirmed from the shown code.

A closure-valued NewSlot targeting an existing field of a locked class passes the line 5 guard and overwrites the field default at line 9, which undermines the immutability comment at lines 5-6; the static-table exception is documented intent and the security impact depends on instance-read semantics outside the shown code, so it is treated as a semantic/robustness concern, not a confirmed CWE.
Resource exhaustion by member growth is capped by the line 12-14 guard; residual DoS risk depends on the unshown magnitude of MEMBER_MAX_COUNT.
Refcount handling of the cloned closure (_base) at lines 24-26 assumes a matching release in unshown destruction code.

verdict.summary: The loop guard at parse_die line 6 computes 'abbrev->count - 1' without checking count > 0. An attacker-crafted DWARF abbreviation with count == 0 makes the unsigned subtraction wrap to SIZE_MAX, so the loop executes with i = 0, 1, 2, ... and performs out-of-bounds writes into die->attr_values[i] (line 7) and out-of-bounds reads of abbrev->defs[i] (line 9), causing memory corruption from a malicious input file.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < abbrev->count - 1; i++) {
		memset(&die->attr_values[i], 0, sizeof(die->attr_values[i]));
evidence.reason: abbrev->count is attacker-controlled (derived from the .debug_abbrev section by an unseen caller) and is used with no validation in the guard. For count == 0 the unsigned expression 'abbrev->count - 1' wraps to 2^64-1, so the guard admits i = 0, 1, 2, ... instead of none; the first iterations reach the memset write at line 7 and the &abbrev->defs[i] read at line 9 past the end of any finite (including zero-size or NULL) attr_values/defs arrays, producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and read. A guard such as 'abbrev->count > 0' or checking i + 1 < abbrev->count is absent.

assumptions: abbrev->count is an unsigned 64-bit value and i is size_t, so 'abbrev->count - 1' wraps to 2^64-1 when count == 0.

die->attr_values and abbrev->defs are finite caller-allocated arrays whose capacity for count >= 2 is not visible in the shown code; the finding relies only on the count == 0 case exhausting any finite capacity.
comp_dir and line_info_offset logic (lines 14-36) is safe as shown: the form whitelist, NULL checks, and strdup/ht_up_insert handling are correct.
limitations: Unchecked return of parse_attr_value at line 9: if it can return NULL on a malformed input, the next iteration calls parse_attr_value(NULL, buf_end - NULL, ...) — whether NULL is returned is determined by unseen code, so this is not a confirmed finding.
strdup(comp_dir) at line 30 requires attribute->string.content to be NUL-terminated; termination is established only by the unseen attribute parser, so a potential overread is unconfirmed.

buf_end - buf at line 9 (ptrdiff_t to size_t conversion) would become a huge size if buf ever advanced past buf_end; nothing in the shown code validates this invariant, but the negative-difference-producing path depends on unseen parse_attr_value behavior.
No injection, crypto, or file/access-control sinks are present in the shown code; the only confirmed class is memory safety via the loop-bound underflow.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf forwards an unvalidated, possibly negative rlen as the memcpy size: a caller-supplied negative len (line 12, admitted by the remain >= len comparison at line 11) or a negative remain (line 17, admitted because line 14 tests only remain == 0) is implicitly converted from int to size_t at line 20, turning the copy into a ~2^32/2^64-byte out-of-bounds write (e.g., len = -1 with remain >= 0).

evidence.reason: The copy size is attacker-influenced and unvalidated: the caller-supplied parameter len flows to rlen = len at line 12 whenever remain >= len (line 11 admits any len <= remain, including negatives), and a negative remain flows to rlen = remain at line 17 because the guard at line 14 excludes only remain == 0, not remain < 0. Any negative rlen is implicitly converted to size_t (CWE-195), so len = -1 with remain >= 0 yields rlen = -1 and a memcpy of (size_t)-1 bytes (0xFFFFFFFF/0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) from dp->data + dp->pos into buf, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); line 21 also moves dp->pos in the wrong direction. No len >= 0 or rlen >= 0 check exists anywhere before this sink.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the start of the shown snippet.
On valid entry, the module invariant 0 <= dp->pos <= dp->logicalSize holds, and dp->data is a valid allocation maintained by unseen code.
buf is assumed by the caller to hold at least len bytes when len is positive.
limitations: The len < 0 trigger requires the unseen caller to pass a negative length; if all real callers pass fixed positive sizes, this is defensive hardening rather than an exploitable path, which caps confidence at 0.7.

A negative remain (pos > logicalSize) would also make rlen negative through lines 10/17, but the shown branch bounds preserve pos <= logicalSize from any valid entry state, so that path depends on an invariant break in unseen code and is not independently confirmed.
No loop, injection, crypto, file, or authorization sinks exist in this function; the analysis is limited to the memcpy size handling.

verdict.summary: In get_visual_text(), the characterwise/blockwise branch computes *lenp as the unvalidated byte-column difference (VIsual.col - w_cursor.col + 1, lines 24/29) and uses it to form *pp + *lenp - 1 passed to mb_ptr2len() (line 35). Neither endpoint column is ever compared against STRLEN(*pp); the only guard, if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0 (line 31), checks the span start, not the span end. When the far-end column exceeds the line's byte length, mb_ptr2len() reads past the line's terminating NUL — a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Sink: *lenp (attacker-position-influenced via the global VIsual.col / w_cursor.col byte columns flowing through lines 24 and 29) is used as an unchecked byte offset into the line pointer *pp and dereferenced by mb_ptr2len(), which reads up to MB_MAXBYTES. The only guards in the shown path — if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0 (lines 31-32) and if (has_mbyte && *lenp > 0) (line 33) — admit the failing case: a nonzero first byte with any positive length. Witness: a 3-byte line "abc" (NUL at index 3), near col 0 with a nonzero first byte, far col 4 yields *lenp = 5, so *pp + 4 points one byte past the NUL and mb_ptr2len() performs an out-of-bounds heap read at line 35. No check anywhere bounds *lenp - 1 to STRLEN(*pp).

assumptions: Line buffers returned by ml_get_curline()/ml_get_pos() are NUL-terminated with the NUL within the allocation, so a read landing exactly on the NUL (col == STRLEN) is in-bounds and mb_ptr2len() returns 1 for a NUL byte.
VIsual.col and w_cursor.col are byte offsets rather than character or virtual (coladd) columns.
mb_ptr2len() reads at most MB_MAXBYTES bytes from the supplied pointer.
limitations: Producing a far-end byte column strictly greater than the line's byte length depends on editor-state machinery outside the shown code (e.g., virtualedit/exclusive-selection col adjustment, or a line shortened under an existing selection); in ordinary same-line charwise states both byte columns stay within the line and the worst-case read lands on the in-bounds NUL, so confidence is capped at 0.6.

In Vim's real callers, blockwise operators are routed through get_visual_block/getvcols rather than get_visual_text(); if that holds, the most likely over-length column states never reach this function.

Narrowing the 64-bit column difference into '*lenp' (int) could wrap negative only for lines longer than INT_MAX bytes (CWE-190); the resulting impact would manifest in unseen callers, so it is not independently confirmed here.
The returned *lenp can include the trailing NUL when the selection ends at/past end-of-line (off-by-one overcount); it has no memory-safety effect inside this function.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The substring scan is memory-safe: the guard 'if (size > r_size(op1))' (line 14) admits only size <= r_size(op1), so count = r_size(op1) - size >= 0, and the do-while 'while (count--)' executes exactly count+1 iterations, checking candidate positions 0..L-size (forward) or L-size..0 (backward). Every '*ptr' read and 'memcmp(ptr, pat, size)' therefore stays within [0, L-1]; the final pointer advance is never dereferenced. No injection, crypto, file, or authz sink exists in the shown code.

assumptions: Operator dispatch guarantees at least two operands for search, so op and op1 are valid operand-stack slots.
Ghostscript's push(2) macro redefines op to the new osp, so op[-1] and op[-3] index the pre-push operand slots, and the caller guarantees stack capacity.
String refs are interpreter-consistent: value.bytes points to a buffer of at least r_size bytes, so pat[0] (for size >= 1) and memcmp with size bytes read within the pattern's bounds.
limitations: On the final no-match iteration, ptr is advanced one-past-end (forward) or one-before-start (backward), which is unspecified C pointer behavior but is never dereferenced; no out-of-bounds access occurs.
The scan is worst-case O(L*size) comparisons but polynomial, iterative, and guaranteed to terminate; it is not a regex with unbounded quantifiers, so no ReDoS (CWE-1333) finding.
An out-of-bounds read would require a string ref whose r_size overstates its allocation, which the shown code cannot create; that invariant is maintained outside this function.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. This is the hardened esp_output_head: the page-frag write path (lines 38-60) is bounded by the allocsz gate at lines 19-21 (tailen <= ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE), the tailroom fast path by the exact tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb) check at line 24, the frag-descriptor write at line 56 by the MAX_SKB_FRAGS check at lines 30-31, and the COW path by skb_cow_data at line 79. No attacker-controlled length or index reaches a memory operation with a too-weak or absent guard within the shown control flow.

assumptions: esp->tailen >= 0 (int) as produced by the ESP output trailer computation; a negative tailen would require an out-of-scope caller bug.

ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE (defined outside the shown snippet) is chosen by the kernel fix for CVE-2023-46813 to be at most the x->xfrag page-frag backing capacity, so ALIGN(tailen) fits the refilled page; its exact value is not visible in the shown code.
esp_output_fill_trailer() writes at most esp->tailen bytes, matching the esp->tailen definition; its internals are not in the shown snippet.
skb length invariants (data_len <= len, len bounded by MTU/GSO ~64 KiB) hold, so the unsigned arithmetic at line 19 cannot wrap in practice.
skb_page_frag_refill() true return guarantees pfrag->offset + allocsize <= pfrag->size when allocsize does not exceed the backing page capacity.
limitations: Theoretical 32-bit wrap of 'skb->data_len + tailen' at line 19 could make allocsz small and bypass the line 20 gate, but reaching it requires an skb of ~4 GiB, contradicting kernel skb length bounds; no concrete witness is reachable, so it is not a finding.

If ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE exceeded the page-frag capacity, a tailen in (page_size, ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE] would overflow the xfrag page at lines 50/52; the shown code provides no check for this, but the kernel-defined constant is the protective bound and its value is outside the shown snippet.
A negative esp->tailen would misbehave in the unsigned comparisons at lines 19/24 and in pskb_put at line 87, but no shown path produces it (out-of-scope caller assumption).
pskb_put/skb_over_panic and skb_cow_data failure handling are defensive kernel mechanisms; no attacker-reachable inconsistency exists in the shown flow.
esp_output_fill_trailer, esp_output_encap, skb_page_frag_refill, and skb_cow_data internals are not in the shown code; their internal safety is relied on per the invariants above.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled input reaches a memory, injection, or crypto sink in uECC_sign_with_k. The nonce k is fully constrained by the line 23 guard (admits k in [1, n-1]; rejects 0 and k >= n) before every use; all word counts and byte sizes derive from trusted curve constants; tmp/s are uECC_MAX_WORDS words; signature writes are bounded by the 2*num_bytes contract; message_hash reads are delegated to the unseen bits2int helper (out of scope). The only visible defects are the reversed bcopy argument order in the little-endian branches (lines 61 and 77), which overwrite the caller's private-key buffer with the blinding value and fail to store the s component, causing invalid signatures on LE builds. Because the written bytes are internal constants/RNG output, the size equals the documented buffer sizes (no out-of-bounds access), and the trigger is compile-time rather than attacker-chosen input, these are recorded as robustness/correctness limitations, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: curve is a framework-internal trusted constant table; for the shipped curve set num_n_words <= num_words, num_words <= uECC_MAX_WORDS, num_n_words*sizeof(uECC_word_t) >= BITS_TO_BYTES(num_n_bits), num_n_bits == num_bytes*8, and num_words_bits is a multiple of the word size so EccPoint_mult's 2*num_words-word write equals 2*num_bytes bytes.
Callers honor the API size contracts: signature = 2*curve->num_bytes bytes, k = num_words words, private_key = BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes.
bits2int caps its read of message_hash at BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes (upstream helper contract; the helper body is not shown).
g_rng_function is framework-internal, and EccPoint_mult accepts initial_Z == 0 per its upstream contract.
limitations: Line 61 bcopy((uint8_t *) tmp, private_key, BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits)) copies tmp into private_key (bcopy is src,dst), reversing the intent shown by the parallel BE branch at line 63 (/* tmp = d */). It overwrites the caller's secret buffer with the blinding value (1 or an RNG value) and, because tmp never receives d, s = tmp * r yields invalid signatures. The written bytes and size are not attacker-controlled (size equals the documented private-key size; no out-of-bounds access), so it fails the taint requirement and is treated as a robustness/correctness defect, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Line 77 bcopy((uint8_t *) signature + curve->num_bytes, (uint8_t *) s, curve->num_bytes) is likewise reversed: the s component is copied from signature into s, so the signature's second half is never written (it retains the point's y-coordinate) and signatures are invalid on LE builds. Same taint analysis; in-bounds; recorded as a limitation.
Any out-of-bounds read of message_hash driven by hash_size (line 70) would occur inside the unseen bits2int helper; the shown call is a pure pass-through, so it is out of scope.
The function trusts caller-supplied k and private_key per the API contract; weak, biased, or reused nonces (or a weak g_rng_function) would break ECDSA security but originate outside the shown code.

The line 23 guard compares only num_n_words words of k; for hypothetical curves with num_words > num_n_words, high words of k would go unchecked. This does not apply to the shipped curve set and is a hardening note only.
The bit-length check at line 73 is a no-op for standard curves (s < n and num_n_bits == num_bytes*8) and has no security effect.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free in eval7(): for a curly-braces name, get_name_len() returns a heap-allocated alias that s and later name_start are rebound to; vim_free(alias) at line 267 frees that buffer, yet handle_subscript(arg, name_start, ...) at line 273 is still handed the dangling name_start whenever the expression continues with a subscript such as '.' or '->'. The guard at line 272 (ret == OK) does not invalidate name_start, so the freed pointer is consumed in subscript handling (read/dereference of freed heap memory), enabling a crash or memory corruption from attacker-controlled expression text.

evidence.snippet: ret = handle_subscript(arg, name_start, rettv, evalarg, TRUE);
evidence.reason: name_start is tainted by attacker-controlled curly-brace name syntax: get_name_len() (line 207) allocates alias for a {name} expression, s is rebound to alias (lines 208-209), and name_start = s is set at line 255 in the evaluate branch. vim_free(alias) at line 267 immediately frees that heap buffer, and line 273 passes the dangling name_start to handle_subscript, which consumes it for [ / ( / . / -> subscript processing when ret == OK (guard only tests evaluation success, not the validity of name_start). Concrete trigger: legacy-script expression '{abc}.x' or '{abc}->m()', which takes the evaluate branch (the '(' at line 222 excludes direct calls), frees the alias at 267, and at 273 dereferences/reads freed heap memory (CWE-416).

assumptions: char_u is an unsigned char type, so isdigit(*(*arg + 1)) at line 31 is not undefined behavior on the ctype tables.
Expression text reaching eval7 is attacker-influenceable in Vim's model (e.g. :eval, :execute, expressions in sourced files/autocommands), with only the NUL terminator bounding the byte string.

get_name_len() allocates a fresh buffer for alias when the name is a curly-braces {expr} name (legacy script), and handle_subscript()'s contract consumes name_start as the base name for subsequent subscripts.
limitations: The dereference of the freed pointer happens inside the called function handle_subscript(), whose body is not part of the shown code; the shown code itself creates the dangling pointer (free at 267, hand-off at 273).

NULL-dereference candidates at lines 164 (rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func) and 169 (ufunc->uf_ret_type->tt_type) require get_lambda_tv() to return OK with an invalid partial/type; that producing path is not in the shown code, so these are not confirmed findings.

The recursion guard (lines 44-49, 281) is balanced and caps eval7 nesting at 1000; deeper-stack exhaustion at that depth is not demonstrated (comment says crash occurs at 10000), so no DoS finding is made.
Reads of **arg / *(*arg + 1) after pointer increments (lines 31, 136-151) land on the in-bounds NUL terminator for a NUL-terminated string and are not treated as out-of-bounds.
Length/alias consistency between get_name_len()'s return and the alias buffer could only be verified in the unseen helper; treated as an invariant rather than a separate buffer-overflow finding.

verdict.summary: The shown code reads one sourced line into a growarray and contains no reachable memory-safety, injection, crypto, or file-handling flaw. The potentially dangerous operations are each guarded: ga_grow(&ga,120) establishes ga_maxlen >= ga_len+120 before every fgets; fgets(buf+ga_len, ga_maxlen-ga_len, fp) writes at most size-1 data bytes plus a NUL, bounding len to ga_maxlen-1; the exact-full-buffer continuation guard (ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1 && buf[len - 1] != '\n') detects the only state where len == ga_maxlen-1 and regrows before the next write; the buffer path regrows by 1 (ga_grow(&ga,1)) before buf[ga.ga_len++]=NUL; buf[len-2]/Ctrl-V backscan accesses are bounded by len>=2 / c>=0; and buflines indexing is capped by buf_lnum >= buflines.ga_len. No attacker-controlled value or index exceeds an allocated region, and no injection/crypto sink exists in this function.

assumptions: ga_grow(&ga, n) on success guarantees ga_maxlen >= ga_len + n (growarray invariant), and ga_maxlen counts total usable element slots starting at 0 after ga_init2.
fgets(buf, size, fp) writes at most size-1 bytes into buf followed by a NUL terminator.
buflines.ga_data is an array of ga_len NUL-terminated char_u* strings maintained by the unseen caller, and sp->fp is an open FILE* in a valid state.
USE_CRNL is a compile-time source-reading mode (Dos/CRLF handling); under it the ga_len semantics are unchanged.
limitations: Lines longer than INT_MAX bytes could truncate the int 'len' on line 40 (cast of a long STRLEN result); triggering it requires allocating a >2 GiB single line and is not a demonstrated path in the shown code, with no amplification (growth is O(line length)) - DoS/robustness concern, no CWE.

Embedded NUL bytes in sourced text truncate the logical line at the first NUL (Vim treats source as text); this is a parsing limitation with no out-of-bounds consequence because all later accesses use the STRLEN-bounded 'len', no CWE.

A single unbroken physical line causes repeated ga_grow/fgets iterations bounded by log2(line length); memory use is proportional to the input and OOM requires allocation failure of a caller-controlled-size buffer, excluded per analysis rules.

ga_concat/ga_grow failure behavior (FAIL without reallocating) is assumed to leave ga_len unchanged, consistent with the standard implementation; under that contract both failure paths (break, return NULL / return accumulated data) are clean.
All behavior of the callers of get_one_sourceline (how sp, fp, and buflines are populated, and what is done with the returned line) is out of scope.

verdict.summary: The leftward fill scan only guards the lower index bound (i >= 0, line 13); a caller-supplied x >= im->sx (or any out-of-range y, which is never checked) reaches gdImageSetPixel/gdImageGetPixel with an out-of-bounds index, causing heap OOB read/write (CWE-787). Independently, the unbounded recursive flood fill (lines 50-51, 73-74) can exhaust the stack on attacker-shaped images (CWE-674).

evidence.reason: The left-scan loop condition 'i >= 0' (line 13) admits i in [0, x] with no upper bound against im->sx, while the rightward loop (line 28) does enforce 'i < im->sx'. Caller-controlled x >= im->sx (e.g., im->sx = 16, x = 16) passes the guard and line 19 writes 'color' one or more elements past the pixel row, an OOB write; y is never checked at all, so y = im->sy or y = -1 is OOB at lines 15/19 with any valid x. The 'y > 0' (line 39) and 'y < im->sy - 1' (line 62) guards protect only the recursive y-1/y+1 accesses, not the initial call.

Recursion has no depth limit. With attacker-influenced image dimensions and a fill region of N non-border pixels (e.g., a 2xN image filled at (0,0)), the above/below passes (lines 39-83) seed about one recursion per row, producing recursion depth proportional to N (up to the pixel count). For N ~ 70,000, ~1M stack frames exceed typical stack limits, crashing the process (DoS, CWE-674); line 73-74 is the symmetric sink.

assumptions: Callers (e.g., gdImageFill, gdImageFilledPolygon, imagefill wrappers) pass coordinates x/y derived from user input without validating them against im->sx/im->sy.
gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are treated as the pixel-array memory operations they perform; their internal bounds behavior is not part of the shown code.
limitations: If the unseen gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel internally re-validate coordinates, the OOB write is reduced to a robustness issue; that internal behavior is unverifiable from the shown snippet.
Recursion depth is bounded by the fill-region pixel count, so the recursion finding is a stack-exhaustion crash (environment-dependent stack size), confidence 0.6.
The x + 1 (line 28) INT_MAX overflow is a subset of the x-out-of-range OOB path and is not reported separately.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the caller-supplied endpoint name into the fixed-size sun_path buffer with strcpy and no length check, so an endpoint name at least as long as sizeof(sun_path) (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS) causes a stack buffer overflow before bind() can reject the path.

evidence.reason: pipePath (line 4) is the attacker-influenceable return of endpoint.name() and reaches this strcpy unvalidated: the only prior guard (lines 5-7) merely rejects duplicate keys and imposes no length bound. sun_path is a fixed-size array (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS), and strcpy writes pipePath.size()+1 bytes including the NUL terminator. A witness value of pipePath length >= sizeof(sun_path), e.g. a 108-character name on Linux, passes the duplicate check and overflows the stack buffer one byte past sun_path (more for longer names), before bind() at line 18 could reject the oversized path.

assumptions: sun_path capacity is implementation-defined but finite (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS); the overflow threshold is sizeof(sun_path) in either case.
endpoint.name() returns the full supplied path material without truncation; no trust invariant for endpoint is established anywhere in the shown code.
limitations: unlink(local.sun_path) (line 16) and chmod(local.sun_path, ...) (line 21) operate on the same unvalidated attacker-influenceable path with no containment to an intended socket directory, which could allow deleting/chmodding arbitrary reachable files (CWE-59/CWE-22 territory), but the privilege boundary and reachable-path set depend on caller constraints not shown here; kept separate from the CWE-121 finding.

A TOCTOU race exists between unlink (line 16) and bind (line 18): another process could recreate a file/symlink at the path in between, but this is a robustness/race concern without a demonstrated privilege impact in the shown code.
chmod-based permissive socket permissions (S_IRWXU on the socket file) are a hardening concern, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId dereferences it->second after a failed idInfoMap lookup: the only guard invokes the STFATAL logging macro, but the shown code contains no return/throw after it, so on a missing id control can fall through and dereference the end() iterator (undefined behavior / crash). The finding depends on STFATAL not provably terminating, which is not established in the shown code.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled id (unvalidated parameter, line 1-2) that is absent from idInfoMap makes find() return the end() iterator at line 2. The guard at lines 3-5 only calls the STFATAL logging macro and the shown code never returns or throws, so control proceeds to this dereference. Any string not present in idInfoMap is a concrete witness passing the guard yet reaching the sink, where dereferencing the past-the-end iterator is undefined behavior (CWE-690).

assumptions: idInfoMap is a std::map-like container whose end() iterator is invalid to dereference.
getInfoForId may be invoked with arbitrary caller-supplied id strings; provenance of id is not shown in this function.
STFATAL is an external logging macro whose exact termination semantics are not part of the shown code.
limitations: If STFATAL provably terminates the process (e.g., aborts like LOG(FATAL)), line 6 is unreachable on the not-found path and the code is safe; that behavior cannot be verified from the shown code.
Concurrent unsynchronized mutation of idInfoMap (iterator invalidation between find and dereference) is not shown in the provided code.
The logged message is a constant literal, so there is no log-injection or format-string issue here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code. update_topline() performs only display geometry: all indices passed to hasFolding() are bounded by body-entry guards (lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count at line 95 before the call at line 98; lnum <= 0 at line 200 before the call at line 202), and the 'scrolloff' arithmetic feeds only comparisons that select scroll helpers, never an index, size, or pointer. No injection, crypto, file, or authn/z sinks are present. Overflow/truncation concerns are demoted to limitations.

assumptions: Vim invariants hold: w_cursor.lnum and w_topline are within [1, curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count], w_height > 0 whenever the line-20 early return is not taken, and botline_forw() strictly advances loff.lnum each call.
hasFolding() returns a fold-end line no greater than ml_line_count, so the loop-increment hasFolding(lnum, NULL, &lnum) followed by ++lnum stays within the guarded range.
curwin/curbuf are valid non-NULL window and buffer pointers supplied by the framework.
limitations: Integer overflow in w_topline + *so_ptr (lines 92, 103) or w_botline - *so_ptr (lines 145, 196) would require 'scrolloff' near LONG_MAX; no trigger is shown in the code and the effect is limited to wrong scroll direction because the hasFolding() calls are still clamped by lines 95 and 200.
Narrowing int save_so = *so_ptr (line 16) with restoration at line 240 silently truncates 'scrolloff' values above INT_MAX; display-only corruption with no security impact.
int overflow in the n/line_count accumulators (lines 173, 194, 207) only affects the choice among scroll helpers.
A hang in the while loop at lines 167-177 would require botline_forw() to fail to advance; no evidence in the shown code and the loop is finite-state under the stated invariants.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder clamps x and y only when they exceed the image size (lines 13-18), leaving all negative y values unclamped. With attacker-controlled y=-1 (and x>=0, border>=0), the left-scan loop (line 20) calls gdImageGetPixel(im, i, y) and gdImageSetPixel(im, i, y, color) with row -1, producing a deterministic heap out-of-bounds read (line 21) followed by an out-of-bounds heap write (line 24).

evidence.reason: y is an attacker-controlled int parameter; the only check on it (lines 16-18, 'if (y >= im->sy) y = im->sy - 1;') admits every negative value because it clamps only the upper bound. Witness x=0, y=-1, border=0 on an image with sx>=1, sy>=1: lines 8-18 all pass, the loop 'for (i = x; i >= 0; i--)' (line 20) executes at i=0, and gdImageGetPixel indexes im->pixels with row -1, an out-of-bounds heap read that occurs before the border comparison. No lower-bound clamp ('y < 0') exists anywhere in the shown code.

The same unclamped negative y from the tainted parameter reaches this write sink in the same left-scan loop: with x=0, y=-1, when the out-of-bounds read at line 21 returns a value != border, gdImageSetPixel writes through im->pixels[-1][0], an out-of-bounds heap write. The guard at lines 16-18 admits y=-1 (it only clamps y >= im->sy), and the loop repeats this for every i down to 0, so up to x+1 OOB accesses occur.

assumptions: im points to a valid gdImage with sx >= 1 and sy >= 1 whose pixels array has exactly sy rows of sx columns; the pixel accessors index im->pixels[y][x] without internal bounds checks.
x and y are treated as caller-supplied (library API) values; the shown code is the component responsible for validating them before use as pixel indices.
limitations: A purely negative x (x < 0) is not a separate finding: the left loop is skipped and the leftLimit == -1 sentinel (line 27) returns.
The OOB write at line 24 fires only when the OOB-read value at line 21 is not equal to border; the OOB read itself is deterministic and unconditional for any x >= 0 with y < 0.
Images with sy == 0 would clamp a non-negative y to -1 (line 16-17) and trigger the same root-cause overflow; treated as the same finding, not a new CWE.
Flood-fill recursion depth is bounded by image height and terminates (filled pixels are skipped), so stack-exhaustion DoS on very tall images is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in the obsolete .gpb pattern branch. With width=height=32768 and bytes=1 the guard at lines 47-51 passes (it bounds per-dimension sizes and the 64-bit gsize product only), but line 164 computes 4*bh.width*bh.height in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, which wraps to 0; g_malloc returns a minimal chunk, and the loop at line 166 (bound ph.width*ph.height = 2^30, enforced equal to bh.width*bh.height at lines 155-156) writes and reads out of bounds at lines 168 and 176 with attacker-controlled bytes, enabling heap corruption/code execution.

evidence.reason: 4 * bh.width * bh.height is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (all operands are guint32/int). The sanitizer at lines 47-51 admits bh.width=bh.height=32768, bytes=1 (32768 <= GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE; G_MAXSIZE/32768/32768/1 >= 1 on both 32- and 64-bit builds) but never bounds 4*width*height < 2^32; here 4*32768*32768 = 2^32 wraps to 0, allocating a minimal chunk instead of 4 GiB. The loop bound at line 166 (ph.width*ph.height == bh.width*bh.height per lines 155-156) is 2^30, so the writes at lines 168 and 176 overflow this allocation from the first iteration.

Attacker-controlled file bytes flow from the BrushHeader read at line 31 and PatternHeader read at line 141 into bh.width/bh.height (lines 40-41) and ph.width/ph.height (lines 146-147); with the witness width=height=32768 the allocation at line 164 wrapped to 0 bytes, and this statement executes for i in [0, 2^30), writing plain_brush[i] (file pixel data read at line 124) at offsets i*4+3 up to 2^32-1, all outside the wrapped allocation (offset 3 already exceeds the ~1-byte g_malloc(0) chunk at i=0). The write is a sink at line 176; the guard at lines 47-51 does not protect it.

assumptions: BrushHeader and PatternHeader integer fields are guint32, so 4*bh.width*bh.height at line 164 (and bh.width*bh.height*bh.bytes at line 121) are evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic on both 32- and 64-bit builds.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is 32768 (GIMP 2.x default), so width=height=32768 passes the check at lines 47-48.

g_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal-size allocation (GLib semantics), so the loop's first out-of-bounds write at line 176 executes; the 1 GiB stacked allocation at line 122 is assumed to succeed on a typical host.
limitations: Reaching the overflow requires a crafted file of at least ~1 GiB of pixel data because line 124 requires read(fd, brush_buf, size) to return exactly w*h*bytes bytes; this is an attacker-chosen file-size cost, not a protection.

gimp_any_to_utf8(temp, -1, ...) at line 109 may over-read (strlen-style scan) if the bn_size file bytes contain no NUL, since the buffer is not NUL-terminated; the scanning operation is delegated to an unseen callee, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

For bytes=18 with version != 3, size = width*height*18 at line 121 can wrap in 32-bit arithmetic despite the 64-bit G_MAXSIZE check at line 51; the wrapped size is used only for a size-matched allocation and read, and the function returns at the depth switch (lines 233-238), so no out-of-bounds access results in the shown code.
Single-shot OOM-abort from the 1 GiB allocation at line 122 (or the 0-byte allocation at line 164) is an unchecked-allocation DoS concern, not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: When id is not a key in idInfoMap, the guard at lines 4-6 only emits the fatal log and does not terminate execution, so the unconditional 'return it->second;' at line 7 dereferences the end() iterator — an out-of-bounds read / undefined behavior that can crash the process or return a stale, unrelated TerminalUserInfo.

evidence.reason: Caller-supplied, unvalidated 'id' flows to idInfoMap.find(id) (line 3); when id is absent, the guard at lines 4-6 admits exactly the not-found set but only logs (STFATAL), with no return/throw/else, so 'it' is still idInfoMap.end() when line 7 dereferences it. Confirmed witness: any id that is not a key in idInfoMap (e.g., an evicted terminal id), producing an out-of-bounds read of the one-past-end iterator.

assumptions: STFATAL is assumed to log without terminating the process (e.g., a fatal-severity stream that does not abort); if it called abort()/exit(), the not-found path would terminate before line 7 and the finding would be unreachable.
id is assumed to be reachable from untrusted callers, e.g., a client-supplied terminal/session identifier; the shown code applies no constraints to it.
idInfoMap is a standard map-like container whose end() iterator must not be dereferenced.
limitations: If the logging framework's FATAL severity aborts the process (as glog LOG(FATAL) does), line 7 is not reached on the not-found path and this is not a vulnerability; the verdict depends on the unseen STFATAL macro/build semantics.
No log-injection finding: the message at line 5 is a static literal and never embeds id.

Impact beyond a crash depends on the fields of TerminalUserInfo, which are not shown; a returned stale object could mis-associate identity at the routing boundary but the concrete data layout is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmable, attacker-reachable vulnerability in get_one_sourceline. All buffer writes and reads are bounded by explicit guards: line 20 guarantees at least 120 bytes of headroom before each fgets (lines 37-38); the full-buffer continue at line 58 requires ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1, which forces len >= 119 on the file path (or len >= 1 on the buffer path), so buf[len-1] is always in-bounds; the buffer path is capped by the buf_lnum < buflines.ga_len check at line 24 and the ga_grow(&ga, 1) guarantee before the NUL write at line 31; the trailing-NL/Ctrl-Z/CR handling is guarded by len >= 1 / len >= 2 (lines 45-47, 61, 64, 77, 104). The loop terminates because every continue consumes file bytes or a buffer line, and the escaped-NL parity check (lines 96-98) is arithmetically correct for both c >= 0 and c == -1. The shown code contains no injection, crypto, or access-control sink.

assumptions: sp->buflines.ga_data entries are NUL-terminated strings built by the caller (ga_concat in line 26 relies on STRLEN), and sp->fp is a valid readable FILE* supplied by an unseen caller.
ga_grow(&ga, n) has the postcondition ga_maxlen - ga_len >= n on OK and leaves the growarray in a consistent state on FAIL.
fgets always NUL-terminates its output within the size given, so STRLEN at line 40 is bounded by the bytes fgets wrote.
Ctrl_V / Ctrl_Z / NUL are single-byte constants and ga_len (bytes used) does not count the terminating NUL for the concat path.
Sourced file content and sourced buffer text are treated as potentially attacker-influenced input; framework fields (fileformat, error, sourcing_lnum) are internal state.
limitations: Integer robustness only: len (int) and the (int)STRLEN cast at line 40 would wrap only for a single logical line exceeding 2^31-1 bytes; no concrete attacker-deliverable value in this context, and the fgets chunk size is constant (120), so this is not treated as a finding.

NUL bytes embedded in the sourced file cause silent truncation of the returned line at the first NUL (STRLEN at line 40 reads past them inside the buffer but reports a shorter length); data-loss/robustness only, no security mechanism broken.

OOM paths (ga_grow FAIL at lines 20-21 and 28-29) abandon or return partial lines; the allocation request is a constant (120) or derived from caller-held data, so the failure is not attacker-scaled within the shown code.

If an unseen caller supplied non-NUL-terminated buflines entries, ga_concat (line 26) would over-read; the actual read occurs inside the helper and depends on a caller invariant, so it is out of scope for the shown lines.
No verdict is offered about other Vim code reached after this function (ga_grow_inner, line_breakcheck, msg_source/emsg internals).

verdict.summary: Heap-based buffer overflow in GetEXIFProperty: when the caller requests all EXIF tags (property "exif:*", which passes the strlen>5 guard at line 449), key is allocated as strlen(property)+1 = 7 bytes (AcquireString at line 761), then FormatLocaleString(key, MaxTextExtent, "%s", description) at lines 783-784 copies a static tag description (up to 28 bytes including NUL, e.g. "exif:InteroperabilityIndex", or 8 bytes for unmapped tags) past the end of that heap allocation. The guard only checks strlen(property) > 5 and never relates property length to description length, so any EXIF profile containing at least one directory entry triggers the out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Sink write: key was allocated at line 761 as AcquireString(property) with size strlen(property)+1; for the concrete attacker-influenced property "exif:*" (length 6, admitted by the only guard at line 449, strlen <= 5 returns), the allocation is 7 bytes. The format call passes MaxTextExtent (~4096) as the size bound, not the real 7-byte allocation, so description (static table value up to 35 chars, e.g. "exif:InteroperabilityIndex" = 28 bytes including NUL, or "unknown" = 8 bytes for unmapped tags) is written out of bounds whenever the value block runs (all != 0 at line 648, reached for every EXIF entry with property "exif:*"). The guard at line 449 does not constrain the write length, so the heap out-of-bounds write is confirmed with the concrete witness property=\"exif:*\" plus any profile with at least one EXIF entry; this is CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow.

assumptions: MaxTextExtent is a large compile-time constant (typically 4096) and FormatLocaleString honors its size argument as an upper bound, so the write is truncated to ~MaxTextExtent rather than bounded by the actual key allocation.
AcquireString allocates exactly strlen(source)+1 bytes.
ReadPropertySignedShort/UnsignedShort/SignedLong and ReadPropertyByte consume 2/2/4/1 bytes respectively and are the standard ImageMagick helpers.
property values such as "exif:*" are passed to GetEXIFProperty by callers implementing property queries (image metadata lookup APIs).
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read during the "Exif\0\0" signature scan (lines 535-547) when length reaches 0 mid-sequence (e.g. profile tail "Ex"): the actual byte read happens inside the unshown ReadPropertyByte helper, so whether it honors length==0 cannot be established from the shown code.

components*tag_bytes[format] at line 626 is a size_t multiplication with a weak overflow check at line 627; wrap-to-large values on 32-bit builds fall into the >4 branch whose bounds (lines 640-644) reject or skip them, and wrap-to-small values are caught by line 627, so no confirmed OOB read is derivable in the shown code.

The EXIFMultipleValues/EXIFMultipleFractions macros appear to read up to number_bytes bytes from p; this is fully bounded by the q bound at lines 610-613 and the dir_offset+number_bytes <= length checks at lines 640-644 (plus line 731 for strings), so no OOB read is confirmed there.
The "unknown" FormatLocaleString write for all==2 (line 799) is unreachable because tag_value < 0x20000 always (tag_offset is 0 or 0x10000 and tags are 16-bit).

Large per-entry allocations (AcquireQuantumMemory at lines 663-666 and 734-737) are size-bounded by profile length and tolerate allocation failure (value==NULL guards), so only a hardening/robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

The heap overflow is triggered only when the caller supplies the wildcard property "exif:*"; if property is always a fixed developer-controlled constant in a given deployment, the parameter-origin taint is reduced, though the shown code places no such restriction.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. update_topline only recomputes window scroll state: all line-number loops are bounded by explicit guards (lines 97, 168-172, 201), the botline block is guarded by w_botline <= ml_line_count (line 141), and the temporary scrolloff override is restored at line 241 with no intervening early return. No memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink exists in the shown code.

assumptions: Vim maintains the invariant 1 <= w_cursor.lnum <= ml_line_count before update_topline runs (check_cursor_lnum at line 22 clamps it on the early-return path).
w_topline and w_botline are editor-maintained window state; validate_botline() at line 139 keeps w_botline consistent.
'scrolloff' (w_p_so / p_so) is a validated non-negative option with a bounded maximum, so *so_ptr >= 0 in all arithmetic.
Called helpers (hasFolding, botline_forw, check_top_offset, scroll_cursor_*) are trusted editor functions; only their call sites in the shown code are analyzed.
limitations: Signed overflow in w_topline + *so_ptr (lines 93, 104) or w_botline - *so_ptr (lines 197, 208-209) is not reachable: w_topline/w_botline are bounded by ml_line_count (memory-bounded) and *so_ptr is option-capped (~1e6), far below LONG_MAX; even on 32-bit long builds ml_line_count <= 2^31-1 with no overflow.
Even if lnum transiently became ml_line_count+1 in the fold loop (line 93), the guard at line 97 breaks before hasFolding (line 99) is called, so no out-of-range line number is ever passed.

n and line_count are int and could in principle truncate large long arithmetic, but they only select between scroll strategies (lines 109-115, 210-213) and never index memory, so any mismatch is a cosmetic scrolling artifact, not a security issue.
No network-, file-, or packet-derived input reaches this function in the shown code; cursor position and scrolloff are editor- and user-configuration-controlled, not attacker-controlled data.

verdict.summary: Missing closing double-quote in the GSER issuer or thisUpdate value makes the content scan consume the entire remaining region (is->bv_len == x.bv_len / tu->bv_len == x.bv_len); advancing x.bv_val by bv_len+1 and subtracting bv_len+1 from the unsigned ber_len_t x.bv_len underflows it, and the subsequent 'eat leading spaces' loop / comma check dereferences x.bv_val[0] out of bounds (lines 79/115 -> 124/132).

evidence.reason: When the issuer content scan (lines 65-77) finds no closing quote, is->bv_len equals x.bv_len, so this subtraction underflows the unsigned ber_len_t (e.g. 36 - 37). Taint: in->bv_val/bv_len (attacker-controlled LDAP/GSER data, line 8) determines is->bv_len and x.bv_len; witness `{issuer "rdnSequence:ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789}` passes the guards at lines 19/21/35/52/58 and reaches line 79 with is->bv_len == x.bv_len. The wrapped length then feeds the out-of-bounds `x.bv_val[0]` read at line 124 (and/or line 132).

Same underflow via the thisUpdate path: the scan (lines 107-111) exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len when no closing quote exists; line 112's length gate (>= 14) still passes, then this subtraction wraps x.bv_len (e.g. 14 - 15). Witness `{issuer "x",thisUpdate "YYYYMMDDHHMMSS}` passes lines 19/21/83/100 and reaches line 115; the subsequent `x.bv_val[0]` dereference at line 124 is out of bounds (x.bv_val now points one past the input berval).

Out-of-bounds read sink: after the length underflow at lines 79 or 115, x.bv_len is a huge wrapped value and x.bv_val points at/outside the end of the input buffer, so this loop's guard evaluates `x.bv_val[0]` first and performs an out-of-bounds read before the `x.bv_len` test (at most one byte past the berval immediately, walking arbitrarily far if that byte is a space). CWE-125: attacker-chosen missing closing quote in `in` (lines 65-77 or 107-111 consuming all of x) triggers the wrap.

assumptions: ber_len_t is an unsigned integer type (OpenLDAP lber), so `x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1` with equal operands wraps to a huge value; if it were signed, the same input still produces an OOB read at line 124 (x.bv_val lands one past the buffer with x.bv_len == -1).
Line numbers refer to the provided snippet with `issuerAndThisUpdateCheck(` as line 1.

The `in` berval is derived from externally supplied (LDAP/network) data by the unseen caller; the function's own syntax validation shows it is treated as untrusted, and the dangerous arithmetic/dereference are entirely within the shown code.
limitations: NULL dereference if `slap_sl_malloc` (line 150) fails: requires an allocation failure and is not attacker-amplified; not counted as a finding.
The `is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1]` read at line 70 can reach at most `x.bv_val[x.bv_len]`, which is the (in-bounds) closing `}` byte of the input, so it is not an OOB access.

When fewer than `n` bytes remain, the strncasecmp calls at lines 35/52/83 stop on the embedded closing `}` byte (never matching issuer/rdnSequence/thisUpdate), so they do not read past the original buffer.
If callers always pass buffers with slack/terminators, the line-124 read may not crash, but it still violates the berval's bounds and is UB; impact depends on allocation layout.
If a caller ever passes only fully trusted static strings, the finding is unreachable; nothing in the shown code documents such an invariant.

verdict.summary: jsP_dumpsyntax only copies an int flag, reads the scalar field prog->type, dispatches to the unseen printers pstmlist/pstm, and emits constant newline characters. No attacker-controlled length, index, string, format specifier, or path reaches a security-relevant operation in the shown code, so no vulnerability is confirmable within its scope.

assumptions: Callers pass a non-NULL js_Ast* prog; the shown code contains no path that produces NULL, so the dereference at line 4 is safe only under that caller invariant.
The rendering functions pstmlist, pstm, and nl are outside the shown scope; any formatting/injection behavior they contain is not attributable to this function.
limitations: A NULL prog supplied by an out-of-scope caller would cause a NULL dereference at line 4; not a finding because the shown code cannot produce NULL.

If the unseen pstmlist/pstm implementations print attacker-controlled AST string nodes with printf-family calls or unbounded recursion, vulnerabilities could exist there, but they are absent from the shown code and out of scope.
Deeply nested attacker-crafted ASTs could cause stack exhaustion inside the unseen recursive printers; not verifiable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the caller-supplied endpoint name into sockaddr_un::sun_path with strncpy but never checks that pipePath fits: a name of exactly sizeof(local.sun_path) bytes (e.g., 108 'a's) leaves sun_path without a NUL terminator. unlink (line 16) and chmod (line 21) then scan it as a C string, reading past the buffer (out-of-bounds read), and bind (line 18) sees an unterminated address, fails, and triggers FATAL_FAIL, aborting the process. The only guard, the duplicate-path check at line 5, tests map membership, not length, so it admits the failing witness.

evidence.reason: pipePath (line 4) is the unvalidated, caller-supplied endpoint name with unbounded length; for a name of exactly sizeof(local.sun_path) bytes, strncpy fills the whole sun_path array and writes no NUL terminator. The resulting buffer is consumed as a C string at line 16 (unlink) and line 21 (chmod), which scan past the 108-byte array (out-of-bounds read), and at line 18 (bind), which fails on the unterminated address and aborts via FATAL_FAIL. The only guard, the duplicate-path check at line 5, constrains map membership, not length, so it admits the 108-byte failing witness.

assumptions: sun_path has its full declared array size (108 bytes on Linux), so the write is capped but the missing-NUL case still occurs
endpoint.name() returns a std::string whose length is unbounded by the shown code
FATAL_FAIL aborts (or throws) on a failed expression, converting the bind/chmod failure into process termination
limitations: Arbitrary-file deletion via unlink(local.sun_path) (line 16) depends on a caller binding attacker data into endpoint and on process permissions; provenance is not visible here, so it is not a confirmed finding
TOCTOU between unlink (line 16) and bind (line 18) has no demonstrated attacker window or impact
The over-read magnitude is bounded by adjacent stack contents and PATH_MAX, and a failing bind ends execution, so no sustained memory corruption or broader disclosure is demonstrated

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable vulnerability in the shown code. All input-derived lengths reaching allocation/copy sinks are bounded by explicit guards (lines 363-365, 507, 526) or by the y_size/y_array validation at lines 182-187; the only arithmetic that could overflow (totlen+oldlen+1 at lines 372/531, col+yanklen+1 at line 602) wraps to a negative int, which converts to a huge size_t and forces alloc() failure followed by a checked break/goto, so it cannot yield an undersized live allocation. Residual multi-GB, guard-absence, and workload concerns are documented in notes.limitations without CWEs.

assumptions: y_size and y_array are consistent: either the register's array with exactly y_size entries (line 135), the single-entry fake register (line 125), or the ALLOC_MULT result sized exactly y_size (line 116); the guard at lines 182-187 runs before any y_array indexing.
In non-Visual paths, curwin->w_cursor.col is a byte column within the current line (editor invariant); the Visual path additionally guards col > oldlen at lines 526-530.
STRLEN results fit int for lines/register contents below 2 GB; alloc() takes size_t, returns NULL on huge sizes, and every allocation result in the shown code is checked before use.
count is non-negative in plain put paths (the -1 sentinel is only used for the '.' register branch at line 59, which returns early).
limitations: Integer-truncation/overflow class: (int)STRLEN() at lines 225/317/348/590 and int size expressions totlen+oldlen+1 (lines 372, 531) and col+yanklen+1 (line 602) are unguarded for operands outside [0, INT_MAX]; with a register line or buffer line exceeding ~2 GB, yanklen could truncate negative and flow into the line-602 allocation and the memmove at line 608. No concrete failing value is demonstrated at practical scale and the [0,INT_MAX] wrap only goes negative (alloc failure), so this is an unconfirmed hardening gap, not a confirmed finding.

Allocation-failure DoS: count*yanklen or count*(yanklen+spaces) near INT_MAX causes huge alloc requests to fail (lines 372, 531), which is a denial path only if the attacker can already supply near-2-GB register content.

Workload DoS: attacker-chosen count drives O(count*y_size) work in the loops at lines 386/536/580; execution is finite-state and terminating (count is a bounded long), so only volume-based CPU cost is possible.
In-place NUL splitting of expr_result at line 104 mutates the caller's expression-result buffer; it is in-bounds but is an aliasing side effect worth noting.

Potential negative/MAXCOL cursor-column states (e.g., getvpos failing sets col = MAXCOL at line 524) are guarded by the col > oldlen check at line 526 in the only path that consumes them; any residual position oddity is cosmetic, with no confirmed memory impact.

verdict.summary: jsP_dumpsyntax contains no security-relevant sink in the shown code: it only assigns an int to module state, NULL-checked dispatch to unseen printer helpers (pstmlist/pstm/nl), and a constant putchar guarded by minify > 1. The only dereference (prog->type) is fully protected by the if (prog) guard, and no memory, injection, crypto, or file operations are present.

assumptions: minify is module-level printer state whose only use in the shown code is the minify > 1 comparison at line 9.
pstmlist, pstm, and nl implement the actual AST printing and are not shown; per the pass-through rule their internals are out of scope.
limitations: Potential injection, recursion-depth/algorithmic-complexity, or memory-safety issues inside pstmlist/pstm/nl cannot be assessed because those function bodies are not present in the shown code.
The side effect of assigning dominify to the global minify at line 2 could affect unseen printer behavior, but no sink consuming that state appears in the shown code.
No dereference of prog before the NULL check is possible: prog == NULL is excluded by the line 3 guard before prog->type is read at line 4.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() trusts the unvalidated col parameter and forms p + col against a line fetched by ml_get_curline(). When the caller-supplied column exceeds the line byte length (or is negative), mb_head_off(p, p + col) reads out of bounds at line 17, a heap OOB read. The only branch guards have_mbyte and !redrawing() never constrain col against the line length; a failing witness is col = L + 1 with has_mbyte enabled, where p + col points one byte past the NUL-terminated line. This matches the real Vim bug fixed by capping col at the line length before the mb_head_off call.

evidence.reason: col is the function parameter (line 1) with no sign, range, or length check before use. Line 16 fetches the line via ml_get_curline(); line 17 forms p + col and mb_head_off dereferences it (initial byte read plus backward character scan). The guard has_mbyte (line 11) admits every col, and the failing witness is col = L + 1 for a line of byte length L (first value past the in-bounds NUL at p + L), or any negative col pointing before the buffer. No protective check bounds col; therefore the read is out of bounds on the heap (CWE-125).

assumptions: has_mbyte is enabled, which is the default in typical multibyte Vim builds and is required to reach line 17.
colnr_T is a signed integer type, so a negative col is representable and is not excluded by the shown code.
ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer whose byte length L is the true in-bounds limit; the shown code never reads that length before building p + col.
mb_head_off() dereferences the pointer it is given, so the pointer arithmetic at line 17 directly produces the out-of-bounds read.
limitations: The exact caller and the editing state that yields col > L (or col < 0) are not shown; per the analysis scope, an unvalidated function parameter flowing to a memory operation in the shown code is sufficient for reachability.

The internal loops of mb_head_off() and curs_columns() are not shown, so only the pointer formation/dereference call at line 17 is directly anchored; curs_columns() consuming the invalid w_cursor.col is a related concern but is not asserted as a separate finding.
The proven impact is out-of-bounds read (crash/info disclosure); no write or code-execution primitive is established from the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in input_bmp_reader: an attacker-controlled biSize of 108 or 124 (read from the file header at line 75) passes the branch guard at lines 188-189 and makes ReadOK at line 193 write 104 or 120 bytes into the 64-byte stack buffer declared at line 4, overflowing it and enabling memory corruption/control-flow hijack when parsing a hostile BMP.

evidence.reason: Bitmap_File_Head.biSize is attacker-controlled file data read via ToL at line 75. The branch guard at lines 188-189 admits exactly biSize == 108 and biSize == 124, producing read lengths biSize - 4 = 104 or 120 bytes into the 64-byte stack buffer declared at line 4. The guard only checks equality and never bounds biSize - 4 against sizeof(buffer), so the sink write overflows the buffer by 40 or 56 bytes with attacker-chosen bytes (CWE-121).

assumptions: ToL/ToS unpack 4/2 bytes little-endian, so biSize, biWidth, biHeight, bfOffs are fully attacker-controllable 32/16-bit values.
ReadOK(fd, dst, n) performs an n-byte read into dst (fread-style) and returns false on a short read, as its name and usage imply.
limitations: ColormapSize unsigned underflow at line 252 could yield a negative size passed to ReadColorMap at line 333, but the actual color-map write occurs in the unseen ReadColorMap, and the signedness of bfOffs/biSize fields is not shown in this snippet.
The (unsigned short) narrowing of biWidth/biHeight at line 349 feeds the unseen at_bitmap_init, so its impact cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
fseek with attacker-controlled bfOffs at line 337 is at most an out-of-file-read robustness concern in the shown code.
The while loop over 'BA' markers (lines 37-52) is bounded by input length and terminates on read failure; it is not a hang finding.
No format-string or log/header/shell injection exists: all LOG/printf uses have literal formats with filename passed only as a %s argument.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced lengths reaching memory sinks are bounded within the shown code: L18 (tailen <= skb_tailroom) protects the L80/L81 linear-tail writes, L36 refill of ALIGN(tailen) protects the L44-L46 frag-page fill, L24 (nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS, admits exactly 0..MAX_SKB_FRAGS-1) protects the L50 frags[] write, L73 (skb_cow_data(skb, tailen)) plus L74 protects the COW path, and L71/L77 recompute esp->esph after any reallocation. No attacker-controlled value can defeat one of these guards, and no injection, crypto, or file/access-control sink exists in the shown code.

assumptions: esp->tailen is produced by the unseen caller (esp_output) from skb->len and crypto parameters, and is non-negative and small (trailer + tfclen + auth size); nothing in the shown code can make it negative or near INT_MAX.

skb_page_frag_refill success implies at least allocsize contiguous bytes remain at pfrag->offset, and skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) implies at least tailen bytes of tailroom at the trailer's tail; both are library/OS contracts defined outside the shown code.
skb_shinfo(skb)->frags[] has exactly MAX_SKB_FRAGS elements.
limitations: A negative or huge tailen (signed/unsigned comparison at L18, ALIGN at L32, pskb_put int at L81) would be unsafe, but producing such a value depends on an unseen caller; it is not established from the shown code.

If tailen could exceed PAGE_SIZE, frag-path safety at L44-L46 would depend entirely on the unseen skb_page_frag_refill implementation re-verifying capacity; that is an out-of-scope pass-through concern.

The L18 fast path can append the ESP trailer at the linear tail of a nonlinear skb (i.e., before existing frags), a packet-layout correctness concern with no attacker-triggered security impact demonstrated in the shown code.
The frag path returns nfrags = old + 2 (L48, L52, L58), an over-count; the unseen caller consumes only the sign of the return, so no security impact is established.
skb->len/data_len/truesize additions and refcount_add (L60-L64) could only overflow with tailen near 2^32, which is unreachable for this caller-derived value.

verdict.summary: In ex_retab() under FEAT_VARTABS, the long values start_vcol/vcol are narrowed to 16-bit colnr_T at the tabstop_fromto() call (lines 98-99). For a buffer line whose whitespace run straddles the 65536-virtual-column boundary, the helper returns a negative space count, so num_spaces/num_tabs (lines 100-101) and len (line 128) go negative. The allocation at line 130 then becomes 1 byte in the concrete witness while mch_memmove at line 134 writes start_col=8198 bytes and the memmove at lines 135-136 writes 57330 bytes starting at new_line-57329, producing heap out-of-bounds writes both past and before the buffer. Trigger: crafted file line (8191 tabs, 6 spaces, 'X', 2 tabs, 'y', 57328 fillers; ts=8, noexpandtab) processed by :retab.

evidence.reason: Allocation-size sink. Taint: file line contents via ptr = ml_get(lnum) (line 65) drive vcol/start_vcol; at lines 98-99 they are narrowed to 16-bit colnr_T, and for a whitespace run straddling the 65536-column wrap the helper returns s=-65527, t=0, making len (line 128) = -65527. Then old_len(65529) - col(8200) + start_col(8198) + len(-65527) + 1 = 1, so a 1-byte buffer is allocated while the subsequent memmoves write far more.

Out-of-bounds write past the heap allocation. With the confirmed witness start_col = 8198 but the line-130 allocation is 1 byte; the guard at line 133 only tests start_col > 0 and line 131 only tests new_line != NULL, so memmove writes 8198 bytes into the 1-byte buffer (8197-byte heap overflow).

evidence.snippet:
mch_memmove(new_line + start_col + len,
				      ptr + col, (size_t)(old_len - col + 1));
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write before the heap allocation. In the same run, start_col + len = 8198 - 65527 = -57329, so the destination is new_line - 57329, while old_len - col + 1 = 65529 - 8200 + 1 = 57330; memmove writes 57330 bytes starting 57329 bytes before the 1-byte allocation. The destination offset uses the attacker-influenced negative len with no check that the offset is within [0, alloc size].

assumptions: FEAT_VARTABS is compiled so the tabstop_fromto branch (lines 95-101) is active; in the #else branch all arithmetic is on long values and keeps len >= 0, so no overflow was found there.

colnr_T is the default 16-bit unsigned short, so the implicit long-to-colnr_T narrowing at lines 98-99 wraps virtual columns at 65536; a 32-bit colnr_T build or a helper with long parameters removes the wrap.
The unseen helper tabstop_fromto returns *spcs = negative left_spaces unclamped when end_col < start_col; if it clamps negatives to 0, the failure is not reachable.
Defaults ts=8, noexpandtab, single-entry vartabstop; the attacker controls the buffer line via a crafted file and the victim runs :retab (e.g. vim -c retab file).
limitations: The colnr_T narrowing and unclamped negative output are in the signature/implementation of the unseen tabstop_fromto helper; if it uses long columns or clamps, this specific witness does not apply.

A wrap producing a hugely negative allocation size (converted to huge size_t) would instead make alloc() fail and is handled by the NULL checks at lines 131 and 161 (OOM path, no write); the confirmed witness avoids this by producing a 1-byte allocation.
The (colnr_T)vcol cast at line 155 can make tab widths logically wrong on very long lines, but allocation and write sizes remain algebraically consistent there; it does not create OOB on its own.
Trailing-whitespace-only content never reaches the retab block (break at lines 153-154), so such lines are left unchanged; not a finding.
There are no command/SQL/HTML/log/crypto sinks in the shown code; the numeric parsing of eap->arg is validated at lines 32 and 50-61.

verdict.summary: The shown singlevar routine resolves a name token and, for globals, emits an indexed access on the environment. The only attacker-derived value (varname from str_checkname, line 2) flows as data into the constant table via codestring (line 9) and into codegen via luaK_indexed (line 10); no memory, injection, exec, crypto, file, or authz sink exists in the shown code, and the lua_assert post-condition (line 8) cannot be violated on any attacker-chosen input path shown here.

assumptions: str_checkname never returns NULL (lexical failures raise via longjmp), so varname at line 2 is a valid interned TString.
ls->fs and ls->envn are set up by the parser before this function is called; ls->envn is the interned _ENV string.
_ENV is declared in the enclosing function scope by unseen parser code, so the second singlevaraux call at line 7 always yields a non-VVOID result, keeping the assertion at line 8 safe.
varname is a syntactically valid identifier whose length is bounded by the unseen lexer's token buffer.
limitations: The lua_assert at line 8 would abort if the unseen parser invariant that _ENV is resolvable were violated, but no path in the shown code can produce VVOID there; the attacker-controlled name does not influence that lookup, so this is an unreachable robustness concern, not a finding.

Bound enforcement for the identifier length and correct constant-table sizing depends on unseen internals of str_checkname and codestring; the shown code passes no attacker-derived size or index to them, so any hypothetical issue there is out of scope.
No other concern was identified; there are simply no security sinks (memory, injection, crypto, file, authz) in the shown code.

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck performs an out-of-bounds read when the attacker-controlled thisUpdate (or issuer) value has no closing double quote: the scan at lines 107-111 exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len, so x.bv_val is advanced one byte past the end of the input buffer and x.bv_len underflows to SIZE_MAX (lines 112-113); the next leading-space loop dereferences x.bv_val[0] (line 122) one byte past the buffer, enabling a crash/DoS and, if that byte is a space, an unbounded further scan. A concrete passing input is b"{issuer rdnSequence:\"   \",thisUpdate \"x}" (40 bytes), which passes the length>=37 and brace checks and triggers the failure in shown code.

evidence.reason: Sink: dereference of x.bv_val[0] occurs before the x.bv_len check, so it executes even with x.bv_len==0 and with an already-wrapped length. Taint: in->bv_val/in->bv_len are the attacker-supplied GSER value, constrained only by length>=37 (line 19) and '{'/'}' checks (line 21); nothing requires a closing quote around the thisUpdate value. Witness: input {issuer rdnSequence:"   ",thisUpdate "x}" (len 40) passes lines 19/21; after consuming `thisUpdate ` and the opening quote, x.bv_val=in+38 and x.bv_len=1; the scan at lines 107-111 finds no closing quote and exits with tu->bv_len==x.bv_len==1; line 112 advances x.bv_val to in+40 (one past the 40-byte buffer) and line 113 underflows x.bv_len to SIZE_MAX; line 122 then reads *(in+40) — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), which also becomes an unbounded forward scan if that byte is a space.

assumptions: ber_len_t is an unsigned type (size_t), so x.bv_len -= tu->bv_len + 1 wraps on underflow.
in is the exact attacker-supplied value with an accurate bv_len; provenance is a function parameter (in the real caller, an LDAP filter/assertion value processed by slapd).
Line 35 (2D8C): is->bv_val assignment and final *is = ni (line 158) write only into caller-provided output slots, not into attacker-chosen addresses.
limitations: The identical missing-closing-quote condition also triggers the same wrap through the issuer path at lines 78-79; counted under the same CWE-125 finding.
strncasecmp over-reads at lines 35/83 when fewer than 6/10 bytes remain in x (e.g. space-only interior) are the same OOB-read class and are not counted separately.
