The byte at in+40 is heap-layout dependent; if it is not a space the read is a single OOB byte (information exposure / possible crash at a page boundary), and if it is a space the scan continues across memory — impact is DoS/info-leak, not reliable RCE.
Unchecked slap_sl_malloc at line 148 could NULL-deref only on allocation failure; the allocation size is not attacker-escalable to force failure, so it is excluded per rules.
No injection, weak-crypto, or authz/authn sinks exist in the shown code; syntax checks for duplicate fields (lines 36/85) are correct.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only attacker-influenced value, varname (line 2), is a lexer-produced identifier used solely as the key for the language's intended env[varname] global lookup; the shown code never uses it as a size, index, format string, or text-execution component, and the constant-table write is delegated to unseen helpers (lines 10-11).

assumptions: ls is a valid LexState created by the Lua parser; ls->fs and ls->envn are initialized, so the lua_assert at line 8 reflects an internal invariant, not an input check.
str_checkname (line 2) returns TStrings only for NAME tokens produced by the lexer, whose content is restricted to Lua identifier characters.
singlevaraux, luaK_exp2anyregup, codestring, and luaK_indexed are trusted compiler internals whose own code is not shown.
limitations: Any overflow inside codestring or luaK_indexed would occur in unseen helper code; the shown function only passes arguments to them, so those writes are out of scope here.
In release builds, a violated internal invariant at line 8 would be undefined behavior, but ls->envn always exists, so it is not attacker-reachable from this fragment.

Attacker-supplied Lua source can influence only varname's identifier content, which is consumed as a bytecode constant key rather than reaching a memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In create_cache_bins, the dyld-cache dependency walk trusts two file-derived values without bounds checks: extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex starts an unbounded scan of depArray (heap OOB read, CWE-125), and depArray[k] & 0x7fff is used to index deps and img, giving an attacker-controlled heap OOB write (CWE-787). The path requires R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER to be set and cache->accel to be present.

evidence.reason: dep_index is computed at line 80 as depArray[k] & 0x7fff, where depArray is filled verbatim from the untrusted file at line 46, so dep_index ranges 0..32767 with no validation. deps was allocated at line 19 with exactly cache->hdr->imagesCount int entries, and no guard in the shown code compares dep_index to that count. A crafted file with imagesCount=4 and a dependency entry depArray[k]=0x0004 makes deps[4]++ write one int past the heap allocation; the same index makes &img[dep_index] at line 83 an out-of-bounds read. Reachability requires R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER (line 13), accel (line 40), a successful dep-list read (line 46), and a filter match at line 67.

k starts at the file-derived extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex (read via read_cache_imgextra, line 50) and increments while depArray[k] != 0xffff. depArray has exactly cache->accel->depListCount entries (allocated line 41, filled line 46), and the loop body contains no k < depListCount bound; the array element is read before any bound test. A start index >= depListCount, or a dep list crafted without the 0xffff sentinel inside [start, depListCount), reads past the heap allocation and can continue indefinitely, disclosing adjacent heap contents and/or crashing.

assumptions: cache->buf and all cache fields used here (hdr, n_hdr, accel->depListCount, accel->depListOffset) are parsed from the untrusted dyld shared-cache file before create_cache_bins runs.
read_cache_images returns an array of hdr->imagesCount entries and read_cache_imgextra returns an array indexable by extras[j] for j < hdr->imagesCount.
R_NEWS0(type, n) allocates n elements of the given type; deps is int[imagesCount] and depArray is ut16[depListCount].
Reaching lines 77-91 requires R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER to be set by whoever invokes the analysis.
limitations: The depArray/deps corruption requires the operator to set R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER; if the attacker cannot control that environment variable, the file alone does not reach lines 79-83.

deps is sized from cache->hdr->imagesCount (header 0) but indexed with each header's hdr->imagesCount at lines 59/65/75/103; a later header with more images than header 0 would cause additional OOB indexing. Not separately reported because it is the same OOB class and requires multi-header file specifics.
r_buf_read_at at line 112 is unchecked, so magicbytes may be read uninitialized at line 113; impact is limited to classification of the sub-bin.
eprintf with %s and file-derived lib_name (lines 72, 88) allows newline/terminal-escape log injection; not rated as a security finding.
Untrusted-size allocations (lines 19, 41) and unchecked strdup/r_list_append results (lines 136-144, 147) are OOM/leak-only issues.
The k-loop can also keep scanning far past depArray until it finds 0xffff in heap memory; this is captured under the CWE-125 finding rather than as a separate hang/DoS claim.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerabilities. All inputs (pdev, ent, cfg_trans, PCI config/device registers) are kernel- or hardware-sourced in the shown scope; the only size/length values are compile-time constants (sizeof at lines 14, 17, 63, 67; addr_size ∈ {36, 64} at lines 61, 65), the only formatted output is a size-bounded snprintf with a fixed-width literal format (lines 146-147) that can emit at most 22 bytes, and every allocation/NULL/error result is checked before use (lines 20, 34, 41, 77-87, 90-93, 96-100, 110-114, 127-138, 155-172) with complete cleanup. No attacker-controlled value reaches any memory, injection, crypto, or authz sink.

assumptions: pdev, ent, and cfg_trans are supplied by the PCI core/driver configuration tables, not attacker-controlled within the shown code's scope.
trans->hw_id_str is a fixed-size field; snprintf truncation at sizeof(trans->hw_id_str) bounds all writes regardless of its actual size.
pdev->device and pdev->subsystem_device are 16-bit PCI config values, so (device << 16) + subsystem_device fits u32 and the %04X format emits at most 22 bytes.
limitations: Device-controlled PCI values (hw_rev, device, subsystem_device) are the only quasi-external data; they reach only a bounded, literal-format snprintf (lines 146-147) and fixed u32 arithmetic (line 145), so no injection or overflow path exists.
Treating HW_REV == 0xffffffff (line 110) as fatal is a robustness/availability heuristic, not an exploitable flaw.
Ignored return of pci_write_config_byte (line 104) and reliance on pcim managed resources are defensive-hardening concerns, not vulnerabilities.
Device-induced behaviors outside the shown code (e.g., interrupt storm handling in ISR paths) are out of scope for this function.

verdict.summary: ex_retab() is not vulnerable as shown. All memory operations are bounded: col never exceeds the current line length (the NUL check at line 153 precedes every index increment at lines 162/164 and the post-rewrite reset at line 147), the allocation at line 130 is exactly start_col + len + (old_len - col + 1) and matches the three disjoint copy/write regions (lines 134-139), and the tabstop divisor is constrained to >= 1 by the guards at lines 50-61 plus the validated 'tabstop' option. Line contents (attacker-controlled file data) and the retab argument were traced through every branch and loop without finding a value that violates these bounds, and no injection, crypto, or auth sinks exist in the function.

assumptions: curbuf->b_p_ts is kept in [1, TABSTOP_MAX] by 'tabstop' option validation, so the fallback at line 61 keeps new_ts >= 1 for the divisions at lines 103-110.
tabstop_set validates 'vartabstop' entries to positive widths, so tabstop_fromto returns non-negative t and s (and thus len = num_spaces + num_tabs >= 0 at line 128 in the FEAT_VARTABS path).
mb_ptr2len never advances col past the terminating NUL (Vim line-scanning invariant for buffer text), preserving the col <= old_len invariant across multibyte lines.
ml_get returns a non-NULL, NUL-terminated line buffer.
eap->line1/line2 are validated by the command dispatcher and the line range is finite.
The analysis assumes a 64-bit 'long' (or any build where the line-length arithmetic cannot overflow), consistent with Vim's mainstream targets; MAXCOL-capped vcol keeps all values well within range.
limitations: If ml_replace (line 140) fails, the newly allocated new_line is retained and processed locally but never freed — a per-line single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled amplification; out of the confirmed-finding bar.
If u_save (line 119) fails, new_line is set to NULL and the remaining lines of the range are skipped (robustness/availability of the command only, no memory safety impact).

After a rewrite the virtual column vcol is not recomputed for the shifted text; a stale (overstated) vcol can only trigger the 'Resulting text too long' early break at lines 156-160, a cosmetic/behavioral limitation with no out-of-bounds consequence.
Behavior of unseen helpers (tabstop_fromto, mb_ptr2len, ml_replace, tabstop_set) is taken per the invariants above; any deviation would reside in code outside this snippet.
An alloc failure (line 131) is checked and breaks out gracefully; DoS would require a line already large enough to exhaust memory, i.e., not attacker-amplified by this function.

verdict.summary: nft_verdict_init is the post-fix revision for the bound-chain verdict UAF (CVE-2024-1086 class): the generic bound-chain rejection (nft_chain_is_bound at lines 52-53) and the set-element bound-chain rejection (desc->flags & NFT_DATA_DESC_SETELEM && chain->flags & NFT_CHAIN_BINDING at lines 54-56) both precede the chain->use++ / data->verdict.chain store at lines 58-59, so no attacker-supplied NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO verdict can pin a bound chain whose lifetime is rule-bound. All other netlink inputs are bounded by the nested-attribute policy (code NLA_U32, chain name <= 31 bytes, maxattr NFTA_VERDICT_MAX for the tb[] array), no memory-mutation, injection, or crypto sink exists in the shown code, and the no-chain/no-id and error paths are fully handled. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: nft_chain_is_bound(chain) evaluates chain->flags & NFT_CHAIN_BINDING, making lines 52-53 and 54-56 test the same flag (the second is a redundant backstop).
nft_verdict_policy constrains NFTA_VERDICT_CODE to NLA_U32, NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN to a NUL-terminated NLA_STRING of at most NFT_NAME_MAXLEN-1 bytes, and NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN_ID to NLA_U32.
nft_chain_lookup / nft_chain_lookup_byid return either a valid chain pointer or an ERR_PTR, never a non-error NULL.
struct nft_data / struct nft_verdict is 16 bytes, so desc->len = sizeof(data->verdict) matches the buffer the caller supplies, and data/desc are non-NULL kernel-internal contract values.
For non-JUMP/GOTO verdicts the caller (nft_data_init path) zeroes *data before init, so data->verdict.chain is not left uninitialized.
limitations: Consumption of the stored verdict (nft_do_chain and set-element eval dispatch) is not in the shown code, so downstream interpretation of high-bit verdict flags (e.g. codes accepted via the masked default branch) cannot be confirmed here.

chain->use counter type and the chain-deletion/refcount-reversal paths are not shown, so a use-counter overflow (requiring tens of thousands of live references) is not confirmable and is out of scope.
A transaction-internal TOCTOU (parsing a verdict referencing a chain that is bound later in the same batch) is not demonstrable from these lines and is not raised as a finding.
Any refusal path (e.g., -EINVAL) is a netlink validation error, not a privilege or integrity break; no DoS amplification is reachable through a loop in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in parse_die: the loop bound at line 7 is the attacker-controlled abbrev->count (parsed from the binary's .debug_abbrev), and the body writes die->attr_values[i] (lines 8, 11) and reads abbrev->defs[i] (line 10) with no capacity check for either array. The guard only proves i < abbrev->count - 1, so an index equal to the real array capacity is admitted whenever count exceeds capacity + 1 (e.g., count=6 with capacity 4 reaches i=4); the shown code has no size parameter for die->attr_values or abbrev->defs and therefore cannot guarantee the accesses stay in bounds.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled abbrev->count (taint source, line 7 loop condition) drives index i into die->attr_values[i]; the only guard is i < abbrev->count - 1, which constrains i solely relative to the same attacker-controlled value and never against the array's real capacity (no capacity parameter is passed to parse_die). A crafted abbrev with count = 6 against an attr_values buffer of capacity 4 admits i = 4, an out-of-bounds write at this memset and at the &die->attr_values[i] argument of parse_attr_value (line 11), yielding heap corruption (CWE-787).

assumptions: abbrev->count and abbrev->defs originate from parsing the untrusted binary's .debug_abbrev data, so count is attacker-controlled with no upper bound enforced in the shown code.
die->attr_values has finite capacity; if the unseen caller always allocates exactly abbrev->count (or more) elements, the loop indices 0..count-2 would be in bounds.
limitations: The OOB write materializes only if the caller's die->attr_values capacity (or abbrev->defs length) is smaller than abbrev->count - 1; because the shown code neither allocates these buffers nor receives their sizes, that mismatch cannot be fully grounded from the shown code alone, which caps confidence at 0.6.

If abbrev->count counts only real attributes (no terminator entry), the count - 1 bound silently drops the last attribute (e.g., DW_AT_stmt_list); this is a functional under-parse, not a confirmed security impact.

If parse_attr_value could return NULL or advance buf past buf_end, the subsequent buf_end - buf computation at line 10 would be invalid; that helper's return behavior is not shown, so this is unconfirmed.
strdup(comp_dir) at line 32 depends on NUL-termination guaranteed by the unseen parse_attr_value; no violation is visible in the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: suggest_trie_walk STATE_REP applies a REP dictionary replacement to the attacker-influenced word buffer fword without bounding tl = STRLEN(ftp->ft_to): when tl > fl, STRMOVE(p + tl, p + fl) shifts the word tail (including the NUL) past the end of the caller-provided fword buffer and mch_memmove(p, ftp->ft_to, tl) writes tl bytes, producing an out-of-bounds write reachable whenever a REP item whose "to" is longer than its "from" prefix-matches the word.

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced tl = STRLEN(ftp->ft_to) (line 1364, from ftp->ft_to taken out of the dictionary REP table gap->ga_data at lines 1335-1341) flows unchecked into STRMOVE(p + tl, p + fl) (1367) and mch_memmove(p, ftp->ft_to, tl) (1370), where p = fword + sp->ts_fidx (1333). The guards that admit this block (1302-1304, 1342, 1348-1349) only require a REP-equipped language, a score/depth budget via TRY_DEEPER, and that ft_from prefix-matches the remaining word; none caps tl or verifies sp->ts_fidx + tl fits the caller-allocated fword buffer. Witness: fword = "a" in a buffer holding the original word plus NUL, REP {from="a", to=<40 bytes>}: fl=1, tl=40, the tail including the NUL is moved to offsets 40-41 and 40 bytes are written at 0-39, i.e. ~40 bytes past the 2-byte buffer (CWE-787, out-of-bounds write).

assumptions: MAXWLEN is the compile-time word-length cap (40) used for the local arrays tword/stack/preword/compflags.
The caller allocates fword with at most enough space for the original bad word and its NUL (the function receives no length/capacity argument and guarantees no slack for REP growth).
REP items (sl_rep / sl_repsal) come from the active spell/aff data that the user can supply, so ft_from/ft_to lengths are treated as attacker-influenced.
su->su_badlen matches the length of su->su_badptr and fword as passed by the caller.
limitations: Bounds for tword[sp->ts_twordlen++] = c (699, 930), compflags[sp->ts_complen] (270, 479-480) and writes at stack[depth+1] depend on TRY_DEEPER/go_deeper which are not in the shown code; a missing/incorrect bound there cannot be confirmed from the shown code alone.

STRCPY(preword + sp->ts_prewordlen, ...) (303) and STRCAT(preword, " ") (554) accumulate into preword[MAXWLEN * 3] across splits/compounds with no shown bound; no concrete overflowing witness could be derived from the shown invariants.
sprintf into changename[depth][80] (e.g., 686-692, 931, 1353-1355) can exceed 80 bytes with MAXWLEN-length words, but it is compiled only under DEBUG_TRIEWALK, so it is unreachable in normal builds.
add_suggestion(su, ..., sp->ts_fidx - repextra, ...) (408, 423) could underflow after repeated growing REP replacements; add_suggestion is not shown, so the impact is unconfirmed.

Short over-reads at the end of fword (fword[sp->ts_fidx + 1] in STATE_DEL, p[1]/p[2] in STATE_SWAP/STATE_SWAP3) read at most one or two bytes into the NUL region with no attacker-chosen extent; no security impact confirmed.
The walk may have exponential worst-case work, but it is constrained by score/depth limits, ui_breakcheck() (1418-1421) and the optional FEAT_RELTIME time limit; no ReDoS finding confirmed.

verdict.summary: 32-bit integer overflow in the brush-buffer size calculation: `size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes` (line 122) is computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, while the sanitize guard (lines 47-51) only bounds the product against 64-bit G_MAXSIZE, so on 64-bit builds a GBR file with version=1, width=32768, height=65536, bytes=2 passes every check and wraps size to 0. g_malloc(0) yields a minimal heap buffer and the case-2 conversion loop (lines 190-207) then performs 2^31 iterations, reading 2-byte values and writing 1 byte per iteration far beyond the allocation (heap OOB read/write). Exploitation requires GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE >= 65536 (e.g., 300000 in GIMP >= 2.10.4) and a 64-bit build.

evidence.reason: Taint: width, height and bytes are attacker-controlled guint32 fields read from the GBR file at line 31 and normalized at lines 40-42. The product is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic; the guard at line 51 checks G_MAXSIZE / width / height / bytes >= 1, which on 64-bit builds only rejects products >= 2^64 and does not constrain the 32-bit intermediate. Witness 32768 x 65536 x 2 passes lines 47-51 (assuming GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE >= 65536) and wraps to size == 0, which is then passed to g_malloc at line 123.

Confirmed OOB read sink: for the witness file (size wraps to 0 at line 122, g_malloc(0) returns a minimal buffer), the loop at line 190 admits i in [0, 2^31) because its bound bh.width * bh.height also wraps to 2^31, and buf advances 2 bytes per iteration, reading up to 4 GiB from an allocation of ~0 bytes past the heap object.

Confirmed OOB write sink: for the same witness (size == 0 at line 122), the loop at line 190 runs 2^31 iterations writing 1 byte at offsets 0..2^31-1 into a minimal heap allocation returned by g_malloc(0) at line 123. The guard at line 51 fails to prevent the size wrap on 64-bit (G_MAXSIZE is 64-bit while the product at line 122 is 32-bit), and the width/height cap at line 47 excludes this input only if GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE < 65536, which the shown code does not establish.

assumptions: GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE (referenced at lines 47-48, defined outside the shown code) is assumed >= 65536 (e.g., 300000 in GIMP >= 2.10.4), so the witness width=32768, height=65536 passes the width/height guard.

64-bit build: gsize/G_MAXSIZE are 64-bit while the line-122 multiplication is 32-bit. On 32-bit builds the guard at line 51 rejects the witness (G_MAXSIZE/32768/65536/2 == 0), so the finding is 64-bit specific.
glib g_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL minimal allocation, making size==0 proceed to the loop.
All BrushHeader fields are fully attacker-controlled file bytes (read at line 31, converted via g_ntohl).
limitations: If GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE <= 30000 (GIMP 2.0-2.8-era builds), no width/height pair can overflow the line-122 product for bytes in {1,2,4} (max 3.6e9 < 2^32), and the bytes=18 paths terminate in a clean error return, so the OOB is unreachable in that configuration.
g_new(gchar, bn_size) at line 97 lets the file's header_size drive an allocation of up to ~2 GiB (bn_size is a positive gint up to 2^31-1); impact is OOM abort (DoS) only and is not elevated.

The pattern path allocation at line 165 (4 * width * height) shares the overflow math but requires the preceding read of width*height bytes (>= 2 GiB for the same witness values) to succeed, making it impractical.
Failures of gimp_image_new/gimp_layer_new/gimp_drawable_get are unchecked; any NULL-return behavior comes from unseen framework code and is out of scope.
g_message/g_set_error formats are fixed strings; filename (caller-supplied path, not file content) is out of the malicious-file threat model.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe() installs a page-cache-backed pipe buffer (lines 35-39) without resetting pipe_buffer.flags, so a stale PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE left by an earlier user write()/drain cycle survives. A subsequent pipe_write() then merges attacker-supplied data directly into the file-backed page-cache page, bypassing the file's write permission (Dirty Pipe, CVE-2022-0847; local privilege escalation).

evidence.reason: The pipe buffer slot selected at lines 21/30 is reused after an attacker-controlled write()/drain cycle that leaves PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE set. This block reinitializes ops/page/offset/len but never buf->flags, and none of the shown guards (bytes cap at lines 11-12, zero check at line 14, sanity() at line 17, pipe_full() at line 32) clears or constrains the flag. The surviving flag makes fs/pipe.c pipe_write() merge attacker data into the file-backed page-cache page, bypassing file write permissions — the Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) root cause, CWE-281.

assumptions: pipe->ring_size is a power of two, so `i_head & p_mask` (lines 21/30) keeps the index inside pipe->bufs[].
pipe->tail/head/max_usage and i->head/i->iov_offset/i->count satisfy standard kernel pipe/iov_iter invariants, enforced by sanity() (line 17) and pipe_full() (line 32).
The page pointer passed in is a valid, refcounted page-cache page supplied by the caller.
limitations: `buf->len += bytes` (line 25) promotes to 64-bit then truncates to unsigned int; overflow would require bytes > UINT_MAX in one call, not demonstrated since callers iterate one page per call — no confirmed memory-safety impact from the shown code.
Wrap of `i->iov_offset`/`i->count` would require near-SIZE_MAX values inconsistent with sane iov_iter state; not demonstrated.

The unauthorized data copy itself executes in fs/pipe.c pipe_write() (unseen); the shown function is the in-scope root cause because it fails to reset the merge-capability flag when installing the page-cache buffer.

verdict.summary: The shown code is plan-executor construction with no attacker-reachable memory, injection, crypto, file, or authz sink. The only hazardous arithmetic (divisions at lines 59 and 114) is fully covered by guards: line 14 admits only numRecords > 100 before line 59, and line 91 requires numRecords != 0 and an engaged bucketUnpacker before line 114 and the dereferences at lines 121/133. The trialStage dereference at line 160 is short-circuit protected. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: sampleSize is non-negative (planner/governor-enforced for the $sample stage).
numRecords is a non-negative collection record-count estimate produced by the framework.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a positively-validated server parameter.
CollectionShardingState::get returns a non-null handle (framework invariant; no null-producing path exists in the shown code).
Line numbers are relative to the start of the provided snippet.
limitations: sampleSize and gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount are passed into SampleFromTimeseriesBucket/UnpackTimeseriesBucket constructors (lines 117–133) whose bodies are not shown; any downstream allocation or behavior driven by these values is a pass-through and out of scope.

A hypothetical gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount of 0 would make the line-114 ratio NaN, but that parameter is not attacker-controlled and no memory/injection/authz sink would be reached; classified as a robustness concern only.
css->... at line 52 relies on a non-null CollectionShardingState::get return; the shown chain contains no null-producing path, so a NULL dereference here is not a confirmed finding.
All arithmetic on numRecords/sampleSize promotes to double; value-range oddities (e.g., negative counts) are excluded by the lines 14/91 guards on every path that reaches a division.

verdict.summary: In the dependency-resolution loop, file-controlled values from the dyld-cache accelerator table drive indices into heap buffers without length checks: dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff allows up to 32767 and is written into deps[] (allocated with hdr->imagesCount entries) at line 81, and the same loop reads depArray[k] and img[dep_index] with no k < depListCount / dep_index < imagesCount bounds, yielding heap OOB write and OOB reads from untrusted file input.

evidence.reason: dep_index is derived at line 80 from file-controlled depArray content read at line 46 (depArray[k] & 0x7fff, admitted range 0..32767). deps was allocated at line 19 with exactly cache->hdr->imagesCount ints (e.g., 1024). A file supplying depArray[k] = 0x5000 yields dep_index = 20480, passing the only guard (the 0x7fff mask) and writing 4 bytes ~19,456 ints past the deps allocation — an attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). No dep_index < hdr->imagesCount check exists anywhere on the path (lines 58-95).

The loop iterates depArray — allocated with depListCount ut16 entries at line 41 — with no k < depListCount term. k is seeded from file-controlled extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex and advanced until a sentinel value is seen: with depListCount=8 and dependentsStartArrayIndex=8 the condition reads depArray[8], and a depList lacking any 0xffff value advances k past the 2*depListCount-byte allocation entirely, a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose only terminator is a data value, not a length bound.

img was produced by read_cache_images with hdr->imagesCount entries (line 32), but dep_index (line 80) is an unmasked-by-size file value in 0..32767. With hdr->imagesCount=1024 and depArray[k]=0x7fff, &img[32767] is a heap read thousands of elements past the img allocation, with no dep_index < hdr->imagesCount check in the shown path (lines 58-95) — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), same taint and gate as the write at line 81.

assumptions: Line numbers refer to the provided listing, numbered from 1 at 'static RList *create_cache_bins(...)'.
img returned by read_cache_images (line 32) has hdr->imagesCount entries and cache->hdr/cache->accel are parsed directly from the untrusted dyld-cache file.
R_FREE frees and NULLs its argument (radare2 convenction), so the cleanup at lines 98-99 and 154-158 does not double-free.
Reachability of the findings requires R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER to be set and at least one image name to match the filter (line 67), which are normal operating conditions of this filter feature.
limitations: deps is allocated once with cache->hdr->imagesCount of the first header (line 19) but indexed by each header's own hdr->imagesCount at lines 59, 65, 75, and 103; a crafted multi-header cache with hdr[1].imagesCount > hdr[0].imagesCount yields the same OOB class via a second trigger — deliberately not added as a separate CWE.
eprintf log lines at 72 and 88 print file-controlled strings with no newline neutralization (log-injection class), reachable but minor impact only; not scored in the verdict.
The depListCount * 2 check at line 46 could wrap in ut32 arithmetic for depListCount >= 2^31, but R_NEWS0 at line 41 would fail the ~4 GB allocation first and goto next — not exploitable.
Memory-exhaustion DoS via attacker-large depListCount repeated per header is guarded by NULL checks (lines 42-44, 51-53) that exit cleanly; not attacker-scalable in a single pass.
NULL dereferences of cache->hdr or cache->accel would require an out-of-scope caller to pass a NULL-bearing cache; not treated as a finding.
cache->maps[maps_index] at line 106 and n_hdr-sized accessors at lines 28-31 are not validated in the shown code, but their bounds are enforced by unseen loader code; flagged for completeness only.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerabilities. All inputs (pdev, ent, cfg_trans) are kernel-provided or static compile-time driver data; no attacker-controlled value reaches any security-relevant sink. Allocations are fixed-size and NULL-checked, all log/printf calls use literal formats with integer arguments, the only string write (hw_id_str, lines 137-138) is size-capped by snprintf, and error paths free each resource exactly once. The unchecked alloc_workqueue (line 165) and unguarded base_params dereference (line 38) are robustness concerns only, with no attacker-tainted or shown-code-reachable NULL path.

assumptions: The Linux PCI probe-callback contract guarantees pdev is non-NULL and fully initialized (dev, irq, device, subsystem_device).
cfg_trans points to static, const driver configuration whose base_params member is always a valid non-NULL pointer.
pcim_iomap_table(pdev) contains an entry for BAR 0 because pcim_iomap_regions_request_all(pdev, BIT(0), ...) succeeded at line 80 before the table read at line 86.
Error-label fall-through at out_free_ict/out_no_pci frees each resource exactly once.
limitations: Unchecked alloc_workqueue return at line 165: if it returned NULL, the pointer is only stored and INIT_WORK is applied to the work struct in this function; any NULL dereference would occur in unshown code (later queue_work), so no confirmed finding.
cfg_trans->base_params dereference at line 38 has no NULL guard, but cfg_trans is static driver data and no shown path can make it NULL; a NULL value could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller.

CSR_HW_REV read at line 100 is device-controlled under a malicious-hardware threat model, but it is consumed only by u32 bit arithmetic (lines 114-115) and a constant-format log (line 133); no memory, index, or injection sink.
Possible truncation of trans->hw_id_str by snprintf at lines 137-138 is bounded by sizeof and has no security impact.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in parse_command_modifiers: when an Ex-mode command line starts with the Visual range prefix '<,'> and ends with no command (use_plus_cmd), the code copies the tail with mch_memmove then STRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "'<,'>+"), which always extends the string one byte past the previous NUL (orig_cmd + 5 + len). No capacity check exists, so a maximum-length Ex-mode line ('<,'> followed by 794 spaces in an 800-byte buffer) writes the terminating NUL one byte past the buffer (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled command line eap->cmd with a '<,'> prefix (line 17) is advanced to cmd_start = orig_cmd + 5 (lines 24-25); after whitespace/colon skipping (34-39) a line ending at NUL in Ex mode sets use_plus_cmd (42-51); branch 328 (eap->cmd > cmd_start) is satisfied by whitespace-only progress and does not check buffer capacity; len = STRLEN(cmd_start) (336) is the full tail length (e.g. 794 spaces), and this STRCPY writes 7 bytes at orig_cmd + len, ending one byte past the previous NUL at orig_cmd + 5 + len (e.g. index 800 of an 800-byte line buffer) - a 1-byte out-of-bounds NUL write with no guarding length/capacity check in the shown code.

assumptions: eap->cmd is non-NULL and NUL-terminated, guaranteed by the exarg_T/ex-line framework.

The Ex-mode line buffer has zero slack when the line is at maximum length (800-byte IObuff in Vim), making the +1-byte extension land out of bounds; the shown code itself imposes no bound regardless of buffer capacity.
limitations: Candidate B: atoi() at line 316 may be fed a huge digit string (integer-overflow UB) only on the ':3 verbose ...' range-shadowing path; impact is confined to the verbose level and no security boundary is broken - not a finding.
Candidate C: the user-supplied filter regex is only compiled here (vim_regcomp, line 191); matching occurs outside the shown code, so ReDoS (CWE-1333) is out of scope.

Candidate D: when vim_regcomp fails, the NUL inserted by skip_vimgrep_pat_ext (line 184) is not restored (break at 192-193 skips the restore at 195-196); this truncates the command string but no memory-safety failure is demonstrated.

Candidate E: the non-plus transform (lines 345-347) is length-preserving (5-byte '<,'> plus leading space/colon are replaced by 1 colon + 5 bytes) and all writes stay within [orig_cmd, eap->cmd); verified safe.
The overflow byte is always the string terminator (0x00), restricting but not eliminating memory-corruption impact.

verdict.summary: Log injection in the NBD meta-context option handler: attacker-controlled query bytes read from the client socket are written verbatim to the debug log via a %.*s format (precision bound by querylen), with no CR/LF neutralization, allowing a remote client to terminate the log line and forge subsequent log entries (CWE-117). All memory-safety candidates (nrinfos read, INFO loop, meta-context query reads, optlen+1 allocation) were verified as fully guarded: line 200 caps exportnamelen at optlen-6, line 209's equality pins the INFO loop's last index to optlen-1, and lines 424/454 cap opt_index at optlen-4 before each 4-byte read.

evidence.snippet:
debug ("newstyle negotiation: %s: %s %.*s",
                   optname,
                   option == NBD_OPT_LIST_META_CONTEXT ? "query" : "set",
                   (int) querylen, &data[opt_index]);
evidence.reason:
Taint: &data[opt_index] holds raw network bytes read by conn_recv_full(data, optlen, ...) (line 370); querylen and the bytes are attacker-chosen from the option payload. The only validation on the shown path is the check_string call (lines 460-461), which bounds querylen against optlen-opt_index and (by contract) rejects NULs, but nothing in the shown code strips CR/LF before the write. Reachability: the client first sends NBD_OPT_STRUCTURED_REPLY (sets conn->structured_replies = true at line 358), then NBD_OPT_LIST_META_CONTEXT with exportnamelen=0, nr_queries=1, querylen=5 and the witness bytes {'a','
','b','
','c'} (no NUL, fits remaining payload), which passes the guard and reaches the sink: debug(...) at lines 464-467 writes those bytes to the log, so embedded '
' terminates the log line and lets the attacker forge subsequent log entries. Impact: log integrity/forgery - CWE-117 (low), because the sink writes the input without neutralization.

assumptions: MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is bounded well below 2^31 (e.g., 64MB), so malloc(optlen+1) cannot wrap uint32 arithmetic and the (int) querylen cast at line 467 is lossless and non-negative.

check_export_name(option, data, len, maxlen) and check_string(option, data, len, maxlen, what) enforce their maxlen arguments (reject len > maxlen), and check_string rejects embedded NUL; the memory safety of the meta-context path (strndup line 413, debug line 467, strncmp lines 474/482) depends on these helper contracts.
The log sink (debug()) writes the formatted message verbatim without escaping CR/LF; this is the standard behavior of nbdkit's debug logger.
Line numbers are 1-based counts from the start of the code as shown in the prompt (no repository file was provided).
limitations: No memory-safety finding: every attacker-controlled index/length is covered by a named guard - line 200 (admits exportnamelen 0..optlen-6, boundary optlen-6 reads end at optlen-1), line 209 (equality forces loop reads to end exactly at optlen-1), lines 424/454 (admit opt_index <= optlen-4, boundary reads end at optlen-1), with minimum-size prechecks at lines 182 and 389 preventing optlen-6/optlen-8 underflow.

If check_export_name or check_string did not enforce their maxlen arguments, the meta-context path would permit out-of-bounds reads (e.g., strndup at line 413, %.*s at line 467, strncmp at lines 474/482); this cannot be confirmed from the shown code because the helpers' internals are not present.
debug(... "%s count: %d", ..., nr_queries) at lines 433-435 passes uint32_t to %d: variadic type mismatch with no memory or injection impact (printing-only) - not treated as a finding.

A client-declared nr_queries up to 2^32-1 cannot cause unbounded work: each loop iteration consumes at least 4 payload bytes, the payload is capped by MAX_REQUEST_SIZE, and lines 454/460-461 force a bounded termination path (error reply + continue).
The log-injection finding requires debug/verbose logging to be enabled at runtime and has no memory-safety impact; severity is accordingly low.

verdict.summary: Under CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY, xfrm_expand_policies() writes the result of xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype() into pols[1] (line 22) without any check that the caller-provided pols array has capacity for two entries; the only count validation is *num_pols == 0 (line 7). With *num_pols == 1 and a single-slot buffer, a non-NULL, non-ERR lookup result produces an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) at index 1, later re-read at line 39.

evidence.snippet:
pols[1] = xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype(xp_net(pols[0]),
						    XFRM_POLICY_TYPE_MAIN,
						    fl, family,
						    XFRM_POLICY_OUT,
						    pols[0]->if_id);
evidence.reason: pols and *num_pols are a caller-supplied buffer/length pair whose only validation in the shown code is the line 7 check for *num_pols == 0 / pols[0] == NULL, which proves a first element exists but never verifies capacity >= 2. Witness: *num_pols == 1 with a one-element array, CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY enabled, pols[0]->action == XFRM_POLICY_ALLOW and pols[0]->type != XFRM_POLICY_TYPE_MAIN (lines 20-21), and a non-NULL/non-ERR result from xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype() (line 27 true, line 28 false). Control then executes the store pols[1] = <ptr> at line 22, writing past the one-element buffer, and line 34/line 39 subsequently read pols[1]. The guard is insufficient: it admits the failing value *num_pols == 1, and no protecting check bounds the array size to >= 2, so the write at line 22 is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY is enabled for the vulnerable path (lines 19-37) to be compiled in.
pols[0] passed by the caller is non-NULL and non-ERR when *num_pols > 0, as enforced by the shown checks at lines 7 and 12.
pols[0]->xfrm_nr and pols[1]->xfrm_nr are u8 values, so the u8-to-int widening at lines 17 and 34 is value-preserving and cannot overflow.
limitations: Actual in-kernel callers of this static function (not shown) allocate pols as a two-element array and pass *num_pols = 1, which would keep the pols[1] store and read in bounds; the finding rests on the function's own absence of a capacity check for a caller-supplied length/buffer pair, per the analysis scope rules.
If *num_pols were ever set larger than the array's valid entries, the loop read pols[i]->action at line 39 would be an out-of-bounds read of the same root cause; not counted as an independent CWE.

The sum *num_xfrms = pols[0]->xfrm_nr + pols[1]->xfrm_nr (lines 17, 34) can reach 12, which may exceed XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6) in a later consumer; that consuming buffer/index logic is not present in the shown code and is therefore out of scope.
No attacker-controlled data reaches a format-string, command, SQL, log, HTTP header, or crypto sink in the shown code; those classes were inventoried and found absent.

verdict.summary: The line-40 guard bounds only bare provider_name length against 0xffff0000, but rrlen (uint16_t) is computed from provider_name + constant terms at lines 45-49, so a provider_name length L = 65536 - (17 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)) (or any congruent value below 0xffff0000) wraps the size_t sum to rrlen == 0. malloc(0) then returns a tiny/maximal NULL-free heap chunk, and at line 55 the size argument rrlen - 1 promotes to int -1 and is converted to SIZE_MAX, so snprintf writes the provider name plus fixed text out of bounds.

evidence.reason: provider_name is a config/file-derived input with no length cap in the shown code. The only guard (line 40) rejects lengths >= 0xffff0000 but admits the witness length L = 65536 - (17 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)), which makes the size_t sum at lines 45-49 wrap to uint16_t rrlen == 0 after truncation. malloc(rrlen) (line 50) then returns a non-NULL pointer, and at this sink rrlen - 1 promotes to int -1 and converts to SIZE_MAX as the snprintf size argument, so the provider bytes are written into a zero-size heap allocation: an out-of-bounds write. The guard's bound is insufficient because it validates the bare provider length instead of the summed rrlen before truncation.

assumptions: sizeof(struct SignedCert) is a compile-time constant S with 17 + 4*S < 65536, so the wrap-to-zero witness length L = 65536 - (17 + 4*S) is a small, physically insertable string length.
malloc(0) returns a non-NULL unique pointer on the target libc (glibc semantics); if it returns NULL the function takes the safe early return at line 53 and the overflow path is not reachable.
dnscenv->signed_certs_count and rotated_certs_count match the actual array sizes (caller invariant, unverified in the shown code).
provider_name is NUL-terminated (caller invariant).
The missing semicolon after `continue` at line 43 is treated as a transcription artifact; the analysis follows the intended control flow.
limitations: The snippet as shown does not compile (line 43 `continue` lacks a semicolon), so taken literally the program fails before running; the intended flow is analyzed instead.
Log-injection / config-list injection of provider_name at lines 8 and 5-7 share the same config-only provenance and low impact; they are not independently scored.
Unchecked strdup at line 71 can pass NULL to cfg_strlist_insert only on OOM, with no attacker-controlled volume scaling; not a finding.
Using rrlen - 1 (not rrlen) at line 55 can drop the trailing quote and produce malformed local-data records in the non-wrapping path; a correctness issue, not a memory-safety one.
On libcs where malloc(0) returns NULL, the overflow is unreachable and the impact reduces to an early failure; exploitability also depends on the ability to set a ~65 KB provider name.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree descends the case-folded trie with an unbounded depth that indexes MAXWLEN-element stack arrays. A crafted .spl spell file containing a word of >= MAXWLEN bytes drives depth past the array bounds, causing stack out-of-bounds writes of attacker-controlled bytes at lines 88-91 and the terminator write at line 60.

evidence.reason: depth counts the bytes of the current word read from byts[] (line 56), which is populated from the attacker-controlled .spl spell file (lines 27-28). No guard caps depth at MAXWLEN-1: the only depth condition is `depth >= 0` (line 37). A word of byte-length L >= MAXWLEN reaches depth == MAXWLEN, so this write plus arridx[curi/wordcount][depth] at lines 89-91 and tword[depth] = NUL at line 60 index the MAXWLEN-element stack arrays out of bounds. Since the written byte c comes directly from the file, the overflow writes attacker-chosen values onto the stack.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is the compile-time element count of arridx, curi, tword, tsalword, and wordcount; valid indices are 0..MAXWLEN-1.
byts and idxs (sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs) are the case-folded trie parsed from the loaded .spl spell file, so their byte sequences and encoded word lengths are attacker-influenced.
A fold-tree word whose byte-length is L causes the descent branch (lines 85-92) to execute exactly L times, bringing depth to L.
limitations: A malicious child index in idxs[n] (line 89) could also drive arridx[depth] outside the byts/idxs arrays at lines 39/42, but whether the unseen .spl loader validates child indices before this traversal is not demonstrable from the shown code, so it is not reported as a separate CWE.
A cyclic back-edge via idxs entries could make the outer loop (line 37) non-terminating, but this is subordinate to the confirmed overflow and not independently confirmed from the shown code.
spell_soundfold (line 61) and tree_add_word (line 65) operate on buffers whose writable lengths are not shown, so any overflow inside them is out of scope here.
words_done is promoted to int in smsg's %d (line 96) and wordcount sums can overflow for pathological files, but neither is a security finding on its own.

verdict.summary: In OP_ARGARY, the guard `if (MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1)` (line 644) admits env lengths down to m1+r+m2+2, but the kd tail reads `stack[m1+r+m2+1]` (line 677), i.e. `e->stack[m1+r+m2+2]`, one slot past the environment's heap buffer. Attacker-controlled bytecode (m1=m2=r=0, kd=1, lv=1, env len=2) passes the guard and triggers a one-slot heap out-of-bounds read whose value is stored into VM register regs[a+2].

evidence.reason: Operand b (decoded at lines 625-629) and lv come unvalidated from attacker-supplied bytecode via proc->body.irep->iseq (line 4), and MRB_ENV_LEN(e) is the heap allocation size of e->stack, set by crafting the enclosing proc's nlocals. The guard at line 644 (`MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1`) admits len == m1+r+m2+2, but with kd=1 this line reads stack[m1+r+m2+1] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+2], exactly one mrb_value past the end; witness m1=m2=r=0, kd=1, lv=1, len=2 passes the guard (2>1) yet reads e->stack[2] on a 2-slot allocation (CWE-125 heap out-of-bounds read).

assumptions: The VM may execute bytecode derived from attacker-controlled data (e.g., mrb_load_file/mrb_load_irep on untrusted files or network payloads); if bytecode is always compiler-verified and trusted, the finding is not reachable.
MRB_ENV_LEN(e) equals the number of mrb_value slots allocated for e->stack.
Release builds compile out mrb_assert, so the debug-only assertion at lines 314-316 does not constrain crafted bytecode.
limitations: OP_BLKPUSH (lines 1159-1183) exhibits the identical one-slot guard shortfall: guard `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` (1170-1171) vs. read `stack[m1+r+m2+kd]` (1181); same CWE-125 root cause, not added as a separate CWE.

The shown dispatch never checks operands against irep->nregs, irep->ilen, irep->plen, or irep->slen (e.g., regs[a] at line 48, regs[a+2] at 230, OP_JMP pc += at 284, OP_JMPUW pc = irep->iseq + a at 330, OP_APOST/OP_HASHADD register writes); crafted bytecode can thereby reach broader OOB read/write paths. These are the same systemic class, not individually confirmed via a separate witness.
No injection (format/command/SQL/header), cryptographic, or file/access-control sinks exist in the shown code.
The confirmed finding is an 8-byte heap over-read, not a write; exploitation would require a deployment that executes untrusted bytecode, which many mruby uses do not.

verdict.summary: The only security-relevant operation is the array read at line 6, whose index is s->reg % sizeof(s->edid_blob). The modulo maps any non-negative reg value into [0, sizeof-1], exactly the array's valid index range, so no out-of-bounds read is reachable and no other sink (injection, crypto, file, authz) exists in the shown code.

assumptions: s->reg is an unsigned type (uint8_t in QEMU's I2CDDCState), so it is never negative; the modulo arithmetic therefore cannot produce a negative index.
s->edid_blob is a fixed-size array member, so sizeof(s->edid_blob) is the exact number of elements being indexed (N), not a pointer size.
I2CDDC() is a container_of-style cast applied to a valid I2CSlave from the bus, so s is never NULL; no NULL-dereference path exists in the shown chain.
limitations: If s->reg were a signed type that could hold negative values, subject to the unseen struct definition, reg % sizeof could yield a negative index and an out-of-bounds read before the array; this is not the case in QEMU, where reg is uint8_t.
A pre-fix version of this function that read s->edid_blob[s->reg] without the modulo would be an out-of-bounds read once reg wrapped past the array size; that code is not the code shown here.

Returning EDID bytes to the guest bus is the device's designed function; even after uint8_t wrap-around the reads repeat valid in-bounds bytes, which is a functional behavior, not a memory-safety or disclosure finding.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in jetp3852_print_page: line_size is accepted up to DATA_SIZE (guard at line 22), but the pad write memset(end_data, 0, 7) at line 45 writes 7 bytes from end_data = data + line_size, reaching indices DATA_SIZE..DATA_SIZE+6 (up to 6 bytes past byte data[DATA_SIZE]). A job whose scanned line size is DATA_SIZE with a nonzero final byte triggers a deterministic out-of-bounds stack write.

evidence.reason: Sink: 7-byte write at end_data. line_size (line 19) is derived from job-controlled width/resolution; the only guard, `if (line_size > DATA_SIZE)` (line 22), admits line_size == DATA_SIZE, so end_data = data + line_size == data + DATA_SIZE (line 29). For a non-blank line with nonzero trailing bytes the while loop (lines 33-34) leaves end_data at that maximum, and memset writes indices DATA_SIZE..DATA_SIZE+6 — 6 bytes past the DATA_SIZE-byte stack array declared at line 10 (CWE-787). The guard would need to enforce line_size <= DATA_SIZE - 7.

assumptions: DATA_SIZE = LINE_SIZE * 8 and the byte data[DATA_SIZE] buffer are the real bounds in the shown code.
line_size is derived from device width/resolution as stated by the error message at lines 23-24.
A non-blank scan line with nonzero bytes at the far end of the line keeps end_data at its maximum value.
limitations: Practical triggering of the overflow requires the device/raster configuration to yield a line_size in the narrow band [DATA_SIZE-6, DATA_SIZE]; the shown code does not rule it out (the guard explicitly admits DATA_SIZE), but the device-initialization code that fixes max width is outside this snippet.

For the first rendered line, bytes of data beyond line_size are uninitialized stack memory that the transpose loop (lines 56-68) still reads and emits to the printer stream; this is a low-impact information-disclosure concern, not counted as a separate finding.
A negative line_size (unchecked at line 22) would make line 45 write before data, but no shown path produces a negative return from gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in get_recurse_data_length(): in the OP_COND case, `alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1)` (line 88) is computed from a pattern-derived link offset embedded in the bytecode and dereferenced at line 89 with no bounds check, so a bytecode value `GET(cc, 1) >= ccend - cc` reads past the end of the compiled code range (CWE-125), giving an attacker-supplied regex a crash/DoS and possible information-disclosure path through the JIT compiler.

evidence.snippet:
alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1);
    if (*alternative == OP_KETRMAX || *alternative == OP_KETRMIN)
evidence.reason: `GET(cc, 1)` reads a LINK_SIZE-byte link offset embedded in the compiled bytecode, which is derived from the attacker-supplied regex pattern, and line 89 dereferences `alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1)` with no bounds check. The only guard on the path is `while (cc < ccend)` at line 20, which constrains `cc` but not `alternative`; witness value `GET(cc, 1) = ccend - cc` passes that guard yet makes `*alternative` read at least one byte past the end of the scanned code range (OOB read, CWE-125). An `alternative < ccend` check is absent before the dereference.

assumptions: `GET(cc, 1)` reads a LINK_SIZE-byte (16- or 32-bit) link offset stored at cc+1, per PCRE2 bytecode conventions; GET2 reads an IMM2_SIZE value.
Contents of the compiled bytecode (opcodes and embedded operand values such as link offsets, group numbers, and name lengths) trace back to the caller-supplied regex pattern.
`optimized_cbracket` is sized by the pattern's bracket count; `PRIVATE_DATA`/`next_opcode` behave per PCRE2 JIT invariants and are not defined in the shown snippet.
The shown code performs only reads; output pointers and `common` are trusted framework state.
limitations: Line 73 `common->optimized_cbracket[GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE)]` is also an unguarded bytecode-derived array index of the same OOB-read class, but group numbers are compiler-encoded and in range for well-formed patterns; not independently confirmed, so no additional CWE is attached.

Advancement via `cc += PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1)` (line 46) and `cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1]` (lines 164/176) trusts compiler-maintained distances; no attacker-sizeable deviation is demonstrated in the shown code.
`next_opcode` returning NULL (lines 194-195) would only trip a debug build assert; in release builds the value is not dereferenced in the shown code.
Integer overflow of `length` would require a pattern with more than 2^31 counted opcodes, which is not demonstrated here.
No allocation-failure, truncation, incomdejection, or injection concerns exist in this function; it has no write, exec, SQL, log, HTTP, crypto, or file sinks.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() accepts a caller-supplied column index col_arg that is clamped only to be non-negative (line 3); the shown path never bounds col by the current line length, so when col exceeds the line length the pointer arithmetic p + col (line 18) is dereferenced by mb_head_off() past the NUL terminator of the ml_get_curline() buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap read (also fed to curs_columns() via w_cursor.col at lines 11/20).

evidence.reason: col_arg (line 1) is a caller-supplied index transformed at line 3 into col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg, which admits any col >= 0 and is the only guard. No check compares col with the length of the line buffer obtained from ml_get_curline() (line 17). With has_mbyte set, this line computes p + col and passes it to mb_head_off(), which dereferences bytes at and behind p + col. A witness value col = linelen + 1 (line length obtained at line 17) passes the line-3 clamp yet makes p + col point past the NUL, so mb_head_off() performs an out-of-bounds read; the same over-large col is stored to w_cursor.col at line 11 and consumed by curs_columns() at line 20. Confirmed CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line buffer with valid indices 0..linelen.
mb_head_off() scans only within [base, p], so its return value is <= col and the subtraction at line 18 cannot drive w_cursor.col below 0.
In the upstream product, ordinary callers (insert-mode paths) pass a cursor column or line length <= linelen; that invariant is not enforced anywhere in the shown code.
limitations: The historical negative-column out-of-bounds class is fully neutralized by the clamp at line 3 (col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg); it is not a finding.

Reachability of the upper-bound OOB depends on an unseen caller supplying col > current line length (e.g., a stale column after the line was shortened); the shown function never increases col itself, so no failing value is synthesized inside the shown code — this is the trusting-a-parameter pattern the rubric treats as in scope.
The actual byte reads occur inside the unseen helpers mb_head_off() and curs_columns(); only the pointer computation p + col and the w_cursor.col assignment appear in the shown code.
Theoretical pointer-wraparound if col approached COLNR_MAX with a high base address is not attacker-reachable and was not treated as a finding.
No injection, crypto, file-handling, or authn/authz sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the NBD_OPT_LIST_META_CONTEXT / NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT path, attacker-controlled meta-context query bytes are written verbatim into the server debug log via debug("%s %.*s", ..., (int) querylen, &data[opt_index]) with no escaping or newline neutralization, letting a remote client inject forged log lines (CWE-117). All memory-safety sinks were verified as protected by explicit guards (optlen <= MAX_REQUEST_SIZE; optlen >= 6 with exportnamelen <= optlen-6; optlen == 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos; opt_index+4 <= optlen; check_string/check_export_name maxlen arguments).

evidence.snippet:
debug ("newstyle negotiation: %s: %s %.*s",
                   optname,
                   option == NBD_OPT_LIST_META_CONTEXT ? "query" : "set",
                   (int) querylen, &data[opt_index]);
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled bytes from the socket (received into data at line 373; offset/length chosen by the client via querylen at lines 459-461) are written unescaped into the debug log via %.*s at lines 467-470. The shown guards (optlen >= 8 at 392, opt_index+4 <= optlen at 427/457, and check_string's maxlen=optlen-opt_index at 463-464) constrain only lengths, not content, so a query such as "x\n2026-09-25 forged" passes every shown check and injects a newline/forged content into the log line (CWE-117).

assumptions: MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is a server-internal constant well below UINT32_MAX, so malloc(optlen+1) (line 38) and the uint32 arithmetic cannot overflow on the shown path; optlen <= MAX_REQUEST_SIZE (line 34) caps every payload-buffer access.

check_export_name (lines 72/226/406) and check_string (line 463) enforce their explicit maxlen argument (len <= maxlen), consistent with the inline duplicate bound at line 203 and the guard at line 427.
All debug()/nbdkit_error() format strings are literals; no attacker-supplied format specifiers reach a printf-family sink.
limitations: Memory-safety candidates were demoted with named protective checks: the nrinfos memcpy (210) is bounded by optlen >= 6 (185) and exportnamelen <= optlen-6 (203), max index optlen-1; the INFO loop (267) is bounded by the equality at 212, max index optlen-1; the meta-context reads (429/459) are bounded by opt_index+4 <= optlen (427/457), and even a uint32 wraparound of opt_index can only produce small in-bounds indices.

The log-injection witness requires check_string (unseen) to admit control characters; if that helper enforces printable-only meta-context strings, the newline witness is not reachable, which keeps confidence at 0.6 rather than >= 0.7.
Impact of the log injection is limited to operator-facing debug logs (verbose mode); it does not enable code execution or data disclosure, hence severity low.

Helper-internal behavior (crypto_negotiate_tls, finish_newstyle_options, check_export_name string policy, send_newstyle_option_reply_* length handling) is outside the shown code and was not treated as a sink.

verdict.summary: In do_mouse(), the tab-page-line drag paths index TabPageIdxs with the input-derived global mouse_col without any bounds check (lines 263 and 321), while the equivalent click path guards the identical access with mouse_col < Columns (line 275). After the attacker triggers a tabline click to set in_tab_line, a drag event carrying mouse_col >= Columns (e.g., 200 with Columns == 80) reaches these reads and performs a heap out-of-bounds read, violating memory safety and potentially crashing Vim.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled global mouse_col (from terminal mouse-event decoding) indexes TabPageIdxs on the drag-in-tabline path with no bound. The same array is only ever validated by mouse_col < Columns on the click path (line 275), proving values >= Columns must be rejected; that guard is absent here. Witness: tabline click sets in_tab_line=TRUE (line 277), then a drag with mouse_col=200 while Columns=80, is_drag=TRUE, mod_mask=0 reaches line 263 and reads TabPageIdxs[200] past the end of the heap array (CWE-125, heap OOB read).

Identical unguarded read on the else-if drag path (mouse_row != 0 or firstwin->w_winrow <= 0): guards are only is_drag and in_tab_line, with no mouse_col < Columns check. A drag event with mouse_col >= Columns after a prior tabline click reaches line 321 and reads past the end of TabPageIdxs (CWE-125, heap OOB read).

assumptions: TabPageIdxs is dimensioned by Columns, as implied by the sole bounds check mouse_col < Columns applied to the same array on the click path (line 275).
mouse_row/mouse_col are global state populated from terminal/input mouse-event decoding, so their values are attacker-controllable input.
limitations: The downstream use of the OOB value (c1) in tabpage_move/tabpage_index (lines 264-265, 322) and goto_tabpage (line 292) could amplify impact, but those functions are not shown, so no separate finding is asserted.
The double-click whitespace skip loop (lines 767-768) terminates because gchar_pos() returns NUL (non-whitespace) at EOF; no hang or OOB is claimed.
No injection, crypto, file-handling, or authz sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All attacker-controlled netlink data is bounded by nla_parse_nested_deprecated and the verdict switch; chain lookups are fully error-checked with IS_ERR before any dereference; writes target caller-provided fixed-size storage with no attacker-controlled length or index. Potential NULL-deref, upper-bit handling, and use-count overflow concerns are helper-contract or volume-dependent hypotheses, not confirmed failures.

assumptions: nft_verdict_policy (used via nla_parse_nested_deprecated at lines 9-10) validates attribute types and lengths, so nla_get_be32 at line 16 reads an in-bounds u32.
nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid return ERR_PTR on failure and never return plain NULL, so the IS_ERR checks at lines 42-43 and 48-49 cover all failure values.
data points to at least sizeof(struct nft_data) of caller-allocated storage; desc->len at line 61 is an output field, not an attacker-controlled bound.
limitations: If a chain-lookup variant returned plain NULL instead of ERR_PTR, IS_ERR at lines 48-49 would not catch it and lines 50/53/56 would dereference NULL; under the actual kernel contract this path does not exist.

Upper bits of data->verdict.code are not independently validated beyond the low-byte switch check, but any harmful use would occur in packet-path consumers outside the shown code, so no sink is present here.
chain->use++ overflow at line 56 would require roughly 2^32 successful bindings to one chain, is bounded by memory, and is not triggered by a single message; it is not a demonstrated failure.
Behavior of unseen callers (e.g., under-sized data buffers) and lifetime/race conditions around chain->use and data->verdict.chain are outside the shown code and not confirmed.

verdict.summary: parseDragons allocates a heap buffer of attacker-chosen size (file length minus offset) but reads fixed 4-byte magic windows at b[0..3] and b[8..11] without requiring size >= 12. A file leaving only 1..11 bytes at the offset passes all guards (lines 4, 8) and memcmp over-reads up to 11 bytes past the heap allocation (lines 44 and 47).

evidence.reason: size = r_buf_size(buf) - off (lines 3,7) is fully attacker-controlled via file length/offset and is only guarded to be >= 1 (lines 4-10); malloc(size) at line 11 creates a buffer of that size. With size == 1 the guard chain admits the path, and this sink reads b[8..11], i.e. up to 11 bytes past the 1-byte heap object: heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing check is size >= 12 before the magic comparisons.

Same taint and guard insufficiency as line 47: with attacker-controlled size in 1..3 (e.g., size == 1), the checks at lines 4-10 are satisfied, yet this sink reads b[0..3], up to 3 bytes past the malloc(size) object (CWE-125).

The allocation whose bound is attacker-derived: size is r_buf_size(buf) - off (lines 3-7) with only an off>=size and size!=0 guard, so the object can be as small as 1 byte while lines 44 and 47 unconditionally read 4-byte windows reaching b+8..b+11.

assumptions: r_buf_size returns the full file length and r_buf_read_at returns the number of bytes read, so the available==size check at line 16 admits a fully populated buffer of exactly `size` bytes.
off is a caller-supplied parsed file offset that may point anywhere in the attacker-controlled file, including near EOF.
D is a debug-only macro, so lines 64-67 are compiled out of production builds.
limitations: Line 65 (r_read_le32(b+12)) performs the same class of over-read (needs size >= 16) but only when the debug `D` block is compiled in; not counted as a separate finding.
Early returns at lines 16-18 and 52-55 leak the malloc'd buffer; these are single-shot leaks with no attacker-controlled volume loop shown, so no CWE.

If the retry magic check fails (lines 58-60), parsing continues into r_coresym_cache_element_new (line 69) with modified/unverified input; the dangerous parse is outside the shown code (hardening concern only).

Truncation of ut64 size to the int length parameter of r_buf_read_at (lines 15, 52) and off+16 overflow at line 69 are not exploitable in the shown code: truncation paths fail the available!=size check and return NULL, and off is bounded by file size.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in the DDC EDID read callback: s->edid_blob is indexed by the guest-controlled s->reg with no bounds check, and s->reg is incremented on every read (line 7), so repeated guest reads can carry the index past the end of the 256-byte EDID buffer and disclose adjacent host memory.

evidence.reason: s->reg is guest-controlled (set from an I2C data byte by the device's offset-selection write handler) and is post-incremented at line 7 with no bounds check on every bus read, then used unvalidated as the index into s->edid_blob at line 6. A guest writing offset 255 and then reading twice drives s->reg to 256, so the second read accesses edid_blob[256], one byte past the 256-byte array (and keeps advancing on further reads). The guard that would make this safe, a check such as 'if (s->reg < sizeof(s->edid_blob)) return 0;', is absent from the shown code, so the witness value 256 reaches the sink line 6 unfiltered, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that leaks adjacent host heap and can destabilize QEMU.

assumptions: The device is QEMU's i2c-ddc slave (hw/i2c/i2c-ddc.c), where s->edid_blob is a 256-byte array and s->reg is written from guest-supplied I2C bytes by the device's write path.
i2c_ddc_rx is invoked once per byte the guest reads on the emulated I2C bus, so repeated reads reach lines 6-7 repeatedly.
The unchecked 's->reg++' at line 7 is the only index source visible in the shown path and imposes no upper bound.
limitations: If s->reg were an 8-bit field wrapped at 256 together with a 256-byte blob, reads would stay in-bounds; the shown code alone does not display the field width or array size, but the absent bounds check means no limit is enforced on the shown path, which is the exploitable condition in the real device.
The impact is primarily host-memory disclosure and potential instability; a hard crash depends on the runaway read crossing an unmapped page boundary, which is not demonstrated from the shown code.

verdict.summary: In restricted (non-root) mode, the option allowlist at lines 90-94 admits '-i'/'--internal-only'; case 'i' then calls mnt_context_disable_helpers(cxt, TRUE) (line 115) and the flow reaches rc = mnt_context_mount(cxt) (line 304) with no compensating restricted-mode check in the shown code. The helper layer that enforces the fstab/'user'-option authorization for unprivileged mounts is disabled, letting a restricted user mount entries/devices reserved for root (CVE-2016-2779 class) - a local authorization bypass.

evidence.snippet:
if (mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) &&
	    !strchr("hlLUVvpris", c) &&
	    c != MOUNT_OPT_TARGET &&
	    c != MOUNT_OPT_SOURCE)
	    exit_non_root(option_to_longopt(c, longopts));
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled option code 'i' ('-i'/'--internal-only') from argv passes this restricted-mode guard because 'i' is a member of the allowlist string "hlLUVvpris". The guard is the only authorization check protecting the privileged mount path; with no other shown check excluding 'i', the flow reaches mnt_context_disable_helpers(cxt, TRUE) (case 'i', lines 114-116) and then rc = mnt_context_mount(cxt) (line 304) with libmount helper execution - and the fstab/'user'-option enforcement it carries - disabled. A concrete witness is a non-root restricted invocation `mount -i -U <uuid-of-root-only-fstab-entry>`: 'i' and 'U' both pass line 91, branch B (lines 257-265) does not exit because only a source is set, and line 304 executes the privileged mount unmounted from the restriction mechanism, an authorization bypass (CWE-863).

assumptions: mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) is true when a non-root user runs the setuid/privileged mount binary; this is libmount-determined and trusted.
usage() terminates the process (util-linux usage() ends in exit()), so branches calling usage(stderr) do not fall through to mnt_context_mount.
mnt_context_set_source() duplicates its argument, so free(srcbuf) after the LABEL=/UUID= sources (lines 151, 157) is not a use-after-free in the shown code.
libmount applies the fstab/'user'-option restricted-mode check on the helper-execution path that -i disables; the shown code contains no compensating enforcement after mnt_context_disable_helpers.
limitations: The final mount(2)/helper invocation and its fstab enforcement are implemented in unseen libmount code, so the privilege consequence depends on that behavior; within the shown code, line 91 is the only gate and it admits 'i'.
Potential quoting/escaping of '"' or '\' in optarg inside the LABEL="%s"/UUID="%s" strings (lines 148, 154) reaches only an opaque context setter; no injection sink exists in the shown code.
All err()/warnx()/usage() format strings are constants; optarg is only an argument to %s, so no format-string vulnerability.
xasprintf allocation failure with a large attacker label is single-shot DoS at most, with no memory-unsafety in the shown code.
Singular source/target labeling, fstab reading (append_fstab), listing output (print_all), helper argv construction, and option-string parsing occur in unseen code and were not evaluated.

verdict.summary: When fopen() fails (an attacker can supply any nonexistent or unreadable path as filename), the error branch (lines 16-19) jumps to the cleanup label and calls fclose(fd) with fd == NULL at line 352. Passing NULL to fclose is undefined behavior; on libcs that dereference the FILE* (e.g., MSVC CRT) this is a NULL pointer dereference that crashes the process — an attacker-triggerable denial of service.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled `filename` flows to `fopen` (line 14), whose NULL return on a nonexistent/unreadable path is admitted by the guard `if (!fd)` (line 16), which sends execution via `goto cleanup` (line 19) to the cleanup label (line 351) with fd == NULL; the unconditional `fclose(fd)` at line 352 then passes NULL to fclose with no NULL check on this path — the only guard (`if (!fd)`) selects the exact NULL-delivering branch, and every other goto-cleanup site has a valid stream. fclose(NULL) is undefined behavior per the C standard and dereferences a NULL stream pointer on implementations that do not tolerate it, yielding a NULL-pointer-dereference crash (CWE-476, DoS only).

assumptions: Bitmap_File_Head/Bitmap_Head fields use the BMP plugin's standard scalar types (guint32 bfOffs/biSize, gint32 biWidth/biHeight, guint16 biBitCnt); these declarations are not in the shown snippet.
at_exception_fatal returns normally, so the `goto cleanup` on line 19 executes and reaches the fclose at line 352.
limitations: ColormapSize (line 253) can underflow, but with guint32 bfOffs/biSize the wrap produces a positive value (~2^30) that the `> 256` clamp (lines 261-262) reduces to 256; a negative value would need signed header types not shown, and any memory-safety consequence would occur inside the unseen ReadColorMap (line 334) — delegated code, out of scope.

The `(unsigned short)` narrowing casts at line 350 truncate attacker-controlled width and negative height; any OOB from a width/height mismatch with image_storage would occur in unseen consumers of the returned bitmap.

The overflow guards at lines 302-303 are effective for the shown arithmetic: clause 1 bounds width*biBitCnt <= 0x7fffffff, and lines 314/321 stay in range; the full ReadImage allocation (lines 341-348) is not shown and is not audited here.
Uninitialized ColorMap palette if ReadColorMap skips all entries, and mishandling of a huge fseek offset (line 338), affect only unseen ReadColorMap/ReadImage behavior.
All LOG calls use literal format strings with filename only as a %s argument, so there is no format-string or log-injection finding.
The fclose(NULL) impact is platform-dependent (glibc returns EOF; MSVC CRT and assert builds crash); consequence is limited to denial of service.

verdict.summary: sug_filltree walks slang->sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs without any bounds checks: arridx[depth] (= idxs[n], line 87) and n = arridx[depth] + curi[depth] (line 51) are file-supplied values used to read byts[arridx[depth]]/byts[n]/idxs[n] (lines 37, 54, 87) and to write idxs[arridx[depth]] (line 40) with no check against sl_fbyts_len/sl_fidxs_len; depth is incremented without a MAXWLEN bound, so tword[depth++] = c (line 86) overruns the stack array. A crafted spell file can set, e.g., idxs[1] = 1003 with sl_fidxs_len = 1000 and byts[1003] = 0, making line 40 a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), with OOB reads (CWE-125) along the same path and a stack overflow when the tree depth exceeds MAXWLEN.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write into slang->sl_fidxs: arridx[depth] is set from file-supplied idxs[n] at line 87 for every depth > 0 and is never checked against sl_fidxs_len (or sl_fbyts_len). Concrete witness: sl_fbyts_len=1005, sl_fidxs_len=1000, byts[0]=1, byts[1]='a', byts[1003]=0, idxs[1]=1003. After one descent depth=1 reaches arridx[1]=1003; the line-37 guard curi[1]=1 > byts[1003]=0 passes and line 40 writes idxs[1003], past the 1000-element fidxs array. No bounds guard protects this write; the only length check in the function (line 77) covers a different read.

Stack OOB write: depth is incremented on every descending step and is never compared against MAXWLEN, the size of tword/arridx/curi/wordcount. A crafted trie with a chain of more than MAXWLEN non-NUL labels (each node count 1 with its child idx pointing to the next node) drives depth to MAXWLEN, at which point line 86 writes tword[MAXWLEN] past the MAXWLEN-element stack array; the subsequent arridx[depth]/curi[depth]/wordcount[depth] accesses (lines 87-89) and the next line-37 read are equally out of bounds (CWE-787, with CWE-125 on the read side).

assumptions: slang->sl_fbyts, slang->sl_fidxs, and slang->sl_fbyts_len are populated directly from the contents of a loaded .spl spell file, so their values are attacker-controlled up to the file size; the loader (not shown) is assumed not to validate every index.
idxs entries are capable of carrying arbitrary values (e.g., 1003 or negative values) as read at line 87.
MAXWLEN is the element count of each local stack array (arridx, curi, tword, tsalword, wordcount), so valid indices are 0..MAXWLEN-1.
limitations: The internals of spell_soundfold() and tree_add_word() are not in the shown code; any flaw strictly inside them (e.g., tsalword handling) is out of scope, though tword's terminator at line 58 is correctly placed for in-range depths.
If the unshown .spl loader fully validates every byts/idxs index and depth before calling sug_filltree, the OOB accesses are prevented; that protection is not demonstrable from this snippet.
smsg(_("Total number of words: %d"), words_done) passes an unsigned to %d; benign and not attacker-influenceable.

A crafted cyclic node-pointer chain can also make the outer while loop (line 35) run unboundedly; this denial-of-service behavior is a secondary manifestation of the same missing-validation root cause as the memory corruption.
The unchecked return value of spell_soundfold() (line 59) is ignored but has no identified security consequence in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only buffer writes are the visual-range fixup at lines 342-343 and 347-349 (mch_memmove/STRCPY), and every admitted path is bounded: the line 328 guard 'eap->cmd > cmd_start' guarantees at least one byte M+S>=1, the NUL checks at lines 42-51 and 67-76 ensure an OK exit never reaches line 349 with eap->cmd at the NUL unless use_plus_cmd routes to the length-non-increasing ' *+' branch, and with L=5+M+S+C the line 349 write occupies [M+S-1, M+S+4] within [0, L-1] while the line 343 write occupies [M, M+3] within [0, 5+M]. Remaining concerns (filter-pattern NUL not restored on vim_regcomp failure, dead atoi branch, tab-number boundary, regex compile-only) are robustness/logic issues or out-of-scope per the analysis rules.

assumptions: eap->cmd points to a NUL-terminated buffer that actually contains the string it denotes, including the optional five-byte '<,'> prefix; this is the standard Vim command-line invariant.
Return values of skip_range/skip_vimgrep_pat_ext remain within the eap->cmd string and comply with the NUL-termination invariant (their internal parsing is unseen).
errormsg, cmod, and eap are valid framework-owned objects for the lifetime of the call.
limitations: In case 'f', if vim_regcomp (line 191) fails, 'break' at line 193 skips '*nulp = c' (line 196) and leaves eap->cmd un-advanced, embedding a NUL in the command line; impact is command truncation/error behavior, not memory corruption or injection (silent truncation, no security impact).

The 'verbose' digit branch (line 313-317) is effectively dead on the shown control flow (line 311 advances p, not eap->cmd, so *eap->cmd is 'v'); even if reachable, atoi has no memory sink in the shown code.
The tab case admits tabnr == LAST_TAB_NR producing cmod->cmod_tab = LAST_TAB_NR + 1 (line 279); the consuming tab-page lookup is outside the shown code, so no failure can be confirmed here.

Regex reached by vim_regcomp (line 191) is attacker-supplied, but the shown code only compiles it; the match (potential ReDoS, CWE-1333) happens in unseen code, so it is out of scope under the stated rules.

checkforcmd_* / STRNCMP reads are bounded by modifier-literal lengths or NUL; an out-of-bounds read would require a caller-supplied non-NUL-terminated buffer, contradicting the stated trust invariant.
No weak-crypto, command/argument injection, SQL/XPath, log/header injection, or authz/authn logic exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory data from the attacker-controlled directory_table without any check that each fixed-size read (sizeof(dirh), sizeof(*dire)) and the dire->size+1 name read fit within the directory region 'size' or the directory_table allocation. bytes and size derive from crafted inode fields ((*i)->data, (*i)->offset, (*i)->start) and the lookup_entry result, so a crafted squashfs image (e.g. (*i)->data == 18, with the directory block last in the table) drives out-of-bounds reads past the end of directory_table, causing memory disclosure or a crash.

evidence.reason: bytes is attacker-controlled (lookup_entry result from (*i)->start at L42, plus (*i)->offset at L48) and size is attacker-controlled ((*i)->data at L49); the only guard is the loop condition bytes < size (L51), which admits bytes == size - 1, after which this 16-byte fixed read reaches up to size + 15.
