No check compares bytes + sizeof(dirh) against size or against the directory_table allocation, so with (*i)->data == 18 and the directory block placed at the end of the table in the crafted image, this read crosses the end of directory_table (OOB read, CWE-125).

dire->size is attacker-controlled (read at L77) and the L82 check (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) only protects the local 265-byte buffer, not the read source; in the inner loop (L70) bytes is never re-checked against size, so the dire->size+1-byte read at directory_table + bytes continues past the directory region and, for a block placed at the end of directory_table (attacker-chosen image layout), past the allocation end (OOB read, CWE-125).

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN == 256 (squashfs 3.x), so the local buffer at L5-7 provides 257 bytes for dire->name; with the L82 guard admitting size <= 255, the L87 copy (<= 256 bytes) and L89 NUL write (index <= 256) stay in bounds.
lookup_entry returns the byte position of the directory block within directory_table (standard squashfs-tools hash-table semantics); the -1 case is handled at L44-46.

directory_table is a global buffer whose start/end are derived from the superblock (directory_table_start/end) and thus from the attacker-crafted image layout, so placing the parsed block at the end of the allocation is attacker-chosen.
struct dir_ent.name is sized SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1, making the L101 strcpy safe given the L82 cap.
limitations: Integer overflow: L48 (bytes += (*i)->offset) and L49 (size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3) mix unsigned values into int; a wrap to a negative bytes would drive directory_table + bytes before the buffer. Signed overflow is UB, so this alternate trigger of the same OOB class is not confirmed independently and is not assigned a separate CWE.
Log injection: TRACE at L90-92 prints attacker-controlled dire->name with %s, allowing newline injection into logs (low severity); demoted to keep the verdict focused on the OOB read.
NULL dereference: *i from read_inode (L17) is dereferenced at L25-29 without a NULL check, but the NULL-producing path is in unseen helper code, so it is a limitation per reachability rules.
DoS-only large realloc (L94-95): allocation size grows with attacker-influenced dir_count but a failure exits cleanly via EXIT_UNSQUASH; not a memory-safety finding.
The guard at L65 (dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT) is effectively unreachable if dirh.count is 8-bit (max 255 -> dir_count 256), but this does not introduce a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML writes a NUL terminator at line[llen + 1] (line 96) one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte `line` buffer whenever an attacker-controlled gopher response line reaches TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes: the clamp at lines 75-78 admits that exact combined size, so the write lands at index TEMP_BUF_SIZE (CWE-787, network-reachable memory corruption). Independently, the gopher `host` field is interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute at lines 239-240 (also 232-233), allowing attribute breakout and script injection in the proxy-served page (CWE-79).

evidence.reason: llen is attacker-controlled: it is the length of a gopher response line found by memchr at lines 68-71, plus gopherState->len accumulated from prior chunks at lines 83-84. The only guard, lines 75-78, enforces gopherState->len + llen <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, so a combined length of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 still passes; with that value llen+1 indexes TEMP_BUF_SIZE, one past the last valid index (TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1) of the line buffer allocated at line 6. Witness: a response line of TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes ending in '\n' with gopherState->len == 0 (guard not triggered; memcpy at line 94 fills indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2) writes the NUL at line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE]; a longer line (clamp path, lines 75-77) reaches the same index.

evidence.snippet: outbuf.appendf(" %s\n", icon_url, host, gtype, escaped_selector, html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: host is carved from the attacker-controlled gopher response line (strchr at lines 122-127) and passed into the HREF attribute without html_quote or rfc1738_escape_part, unlike name (html_quote) and escaped_selector in the same call. Witness host = '"><script>alert(1)</script>' in line `1spam\tspam\t"><script>alert(1)</script>\t70\n`: the quote terminates HREF="gopher://..." and the injected <script> executes in the HTML page served by the proxy.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the pasted function, starting at the gopherToHTML signature (line 1).
TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the byte capacity of the `line` buffer created by LOCAL_ARRAY at line 6; valid indices are 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1.
inbuf/len carry the response body of the remote gopher server named by the user-chosen gopher URL, so line contents, per-line lengths, and the host field are attacker-controllable (open-proxy model).
gopherState->len is kept in [0, TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1] by the clamp at lines 75-78 and the reset at line 92.
limitations: The shown code does not reveal whether LOCAL_ARRAY allocates on the heap or the stack; the one-byte NUL overflow is at minimum memory corruption/DoS, with full remote exploitability depending on that allocator detail.

CSO atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) at lines 269/271 with a possible NULL token is guarded: under C strtok semantics a NULL s_code or s_recno implies result is also NULL, and the `if (!result) break;` at lines 266-267 (and 291-292) executes before the atoi calls; therefore no confirmed NULL deref.
Overlong gopher lines are deliberately truncated at lines 75-78 (logged 'Buffer overflow. Lost some data'); the memcpy operations themselves remain in bounds.
The XSS finding (CWE-79) matters only when the generated HTML is rendered in a browser at the proxy origin; the CWE-787 buffer overflow finding does not depend on that condition.

verdict.summary: thread_call passes the caller-stack count nparams (line 5) straight into sq_call on the coroutine (line 9) without comparing it to the callee's declared parameter count or reserving coroutine stack space. With the thread function declaring more parameters than the call supplies (e.g. t.call() on a function with many parameters), the frame setup writes the missing parameters past the coroutine's stack top, producing a heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Taint: the attacker controls the coroutine's function (declared parameter count P, via newthread(closure)) and nparams (line 5 via the call-site argument count; t.call() yields nparams=1). Flow: line 4 admits any OT_THREAD receiver, then lines 6-8 fill the coroutine stack with exactly the roottable plus the moved arguments (nparams slots above the base), leaving no slack; the unchecked method call is this use of nparams at line 9. Failure: when P > nparams (witness: newthread(function(a1..a255){}) then t.call()), the call's frame setup pads P-nparams missing parameters by writing them at coroutine slots just past the occupied top, overrunning the coroutine's stack allocation (heap OOB write). The only guard (line 4) validates the receiver type only and does not constrain nparams vs P; the caller-side loop bound is sound (i<=nparams equals the valid stack top), so the flaw is the unvalidated count reaching this call.

assumptions: Native-call stack layout: slot 1 is the receiver ('this') and sq_gettop counts it, consistent with the line 3/4 type check requiring a thread at index 1.

The coroutine's frame setup (inside sq_call / SQVM::Call, not shown) pads missing declared parameters by writing consecutive slots above the provided ones without bounds-checking or growing the coroutine stack.
limitations: The exact overflow extent and any in-bounds margin depend on SQVM::Call's parameter padding and on the coroutine's initial stack size set by newthread, both outside the shown code.
When the thread function declares no more parameters than nparams, no overflow occurs on the shown path (surplus arguments are only truncated, a semantic issue).
The line 7-8 loop itself is not an out-of-bounds read of the caller stack: sq_gettop at line 5 returns the true top and the strict bound i<(nparams+1) admits only i<=nparams.
No injection (format-string/command/query/header), crypto, or file-handling sinks exist in this function.
If the embedding treats scripts as fully trusted, the attacker model weakens, but the memory-corruption class remains.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled input reaches a dangerous sink in the shown code. The floating-point ratio divisions (lines 66-67 and 123-124) are protected by exact guards: the sharded-path denominator requires numRecords > 100 (line 14, so the denominator is at least 5.05 and never zero), and the timeseries-path denominator requires numRecords != 0 (line 91) plus a trusted positive server parameter gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount; the bucketUnpacker dereferences are guarded by line 91, and rsRandCursor is null-checked at line 35. There are no memory, injection, crypto, or file sinks in the shown code, so no CWE is confirmed.

assumptions: sampleSize flows from the user-supplied $sample size argument parsed by an unseen caller; numRecords is a caller-supplied catalog estimate.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a trusted server parameter (admin configuration, positive default), not query-controlled.
coll, expCtx, opCtx->lockState(), CollectionShardingState::get(...), and coll->getRecordStore() satisfy MongoDB-internal invariants (collection locked, non-null handles) for a valid CollectionPtr.
BucketUnpacker is engaged only when the pipeline is unpacking a time-series bucket collection, consistent with the line 91 guard.
limitations: If the trusted server parameter gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount were misconfigured to 0, the timeseries division at line 124 could produce 0/0 NaN (or inf/NaN) in minAdvancedToWorkRatio; this is not attacker-reachable in the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding and carries no CWE.

Negative or zero sampleSize passes the early-return gates and flows into TrialStage/SampleFromTimeseriesBucket (lines 77-82, 127-137, 145-150); stage semantics are outside the shown code, so impact is unconfirmed and out of scope.

Potential NULL dereferences of coll->getRecordStore() (line 34) and CollectionShardingState::get(...) (line 49) would require broken framework invariants that attacker input cannot produce in the shown code.
The 'first 100 works()' trial loop, ARHASH retry logic, and any algorithmic-complexity behavior are implemented inside unseen PlanStage classes, so they cannot be validated here and are out of scope.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-reachable vulnerability in the shown code. All reads/writes of the heap buffer b are bounded: size >= 32 (line 11) covers the constant-offset memcmp/r_read_le32 accesses, malloc(size) matches the r_buf_read_at length (len after st64-to-int narrowing never exceeds size), successful read windows [off, N) and [off-8, N-8) stay within the file, and every short/failed read is caught by the available != size checks (lines 19, 59) before b is used. Residual concerns are single-shot in scope: a negative off admitted by the one-sided guard at line 4 inflates malloc(size) without subsequent memory corruption, and the two read-failure returns (lines 21, 61) leak b instead of freeing it; these are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at never writes more than its length argument and returns the number of bytes actually transferred (or a negative/error value on failure), so the available != size checks at lines 19 and 59 truthfully reflect a short or failed read.
off is caller-supplied and attacker-influenced, including possibly negative values via sign-extension of 32-bit file fields; the shown code applies no non-negativity check.
The D { ... } block (lines 69-72) is a debug-only construct; even if executed, the b+12 read is in-bounds because size >= 32.
limitations: Negative off: the guard at line 4 (off >= size) is one-sided, so off < 0 passes; size -= off (line 7) then inflates size beyond the file length and malloc(size) (line 14) can request ~2 GiB. Impact is a single-shot oversized allocation that is never written: r_buf_read_at fails, available != size forces return NULL, and the memory is released or (see leak) leaked. No memory corruption results, and DoS volume does not scale with attacker input in a loop in the shown code, so this is not raised as a finding.

Missing free(b) on the two read-failure returns (lines 21 and 61) leaks the buffer (up to ~2 GiB when off is very negative). This is a single-shot leak per invocation with no attacker-controlled repetition loop in the shown code, so it is not raised as a finding.

int arithmetic on off (off - 8 at line 58, off -= 8 at line 64, off + 16 at line 74) can overflow for |off| near 2^31 (e.g., files or offsets near/above 2 GiB); the wrapped value flows only into the unseen constructor r_coresym_cache_element_new or into the checked read-failure path, so no memory operation in the shown code consumes an overflowed value.
Behavior of r_coresym_cache_element_new (line 74) with off + 16 (including offsets past EOF or wrapped) is outside the shown code and not assessed.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads from directory_table using attacker-controlled byte offsets and copy lengths without any check against the directory-table buffer boundary. The guards that exist (dir_count <= SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT at line 64, dire->size < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN at line 81) bound the entry count and the on-stack name buffer, but never verify that bytes + read_len stays within the heap directory table, so a crafted squashfs image (oversized inode data/offset, or an entry with size 255 positioned at the end of the table) causes heap out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125), yielding crash/DoS and disclosure of adjacent heap bytes into extracted names.

evidence.reason: The read length dire->size + 1 and the base directory_table + bytes are both attacker-controlled (dire->size is parsed from image bytes at lines 72-77; bytes is derived at lines 42/47 from lookup_entry plus the attacker-chosen (*i)->offset/(*i)->start, and the loop bound size = (*i)->data + bytes at line 48 is attacker-chosen too). The only guard before this sink, at line 81 (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN), admits dire->size = 255 and therefore a 256-byte copy, and the line 64 guard bounds only dir_count, so no check prevents a copy that starts near or past the end of the directory_table heap allocation. Concrete witness: directory entry with size=255 when bytes leaves fewer than 256 readable bytes in directory_table (or an inode whose data/offset make the line 50 loop continue past the table end), causing an out-of-bounds heap read that can crash or leak heap bytes into dire->name, later strcpy'd at line 107 into dir->dirs[].name and printed at lines 96-97.

assumptions: Line numbers refer to the provided function text, counted from the first line ('static struct dir *squashfs_opendir(...)').

Standard squashfs layout is assumed where the snippet does not define it: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN = 256, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT = 256, packed 4-byte dir_header_2 and 5-byte dir_entry_2, so the 262-byte stack buffer at lines 5-7 keeps the name writes at lines 86-88 in bounds.
directory_table is a heap buffer whose total size is fixed by an unseen allocation; the shown code never reads or enforces that size.
read_inode returns a valid, non-NULL inode on the analyzed path so lines 25-30 dereference safely.
limitations: A NULL dereference of *i at lines 25-30 is not confirmed because whether read_inode can return NULL on crafted input is outside the shown code.
Integer overflow in the realloc length at lines 100-101 would require roughly 2^31 directory entries (multi-GB image) and is preempted by the confirmed OOB read; treated as robustness only.
Path traversal through crafted directory names is mitigated by the check_name call at line 91, but check_name's implementation is not shown, so a bypass cannot be confirmed from this code alone.
If lookup_entry can return negative values other than -1, the same missing-bounds issue manifests as an under-run read; this is folded into the main CWE-125 finding.
Format strings in TRACE/ERROR calls use constant format strings; no format-string injection is present.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All attacker-controlled option values reach dangerous downstream operations only through guarded paths: the restricted-mode whitelist (lines 90-94) admits only {h,l,L,U,V,v,p,r,i,s} plus --target/--source and excludes -o/-O/-t/-T/-B/-M/-R etc. for non-root callers, and positional argv access is bounded by the argc==1 / argc==2 equality guards (lines 278, 287-288). The only unconstrained attacker value is the -L/-U label embedded unescaped in LABEL="%s" / UUID="%s" (lines 148, 154), but tag parsing and mounting happen inside unseen libmount code, so no in-scope injection effect or broken security mechanism is demonstrable; that concern is recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) is true for non-root invocations, which activates the option whitelist at lines 90-94.
argv strings are NUL-terminated and bounded by OS exec argument limits.
Actual mount() authorization (fstab user-entry policy, device resolution) is enforced inside libmount, which is outside the shown code; sanitize_env() likewise runs unseen.
limitations: The -L/-U label/UUID value is interpolated unescaped into LABEL="%s" / UUID="%s" (lines 148, 154): a label containing a double quote can break the quoted tag syntax (e.g. optarg x" produces LABEL="x""). This is not confirmed as a finding because the tag parsing/mounting sink is in unseen libmount code (the shown lines only construct and forward the string), no concrete injection effect or policy bypass is demonstrable from the shown code, and the invoker supplies the label to their own mount invocation, so no privilege boundary is crossed within the shown code unless mount is installed setuid-root with a libmount policy bypass - untestable here.

-o/-O/-t/-T reach libmount option/type/file setters (lines 137, 141, 166, 244-248) with attacker-controlled data, but are unreachable for restricted callers due to the whitelist at lines 90-94; for root callers the input is trusted by the security model.

Any flaw inside libmount (option parsing, fstab parsing, mount syscall policy, tag resolution) or inside sanitize_env()/append_fstab()/exit_non_root() is out of scope because those implementations are not shown.
No memory-safety sink (copies, pointer arithmetic, length-derived allocations used for indexing) exists in the shown code; xasprintf uses only a fixed %s format.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory metadata from directory_table + bytes where bytes is a signed int derived from attacker-controlled inode fields. Lines 47-48 can wrap bytes negative and size positive (e.g., offset=0x80000000, data=0xFFFFFFFF with lookup result 0), so the only guard, while(bytes < size) at line 50, admits memcpy reads from directory_table + bytes far outside the allocation, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled inode fields reached at line 17 populate (*i)->offset and (*i)->data. Line 47 (bytes += (*i)->offset) and line 48 (size = (*i)->data + bytes) use unsigned 32-bit addition then convert back to signed int, so with lookup_entry returning 0, offset=0x80000000 and data=0xFFFFFFFF, bytes becomes INT_MIN (-2147483648) and size becomes INT_MAX (2147483647). The only guard, while(bytes < size) at line 50, then admits this statement, which copies sizeof(dirh) bytes from directory_table - 2147483648, i.e. before the directory-table buffer — a confirmed out-of-bounds read. No shown check bounds bytes against the allocation; the == -1 test at line 43 cannot catch wrapped negatives.

assumptions: read_inode (line 17) and lookup_entry (line 42) return values derived directly from the untrusted image, so (*i)->start/offset/data and the table position are attacker-controlled.
lookup_entry returns a non-negative block offset or exactly -1; the -1 branch is the only negative value it produces.
struct dir_ent.name has at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 capacity, which with the guard at line 81 makes the strcpy at line 107 in bounds (definition not shown in the snippet).
limitations: TRACE at lines 96-98 prints attacker-controlled directory names (%s) without neutralization; newline/control-byte log forging on stderr is low impact and the trace may be compiled out, so it is not counted as a finding.
Attacker-controlled iteration volume can drive repeated realloc growth at lines 100-101 (memory-exhaustion DoS); not confirmed as a distinct vulnerability.

For non-wrapping bytes values, whether directory_table offsets stay inside the actual allocation depends on lookup_entry's unseen loading guarantees; the negative-wraparound witness at lines 47-48 stands on the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every in-function memory operation on ccline.cmdbuff (Ctrl-U copy loop L492-495, K-RIGHT L547-561, K-LEFT L569-582, ex-mode backslash read L397) is guarded by the invariant 0 <= cmdpos <= cmdlen with NUL termination at cmdlen, and every mutation visible in this function preserves that invariant, with explicit boundary values (cmdpos == cmdlen after Ctrl-E; cmdpos == 0 guard before decrement) proving safety. The attacker-controlled key stream reaches dangerous operations only inside unshown helpers (put_on_cmdline, nextwild, ExpandOne, showmatches, add_to_history, bracketed_paste, cmdline_erase_chars, incsearch), which are out of scope of the shown code.

assumptions: The global ccline fields (cmdbuff/cmdlen/cmdpos) are maintained by unshown helpers (init_ccline, put_on_cmdline, cmdline_erase_chars, cmdline_paste, bracketed_paste, cmdline_browse_history, cmdline_insert_reg) so that 0 <= cmdpos <= cmdlen and cmdbuff is NUL-terminated at cmdbuff[cmdlen], with an allocation of at least cmdlen+1 bytes.

IObuff is sized (IOSIZE bytes) well beyond MB_MAXBYTES, so mb_char2bytes(c, IObuff) at L878 cannot overflow it; c reaching L878 is either a plain byte or a char encodable for the current encoding, since special keys are filtered through IS_SPECIAL at L852/L872.
safe_vgetc()/get_literal()/get_digraph() return sanitized codepoints, and the unshown helpers enforce their own internal bounds when receiving ccline.cmdbuff and ccline.cmdlen from this function.
limitations: Potential memory-safety or injection bugs inside the unshown helpers (put_on_cmdline, the completion engine nextwild/ExpandOne/showmatches, bracketed_paste, cmdline_paste, cmdline_insert_reg, add_to_history, abbreviation handling, incsearch highlighting) cannot be confirmed from the shown code; those sinks are absent here and therefore out of scope.

If any unshown helper ever broke the invariant and left cmdpos > cmdlen, the Ctrl-U handler (L489-495) would perform an out-of-bounds copy/NUL write; no shown-code path can produce such a state, so no concrete witness exists and this remains an assumption-dependent concern, not a finding.
The typed command string is executed later by unseen callers; command execution of the user-typed buffer is intended functionality and no injection sink is present in the shown code.
Recursion via CmdlineEnter/CmdlineChanged autocommands is capped by the depth == 50 check at L72-77, so unbounded recursion is not reachable in the shown code.
An out-of-memory failure of init_ccline (L69) jumps to theend and returns whatever ccline.cmdbuff is (possibly NULL); the shown code never dereferences that NULL on this path.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory metadata with memcpy from directory_table + bytes, where bytes and the loop bound size are derived from unvalidated, attacker-controlled image fields ((*i)->offset at line 47, (*i)->data at line 48) and are never checked against the actual size of the directory_table allocation. The only guard, while(bytes < size) at line 50, admits bytes values far past the end of the heap buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read that crashes unsquashfs and can disclose heap contents, including via the TRACE print at line 89.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled bytes (lookup_entry result at line 42 plus unchecked (*i)->offset at line 47, advanced at lines 61/78/106) reaches this heap read with no check against directory_table's allocation. The loop guard bytes < size at line 50 uses size = (*i)->data + bytes (line 48), an attacker-controlled value never compared to the table length; witness: (*i)->data = table_len + 1 makes every bytes >= table_len pass the guard and dereference out of bounds (CWE-125 heap over-read).

Same unguarded index: the read at directory_table + bytes with length dire->size + 1 occurs with bytes advanced past the heap allocation while bytes < size still holds. The line-81 check (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) limits the copy length to 256 bytes but does not constrain the read position, so a crafted image with large (*i)->data drives this memcpy out of bounds; the over-read bytes are then printed by TRACE (line 89).

assumptions: Line numbers refer to the code as presented, starting at line 1.

SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256 and squashfs_dir_entry_2 is a packed struct with sizeof 6 and a name area starting at offset 6, giving the stack name area 257 bytes; struct dir_ent carries char name[SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1], so strcpy at line 100 always fits.
directory_table is a heap buffer whose allocation size is fixed before squashfs_opendir runs and is never referenced in the shown code.
The attacker fully controls the squashfs image, including inode fields, directory table contents, and the lookup hash table.
limitations: The stack name copy is protected by the guard at lines 81-84: dire->size <= 255 makes the memcpy at line 86 write at most 256 bytes into the 257-byte name area and line 88 touch at most index 256; no stack overflow is confirmed in this code.

The realloc size arithmetic at lines 93-94 ((dir->dir_count + DIR_ENT_SIZE) * sizeof(struct dir_ent)) could overflow only with roughly 2^31 directory entries, unreachable before the heap over-read at lines 56/86 crashes, so it is not independently confirmed.

bytes += (*i)->offset at line 47 can wrap bytes negative when the inode offset field is wide, causing reads before directory_table; this is treated as the same CWE-125 class rather than a separate finding.

Name bytes copied at line 86 are passed to TRACE '%s' at line 89 without sanitization, so newline characters can appear in log output; impact is limited to log forgery in debug builds and is not a confirmed security boundary.
read_inode error behavior is outside the shown code; the malloc/realloc failures are checked (lines 20, 95), so no NULL dereference is reachable from the shown statements.
Memory disclosure via TRACE depends on the trace macro being compiled in.

verdict.summary: In FEAT_GUI builds, check_termcode() takes key_name directly from raw input bytes (key_name[0]=tp[1], key_name[1]=tp[2], lines 101-102) and, when they form a mouse/extra-key code, unconditionally calls get_bytes_from_buf(tp + slen, bytes, 4) at line 361 without checking slen + 4 <= len. The only guard, num_bytes == -1 (lines 363-364), is structurally dead because get_bytes_from_buf() takes no length argument and always returns the fixed count. A 3-byte crafted input (len == 3: CSI + KS_EXTRA + KE_MOUSELEFT/KE_MOUSEUP family) starts the read at tp+3 and consumes up to 3 bytes past the end of the input region, an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125); the same unguarded pattern exists in the KS_MENU, KS_TABLINE, and scrollbar handlers.

evidence.reason: tp and len come from the attacker-influenceable input region (lines 46-47 or 53-54; len = remaining bytes). When gui.in_use, lines 96-102 set slen=3 and key_name from raw input bytes tp[1]/tp[2], so a 3-byte input (len == 3) whose bytes equal CSI, KS_EXTRA and KE_MOUSELEFT (etc.) reaches this line, where tp + slen == tp + 3 is the NUL sentinel written at line 85. get_bytes_from_buf() copies exactly 4 bytes starting there, reading up to 3 bytes past the end of the input region (past the allocation at buffer tails); its signature has no length parameter, so num_bytes is always 4 and the only guard at lines 363-364 (num_bytes == -1) can never reject the short buffer — the missing check is slen + 4 <= len. The over-read bytes also flow into mouse_col/mouse_row (lines 365-366) and inflate slen to 7 (line 367).

assumptions: FEAT_GUI is defined and gui.in_use is true for the primary path.

The scanned bytes (typebuf content or buf[]) are attacker-influenceable: untrusted terminal/remote input, pasted bytes scanned into a GUI build's input queue, or fuzz input; byte values are fully selectable by the sender.

get_bytes_from_buf()/get_long_from_buf() take no buffer-length argument, so they copy a fixed number of bytes and cannot signal a shortage; therefore num_bytes can never be -1 at the call sites shown.
limitations: The same missing len bound affects sibling GUI sinks in the shown code: KS_MENU get_long_from_buf(tp + slen, ...) (line 427), KS_TABLINE/KS_TABMENU get_bytes_from_buf(tp + slen, ...) (lines 448, 461), and the KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR loops whose conditions read tp[j+1]/tp[j+2] unbounded by len (lines 479-497, 508-518); they are treated as the same CWE-125 class, not separate findings.
Out-of-allocation reads require the input to end at the tail of the heap block; with allocator slack the read still exceeds the validated length but stays inside the allocation.

tp[len] = NUL (line 85) writes one byte at buf[*buflen] in the buf path; safety depends on a caller invariant (spare NUL slot) not shown or verifiable here, with no attacker-visible length in the shown code - not confirmed.

In a stock GUI the event bytes are normally generated by the GUI layer; the trigger applies where attacker-controlled bytes are actually scanned (untrusted terminal/remote input, pastes into the input queue, fuzzing of check_termcode).
Internal bugs in the not-shown helpers (handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs, check_termcode_mouse, put_string_in_typebuf, modifiers2keycode) are out of scope.
Non-GUI builds contain no in-shown unbounded dereference; the main matching loop's partial-sequence and pointer guards (lines 127-128, 172-183, 223-224, 240-246) fully cover their indexed accesses.

verdict.summary: In jetp3852_print_page, raw raster bytes copied by gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines (lines 34-35) are used unvalidated as indices into the 8-element static arrays spr40/spr8/spr2 (lines 53-55) at lines 58-65. Any non-blank scan line containing a byte value >= 8 (e.g., pixel value 0xFF) indexes past the buffer end, causing an out-of-bounds read; the resulting word is written through odp to the printer stream. The only guards present, memset (line 15) and the line_size <= DATA_SIZE length check (line 26), constrain initialization and length but never restrict the copied byte values to the 0..7 range the tables require.

evidence.reason: dp[0..7] hold raw raster bytes filled by gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines at lines 34-35 with no value sanitization, and they are used directly as indices into spr40/spr8/spr2, each declared as exactly 8 ulongs at lines 53-55. The transpose loop (lines 48-50) reaches this statement for every non-blank line (line 39 guard), and any scanned byte value in 8..255, e.g. 0xFF, produces index 8..255 on an 8-element array, an out-of-bounds read. The guards relied upon are insufficient: memset (line 15) only zeroes bytes beyond line_size and line 26 only bounds the copy length (line_size <= DATA_SIZE), neither restricts byte values to 0..7; the adjacent memory read is folded into pword (lines 66-68) and emitted to the printer stream via gp_fwrite (lines 107-108).

assumptions: LINE_SIZE is a compile-time constant (e.g., 1024) so DATA_SIZE = LINE_SIZE*8 is an exact multiple of 8, yielding exactly LINE_SIZE transpose iterations.
gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line and gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines behave as documented, returning a non-negative scan-line size for the copy length.
The page raster content passed to this device is derived from the document being printed and is therefore considered attacker-influenced.
limitations: The spr-table OOB read (CWE-125) would not trigger if an unseen device invariant guaranteed every copied raster byte is <= 7; the shown code never establishes such an invariant, and its own comment (lines 13-14) states that bytes > 7 break the tables, which only the memset partially addresses.

A negative line_size would pass the line 26 check (< or == DATA_SIZE) and, converted to an unsigned length inside gdev_prn_copy_scan_lines, could cause a large out-of-bounds copy; producing it requires gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line to return a negative value, which is outside the shown code, so this is recorded as a hardening concern without its own CWE.
A very large pdev->height causes a long outer loop (lines 32-111) with attacker-influenced page size; it terminates on finitely many lines, so it is a robustness/DoS concern, not a confirmed finding.
Printer-protocol values (cntc1/cntc2/vtp at lines 78, 91-93) derive from sizes and are written through literal-format calls; they are not treated as an injection sink for printer output.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every write into 'buf' is bounded by the allocation at line 32 (STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5); with BASENAMELEN = 256 and readdir d_name capped at NAME_MAX = 255 bytes, the worst-case surplus at lines 150/157-158/164 is d_name + "/**" - "**" <= 256 bytes, which fits the 261-byte slack with a ~4-byte margin. The '**' recursion is depth-capped by 'stardepth < 100' and each recursive call re-allocates a fresh buffer sized for the grown path, so surplus does not accumulate. The suspected out-of-bounds write, ReDoS, and DoS candidates all fail confirmation with a concrete witness in the shown code.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN >= 260 (Vim defines 256; the line-31 comment 'make room for file name' indicates it is the slack for one directory entry), making the 261-byte slack admit the worst-case 256-byte write surplus.
POSIX readdir returns d_name as a NUL-terminated array of at most NAME_MAX = 255 bytes, so d_name never exceeds the allocation slack.
path is a NUL-terminated string and wildoff is always >= 0 and <= the first-wildcard offset at every call site in the shown code (lines 125, 160, 169).
vim_regfree(NULL) is a no-op in Vim's regexp layer, so freeing regmatch.regprog when EW_NOTWILD prevented compilation (line 204) is safe.
limitations: Size-safety of lines 123, 150, 157-158 and 164 rests on the unshown BASENAMELEN macro: if BASENAMELEN < 260, a d_name of ~253+ bytes overflows buf at line 150 (unbounded STRCPY), and lines 157-158 overflow in a '**' chain; no such macro value is visible in the provided code, so no concrete failing witness can be given.

vim_regexec at lines 145-146 matches a user-derived pattern against attacker-influenced file names, but no pattern that survives file_pat_to_reg_pat (line 93) and causes catastrophic backtracking in the unseen vim_regcomp/vim_regexec implementations could be exhibited, so CWE-1333 is unconfirmed.

The readdir loop (lines 136-198) at the top level (stardepth == 0) never calls ui_breakcheck(), so expanding '*' over a huge directory runs without Ctrl-C checks; bounded by directory contents, this is a robustness/DoS consideration, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Line 148 compares d_name against path + (s - buf); backslash removal before s shifts the offset in buf, which can cause wrong matches but keeps the read inside path's bounds, so it has no security impact.

The MACOS_CONVERT mch_memmove at line 188 copies mac_precompose_path output of unverified size, but precomposition does not lengthen strings and the block is OS-specific, so it is not substantiated as a finding.

verdict.summary: In get_recurse_data_length() (pcre2_jit_compile.c), the OP_KET branch advances cc by PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) (line 49), a machine word embedded in the compiled pattern, with no bound check against ccend; a crafted regex-derived bytecode can push cc past the end of the compiled-code buffer so the while (cc < ccend) loop dereferences *cc (line 24) out of bounds — a heap OOB read (CWE-125) reachable from attacker-supplied patterns when JIT compilation is enabled.

evidence.reason: PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) is a length/index embedded in the compiled code and derived from the attacker-supplied pattern via the compile/JIT passes; it is consumed without validation. The guard `if (offset != 0)` (line 44) only decides whether the skip runs, and SLJIT_ASSERT (line 48) only checks the value is nonzero. Neither compares it with the bytes remaining until ccend (or until the underlying allocation end): any skip value V with 1 + LINK_SIZE + V greater than the remaining bytes passes the guard and leaves cc beyond the segment. The loop-head test (line 21) is evaluated only on the next iteration, after the overshoot is committed.

Sink: after the unclamped advance at line 49 (or the same-class advances via GET(cc,1) at lines 106/179, cc[1] at lines 202/214, extralen at lines 118/131/144, or next_opcode at line 231) moves cc past ccend and past the end of the compiled-code allocation, the next iteration re-enters while (cc < ccend) and dereferences *cc out of bounds (heap-buffer-overflow read, CWE-125). The final SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend) (line 236) is compiled out in release builds and is not a runtime bound check.

assumptions: cc/ccend delimit a segment of the pcre2 compiled bytecode produced by pcre2_compile from the pattern text, and pcre2_jit_compile invokes get_recurse_data_length() on it; the pattern text is attacker-controlled (e.g., a user-supplied regex compiled with JIT).
SLJIT_ASSERT is debug-only and is not relied on as a bounds check in release builds.
Values read via PRIVATE_DATA/GET/GET2/cc[1]/GET_EXTRALEN are stored in the bytecode at positions determined by pattern structure (opcode sizes, link lengths, argument lengths).
limitations: The exact pattern text that makes the compiler emit an inconsistent PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1)/link value is produced by unshown compile.c/JIT passes; real-world pcre2 JIT CVEs confirm such inputs exist, but the concrete triggering regex is not derivable from the shown code alone, capping confidence at 0.7.

The OP_COND probe (`alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1); *alternative`, lines 106-107) and the XCLASS/MARK/SKIP_ARG advances (`cc += size` line 187, `cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1]` lines 202 and 214) exhibit the same unclamped embedded-length class; not counted as separate CWEs.
A downstream heap write (CWE-787) would depend on the unshown set_recurse_data_length()/allocation logic and could not be independently confirmed from the shown code.
Integer overflow of the int `length` accumulator would require more than 2^31 counted slots and is not realistic.

verdict.summary: n_start_visual_mode() contains no security-relevant sink: the caller-supplied character c is only stored in VIsual_mode and compared to Ctrl_V, never used as an index, size, pointer, or format string; w_virtcol is recomputed by validate_virtcol() and consumed by the out-of-scope coladvance() helper; there are no memory, injection, crypto, file, or authz operations in the shown code.

assumptions: The unseen caller is expected to pass a Visual-mode character (e.g., Ctrl_V, 'v', 'V') for c, but correctness of that invariant is not needed for the verdict because c is never used in a security-relevant operation in the shown code.
validate_virtcol() derives w_virtcol from editor cursor state, and coladvance() is assumed to internally bound/clamp the cursor column; their logic is outside the shown code.
limitations: Potential memory-safety issues inside coladvance(), foldAdjustVisual(), setmouse(), conceal_cursor_line(), conceal_check_cursor_line(), or trigger_modechanged() are out of scope because the dangerous operations are in unseen code (pure pass-through per the reachability rule).

If an out-of-range value were stored into VIsual_mode via line 8, it could make editor state inconsistent, but no consumer of VIsual_mode is shown, so this is a robustness concern without a demonstrable security impact.
trigger_modechanged() at line 25 may fire user-defined autocommands; that is by-design interactive-editor behavior, not a vulnerability introduced by the shown code.

verdict.summary: The shown code contains no security-relevant sink: parameter c is only compared against the constant Ctrl_V (line 15) and stored into a fixed-width global (line 8); all other operations are guarded state updates of framework-maintained globals. There are no buffers, loops, memory operations, injection sinks, crypto operations, or file/authz logic, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: curwin is a valid global window pointer per Vim's runtime invariant; no NULL-producing path exists in the shown code (lines 4-5, 15-20, 42-46).
Ctrl_V, VE_BLOCK, TAB, INVERTED, and NUL are compile-time constants, giving the comparisons at lines 15 and 42 and the assignment at line 37 fixed semantics.

Helper functions (trigger_modechanged, validate_virtcol, coladvance, foldAdjustVisual, setmouse, conceal_check_cursor_line, gchar_cursor, get_ve_flags) are outside the shown code; their internals are not assessed.
limitations: Parameter c (line 1) is stored into global VIsual_mode at line 8 without validation, but the shown code never uses c as an index, size, format string, or pointer, and an int-to-int store cannot overflow; no sink line exists to trigger.

coladvance(curwin->w_virtcol) at line 18 could move the cursor into positions handled by unseen code, but the actual buffer/window writes occur inside coladvance(), which is not part of the shown code, and the argument is produced by validate_virtcol() at line 17 on the same guarded path.
A NULL curwin is not reachable from the shown code (no allocation/parse that can fail precedes its use), so no NULL-dereference finding applies.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All dereferences are guarded: the entry checks handle NULL/zero counts and ERR_PTR pols[0], the sub-policy branch handles NULL and error results from xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype before incrementing *num_pols, and the loop uses a strict i < *num_pols bound whose maximum index stays within the caller's policy array under the kernel's XFRM invariants. The only remaining concerns require an out-of-contract caller state.

assumptions: CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY implies the caller's pols array has at least two slots (e.g. XFRM_POLICY_TYPE_MAX + 1), with slot 1 reserved for the expanded main policy.
The caller passes *num_pols == 1 at most before expansion, with pols[0] non-NULL, non-ERR, and each counted entry valid.
xfrm_nr is a small bounded counter (u8-domain), so the maximum sum of two policies (≤510) cannot overflow int.
xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype returns NULL, a valid pointer, or an error pointer encoded within the kernel IS_ERR range.
limitations: pols[1] is written at line 20 without an explicit capacity check; if an out-of-contract caller passed a one-element array, this would be an out-of-bounds write, but no shown path or attacker-controlled value produces that state.
The loop at lines 35-39 dereferences pols[i] without a per-element NULL check; a NULL entry for i >= 1 can only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller, and the shown code never creates one.

If a hypothetical caller passed *num_pols >= 2 and pols[0] was a sub-policy, the branch would overwrite pols[1] and grow the count to 3 while leaving slot 2 untouched; this requires an unseen caller state outside the kernel's usage contract, so it is not confirmed reachable from the shown code.
The error path's xfrm_pols_put(pols, *num_pols) at line 27 is safe only while *num_pols is 1 at that point; the same hypothetical caller state (initial *num_pols >= 2) would also break that path.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir walks directory_table with a cursor and loop bound set entirely from attacker-controlled inode fields (bytes += (*i)->offset and size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3, lines 48-49). The loop guard only checks bytes < size, and the reads at lines 52, 66, and 76-77 are never checked against the directory_table allocation, so a crafted squashfs image (e.g., inode data ~1e9 with an offset placing bytes near the table end) drives heap out-of-bounds reads, causing crashes and potential heap disclosure (CWE-125). The guards at lines 60-63 and 71-74 cap only the entry count and name length, not the read cursor.

evidence.reason: bytes is attacker-set via (*i)->offset (line 48) and size via (*i)->data (line 49); the loop guard at line 51 requires only bytes < size, and no check compares bytes + sizeof(dirh) with the directory_table allocation. An inode with data ~1e9 and an offset placing bytes within 12 bytes of the table end passes the guard, and this 12-byte read extends past the heap buffer (heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

dire->size (0..255 after the guard at line 71) controls a read of dire->size + 1 bytes from directory_table + bytes with no check that the range lies within the directory_table allocation or even within the logical size region; combined with attacker-set bytes/size (lines 48-49), this reads up to 256 bytes past the buffer when bytes is near the table end (heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

assumptions: struct dir_ent contains char name[SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1] (257 bytes), so the strcpy at line 90 stays in bounds given the line 71 guard; the struct definition is not shown.

directory_table is a heap buffer of finite size (the decompressed directory table loaded elsewhere); the OOB read is relative to that unseen allocation, which the analysis rubric treats as in-scope because the dangerous read itself is in the shown code.
dire->size is unsigned short (squashfs format), so the guard at line 71 rejects only values >= 256 and admits 0..255.
TRACE is debug-only output and may be compiled out.
limitations: The header/entry/memcpy OOB read assumes an unseen caller does not pre-validate inode offset/data against the directory_table length; no such constraint exists in the shown code.

32-bit-only integer wrap in the realloc sizing at lines 83-84 (multiplication in int before size_t promotion) could undersize dir->dirs and overflow at the line 90 strcpy once dir->dir_count reaches about 2^31/sizeof(struct dir_ent) entries (roughly 16M entries / ~200 MB table); on 64-bit builds size_t promotion prevents the wrap, so it is not confirmed as the primary issue.

Log injection through TRACE at lines 79-81: attacker-controlled directory names may contain newlines written to the debug log without neutralization; low severity and debug-only, so no CWE is attached.
Truncation of size to int at line 49 ((*i)->data + bytes - 3 > INT_MAX makes size negative and skips the loop) is not itself a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The function is the post-CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe) fixed copy_page_to_iter_pipe(): every page-cache pipe buffer is initialized with buf->flags = 0 (clearing PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE), the merge path is confined to the same page at a continuous offset, ring indexes are masked to [0, ring_size-1], and the slice write is gated by pipe_full(). All length arithmetic is bounded (bytes capped to i->count; byte counts capped to MAX_RW_COUNT by kernel callers), so no exploitable out-of-bounds, truncation, or flag-inheritance path is reachable in the shown code.

assumptions: pipe->ring_size is always a power of two (enforced by alloc_pipe_info()/pipe_set_size()), so i_head & (ring_size - 1) at lines 21 and 30 bounds the ring index to [0, ring_size-1].
sanity(i) at line 17 validates ITER_PIPE state invariants (i->head vs pipe->head, i->iov_offset vs last buffer offset) under PIPE_PARANOIA.

Kernel read/splice length import paths cap i->count at MAX_RW_COUNT (0x7ffff000) and offset is reduced modulo PAGE_SIZE before this function, so offset + bytes and the 32-bit buf->len stores cannot overflow.
i->head lags pipe->head by one after a fill (lines 42-44), which is what makes the line 21/23 merge probe land on the last-filled buffer on the next call.
limitations: If an unseen caller ever passed bytes >= 2^32, buf->len = bytes (line 40) / buf->len += bytes (line 25) would truncate the 32-bit len and offset + bytes (line 43) could wrap; no attacker-reachable call chain passes such a count (all syscall entry points cap at MAX_RW_COUNT), so this is a hardening concern, not a confirmed finding.
If pipe->ring_size were ever not a power of two, the mask at lines 21/30 would not bound the index; ring_size is fixed by kernel pipe allocation and is not attacker-controlled.

The Dirty-Pipe-style page-cache overwrite would be real without line 36 (as in upstream v5.16), but the shown code contains buf->flags = 0, which excludes the required CAN_MERGE-on-page-cache-buffer witness, so that concern is not reachable here.
A NULL/bogus pipe or iterator dereference would require the unseen caller to pass an invalid struct iov_iter/pipe; the shown path never produces NULL and sanity(i) gates the state.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received trusts attacker-influenced HCI frame bytes: aid_len (from skb->data[1]) and params_len (from skb->data[aid_len+3]) are used as memcpy lengths and array indices with no check tying them to skb->len. The line 22-24 guard is bypassed whenever skb->data[0] is the AID tag, and the line 33 check only caps aid_len at sizeof(aid). A short frame such as skb->len=10 with aid_len=16 triggers an out-of-bounds read of skb->data and an out-of-bounds write past the 8-byte transaction allocation; for frames with skb->len-2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) the line 47 check underflows and admits any params_len, overflowing at the params memcpy.

evidence.reason: transaction->aid_len is copied from attacker-influenced skb->data[1] (line 30) and used as the memcpy length without any bound relating it to skb->len. The guard at lines 22-24 (len < NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH+2 && data[0] != AID_TAG) passes for short frames whenever data[0] == 0x81, and the check at line 33 only enforces aid_len <= sizeof(aid)=16, which caps the destination array but not the source. Witness: skb->len=10, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=0x10 (16 <= 16, guard passes) -> memcpy reads indices 2..17, 8 bytes past the end of a 10-byte skb payload, and writes 16 bytes at struct offset 4 of the 8-byte devm_kzalloc(dev, skb->len-2) object, a heap-buffer overflow.

params_len is read from skb->data[transaction->aid_len + 3] (line 44) without checking that index against skb->len, and the only validation (line 47) compares it to (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) in unsigned arithmetic: when skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) the subtraction underflows, so any params_len (0..255) is admitted. The memcpy then reads skb->data[aid_len+4 .. aid_len+3+params_len] beyond skb->len and writes params_len bytes past the undersized transaction allocation, extending the same missing-length-check flaw to a second OOB write/read sink.

assumptions: skb and its payload (skb->data, skb->len) are treated as attacker/peer-influenced input because they are bytes of a received NFC HCI event frame; the shown code performs no validation of their origin or contents.

sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) covers u32 aid_len + aid[16] + params_len (≈21 bytes, per the ETSI 102 622 table quoted in lines 15-21); the exact value is not needed for the confirmed source OOB read, only for the write-overflow arithmetic.
NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG is 0x81, the tag value an attacker can place in skb->data[0] to defeat the length guard.
limitations: The guard also reads skb->data[0] when skb->len == 0 and skb->data[1] is read when skb->len == 1; these are earlier manifestations of the same flawed guard and are subsumed by the primary finding.
For skb->len == 2, devm_kzalloc(dev, 0) may return a ZERO_SIZE_PTR-class object and crash at the line 30 store; same root cause, not a separate finding.

Whether a real deployment lets an NFC peer or corrupted controller synthetically control these bytes depends on the transport environment; the shown code itself imposes no constraint that would prevent it.
Exploit impact (info leak vs. corruption/DoS) depends on allocator layout and is not determinable from the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: addBinding contains complete integer-overflow and bounds protections. The attacker-controlled uri length (len) is guarded by 'len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE' (lines 69, 94) and by a size_t-overflow guard under '#if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX' (lines 74, 98); REALLOC/MALLOC failures are checked (lines 82, 106). The destination allocation is always len + EXPAND_SPARE, strictly larger than the memcpy size, so the memcpy (line 113) and the indexed write b->uri[len-1] (line 115) stay in bounds. The namespace-comparison loop (lines 45-52) is protected by short-circuit 'len > xmlLen ||' guards. No reachable memory-safety, injection, or crypto finding exists.

assumptions: uri is a valid null-terminated XML_Char string (invariant established by the parser before calling addBinding).
EXPAND_SPARE is a positive constant (>= 1), so len + EXPAND_SPARE always exceeds the copied length.
b->uriAlloc accurately reflects the size of the previously allocated b->uri buffer on the free-list path.
limitations: Theoretical int overflow if strlen(uri) == INT_MAX and m_namespaceSeparator is set would wrap len negative on len++ (line 64), but this requires a single string of ~2 GiB and the subsequent oversized allocation would fail and return XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY before the memcpy; not a feasible reachable failure.

The '#if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX' size_t-overflow guard is intentionally compiled out on 64-bit targets where size_t is 64-bit and the bounded len cannot overflow the allocation size; this is correct and not a vulnerability.
Callback dispatch to m_startNamespaceDeclHandler (lines 127-129) delegates to unseen code; no injection or memory-safety concern is attributable to the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The pointer-difference length passed to win_linetabsize() is bounded by the same-buffer guard at the function head (rex.reg_buf == curbuf && VIsual.lnum != 0) plus the engine invariant that rex.input lies within the NUL-terminated rex.line, and MAXCOL is explicitly neutralized before the blockwise column arithmetic. The remaining concerns (an OOB read if the unseen engine ever violated the input-within-line invariant, and signed overflow of bot.col + 1 when bot.col == MAXCOL that only flips the returned boolean) lack a concrete failing witness in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: rex.line points to the NUL-terminated current line of the matched buffer and rex.input lies in [rex.line, rex.line + STRLEN(rex.line)]; this is maintained by the unseen regexp engine and never violated inside the shown code.
colnr_T is a signed int with MAXCOL == 0x7fffffff, matching Vim's type definitions.
The guard 'rex.reg_buf != curbuf || VIsual.lnum == 0' at line 14 is sufficient because the caller only sets VIsual.lnum to a line number of curbuf.
limitations: If the unseen engine ever violated the invariant that rex.input points within rex.line, the length (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line) passed to win_linetabsize() at line 68 could exceed the line allocation and cause an out-of-bounds read inside that unseen helper; the shown code itself cannot produce such a value, so this is out of scope per the pass-through rule.

At line 55, 'bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')' with bot.col == MAXCOL (0x7fffffff) and an inclusive/old selection performs signed-overflow UB; the concrete two's-complement result only makes the comparison true and rejects the match, with no memory-safety impact demonstrated.
The narrowing casts at lines 53 and 68 could wrap only for lines at least 2^31 bytes, which Vim's colnr_T-bounded line model cannot produce; classified as theoretical.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) with matching out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) in st21nfca_connectivity_event_received. Attacker-controlled NFC HCI event bytes set aid_len and params_len which are used as memcpy sizes without bounds checks: the only guard (lines 22-24) uses && and caps nothing, and no check limits aid_len to NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH or to skb->len. A crafted skb (e.g., len=7, data[0]=0x81, data[1]=0xFF) passes the guard and copies 255 bytes into a 5-byte devm_kzalloc buffer at line 31-32 (overflow), while also reading past skb->data; a second copy at lines 40-41 overflows the same allocation for large params_len. This is reachable over the NFC air interface and causes kernel heap corruption.

evidence.reason: Taint: skb->data[1] (attacker-controlled HCI event byte) is stored into transaction->aid_len at line 30 with value range 0-255 and never validated. Sink: memcpy at lines 31-32 copies aid_len bytes into the 16-byte transaction->aid inside an allocation of only skb->len - 2 bytes (line 26). Reachability: the guard at lines 22-24 uses && so it admits the concrete witness len=7, data[0]=0x81 (and admits all len>=7 packets), and it imposes no bound on aid_len; witness data[1]=0xFF gives aid_len=255 into a 5-byte allocation, overflowing the heap by ~250 bytes and reading 255 bytes from skb->data[2..256] past the 7-byte payload. Primary impact: kernel heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the source-side copy also performs an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Taint: params_len is read from skb->data[aid_len + 3] at line 39 (range 0-255) with the index and size unconstrained, and the params flexible array has no bytes beyond the skb->len - 2 allocation (line 26). Reachability: for a packet with len=400, aid_len=255, and params_len=255, only 400-2-4-255=139 destination bytes are available but 255 are copied, overflowing the same heap allocation; on short skbs the overflow is even larger. Impact: second confirmed instance of the same heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) from the same unchecked-length root cause.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction is the standard kernel definition with u8 aid[NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH] where NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH == 16 and a trailing flexible params array; the fixed 16-byte aid array and flexible params are relied on for the overflow math.
skb->data and skb->len describe the HCI event payload received from the NFC controller/peer and are therefore attacker-influenced over the air; the shown code consumes them directly.
skb->len is unsigned, so skb->len - 2 wraps for len < 2.
limitations: skb is freed only at line 49, so the early -EPROTO/-ENOMEM returns at lines 24, 28, and 37 leak the skb and the devm allocation per malformed event; this is a slow-leak/DoS robustness concern, not the primary memory-safety finding.

skb->len - 2 underflows to a huge size when skb->len < 2, but the NULL check at line 27 converts that path to -ENOMEM rather than a dereference; it is recorded as defensive hardening, not a separate finding.

The over-the-air reachability of the HCI EVT_TRANSACTION path depends on NFC controller/stack configuration outside this function; regardless, the payload bytes handled here are attacker-controlled, which is sufficient for the confirmed sinks.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual performs only in-line pointer arithmetic and column comparisons over regexp-engine-managed line pointers. The line re-fetch at line 70 re-anchors rex.input to the freshly fetched line before win_linetabsize reads it, and the only overflow-prone expressions (bot.col + 1 at line 55, end - 1 at line 74) overflow only from trusted sentinel states (MAXCOL / 0) and fail closed (return FALSE). No attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or file sink unconstrained in the shown code.

assumptions: colnr_T is signed int and MAXCOL == INT_MAX (per Vim's vim.h), so MAXCOL + 1 wraps negative and makes the line-55 condition always true (fail-closed rejection).
The regexp engine maintains rex.line <= rex.input <= rex.line + strlen(line), and reg_getline()/ml_get() return NUL-terminated line buffers; these invariants are established by unseen engine code.
VIsual/cursor columns and b_visual.vi_* values come from trusted editor UI state, not from attacker-controlled file bytes.
limitations: No confirmed finding: the memory-relevant operations (pointer subtraction line 51, re-anchoring line 71, win_linetabsize read line 73) are reached with col fully determined by engine invariants and re-anchored after the getvvcol() line flush by the re-fetch at line 70; no concrete witness value violates bounds on a shown path.

Integer wrap at line 55 (bot.col == MAXCOL) and line 74 (end == 0 with exclusive selection) causes only spurious FALSE (fail-closed); it breaks no security mechanism, so it is a robustness concern, not a CWE-190 finding.

A NULL dereference of rex.line at lines 71/73 if reg_getline() returned NULL is unconfirmable: the NULL-producing path is outside the shown code and the same rex.lnum already produced a valid line before getvvcol().
getvvcol(), win_linetabsize(), and reg_getline() are not shown; any defect inside them is out of scope.
The shown code contains no loops, so loop-bound and read-position-invariant analysis is vacuous.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create sizes flow using num_actions, a count of expressions whose offload_action succeeded (lines 11-13, 21), but the second loop (lines 35-45) invokes expr->ops->offload for every expression whose offload is non-NULL regardless of that count, with no capacity check. An expression that has offload but no successful offload_action passes the line 36 guard and appends an action at line 40 into a flow allocated without a slot for it, producing a heap out-of-bounds write reachable from attacker-controlled nftables rule contents.

evidence.reason: flow is allocated at line 21 with capacity derived only from num_actions, which line 13 increments solely for expressions whose offload_action is non-NULL and returns nonzero. The loop guard at line 36 admits every expression with offload set, including expressions with offload_action NULL/false that were never counted, and line 40 then allows their offload to append actions beyond the allocated capacity. The witness is any rule expression with ops->offload set, ops->offload_action absent or returning 0, and an offload that appends at least one action, in a rule whose num_actions is at least 1 so line 18 does not reject it. No check between lines 21 and 40 bounds the total appended actions to num_actions, so the write at line 40 is an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787).

assumptions: nft_flow_rule_alloc(num_actions) allocates capacity for exactly num_actions flow actions.
expr->ops->offload can append one or more actions into flow during the second loop.
The expression list of rule is finite and bounded by netlink rule size, so both loops terminate and num_actions cannot overflow.
rule contents are netlink-supplied, i.e. the attacker selects which expression ops appear in the rule.
limitations: The concrete failing ops table (an expression with offload set, offload_action absent/0, and an action-appending offload) is not shown in this snippet; the overflow fires only if such callback semantics exist in the kernel's expression ops.
A rule containing only match-style offloads that append no actions would not overflow; the demonstrated failure requires at least one uncounted action-appending expression.

nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan(ctx, flow) at line 46 could add further unaccounted actions, but its body is not shown and any write there is delegated to unseen code, so it is not an independent confirmed finding.
Null dereference of expr->ops is not confirmed; it depends on an unseen kernel invariant and the shown code guards the ops fields it dereferences.

verdict.summary: The shown apprentice_load code contains no confirmed, attacker-triggerable vulnerability. The directory-entry path is built with a size-bounded snprintf into mfn (line 42), estrndup's length is capped to min(mflen, sizeof(mfn)-1) (line 64) so it never reads past mfn's initialized bytes, and the filearr growth guard (lines 52-63) guarantees files < maxfiles at every store (line 64). Remaining concerns (stat-to-load TOCTOU, qsort(NULL,0,...), uint32_t vs size_t width, OOM-only leaks) require magic-directory write access or >2^32 entries and are documented as limitations.

assumptions: fn (magic database path) is caller-supplied; in shown code its only consumers are stat/opendir/snprintf/load_1, all size-bounded.
snprintf with size sizeof(mfn) always NUL-terminates mfn and writes at most sizeof(mfn)-1 bytes (C standard).
PHP's estrndup copies exactly len bytes and appends a NUL; the cap at line 64 equals strlen(mfn) in every branch.
Helper functions (load_1, set_text_binary, coalesce_entries, magic_entry_free, cmpstrp, apprentice_sort) are outside the shown code.
limitations: TOCTOU between stat(mfn,...) at line 49 and the deferred load_1 at line 69: a symlink swap requires write access to the magic database directory, which already grants control of the parsed magic content; no privilege boundary is crossed within the shown code.

qsort(NULL, 0, sizeof(*filearr), cmpstrp) at line 67 when the directory has no regular files is strictly unspecified C behavior but is a no-op in practice (glibc qsort returns for n==0); robustness nit, no demonstrated failure.
uint32_t i (line 4) compared against size_t files/count (lines 68, 80) would only wrap with more than 2^32 directory entries or magic entries and a multi-GB filearr; not attacker-reachable.
maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr) (line 55) could overflow size_t only beyond SIZE_MAX/8 entries; same unreachable scale.
filearr is not freed on the snprintf-error (line 47) or realloc-failure (line 61) paths: single-shot leak requiring OOM, no compounding attacker control.
Silent truncation of mfn when fn/d.d_name exceeds MAXPATHLEN-1: no memory-safety impact (line 64 cap); the truncated path either fails stat and is skipped or names a real file.

Memory DoS by flooding the magic directory with files: per-entry allocation is tiny and the volume requires write access to the magic directory, so it does not scale with attacker input on the shown path.
The mset loop at line 80 terminates only if set_text_binary (line 85) makes progress; that helper is not shown, so non-termination cannot be anchored to the shown code.

verdict.summary: 32-bit integer overflow in prealloc_elems_and_freelist: elem_size * smap->map.max_entries is computed in u32 arithmetic and wraps before the implicit widening to size_t, so bpf_map_area_alloc (line 6) receives an undersized or zero size while pcpu_freelist_populate (line 15) still populates max_entries slots at the full elem_size stride, causing kernel heap out-of-bounds writes and potential privilege escalation. Both operands derive from the attacker-controlled BPF_MAP_CREATE attributes and the only guard (if (!smap->elems)) does not detect overflow.

evidence.reason: Taint: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries come from the attacker-controlled bpf() syscall attributes and reach this allocation size unvalidated. The product elem_size * max_entries is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (both operands are u32) and only then widened to size_t, so e.g. max_entries=2^29 with elem_size=20 yields 20*2^29=5*2^32, which wraps to 0; bpf_map_area_alloc(0) returns a non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR, the if (!smap->elems) guard on line 8 admits it, and pcpu_freelist_populate on line 15 then lays out max_entries slots of elem_size bytes against a zero-size or 4-byte allocation, making the slot at elems+20 already out of bounds. No check constrains max_entries or promotes the product to 64-bit before use.

assumptions: 64-bit kernel where size_t is 64-bit and u32 is 32-bit unsigned int.
struct stack_map_bucket is 4 bytes on 64-bit ({u32 nr_entries; u32 ips[];}).
Attacker can reach BPF_MAP_CREATE (unprivileged BPF or CAP_BPF), supplying map attributes incl. max_entries and value_size.
kmalloc(0)/ZERO_SIZE_PTR behavior on the target: allocation of wrapped size 0 returns a non-NULL pointer.

Caller-side validation of value_size (e.g., restricted to 8/16) is not present in the shown code; the overflow witness relies on max_entries alone and remains valid even if max_entries is capped near 2^30.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds write occurs inside the called pcpu_freelist_populate and the subsequent stack-map update path, which are not shown; the shown code is the source of the incorrectly sized allocation and the inconsistent stride/count passed to it.

If an external (unshown) caller imposed a much tighter max_entries cap such that elem_size * max_entries can never exceed UINT32_MAX, this exact trigger would not fire; no such bound exists in the shown code, where a caller-supplied length is used after an absent check.
elem_size = sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) + value_size could itself wrap if value_size were near UINT32_MAX; this is the same root-cause class and is not counted as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, rule-satisfying vulnerability in the shown code. Every file-derived size reaching a memory sink is bounded by an identifiable guard: colors <= 2^bits <= 256 before the colormap alloc/read/loop (L249-251, L306-325); the pixel buffer is allocated at rows*max(bytes_per_line, columns+256) which is >= the ReadBlob length rows*bytes_per_line, with a count!=length check (L336-348); and every per-case conversion stride (1/4/8/16/24/32 bpp) is provably <= the allocated stride, keeping all *p reads and SetPixelIndex writes inside their buffers (L360-704). The weak length/8 pre-check (L337) and the columns+256 allocation term only permit bounded, cleanly-failing allocation attempts (DoS), and the remaining concerns (32-bit size_t wraparound in bytes_per_line/length, undefined mask<<32 shift counts, and DecodeImage internals) are platform-dependent or outside the shown code. No format-string, command, SQL, crypto, or header sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: Analysis assumes a 64-bit size_t/ssize_t platform (matches the evaluation environment); all shown bounds and per-case stride identities are proven for that model.

ReadBlobLSBLong/ReadBlobLSBShort return 0 on EOF without causing memory effects, and OpenBlob/SetImageExtent/AcquireVirtualMemory/AcquireQuantumMemory fail cleanly (MagickFalse/NULL) on exhaustion, as handled by the shown L292-295, L304-308, L342-344, L352-354 checks.
QueueAuthenticPixels/GetAuthenticIndexQueue return regions of exactly image->columns pixels for the requested row, and colormap arrays are allocated with exactly image->colors entries.
limitations: 32-bit size_t wraparound: bytes_per_line = 4*((columns*bits+31)/32) (L335) and length = rows*bytes_per_line (L336) can overflow for columns/rows near 2^31, defeating the length/8 pre-check (L337) and causing allocation size, read length, and conversion strides to disagree; whether a live undersized buffer results depends on unseen AcquireVirtualMemory/SetImageExtent overflow and memory-limit behavior, and the platform word size is not specified, so this could not be confirmed with a concrete witness.

Bit-counting mask loops can evaluate mask << 32 (undefined behavior) for all-ones masks; they remain finite via the '> 32U' break and have no memory impact on x86/ARM (shift counts masked mod 32), so this is a robustness concern, not a finding.
The RLE expansion happens inside unseen DecodeImage (L356-357); only its buffer and columns*rows argument are in the shown code, so that write is out of scope per the pass-through rule.

The length/8 > GetBlobSize pre-check (L337) is weaker than length > GetBlobSize and does not bound the columns+256 allocation term, so crafted small files can force large transient allocations with ~16x amplification; all such paths fail cleanly in the shown code (NULL checks, count!=length throws), making it a DoS/resource concern only.
Debug-only log statements pass size_t arguments to %u formats (e.g., L115, L121); type-mismatch UB in logging only, no attacker-controlled output or security impact.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The attacker-controlled URI length flows only into guarded allocations (len <= INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE at lines 80/108; size_t product bound at lines 89/116) and an in-bounds memcpy whose length is either the URI length or URI length + 1 (its NUL terminator); the separator write index at line 132 is unreachable when len == 0 because the guard at line 131 is identical to the guard that caused len++ at line 75.

assumptions: uri is a non-NULL, NUL-terminated XML_Char string, so its storage contains exactly s+1 XML_Chars including the terminator and the strlen-style loop at line 45 terminates.
prefix->name is an internal NUL-terminated string, making the fixed reads at lines 33-42 within storage.
EXPAND_SPARE is a small positive constant, so the allocated capacity len + EXPAND_SPARE is strictly greater than len.
parser state fields (m_ns, m_namespaceSeparator, m_freeBindingList, m_dtd, m_startNamespaceDeclHandler) are trusted framework-internal values.
On 32-bit builds the guards at lines 89/116 also transitively bound the subsequent memcpy size because b->uriAlloc was produced by the same guarded allocation path.
limitations: A URI longer than INT_MAX XML_Chars (~2^31 characters) would overflow the int loop counter at line 45 before the overflow guards apply, but reaching that requires an infeasibly large attacker document/attribute; the path is not demonstrable within the shown constraints, so it is not a confirmed finding.
Very large but sub-INT_MAX URIs can request large allocations; allocation failure merely returns XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY and is a robustness/DoS concern, not a memory-safety finding.
Uses of the resulting BINDING and the start-namespace-declaration callback at lines 144-146 occur in unseen caller code and are out of scope.
No injection, crypto/entropy, file/access-control, or authz sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: http_isfiltered indexes the fixed-size fm->hdf[] and fm->hd[] arrays with the caller-supplied parameter u, which the shown code never bounds-checks; any u >= HTTP_HDR_MAX performs an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at lines 6 and 8, followed by a dereference of an invalid header pointer, enabling info disclosure or a crash.

evidence.reason: The unsigned parameter u arrives from the caller with no constraint imposed on the shown path and is used to index the fixed-size fm->hdf[] array. There is no u < HTTP_HDR_MAX (or u < fm->nhd) guard anywhere in the function; the only guards (lines 9 and 12) validate the data read out of the arrays, not the index. A concrete failing witness is u = HTTP_HDR_MAX, which passes every shown check and reads one byte past the end of fm->hdf[].

The same unvalidated u is used a second time to read the pointer fm->hd[u] from the fixed-size fm->hd[] array. With u = HTTP_HDR_MAX (or larger) — admitted because the shown code never tests u's upper bound — this reads past the array, and the resulting garbage pointer is dereferenced immediately by strchr, turning the out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) into a likely crash or adjacent-memory disclosure.

assumptions: fm points to a live, framework-managed struct http whose hd[u].b strings are NUL-terminated, so strchr at line 8 never reads past the string end once hd[u] itself is valid.
http_hdr_flags at line 11 only reads the [b, e) header-name range, where e is the first ':' found by strchr and therefore lies within the same string as b.
fm->hdf[] and fm->hd[] are fixed-size arrays (HTTP_HDR_MAX entries); the failure requires u to reach or exceed that bound.
limitations: In the real product, unseen callers iterate u over [0, fm->nhd) with fm->nhd capped by the parser, which would keep u in range; that invariant is not present in the shown code and therefore cannot serve as the protective check.

NULL dereference of fm or fm->hd[u].b is not confirmable from the shown code because no in-function path produces NULL for these values; it would require caller-invalid state, so it is not reported as a finding.
No injection, weak-crypto, file-handling, authz, or ReDoS concerns exist in the shown code because none of the corresponding sinks are present.

verdict.summary: e1000_send_packet passes the guest-influenced and completely unvalidated `size` parameter directly to `qemu_send_packet` (line 10) or `nc->info->receive` (line 8), with neither a sign check (`size > 0`) nor an upper bound relative to `buf`. A negative value such as -1 is widened to a size_t byte count of ~2^64-1 at the iov boundary, forcing a host out-of-bounds read from `buf` — guest-to-host memory disclosure and emulator crash (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: The caller-derived `size` parameter (line 1) is unconstrained in the shown code — there is no `size > 0` and no `size <= capacity(buf)` guard anywhere on the path from line 2 to line 10. Any negative value (e.g., -1) reaches this sink unchanged and is widened to a size_t iov length of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF when the packet is transmitted, so the backend reads past the end of `buf`; a positive `size` exceeding the backing buffer capacity triggers the same OOB read. The only branch (line 7) selects between this sink and line 8 and constrains neither value.

In the guest-selectable loopback branch (line 7), the same unvalidated `size` reaches `nc->info->receive`, which consumes `size` as the byte count read from `buf`. With no length validation in the shown code, a negative value (widened to a huge unsigned byte count) or any value above the buffer's capacity causes a host out-of-bounds read on this branch as well, duplicating the CWE-125 failure of the non-loopback path.

assumptions: `qemu_get_queue(s->nic)` returns a non-NULL `NetClientState` (framework invariant in QEMU), so line 6 introduces no NULL hazard.
`buf` points to a caller-owned staging buffer of finite fixed capacity, and `size` is not bounded to that capacity anywhere in the shown code.
Both `qemu_send_packet` and the net-backend `receive` callback treat the passed integer as the exact byte count to read from `buf`.
limitations: `inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count(s, buf)` (line 12) inspects leading bytes of `buf`, but its body is not shown; if `buf` is a fixed-capacity staging buffer, reads of a few bytes remain in-bounds regardless of `size`, so no OOB is confirmable for it.

`e1000x_increase_size_stats(s->mac_reg, PTCregs, size)` (line 13) receives the 6-element static array `PTCregs` (lines 3–4) with no `-1` sentinel; if its (unseen) consumer loop iterates until a sentinel, it could read past the array and use garbage register indices. The write loop is outside the shown code and the indices are build-time constants, so this is not confirmed.
A NULL `buf` dereference is not confirmable because the shown code never produces NULL; it would require an unseen caller to supply one.
The real upstream QEMU TX-descriptor path may cap `size` before calling this function, but that protective check is not shown, so per the scoping rules it is not credited toward the verdict.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability.
