The cursor-column walk (lines 94-104) is bounded by the new_cursor_col >= 0 guard (line 97) and the NUL break (lines 101-102), so reads stay within [0, strlen]; the spaces-insertion buffer alloc(i+1) (line 113) exactly matches the writes at indices 0..i (lines 117-119), with i >= 1 forced by the loop invariant and the vcol != w_virtcol branch; the VREPLACE write new_line[w_cursor.col] = NUL (line 199) is bounded by the cursor-math in every cursor branch (col <= new line length); and all allocation results are NULL-checked (lines 114, 190-191, 195-196).

assumptions: Vim invariants relied on: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer and curwin->w_cursor.col <= strlen(current line) is maintained by editing/movement code outside this function.
alloc() and vim_strsave() return NULL on failure rather than aborting; the NULL paths are checked before use (lines 114, 190-191, 195-196).
mb_ptr2len() returns a length >= 1 for non-NUL positions and lbr_chartabsize() contributes >= 1 per non-NUL character (implementations outside the shown code).
Parameters type/amount/round/replaced/call_changed_bytes come from internal callers and are only passed through to delegated functions, never used to index or size memory in the shown code.
limitations: i = w_virtcol - vcol (line 112) has no explicit upper bound, but it scales linearly with the current line's display width and the allocation failure at line 113 is handled at line 114, so no compounding attacker-controlled DoS is demonstrable.
The VREPLACE write at line 199 is safe only while the unseen editor invariant w_cursor.col <= line length holds; a hypothetical caller violating that invariant is out of scope.
Correctness of mb_ptr2len/lbr_chartabsize on malformed multibyte text (including not reading past the terminating NUL) is delegated to code not shown here.

No integer-overflow witness for vcol/i could be constructed: reaching INT_MAX screen columns would require a line whose byte length approaches INT_MAX, with the allocation-failure path handling the result.

verdict.summary: http_isfiltered reads fm->hdf[u] (line 6) and fm->hd[u].b (line 10) using the caller-supplied header index u, which the shown code never validates against the arrays' upper bound. The only guard, 'u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST' (line 8), is a pseudo-header discrimination test: it excludes only u in [0, HTTP_HDR_FIRST-1], admits every u >= HTTP_HDR_FIRST unbounded, and is evaluated after the first dereference. Any u at or beyond the element count of hdf/hd (e.g., the HTTP_HDR_LAST extent) causes an out-of-bounds read that can leak adjacent memory or crash the worker when strchr scans an out-of-range header pointer (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Caller-supplied unsigned index u is used to subscript fm->hdf before any bound check exists on the shown path: the only comparison, 'u < HTTP_HDR_FIRST' at line 8, executes after this access and tests only a small pseudo-header constant, so it cannot exclude u at or beyond the array's element count. A value u >= sizeof(fm->hdf)/sizeof(fm->hdf[0]) (e.g., the HTTP_HDR_LAST extent) performs an out-of-bounds read at this sink.

This indexed read is reached only when the line-8 guard passes, i.e. u >= HTTP_HDR_FIRST, but that guard caps nothing above, so it admits u at or beyond the fm->hd element count. The same uncontrolled parameter u then drives strchr over an out-of-bounds header pointer, yielding an OOB read/crash; no comparison against the array size is present anywhere in the shown code.

assumptions: fm is non-NULL and points to a valid struct http whose hdf/hd arrays are indexed by header-slot index u; this invariant is enforced only by unseen callers and is not checked in the shown code.
The exact element counts of fm->hdf and fm->hd are defined in the struct/table outside this snippet; the nominal extent is the HTTP_HDR_LAST constant, which the shown code never compares u against.
When u is in range, fm->hd[u].b points to a NUL-terminated header string, so strchr is well-defined for in-range indices (Varnish storage invariant).
limitations: The precise numeric failing value depends on the unseen array sizes; the confirmed witness is any u >= the element count of hdf/hd (for example, the HTTP_HDR_LAST extent), which no shown check excludes, hence confidence 0.6 rather than >= 0.7.
A NULL or tombstone fm->hd[u].b (unused slot) would make strchr(NULL, ':') undefined, but producing that state requires initialization/state from unseen code, so it is not confirmed as a finding.

Whether a real network attacker can directly influence the value of u depends on unseen callers (in Varnish, iteration over parsed header slots bounded by fm->hdrs); the finding rests on the shown code's absence of any upper-bound validation of the parameter.

The semantics of 'f->flag & how' (any-bit match against possibly multi-bit flag masks) and of returning 0 for colon-less headers are intended filter behavior with no confirmed security class in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in squashfs_opendir: attacker-controlled directory inode fields set the read position and loop bound (bytes = lookup + (*i)->offset, size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3, lines 48-49) with no bound against the directory_table heap allocation; the only guard, 'while(bytes < size)' (line 51), uses the same attacker-derived size and admits positions where the 12-byte header/entry reads at lines 52 and 66 (and the name memcpy at lines 76-77) run far past the buffer, causing crash/UB.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap read: bytes is set at line 48 as lookup_entry result plus attacker-controlled (*i)->offset and is only guarded by 'while(bytes < size)' where size is computed at line 49 from attacker-controlled (*i)->data. The guard admits bytes = table_size - 2, so this fixed-size read copies 12 bytes starting 2 bytes before the end of the directory_table heap buffer; no check constrains bytes or size against the buffer allocation.

Same uncontrolled read position reaches the per-entry read: bytes increased only by sizeof(dirh) at line 57, with no remaining-space or table-bound check before this 12-byte fetch. With the same witness (bytes near/exceeding the table end and size inflated via (*i)->data), the entry read dereferences directory_table + bytes out of bounds, driven by the unvalidated on-disk inode fields obtained at line 17.

assumptions: directory_table is a single heap allocation sized to the uncompressed directory table, so positions beyond its end are out of bounds.
read_inode (line 17) copies on-disk inode fields start/offset/data into *i without size validation, so these values are attacker-controlled from the image.
SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER/SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY perform fixed-size (12-byte) structure copies from the source address.
limitations: The corrupted: path (lines 109-111) as shown lacks a return statement, so it falls off the end of a non-void function (UB) on attacker-triggered invalid names; if the full upstream function returns NULL there, any dereference would occur in an unseen caller and is not confirmed here.
TRACE at lines 55-56 passes long long bytes to %d; fixed-format mismatch is benign UB with no injection.
Memory disclosure via OOB-derived directory names is not demonstrated: names are capped at 256 bytes and NUL-terminated, and any use in extraction/printing happens outside the shown code.
CPU/memory exhaustion from a huge attacker size is secondary to the confirmed OOB read and is not scored separately.

verdict.summary: e1000_send_packet validates neither `size` nor the valid length of `buf` before using it. In particular, line 12 unconditionally calls inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count(s, buf), which reads buf[0] (and up to 6 bytes for broadcast detection) without any length argument, on both the loopback and normal paths. A guest-supplied zero-length TX packet (size == 0) reaches this call and produces an out-of-bounds read past the valid packet data.

evidence.reason: The guest-controlled length `size` (derived from the TX descriptor `len` field, 0..65535) is never checked in this function. After either branch (lines 7-11) control always reaches line 12, which invokes inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count(s, buf) without supplying any bound. That helper dereferences buf[0] (and compares up to 6 bytes for the broadcast/multicast check) regardless of `size`, so the concrete witness size == 0 (a descriptor with len set to 0 and EOP) reads one byte past the zero-length packet: an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The only guard that would block this (e.g., an `if (size > 0)` gate before line 12) is absent.

assumptions: `buf`/`size` are caller-supplied from the e1000 TX path, where `size` equals the guest-controlled 16-bit TX descriptor length (0..65535); the shown code contains no check establishing size > 0 or bounding size to the buffer allocation.
inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count reads `buf[0]` as its first action and compares up to 6 bytes for broadcast/multicast classification; the shown call passes no length, so the helper has no bound.
limitations: The helper bodies and the caller (process_tx_desc) are not shown, so the exact backing allocation of `buf` is not visible; per the scoping rule a buffer allocated by an unseen caller does not excuse the missing size check, but the allocation semantics limit the confirmed trigger to the size == 0 witness rather than an oversized-size witness.
Negative sizes are not reachable from the real TX path (the length field is unsigned 16-bit), so the confirmed trigger is size == 0, not size < 0.
qemu_send_packet/qemu_receive_packet (lines 8/10) consume the same unvalidated `size` in internal copies; this is the same root cause and is not counted as a separate finding.
If an unseen caller guaranteed size >= 1 on every invocation, the buf[0] dereference would be in-bounds; the shown function imposes no such guarantee and none is stated.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled value reaches a security-relevant sink unconstrained within the shown code. The expr->ops dereferences at lines 11 and 35 are protected by the parse-time invariant that ops is always non-NULL for a fully parsed nft_rule; loop bounds derive from the trusted rule size via nft_expr_first/more/next; the action count at line 12 matches the flow allocation at line 20 under the NFT_OFFLOAD_F_ACTION contract; and all error paths assign err and free ctx/flow consistently. Remaining concerns (helper-bounded action writes, NULL ops, int overflow, two-pass TOCTOU) lack a concrete failing witness in the shown code and are out-of-scope.

assumptions: expr->ops is always non-NULL for any rule that reached this function, because nf_tables expression parsing rejects unknown expression types before a rule is committed.
The nft_expr_first/nft_expr_more/nft_expr_next helpers advance by trusted ops->size and terminate at the rule blob end, bounding both loops (lines 10-15, 34-44).

Every expression with ops->offload_flags & NFT_OFFLOAD_F_ACTION is offloaded to exactly one action slot, so the num_actions count at line 12 matches the allocation at line 20; the shown code does not itself write more actions than counted.
The rule contents are stable between the two traversals; no mutation of rule appears between lines 9-15 and 34-44, and the caller is assumed to serialize rule updates.
Rule size and expression count are bounded by netlink message and nf_tables rule-size limits enforced in the unseen caller, making num_actions int overflow (line 12) unreachable.
limitations: If the parse-time invariant on expr->ops were ever violated, line 11 or line 35 would NULL-dereference, but the NULL-producing path is outside the shown code (CWE-476 not confirmed).

If an offload callback in an unseen module added more actions than counted (e.g., without NFT_OFFLOAD_F_ACTION being set), line 39's dispatch could lead to a heap OOB write inside nft_flow_rule_add_action; the write and the concrete witness expression are outside the shown code, so this is not a confirmed finding.
A two-pass TOCTOU (count at lines 9-15 vs. offload at lines 34-44) would require concurrent mutation of rule, which is neither present in the shown code nor demonstrated to be reachable.
Allocation-size arithmetic inside nft_flow_rule_alloc(num_actions) at line 20 is bounded only by unseen rule-size checks in the caller; not a finding in the shown code.
Failure cases that depend on allocation failure (lines 21, 27) with attacker-controlled volume are not demonstrated and would only be DoS-relevant, not memory safety.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes attacker-controlled devname, mountpoint, and fstype verbatim into /etc/mtab (MOUNTED) via addmntent at line 86 with no neutralization of whitespace or newlines; a mountpoint such as "/mnt/x\n/dev/fake /mnt/x ext2 rw 0 0" terminates the real record and injects a forged second record that getmntent-family consumers (mount -a, umount -a, df) parse as a genuine mount, corrupting the system mount table. All memory copies in the function are bounded by strlcat against a calloc(MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, 1) buffer, so the issue is record/CRLF injection, not memory safety.

evidence.reason: Sink: addmntent serializes the struct into MOUNTED (/etc/mtab) with fields separated by whitespace and records by newlines. Attacker-controlled devname, mountpoint, and fstype are assigned with no content check at lines 58-60 (and mount_user at 80-81); the only guard before the write, `if (mountent.mnt_opts)` at line 62, tests allocation success, not data content. A mountpoint of "/mnt/x\n/dev/fake /mnt/x ext2 rw 0 0" passes every check and is written verbatim, terminating the real record and injecting a forged second record that getmntent-family consumers (mount -a, umount -a, df) treat as a real mount (CWE-93, low severity).

assumptions: Callers of add_mtab build devname/mountpoint/fstype from mount(8) command-line arguments; the shown code imposes no constraints on these parameters, so per the analysis rules they are attacker-controlled inputs.
getmntent-family parsers treat a newline as a record terminator and whitespace as a field separator for mtab format.
Non-root reachability of add_mtab implies the caller already authorized the mount; root callers can edit mtab directly, which bounds the injection severity to low.
MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN is large enough that normal usernames and option fragments do not truncate; truncation is safe regardless.
limitations: No memory-safety flaw found: every write into mountent.mnt_opts is a strlcat bounded by MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN against a calloc(MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, 1) buffer, so the maximum string length is MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN-1 characters plus a terminating NUL; longer input is silently truncated, which is not a violation.

If calloc fails, mountent.mnt_opts stays NULL and NULL reaches addmntent; the allocation size is a constant rather than attacker-controlled, so this is a robustness limitation, not a confirmed finding.
Authorization for the mount itself (whether a non-root user may write mtab) is decided by unseen caller code; the shown function has no authz check of its own, so no authz-bypass finding is made.

The double unlock possible via atexit(unlock_mtab) combined with explicit unlock_mtab() calls on error paths (lines 53, 92) is a locking robustness concern, not an attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code.

Real-world impact of the mtab injection is limited because the writing user is already permitted to append their own mount record; the effect is integrity/confusion for mtab consumers rather than direct privilege escalation.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents can hang the X server indefinitely: if affectWhich sets the XkbMapNotify bit (0x2) together with any other bit, the loop at line 25 skips that bit via the 'ndx == XkbMapNotify' continue at lines 26-27 before maskLeft is cleared at line 28, so maskLeft never reaches 0 and the loop spins forever (ndx grows without bound, bit becomes 0 after 32 shifts and continues matching nothing). A single crafted xkbSelectEvents request with affectWhich=0x0003, clear=0, selectAll=0 triggers it after one harmless 4-byte swap, denying service.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled affectWhich (swapped at line 8) becomes maskLeft at line 24. With affectWhich=0x0003 (XkbMapNotify bit 0x2 plus XkbNewKeyboardNotify bit 0x1), clear=0, selectAll=0: ndx=0 clears bit 0x1; ndx=1 hits the 'ndx == XkbMapNotify' disjunct at line 26 and continues at line 27 before 'maskLeft &= ~bit' at line 28, so maskLeft keeps 0x2 forever; for ndx>=2 'bit & maskLeft' is 0 and after ndx=32 bit is permanently 0, yet the loop condition 'maskLeft != 0' at line 25 stays true. The loop never terminates and line 75 is never reached, hanging the X server; no loop bound or exit guard constrains this admitted value.

assumptions: The X server framework guarantees the full declared request (stuff->length * 4 bytes) is present in client->requestBuffer before this handler runs, so dataLeft at line 23 accurately bounds the trailing bytes.
xkbSelectEventsReq fields are CARD16 after swap; in particular affectWhich is 16-bit, so maskLeft only ever contains bits 0..15.
limitations: Size-1 events (XkbCompatMapNotify, XkbBellNotify, XkbActionMessage, lines 44-47) pass the line 53 guard with dataLeft >= 2 but consume 4 bytes (lines 63-66). This cannot underflow unsigned dataLeft because dataLeft is always a multiple of 4 (line 23, decremented by 4 or 8 at line 67), so dataLeft values 2 or 3 are unreachable and no out-of-bounds read is reachable from this path.
ErrorF at lines 70-71 passes unsigned dataLeft to a %d specifier; cosmetic type mismatch only, no format-string injection because the format is constant.
The default case at lines 49-51 safely rejects unknown event bits 12-15 with BadValue; not a finding.

verdict.summary: In unix_expandpath(), the buffer 'buf' is allocated as STRLEN(path) + BASENAMELEN + 5 (line 32), but a directory entry name returned by readdir() is copied into it with an unbounded STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) at line 150. The guard at lines 141-148 checks dot-file policy and pattern match only, never name length, so a name longer than BASENAMELEN + ~5 - (e-s) bytes overflows the heap allocation (e.g. a 200-byte non-dot filename matching pattern '*' in a scanned directory), enabling memory corruption. This is the known Vim unix_expandpath heap overflow (CVE-2017-5953 class).

evidence.reason: dp->d_name comes from readdir() (line 138), i.e. attacker-controlled filesystem data when the scanned directory is writable by the attacker, and its length is bounded only by NAME_MAX (>=255), never by the shown code. The allocation at line 32 limits buf to STRLEN(path)+BASENAMELEN+5 bytes, so the tail capacity at 's' is only ~105+(e-s) bytes for a single-wildcard component. The guard at lines 141-148 admits any non-dot name matching the pattern (e.g. 'A' repeated 200 times against pattern '*'), and line 150 then writes 201 bytes, overflowing the heap buffer by roughly 95 bytes — a confirmed out-of-bounds write with no length check anywhere on the path between readdir and the sink.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is 100 (standard Vim build), giving buf capacity STRLEN(path) + 105.
path is NUL-terminated and shorter than INT_MAX, so the sequence-phase copies (lines 45-71, 123) stay in bounds.
The scanned directory can contain attacker-created entries, e.g. /tmp or any shared/writable dir named in the pattern.
readdir() can return names longer than BASENAMELEN+5 (NAME_MAX >= 255 on common platforms).
limitations: Lines 157-158 and 164 (STRCPY of "/**" and path_end) overflow only as a consequence of the same root cause at line 150; they are not separately counted as a distinct CWE.

vim_regexec() (line 145) against attacker-controlled d_name with user-chosen patterns could be a ReDoS concern, but the pattern is usually not attacker-controlled in the expansion flow; not confirmed.
vim_regfree(regmatch.regprog) at line 204 can be called with NULL under EW_NOTWILD; safety depends on unseen vim_regfree implementation, out of scope.
The macOS precompose path (#ifdef MACOS_CONVERT, lines 183-193) may copy a lengthened precomposed string into buf without re-checking capacity; not confirmed and platform-gated.
No other memory-safety or injection sink was found: no format strings, no command/exec construction, no SQL/query building, and no authz logic in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Attacker-controlled file values reaching memory operations are bounded by explicit checks in the shown code: the image_type whitelist (lines 69-79), the bits_per_pixel check (lines 91-93) capping all reads to the 4-byte pixels[] buffer, colormap allocation sized exactly to image->colors with fill loops bounded to [0, colors) (lines 188-194, 258), ConstrainColormapIndex at colormap lookups (lines 312-313, 348-349), the comment buffer allocated id_length+MagickPathExtent with id_length <= 255 (lines 147-155), and the row-offset invariant keeping offset < rows at every loop-top so image->rows-real-1 cannot underflow (lines 273-275, 398-402). No injection, crypto, file-path, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: AcquireImageColormap(image, n) allocates exactly n entries and returns MagickFalse for n == 0 or on allocation failure (called at lines 132 and 190; both failure paths throw).
ConstrainColormapIndex clamps or rejects indices outside [0, image->colors) for an allocated colormap (lines 312-313, 348-349).
QueueAuthenticPixels(image, 0, y, columns, 1) returns a cache row of columns pixels including all channels, or NULL, which is checked at lines 277-278.
ReadBlob/ReadBlobByte/ReadBlobLSBShort perform bounded reads; short reads/EOF are caught by the explicit count checks and EOFBlob() at lines 89, 293, 334-335, 357-358, 369-370, 413.
A newly acquired image has image->colors == 0, so the colormap_type != 0 path always allocates at least colormap_index entries (lines 188-191).
limitations: For 24-bit images with alpha_trait set (e.g., bits_per_pixel == 24 with alpha_bits > 0), the case-24 branch (lines 352-362) never assigns pixel.alpha, so SetPixelAlpha at line 386 writes a stale value carried from an earlier pixel; impact is confined to image content the attacker already fully controls, with no trusted-boundary disclosure.

Large dimensions/colormaps (up to 65535x65535 pixels or 1<<bits_per_pixel colors) can demand large allocations, but sizes are attacker-bounded, allocation failures throw ResourceLimitError, and no dereference follows those failure paths.
The bits_per_pixel check admits values 2..14, which decode through the shared 1-byte default case; this is format tolerance rather than memory unsafety given the 4-byte pixels[] buffer.

Analysis relies on the helper contracts in assumptions; if a helper allocated fewer entries than requested, the corresponding loops would overflow, but that failure mode is not present in the shown code.
SetImageProgress cancellation (lines 407-409) can leave status == MagickFalse and trigger the spurious CorruptImageError at lines 378-379; robustness quirk only, no security impact.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code. The main loop is bounded by BOTH the qfp==NULL break (lines 71-73) and lnum<qfl->qf_count (line 51), so no iteration dereferences a NULL qfp; callback strings are NULL/type-guarded (lines 58, 61-62); the only remaining risky sinks (dirname/path write inside qf_buf_add_line, qf_start==NULL or stale old_last states, callback re-entrancy) depend on unseen callees or caller invariants and are out of scope under the analysis rules.

assumptions: Callers preserve the qf_list_T invariants: qfl->qf_start is non-NULL whenever qfl->qf_count > 0, and a non-NULL old_last is a live node of qfl whose qf_next chain covers the remaining entries; under these, qfp is non-NULL at every dereference (lines 65-66, 69) and ml_delete(lnum+1) (line 81) hits the trailing empty line.
ml_delete validates out-of-range line numbers (returns FAIL / internal error), so line 81 cannot corrupt memory even in the empty/0-count edge case.
tv_get_string_chk (line 60) returns NULL only on type errors, which the invalid_val flag (lines 61-62) fully contains.
limitations: Potential NULL dereference at lines 65-66 if qfl->qf_start == NULL with qf_count > 0, or if old_last is not a live node of qfl; the NULL-producing state can only be supplied by an unseen caller, so it is not reachable from the shown control flow.
Path construction into dirname[MAXPATHL] (line 25) and the actual buffer line writes happen inside the unseen qf_buf_add_line (lines 65-66); any overflow or injection there is out of scope.

Re-entrancy: the quickfixtextfunc callback (line 46) and BufReadPost/BufWinEnter autocommands (lines 98-101) can mutate the quickfix list or buffer during iteration, potentially invalidating qfp/qftf_li (use-after-free); no concrete trigger path is demonstrable within the shown code.
ml_delete(lnum + 1) (line 81) would target a wrong line if qf_buf_add_line returned FAIL (line 66-67), e.g. after an allocation failure; excluded per the unchecked-allocation rule.
The qf_count == 0 case calls ml_delete(1) on an already-emptied buffer (line 81); ml_delete's bounds validation makes this fail safely.

verdict.summary: tc_new_tfilter contains no confirmed, reachable vulnerability. All attacker-controlled values that reach memory/index operations are constrained by explicit guards in the shown code: CAP_NET_ADMIN capability gate (line 25) before any mutation, nlmsg_parse_deprecated with sizeof(*t) minimum and rtm_tca_policy (lines 31-34) before reading tcmsg fields, the IFNAMSIZ name-length check that rejects over-long TCA_KIND before name[16] is used (lines 65-69), and the TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK bound on TCA_CHAIN before tcf_chain_get indexes the block (lines 94-100). Every q/block/chain/tp pointer dereference is protected by an explicit NULL or IS_ERR check in the shown paths, and no injection, weak-crypto, or authz-bypass sink exists in the function.

assumptions: rtm_tca_policy (passed at line 31) is the kernel-internal policy covering TCA_MAX attributes including TCA_KIND and TCA_CHAIN types/lengths.
tcf_proto_check_kind (line 65) enforces a bounded copy into name[IFNAMSIZ], consistent with the 'name too long' -> -EINVAL contract shown at lines 66-68.
tcf_chain_get (line 100) safely handles the admitted chain_index range [0, TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK].
chain->flushing (line 119) is a transient flag cleared when the concurrent flush completes, so the -EAGAIN replay loop (lines 218-224) terminates.

qdisc/block/filter lookup helpers (__tcf_qdisc_find line 61, __tcf_qdisc_cl_find line 82, __tcf_block_find line 86) return errors for invalid ifindex/block ids, as their errors are checked at lines 62, 83 and 88.
limitations: Helper internals (tcf_proto_check_kind, tcf_chain_get, tcf_chain_tp_find, tcf_proto_create, tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique) are not shown, so their exact bounds and refcount behavior are framework-internal invariants.

Lifetime/refcount races between concurrent tcf_chain flush and the unlocked use of tp (after mutex_unlock at lines 142/158) depend on helper refcounting that is outside the shown slice and cannot be confirmed as a finding.
Potential NULL q->ops->cl_ops for exotic qdiscs is not analyzable here; __tcf_qdisc_find is assumed to only return qdiscs valid for tfilter use.
If rtm_tca_policy lacked a TCA_CHAIN entry, nla_get_u32 at line 94 could read an undersized attr; the policy is a trusted kernel-internal constant outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot contains no attacker-controlled input reaching a security sink. The only memory writes are a single UINT32 store guarded by a NULL check (line 12-13) and MemorySet with the compile-time size sizeof(*object) (line 16); the loop bound i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS (line 7) keeps all s_objects accesses strictly within bounds. No injection, crypto, file, or authz operations are present.

assumptions: s_objects is declared with at least MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements, so indices 0..MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1 are valid.
TRANSIENT_FIRST + MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS - 1 stays within the valid transient object handle range.
handle is either NULL or a valid writable buffer supplied by the caller.
limitations: A non-NULL but dangling/invalid handle is a caller-contract violation outside the shown code; the shown code cannot validate pointer validity and its NULL guard is the only applicable check.
No attacker-controlled length, index, or data value reaches any memory, injection, crypto, or access-control operation in the shown code, so no candidate reached confirmation.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The authorization gate (if (!maywrite)) at lines 36-39 fully covers both DB write sinks (cyrusdb_delete line 68, cyrusdb_store line 93), and the remaining in-function sinks (memcmp line 33, quota arithmetic line 44, DEBUG-only syslog) are sound. Memory-safety operations are delegated to unseen size-capped helpers (make_key with sizeof(key), make_entry) and are out of scope.

assumptions: struct buf.len is an int (signed) and quota_t is a signed long long, so the subtraction at line 44 is signed and cannot unsigned-underflow.
IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED is a nonzero error constant, making the if (r) goto out at line 38 unconditionally bail when maywrite is false.
make_key is called with sizeof(key) (MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1), bounding keylen; its internal write is an unseen helper.
limitations: The DB key construction (make_key) and value encoding (make_entry) write into the key/data buffers; their internal bounds checks are not in the shown code and were not analyzed.
The quota delta at line 44 would be a signedness/underflow concern only if quota_t were unsigned or narrower than buf.len; with the standard Cyrus types it is signed-correct.
A caller-supplied struct buf with len > 0 but s == NULL would be dereferenced only inside the unseen make_entry, not in this function.
The identical-value early return (lines 33-34) returns success without checking maywrite, but performs no write, so it has no security impact.

verdict.summary: add_mtab() writes attacker-controlled devname, mountpoint, and fstype strings verbatim to /etc/mtab via addmntent() without any character or length neutralization, so an unprivileged mount user can inject newline/whitespace separators and forge or corrupt mount-table entries in a root-owned file parsed by other privileged tools (CWE-93).

evidence.reason: devname, mountpoint, and fstype are attacker-controlled argv strings assigned verbatim at lines 74-76 and passed to addmntent(), which writes them per the standard format '%s %s %s %s %d %d\n' with single-space field separators and no escaping. No branch between lines 74 and 102 (fd/fstat checks and the post-write return check at line 103) filters characters, so a mountpoint such as '/tmp/m\nx /dev/shm ext2 rw 0 0' — legal as a pathname, so mount(2) succeeds — is written raw at line 102, ending the real mtab entry early and forging a second line; a space in devname or mountpoint shifts the whitespace-delimited columns instead. An unprivileged caller (whose path is explicitly supported by the uid != 0 / mount_user handling at lines 12-13) thus gains the ability to inject arbitrary data into the root-owned /etc/mtab consumed by mount, umount, and related tooling.

assumptions: mount is invoked as a setuid-root binary by unprivileged local users; the code's own uid != 0 / setreuid handling and the 'prevents unprivileged users from sending signals' comment establish this entry path.

The standard C library addmntent() writes fields with fprintf('%s %s %s %s %d %d\n') and performs no backslash/octal escaping (glibc behavior); a libc that does escape newlines would neutralize the newline vector outside the shown code.
mount(2) accepts device/mountpoint name strings containing whitespace and newlines provided the path is valid, so such characters survive into add_mtab().
limitations: If the calloc() of mnt_opts (line 77) fails, mountent.mnt_opts is NULL and line 102 would pass NULL to addmntent's '%s'; this requires an allocation failure on a fixed compile-time-constant size with no attacker control over size or volume, so it is not a confirmed finding.

The fstat() at line 65 is not followed by a regular-file/nlink check, so a symlinked /etc/mtab is not detected (a hardening gap upstream later addressed), but an unprivileged attacker cannot create or replace /etc/mtab, so this is not attacker-reachable in the shown code.

Early-return paths at lines 22, 28, 34, and 39 skip restoring the blocked signal mask and disabling DAC override; the impact is confined to the exiting mount process with no attacker-controlled value.
Over-long username/device strings are silently truncated by the bounded strlcat() calls (lines 79-97) with no security impact.
If the target libc escapes mtab special characters, the injection is neutralized there rather than in the shown code, which would reduce this finding to an input-validation hardening concern.

verdict.summary: expand_case_fold_string derives len from enclen(reg->enc, p) without checking len <= end - p; with a truncated multibyte tail at the end of a StrNode, the n==0 path sets foldp=p, fold_len=len (lines 67-68) and onig_node_str_cat (line 87) reads past the heap buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

evidence.reason: len at line 32 (enclen on attacker-controlled pattern bytes) is never validated against end - p; the only guard, 'while (p < end)' (line 24), admits p = end-1. For n==0, lines 66-68 set foldp = p and fold_len = len, so this sink copies [p, p+len). Witness: truncated UTF-8 3-byte char at the tail (enclen returns 3, end - p == 2) passes the line 24 guard and line 87 reads 1 byte past the heap-backed StrNode buffer.

assumptions: The StrNode byte range [start, end) is treated as attacker-supplied regex pattern text (standard threat model for a pattern compiler); reg->enc / reg->case_fold_flag are trusted framework state.
Encoding callbacks honor their documented contracts for well-formed input (items[] and buf sizes), so those paths are not attacker-tunable.
Line numbers count from the first line of the pasted snippet.
For encodings whose case-fold lookup is end-unaware, the same over-read occurs inside the line 25 macro instead of line 87.
limitations: Practical triggerability of the truncated-multibyte witness also depends on the unseen parse pipeline not rejecting invalid code points before a StrNode is created; the shown code itself provides no such validation, but full-library reachability is not proven here.
Unseen-helper recursion via expand_case_fold_make_rem_string (line 138) would need a single character with more than 8 fold codes, exceeding the encoding item-count contract; unconfirmed.
Write into buf (lines 62-63) relies on the ONIGENC_MBC_CASE_FOLD_MAXLEN encoding contract; no attacker-controlled route to exceed it was identified.
Exponential alternative expansion is capped by lines 94-95 (break at alt_num > 8), so the historical complexity DoS is not present in this shown code.
Silent skip of dangling tail bytes when p advances past end (lines 132, 135) has no security impact.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown teardown path. There are no injection, crypto, file-handling, or memory-safety sinks reachable with attacker-controlled data: no user lengths/indices, no loops, and the free ordering (nci_unregister_device -> nci_free_device -> kfree(priv)) leaves no use of freed pointers in the shown code. The dangerous-looking chained dereference of priv->ndev->nfc_dev at line 5 cannot be confirmed because the shown code contains no NULL-producing path; a NULL there would be caller-supplied and is out of scope. UAF/double-free and teardown-race concerns depend entirely on unseen helper implementations and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: priv points to a live nfcmrvl_private allocated by the unseen probe/register path, and priv->ndev is valid at entry.
priv->ndev->nfc_dev is non-NULL because it is populated only when nci_register_device() succeeds, which precedes any call to this unregister function.

The helper functions (nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit, nci_unregister_device, nci_free_device) do not free priv or ndev, so line 14 and line 15 are single frees with no later use in the shown code.
limitations: Line 5 dereferences priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress with no NULL check; a NULL can only originate from a caller/registration path not shown, so this is a potential NULL-deref robustness issue, not a confirmed finding (no CWE).

A use-after-free or double-free would require the unseen helper bodies to free priv or ndev, or an in-flight firmware-download worker to touch priv after kfree(priv) at line 15; none of that is visible or confirmable in the shown code (no CWE).
The unregister/free/kfree ordering is safe with respect to the uses shown; any hazard requires hidden callback or worker code outside this function.

verdict.summary: In the octet-counting framing path, the digit accumulator at line 33 has no range check or digit-count cap, so an attacker-controlled count overflows the signed int. A negative iOctetsRemain flows to octatesToCopy (line 98), evades the guards at lines 100 and 103, and is passed to memcpy (line 108) where it is converted to a huge size_t, causing an out-of-bounds heap write and read in a network-facing daemon.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled digit bytes from the socket (c from **buff, line 10) are accumulated without any digit-count or range cap. 12 '9' digits overflow the signed int to -727,379,969 (two's-complement), and the value is later used as the memcpy length at line 108.

octatesToCopy is copied from pThis->iOctetsRemain at line 98. When the overflowed remainder is negative (-727,379,969), guard at line 100 (buffLen < negative) does not fire and guard at line 103 (negative + iMsg > iMaxLine) does not fire, so the negative int is converted to size_t (~1.8e19) and memcpy writes far past the pMsg heap buffer and reads past *buff, corrupting memory (CWE-787, CWE-190).

assumptions: The caller guarantees buffLen >= 1 so `char c = **buff;` (line 10) is in-bounds, and advances *buff by one byte after each call, as implied by the `- 1` in `*buff += (octatesToCopy + octatesToDiscard - 1);` at line 111.

pMsg is a caller-allocated buffer of at least iMaxLine bytes, and iMsg is maintained in [0, iMaxLine] by the shown code (lines 92-93, 103-106); for non-negative octetsToCopy the memcpy length is capped at iMaxLine - iMsg.

Signed overflow at line 33 is assumed to wrap two's-complement as on the target platforms (gcc/clang x86-64 and ARM); in strict ISO C it is undefined behavior, so the failure remains UB rather than defined-safe behavior.
limitations: Log injection possibility at lines 69-70: attacker bytes from *buff are printed via `%.*s` into LogError without neutralization, but the precision is capped at 32 bytes and the downstream log sink is outside the shown code, so it is not reported as a CWE.

isdigit() at lines 14 and 32 is called with a possibly negative char value (bytes >= 0x80) made by `char c = **buff;` (line 10), which violates the ctype contract; impact is limited to a libc table over-read with no demonstrated exploit.

A zero-octet frame (count "0 " followed by data) makes octatesToCopy + octatesToDiscard == 0 at lines 100-111, so *buff has zero net advance while the caller decrements buffLen; this is a state-accounting anomaly rather than a memory-safety bug.

If a compiler eliminated the signed-overflow path under strict overflow assumptions, the failure mode would be undefined rather than the wrapped negative value; the memcpy OOB write is confirmed for normal daemon builds.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents is not vulnerable in the shown code. The dangerous byte-swap loop over the request tail is fully guarded: REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE (line 6) ensures dataLeft >= 0; the per-detail check `if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;` (line 53) rejects insufficient remaining data for every reachable value, because SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) = 16 (seven swapped CARD16 fields plus two opcode bytes) makes dataLeft a multiple of 4 through line 23 and all decrements (4 or 8 at line 67); pointer advance (line 66) and the final leftover check (line 69) keep access within the request buffer; unknown event bits return BadValue (lines 49-51); the loop terminates in at most 16 iterations. The only apparent gap (a size-1 detail admitted with dataLeft == 2 but consuming 4 bytes, which would underflow dataLeft and cause subsequent out-of-bounds swaps) requires dataLeft == 2, which is unreachable because dataLeft is always congruent to 0 mod 4.

assumptions: SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is 16 bytes: 2 CARD8 opcode bytes plus the 7 CARD16 fields (length, deviceSpec, affectWhich, clear, selectAll, affectMap, map) made visible by the swaps at lines 5-12.
client->req_len is the request length in 4-byte words, and the DIX dispatcher guarantees the request buffer holds exactly req_len*4 bytes.
XkbMapNotifyMask is bit 1, so maskLeft (line 24) excludes only XkbMapNotify; the ndx == XkbMapNotify skip at line 26 is redundant but harmless.
Valid XKB event indices for the details loop are exactly those enumerated in the switch (lines 32-48); any other bit triggers the default BadValue return.
limitations: The size-1 detail path (lines 44-47, 63-64) consumes 4 bytes while its guard only requires 2; this would underflow the unsigned dataLeft (line 67) and permit out-of-bounds swaps on a later iteration (lines 56-61) only if dataLeft == 2 were reachable, which is excluded by the dataLeft ≡ 0 (mod 4) invariant derived from SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) = 16 and decrements of 4 or 8.

The final check `if (dataLeft > 2)` (line 69) tolerates up to 2 trailing bytes, but with the same modular invariant the only passing leftover value is 0; any parsing of tolerated trailing bytes would occur in the unshown ProcXkbSelectEvents, which is out of scope.

Byte-order or semantic handling of the detail values consumed by size-1 entries (BellNotify, ActionMessage, CompatMapNotify) is not analyzed because no security-relevant sink for those values appears in the shown code.
Authorization for the XKB device (line 75, ProcXkbSelectEvents) is outside the shown code and is not assessed here.

verdict.summary: NULL-pointer dereference in the gzip-header EXTRA parsing of inflate(): when the FLG byte sets FEXTRA and XLEN is nonzero, `len = state->head->extra_len - state->length` (line 144) dereferences `state->head` before the NULL check at lines 145-147. With the default configuration (app never called inflateGetHeader, so state->head == NULL), a crafted gzip stream crashes the decompressor (DoS, CWE-476).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled FLG bit 0x0400 (line 87) and XLEN (line 128) drive mode EXTRA with copy>0 (lines 141-143), reaching an unconditional dereference of state->head at line 144. The guard at lines 145-147 (`state->head != Z_NULL && ...`) covers only the zmemcpy one statement later, not this read; every other gzip-header access in the shown code (lines 52, 98, 107, 116, 129, 135, 180, 202, 216) is NULL-guarded, so head==NULL is an expected default. Witness: gzip stream `1f 8b 08 04 00 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00` (FEXTRA, XLEN=1, one extra byte) with head==NULL dereferences NULL and crashes at line 144 (CWE-476).

assumptions: GUNZIP is defined (the gzip header path, including FLAGS/TIME/OS/EXLEN/EXTRA, is compiled in).

The embedding application uses the default configuration where inflateGetHeader() was not called, so state->head is NULL — a state the shown code itself treats as valid via its repeated `state->head != Z_NULL` guards.
PKZIP_BUG_WORKAROUND and INFLATE_STRICT are undefined (default builds), so the nlen/ndist cap at line 321 and the sane/whave distance checks are active.
Line numbers are relative to the provided snippet, which begins at `int ZEXPORT inflate(strm, flush)`.
limitations: The NULL dereference requires head==NULL; if an embedder always calls inflateGetHeader() before inflating gzip data, head is non-NULL and line 144 does not fault (the subsequent guard still prevents the zmemcpy).

The EXTRA-field zmemcpy (lines 148-150) is not an out-of-bounds write: line 147 (`len < state->head->extra_max`) and the `extra_max - len` clamp fully bound it; the historical CVE-2022-37434 pattern is fixed here.
Bulk copies delegated to inflate_fast (line 443) and updatewindow (line 660) are not present in the shown code; any flaw there is out of scope.
No ReDoS/weak-crypto/log-injection findings: decoder loops are finite-state over bounded input, crc32/adler32 are integrity checksums, and Tracev/Tracevv use constant format strings.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot contains no confirmed vulnerability. The only pointer write (*handle, line 13) is fully guarded by if(handle) at line 12, and the only array access (s_objects[i], lines 9/15) is bounded by the strict loop condition i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, which admits indices 0..MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1 only. The MemorySet size is the compile-time sizeof of the target member, and handle arithmetic uses a bounded index plus a trusted constant with no attacker-controlled inputs or injection/crypto/file/authz sinks in the shown code.

assumptions: s_objects is declared elsewhere with at least MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements, matching the loop bound.
TRANSIENT_FIRST and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS are the standard trusted TPM constants, so i + TRANSIENT_FIRST in UINT32 arithmetic cannot wrap.
TPMI_DH_OBJECT is a fixed-size handle type (UINT32), so the single store at line 13 fits the caller's buffer.
handle is supplied by framework-internal callers as an out-parameter; its pointer value is not attacker-controlled in the shown code.
limitations: If TRANSIENT_FIRST were chosen near UINT32_MAX and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS large, i + TRANSIENT_FIRST could wrap and alias handle ranges; this depends on unshown trusted constants and is not triggered by any attacker input, so it is not a confirmed finding.

If a caller passed a handle pointer aliasing memory inside s_objects, the write at line 13 could be clobbered by MemorySet at line 15; that would be a caller contract violation rather than a reachable attacker-triggered flaw.
The snippet has no concurrency controls; simultaneous slot allocation from multiple contexts is not addressed and is out of scope of the shown code.

verdict.summary: In win_redr_status, the default status line is assembled in NameBuff (MAXPATHL bytes) without any check that len has room. When the translated buffer name is MAXPATHL-1 bytes and any suffix flag (help/preview/changed/readonly) is set, line 53 writes a space into the last byte, destroying the NUL terminator and setting len = MAXPATHL; the following suffix block reads STRLEN(p + len) at one-past-the-end (line 57/63/73/78) and screen_puts then scans the unterminated string (line 117), producing an out-of-bounds read. If that read finds a non-NUL byte, len grows past MAXPATHL and the next suffix's MAXPATHL - len underflows to a huge size_t, escalating to an out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled buffer-name length flows from get_trans_bufname (line 43) into len. With a name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes, the guard at lines 47-53 admits the value and line 53 writes the space into NameBuff[MAXPATHL-1], replacing the NUL so that len becomes MAXPATHL (one-past-end) and the string is unterminated. Line 72 then calls vim_snprintf with maxlen 0 (no write), and this STRLEN reads starting at p + MAXPATHL, outside NameBuff, until it finds a NUL; if it returns r >= 1, len becomes MAXPATHL + r and the next suffix (line 77-78) passes the negative MAXPATHL - len to vim_snprintf as a huge size_t, writing out of bounds. No len < MAXPATHL check exists before line 53, this read, or the later suffixes, so the border value MAXPATHL-1 is admitted and triggers the OOB read (CWE-125).

assumptions: NameBuff is char_u[MAXPATHL] and get_trans_bufname NUL-terminates it with at most MAXPATHL-1 bytes, so len is in the range 0..MAXPATHL-1 before line 53.
vim_snprintf writes at most maxlen-1 characters plus a NUL, and writes nothing when maxlen is 0.
mb_ptr2len and mb_ptr2cells return at least 1 per byte/character, so the multi-byte loop at lines 98-100 terminates and, for a NUL-terminated string, never indexes past STRLEN(p).
The operating system permits a file path (buffer name) of MAXPATHL-1 bytes, e.g., a 4095-byte path when MAXPATHL equals PATH_MAX (4096).
limitations: The escalation to an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) at the second suffix depends on the byte immediately following NameBuff being non-NUL and on that memory being writable; it is layout-dependent and therefore not listed as an independently confirmed CWE.
The multi-byte truncation at lines 104-105 overwrites the last byte of a multibyte character with '<'; this is an in-bounds write and only a display artifact when the string is NUL-terminated.
The custom-statusline path (redraw_custom_statusline, line 36) is delegated to unshown code and was not analyzed.
No format-string, command, SQL, log, header, or crypto sinks exist in the shown code, so no injection or weak-crypto findings were formed.

verdict.summary: In win_redr_status, the status-line buffer append writes a space at `*(p + len++) = ' '` without writing a new NUL terminator. When the space is appended but no subsequent marker snprintf runs (specifically a changed terminal buffer: bufIsChanged true, bt_terminal true, so the `[+]` append is skipped by the `!bt_terminal` guard and no other marker applies), the original NUL is overwritten and `screen_puts(p, ...)` reads past the logical end of the NameBuff string into stale bytes — a heap over-read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: This write overwrites the NUL that previously terminated the string at p[len] and increments len without writing a new terminator. When the shared guard (bt_help || p_pvw || bufIsChanged || b_p_ro) is true but none of the following vim_snprintf marker blocks executes (the only such case is bufIsChanged && bt_terminal, because the `[+]` append at lines 68-76 is disabled by the `!bt_terminal` guard), no NUL is written and the string passed to screen_puts is unterminated at its logical end. len originates from STRLEN(NameBuff), and NameBuff is filled by get_trans_bufname from the buffer's attacker-influenced file name (Phase 1 taint).

This sink reads p (pointing into NameBuff) until NUL. On the changed-terminal-buffer path, the string is not NUL-terminated after the space appended at line 55, so screen_puts reads past the logical end into stale buffer bytes — an out-of-bounds/stale read (CWE-125). The reachable trigger is: a terminal buffer with bufIsChanged true, where the `!bt_terminal` guard (line 70) suppresses the `[+]` append and no bt_help/p_pvw/b_p_ro marker runs.

assumptions: NameBuff is a static char_u[MAXPATHL] global that get_trans_bufname always fills as a NUL-terminated string, so the space at line 55 overwrites a real NUL.
vim_snprintf always writes a NUL, so the four marker appends (lines 58, 64, 74, 79) always keep the string terminated.
limitations: The over-read may remain bounded within the physical NameBuff array because NameBuff is a zero-initialized static global and prior fills leave a NUL somewhere inside it; a true read past the physical buffer end depends on memory state, so severity/confidence are moderate.
The precise attacker trigger requires a terminal buffer in a changed state (bufIsChanged && bt_terminal) with a crafted file name, which is stateful rather than unconditionally reachable.

No out-of-bounds write was found: every vim_snprintf uses size MAXPATHL - len (keeping len <= MAXPATHL-1), and both `*p = '<'` writes (lines 107, 115) land within the string; the mbyte loop (lines 100-102) terminates and never lets i-1 exceed the string length.

verdict.summary: In the control-byte walk of mobi_parse_index_entry, attacker-controlled tagx->tags_count and per-tag control_byte values advance the control_bytes pointer (line 62) without any check against the entry end (buf->maxlen set at line 20) or the underlying buffer, and line 66 dereferences control_bytes[0]. A crafted INDX record placing a short final entry at the end of the buffer and declaring many control bytes drives the read past the heap allocation, causing an out-of-bounds read (info disclosure / crash).

evidence.reason: control_bytes is initialized to buf->data + buf->offset (line 41) and incremented once per tag with control_byte == 1 (line 62) for up to tagx->tags_count attacker-chosen iterations (loop bound, line 60); the only bound ever established for this region is buf->maxlen = buf->offset + entry_length (line 20), and the entry-length guard (line 16) does not constrain the pointer walk. With a 4096-byte record, offsets placing the last entry at offset 4093 with entry_length 2 (passes line 16), label byte 0, and 3 tags (two with control_byte == 1, one with control_byte == 0), line 66 reads data[4096], one byte past the allocation; larger tags_count extends the read arbitrarily past the entry and buffer end. No comparison of control_bytes against the buffer end exists in the shown code.

assumptions: mobi_buffer_get8/get_varlen honor buf->maxlen as the hard read bound and signal an error instead of aborting, so all logical reads are bounded by the entry-length region set at line 20.
buf->maxlen equals the valid extent of buf->data (the invariant every mobi_buffer_* call in the shown code relies on).
The caller bounds curr_number so that offsets[curr_number + 1] is a valid array element, and tagx->tags has at least tags_count elements.
limitations: entry_length underflow (line 7, unsigned size_t subtraction on non-monotonic offsets) and wraparound of the guard sum at line 16 can corrupt buf->maxlen at line 20 with buf->offset already past it; the effect merges into the same control_bytes OOB read and is not needed for the confirmed finding.

strncpy at line 38 could read past text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX] only if the unseen decoders at lines 29/31 return a label length >= INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX; their behavior and the constant's value are not shown, so this is unconfirmed.
Line 7 reads offsets[curr_number + 1] before any in-function bounds check; it depends on the unseen caller bounding curr_number.
NULL derefs of ordt/tagx/buf would require a buggy caller; allocation-size multiplies at lines 52/97 overflow only on 32-bit with a huge tags_count.
The OOB read window is limited to roughly tags_count bytes past the entry; impact assessed as info disclosure and crash, not arbitrary write.

verdict.summary: qf_fill_buffer contains no reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. All dangerous constructs are guarded: the qfp walk is NULL-checked immediately after every advance (lines 71-73) and initialized non-NULL (lines 23, 39-42); qftf_li dereferences are guarded (lines 48, 58, 75); tv_get_string_chk NULL is handled (lines 61-62); the lnum loop is strictly bounded by `lnum < qfl->qf_count` (line 51) with monotonic increment and no underflow; and the only remaining memory operations (qf_buf_add_line, ml_delete) are delegated to unseen, bounds-checked helpers, making any defect there out of scope. No injection, crypto, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: Framework invariant: qfl->qf_start == NULL iff qfl->qf_count == 0, so the line-23 guard implies qf_count >= 1 on entry to the loop.
qf_buf_add_line and ml_delete are assumed to be bounds-checked helper functions that copy their inputs; their internals are not in the shown code.
ml_append-style add semantics: each loop iteration adds one line, leaving the original empty line at position lnum+1, which line 81 then removes.
tv_get_string_chk returns NULL only on a non-convertible typval, and NULL is an accepted default-text input for qf_buf_add_line.
limitations: Potential OOB/use-after-free inside qf_buf_add_line, call_qftf_func, or ml_delete cannot be confirmed because those operations are not implemented in the shown code (out of scope per the pure-pass-through rule).
If qf_buf_add_line triggers autocommands that mutate the quickfix list during the loop, qfp/qftf_li could dangle; this is not demonstrable from the shown code.
Integer overflow of (lnum + 1) at line 46 requires a quickfix list of ~2^63 lines, which is not attacker-reachable under memory limits.
The delete-all loop (lines 18-19) would hang only if ml_delete repeatedly failed at the memfile layer, which is not attacker-controlled input.
Inconsistent qfl->qf_count vs. actual list length is handled by the NULL break at lines 72-73 and the FAIL break at line 66, so it produces only early termination, not memory unsafety.
Displaying user-supplied quickfix text in the quickfix buffer is by design and carries no injection sink in this function.

verdict.summary: The classic alt_num case-fold expansion overflow/blowup pattern is present but fully guarded: line 55 multiplies alt_num by (n+1) and line 56 breaks once alt_num > THRESHOLD_CASE_FOLD_ALT_FOR_EXPANSION (8). Since the encoder contract bounds n by the items array size (ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM, line 8) so n+1 <= 4, the largest value line 55 can produce before the check is 8*4 = 32, far below INT_MAX, so signed overflow cannot bypass the cap; at most 2-3 characters are expanded (~64 nodes) and the remaining tail is folded into a single node (lines 96-120), keeping total work linear in the input length. All heap-node allocations in the shown code are null-checked. No attacker-controlled value reaches a dangerous operation in the shown code without a sufficient bound, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_BY_STR writes at most ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM items (the size of the items array at line 8), so n in the n>0 branch is <= 3 and n+1 <= 4.
The pattern parser validates encoding before building STR nodes, so enclen(enc, p) <= end - p for every p reached in the loop and len >= 1.
int is 32-bit, so the safe maximum observed by the line 56 check is 8*4 = 32.
limitations: Line 55's alt_num accumulation would become exploitable only if some encoder/helper returned n >= ~2^28 (violating the items-array API contract), letting a single multiplication wrap alt_num to <= 8 and defeat the line 56 guard; the shown code cannot produce such an n, so this is not a confirmed finding.

Line 51's onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) could over-read if enclen ever returned a length exceeding the remaining bytes (truncated multibyte tail); reachability depends on the unseen parser's validation, so no concrete witness exists in the shown code.

If enclen returned 0 for some byte, p += len (line 93) would never advance and the loop would not terminate; oniguruma encodings return >= 1 and upstream validation prevents it, so this is unconfirmed here.
Memory-safety defects inside expand_case_fold_string_alt (line 66) and expand_case_fold_make_rem_string (line 99) are not in the shown code (pure delegation), so they are out of scope.
This excerpt matches the post-CVE-2020-26159 fixed form; the historical pre-fix code that lacked the line 56 threshold is not the code under analysis.

verdict.summary: mobi_parse_index_entry walks the entry control bytes with an unbounded pointer: control_bytes is advanced once per attacker-controlled tag with control_byte==1 (line 66) inside a loop bounded only by the file-controlled tags_count (line 64), with no check against control_byte_count or the record buffer size, so a crafted MOBI can drive control_bytes[0] (line 70) far past the heap record allocation — a heap out-of-bounds read causing crash/DoS and potential information disclosure.

evidence.reason: control_bytes is set to buf->data + buf->offset (line 45) and incremented (line 66) for every tag whose file-controlled control_byte equals 1, inside a loop whose bound is only the file-controlled tagx->tags_count (line 64). No guard anywhere in the shown code limits the number of increments to tagx->control_byte_count or to the buffer allocation size (buf->maxlen), so with a crafted MOBI whose TAGX record lists 8191 leading tags with control_byte==1 followed by one tag with control_byte==0 in a 4 KiB INDX record, control_bytes points ~7 KB past the heap record when line 70 dereferences control_bytes[0] — a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: The caller allocates idxt.offsets with at least entries_count+1 elements, so offsets[curr_number+1] (line 7) is in bounds.
The caller allocates indx->entries with total_entries_count elements, so entries[entry_number] is in bounds after the line 10 guard.
tagx->tags points to an array of tagx->tags_count elements allocated from the TAGX record.
buf->data/buf->maxlen reflect the heap record allocation, so reads at data+maxlen or beyond are out of bounds.
INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX >= 255, so the initial label_length (0-255) does not exceed the text buffer.
limitations: Stack OOB read at line 42 (strncpy reading label_length+1 bytes from text) cannot be confirmed: the shown code does not establish that mobi_getstring_ordt or mobi_indx_get_label can return a length above INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX, and the writes into text occur inside those unseen helpers.

Unsigned underflow of entry_length at line 7 (offsets[curr_number+1] < offsets[curr_number]) can bypass the line 16 guard via size_t wrap, but the resulting smaller buf->maxlen does not demonstrably lead to an OOB read/write in the shown code.

value_count * tag_value_count (line 114) can overflow uint32, but the INDX_TAGVALUES_MAX cap makes this only reduce iterations; the inner loops (lines 115-127) are guaranteed to terminate because tagvalues_count increments every iteration.
Casting tagx->control_byte_count to int at line 46 could become negative for counts above INT_MAX, but the seek is performed by the unseen mobi_buffer_seek, so any impact is unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: qh_help does not contain a confirmed vulnerability. The attacker-controlled buffer 'buf' is used only as a %s argument to nsock_printf* calls whose format strings are compile-time literals, so no format-string, injection, or out-of-bounds flaw is reachable in the shown code; the 'len' parameter is unused.

assumptions: The nsock_printf* family behaves like standard printf-family functions, interpreting only the format string and treating additional arguments strictly as data.
qhandlers and qh_find_handler return valid, non-cyclic handler structures as framework-internal invariants.
limitations: If nsock_printf* deviated from printf-family semantics (e.g., treating variadic data as format text), a format-string issue could arise, but no such behavior is shown and it is not assumed.
The handler invoked at line 22 is not shown; any vulnerability inside an unseen handler's implementation is out of scope for this snippet.
The unused 'len' parameter could be a latent trust-boundary concern if a caller expected it to bound 'buf', but no such bound is enforced or used in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in `size = bytes_per_line * hh` (line 87): width/height are read from the attacker-controlled file via `sscanf` and cast to guint with no upper bound (only the zero check at line 77). A crafted XBM with width=2147483647 and height=15 makes the 32-bit product wrap to 0xF0000000, which is stored as a negative int and passed to `g_malloc` (line 88) as ~4 GiB; GLib aborts the process when the allocation fails, giving an attacker-controlled crash/DoS. The fill loops themselves are not exploitable for an overwrite because bytes_per_line is provably always even (so size is even and both loops write exactly size bytes).

evidence.reason: ww and hh are attacker-controlled: they are parsed with `sscanf (line,"#define %s %d",name_and_type,&value)` from file bytes read by `fgets` (line 30) and cast to guint at lines 41/43. bytes_per_line (line 85) and the product at line 87 are computed in 32-bit arithmetic; the only guard, `if (!ww || !hh)` (line 77), rejects only zero and admits the witness. Witness: width=2147483647 gives bytes_per_line=0x10000000, height=15 makes the product truncate to bit pattern 0xF0000000, stored as negative int and passed to g_malloc as gsize≈4026531840, which fails and terminates the process via GLib's fatal allocation error — a single crafted file causes a crash (DoS) and the allocation no longer matches the declared dimensions.

assumptions: fstream content is attacker-controlled (user-supplied XBM image file).
int/guint are 32-bit, so the product at line 87 truncates modulo 2^32 and a high-bit pattern becomes a negative int.
g_malloc terminates the process via g_error when the requested allocation fails, per GLib semantics.
MAX_SIZE is a compile-time constant (256 in the original GIMP source).
limitations: The classic heap-buffer-overflow consequence of this overflow is NOT confirmed in the shown code: (ww+7)/8+padding is always even for every ww in [0, 2^31-1] (parity argument: r=ww%16 gives 2k+2, 2k+2, or 2k for r∈[1,8], r∈[9,15], r=0 respectively), so size is always even and both fill loops write at most exactly `size` bytes, matching g_malloc(size). No out-of-bounds write witness exists.
An odd `size` (which would make the version10p loop write one byte past the end, e.g., ww=17, hh=3) is unreachable: padding makes bytes_per_line even, giving size=12 for that witness.
A caller-side out-of-bounds read (huge published width/height at lines 117-119 with an undersized `data`) is out of scope because the decoding operation is not in the shown code.
In the version10p padding case (ww%16 in 1..8) the high byte is skipped (line 98-99), leaving uninitialized g_malloc bytes as image data; no demonstrated security impact.
Hotspot parsing can decrement `type` to name_and_type-1 (lines 45-46) but that pointer is never dereferenced afterwards.
The unbounded %s into name_and_type is safe: the truncation guard (lines 31-32) admits only lines of length <= MAX_SIZE-2, so token+NUL cannot exceed the buffer.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar: the CP950 PUA lookup loop (lines 51-55) can exit without a match, leaving k equal to the row count N, and line 57 unconditionally dereferences cp950_pua_tbl[k] one row past the end of the static table. k and the (c1, c) pair derive from attacker-controlled input bytes (lines 1, 20, 30), so a crafted CP950 byte sequence triggers an over-read that can leak adjacent memory or crash the process.

evidence.reason: k is the loop index from lines 51-55; when no row satisfies the membership test at line 52 (the guard at lines 45-49 admits ~6,500 (c1,c) pairs, e.g. c1=0xC6 with any c in 0xA1..0xFE via line 49, while table rows cover only finite intervals), the loop exits with k == sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4) == N. No post-loop `k < N` check exists in the shown code, so this dereference of cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] reads one row past the array end. c1 comes from filter->cache (line 30), set from an attacker-controlled lead byte at line 20, and c is the attacker-controlled current byte (line 1), making the over-read triggerable by crafted input (CWE-125: information disclosure / DoS).

assumptions: c is a single input byte (0..255); the conversion engine invokes this filter once per byte of the decoded text.

verdict.summary: Not vulnerable as shown. The allocation-size arithmetic is done in u64 (`u64 elem_size` plus the explicit `(u64)` cast of `smap->map.value_size`), so `elem_size * smap->map.max_entries` cannot wrap for any u32 value_size/max_entries (max product `(C + 2^32-1)*(2^32-1) < 2^64`); a product too large to satisfy makes `bpf_map_area_alloc` return NULL, which the check at line 9 converts to a clean -ENOMEM, and the freelist-populate count/stride match the allocated size exactly. No memory-safety, injection, crypto, or access-control flaw is confirmable in the shown code; the only residual concern (u32 stride/offset arithmetic inside the unseen `pcpu_freelist_populate` for >4 GiB allocations) is delegated to code not shown and is recorded as a limitation without a CWE.

assumptions: `smap->map.value_size` and `smap->map.max_entries` originate from the `BPF_MAP_CREATE` bpf() syscall attributes (attacker-influenced) and are u32.
The unseen caller `stack_map_alloc` enforces `value_size` in {0, 8} and `max_entries > 0` with memory charging, keeping `elem_size` small in practice.
On 64-bit builds, `bpf_map_area_alloc`'s size parameter does not narrow the u64 product.
limitations: If `elem_size` could exceed u32 (e.g., an unbounded `value_size`), the implicit u64->u32 narrowing at the `pcpu_freelist_populate` boundary and the u32 `i * size` offset arithmetic inside that unseen helper could wrap and point the freelist at wrong addresses; the write loop itself is not in the shown code, so this is delegated and unconfirmed (no CWE).

On 32-bit builds the u64 product would be narrowed to size_t at the `bpf_map_area_alloc` boundary; this build is not demonstrated, and the caller-side `value_size` invariant keeps `elem_size` far below u32 wrap.
Memory-exhaustion DoS by a very large `max_entries` is bounded by the NULL check / -ENOMEM path in the shown code and by caller charge limits; the shown code contains no attacker-scaled loop.

verdict.summary: tipc_crypto_key_rcv() copies an attacker-controlled keylen (u32 from packet bytes at line 24) into a kmalloc(size) buffer at lines 26-27 before the size sanity check at line 30, permitting a remote heap out-of-bounds write (and out-of-bounds read) from a TIPC key-exchange message.

The destination skey->key starts at offset TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32) = 36 in an object allocated with only size bytes at line 17 (u16 msg_data_sz, max 65535, unvalidated); the writable region is size-36 bytes. The only guard, line 30 (size == tipc_aead_key_size(skey)), executes after this memcpy and cannot prevent the overflow. Witness: size=36, keylen=5 passes line 10 and kmalloc(36), then this memcpy writes 5 bytes at offset 36, overflowing the 36-byte object; keylen=0xFFFFFFFF yields a near-4GB write. Confirmed CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME is 32 and struct tipc_aead_key lays out keylen (4 bytes), alg_name[32], and a trailing flexible key[] array, so skey->key begins at offset 36 as implied by the code's use of data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32).
hdr arrives from the TIPC network receive path, so key_gen, size, data, and keylen are attacker-influenced; no caller-side validation of msg_data_sz is shown or assumed.
limitations: Packet-payload out-of-bounds reads (line 24 requires size>=36, line 25 requires size>=32, and the line 26 source read requires size>=36+keylen) are not separately enumerated as findings; they share the same unvalidated-length root cause as the confirmed CWE-787.
tipc_aead_key_size(skey) can overflow int for keylen > 0x7FFFFFFB, but that only affects the post-copy check and is not an independent reachable failure.
kmalloc failure at line 18 is handled cleanly and is not a finding.

verdict.summary: write_entry stores the return of make_key() into keylen without validating it against the 1025-byte stack buffer `key`, then passes (key, keylen) to cyrusdb_delete()/cyrusdb_store() (and read_old_value()). When attacker-influenced mboxname/entry/userid lengths make the serialized key exceed sizeof(key), make_key truncates the buffer but keylen is still oversized (or negative), so the DB layer reads past the end of `key` - an out-of-bounds read that can crash the server or corrupt/confuse annotation keys.

evidence.snippet: r = cyrusdb_store(d->db, key, keylen, data.s, data.len, tid(d));
evidence.reason: keylen is produced by make_key() at line 26 from attacker-influenced mboxname/uid/entry/userid into the 1025-byte `key` buffer (line 12); no shown statement between lines 26 and 93 constrains keylen (no keylen < 0 and no keylen <= sizeof(key) check). With a mailbox name near MAX_MAILBOX_PATH plus any entry/userid, the serialized key exceeds 1025 bytes, make_key truncates the buffer and returns a length >= sizeof(key) (or a negative error), and cyrusdb_store() reads keylen bytes from `key`, reading past the end of the stack buffer. The same unvalidated keylen also reaches read_old_value() at line 30 and cyrusdb_delete() at line 68.

The same unvalidated keylen from line 26 reaches cyrusdb_delete() on the deletion path (value->len == 0 && uid == 0); an oversized or negative keylen makes the DB layer read beyond the 1025-byte `key` stack buffer (CWE-125), enabling a crash/denial of service.

assumptions: make_key writes at most sizeof(key) bytes into `key` (truncates rather than overflows the buffer) and reports the produced/needed length (or a negative error code) via its int return.
struct buf invariants hold in normal operation: value->s and oldval.s are non-NULL whenever ->len > 0.
mailbox->name is bounded by the caller (MAX_MAILBOX_PATH); entry/userid lengths are bounded only by unseen protocol/API-level checks.
The CYRUSDB_AGAIN retry loops (lines 67-69, 92-94) terminate because the helper returns CYRUSDB_AGAIN only transiently.
limitations: Quota diff at line 39 performs unsigned arithmetic when oldval.len > value->len (wrap to ~2^64 before conversion to quota_t); the resulting sign/accounting behavior depends on unseen mailbox_quota_check/update code, so it is not confirmed as an exploitable quota bypass.
memcmp at line 34 dereferences value->s when value->len > 0; a NULL value->s with len > 0 would crash, but that requires an unseen caller to violate the buf invariant.

The NULL-userid guard at line 83 is skipped for empty values (tombstone path at line 74), writing a tombstone key with an empty userid component; requires an unseen caller to pass NULL userid for a message annotation and is a data-integrity concern only.
The maywrite check (lines 43-46) runs only on the mailbox path; prefix/server annotations (mailbox == NULL) rely on authorization performed by the unseen caller.
DEBUG-only syslog calls at lines 63/88 log value->s and key_as_string() output without neutralization; log-injection risk exists only in debug builds.

verdict.summary: No confirmed in-scope vulnerability. The argument-copy loop (lines 8-9) is bounded by the reservation at line 6 (nparams+3 >= nparams items actually written), the guard at line 4 fully covers _thread(o) use, and sq_call's params matches the exactly nparams items pushed. The only failure mode for the reservation is an allocation (OOM) failure caused by the discarded sq_reservestack return, which is an unchecked-allocation robustness concern routed to limitations.

assumptions: Squirrel thread stacks grow on demand: sq_reservestack grows via GrowStack, so on the normal path the reserved bound nparams+3 covers the nparams items pushed at lines 7-9.
sq_call(v, params, ...) counts params as this + arguments, and sq_gettop(v) >= 1 while this native executes because the VM frame always references the callee/this at relative index 1.
nparams is bounded by the caller VM's actually allocated stack capacity, so SQInteger overflow of nparams+3 is unreachable.
limitations: Line 6 discards the sq_reservestack return value; if GrowStack/sq_vm_malloc fails, lines 7-9 write into an unreserved target stack. No concrete witness exists without allocator failure, so this is treated as an unchecked-allocation robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.
Integer overflow of nparams+3 and of the loop index is theoretically possible but unreachable because nparams cannot exceed an allocated VM stack.
Reentrancy (o == the running VM, i.e. _thread(o) == v) is not reachable through the standard-library API visible in the shown code, so a self-corruption scenario is not confirmed.

sq_move(v,_thread(o),-1) (line 11) and the _lasterror assignment (line 15) rely on framework invariants (result on target top after SQ_TRUE retval; refcounted copy) that the shown code does not break.

If a Squirrel variant caps thread-stack growth at creation size, the unchecked reservation at line 6 would become an attacker-controlled stack overflow; that variant-dependent invariant is not established by the shown code.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmed in nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev. The function receives only trusted framework-internal state (priv and its registration-time fields), contains no injection, crypto, or access-control sinks, and its memory operations are ordered so that every dereference of priv->ndev / nfc_dev (lines 3, 6) precedes the sole releases (nci_free_device at line 14, kfree(priv) at line 15), with no dereference after a release. The dangerous-looking deref chain is protected by this visible lifetime ordering plus the NCI API contract visible in the same function, in which nci_unregister_device detaches the device and nci_free_device releases it.

assumptions: priv is a live nfcmrvl_private object on entry; nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev is reachable only on the unregister/remove path after successful registration, so priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev are non-NULL and point to live objects.

Per the NCI API pairing visible in the shown code, nci_unregister_device(ndev) (line 5) detaches ndev from the NFC subsystem but does not release ndev or nfc_dev memory; the sole releases are nci_free_device(ndev) (line 14) and kfree(priv) (line 15).
priv->config.reset_n_io is probe-time configuration from trusted device-tree/platform data, not attacker-controlled.
limitations: A use-after-free of priv->ndev->nfc_dev at line 6 would require nci_unregister_device's unseen body to free those objects; no shown code frees them before line 6, and the shown pairing with nci_free_device at line 14 indicates release happens later, so this is not confirmable from the shown code (no CWE attached).

A NULL-pointer dereference at line 6 would require priv, priv->ndev, or nfc_dev to be NULL; the shown code contains no NULL-producing path, so this is an out-of-scope caller-invariant concern (no CWE attached).
Calling nci_unregister_device before nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort/deinit (lines 5-9) is a potential robustness/ordering concern, but no security impact is demonstrable in the shown code.
A double free of ndev or priv would require an unseen caller to release the same object again; not supported by the shown path.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerabilities: attacker-controlled buf reaches only %s arguments of fixed literal format strings (lines 25, 29), there are no memory-writing operations, and the only dereference of qh is fully guarded by the NULL check at line 23.

assumptions: buf is NUL-terminated by the caller; all reads via !*buf and strcmp at lines 5, 12, and 22 rely on that contract.
Registered handlers (qh->name, qh->description, qh->handler) are non-NULL trusted data installed by registration code; qhandlers is a finite acyclic list.

Not confirmable from the shown code because the buffer is not constructed here.
