verdict.summary: The STUN parser writes attacker-chosen pointers past the fixed-size msg->attr[] array: msg->attr_count is incremented per attribute (line 61) and used to index msg->attr[...] (line 36) with no capacity check, so an attacker sending many small attributes (e.g., 25 zero-length attrs in a 120-byte message, up to ~16384 attrs in a 65535-byte message) triggers an out-of-bounds write at line 40. Additionally, header fields (lines 10/25) and the attribute length field (line 41) are read before any buffer-length validation, enabling 1-2 byte out-of-bounds reads (e.g., buf_len=2 or a message whose attribute area is 3 bytes).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds pointer write: msg->attr_count (attacker-controlled via header length at line 25 and per-attribute length at line 41, incremented at line 61) indexes msg->attr[...] at line 36, and this write executes before the line 44 guard. There is no check bounding attr_count against the fixed array capacity; the line 26 and line 44 guards bound only byte consumption (len <= msg_len), admitting arbitrarily many 4-byte attributes. Witness: buf_len=120, msg_len=100, 25 attributes of length 0 write indices 0..24; up to 16384 writes reaching index 16383 are possible (msg_len=65535).

Out-of-bounds read before validation: the 2-byte length field at p_attr+2..p_attr+3 is read before the guard at line 44, so a loop entry with msg_len=3 (buf_len=23, header length field=3) reads one byte past the 23-byte buffer. The same late-validation pattern affects the header: with buf_len=2, line 25 reads msg->hdr->length at offsets 2..3 of a 2-byte buffer before the line 26 check (which then rejects via unsigned underflow). Triggering values are attacker-controlled network message lengths (lines 25, 41).

assumptions: msg->attr is a fixed-size array in the pjstun_msg structure (e.g., PJSTUN_MAX_ATTR_COUNT entries), which is why indexing it without a capacity check at lines 36/40 is an overflow for any practical capacity < 16384.
The caller passes attacker-received datagram bytes and the actual received length as buf/buf_len, which is the standard usage of this parser on network input.
limitations: The exact capacity of msg->attr[] is defined in an unseen struct, but per the OOB rule an attacker-controlled index reaching a memory operation in the shown code with an absent check is a finding regardless.

The OOB header reads (lines 10/25) only trigger for buf_len <= 3 because for buf_len >= 4 the header bytes fit and the line 26 underflow comparison safely rejects shorter buffers afterward; impact is a 1-2 byte over-read.
Unaligned struct-pointer casts of byte buffers (lines 9, 33, 40) are undefined behavior on strict-alignment platforms; not scored as a confirmed finding.
Log sinks use constant format strings with integer arguments, so no format-string or log-injection risk.
The loop always terminates (len >= 4, msg_len strictly decreases); no hang/DoS finding.
A caller that separately guarantees buf_len >= 20 before calling would eliminate the header over-read trigger but not the unbounded attr_count write.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in inbound_cap_ls: the attacker-controlled CAP LS extension list is split without limit and every whitelisted token is appended with unbounded strcat into the 256-byte stack buffer. 19 repeated 'multi-prefix' tokens overflow the buffer (first out-of-bounds write, a NUL at index 256, occurs on the 19th append at line 30), and the overrun grows with the token count, enabling a malicious IRC server to crash or corrupt the client.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled extensions_str is split without a token limit at line 15 and iterated at line 19; each token equal to "multi-prefix" passes the equality-only guard at line 28 and appends the 13-byte literal at line 30. buffer is fixed at 256 bytes (line 4) and starts at length 9 (line 17). After 19 matching tokens the 19th strcat writes a NUL at index 256, one byte past the array, and the loop (line 19) does not stop, so further tokens keep writing out of bounds. Witness: extensions_str = "multi-prefix " x 19.

assumptions: extensions_str originates from the remote IRC server's CAP LS payload, making it attacker-controlled network data.
g_strsplit with max_tokens=0 returns a NULL-terminated vector containing every space-separated token with no count cap.
A normal IRC line can carry the ~247-byte payload needed for the first out-of-bounds write, so message-length limits, if any exist in the caller, do not prevent the overflow.
limitations: EMIT_SIGNAL_TIMESTAMP internals are not shown, so any downstream handling of the emitted strings is out of scope.
tcp_sendf at line 93 uses a literal "%s\r\n" format string; buffer is passed as data, so no format-string injection finding applies.
No regex, crypto, or file/access-control sinks exist in the shown code, so no ReDoS, weak-crypto, or file-handling findings apply.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in load_buffer's beach: cleanup path: obj is initialized to NULL (line 11) and every branch that jumps to beach (line 15 on a NULL prelink_range from get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0, line 21, line 31, line 41) leaves it NULL, yet line 67 unconditionally executes obj->cache_buf = NULL, crashing the process when an attacker-supplied Mach-O triggers the prelink-info lookup failure.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled file bytes reach get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 (line 13); when the helper returns NULL for a crafted Mach-O, the guard at line 14 admits the NULL value via goto beach (line 15) while obj is still NULL (line 11). No subsequent check verifies obj != NULL before line 67 dereferences it, so the write obj->cache_buf = NULL executes on a NULL pointer, causing a crash (CWE-476). The same NULL dereference is reached on the failure branches at lines 21, 31, and 41, which either leave obj NULL or R_FREE it to NULL before jumping to beach.

assumptions: radare2's R_FREE macro frees the pointer and sets it to NULL, which is why obj is NULL on the beach paths at lines 31 and 41.

get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 can return NULL for malformed/attacker-chosen input (its internals are not shown, but the shown code explicitly handles the NULL return, and a NULL return is induced by file contents, not by an errant caller).
r_buf_ref does not fail in a way that matters here; the early-return leak at lines 5-8 is non-compounding.
limitations: The early return at lines 6-8 when MACH0_(new_buf) fails leaks the fbuf reference taken at line 2; this is a single-shot leak that does not compound with attacker-controlled volume, so it is not a finding.

The allocation-failure path (lines 19-22, R_NEW0) also reaches the NULL dereference at line 67, but allocation failure without attacker control of the allocation size is not treated as a separate finding.
Memory-safety issues inside the helper functions (MACH0_(new_buf), get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0, r_cf_value_dict_parse, swizzle_io_read) are outside the shown code and are not assessed.

verdict.summary: Pattern-effect cell values (`pat->data[i][index]`, i.e. module-file data) are used unvalidated as indices into the `fxColors`/`extFxColors` color palettes. Line 200 executes `fxColors[data]` for every value `<0x10`, including negatives other than the -1 sentinel (e.g. -2, read before the palette); line 218 executes `extFxColors[data-0xe0]` for every value `>=0xe0` with no upper bound (e.g. `data=0x100` gives index `0x20`, one past a 32-entry palette). The only guards are the `==-1` sentinel and the value-band chain (lines 194, 199-217), which neither establish a low bound nor a high bound for the index, so the reads are out of bounds (CWE-125), causing a crash or reading adjacent static memory into the renderer.

evidence.reason: Taint: `pat->data[i][index]` is an attacker-controlled pattern-cell value from the module file. The shown guards (line 194 `==-1`, and the `<0x10 ... <0xe0` bands at lines 199-217) only exclude the -1 sentinel and band values; the final `else` admits every value `>=0xe0` with no upper bound. A cell value `0x100` passes the chain and reaches this sink, computing index `0x100-0xe0=0x20`, out of bounds for a 32-entry `extFxColors` palette (and any value > 0x11F is progressively farther OOB). The out-of-bounds read target/garbage is then used to index `uiColors` in the same statement, i.e. a second OOB read feeding `ImGui::PushStyleColor`.

Same taint source: `pat->data[i][index]` from module-file data. The guard immediately above (line 199 `pat->data[i][index]<0x10`) admits every negative value besides the -1 sentinel; a cell value of -2 passes line 194 (`==-1` fails) and line 199, executing `fxColors[-2]`, an out-of-bounds read before the 16-entry palette. There is no lower-bound check on the index in the shown code (contrast the instrument guard at lines 120-121 and the volume clamp at lines 158-160).

assumptions: `fxColors` and `extFxColors` are the standard fixed-size rendering palettes of this codebase (16 and 32 entries respectively), matching the 0x00-0x0F and 0xE0-0xFF bands used by the surrounding guards; the negative-index and >=0x20-index bounds follow from those assumed table sizes.

`pat->data[i][col]` cells originate from a module file loaded from disk (attacker-controlled contents when opening untrusted songs), and the shown code reads them without range validation apart from the sentinel/branch checks cited.

Supporting invariants relied on for the non-findings: `pat[i]` rows are allocated with `e->song.patLen` rows; each pattern row has exactly `4 + 2*effectRows` columns matching `e->song.pat[j].effectRows`; `chanShow`/`chanCollapse` are sized consistently with `chans`; `volColors` has at least 128 entries.
limitations: `patChanX[chans]` (line 274) is an unconditional member-array write at index `chans` with no capacity check, but the capacity of `patChanX` is not shown and the trailing-column write suggests the array is sized `chans+1` by design, so no concrete failing witness is available.

`sprintf` into `static char id[32]` (lines 87, 118, 130, 155, 161, 195, 198, 243, 245): with realistic bounds (patLen <= 65536, chans <= 128, effectRows <= 128, noteName <= 5 chars) the longest output is ~27 bytes; overflow would additionally require ~10-digit `i`/`j` values and a longer `noteName`, so this is unconfirmed.

NULL dereferences of `patCache[j]` (line 72) and `e->song.ins[pat->data[i][2]]->type` (line 123, whose index is range-guarded at 120-121): nullness would have to be produced by an unseen caller/loader, which is out of scope per the analysis rules.
`noteName()` internals (indexing note-label tables with unvalidated note-cell values) are not part of the shown code, so any OOB inside it is out of scope.

If `e->song.pat[j].effectRows` ever differed from the actual column allocation of `patCache[j]->data`, the reads `pat->data[i][index]`/`[index+1]` inside the k-loop (lines 195-246) would be OOB; that mismatch is unconfirmed and violates the assumed invariant.
No injection, weak-crypto, or algorithmic-complexity concerns are present: format strings are literals, there is no regex, and both loops always terminate.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg performs out-of-bounds reads because it dereferences the STUN header and the 4-byte per-attribute header without first validating the remaining buffer length. With msg_len in {1,2,3} (a 21-23 byte datagram admitted by the equality check at line 27), the loop condition `msg_len > 0` at line 36 permits an iteration whose `(*attr)->length` read at line 42 extends up to 3 bytes past the end of buf; the post-read check at line 45 cannot prevent it. A second instance of the same missing-minimum-length root cause reads `msg->hdr->type` at line 11 before any size check, so buf_len < 4 also over-reads. No data is written or disclosed by the shown code and crash requires crossing a page boundary.

evidence.reason: msg_len is attacker-controlled via the STUN header length field (line 26) and is the exact remaining byte count after the header, since line 27 admits every value satisfying msg_len == buf_len - 20 including 1, 2, and 3. The loop condition at line 36 (`msg_len > 0`) admits those values, but reading `(*attr)->length` dereferences p_attr+2..p_attr+3 and needs 4 remaining bytes. With a 21-byte BINDING_REQUEST (msg_len=1), the read lands 2 bytes past the end of buf (1 byte past for msg_len=2, 2 for msg_len=3). The `msg_len < len` guard at line 45 runs only after the read and always errors for msg_len<4 because len>=4, so it cannot protect the sink. Confirmed out-of-bounds read, CWE-125.

buf_len is the caller-supplied network datagram length and no size check precedes this dereference: with buf_len in {0,1} the 2-byte read of msg->hdr->type at buf[0..1] is out of bounds by 2 or 1 byte(s). The only length guard (line 27) executes later on the same path and, via unsigned subtraction, protects only subsequent code, so this sink is unconstrained in the shown code. Same missing-minimum-length root cause as the attribute-header read, CWE-125.

assumptions: buf and msg are non-NULL by caller contract; buf_len is the exact size of the readable region of buf (parameter trust).
pjstun_msg_hdr is 20 bytes and pjstun_attr_hdr is 4 bytes with type at offset 0 and length at offset 2, per the sizeof/cast usage shown.
limitations: For msg_len in {1,2,3}, the OOB bytes only feed the len computation and the parser always returns PJLIB_UTIL_ESTUNINATTRLEN; there is no attacker-observable disclosure or memory write in the shown code, and a crash requires the over-read to cross an unmapped page.
All PJ_LOG calls use literal format strings with numeric arguments, so no format-string or log-injection finding applies.
No exec, SQL, path, file, or crypto sinks appear in the shown code; the u16 narrowing at line 60 is guarded (len <= msg_len) and value-preserving.

verdict.summary: fiber_switch copies len values from the caller-supplied argument array a into the target fiber stack with no check that a actually holds len elements. The length len (and the pointer a) are function parameters whose provenance is the VM's Fiber#resume/transfer argument handling; the only validation in the shown code is the unrelated c->ci->proc guard (lines 32-34), and the stack extension on line 35 bounds only the destination. An attacker-influenced len larger than the real size of a causes an out-of-bounds read at line 39 (while (b<e) { *b++ = *a++; }), which can crash the interpreter or leak memory.

evidence.reason: Line 39 dereferences *a in a loop that executes exactly len times (bound set by e = b + len on line 37), but no shown check validates len against the number of valid elements in a, and no guard (status switch 10-25, c->ci->proc check 32-34) restricts len. mrb_stack_extend on line 35 bounds only the destination b/stbase+1, not the source a. Caller-supplied len=10 with a buffer holding fewer values reads a[1..9] out of bounds at this sink (CWE-125).

assumptions: fiber_check (line 3) and fiber_check_cfunc (line 8) validate the fiber object and context state.
mrb_stack_extend (line 35) guarantees stend >= ci->stack + len + 2, and for a created fiber ci->stack == stbase, making the destination writes at stbase[1..len] in-bounds.
fiber_switch_context (line 28) correctly makes c the current context and preserves a (pointing into the old context).
Canonical VM callers normally pass len equal to the number of elements at a; this does not remove the in-scope absent check per the analysis rules.
limitations: The write side of the copy (stbase[1..len]) is excluded from the finding because its protecting check, mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) at line 35, is present; a write overflow would require the unshown helper contract or creation-time ci->stack invariant to fail.
Negative len skips the loop (e < b); only c->cibase->n becomes negative (line 44), with no memory impact in the shown code.
len+2 arithmetic overflow (len near MRB_INT_MAX) is not a finding because an argument array that large is infeasible through the VM path.
Callinfo bounds for c->ci-- (line 42) and c->ci[1].stack[0] (line 50) depend on unshown mruby callinfo-layout invariants and were not confirmed.
No injection (format string, exec, SQL, log/header), weak-crypto, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The shown glue function performs no memory, injection, crypto, or access-control operation on attacker-controlled data. Every pointer it dereferences (main_mach0, prelink_range, obj, pending_bin_files) is NULL-checked on the shown path with the excluded set exactly {NULL}, all prelink_range reads precede its free, and no loop exists. The only attacker-derived values (filetype, range offset/size, pa2va_* fields, chained_starts) are passed unchanged into unseen helpers (r_cf_value_dict_parse, swizzle_io_read), which is a pure pass-through absent from the shown code and therefore out of scope.

assumptions: bf, bin_obj, and buf are framework-supplied and valid (RBinFile/RBuffer invariants); the shown code contains no checks for them, and no attacker path controls them.
Helper functions preserve the refcount contract: r_buf_ref (line 2) is balanced by r_buf_free (66) or by obj->cache_buf ownership (48).
unseen helpers are assumed not to perform undefined behavior on their own; any such behavior is outside the shown code.
limitations: Attacker-controlled Mach-O fields flow to unseen functions: prelink_range->range.offset/size into r_cf_value_dict_parse (lines 26-27) and pa2va_exec/pa2va_data plus chained_starts into swizzle_io_read (lines 49-50, 58-60), with no bounds validation shown; those are pass-throughs to unseen parse/read code, so any memory-safety issue there cannot be confirmed from the shown code (no CWE).

Line 7 returns without r_buf_free(fbuf), leaking the line-2 ref; rebase_info is not freed on failure paths (lines 14/18/25/35). These are single-shot leaks with no attacker-controlled repetition in the shown code.
An OOM in r_buf_ref or allocations producing NULL is not attacker-controlled and does not reach a shown dangerous sink.
No loop is present, so loop-bound, index-vs-size, and read-position analyses do not apply.

verdict.summary: The fastrpc_dma_buf_attach callback receives only framework-internal dma_buf/dma_buf_attachment objects and reads driver-initialized fields (dev, virt, phys, size, lock) from dmabuf->priv. All mutations are constant-size allocations, a checked dma_get_sgtable call (error path returns -EINVAL and frees the allocation), a static-format dev_err, and a mutex-protected list_add. No attacker-controlled value reaches any memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink, so no vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code.

assumptions: dmabuf->priv always points to a valid, initialized struct fastrpc_buf set by the driver when the dma_buf was created/exported.
dmabuf and attachment are framework-managed objects supplied by the DMA-buf subsystem, not directly by userspace.
FASTRPC_PHYS() only translates the driver's internal phys field and does not introduce attacker data.
limitations: If an unseen caller could supply dmabuf->priv == NULL, line 5 would dereference NULL; the shown code never produces that state, so it is out of scope.
buffer->size and buffer->virt are passed to dma_get_sgtable without re-validation, but they originate in driver internals and no attacker influence reaches them in the shown code.
No loop exists here, so unbounded-iteration/algorithmic-complexity concerns do not apply to this function.

verdict.summary: EvalGatherNd validates gather indices only for negativity (lines 6-12) before dispatching them unchanged to the GatherNd kernels (line 16). Indices equal to or larger than a params dimension pass the check and yield a flat offset past the params buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap read in the gather kernel; an adversarial TFLite model controls these values.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled indices from the model tensor (read at line 4) reach this dispatch unvalidated: the guard at line 7 / line 12 admits every value >= 0, e.g. index value 2 for a params dimension of size 2, with no upper-bound comparison against params->dims anywhere on the shown path. The dispatched kernel then computes the flat offset from that index and reads params memory beyond the buffer (CWE-125 OOB read); the smallest passing-but-failing witness is any index == dim size or larger.

assumptions: TFLite's invariant that indices->bytes matches the allocated indices buffer makes the validation-loop read at line 7 in-bounds.
The threat model is a crafted/adversarial TFLite model, so the indices tensor contents and shapes are attacker-controlled.
IndicesT is a signed integer type, making the '< 0' comparison meaningful.
limitations: The faulting memory instruction itself is inside the unshown templated GatherNd/GatherNdString kernels; if those kernels independently confine indices to the params dimensions, the OOB would not materialize, but the shown code provides no such bound.
The negative-index failure mode is already contained by the present sign check; only the missing upper-bound validation is the residual issue.
If IndicesT were an unsigned type, the '< 0' check would be vacuous; this is a robustness concern, not an independent finding, since negative values are then unrepresentable.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader guards the header reads with `length < sizeof(bh)`, which compares against the size of the pointer `bh` (8 bytes on 64-bit) instead of the size of the blobheader struct (>= 10 bytes for the five fields dereferenced here). An attacker-controlled blob of 8..sizeof(*bh)-1 bytes passes the guard and triggers out-of-bounds reads of bh->min_version, bh->version, and bh->flags.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink: with caller-supplied `length == 8` (equal to `sizeof(bh)` for a 64-bit pointer, so the line-7 guard `length < sizeof(bh)` admits it) and the attacker setting `bh->totlen = htonl(8)` to pass line 14, this dereference of `bh->min_version` reads a field beyond the 8-byte `data` buffer (the five header fields occupy at least 10 bytes), leaking adjacent memory or faulting. The protecting check is insufficient: it bounds against the pointer size rather than `sizeof(*bh)`.

Reached whenever `min_version <= BLOB_HEADER_VERSION`; for any length in [8, sizeof(*bh)-1] that passed the line-7 guard, these additional header reads (`bh->version`, `bh->flags`) also sample memory past the end of the `length`-byte buffer supplied by the caller, with results written out through the output pointers.

assumptions: `blobheader` contains at least the five fields dereferenced in the shown code (totlen 32-bit, hdrsize 16-bit, version 8-bit, flags 16-bit, min_version 8-bit), so sizeof(blobheader) >= 10 > sizeof(blobheader*) == 8 on a 64-bit build (and > 4 on 32-bit, making even `length == 4` unsafe).
The caller passes `length` equal to the actual allocated size of `data`.
`BLOB_HEADER_VERSION` is a small compile-time constant and does not affect the over-read.
limitations: The returned `*dataoffset` (from `ntohs(bh->hdrsize)`) is not validated against `length`; a caller that later indexes the blob with it could go out of bounds, but that consuming operation is absent from the shown code.
NULL `data` or NULL output pointers would dereference only if an unseen caller violates its contract; the shown code cannot produce NULL.
The logprintf calls are not injection sinks: all formats are literals and all arguments are numeric.
There is no loop in the shown code, so no ReDoS or algorithmic-complexity concern applies.
The exact struct layout/padding is not shown; the over-read conclusion requires only sizeof(*bh) > sizeof(bh), which follows from the shown field accesses.

verdict.summary: The delete path decrements pos below zero (line 41) before the bounds guard (line 45), which only checks the upper end because d+l collapses to decoded+*decoded_size. With rule bytes {0x02,0x05,0x03,0x05} and initial size 0, pos becomes -1, causing an out-of-bounds read of decoded[-1] at line 49 and, if that byte matches the rule byte, an out-of-bounds write via memmove at line 53.

evidence.reason: Attacker-chosen rule bytes set mod='d', dir='<' with pos=0, then the delete branch decrements pos to -1 at line 41. The guard at line 45 admits pos=-1: l=*decoded_size-(-1)>=0 and d+l=decoded+*decoded_size always satisfies the upper bound, so no lower-bound check protects this dereference. Reading decoded[-1] is an out-of-bounds read; if that byte equals c, the memmove at line 53 writes one byte before the decoded buffer.

assumptions: decoded is allocated with at least INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes and *decoded_size initially lies in [0, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX], matching what the shown upper-bound checks assume.
rule is NUL-terminated, so the loop at line 7 terminates.
limitations: The one-byte out-of-bounds write at line 53 only occurs if the byte immediately before decoded equals the attacker-chosen rule byte c; the out-of-bounds read of decoded[-1] at line 49 occurs unconditionally on the witness path.
Potential additional over-read via debug_print("%s", decoded) on a non-NUL-terminated decoded buffer is not separately analyzed.
Unseen-caller contract violations such as an initially negative *decoded_size or a decoded buffer smaller than INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX would create additional out-of-scope corruption paths.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All buffer writes are bounded: strcpy uses a 9-character constant into a 256-byte buffer, every append uses g_strlcat with sizeof(buffer)=256 (max 255 bytes + NUL), the only network write uses the literal format "%s\r\n" so buffer content is never treated as a format string, and both loops are strictly bounded (NULL-terminated token array; x < G_N_ELEMENTS(supported_caps)). The remaining concerns (CRLF injection into the echo, tags_data NULL, g_strsplit failure) are not reachable through the shown path and carry no cross-trust-boundary impact.

assumptions: extensions_str is a single IRC message parameter delivered by a line-based message reader that splits the byte stream on CR/LF, so the parameter cannot contain raw newline bytes even though a malicious server controls its content.
g_strsplit returns a NULL-terminated token array per GLib contract, so the outer loop bound equals the token count.
supported_caps is a fixed compile-time array, so G_N_ELEMENTS(supported_caps) is valid and the inner loop is constant-bounded.
serv and tags_data are always non-NULL at framework call sites; the shown code never constructs a NULL for either.
buffer is exactly 256 bytes, so the "CAP REQ :" literal (10 bytes) and the g_strlcat cap of 255 content bytes leave no overflow margin.
limitations: CRLF/newline injection into tcp_sendf (line 52) would require CR or LF inside extensions_str; IRC line framing excludes it, and the sink sends to the same server that supplied the payload, so no cross-trust-boundary impact. No CWE assigned.
tags_data is dereferenced without a NULL check (lines 11, 51); a NULL could only be supplied by an unseen caller, so the NULL-producing path is absent from the shown code. No CWE assigned.

g_strsplit (line 13) is unchecked; on allocation failure extensions would be NULL and the loop at line 17 would dereference it, but the allocation is sized by a bounded IRC line so failure is not attacker-scalable. No CWE assigned.
A capability list longer than 255 bytes is silently truncated by g_strlcat, which can drop requested capabilities, but truncation has no security impact. No CWE assigned.

verdict.summary: 32-bit unsigned overflow in the APNG frame-buffer sizing (rowbytes = w * 4; imagesize = h * rowbytes, both unsigned int) lets an IHDR width/height that passes the line 43 cMaxPNGSize guard wrap the allocation size to a tiny/zero value; the same attacker-controlled dimensions then drive a ~h*w*4-byte libpng decode write through the undersized row buffer (line 174), producing a heap buffer overflow. The guard bounds each dimension but never the product.

evidence.reason: w and h are attacker-controlled unsigned ints read from the IHDR chunk (lines 40-41) and admitted by the line 43 guard (w,h <= cMaxPNGSize = 2^30). Both products are 32-bit unsigned: rowbytes = w*4 wraps for w >= 2^30, and imagesize = h*rowbytes wraps whenever h*4*w >= 2^32. Witness w = h = 32768 (passes line 43): rowbytes = 131072, imagesize = 32768*131072 = 2^32 == 0, so line 56 allocates a 0-byte heap object while processing_data at line 174 decodes h*w*4 = 4 GiB of RGBA through frameRaw.rows (lines 57-58) into it, overflowing the heap; the same wrapped row pointers are later indexed in the copy loop (lines 112-124). The line 43 guard is insufficient because it caps each dimension but never the product 4*w*h < 2^32, and no 64-bit widening or post-allocation check exists.

assumptions: cMaxPNGSize == 1u << 30 (standard libjxl constant); the wrap witness w = h = 32768 works for any cap >= 2^15, so the finding does not depend on the exact constant.
read_chunk stores the full raw chunk size in CHUNK.size (chunkIHDR.size == 25 at line 39 implies size = 12-byte header/CRC + payload) and provides chunk.p with at least that many bytes.
processing_data/processing_finish drive libpng to write h rows x (w*4) bytes of RGBA8 data through frameRaw.rows using the width/height present in chunkIHDR (lines 40-41, 159).
Line numbers are relative to the provided excerpt beginning at line 1.
limitations: In every overflow witness, the OOB write itself executes inside libpng during processing_data (line 174) before processing_finish can succeed, so the shown pixel-loop reads at lines 112-124 over the wrapped row pointers are not independently reachable; the shown code still owns the wrapping arithmetic and the undersized allocation that make the overflow possible.

fcTL chunks are read at offsets 12..33 (lines 142-149) and copied at offsets 12..19 (line 159) with no chunk.size >= 34 check; a zero-length fcTL after acTL would read up to 22 bytes past a 12-byte chunk buffer (OOB heap read), and garbage w0/h0/x0/y0 could then pass the line 151-153 value guard. Not counted as a second CWE because chunk.p's exact allocation size is produced by the unseen read_chunk.

Divide-by-zero DoS: delay_den is read from fcTL data at line 147 and never checked for zero; line 78 (delay_num * 1000 / delay_den) raises SIGFPE for delay_den == 0, reachable via IHDR + fcTL(delay_den=0) + IDAT + IEND. DoS only; no memory-safety impact.

Attacker-set dimensions up to 2^30 can make sub_frame/sub_frame_alpha (lines 105-106) and rows (line 57) request up to ~2^62 bytes / 8 GiB; an uncaught std::bad_alloc is an allocation-failure DoS, excluded by the rules.
The IEND success path (lines 137-140) breaks without freeing chunk.p (a roughly 20-byte leak per decoded image; does not compound with attacker-controlled volume).
png_ptr/info_ptr (lines 7-8) are declared uninitialized; safe only if the unseen processing_start initializes them by reference; NULL-on-error behavior is unverified.

fdAT handling (lines 179-180) writes only at offsets 4..11, which is within any chunk of size >= 12, and chunk.size-16 / chunk.size-4 underflow for short chunks only corrupts the synthesized sequence/IDAT bytes fed into the compressed stream (no shown-code memory impact). isAbc(chunk.p[4..7]) at lines 185-186 is likewise in-bounds for every chunk (size >= 12).
JXL_WARNING at line 34 uses a fixed "%s" format with a decoder hint string; no format-string injection.

verdict.summary: TransposeShapeFn validates perm entries only with `in_idx >= rank || in_idx <= -rank`, which admits every negative value in [-rank+1, -1] and passes it unmodified to `c->Dim(input, in_idx)` (line 55) as an index into the rank-element input dimension array. An attacker-supplied permutation such as [0, 1, -1] for an input of rank 3 yields in_idx = -1 at i = 2, passes the guard, and causes an out-of-bounds heap read during shape inference of a crafted model.

evidence.reason: in_idx is read from the attacker-controlled perm tensor (line 50, fed by lines 41-46). The only guard, line 51 (`if (in_idx >= rank || in_idx <= -rank)`), admits the full interval [-(rank-1), rank-1], including negatives that are invalid indices into the rank-element input dimension array consumed at line 55; there is no second check enforcing in_idx >= 0 before the indexing call. Concrete witness: input rank 3 with perm = [0, 1, -1] — at i = 2, in_idx = -1 fails both `-1 >= 3` and `-1 <= -3`, passes the guard, and `c->Dim(input, -1)` performs an out-of-bounds read of the input shape's dimension storage (CWE-125).

assumptions: perm is a constant input tensor whose element values are attacker-controlled (e.g., embedded in a crafted model/GraphDef), and c->input_tensor(1) returns it while shape inference runs.

Each perm entry is converted precisely (int32 or int64) and the element count of perm equals rank, enforced by WithValue(perm_elems, rank, ...) at line 36 together with the framework invariant that a tensor's data size matches its shape, so the data[i] reads at line 50 stay in bounds.
c->Dim(input, index) consumes the passed index directly against the input shape's dimension array; the shown code provides no non-negative constraint before the call at line 55.
limitations: If the specific InferenceContext::Dim implementation bounds-checks negative indices and returns an unknown dimension, the negative-perm case degrades to loss of shape information instead of an OOB read; the line 51 guard still demonstrably fails to constrain in_idx to [0, rank-1] for its later use.

dims.resize(rank) at line 32 can be driven with an attacker-chosen huge rank from perm_shape (e.g., perm_shape=[N] with unknown input rank and no perm value, rank=N via line 19), causing std::length_error/bad_alloc during shape inference; treated as an unchecked-allocation DoS and not counted as a second CWE.

The int32_t loop counters (lines 49 and 58) compared against int64_t rank can overflow only for rank > INT32_MAX, which requires an impractically large perm tensor (>= 8 GB) or equally huge shapes, so it is not a confirmed practical failure.

An OOB inside the AsInt64 helper would require perm's data buffer to hold fewer elements than perm_shape claims; this is prevented by the framework tensor/shape consistency invariant and is not observable in the shown code.
A non-int32/non-int64 perm dtype falling into the else branch at line 46 would misread element widths, but the Transpose op's type constraint admits only int32/int64, so this path is not reachable.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled S3M order count overflows a fixed-size order list. header->ordnum comes from f.readWord() (line 24) with no cap (unlike insnum/patnum, capped at lines 31/34); the loop at line 82 then copies up to 65535 non-0xFF file bytes into header->ord at line 87. The break on 0xFF (line 84) is data-dependent and bypassable by the file content, so ordnum > 256 writes past the array, corrupting adjacent module memory.

evidence.reason: header->ordnum is read from the untrusted file at line 24 (f.readWord(), range 0..65535) and is used unchanged as the loop bound at line 82, so j reaches ordnum-1 (up to 65534). The guard at line 84 (orders[i] == 255) is not a size check: orders[] is filled from the file at line 79, so an attacker supplies non-0xFF bytes and defeats it. With ordnum = 257 and 257 non-0xFF order bytes, the write at this line targets header->ord[256], out of bounds for a 256-entry order list (boundary proof: ordnum = 256 writes indices 0..255 and is safe; 257 is the first failing value). There is no j-cap and no ordnum > 256 rejection in the shown path, unlike the adjacent caps for insnum (line 31) and patnum (line 34).

assumptions: header->ord is a fixed-size member array of TXMHeader (the S3M order list), conventionally 256 entries per the format; its exact size is not printed in the supplied code. Any size < 65536 makes the write at line 87 overflow for a sufficiently large ordnum.

module->instr, module->smp, and module->phead are sized to hold at least MP_MAXINS instruments, the maximum sample count, and 256 patterns respectively, so indices up to the enforced caps are in-bounds.
safeRead(packed, index, size, ...) advances index and bounds-checks against size; under that semantics the packed-pattern loop (lines 305-348) terminates and reads only within packed[0..size+5).
limitations: If TXMHeader::ord were 65535+ entries or dynamically backed, the order-write overflow would not occur; that size is not visible in the given code, which is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.

Bounds of smp[s], instr[i], phead[i] cannot be fully confirmed without the module struct definitions (MP_MAXSAMPLES/MP_MAXPAT); if those arrays are sized exactly at the format caps the indices are safe.
orders is leaked on the early MP_LOADER_FAILED returns after line 26 (paths through lines 31-35); bounded single-shot leak with no security impact.
The signed subtraction at line 156 can invoke undefined behavior on extreme values but is immediately clamped to >= 0 and does not reach any memory sink in the shown code.

The guarded reads after attacker-controlled seek offsets (lines 136/281/382) may change what bytes are parsed, but no out-of-bounds access or injection arises from the offset itself in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The only size-indexed memory write (njs_scope_value at L34) is governed by an engine-internal bytecode-validated index rather than unvalidated attacker data; the await frame is engine-managed; and there are no injection, crypto, or file/access sinks. Candidate concerns (index bounds, NULL await frame, memory-error leak, free/exec UAF) fail taint/reachability with a concrete witness or are delegated to unseen helpers.

ctx->await is non-NULL because the await instruction allocates and links the async frame into the context before the fulfillment reaction can be dispatched.
ctx->pc and ctx->capability reference the currently-executing validated bytecode and the capability created by the await instruction.
limitations: The L34 write has no bounds check in the shown code; its safety rests on the unseen bytecode/context-creation invariant. Without a concrete out-of-range witness, an OOB write is an unconfirmed hypothesis and the authoritative validation is outside the shown code.
async_frame = ctx->await (L17) is dereferenced at L18 without a NULL check; the NULL-producing path is not shown, so no concrete NULL dereference is reachable in the shown code.

The NJS_ERROR/njs_is_memory_error early return (L58-60) skips njs_async_context_free: a resource leak only on internal OOM, not attacker-parametrized allocation volume, so it is a single-shot leak and not a confirmed finding.

Use-after-free hypotheses around njs_vmcode_interpreter, njs_function_call, and njs_async_context_free cannot be confirmed: the actual free/execution is delegated to unseen functions and the shown control flow provides no failing witness.
Potential OOB read through njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) depends on the unseen macro guard, while nargs is dispatcher-controlled rather than attacker-controlled in this code.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints: the moveable-entry branch indexes bin->segment_entries[segnum - 1] at line 60 with only a segnum > 0 guard (line 59), missing the upper bound segnum < SegCount that the fixed-entry branch enforces at line 63. An attacker-controlled NE file can set segnum (ut8, up to 255) above SegCount, reading past the segment-entries array.

evidence.reason: segnum is read from the attacker-controlled entry-table byte at line 56 and is guarded only by segnum > 0 at line 59 before being used as segment_entries[segnum - 1] at line 60. The fixed-entry branch at line 63 requires bundle_type < SegCount before the same array is indexed, establishing that segment_entries has SegCount elements. A file with SegCount = 1, bundle_type == 0xff, and segnum = 2 passes the guard and reads segment_entries[1], an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125); the concrete path is the while/for loops at lines 28-40 with the bounds check at line 41 satisfied.

assumptions: segment_entries is allocated with SegCount elements, consistent with the fixed-entry guard at line 63.
NE header fields (EntryTableLength/Offset, SegCount, csEntryPoint) are non-NULL and within their declared types, as set by the loader that calls this function.
limitations: The entry_table reads at lines 37 and 58 are gated by checks (lines 29 and 41) that are off by one for the subsequent read positions (tableat + off == r_buf_size - 1 allows reading one byte past the buffer); whether this is a genuine OOB depends on entry_table being backed by bin->buf at tableat, which the shown code does not state.

If entry_table is instead a separate allocation of exactly EntryTableLength bytes, the inner loop (lines 40-70) can advance off past EntryTableLength without re-checking it, producing a larger heap OOB read; the allocation extent is outside the shown code, so this is not confirmed here.
Potential size_t wraparound of tableat on 32-bit builds (ut32 header_offset + ut16 EntryTableOffset) is not analyzed because the build width is not shown.

verdict.summary: testBackingParse is a unit-test harness operating only on compiled-in, trusted test data (data->backing/data->expect/data->rv) and library-returned XML. All fprintf calls use constant format strings; STRNEQ at line 35 is provably guarded against NULL operands by the control flow at lines 12-13/15/20-21/23-27 (expect) and 29-30 (xml). No attacker-controlled input reaches any injection, memory, crypto, or access-control sink in the shown code, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute sets *src to NULL on failure (libvirt API contract), making the expect==NULL/failed-parse path exit at line 20-21.
virBufferContentAndReset returns NULL only when the buffer content is unavailable, and otherwise returns a NUL-terminated allocated string.
STRNEQ performs a bounded comparison of two NUL-terminated strings and is reached only with non-NULL operands.
limitations: Test strings (data->backing) are printed verbatim to stderr (lines 24-25, 36-39); this would be at most low-impact log-line injection in a security log, but the data is compile-time trusted, so no CWE is assigned.
XML escaping of the parsed backing source occurs inside virDomainDiskSourceFormat (unseen caller-side code); the shown code is a pass-through, and the input is trusted.
If the libvirt API contract on src==NULL-after-failure were violated, the redundant check at line 23 still catches expect==NULL with a non-NULL src before line 35.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in fiber_switch: when a non-created fiber (e.g., SUSPENDED) is resumed with vmexec, line 57 writes an attacker-influenced mrb_value to c->ci[1].stack[0] — one slot past the resumed context's top callinfo — with no bounds or capacity check; the only guard is the boolean vmexec flag. An attacker-controlled fiber (single-frame body, high call depth) can corrupt the interpreter heap.

evidence.reason: c->ci is the resumed fiber context's top-callinfo pointer, repositioned by fiber_switch_context (line 28) and, on the created path, by c->ci-- (line 36); no shown check bounds ci[1] against the callinfo region. value originates from fiber_result(mrb, a, len) (line 55) and is attacker-influenced (resume arguments). The path is reachable with status != MRB_FIBER_CREATED and vmexec == TRUE (a yielded/transferred fiber resumed from VM bytecode, lines 54-56); the only guard, if (vmexec) (line 56), constrains the mode but not the index geometry. When the fiber's callinfo stack is at its last slot (e.g., single-frame body resuming from Fiber.yield), the constant index 1 writes one mrb_value past the allocated region — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: Callers uphold the argument-count contract: len >= 0 and a contains at least len entries.
fiber_check/fiber_check_cfunc validate self, and fiber_switch_context/mrb_stack_extend operate on the now-current context c.

The created-path argument copy is safe: len >= 15 is clamped (lines 40-41) and, for len <= 14, mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) (line 44) covers stbase[0..len+1]; the loop b<e (line 47) writes indices 1..len with max index 14, with boundary value len=14 provably inside the allocation.
limitations: The OOB-ness of line 57 depends on the callinfo-region capacity set by unseen fiber setup (fiber_setup/fiber_switch_context); if the runtime reserves a spare slot above the top ci for vmexec returns, the write only overflows when the fiber's call stack fills the region (attacker-controlled call depth). This hidden invariant, not a shown protective check, limits confidence to 0.6.

c->ci-- (line 36) followed by c->ci->proc/c->ci->pc (line 63) could read before cibase only if the dummy callinfo sits at the region base; that setup invariant is not shown, so no secondary CWE-125 finding.
A negative len (signed mrb_int) would skip the copy and store a negative c->cibase->n (line 51), but negative argument counts are not reachable from valid callers.
MRB_PROC_ENV(c->cibase->proc)->stack[0] (line 52) NULL-deref not confirmed: proc is checked non-NULL (line 32) and env stack layout is unshown.
No injection, weak-crypto, or file/access-control sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. testBackingParse is a unit-test helper that only issues fprintf calls with fixed literal format strings and passes values as %s/%d arguments; the only unsanitized data written to stderr (data->backing, data->expect, xml) originates from trusted static test data with no attacker-controlled channel, and all parsing/buffer allocation is delegated to library code not present in the shown function. NULL-value paths are fully guarded (expect by lines 11/19/22, xml by line 29), and the shown code contains no memory, crypto, exec, SQL, or access-control operations.

assumptions: testBackingParse is invoked only by the local test driver with pointers to compile-time-initialized testBackingParseData entries, so data->backing/expect have no attacker-controlled provenance.
virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute returns 0 or -1 and virDomainDiskSourceFormat returns < 0 on failure, matching the comparisons used here.

limitations: Log-shape injection into stderr via the %s arguments at lines 23-24 and 35-38 (e.g., a newline inside data->backing) is possible only with trusted static test data; it has no security impact and carries no CWE.

Memory safety of the backing-store parse and of virBuffer/virDomainDiskSourceFormat internals is out of scope: the shown code is a pure pass-through that delegates parsing and allocation to unseen callees.

Calling testBackingParse with NULL args or NULL data->backing would fault at line 8/14 only if the unseen harness supplies invalid pointers; there is no attacker-controlled channel, so this is a robustness limitation, not a finding.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled inflate rule bytes are inserted verbatim into `decoded` (line 33) and then written unneutralized to the debug log via `%s` on the error paths (lines 29, 46); a `0x0A` rule byte reaches the `%s` output and splits the log line, enabling log-injection/forged log entries. All memory accesses are, however, correctly bounded by the guards at lines 28 and 41 (`pos < 0`, `l < 0`, exclusive end `<= decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX`), so no out-of-bounds flaw is confirmed.

evidence.reason: Rule bytes (attacker-controlled, read at line 7) are inserted into `decoded` at line 33, and `decoded` is passed to a `%s` log sink with no newline/syntax neutralization. Concrete witness rule = {0x41, 0x0A, 0x04, 0x42, 0x00} yields decoded="\nA" (size 2); after 0x04 sets delete direction '>' and resets pos=0 (line 13), 'B' at line 45 mismatches decoded[0]=='\n', executing line 46, which emits the raw 0x0A into the log and forges a new line boundary (CWE-117). The guards at lines 28/41 do pass for this path, so they do not prevent the log injection.

assumptions: INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX equals the allocation size of `decoded`.
`rule` is NUL-terminated by the caller; the loop at line 7 reads until c == 0.
`debug_print` is compiled in and writes to a stderr/log sink.
`*decoded_size` initially lies within [0, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX] per caller contract, though out-of-contract values are still rejected before any access by the guards at lines 28 and 41.
limitations: Memory safety is verified safe: guards at lines 28 and 41 enforce 0 <= pos <= *decoded_size and exclusive access end <= decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX; boundary cases (pos == *decoded_size with l == 0 and *decoded_size == SIZEMAX-1) stay in bounds, and the next full-buffer operation is correctly rejected.

Pointer formation `decoded + pos` with a negative pos (lines 25, 26, 38, 39) is evaluated before the check and is formal UB, but no dereference/memmove occurs on that path, so no reachable OOB access exists.

The `%s` on a possibly non-NUL-terminated `decoded` could over-read, but the read executes inside `debug_print`'s printf internals (not shown), so it is out of scope by the pass-through rule; it is also debug-build only.
The log-injection sink is a debug stderr log, limiting real-world impact; severity is kept low.
A rule stream without a NUL terminator would cause line 7 to over-read, but this depends on a caller-provided contract, not on the shown code.

verdict.summary: The slice-builder loop (rows 117–127) derives its exit bound from unvalidated attacker-controlled row_remapping values (max_old_row). With row_remapping = {0, INT64_MAX}, the expression max_old_row - row_start + 1 overflows int64_t: row_start wraps to INT64_MIN and subsequent slice_length is 0, so row_start never advances and the loop never exits, pushing TensorSlice objects onto tensor_slices indefinitely (unbounded memory growth / hang). No shown guard caps max_old_row against tensor_shape.dim_size(0) or INT64_MAX.

evidence.reason: max_old_row is tainted from the attacker-controlled row_remapping input tensor values (lines 25–33) with no range validation in the shown code; guard at line 111 only requires max_old_row >= 0, never bounding it against tensor_shape.dim_size(0) or INT64_MAX. Witness: row_remapping = {0, INT64_MAX} yields INT64_MAX - 0 + 1 = INT64_MIN (signed overflow) on the first pass, then INT64_MAX - INT64_MIN + 1 = 0, so row_start stays at INT64_MIN <= INT64_MAX forever; the loop never terminates and tensor_slices.push_back (line 125) grows memory without bound (CWE-835, availability/DoS).

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap (line 18) is assumed to accept the attacker-chosen remapping values, since the shown code imposes no value-range constraint before line 25.
Op attributes num_rows_, num_cols_, max_rows_in_memory_ are assumed attacker-controllable (set by the party constructing the op/graph), consistent with TensorFlow semantics.
Signed-overflow wraparound is assumed to follow standard two's-complement behavior of mainstream compilers.
limitations: The real out-of-bounds index of id_present by raw remapping values would occur inside the unshown RemapVectorToMap helper; per the scoring rules the dangerous store is absent from the shown code, so it is recorded here without a CWE.

If an unseen caller/version of RemapVectorToMap (or LookupSlice/SliceTensorShape) range-rejects out-of-range values, the infinite-loop finding becomes unreachable; the shown code itself contains no such check.

verdict.summary: In snd_pcm_oss_sync(), the only guard on runtime->oss.buffer_used is `buffer_used > 0` (line 26); when buffer_used exceeds period_bytes, the unsigned subtraction at line 30 underflows to ~SIZE_MAX, so snd_pcm_format_set_silence() at lines 31-33 writes an enormous number of silence samples at runtime->oss.buffer + buffer_used, well beyond the period-sized OSS buffer. evidence.reason: runtime->oss.buffer_used is attacker-influenced runtime state (set via the OSS write ioctls) and the only constraint imposed by the shown code is `buffer_used > 0` at line 26 — no bound against runtime->oss.period_bytes. For period_bytes=4096 and buffer_used=4097 the guard admits the value, the subtraction at line 30 wraps as unsigned size_t to ~SIZE_MAX, size becomes ~(SIZE_MAX*8)/width samples, and this sink writes that many samples starting at buffer+4097, i.e. one byte past the 4096-byte period buffer; the size_t-to-unsigned-int narrowing inside the sink does not reduce the count to a safe value. The missing protective check (buffer_used <= period_bytes or a clamp) is absent, yielding a kernel heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: runtime->oss.buffer is a heap region of period_bytes, and period_bytes is the maximum valid fill count for buffer_used.
period_bytes >= 1 and width >= 1 are guaranteed by validated fragment/format ioctls executed before SYNC (SNDCTL_DSP_SYNC) reaches this code.
The function is reachable by a local user holding an OSS PCM device fd.
limitations: Producing buffer_used > period_bytes depends on caller-side paths (snd_pcm_oss_write3/capture) that are not shown; per scope rules the sink and the missing bound are in the shown code, but the exact producing sequence is not demonstrated here.

The else-if branch (lines 37-45) has the same unsigned-underflow shape if period_ptr > period_bytes, but period_ptr is normally bounded by the capture read path, so it is not independently confirmed and carries no CWE.

verdict.summary: fastrpc_dma_buf_attach leaks the kzalloc'ed fastrpc_dma_buf_attachment 'a' when dma_get_sgtable() returns a negative value: the ret<0 branch at lines 14-17 returns -EINVAL without calling kfree(a). limitations: Exploitation of the leak requires dma_get_sgtable() to fail for an attacker-reachable buffer configuration; the shown code does not prove that failure is attacker-forcible, so severity is capped at low and confidence at 0.7.

verdict.summary: The JPEG segment parser in ljpeg_start can hang forever on a crafted/truncated file: fread return values (lines 13, 17) are unchecked, so once the file is exhausted the attacker-chosen bytes left in data[0..3] keep tag permanently at a value (e.g. 0xff01) that passes the line 16 guard and never equals 0xffda, making the do-while exit at line 40 unreachable — an unbounded busy-loop denial of service.

evidence.reason: The loop re-runs while tag != 0xffda, and tag (line 14) is recomputed only from data[0..1], which in turn is filled only by the unchecked fread calls at lines 13 and 17. File bytes 'FF D8 FF 01 00 04 FF 01' make iteration 1 parse marker 0xff01 (admitted by the line 16 guard since 0xff01 > 0xff00, with no matching switch case); the next iteration's fread at line 13 hits EOF and returns 0 leaving data[0..3] = FF 01 00 04, so tag stays 0xff01, len stays 2, the switch remains a no-op, and line 40's condition never becomes false — a genuinely unbounded busy loop (CWE-835), not a guaranteed-termination state.

assumptions: fread at EOF returns 0 and leaves the destination buffer unchanged (standard behavior on glibc/Apple libc).
make_decoder_ref, jhead's huff[] layout, dng_version, FORC, merror, zero_after_ff, and the caller's use of ifp are outside the shown code.
Line numbers are counted from the first line of the provided function (line 1 = 'int CLASS ljpeg_start ...').
limitations: The DHT parsing at lines 30-31 delegates all dereferences to make_decoder_ref, whose internal reads may overrun data[] when len is near 65535; because that dereference is not in the shown code, a CWE-125 verdict cannot be confirmed (pass-through to unseen code).

Segment-metadata reads at lines 20, 23-25, 34-35, and 38 can read past the actual segment length when len is small, but all indices stay within the fixed 0x10000-byte array, so the effect is stale-data/metadata corruption, not out-of-bounds access or memory corruption.

SOS-before-SOF input can reach calloc(0, 4) at line 48; behavior depends on the allocator and downstream code (not shown) and is not a memory-safety issue in this function.
Unchecked fread results also mean truncated files can yield metadata from stale buffer bytes; this is the same root cause as the confirmed loop, with no independent additional CWE assigned.

verdict.summary: The S3M order-list copy loop writes an unbounded number of bytes into the fixed-size header->ord array: header->ordnum is read raw from the file (f.readWord(), line 24) with no cap, the order bytes are attacker-controlled (f.read(orders,1,header->ordnum), line 75), and the only loop exit besides i<ordnum is an attacker-removable 0xFF terminator (lines 80-81). j reaches ordnum-1 (up to 65534), so header->ord[j++] = orders[i] (line 83) overflows the 256-entry order array (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write) on a crafted module file.

evidence.reason: orders[i] and the iteration count are fully attacker-controlled: header->ordnum is read raw from f.readWord() at line 24 (range 0..65535, never capped), and the order bytes are loaded by f.read(orders,1,header->ordnum) at line 75. The only guarding condition before the write is 'if (orders[i] == 255) break;' at lines 80-81, which the attacker defeats by supplying no 0xFF bytes. The loop at line 78 therefore admits j = 0..ordnum-1 (up to 65534), with no comparison against the capacity of header->ord (a fixed-size TXMHeader member, 256 entries in the reference definition). Witness: a file with ordnum=300 and 300 non-0xFF order bytes drives j=300, writing ~44 bytes past the array; ordnum=0xFFFF extends the overrun to ~65 KB. The missing check is a j/ordnum bound against the ord array size before this write; the reachable path (lines 24, 75, 78-83) is entirely inside the shown function.

assumptions: header->ord is a fixed-size member array of TXMHeader (256 entries per the reference ModPlug-family definition, matching the S3M song-length limit); the shown code never references its size, but j is bounded only by the file-supplied ordnum (<= 65535), which exceeds any plausible fixed capacity.
The malicious file supplies at least header->ordnum order-list bytes so f.read(orders, 1, header->ordnum) at line 75 fills the allocated buffer as requested.
module->smp, module->instr, and module->phead are allocated by the unseen caller with at least as many entries as header->insnum / header->patnum.
limitations: Sample-array indexing (smp[s] at lines 138-181, 291, 382, 395; s incremented at lines 203 and 397 up to insnum <= 65535, no bounds check in this function) would overflow if module->smp is smaller than the file-supplied insnum, but the array capacity is not visible in the shown code, so it cannot be confirmed and no CWE is attached.
Instrument/pattern targets (instr[i] at lines 193/201/232, phead[i] at line 358) share the same capacity uncertainty.

Pattern decode (lines 300-343) is verified safe: row is capped at 64 by the break at lines 309-314 (writes occur only at row <= 63), chn is masked to 0..31 at line 319, so the maximum slot offset row*160 + chn*5 + 4 = 10239 stays inside the 64*32*5 = 10240-byte pattern buffer (line 248); the while(index<size) loop terminates because size <= 65533 (lines 280-282) and safeRead either advances index or returns its default, driving row to the 64 cap.

The mp_sint32 looplen computation at line 151 relies on implementation-defined signed casts of dwords > 0x7FFFFFFF; negative results are clamped to 0 and any downstream effect lies in unseen conversion code.
Allocation-volume concerns (insnum/patnum up to 65535; per-pattern packed buffers up to 65538 bytes) are bounded per allocation and freed per iteration, so they are not confirmed findings.
Bounds handling inside XMFileBase (read/readWords/seekWithBaseOffset) and the behavior of convertS3MPattern / loadModuleSample are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: _gdContributionsAlloc's failure-cleanup loop decrements an unsigned index and tests "u >= 0", which is always true; an attacker-controlled windows_size (e.g. 536870912 with line_length 1) makes overflow2() at line 23 fire, enters the branch at line 28, and drives u into an infinite loop that indexes ContribRow out of bounds at line 31 and frees arbitrary pointers, causing denial of service and memory corruption.

The loop then reads `res->ContribRow[u].Weights` for u = UINT_MAX, UINT_MAX-1, ... — far beyond the line_length-element array — and gdFree()s the resulting arbitrary pointer values, never terminating. Concrete trigger: attacker-controlled `line_length = 1` and `windows_size = 0x20000000` make the overflow2() check at line 23 true (product 2^32), setting overflow_error = 1, so the branch at line 28 is taken at the first iteration with no guard bounding u before the wrap.

assumptions: line_length and windows_size are caller-supplied unsigned ints; in libgd these derive from image dimensions/filter parameters, but reachability here does not depend on the caller since both are function parameters consumed directly by the shown code.
limitations: A single per-row Weights allocation may reach ~4 GB when windows_size is large but does not overflow (line 26), a possible memory-exhaustion DoS; callers may bound windows_size elsewhere, and the confirmed cleanup bug already covers the malloc-failure symptom.
The failure path returns NULL without freeing res or res->ContribRow (lines 29-34), a single-shot leak with no confirmed attacker-controlled volume amplification in the shown code.
Malloc failure alone could also reach the broken cleanup loop, but the overflow witness above is attacker-verifiable and does not rely on allocation failure.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in _gnutls_server_select_suite: the first two-byte scan loop reads data[i + 1] before the datalen % 2 parity check executes, so an attacker-controlled odd cipher-suite length (e.g. datalen = 1) reads one byte past the end of the client-supplied buffer.

print_connection_info, print_bandw, and print_attr honor the length argument they are passed and return negative when space is insufficient, so the conn/bandw/attr writes are bounded.
pj_memcpy behaves like memcpy (copies exactly the given byte count).

No independent second CWE is confirmed: the port/port_count digit overhead (max 23 bytes) fits within the 36-byte slack, and no injection, crypto, or access-control sinks exist in the shown code.
The conn/bandw/attr helpers are not shown, so their internal correctness is not analyzed; they are reached with explicit remaining-length bounds.

The internal size/format validation performed by tipc_uaddr_valid (line 20) is not shown; if that helper lacked its sizeof check, OOB reads of msg_name would be possible, but that hypothesized flaw is not in the shown code and the guard call is the shown protection.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints: the entry-table index `off` is advanced past the last guarded position and dereferenced without a fresh bound check. The bundle_type read at line 38 and the 2-byte r_read_le16 in the moveable branch at line 62 can each read one byte past the end of the entry table/file buffer on a crafted NE file (e.g., EntryTableLength spanning to EOF with a non-zero last bundle-length byte, or the moveable layout reaching off == EL-1 where EL is the full remaining length).

Witness: with EntryTableLength == remaining buffer length N and off == N-1 (reached after the line-42 guard stops the previous bundle), the last byte is a non-zero bundle_length, and this read accesses absolute index tableat+N, one byte past the buffer.

In the moveable (0xff) branch, after off++ at line 50 and off += 2 at line 56, the guard at line 59 only breaks when off > EntryTableLength, so it admits off == EL-1, while this 2-byte read requires off+1 <= EL-1. Witness: off0 (=EL-7) with EL == remaining buffer length N lets off reach N-1 past the line-42 guard (N-5+4 < N), so the second byte of segoff is read at absolute index tableat+N, one byte past the buffer. The fixed branch's guard (off+2 >= EL -> break, line 67) correctly excludes this case, showing the missing bound.

assumptions: entry_table is anchored at file offset tableat within bin->buf, so reads at bin->entry_table + off correspond to buffer indices tableat + off; the failure is identical if entry_table is a separate allocation of EntryTableLength bytes, because the over-reads occur at its final byte.

The skip branch (off-- / break at lines 52-54) shifts parsing by one byte and discards the rest of a bundle; it is a functional/parsing bug but stays in bounds, so it is not reported as a security finding.
Allocation volume (~ EntryTableLength/2 RBinAddr) is bounded by the declared table length and does not amplify beyond file size; not treated as a DoS finding.
No NULL dereference is reachable in the shown code: entry_table, r_list_newf, R_NEW0, and r_bin_ne_get_segments results are all NULL-checked.
No injection, weak-crypto, or access-control sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID, *out_len is set from the client-controlled max_out_len (clamped at 64) while only 48 of the 64 bytes of the uninitialized talloc_array buffer are written. A client requesting max_out_len between 49 and 64 (e.g., 64) makes the reply advertise up to 16 uninitialized heap bytes, which are disclosed to the remote client.

verdict.summary: Missing bounds check before R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) at line 9 allows a 2-byte out-of-bounds read when the input buffer ends inside the attribute header (sz < 8) and attr is non-NULL.

evidence.reason: offset is unconditionally 6 after line 6, and R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads buffer[6] and buffer[7] with no offset+2 <= sz check. buffer/sz are attacker-controlled file bytes/size. With sz == 6 and attr non-NULL (not ruled out by the shown code), both bytes are out of bounds; with sz == 7, byte 7 is out of bounds. The line 14 guard executes later in the loop and does not protect this read.

assumptions: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT performs an unchecked two-byte read at buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+1]; its definition is not shown and the shown code performs no bounds check before the call.
buffer points to at least sz bytes of attacker-influenced file data.
r_bin_java_default_attr_new can return non-NULL when sz is as small as 6; the shown code places no contrary constraint.
limitations: OOB access inside r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new when sz - offset (line 17) is less than the nested parser needs is not confirmed because the faulting operation is in unseen code.
offset += bsm->size (line 19) can over-advance or wrap only if bsm->size is attacker-controlled and unvalidated; bsm->size's origin and constraints are not shown.
attr->size = offset (line 25) may overstate consumed bytes, but any resulting fault occurs in unseen downstream consumers.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The function performs fixed-size allocations with NULL checks on the structs it dereferences, stores the caller's src_buf/src_buf_sz pair without consuming it, and appends the new encoder to a caller-owned list under a non-NULL guard. The unchecked kstrdup/vzalloc results, the untrusted src_buf/src_buf_sz pair, and the cyclic-list assumption are only consumed by unseen code (e.g., vidtv_s302m_encode), so they are pass-through/robustness concerns, not findings in this function.

assumptions: args.head, when non-NULL, points to a valid, acyclic caller-owned list of vidtv_encoder nodes; the shown loop relies on tail->next == NULL to terminate.
args.src_buf, when non-NULL, refers to a caller-owned buffer of at least src_buf_sz bytes; the shown function never reads or writes it.
The leading '*' on the first line is a snippet artifact; upstream declares 'struct vidtv_encoder *vidtv_s302m_encoder_init(...)'.
limitations: e->src_buf/e->src_buf_sz (lines 22-23) are stored unvalidated; a mismatched buffer/size pair could cause an out-of-bounds read in vidtv_s302m_encode, but that sink is not present in the shown code (pure pass-through), so it cannot be confirmed here.

kstrdup(args.name, GFP_KERNEL) (line 14) and vzalloc(VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ) (line 16) results are not NULL-checked; a failure would leave NULL pointers for unseen code, but allocation failure is not attacker-controlled and no dereference occurs in this function.
while (args.head->next) (line 51) would not terminate on a cyclic list; a cycle cannot be produced within the shown code.
On ctx allocation failure (lines 29-32), kfree(e) leaks e->name and e->encoder_buf; single-shot, constant allocation sizes, no attacker-controlled volume, no security impact.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in snd_pcm_oss_sync(): runtime->oss.buffer_used and runtime->oss.period_ptr are only checked to be > 0, never bounded by runtime->oss.period_bytes. An attacker-influenced value larger than period_bytes makes the unsigned subtraction (period_bytes - buffer_used / period_bytes - period_ptr) wrap to ~2^64-1, so the computed frame count passed to snd_pcm_format_set_silence() becomes enormous and writes far past the end of runtime->oss.buffer (lines 31-33 and 42-44).

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced runtime->oss.buffer_used reaches this memory write guarded only by `buffer_used > 0` (line 26). With period_bytes = P and buffer_used = P+1 (admitted by the guard), the unsigned subtraction at line 30 wraps size to ~(2^64-1)/width frames, so this call writes from buffer+P+1 far beyond the period-sized buffer: confirmed out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the missing check is `buffer_used <= period_bytes`.

Attacker-influenced runtime->oss.period_ptr reaches this memory write guarded only by `period_ptr > 0` (line 37). With period_ptr = period_bytes+1 (admitted by the guard), line 41 wraps size to 2^64-1, and size*8/width frames are written at runtime->oss.buffer, overflowing the period buffer: same out-of-bounds-write class (CWE-787); the missing check is `period_ptr <= period_bytes`.

assumptions: runtime->oss.buffer is a period-sized allocation (capacity period_bytes), as usual in the OSS emulation setup; the allocation itself is not shown.
runtime->oss.buffer_used, runtime->oss.period_ptr, and runtime->oss.period_bytes are settable from the OSS device ABI (write sizes and fragment/format/parameter ioctls) by a local user.
runtime->period_size is nonzero after snd_pcm_oss_make_ready(), so the modulo at line 53 is not treated as a confirmed divide-by-zero.
limitations: A divide-by-zero or endless loop if snd_pcm_format_physical_width() returned 0 for the selected format is unconfirmed from the shown code alone (no witness value derivable here).
A divide-by-zero at line 53 if runtime->period_size could be 0 is unconfirmed; it depends on helper/setup invariants not shown.

The precise setup that lets buffer_used/period_ptr exceed period_bytes (e.g., shrinking fragments between writes and sync) lives in OSS write/parameter helpers outside the shown code; per scope, the shown path itself lacks the required upper-bound check.
Local access to the OSS PCM device nodes is an access-control precondition outside the shown code.
Potential 32-bit overflow of `size * 8` (line 44) is a consequence of the same unsigned wrap, not an independent finding.

verdict.summary: cvtchar returns len=2 when the input string ends with '^' immediately before the NUL terminator (lines 38-43): it reads the NUL, masks c to 0, and unconditionally reports two consumed characters. The consuming parse loop then advances past the terminator and dereferences one or more bytes beyond the end of the terminfo string, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) reachable with a crafted terminfo entry ending in '^'. The shown code lacks the c=='\0' -> len=1 guard that the analogous trailing-backslash case (lines 17-19) demonstrates.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled terminfo string content provides the witness input "^" (bytes 0x5E 0x00): line 7 selects case '^' (line 37), line 38 reads the NUL into c, line 42 masks c to 0, and line 43 unconditionally sets len=2 returned at line 62. The caller's parse loop advances sp by len, i.e. past the NUL terminator, and dereferences memory beyond the string — an out-of-bounds read. The required guard (if c == '\0' then len = 1), which would admit exactly the single '^' character and exclude the overshoot, is absent; the analogous trailing-backslash handling at lines 17-19 shows the intended protective pattern. Confidence is reduced to 0.6 because the final dereference occurs one step downstream in the unseen consuming loop.

assumptions: sp points into a NUL-terminated C string, so sp[1] is always readable when sp[0] != '\0'.
The unseen caller consumes the return value as a pointer-advance amount (sp += len) and dereferences sp again after advancing.
limitations: The out-of-bounds dereference itself executes in the caller's loop, which is not part of the shown code; the shown code is where the faulty length is computed and the missing guard resides.
Digit over-consumption and modulo-256 wrap in the octal loop (lines 26-29) are logic flaws only; all reads stay within the string and no memory operation is affected (no CWE).
Writes through dp (lines 50-60) are delegated wholly to the unseen save_string/save_char helpers, whose bounds are not shown, so no buffer-overflow finding is made here.
Returning len=0 on NUL (line 47) could only hang a caller that loops on a zero advance; no such caller is shown.

verdict.summary: In _gdContributionsAlloc, if the per-row window allocation guard overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) trips on the first loop iteration (u == 0), the cleanup path executes u-- on an unsigned int, wrapping 0 to 4294967295; the follow-up loop then indexes ContribRow[0..UINT_MAX] while the array holds only line_length entries, performing out-of-bounds reads and gdFree() of arbitrary memory (heap corruption / crash).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled parameter windows_size reaches overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) at line 23 unvalidated; with witness line_length=1 and windows_size=0x20000000 the guard trips at u==0, the u-- at line 30 wraps 0 to UINT_MAX (2^32-1), and the inclusive loop at line 31 admits i=0..UINT_MAX: line 32 reads res->ContribRow[i].Weights for i>=1 far beyond the 1-entry allocation and passes the garbage word to gdFree (OOB read, CWE-125, plus invalid free). The line-23 guard only protects the line-26 allocation; it does not protect the decrement, and no u>0 check exists before the wrap.

assumptions: overflow2 returns nonzero when its arguments' product cannot be safely represented, as its name and guarded use indicate; on 64-bit with sizeof(double)=8, windows_size >= 2^29 trips it.
gdFree is NULL-safe (equivalent to free() on NULL) so the inclusive i<=u bound is harmless in the u_fail>=1 case where entry u_fail holds NULL.
ContributionType contains at least the member double *Weights, so sizeof(ContributionType) is 8 on 64-bit builds.
gdMalloc returns NULL on allocation failure; every call site in the shown code checks for NULL.
limitations: The same wrap can also be reached when the first gdMalloc for Weights fails purely by allocator failure; that trigger is not attacker-selected and is only a robustness concern, not part of the confirmed finding.

End-to-end exploitability in a full GD scaling chain depends on the unseen caller passing a windows_size large enough to trip overflow2 (e.g., >= 2^29); within the shown code the parameter is unvalidated, so the failure is reachable per the analysis rubric.
During the overflow-error cleanup, entry 0's Weights is uninitialized gdMalloc memory; the read/free of it is part of the same confirmed underflow path, not a separate independent defect.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All allocations use constant sizes and their failure paths are properly handled; args.name is copied under the caller's NUL-terminated C-string invariant (kstrdup at line 14); the src_buf/src_buf_sz pair is stored verbatim but no memory operation in the shown code consumes it, so any OOB would occur in the unseen vidtv_s302m_encode (delegated pass-through); and the list-walk loop at lines 52-53 terminates on the framework-maintained acyclic, NULL-terminated encoder list.

assumptions: args.name, when non-NULL, points to a NUL-terminated kernel string (the vidtv bridge supplies static/module-parameter strings), satisfying the C-string contract required by kstrdup at line 14.
args.head points to a NULL-terminated, acyclic list of struct vidtv_encoder nodes; the driver maintains this invariant, which is what bounds the while loop at lines 52-53.
Field widths follow the upstream header conventions: args.es_pid is u16 and args.src_buf_sz is an unsigned byte count.
limitations: args.src_buf/args.src_buf_sz are stored with no bound check (lines 25-26); any out-of-bounds read would occur inside vidtv_s302m_encode, which is only referenced as a pointer at line 38 and whose body is outside the shown code — a pure pass-through, out of scope.

kstrdup's return at line 14 is unchecked; a GFP_KERNEL OOM leaves e->name NULL, but no dereference of e->name occurs in the shown code (kfree(NULL) at line 66 is safe), and the allocation size is not attacker-controlled.

The while loop at lines 52-53 would not terminate on a cyclic args.head, but that list is framework-internal and acyclic; no attacker-controlled input supplies it on the shown path (a caller-contract concern, not demonstrated reachable).

If args.name were a non-NUL-terminated pointer, kstrdup at line 14 would read out of bounds; the shown code has no length argument to verify this, so it is a caller-contract limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID returns a 64-byte talloc_array buffer of which only bytes 0-47 are initialized (push_file_id_16 x2 + memcpy at lines 55-57); *out_len is attacker-controlled via max_out_len (line 47) and can be 48..64, so 16 uninitialized heap bytes (offsets 48-63) are returned to the SMB client at lines 58-59. The leak is repeatable on attacker demand, disclosing server heap contents (CWE-908/CWE-200). All other FSCTL cases are adequately guarded against OOB/injection on the shown paths.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled max_out_len (line 9) sets *out_len to min(max_out_len,64) at line 47, and talloc_array at line 49 allocates without zeroing. The writes at lines 55-57 initialize only offsets 0-47; offsets 48-63 remain uninitialized and are returned to the client via *out_data at lines 58-59 whenever max_out_len >= 48 (witness: max_out_len=64). There is no guard limiting *out_len to the initialized prefix, so each repeatable FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID request (function is attacker-selected at line 15) discloses 16 bytes of server heap, an uninitialized-memory read (CWE-908) exposing sensitive information (CWE-200).

assumptions: Samba talloc_array allocates without zeroing (talloc_zero_array is required for zeroing); talloc_zero_array at line 144 confirms the distinction in this codebase.
push_file_id_16 writes exactly 16 bytes (two 64-bit file-id components) at each call site.
The smbd caller transmits exactly *out_len bytes of the returned buffer to the SMB client.
shadow_data fields from SMB_VFS_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA (line 115) are trusted server-side VFS state, not request-controlled.
limitations: FSCTL_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA: labels_data_count (lines 128-129) is a uint32 product that could wrap given num_volumes > ~2^30, but num_volumes originates from the VFS snapshot backend and is not attacker-controlled on the shown path, so the overflow is unconfirmed and not a finding.
