DEBUG log writes at lines 27-30 and 118-123 embed attacker-influenced filenames/connectpath via %s; filenames may legally contain control bytes (e.g., 0x0A) on POSIX, enabling low-impact log forgery. Kept as a hardening note, not added as a second CWE per single-focus discipline.
FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID with max_out_len < 48 only truncates the response (no overflow, no additional exposure beyond the uninitialized-range finding).
srvstr_push and sid_parse internals are not shown; their result handling here is bounded by the passed lengths (2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL), sid_len <= in_len-4).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The format-string parse on line 7 is delegated to the unseen luaO_pushvfstring, the source:line message assembly on line 10 is delegated to the unseen luaG_addinfo, and the only explicit guard (isLua(ci), line 9) exactly covers the ci_func(ci)->p dereference it precedes. All pointer reads operate on VM-invariant data; there are no attacker-controlled sizes, indices, or injection sinks in this function.

assumptions: L is a valid lua_State with a non-NULL, current L->ci while this C function executes (Lua VM invariant).
luaC_checkGC(L) on line 5 does not reallocate or invalidate the CallInfo chain referenced by the ci captured on line 2.
For isLua(ci) true, ci_func(ci) is a valid closure whose proto stays alive via the stack-anchored closure (VM invariant).
msg on line 7 is either a valid pointer into a live TString or the callee raises an error; no NULL-producing path is shown.
limitations: If an unseen caller ever passes attacker-controlled text as fmt (e.g., luaL_error(L, user_string) misuse), a format-string vulnerability could result; the dangerous parse occurs inside the unseen luaO_pushvfstring, and this function is a pure pass-through, so it is out of scope of the shown code.

ci_func(ci)->p->source is forwarded to the unseen luaG_addinfo on line 10; any message-injection concern from a hostile chunk name would materialize in that unseen concatenation, so it cannot be confirmed here.
A NULL dereference of ci or ci_func(ci)->p is not reachable from any value satisfying the VM invariant in the shown code; only an invalid caller-supplied state could produce it.
The shown code applies no input validation to fmt, but no attacker-controlled path into fmt exists within the shown control flow.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in _gnutls_server_select_suite: an odd-length, attacker-controlled cipher-suite list reaches data[i + 1] at lines 17 and 30 inside the first scan loop, before the datalen % 2 parity check at lines 78-81 executes, producing a pre-authentication 1-byte read past the end of the peer-supplied buffer.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled datalen (peer cipher-suite length, unvalidated for evenness before first use) and data[0] (peer-selected byte) reach the memory read data[i+1]: with datalen=1 and data[0]=0x56 (GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR), the loop at line 13 admits i=0 and line 30 reads index 1 = datalen, one byte past the valid range [0,datalen). The guard i < datalen admits this index, and the parity check at lines 78-81 executes only after this loop, so it does not protect the access; the identical trigger applies to line 17 for data[0]=0x00 when safe renegotiation is enabled. Impact: pre-authentication 1-byte out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), comparison oracle or crash on a page boundary.

assumptions: The data buffer is exactly datalen bytes, so valid indices are 0..datalen-1; line numbers are relative to the pasted snippet starting at the function signature.
GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR == 0x56 and GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR == 0x00.
cipher_suites_size returned by the internal helpers stays even and within MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE.
limitations: server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites (lines 42-44) also receives the unvalidated odd datalen, but its internal handling is not shown, so no direct claim is made for it.
If datalen approached UINT_MAX, i += 2 could wrap and the first scan loop would not terminate; TLS message lengths cannot reach that range, so this is not rated as a finding.
Impact of the confirmed read is a single byte past the end: a crash requires crossing an unmapped page, otherwise it is a 1-byte comparison oracle.
An unseen caller could in principle enforce even suite length earlier, but that would not repair the shown code's own misplaced parity guard.

verdict.summary: Unbounded sprintf() into the fixed global big_buffer via suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename): when built with CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE, an over-long configuration file name from config_main_filelist (command-line -C) overflows big_buffer before any ownership/trust checks run, enabling local memory corruption / privilege escalation in setuid-root Exim.

evidence.reason: suffix (line 16) points to filename + Ustrlen(filename) inside the big_buffer_size-byte global big_buffer; filename is returned by string_nextinlist (line 10) from config_main_filelist, which is derived from the attacker-influenced -C argument and can fill big_buffer up to big_buffer_size-1 bytes. This sprintf writes up to 279 bytes with no length check, so for strlen(filename) >= big_buffer_size - 279 the write passes index big_buffer_size-1 and corrupts memory past big_buffer (CWE-120). The uname() guard (line 22) only ensures uts.nodename is valid and does not check remaining space; concrete witness: filename of length big_buffer_size-1 with a 256-byte nodename.

Same unguarded write pattern as line 25: writes up to 258 bytes at suffix, which has only big_buffer_size-1-strlen(filename) bytes of space. The guards in scope (uname at line 22, config_file == NULL at line 27) constrain nodename availability and open attempts, not buffer space, so a filename of length >= big_buffer_size-257 overflows big_buffer.

Most unconditional variant: under CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID it runs whenever the file open is still NULL, with no uname() dependency. It writes up to 22 bytes at suffix and overflows big_buffer whenever strlen(filename) >= big_buffer_size-21; no size check exists anywhere on the shown path (the if at line 39 tests only file-existence).

assumptions: big_buffer is a fixed-size global of big_buffer_size bytes and string_nextinlist NUL-terminates each item within it, so a list item can be up to big_buffer_size-1 bytes long.

config_main_filelist is attacker-influenced in the local threat model: Exim seeds it from the command-line -C argument (argv) or build-time CONFIGURE_FILE, and its length is not bounded by the shown code.
The vulnerable sprintf block is compiled only when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE is defined at build time; the no-fancy-processing build (line 57) is not affected.

Exim's main binary is commonly installed setuid-root, which escalates the impact of the confirmed out-of-bounds write; the overflow executes before the trusted_config ownership checks at lines 85-105.
limitations: Log injection via a newline embedded in the attacker-supplied config filename reaching log_write at lines 74-79 is unconfirmed (Exim's log_write may neutralize newlines) and is low-impact; no CWE assigned.

Potential NULL dereference at line 371 (Ustrtol(s, ...)) if expand_string(host_number_string) at line 370 returns NULL — unlike the sibling expansion sites at lines 222-225, 234-237, and 292-295 there is no NULL check. It is reachable only through a root-controlled config value that fails expansion, or in unprivileged untrusted-config mode where impact is a local crash; treated as a robustness concern, no CWE assigned.
host_number is not range-checked for negative values (only n > LOCALHOST_MAX at line 376), but no consuming sink is shown in the provided code.
The for(;;) block at lines 183-204 terminates after at most two iterations (af is forced to AF_INET and breaks), so it is not a hang.
The fstat() ownership/mode check at lines 85-105 is a correct trust guard but cannot protect the earlier sprintf overflow because it executes after the writes and only when trusted_config is set.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All buffer accesses are guarded: line 9 (`offset + 8 > sz`, requiring sz >= 14) protects the u2 read at line 13, and the `offset >= sz` break at line 18 precedes every use of `buffer + offset` / `sz - offset` at line 21, so even a fully attacker-controlled `bsm->size` (line 23) cannot push `offset` past `sz` before the next guarded use. The loop is bounded by a u16 counter (max 65535) and terminates.

assumptions: `r_bin_java_default_attr_new` returns non-NULL only after legally consuming the 6-byte attribute header, making `offset = 6` inside the `if (attr)` branch valid.
`buffer`/`sz` are a valid pointer/length pair with `sz` being the attribute data region's exact byte length.

The real `r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new` honors its `(buffer, sz - offset)` pair and caps its reported `bsm->size` (argument count is a u16), so `offset += bsm->size` cannot wrap `ut64` or silently stay in bounds while ignoring the passed size.
limitations: An actual over-read would occur inside the unshown `r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new` if it parses without its own bounds checks; the shown code is a pass-through that hands it the correct remaining length, so that read is out of scope (dangerous operation absent from the shown code).

If a helper-reported `bsm->size` overstates consumed bytes, `attr->size` (line 29) can exceed the attribute's real length; any resulting out-of-bounds parse would be in the unseen caller that consumes `attr->size`, which is out of scope.
Non-progress `bsm->size == 0` repeats reads at a fixed in-bounds offset but is capped at 65535 iterations (u16 count) — terminates, no hang/DoS finding.
`if (offset + 8 > sz)` (line 9) is stricter than needed for the two-byte read at line 13 and rejects some valid small attributes; this is over-restriction, not a vulnerability.
Allocation failures of `r_list_newf` or of helper-created objects are single-shot and not attacker-scaled in the shown code; no compounding memory-exhaustion finding.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in ga_concat_shorten_esc: the run-counting loop advances `s += clen` using the first character's byte length, but `mb_ptr2char(s)` can return an equal codepoint for an invalid byte with a different length (e.g. string bytes C3 83 C3 00 makes clen=2 and `s` skip the NUL to one past the 4-byte buffer), so the reads at the `while` condition and the resumed `*p` dereference cross the end of `str`, causing a crash/DoS (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled bytes of `str` (parameter, no length/validity check except `str == NULL` at line 10) fix `clen` at line 21 from the first character (valid U+00C3, 2 bytes -> clen=2). For the witness string {0xC3,0x83,0xC3,0x00} in a 4-byte buffer, `mb_ptr2char(str+2)` returns the Latin-1 fallback 0xC3 for the invalid byte, equal to `c`, so the guard `*s != NUL && c == mb_ptr2char(s)` admits the iteration; `s += clen` then moves `s` to offset 4, one past the allocation, and the line-22 condition re-reads `*s` out of bounds (and can continue walking if OOB bytes match). The guard is insufficient because it never verifies that the matched character's byte length equals `clen`, so it cannot prevent stepping over the NUL terminator. Confirmed failing witness: `str = {0xC3,0x83,0xC3,0x00}`; sink read at line 22 after the line-25 advance.

assumptions: str is a NUL-terminated buffer.
mb_ptr2char_adv advances s by the byte length of the character at p, so clen = s - p is that byte length (>= 1 for the non-NUL start of each outer iteration).
Vim's UTF-8 decoder returns the raw byte value (Latin-1 fallback, length 1) for invalid/truncated sequences, which is what makes an invalid 0xC3 byte compare equal to valid U+00C3.
gap points to a valid grow array (caller invariant).
limitations: The caller that supplies `str` is not shown; the finding assumes the string can contain malformed UTF-8 bytes, which is common for file/message content in Vim.

Whether the single OOB read crosses an allocation boundary depends on the buffer containing `str`; it is guaranteed to pass the string terminator, and is a heap-buffer-over-read for a minimal 4-byte allocation of the witness string.
OOB bytes are not copied to output (they only steer loop control and same_len), so the impact is crash/denial-of-service rather than direct memory disclosure.
Potential INT_MAX overflow of `same_len` via an unbounded OOB walk was not confirmed as a separate triggerable class and is subsumed by the OOB finding.
No injection sink exists in the shown code: ga_concat_esc escapes output and the only format string is a constant "%d".

verdict.summary: cvtchar parses backslash/caret escape sequences from a NUL-terminated string and emits terminfo push notation. No confirmed vulnerability exists in the shown code: every read is bounded by the terminator (the octal loop at lines 26-27 tests isdigit(UChar(*sp)) before each read and stops on the NUL, so it can never advance past the last byte; the *++sp reads at lines 9 and 39 execute only after a verified '\\' or '^' at *sp and at worst read the terminator), the 8*c+d arithmetic at line 27 stays in int domain with defined modulo-256 truncation, and the emitted writes (lines 52-64) are fixed-width and go through the unseen save_string/save_char helpers. No injection, crypto, or access-control sinks are present. Remaining concerns (non-NULL/NUL-terminated sp contract, octal quirk accepting digits 0-9 with value wraparound, helper-buffer capacity) are caller-contract or out-of-scope and are recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: sp points to a valid, non-NULL, NUL-terminated C string; the shown code imposes no other bound on sp.
UChar(x) yields an unsigned char value, so isdigit/isgraph receive arguments representable as unsigned char (conformant per C standard).
dp is a growable output buffer managed by the unseen save_string/save_char helpers.
Line numbers are counted from the inline snippet as provided and are approximate, not from a repository file.
limitations: A NULL or non-NUL-terminated sp would cause a NULL dereference or out-of-bounds read, but no path in the shown code produces that state; it is a caller-contract violation, so it is out of scope.

The octal branch (lines 21-29) accepts any digit '0'-'9' and an unlimited digit run; the accumulated value is truncated modulo 256 into unsigned char (e.g., a run decoding above 255 wraps), and '8'/'9' are misinterpreted as octal digits. This is a decoding/correctness quirk with no memory-safety or injection impact in the shown code.
Any capacity overflow in the dp accumulation depends entirely on the unseen save_char/save_string implementations, which are not part of the shown code.
The NUL arm of the inner default branch (line 33, len=1 when c==0) is unreachable because a backslash followed by NUL is handled by the '\0' case at line 17; harmless dead logic, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All attacker-controlled header values are bounded by guards before use: ldblk is restricted to [0,9999] (line 55), nameLen to <= 0xFFFF (line 83), dims are nonzero (lines 103-104) and at most 2^32-1 via unsigned int fields. The only in-scope memory operation, ReadBlob at lines 163/190, requests depth/8*image->columns bytes, the same geometry used to configure the QuantumInfo pixel buffer (lines 153-157), and is EOF-bounded. Loop index image->rows-y-1 (line 166) stays in [0, rows-1] under the strict y < rows bound. The remaining suspicious sinks (FixSignedValues, InsertComplexDoubleRow/FloatRow, ImportQuantumPixels, SetImageExtent) delegate their memory operations to unseen callees, so their safety cannot be confirmed or refuted from the shown code; concerns such as CPU-cost loops on huge declared extents, uninitialized data on short reads, and ping-path mis-seeks are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: LP64 build (64-bit size_t/ssize_t/long) matching modern ImageMagick defaults; on ILP32, rows >= 2^31 become negative in the (ssize_t) casts and the row loops are skipped, and ReadBlobLSBLong values >= 2^31 are rejected as negative in ldblk by line 55.
ReadBlobLSBLong/MSBLong each consume exactly 4 bytes and return at most 2^32-1.

GetQuantumPixels (line 157) returns a buffer sized by the same depth/columns configuration selected by SetQuantumFormat/SetQuantumDepth (lines 153-154) and SetImageExtent (line 115); ReadBlob returns -1 only on hard error and 0/short counts at EOF otherwise.
image_info->ping, number_scenes and scene are framework-controlled and trusted.
limitations: Delegated sinks: FixSignedValues(image,q,(int) image->columns) at line 173 (int truncation of columns >= 2^31), InsertComplexDoubleRow/InsertComplexFloatRow at lines 194/196, ImportQuantumPixels at lines 170-171, and SetImageExtent at line 115 all perform their actual memory operations inside unseen functions, so any OOB/count misuse there is a pure pass-through and not confirmable in the shown code.

CPU-cost DoS: a minimal file declaring nRows/nCols near 2^32-1 makes the row loops at lines 158/185 run up to ~4.29e9 iterations because short reads (count==0) at lines 163/190 do not break, only count==-1; this is a finite, guaranteed-terminating loop (pathological runtime, not a hang finding), and extreme extents are typically rejected by the delegated SetImageExtent resource limits before the loops.

Uninitialized heap data: truncated rows cause ReadBlob (163) to fill only part of the freshly acquired quantum buffer; the remainder flows into the delegated ImportQuantumPixels at 170, but the exposure is bounded by one row buffer (single-shot, does not compound with attacker volume) and the conversion/write is delegated.
pixels from GetQuantumPixels (line 157) is dereferenced by ReadBlob at 163 without a NULL check; this requires the unchecked allocation to fail, which is out of scope.

Ping-path seek (line 109) computes HDR.nCols*ldblk using the MOPT type code rather than the element size, and the product can wrap on 32-bit unsigned arithmetic; impact is parser mis-alignment/incorrect skip, not a memory-safety failure in the shown code.
The complex-row casts at lines 194/196 reinterpret the same row buffer as double/float pairs; whether the callees read past it is delegated to unseen code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code: ioctl flag operations use guarded, in-bounds 32-bit values; oldflags is never read on a GETFLAGS failure; fd ownership and cleanup are consistent on all paths; and the only error output uses a fixed format string. Candidate narrowing and path-handling concerns lack a concrete failing witness with security impact.

assumptions: a is a valid, non-NULL archive_write_disk context for the lifetime of the call.
A caller-supplied fd >= 0 remains valid and is owned by the caller; the function only closes fds it opened itself.
The underlying file-flag ioctl ABI operates on 32-bit flag values; this is the range relevant to FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/SETFLAGS.
limitations: Narrowing of unsigned long set/clear into int at the newflags assignment is a type/robustness concern, but no concrete 32-bit flag value was found that changes the kernel-visible result or breaks any security mechanism; no CWE is assigned.

open(name, ...) with an archive-derived name and the absence of path/symlink normalization are not exploitable within the shown control flow without caller path-validation or privilege context; whether this matters depends on unseen caller behavior, so it is not confirmed here.
oldflags cannot be consumed uninitialized: the only consumption follows a successful GETFLAGS, and failure jumps to the fail label before any read.
fd leaks and double-close were checked across all branches and were not found.

verdict.summary: Balloc uses the unvalidated caller-supplied index k to read (line 7) and write (line 8) freelist[k]; any k outside the freelist's fixed range (including negative k, or k at/above its length) yields an out-of-bounds read followed by an out-of-bounds write, with no bounds check in the shown code. The same missing bound check also allows 1 << k (line 10) to overflow and produce an undersized/wrong-capacity allocation via lines 11-13.

evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced parameter k (line 1) flows unvalidated into the freelist index read at line 7 and this write at line 8; the only conditional (line 7) checks the fetched pointer's NULL-ness, not whether k is within the freelist's bounds, so a witness such as a negative k or k equal to/greater than the freelist length defeats it and causes an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) with a preceding out-of-bounds read at line 7.

assumptions: freelist is a fixed-size static array (as in dtoa, a small Kmax-sized table) whose exact length is not declared in the shown code; the failure occurs for any k outside its bounds regardless of its exact size.

k originates in the caller (dtoa parsing/formatting internals) and is influenced by integer/exponent content of processed input; per scope, the in-scope fact is that the shown code applies no constraint to it.
limitations: The integer-overflow variant in lines 10-13 (1 << k can overflow/UB for k >= 31; (x-1)*sizeof(Long) can wrap, with rv->maxwds recording the wrong capacity) shares the same missing bound check but exploits implementation-defined shift/wrap behavior; the actual overflowing word writes occur in callers not shown, so it is not given a separate CWE.
NULL dereference at lines 12/16 after the unchecked MALLOC at line 11 requires allocation failure and is at most a DoS/robustness concern; not treated as a confirmed finding.
No injection, crypto, file-handling, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds heap read in lprn_is_black: y0 is clamped with '% maxY' but the outer loop adds y (0..nBh-1) without re-wrapping, so row indices up to maxY+nBh-2 reach ImageBuf past its block-sized allocation and are dereferenced at line 15. Job-influenced geometry/block parameters (r, h, nBh, nBw, BlockLine) provide the taint; e.g. BlockLine=8, nBh=8, r=7, h=8 yields y0=7 and reads rows 8..14 out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Tainted index reaches a memory read: r/h (page geometry) and nBh/nBw/BlockLine (device block parameters, settable per job) flow unvalidated into the line 13 expression and the line 15 dereference. The only guard, '% maxY' on line 11, bounds y0 to [0, maxY-1] but not the consumed row y0+y; for BlockLine=nBh=8, r=7, h=8, y0=7 and the loop reads rows 7..14, so rows 8..14 are up to 7*bpl bytes past the block-sized ImageBuf — a confirmed OOB read at line 15.

assumptions: lprn->nBh, nBw, BlockLine and ImageBuf are initialized by unseen device code, with ImageBuf sized for the block extent (BlockLine/maxY rows); bpl from gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line is positive.
r, h, bx originate from job-driven page raster geometry in the unseen caller, which is attacker-influenced when Ghostscript processes untrusted documents.
limitations: Division/modulo by zero at lines 9 and 11 (nBh == 0, or nBh > BlockLine making maxY == 0) is a DoS-only concern whose trigger depends on device-parameter validation in unseen put_params code; not confirmed as a separate finding.
A negative y0 (C '%' with r + h < bh) would read before ImageBuf; same root cause and covered by the primary finding, no separate CWE.
Horizontal out-of-bounds would require bx*nBw + nBw > bpl, which depends entirely on the unseen caller's loop bounds; not confirmed here.

verdict.summary: luaG_runerror contains no attacker-reachable dangerous operation: fmt at line 7 is bound to compile-time literals from internal VM callers (the function is internal and not Lua-callable), attacker strings only ever arrive as vararg data consumed by Lua's safe bounded formatter, and the stack fix-up at lines 11-12 operates on exactly the two slots created by the line-7 and line-10 pushes under stable VM invariants. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: luaG_runerror is an internal VM helper (LUAI_FUNC in ldebug.h), not exported through lua.h/lauxlib.h and not callable from Lua scripts; all callers pass literal format strings, so fmt at line 7 is not attacker-controlled.
luaO_pushvfstring is Lua's own bounded, buffered formatter and pushes exactly one TValue on success.
luaG_addinfo pushes exactly one TValue (the source:line-enriched message) before the fix-up on lines 11-12.
L->ci is non-NULL while an error is being raised, and L->top is always in-bounds as maintained by the VM; isLua(ci) fully guards the ci_func(ci)->p dereferences on line 10.
limitations: If an out-of-band change ever let input-derived format syntax reach fmt, line 7 would become a format-string hazard (CWE-134); not reachable given the current internal call sites.

Attacker-influenced strings embedded in msg (e.g., __name metamethod values) can contain newlines; log/header/query injection would require an unseen host sink that writes the message, which is absent from the shown code.

An OOM inside luaO_pushvfstring or luaG_addinfo would longjmp before the stack fix-up; that is an unverified allocation-failure path with no attacker-controlled size and is excluded as DoS-only hardening.
The shown code contains no loops, so loop-bound analysis does not apply.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImage computes the next object offset as filepos += MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize + 4 + 4 in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. A crafted MAT file with ObjectSize = 0xFFFFFFF8 makes the delta wrap to 0, so filepos never advances; the object parser loop (while(!EOFBlob(image))) re-seeks to the same offset and re-parses the same miMATRIX object forever, never reaching EOF. Each iteration also allocates a new image and appends it to the list, so the hang is accompanied by unbounded memory growth — an attacker-controlled denial of service (CWE-835, caused by CWE-190 wraparound).

evidence.reason: ObjectSize is attacker-controlled 32-bit unsigned data read at line 91 and is added with no bound check. For ObjectSize = 0xFFFFFFF8, the sum ObjectSize+4+4 wraps modulo 2^32 to 0, so filepos is not advanced. The enclosing loop (line 83) then re-seeks to the identical offset (line 86), re-reads the same header (lines 89-91), and — with DataType = miMATRIX and a small valid matrix body — re-parses successfully each iteration while EOFBlob stays false because the blob position remains inside the file; the only exit guards (lines 90, 92, 408) are all bypassed, producing an unbounded hang plus unbounded image-list growth.

assumptions: MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize, SizeX, and SizeY are 32-bit unsigned fields, matching the unsigned int return type of ReadBlobXXXLong (line 25) and the MAT v5 format.
z2qtype has at least 4 entries, so indices 0..3 (enforced by lines 128/131 and the decrement loop at line 330) are in bounds.
AcquireQuantumMemory and SetImageExtent internally reject arithmetic overflow; SetImageExtent failure aborts via line 267 before BImgBuff is used.

The image 'next' structures created by AcquireNextImage (line 407) share the file blob, which is why SeekBlob/EOFBlob on the current image reflect the same underlying file across iterations (standard ImageMagick multi-frame coder behavior).
limitations: Integer wrap of ldblk (e.g., 8*SizeX ≡ 0 mod 2^32 at line 230) can under-allocate BImgBuff (line 270) such that ImportQuantumPixels (lines 304/314) over-reads heap; this is not confirmed because the access occurs inside an unshown helper and requires SetImageExtent (line 265) to succeed for a multi-GB pixel cache, so no guaranteed failing witness exists.

Attacker-controlled huge ldblk/extents cause multi-GB allocation attempts at lines 265/270, but failure is handled by ThrowReaderException (line 272) or early return (line 267), so impact is an error-path resource-exhaustion concern without memory corruption.

line 242 (image->colors = one << image->depth) shifts a size_t by 64 when depth is 64 (lines 207/221), which is undefined behavior, but the result only feeds the colors value and no shown memory operation depends on it.

A possible use-after-free of image2 after DeleteImageFromList(&image2) at line 394 was examined for the Frames>0 path (line 417-422); DeleteImageFromList(&image2) nulls image2 for a singleton list and line 420 then resets it to image, so the shown control flow does not confirm a UAF.
No injection, weak-crypto, or authz issues exist in the shown code; all log-format call sites use numeric specifiers on bounded or numeric data.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in ReadMATImageV4's complex-pixel branch: when HDR.imagf==1 and HDR.Type[1] selects depth 8 or 16 (Type[1] in {2,3,4,...}), the row buffer is filled with only depth/8*columns bytes but is passed to InsertComplexFloatRow as a float array of columns elements (4*columns bytes), over-reading up to 3*columns heap bytes per row for every image row.

evidence.reason: Type[1] is an attacker-chosen file digit derived from ldblk (lines 57-60) with only Type[3]==0/Type[2]==0 enforced (lines 61-64), and imagf is a file field (line 69) checked only to be 0 or 1. For witness header ldblk=1200 (Type[1]=2), dims 64x64, imagf=1, nameLen=0, the switch (lines 123-149) sets depth=16, so pixels (line 157) is a 2*columns-byte row buffer filled at line 190 with depth/8*columns bytes; the else branch at line 196 then passes it as a float array of image->columns elements, consuming 4*columns bytes and reading 2*columns (depth=16) or 3*columns (depth=8, Type[1]=4 or 5-9) heap bytes past the allocation, per row for image->rows rows. The guard at line 193 only splits 64-bit double from float and admits every other Type[1] value; no depth-consistency check protects the sink.

assumptions: 64-bit target: size_t is 64-bit, so (size_t)HDR.nRows and depth/8*image->columns widen without loss; the depth/8*image->columns product (max ~3.4e10) fits.
GetQuantumPixels returns a per-scanline gray buffer of at least depth/8*image->columns bytes, consistent with the code's own ReadBlob usage at lines 163 and 190.
InsertComplexFloatRow/InsertComplexDoubleRow consume one float/double per pixel across image->columns pixels, matching the element-count cast at line 196 (and line 194).
limitations: 32-bit integer overflow of depth/8*image->columns (lines 163/190) would only shrink the read (wrapped value is smaller), so no OOB results; not applicable on the assumed 64-bit build (CWE-190 not confirmed).
Unchecked NULL return of GetQuantumPixels (line 157) would be dereferenced by ReadBlob, but only if the allocation fails (OOM-dependent, attacker does not control that size); excluded per rules.
A truncated file causing 0 <= count < requested (not -1, lines 164/191) lets ImportQuantumPixels/InsertComplex* consume stale in-bounds buffer bytes; uninitialized-data hardening concern, no CWE.

Ping-mode seek arithmetic (lines 108-109, HDR.nCols*ldblk with ldblk==Type[0] after line 60) does not match the true data extent and can misparse following images in ping mode, but it is a seek-only logic issue with no memory sink; no CWE.
The nameLen EOF path (line 94-98) breaks only the inner skip loop and continues parsing zeros; subsequent zero-dimension check (lines 103-104) prevents harmful access.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled __u16 stream_num is multiplied by sizeof(__u16) and stored into a __u16 stream_len (line 6) with no bounds check; when stream_num=65535 (out=1, in=0), stream_len=65534 and outlen wraps to 14, so sctp_make_reconf at line 15 reserves only 14 payload bytes while lines 26+29 append 16+65534=65550 bytes, an out-of-bounds skb/heap write of 65536 bytes. The identical wrap affects the in-branch copy at line 40 and stems from the 16-bit truncating arithmetic at lines 6, 12, and 13 (CWE-190) feeding the write sink (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: stream_num is attacker-controlled (userspace SCTP_RESET_STREAMS setsockopt, __u16, no validation in the shown code). The copy length stream_len truncates at line 6 (65535*2 = 131070 → 65534) and outlen truncates at line 12 ((16+65534) → 14), so line 15 allocates only 14 payload bytes. With out=1 and in=0, the branch at line 19 is taken (outlen=14) and this sink copies 65534 bytes after the 16-byte outreq header — 65550 bytes into a 14-byte allocation, a 65536-byte out-of-bounds write. The guard at line 28 (if (stream_len)) only checks non-zero and admits stream_len=65534. The mirrored sink at line 40 repeats the same overflow for the in-request branch.

assumptions: sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_outreq) == 16 and sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_inreq) == 8 (4-byte param header plus three / one __u32 fields).
sctp_make_reconf reserves chunk payload space for exactly the passed length (plus standard SCTP framing overhead), so a wrapped outlen/inlen directly under-allocates the payload.
sctp_addto_chunk performs the requested-length copy into the chunk skb without re-validating the copy against the reserved payload length (kernel implementation appends via skb_put_data).
callers supply a stream_list buffer of at least stream_num*2 bytes copied from userspace; no second length is available to this function.
limitations: The shown code has no loops; all paths are straight-line after the two branches.
A NULL stream_list supplied with stream_num > 0 would fault at lines 29/40, but the shown code cannot itself produce NULL, so it is out of scope.
Caller-side caps (e.g., stream_num bounded by the association's in/out stream counts) are not shown; without them, stream_num up to 65535 is reachable and still triggers the truncation.

When stream_len wraps, htons(outlen)/htons(inlen) transmit truncated parameter lengths and some stream ids are silently dropped — a protocol-correctness issue with no independent security impact, not counted as a separate CWE.
If the underlying skb machinery detects the overrun it panics (skb_over_panic) rather than corrupting memory; either outcome is a kernel memory-safety failure.

verdict.summary: Balloc() validates only the upper bound on its index parameter: `if (k > Kmax)` triggers a fatal zend_error but nothing rejects k < 0. A negative k (e.g., -1) passes the only guard and reaches `freelist[k]` at line 11 (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125); if that read yields a non-NULL entry, line 12 performs an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), and the else path executes `x = 1 << k` (line 14), which is undefined behavior for negative k. Since k is a caller-supplied index derived from numeric parsing and the shown code imposes no lower-bound check, an attacker-influenced k can corrupt memory.

evidence.reason: k is the function parameter with no lower-bound validation: the only guard, `if (k > Kmax)` at line 6, excludes only values above Kmax (and only if zend_error(E_ERROR) is non-returning), so negative values are admitted. Witness k = -1 evaluates the guard false and reaches line 11, where freelist[-1] reads before the freelist array (CWE-125); if that OOB read returns a non-NULL value, line 12 writes rv->next to freelist[-1] (CWE-787); otherwise line 14 executes `1 << -1`, which is undefined behavior. The missing check is `k < 0` before indexing/sizing.

assumptions: zend_error(E_ERROR, ...) is fatal/non-returning under PHP Zend semantics; the upper-bound guard at line 6 depends on this, otherwise k > Kmax also reaches freelist[k] out of bounds.
Kmax and the freelist array (Kmax+1 entries) are defined in unseen surrounding code; the shown function's only index constraint is the line-6 guard.
k originates from dtoa caller arithmetic on user-influenced numeric values; the shown code itself imposes no invariant that k >= 0.
limitations: The exact value of Kmax is not shown; if a build defines Kmax >= 31 (int width), `1 << k` at line 14 can overflow into the sign bit even for an in-range k — unconfirmed without Kmax.

The out-of-bounds write at line 12 additionally requires the out-of-bounds read at line 11 to yield a non-NULL value (memory-layout dependent); the out-of-bounds read itself is unconditional once a negative k reaches line 11.

Whether a specific dtoa caller can actually produce a negative k is not visible in the shown code; this does not remove the finding because the shown function itself lacks the required lower-bound check.
No separate integer-overflow finding is reported for `sizeof(Bigint) + (x-1)*sizeof(Long)`: it cannot overflow for typical small-Kmax builds.

verdict.summary: Integer truncation in sctp_make_strreset_req: the attacker-controlled __u16 stream_num flows into __u16 stream_len (line 6) and __u16 outlen/inlen (lines 12-13). With stream_num=32767 the sum 16+65534 wraps outlen to 14 and inlen to 6, so sctp_make_reconf (line 15) allocates only 24 bytes, yet the guarded copy sctp_addto_chunk(retval, stream_len, stream_list) at line 29 writes 65534 bytes from attacker-controlled stream_list — a confirmed kernel heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787 consequence of the CWE-190 wraparound).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled parameter stream_num (__u16, unvalidated in the shown code) yields stream_len=65534 on line 6 for stream_num=32767. The size_t sum 16+65534 truncates to __u16 outlen=14 on line 12 and inlen=6 on line 13, so sctp_make_reconf on line 15 allocates only SCTP_PAD4(14)+SCTP_PAD4(6)=24 bytes. The guards at lines 19 and 28 both pass (14 != 0, 65534 != 0), and this line copies 65534 bytes from stream_list into the ~24-byte chunk payload, a confirmed heap out-of-bounds write. No guard bounds stream_len against the allocation size.

assumptions: Line numbers are taken from the presented snippet starting at the function declaration (line 1).
stream_num is fully attacker-controlled in the shown code (e.g., SCTP_RESET_STREAMS ioctl or an in-band peer request); bytes copied from stream_list are attacker-chosen.
sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_outreq)=16 and sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_inreq)=8 (packed param_hdr + __be32 fields), and SCTP_PAD4(x)=((x)+3)&~3, per the SCTP ABI.
limitations: seq/tsn underflow (lines 23-24) only fills protocol header fields; no memory-safety or injection sink in the shown code.
A NULL stream_list with stream_len>0 would crash at lines 29/40, but the shown code never produces NULL; only an out-of-scope caller could supply it.
If an unseen caller capped stream_num below 32760, the wrap witness would be unreachable, but no such cap is visible in the shown code.
Truncation-only cases where stream_len collapses to 0 cause no memory corruption and are not reported.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Attacker-controlled inputs (dlen, msg_name payloads/length) are constrained on every path to the sinks: dlen is capped at TIPC_MAX_USER_MSG_SIZE before tipc_msg_build (lines 16-17, 97); every read of the user-supplied tipc_uaddr is gated by tipc_uaddr_valid(ua, m->msg_namelen) at line 20; the destination branch admits only TIPC_SERVICE_ADDR / TIPC_SOCKET_ADDR / TIPC_SERVICE_RANGE before header construction (lines 60-70); and the ua==NULL fallback rebinds to the in-socket tsk->peer (line 39) with state/type guards at lines 40-55. Unconfirmed concerns (validator internals, zero-length send skb_peek, the peer-alias reinterpretation) are recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: TIPC_MAX_USER_MSG_SIZE == 65535, so the line 16-17 guard admits dlen in [0, 65535] and the int/size_t comparison at line 98 cannot truncate.

tipc_uaddr_valid (invoked at line 20) is the protective check for the line 6 cast: it rejects invalid address-type values and requires msg_namelen to cover the fields the address type actually uses; its exact internal bound is outside this snippet.

m->msg_name points to the per-call kernel copy of the user sockaddr (sockaddr_storage-sized buffer) and msg_namelen is non-negative; tsk->peer is a member of struct tipc_sock, so the line 39 reinterpretation cannot read outside tsk.

Called routines (tipc_send_group_*, tipc_nametbl_lookup_anycast, tipc_node_get_mtu, tipc_msg_build, tipc_msg_skb_clone, tipc_node_xmit, tipc_wait_for_cond/connect) are evaluated per the shown-code-only rule; their correctness is assumed.
The function is invoked only from the kernel socket layer on a validated socket, so sock->sk is non-NULL.
limitations: If tipc_uaddr_valid only validated the addrtype value and not per-field msg_namelen coverage, undersized msg_name buffers could expose kernel-copied bytes to the ua->lookup_node/ua->sa.* reads at lines 63-64/85-86; this cannot be confirmed from the shown code because the validator's bound is in an unseen helper, so it is not a finding.

The line 39 fallback reinterprets the 8-byte tsk->peer as struct tipc_uaddr; accesses stay inside struct tipc_sock but depend on the struct layout — a logic quirk with no demonstrated out-of-bounds access or privilege-boundary crossing.

A zero-length send (dlen==0) could in principle hand skb_peek(&pkts)==NULL to the line 106 tracepoint if tipc_msg_build returned 0 with an empty queue; whether that queue state is reachable depends on unseen tipc_msg_build internals.

Concurrent mutation of tsk->group/tsk->peer/sk state by other threads and any historical TIPC bugs inside tipc_msg_build/tipc_node_xmit (e.g., reassembly/MTU overflow classes) are outside the shown single-threaded path.

verdict.summary: virtbt_rx_handle reads skb->data[0] and calls skb_pull(skb, 1) without first verifying skb->len >= 1, so a zero-length frame from the virtio device causes an out-of-bounds read of the skb data region and an unsigned underflow of skb->len before the frame is forwarded to hci_recv_frame.

evidence.reason: skb->len is attacker-controlled (device-supplied used length passed by the caller) and the shown code imposes no length check before this read. A zero-length frame (skb->len == 0) reaches line 5 and reads one byte outside the valid data region; the subsequent skb_pull(skb, 1) at line 6 underflows skb->len to 4294967295, so the corrupted frame is forwarded to hci_recv_frame at line 14 for recognized packet types.

assumptions: The caller builds skb from virtqueue_get_buf(vq, &used_len) and sizes the frame from the device-supplied used length without a minimum-length guarantee.
vbt->hdev and the storage written by hci_skb_pkt_type are valid, as guaranteed by driver probe.
limitations: Downstream parsing inside hci_recv_frame is not shown, so the exact corruption impact there is not analyzed.
Depending on headroom layout the single-byte read may land inside the skb allocation rather than outside it; it is still outside the data region defined by skb->len.
The shown code contains no loops and no other injection, crypto, or file-handling sinks, so no other vulnerability classes apply here.

verdict.summary: block_insert computes `offset` at L44 as `bdp->textcol + bdp->textlen - (spaces != 0)` in the append branch; with `textcol==0`, `textlen==0` and `endspaces!=0` this yields -1, and L67 passes it to `mch_memmove` as `(size_t)offset` (2^64-1), writing far past the `newp` allocation and reading past `oldp`. No shown guard bounds `offset`: L23-24 only skips insert-mode short lines, and L58-59 clamps `spaces`, not `offset`.

evidence.reason: `offset` is tainted from block_prep-derived bdp fields at L34/L44/L51-52 and only decremented at L56. In the append non-short branch (L39-45), when bdp->textcol==0, bdp->textlen==0 and bdp->endspaces!=0, L44 yields offset==-1; neither the L23-24 guard (covers only b_insert && is_short) nor the L58-59 spaces clamp bounds `offset`. L67 then casts -1 to the size_t copy length (SIZE_MAX), causing an out-of-bounds write past `newp` and an out-of-bounds read from `oldp`; this is a heap OOB write (CWE-787) with no protecting check on the value.

assumptions: Line numbers are assigned to the pasted snippet starting at 1.
colnr_T behaves as a signed integer here; if it were unsigned, the same unclamped computed value would wrap to a near-maximum size_t and still produce the OOB at L67.

The helper `block_prep` (L22) is not shown; the finding uses a field combination (textcol==0, textlen==0, endspaces!=0, is_short==FALSE) that the shown arithmetic at L41/L44 explicitly permits to reach offset==-1.
limitations: The exact circumstances inside the unseen `block_prep` that produce that field combination (e.g. a block selection inside a leading TAB) cannot be verified from the shown code alone.
The variant where offset exceeds STRLEN(oldp) (L67/L91 OOB read) is not independently confirmed without block_prep semantics; it shares the same missing-clamp root cause as the confirmed write.
Storing a negative `curbuf->b_op_end.col` at L101 would corrupt editor state used elsewhere, but the consumer is outside the shown code.
Allocation failure at L64-65 is handled by the NULL check and is not a finding; no injection, crypto, or file-handling sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The sole attacker-influenced path sink, open(name, ... O_NOFOLLOW) at lines 37-38, is protected by O_NOFOLLOW for the final path component, by the myfd<0 failure return (lines 41-42), and by the S_ISREG/S_ISDIR mode gate (lines 32-33); actual flag writes via FS_IOC_SETFLAGS are bounded by kernel ownership/capability checks. There are no memory, injection, crypto, or loop-based issues in the shown code. Residual link-following and TOCTOU concerns depend on unseen caller sanitization and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: name is a valid NUL-terminated C string, as guaranteed by the libarchive entry API.
a is a valid struct archive_write_disk object and archive_set_error accepts the errno value.
The ioctl flags argument is int-compatible on the target platform, matching the int oldflags/newflags locals.
limitations: O_NOFOLLOW only constrains the final path component; a name whose leading components are attacker-created symlinks, or a hard link, would still reach open() at line 38 — mitigation then depends on the unseen caller's path sanitization and kernel ownership/capability checks on FS_IOC_SETFLAGS, so this is a hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability of the shown code.

When fd < 0, the object referenced by name could in principle differ from the object the caller validated (TOCTOU-style); the shown single-threaded sequence contains no concurrent mutation, so no concrete failing witness exists.
Silent ARCHIVE_OK return when open()/ioctl() fails (e.g., ELOOP, EACCES) may skip flag application without reporting — robustness concern, no security impact.
set/clear are not whitelisted, but arbitrary bits only flow through the ioctl flag mask and are ultimately subject to in-kernel checks; the narrowing at line 61 cannot affect any size or index.

verdict.summary: parse_rtcp_bye trusts the RTCP BYE reason-length octet at packet offset 8 without bounding it by the remaining packet size. The guard `size > 8` only proves octet 8 exists, while pj_memcpy then reads `reason.slen` bytes from `pkt+9`; a 9-byte packet whose offset-8 byte is 1 (or up to 255) causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 255 bytes past the packet buffer, which is copied into `peer_sdes_buf_` and logged, leaking heap contents and potentially crashing.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled packet bytes supply the length: `*((pj_uint8_t*)pkt+8)` (line 10, range 0..255) is passed through `PJ_MIN(sizeof(peer_sdes_buf_), ...)` and becomes `reason.slen`. The only guard, `size > 8` (line 8), admits `size == 9`, for which valid indices are 0..8, yet the copy reads from `pkt+9`; a witness of `size = 9` with `pkt[8] = 1` copies 1 byte already past the end, and `pkt[8] = 255` over-reads 255 bytes. `PJ_MIN` caps the destination write but not the source read, so the sink at lines 11-12 reads out of bounds (CWE-125).

assumptions: `pkt`/`size` describe a received RTCP BYE packet, so the octet at offset 8 is attacker-controlled network data; no caller-side length re-validation is visible in the shown code.
`sess->stat.peer_sdes_buf_` has the capacity implied by the `sizeof` used in the `PJ_MIN` at line 9, so the destination write is bounded.
limitations: The immediate caller is not shown; remote reachability is inferred from this being an RTCP parser, and if an unseen caller guaranteed `size >= 9 + len` the over-read would be prevented — no such guarantee appears in the shown code.
Whether the over-read crashes or only leaks depends on memory layout past the packet buffer; leak exposure depends on PJ_LOG visibility, so information-disclosure/DoS impact is conditional.
Lack of explicit NUL-termination of `peer_sdes_buf_` is only a robustness concern because the log uses `%.*s` with an explicit length.

verdict.summary: In readconf_main, when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID are compiled in, `suffix` is set to the end of the filename inside the fixed-size `big_buffer` (line 16) and `sprintf` appends the euid/nodename suffix with no check of remaining buffer space (lines 25, 30, 41). A config-file list entry (attacker-influenceable via `exim -C`) as long as `big_buffer_size - 1` bytes drives an out-of-bounds write of up to ~279 bytes past `big_buffer`, corrupting memory during configuration load (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: `suffix` was computed at line 16 as `filename + Ustrlen(filename)` where `filename` is a copy of an item from `config_main_filelist` (settable via the -C command line) placed at the start of `big_buffer` by `string_nextinlist` (line 10), so it can legally extend to `big_buffer_size - 1` bytes. This sprintf writes 3..279 bytes at `suffix` with no guard comparing `Ustrlen(filename) + needed` against `big_buffer_size`; the `%.256s` cap only bounds `uts.nodename`, not the write position. With `big_buffer_size` = 20000 and a 19999-byte filename, `suffix = &big_buffer[19999]` and the write (e.g., ".0.x\0") lands 4+ bytes past the end of `big_buffer` — a confirmed out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: `big_buffer` is a fixed-size buffer of `big_buffer_size` bytes (typically BIG_BUFFER_SIZE = 20000) and `string_nextinlist` copies each list item into its start, NUL-terminated, with a maximum item length of `big_buffer_size - 1`.

The vulnerable suffix-append branch compiles only when `CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE` and/or `CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID` are enabled at build time; both branches are present in the shown source (lines 15, 20, 38, 53).
`config_main_filelist` is attacker-influenceable through the `-C` command-line argument (argv); per lines 85-86 this path sets `config_changed` and the code gives away privilege at startup.
limitations: Line 391 `Ustrtol(s, ...)` dereferences `s = expand_string(host_number_string)` (line 390) with no NULL check; the NULL-producing path requires a failed expansion of an admin-supplied config option, which is not attacker-controlled here, so it is not confirmed as a vulnerability.
Line 400 stores `n` into `host_number` with only an upper-bound check (`n > LOCALHOST_MAX`); a negative value is accepted, but any misuse occurs outside the shown code.
Lines 78-82 log `config_main_filelist`/`filename` verbatim via `%s`; newline injection into logs is possible only with same-user `-C` input, with no privilege boundary crossed.

The overflow's escalation impact is not established from the shown code: the attacker-controlled `-C` path drops privilege before this point (lines 85-86), and the compiled-in default config list is not attacker-controlled.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in PQconnectPoll. Every attacker-influenced length/index reaching memory or allocation operations is bounded by explicit guards (auth-message length caps [8,2000] for 'R' and [8,30000] for 'E', body-availability gate at line 1095, port range [1,65535] at line 131, socket-path length < UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN at line 173, host-array bound whichhost < nconnhost at line 85) or by the OS getaddrinfo contract (ai_addrlen <= sizeof(sockaddr_storage)) for the memcpy at line 280. All format strings are literal with attacker data only as arguments; queries are constant literals; requirepeer fails closed; SSL/GSS retries are one-shot and the post-handshake unencrypted-data checks abort.

assumptions: conn is a valid PGconn produced by PQconnectStart/PQconnectdb/PQconnectStartParams, so whichhost starts in [0, nconnhost-1] and connhost[] has nconnhost entries.

The getaddrinfo/pg_getaddrinfo_all contract guarantees ai_addrlen equals the concrete sockaddr size for ai_family (sockaddr_in 16, sockaddr_in6 28, sockaddr_un <= 110 bytes), all <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage), so memcpy at line 280-281 cannot overflow conn->raddr.addr regardless of the attacker-chosen hostname/hostaddr/port strings.

Unix-domain path construction via the UNIXSOCK_PATH macro (line 172, implementation not shown) is a bounded writer into portstr[MAXPGPATH]; the shown strlen check at line 173 then limits the value handed to pg_getaddrinfo_all.
The unseen buffer helpers pqGetc/pqGetInt/pqGets_append/pqParseInput3 maintain inStart <= inCursor <= inEnd and return error instead of reading past inEnd.

pqsecure_open_client/pqsecure_open_gss, pqBuildStartupPacket3, pqGetErrorNotice3, and pg_fe_sendauth internals are outside the shown code; their inputs in the shown code are pre-validated (msgLength caps, constant data, or locally built packets).
limitations: No explicit numeric guard before memcpy(&conn->raddr.addr, addr_cur->ai_addr, addr_cur->ai_addrlen) at lines 280-281; safety is by OS getaddrinfo contract rather than a shown check, so it is a hardening observation, not a confirmed OOB (no attacker-chosen string can inflate ai_addrlen past sockaddr_storage).

A malicious server could stream 'E' bytes without a newline through the pre-3.0 path (pqGets_append at line 1068) to grow conn->errorMessage; the growth occurs inside the unseen helper and impact is DoS-only against a client that chose to connect, so it is not a confirmed finding in the shown code.

Connection parameters containing newlines (host/hostaddr/port) are copied verbatim into conn->errorMessage (e.g., lines 149-151, 162-164). If an unseen caller logs PQerrorMessage, this could amount to log injection, but the log write is outside the shown code and the data is the connector's own configuration, so it is demoted.

SSL/GSS 'prefer'/'allow' fallback-to-plaintext paths (lines 876-884, 1140-1179) are user-selected documented downgrade semantics and retry at most once; they are not treated as a code-level weak-crypto finding.

verdict.summary: fname_match contains no confirmed vulnerability. The only memory operations are home_replace_save's allocation at line 18 (NULL-checked at line 19 before use, freed exactly once at line 21, and never returned) and vim_free. Regex calls at lines 13/19 are guarded against NULL name/p by lines 9 and 19, and the regex engine/pattern compilation are outside the shown code. No injection, crypto, file-access, or authz sinks exist in the function.

assumptions: rmp is a valid non-NULL regmatch_T* supplied by the caller; the shown code contains no path that produces a NULL rmp.
p_fic is trusted framework global state.
name and p are NUL-terminated strings as consumed by the unseen vim_regexec/home_replace_save implementations.
The regex pattern inside rmp->regprog and the regex engine implementation are not part of the provided shown code.
limitations: ReDoS (CWE-1333) cannot be confirmed: the actual regex evaluation and pattern compilation occur in unseen code (vim_regexec is a pass-through in this snippet), and the pattern's provenance, quantifiers, and engine backtracking behavior are unobservable here.

A NULL rmp dereference at line 12 (rmp->rm_ic) is reachable only if an unseen caller passes rmp == NULL; the shown code never produces that value, so it is treated as a caller-supplied limitation, not a finding.
Allocation-size/copy logic inside home_replace_save is not shown, so any size-derived memory error there is outside this snippet's scope.
The behavior of returning the original name (line 20) even when only the HOME-replaced form matched is a logic quirk with no demonstrated security impact.
No loops exist in the function, so loop-bound/iteration analysis is vacuous.

verdict.summary: stl_update_connects_remove_1 indexes stl->neighbors_start[facet_num] after validating only facet_num < 0; any facet_num >= number_of_facets passes the guard and reads out of bounds on the heap (e.g., facet_num == stl->stats.number_of_facets reads one element past the end), enabling crashes or heap information disclosure from crafted STL-derived input.

evidence.reason: facet_num is a caller-supplied, attacker-influenced index whose only guard is `facet_num < 0` (line 6); the upper side is unconstrained, so the value facet_num == number_of_facets (the allocated length of neighbors_start) passes the guard and dereferences neighbor[0] one element past the heap allocation at line 10 (similarly lines 11-12), causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: neighbors_start is allocated with one entry per facet (stl->stats.number_of_facets) by unseen caller code, and is indexed by facet number.
facet_num originates from user/file-derived facet indices in libstl callers, so it is treated as attacker-controlled.
limitations: Repeated removal of the same facet could underflow the stats counters (signed int UB), but no attacker-relevant impact was demonstrated.
j == 3 (all neighbors -1) simply takes no branch; no security impact.
No other sink classes (injection, crypto, file ops) exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: pxa3xx_gcu_write truncates the user-controlled size_t count into a signed 32-bit int (line 9) with no range check. On 64-bit kernels a huge count (e.g. 0x340000000) makes words negative, which passes the upper-bound-only guard at line 17 and bypasses the required lower bound. The negative words*4 product wraps to a large positive length supplied to copy_from_user (line 37), overflowing the fixed BATCH_WORDS*4-byte kernel buffer with attacker data, and the same tainted value is used as an out-of-bounds array index at line 49.

evidence.reason: count is attacker-controlled via write(); line 9 computes words = (int)(count/4), so count = 0x340000000 yields words = -805306368. The guard at line 17 (words >= PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS) admits all negative values, so execution reaches this sink; the int product words*4 wraps to 1073741824 and is widened to unsigned long, copying ~1 GiB into the BATCH_WORDS*4-byte buffer->ptr allocation — a confirmed heap out-of-bounds write sized by attacker input.

The same truncated words value reaches this index after passing the upper-bound-only check at line 17. For count = 0x340000000, words = -805306368 (and for count = 2^34-4, words = -1), so the write of 0x01000000 lands outside the BATCH_WORDS-word array — an out-of-bounds write into adjacent kernel memory.

assumptions: 64-bit kernel build where size_t is 8 bytes and int is 4 bytes; on 32-bit builds count/4 cannot exceed INT_MAX, so the truncation does not trigger there.
PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS is a small positive compile-time constant and the batch buffers hold BATCH_WORDS words, so every negative words value passes the line-17 guard regardless of its exact value.
buffer->ptr is the BATCH_WORDS-word data area of the batch object, so valid indices are 0..BATCH_WORDS-1 and valid copy sizes are at most BATCH_WORDS*4 bytes.
limitations: Exploitation as privilege escalation additionally requires write access to the pxa3xx-gcu device node; with a root-only node the direct trigger is limited to that principal, though the overflow still corrupts kernel memory.

copy_from_user with the wrapped length can fail access_ok and return -EFAULT before line 49 executes, but the attacker can mmap the ~1 GiB source range to make the overflow copy succeed fully; even a partial copy corrupts the heap.
buffer->length (line 46) stores the negative/truncated words value; its consumers are outside the shown code, so no separate finding is claimed from it.
priv->shared->num_words += words (line 14) can wrap a statistics counter with negative words; not security-relevant.
No loops are present in the shown code, so no loop-bound or ReDoS concerns apply.

verdict.summary: stl_update_connects_remove_1 indexes stl->neighbors_start with facet_num after only an stl->error check (lines 4-8); a caller-supplied facet_num outside [0, stl->stats.number_of_facets) causes an out-of-bounds heap read whose values feed the stats-decrement branch.

evidence.reason: facet_num is a caller-supplied int reaching the array-index sink with no bounds check in the shown code; the only guard, `if (stl->error) return;` (line 4), does not constrain it. neighbors_start holds stl->stats.number_of_facets entries, so facet_num == number_of_facets or facet_num == -1 passes the guard and performs an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125), and the OOB values feed j, which selects the stats counter decremented at lines 10/12/14.

assumptions: stl->neighbors_start is a heap allocation of stl->stats.number_of_facets stl_neighbors entries, per the library's allocation invariant (set up outside this function).
facet_num originates from facet indices derived from the input STL file in the removal/merge pipeline, so it is attacker-influenced.
limitations: Whether a particular unseen caller passes an out-of-range facet_num is not shown; the shown code itself provides no protection, so per the analysis rules the OOB index is treated as a confirmed finding.
Stats counters can underflow if decremented when already 0 (e.g., double facet removal); this needs extra state and is only statistics corruption, not an independent CWE.
NULL stl dereference is out of scope: the shown code never produces a NULL pointer.
The references to neighbors_start[1]/[2] on the same line yields the same OOB class as neighbor[0]; treated as one finding.

verdict.summary: The m= line length gate at line 9 computes len >= media.slen+transport.slen+36 in unsigned pj_size_t with no overflow check. An attacker-controlled token-length pair whose sum wraps (e.g., media.slen=0xFFFFFFFF, transport.slen=0 on a 32-bit build, RHS becomes 35) lets the gate pass an undersized buffer, and line 14's pj_memcpy then writes media.slen bytes out of bounds, corrupting memory (CWE-190 leading to CWE-787).

evidence.reason: m->desc.media.slen is attacker-controlled SDP token length and is not capped anywhere in the shown code. The only guard before this copy, line 9 (`if (len < (pj_size_t)m->desc.media.slen+m->desc.transport.slen+12+24) return -1;`), sums media.slen + transport.slen + 36 with no overflow check: with media.slen=0xFFFFFFFF, transport.slen=0 on a 32-bit pj_size_t build the RHS wraps to 35, so len=64 passes the guard, and this memcpy copies ~4 GiB into the 64-byte buf, an out-of-bounds write (and OOB read of media.ptr).

assumptions: m->desc.port and m->desc.port_count are pj_uint16_t, so pj_utoa emits at most 5 digits + NUL.
print_connection_info/print_bandw/print_attr validate their own len argument and return negative on failure, so no write boundary is violated inside the shown advance logic.
In the real PJSIP pipeline, m->desc.fmt_count is capped at PJMEDIA_MAX_SDP_FMT by the SDP parser, which is unseen here.
limitations: Triggering the confirmed overflow requires token lengths whose sum approaches 2^32 (32-bit pj_size_t) or 2^64 (64-bit), i.e., input strings of ~4 GiB or larger, which real SIP/SDP message-size limits make practically undeliverable; the shown code itself imposes no such cap.
Cast of `end-p` (ptrdiff_t) to int at lines 46/55/64 only becomes negative for len > INT_MAX, and the unshown callees are expected to fail closed on negative length.
If a caller violated the unseen invariant fmt_count <= PJMEDIA_MAX_SDP_FMT, loop access m->desc.fmt[i] at lines 28-31 could read beyond the fixed array; not independently reachable in the shown code.
Signed/unsigned comparison `end-p > m->desc.fmt[i].slen` at line 28 only misbehaves if p already exceeds end due to a prior overflow, which the shown guards otherwise prevent.

verdict.summary: ga_concat_shorten_esc performs an in-bounds, terminating scan of a NUL-terminated string: the NULL input is handled (lines 10-14), every dereference of *s is short-circuited by *s != NUL (line 22), clen >= 1 for any non-NUL byte (line 20-21), same-character runs preserve character boundaries, the collapse jump p = s - 1 (line 35) stays within [str, NUL], and the only formatted output uses vim_snprintf with "%d" into a fixed buffer (line 32). No attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink with an insufficient guard. Multibyte-reprocessing output duplication and unseen caller contracts are documented as limitations.

assumptions: str is a well-formed NUL-terminated C string; all bounds reasoning relies on the terminator being present and at an in-bounds address.

mb_cptr2char_adv and mb_ptr2char follow Vim's standard behavior: a non-NUL byte advances by at least one byte, and a decoded char equal to c has the same byte length (clen) as c, keeping s on character boundaries.
NUMBUFLEN is at least 100 bytes and vim_snprintf truncates as documented.
ga_concat and ga_concat_esc operate correctly on the grow array and escape/append exactly the requested bytes; their internals are outside the shown code.
limitations: The else-branch (line 38) outputs the full character via ga_concat_esc(gap, p, clen) but the for-loop's ++p (line 16) advances only one byte, so the continuation bytes of a multi-byte character are re-processed as standalone one-byte characters, duplicating/mangling output text for non-ASCII input. This is a correctness defect with no demonstrated memory-safety or injection impact.

A caller supplying a non-NUL-terminated buffer, or passing str that aliases gap->ga_data (whose reallocation inside ga_concat could invalidate str), would break the function's contract; neither condition is established by the shown code.

The adequacy of the escaping performed inside ga_concat_esc (e.g., neutralization of terminal-control sequences) is delegated to unseen helper code and is therefore out of scope as a pass-through sink.

Reads performed inside mb_ptr2char/mb_cptr2char_adv (up to the first non-continuation byte, which is the NUL at end-of-string) are helper-internal and were analyzed only for completeness; no shown-code dereference passes the NUL position.

verdict.summary: The split() helper performs in-bounds pointer writes on all realistic inputs: each token write at line 17 and the NULL terminator at line 32 occur at index i against a capacity of i+1 slots, and all error paths free exactly the owned objects once. The only notable defect, the guard at line 8 (if (!tmp && result)) failing to catch a NULL from the very first realloc and then dereferencing result at line 17, requires an environment-driven failure of a fixed 8-byte allocation whose size is not attacker-controlled, so it is a robustness/DoS limitation rather than a confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability.

assumptions: dupstr (line 2, 17) returns a malloc'd NUL-terminated copy of its argument and is not shown.
arg and delim are valid NUL-terminated strings supplied by the caller; NULL arg/delim would be a caller contract violation.
The caller owns and frees the returned array; no caller code is shown.
strtok is used in a single-threaded context; its internal static state is not synchronized.
limitations: If the first realloc at line 7 fails (8-byte allocation, i==0, result==NULL), the guard at line 8 is false, so line 17 writes through a NULL result pointer (CWE-690/476 class). This requires an allocator failure on a fixed, non-attacker-controlled size and only yields a crash; per the allocation-failure rule it is not a confirmed finding.
The int counter i at lines 4/17/23/32 can only overflow with >= 2^31 tokens (~2 GiB input), which is practically unreachable; flagged as theoretical signed-overflow/DoS only.
dupstr(cptr) at line 17 is unchecked; on failure a NULL entry is stored, truncating the result list early (robustness, no OOB in the shown code).
An input with zero tokens makes split return NULL, indistinguishable from the allocation-failure return; callers cannot detect OOM vs. empty input (robustness).

verdict.summary: In ReadMATImage, the file-controlled Frames field (coders/mat.c:133, read via ReadBlobXXXLong for DimFlag==16) is never validated. At coders/mat.c:416 the unsigned counter is pre-decremented in if(--Frames>0): Frames==0 wraps to UINT_MAX and Frames==0xFFFFFFFF yields up to ~4.29e9 re-entries through goto NEXT_FRAME (line 420, label line 180). Every iteration re-runs SetImageExtent (line 265), RotateImage (line 373) and AcquireNextImage (line 406), allocating fresh pixel caches whose size is also attacker-chosen (SizeX/SizeY), so a tiny crafted MAT file causes effectively unbounded CPU and memory consumption (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Frames is read directly from the attacker-controlled file at line 133 (DimFlag==16 case) with no lower- or upper-bound check, and is unsigned. With Frames==0 the pre-decrement wraps to UINT_MAX (defined unsigned arithmetic), so --Frames>0 is true and control loops back to the NEXT_FRAME label (line 180); with Frames==0xFFFFFFFF it is true for 2^32-1 iterations. Each re-entry re-executes SetImageExtent (line 265), RotateImage (line 373) and AcquireNextImage (line 406) on attacker-chosen SizeX/SizeY, so the iteration count and per-iteration allocation volume are both attacker-controlled and are not bounded by the input file size, enabling denial of service (CPU/memory exhaustion) from a small file.

assumptions: MATLAB_HDR.SizeX/SizeY are size_t (64-bit on mainstream builds), making the ldblk multiplications (2x/4x/8x SizeX, lines 196/202/208/217/230) exact; on such builds the BImgBuff path (allocation line 270, per-row reads line 297, ImportQuantumPixels lines 304/314) stays in bounds, and oversized ldblk only causes a clean allocation-failure throw.
z2qtype is a static array with at least 4 entries, so z2qtype[z] for z in {0,1,2,3} is in bounds.
SetImageExtent (lines 265-267) enforces the configured resource/policy limits, which is the only cap on attacker-chosen SizeX/SizeY on 64-bit builds.

DeleteImageFromList destroys the removed image and rewrites the pointer argument (ImageMagick list semantics), which keeps the compressed-temp image2 lifecycle self-consistent in the shown control flow.
limitations: Integer overflow in ldblk = (ssize_t)(8 * MATLAB_HDR.SizeX) (also 2x/4x variants, lines 196/202/208/217/230) leading to an undersized BImgBuff and OOB read in ImportQuantumPixels (lines 304/314) is only real when MATLAB_HDR.SizeX is 32-bit in arithmetic (32-bit size_t platform); the MATHeader definition is not shown and LP64 builds are safe, so this is not confirmed.
image->colors = one << image->depth with file-controlled depth==64 (lines 207/221 => line 242) is undefined-behavior shift but has no attacker-visible memory effect.

ReadBlobDoublesXXX/ReadBlobFloatsXXX return values are unchecked (lines 348/356); on truncated files the row written to pixels contains stale/leftover buffer bytes, but it is prior file-derived data, not cross-user heap disclosure.
remove_utf8(clone_info->filename) (lines 400/432/477) could delete the input path if an unseen caller passes image_info->file != NULL without a temp-file replacement; caller state is out of scope.
The scanline loop index i is signed int (line 286) and could overflow for SizeY > INT_MAX, but reaching it requires a multi-GB input file and the short-read guard (line 297) aborts far earlier.
Frames loop is mathematically finite (at most 2^32 iterations) and impact is availability-only; no memory-corruption primitive was confirmed in the shown code on 64-bit builds.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write when loading XM patterns: attacker-controlled 16-bit phead[y].rows and header->channum are multiplied at line 278 (rows*channum*6) in 32-bit int arithmetic; a wrapping product (e.g., rows=65535, channum=21846 -> allocated 131,068 bytes) passes the NULL check while the fill loops at lines 302-303 write rows*channum*6 = 8.59 GB through the writes at lines 373-379, overflowing the heap buffer.

evidence.reason: File-controlled values flow to the out-of-bounds heap write: header->channum (line 49, 16-bit word from file, unvalidated) and phead[y].rows (line 264, 16-bit word from file, unvalidated) are multiplied at line 278 as 32-bit ints. Witness rows=65535, channum=21846: 65535*21846*6 = 8,590,065,660 wraps to 131,068, so new mp_ubyte[131068] succeeds and passes the only guard (NULL check at lines 281-284), while the loops at lines 302-303 iterate 1,431,677,610 times and these unconditional writes at bc..bc+5 overflow the 131,068-byte buffer after ~21,845 cells (bc reaches 8,590,065,660). No check bounds rows/channum/bc against the wrapped allocation size.

assumptions: mp_uword is 16-bit unsigned, mp_sint32/mp_uint32 are 32-bit, and 32-bit int multiplication wraps (two's complement) on the build targets.

MP_MAXINSSAMPS=96 and XM_ENVELOPENUMPOINTS=12, so the insData envelope parsing consumes at most 210 of the 230 bytes (safe); MP_MAXSAMPLES is the module sample-array capacity used for the s>=MP_MAXSAMPLES checks.
module->instr/smp/phead are fixed-capacity arrays; insnum is capped at MP_MAXINS at lines 58-59 so instrument/pattern loops stay within the number of entries.
limitations: Confirmed but secondary CWE-125: smpReloc[nbu[sc]] at lines 229/232 and 596/599 indexes a MP_MAXINSSAMPS-element array with a raw file byte 0..255; bytes >= 96 cause an OOB stack-array read whose value is merely written into instr[y].snum (info-only impact).

Confirmed but secondary CWE-787: smp[g+s] writes at lines 544-552 overflow when accumulated s is within 2*samp of MP_MAXSAMPLES (the guard at 628-630 bounds s, not g+s; e.g., s=350, 96 samples, index 400 reached on iteration 25); the 0x102/0x103 branch at lines 177-185/247 has no s cap at all.

Confirmed but secondary CWE-190/787: MODPLUG 'text' extension at lines 778-783 computes len+1 (wraps to 0 for len=0xFFFFFFFF), allocates/zeroes 0 bytes, then f.read(module->message,1,len) writes remaining file bytes into the 0-byte allocation (or NULL).
hdrsize-=4 at line 36 can wrap a small unsigned hdrsize to ~4GB, making line 42 a multi-GB allocation followed by a huge read (DoS/uncaught allocation failure, no direct corruption shown).
Minor heap OOB read: buffer[pc] at lines 308-343 can advance pc past phead[y].patdata by up to 5 bytes when pattern data is truncated.
VERBOSE printf calls (lines 198, 451, 566) use literal format strings with numeric/array args; no format-string injection.
The hdrBuff size computation (line 39) and histogram/GC loops were not found to contain additional memory-safety defects within the shown code.

verdict.summary: fuse_make_bad performs a single atomic bit-set at a compile-time constant offset within a kernel object derived from the inode parameter. No attacker-controlled index, size, length, or value reaches any security-relevant sink; there are no branches, loops, casts, or arithmetic to validate. The only theoretical concern (dereferencing a NULL inode) cannot be reached from within the shown code and is out of scope.

assumptions: inode is a valid, non-NULL kernel inode supplied by the VFS/FUSE core, as required for any fuse inode callback.
get_fuse_inode resolves to a valid struct fuse_inode via container_of at a compile-time offset.
FUSE_I_BAD is a compile-time constant bit number and state is a fixed struct member.
limitations: A NULL or invalid inode would cause a fault, but the shown path cannot produce NULL (no allocation or parse in the shown code), so it would require an out-of-scope caller violating the VFS contract; no CWE assigned.
There is no bounds/arithmetic surface in the shown code, so no missing guard can be identified.

verdict.summary: hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc_wait trusts the firmware-supplied reply length fw.len (filled at L13-L16 via hw_atl_utils_rpc_state_get) and passes (fw.len + 3) / 4 dwords to hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords (L34-L40) after only excluding the 0xFFFF retry marker (L29) and zero (L32). fw.len can be up to 0xFFFE, producing up to 16384 dwords (64 KiB) written into the small fixed-size self->rpc mailbox, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) corrupting adjacent kernel memory.

evidence.reason: fw.len is tainted device/firmware data returned by hw_atl_utils_rpc_state_get (L13-L16) and is the only length source for this write. The guards in the shown path (loop exit at L29 requiring fw.len != 0xFFFF, and L32 requiring non-zero) admit every value in [1, 0xFFFE]; e.g., fw.len = 0xFFFE passes both and yields (0xFFFE+3)/4 = 16384 dwords (64 KiB) written into the fixed-size self->rpc mailbox, and even fw.len = 0x200 yields 128 dwords, exceeding a 96-dword payload. No cap on fw.len relative to the destination capacity exists in the shown code, so the admitted values directly produce the OOB write (CWE-787) at this sink.

assumptions: self->rpc is the standard small mailbox struct (len field + HW_ATL_RPC_MAX dwords, total ~388 bytes) embedded in aq_hw_s; its definition is outside the shown code, but any realistic mailbox is far smaller than the 64 KiB max write.
fw.len is a narrow bitfield whose maximum useful value is bounded by the 0xFFFF retry marker, so the post-loop maximum is 0xFFFE.
Threat model treats NIC firmware/device MMIO as untrusted (emulated/virtualized device or compromised/updateable firmware), consistent with the upstream fix to this function.
limitations: The implementation of hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords is not shown; the semantics that it writes 'dwords' count words to the destination are inferred from usage and the known upstream fix.
self->rpc_addr is also device-controlled, but its assignment occurs outside the shown code, so a separate address-taint claim is not independently confirmed.
The do-while retry loop (L8-L29) is bounded per iteration by the 100000 us poll timeout, so no hang or unbounded-loop finding is made.

If the NIC firmware is immutable trusted hardware in a given deployment, practical exploitability is reduced, but the shown code path and the resulting OOB write are identical for any firmware value in [385, 0xFFFE].

verdict.summary: sixpack_close is a teardown with no confirmed vulnerability: tty->disc_data is nulled under disc_data_lock (lines 3-6), NULL-guarded (line 8), and the frees at lines 22-24 are preceded by the refcount/complete handshake (lines 13-14), netif_stop_queue (line 16), del_timer_sync (lines 18-19), and unregister_netdev (line 20), so no attacker-controlled input reaches a memory sink in the shown code.

assumptions: The refcount/complete protocol is maintained by unshown code: new references to sp are taken while disc_data_lock is held, and sp->dead is completed exactly once when the last holder releases its reference.
tty points to a valid tty_struct installed with this line discipline, per the TTY core close path.
limitations: A use-after-free from a concurrent transmit path writing to sp->xbuff cannot be confirmed: the write operation lives in unshown code (sixpack_xmit), so the dangerous operation is absent from the shown code.
A NULL sp->dev at lines 16/20/24 is not produced by any path in the shown code; only an out-of-scope caller could supply it.
A hang in wait_for_completion (line 14) would require the unshown completion signal to never fire; the shown sequence is finite and contains no self-deadlock.
Freeing buffers with wrong sizes or partial initialization is not assessable here since allocation/setup occurs outside the shown function.

verdict.summary: split() has two allocation-failure-dependent memory-safety bugs.
