No reachable NULL dereference was found: the only NULL-capable producer is checked at lines 17-19.

verdict.summary: networkstatus_parse_vote_from_string dereferences the return value of find_by_keyword() without a NULL check for several mandatory header keywords (K_VOTE_STATUS line 67, K_PUBLISHED line 86, K_VALID_AFTER line 110, K_FRESH_UNTIL line 114, K_VALID_UNTIL line 118, K_VOTING_DELAY line 122, K_KNOWN_FLAGS line 158). A remote attacker who supplies a networkstatus document (vote/consensus/opinion) omitting any of these keywords makes find_by_keyword() return NULL and the shown code reads tok->n_args / tok->args[0], causing a NULL-pointer crash (remote DoS). The K_NETWORK_STATUS_VERSION site shows the intended pattern (tor_assert(tok) at line 41) is missing at these sites.

evidence.reason: tok is the return value of find_by_keyword(tokens, K_VOTE_STATUS) at line 66. The keyword set is attacker-controlled via the network-supplied document s; header tokenization (lines 29-35) does not require 'vote-status' to be present, so a document containing 'network-status-version' but omitting 'vote-status' yields tok==NULL, and line 67 dereferences tok->n_args (NULL read, SIGSEGV). No NULL guard exists between line 66 and this deref, unlike line 41.

tok is find_by_keyword(tokens, K_PUBLISHED) from line 85, reached for NS_TYPE_VOTE/NS_TYPE_OPINION. A vote document that includes 'vote-status vote' but omits the 'published' line passes all prior checks (lines 17-83) and dereferences tok->args[0] while tok==NULL (CWE-476), crashing the parser.

tok is find_by_keyword(tokens, K_VALID_AFTER) from line 109. For a consensus document (ns_type==NS_TYPE_CONSENSUS, 'vote-status consensus' set at lines 70-71, optional K_CONSENSUS_METHOD skipped at lines 98-99), omitting the 'valid-after' line is not rejected anywhere on the path and yields tok==NULL; tok->args[0] is then read at line 110, a NULL-pointer dereference reachable from attacker-controlled document content.

tok is find_by_keyword(tokens, K_KNOWN_FLAGS) from line 155 with no NULL check. A document that supplies all earlier mandatory keywords (vote-status, valid-after, fresh-until, valid-until, voting-delay) but omits the 'known-flags' line reaches this loop condition with tok==NULL, dereferencing tok->n_args (CWE-476).

assumptions: find_by_keyword() returns NULL when its keyword is absent from the token list, per the contract of find_opt_by_keyword/find_by_keyword used throughout this code; the NULL-producing path is internal to that called function and reachable with no prerequisite in the shown code.
s is a NUL-terminated, network-received document (tor_assert(s) at line 17 is the only constraint shown).
DIGEST_LEN=20 and HEX_DIGEST_LEN=40, so 40 hex characters decode to exactly 20 bytes at the base16_decode sites.
limitations: Non-termination of the 'while (!strcmpstart(s, "r "))' loop at line 298 depends on the unshown routerstatus_parse_entry_from_string advancing s; the shown code alone cannot confirm a hang, so it is recorded here with no CWE.

Attacker-reachable assertion aborts for arg-count shortfalls (lines 122, 203, 249, 396) are deliberate assertion defenses (CWE-617-class DoS); they do not dereference attacker-influenced memory beyond the assert and are not the primary finding.
K_LEGACY_DIR_KEY's tok->args[0] at line 278 assumes the unshown token table enforces >=1 arg; unconfirmable from the shown code.
smartlist_get(footer_tokens, 0) (line 361) and smartlist_get(ns->voters, 0) (line 279) were examined and are guarded by lines 360 and 267-270 respectively; not findings.
All base16_decode sites are exact-fit 40-char-to-20-byte operations guarded by strlen==HEX_DIGEST_LEN; not findings.
log_warn %s sites cannot be log-injected because tokenizer args are whitespace-delimited (no CR/LF can survive); not findings.
SHA-1 document digests and the DIGEST_SHA1 default (lines 210, 392, 467) are protocol-design choices, not an exploitable weakness in the shown code.
Additional identical NULL-deref instances (K_FRESH_UNTIL line 114, K_VALID_UNTIL line 118, K_VOTING_DELAY line 122) share the same CWE-476 root cause and are subsumed by the finding.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free in atusb_disconnect: ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) at line 17 releases the ieee802154_hw allocation that contains the atusb struct (hw->priv), but line 20 still reads atusb->usb_dev and passes the stale pointer to usb_put_dev(). Every disconnect/unbind executes this sequence unconditionally with no guard between the free and the use, yielding a UAF read of freed kernel memory and a put_device() refcount write through a dangling pointer (CWE-416).

evidence.reason: Taint: atusb originates from usb_get_intfdata(interface) at line 3 and is freed by ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw) at line 17 (hw->priv lies inside the freed wpan_phy/ieee802154_hw allocation). Reachability: the shown path is unconditional - there is no branch, NULL check, or refcount between line 17 and line 20, so any device disconnect/unbind reads atusb->usb_dev from freed memory and hands the stale pointer to usb_put_dev()/put_device(), a refcount write through freed data. Impact: use-after-free read of kernel memory with potential crash and, under slab reuse, refcount corruption (CWE-416). The protective ordering used elsewhere (usb_put_dev before ieee802154_free_hw) is absent here.

assumptions: atusb is the driver-private data allocated via ieee802154_alloc_hw(sizeof(struct atusb), ...), so it lives inside the ieee802154_hw/wpan_phy allocation and is freed by ieee802154_free_hw(); this is the documented API ownership contract.
usb_get_intfdata(interface) is non-NULL on the disconnect path because the USB core invokes disconnect only for a successfully probed, driver-bound interface.
limitations: NULL dereference of atusb at line 5 is not a confirmed finding: no shown path produces a NULL interface data pointer, so it fails the reachability test.
No branches or loops exist in the shown function; all statements run in a fixed sequence.

Exploitation beyond a crash (arbitrary refcount corruption) additionally depends on the freed slab being reclaimed with attacker-controlled contents between line 17 and line 20; absent that, the impact is undefined-behavior/UAF read and kernel crash.
No injection, weak-crypto, file-handling, or OOB index candidates were present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is confirmable in ins_bs from the shown code. The pointer-arithmetic sinks are each protected: the softtabstop reads at lines 210-211 sit behind `curwin->w_cursor.col > 0` (line 209); the looped read at line 248 is only evaluated while `vcol > want_vcol` (line 247) with `want_vcol >= 0` and vcol equal to the cursor's virtual column (0 at column 0), so the dereference never runs at col == 0; the trim write at line 128 is behind `len > 0` (line 127); `cpc` (line 14) exactly matches utfc_ptr2char's MAX_MCO-entry contract; and the word loop (lines 285-356) exits on `col > mincol` with mincol >= 0, never calling dec_cursor() from col == 0 in a non-RIGHTLEFT build. The revins (FEAT_RIGHTLEFT) bypass and unshown helper invariants (ins_bs_one, dec_cursor, ml_get at line 0) are recorded in limitations rather than findings, since the failing operation would occur outside the shown code.

assumptions: ml_get_cursor() returns the line text pointer at byte offset col, with 0 <= col <= STRLEN(line); the line's NUL terminator and bytes 0..STRLEN-1 are in-bounds in Vim's memline.

ins_bs_one() maintains the invariant vcol == virtual column of the cursor by subtracting the displayed width (>= 1) of the deleted ASCII space/TAB from vcol; utfc_ptr2char() writes at most MAX_MCO entries into the supplied array.
Vim enforces maximum line lengths well below the range of colnr_T, so the (colnr_T)STRLEN / (int)STRLEN casts at lines 90 and 126 cannot truncate in practice.
Threat model is the standard 'crafted file opened in Vim plus user/rescripted insert-mode backspace'; there are no shell/SQL/log/header/HTML or crypto sinks in the function.
The main safety argument assumes a non-FEAT_RIGHTLEFT build (revins path analyzed separately as a limitation).
limitations: The repeated read `*(ml_get_cursor() - 1)` at line 248 has no inline `col > 0` check; its safety rests on the indirect bound `vcol > want_vcol` (line 247) with want_vcol >= 0 and the vcol==virtual-column invariant. If ins_bs_one() (unshown) ever desynchronizes vcol from the cursor position, this becomes a one-byte heap OOB read (CWE-125) — no failing witness is derivable from the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.

With FEAT_RIGHTLEFT and revins_on, `!revins_on &&` at line 26 bypasses the line-1/col-0 guard, and `revins_on ||` at line 350 plus dec_cursor() at lines 177/226/290 can move the cursor to line 0; the actual out-of-bounds behavior would occur inside the unshown dec_cursor()/ml_get(0) helpers (pass-through), and the inc_cursor()/coladd interactions at lines 51-52 and 59-72 leave reachability unproven from this code alone.

Heap-buffer writes during deletion/insertion (del_char, ins_str, ins_char, do_join, fix_indent) and replace-stack helpers (replace_pop, replace_do_bs, mb_replace_pop_ins) are all delegated to unshown code; any flaw inside them is outside the scope of the shown function.
No confirmed finding means likelihood-based candidates (softtabstop read at col 0, revins line-0 walk) carry no CWE per the scoring rules.

verdict.summary: In jfs_evict_inode, ji->active_ag is used directly as an index into bmap->db_active at line 35, protected only by the sentinel check `if (ji->active_ag != -1)` at line 33. That guard admits every value other than -1, including indices >= the allocation-group count (witness: active_ag == db_maxag, one past valid index db_maxag-1) and negative non-sentinel values (e.g., -2). The atomic_dec read-modify-write at line 35 therefore performs an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) for any such non-sentinel value, producing memory corruption, kernel crash, and potential privilege escalation.

evidence.reason: ji->active_ag is used as an array index into bmap->db_active (valid indices [0, db_maxag-1] per JFS db_active sizing). The only guard is the preceding `if (ji->active_ag != -1)` (line 33), which admits every value except the -1 sentinel: no lower bound that the index be >= 0 and no upper bound that it be < db_maxag. Concrete witnesses `ji->active_ag == bmp->db_maxag` (one past the end) and `ji->active_ag == -2` (before the start) both pass the guard and reach the read-modify-write at this sink, causing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The value's producer is outside this function (allocation/iget state or uninitialized slab data), which per the analysis scope need not be shown; the dangerous operation and the insufficient guard are both present in the shown code.

assumptions: inode is a valid, non-NULL VFS inode; evict_inode is only invoked by the VFS on a live inode.
bmap->db_active is allocated with one entry per allocation group (db_maxag) by the unseen dbMount(), so valid indices are [0, db_maxag-1].

ji->active_ag is produced outside this function (JFS allocation/iget code, or stale/uninitialized inode state); its exact producer is not in the shown code, which is permitted by the reachability rule for sinks present in the shown code.
limitations: The concrete external path that places an out-of-range value into ji->active_ag (e.g., uninitialized slab state after a failed iget, or stale state) is not demonstrated here, which caps confidence at 0.7 rather than higher.

If in the target kernel tree the invariant that active_ag is always in [0, db_maxag-1] holds on every path, this becomes a hardening/robustness concern; the shown code itself cannot establish that invariant and provides no range check at the sink.

BUG_ON at line 30 depends on anon_inode_list state maintained by unseen code; no attacker-reachable path to a non-empty list is demonstrated in the shown control flow, so it is not a confirmed vulnerability.
diFree, jfs_free_zero_link, dquot_*, truncate_inode_pages_final delegate their logic to unseen callees; any faults inside them are out of scope.
Line 5's jfs_info call uses a compile-time literal format with a matched %p argument; no format-string or log injection is possible.

verdict.summary: Attacker-influenced lengths and indices are constrained before every buffer use: iend is capped by MAX_SCAN_SIZE (lines 75-78) and bounds the iend+2-byte allocation (79), the decode call at line 212 is protected by the `i > iend` guard (209-211) so buf+i stays within buf[0..iend] with non-negative length iend-i, and the loop terminates via `i >= iend` (448). The only suspicious format-string path writes flag names into comments without the '%' sanitization applied on the sibling path, but no printf-family consumer of that data exists in the shown code, so it is out of scope.

assumptions: MAX_SCAN_SIZE is a small positive constant well below INT_MAX, so the ut64->int narrowing of iend at line 71 cannot admit a range larger than the intended cap.
radare2's function invariant min_addr(fcn) <= fcn->addr <= max_addr(fcn) holds, so size_t i = addr - start (line 152) does not underflow in the `str == "f"` path.
Unseen callees honor their contracts: r_anal_op respects the length argument (iend - i), r_io_read_at respects the buffer size, and get_next_i bounds i within the scan range.
core, core->anal and core->anal->cur are non-NULL framework invariants at every dereference in the shown code.
limitations: The int truncation at line 71 (iend = end - start) can wrap a huge requested range to a small positive iend; this only shrinks the admitted scan and never enlarges a buffer or pointer offset in the shown code, so no OOB is reachable from it.

At the boundary i == iend the shown code passes length 0 to r_anal_op (line 212); the pointer remains in-bounds, but whether a decoder over-reads despite len=0 depends on the unseen r_anal_op implementation.

The MIPS ADD path stores f->name into a meta comment (line 326) without the '%' replacement applied to is_string_at output at line 332; any format-string crash would occur in the unseen downstream agf consumer, which is absent from the shown code.
Unchecked strdup results (lines 101, 124) can be NULL only on OOM with trusted register-profile strings; not attacker-controlled.
ESIL parse/hook internals (r_anal_esil_parse, esilbreak_mem_read/write/reg_write) are not shown; their behavior is not assessed here.
Potential pathological runtime from a huge op.size or from get_next_i backtracking is unconfirmed: the shown loop is finite-state and always makes progress.

verdict.summary: In the fallback path of get_lisp_indent(), `col` is the byte column of the matched parenthesis while the loop at lines 97-101 advances one character per decrement; on lines whose prefix contains multibyte characters the loop reaches the line's NUL with `col > 0`, then `that++` at line 114 steps one byte past the NUL and the whitespace-skip reads at lines 118-122 (`VIM_ISWHITE(*that)`, `lbr_chartabsize(line, that, ...)`) perform a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Triggered by opening a crafted file whose line shapes satisfy the shown path.

evidence.reason: Taint: `that = ml_get_curline()` (line 88) returns the attacker-controlled line, and `col = pos->col` (line 86) is the byte column of the matched paren returned by `findmatch()` (lines 17/18/22); neither is validated against the line's character count. In the loop at lines 97-101, `lbr_chartabsize_adv(line, &that, ...)` advances `that` by one character and `col--` decrements by one per character, so for a line of e.g. 21 two-byte characters plus '(' at byte column 42 (22 characters total), the loop stops at the NUL with `col = 20`; the branch at line 109 fails, and `that++` at line 114 moves `that` one byte past the NUL. The sink read `VIM_ISWHITE(*that)` and `lbr_chartabsize(line, that, ...)` at lines 118-120 then read heap bytes beyond the line buffer; the guard `while (*that && col)` at line 97 establishes no character-count invariant and neither whitespace loop (lines 118, 164) tests `*that != NUL`, so no shown check prevents the one-past-NUL pointer from reaching the sink.

assumptions: `ml_get_curline()` returns a NUL-terminated line buffer, and bytes beyond the NUL are not guaranteed to be within the allocation.
`findmatch()` returns a valid buffer position whose `col` is a byte column (`colnr_T`), consistent with its use at lines 84-86.
`lbr_chartabsize_adv()` advances `that` by one character (1-4 bytes) and returns that character's display width.
`VIM_ISWHITE(x)` evaluates the byte `x` against space/tab.
limitations: The read past the NUL may land in allocator slack of Vim's line buffer, so practical impact is typically an ASan-detectable out-of-bounds read rather than a guaranteed crash.

Reaching the vulnerable fallback requires `amount == -1` (line 82), i.e. the extra-trick loop at lines 33-80 must not find an intervening line with `parencount == 0`; attacker file layout and cursor placement in the editor must satisfy that path.
Lines consisting only of single-byte (ASCII) characters cannot trigger the overflow because byte column equals character count.
No write, exec, format-string, SQL, logging, or auth sink exists in the shown code; the only confirmed class is memory safety (read), so only CWE-125 is reported.
Invoking `get_lisp_indent()` requires an interactive editor action (e.g. reindent with `lisp`/`lispoptions`); opening the crafted file alone does not execute the function.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in bgp_capability_msg_parse: memcpy at line 51 copies sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) (4) bytes from pnt+3, while the only guard (line 43) bounds the optional payload by the attacker-controlled hdr->length. A capability with hdr->length in 0..3 (e.g., a 3-byte message with length=0) passes both length checks but reads up to 4 bytes past the message end.

evidence.reason: hdr->length is an attacker-controlled capability byte (read at line 25) and the guard at line 43 only ensures pnt + hdr->length + 3 <= end, i.e. that hdr->length payload bytes exist after the 3-byte header. The sink copies a fixed 4 bytes from pnt+3 with no requirement that hdr->length >= 4, so a message with hdr->length 0..3 (e.g., total remaining length 3 with header {SET, any, 0}, passing both line 18 and line 43) reads 1-4 bytes past end. The read is unconditional of hdr->code and feeds the MP branch (lines 55-57), so the OOB bytes can reach logs via iana_afi2str/iana_safi2str.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) == 4 (2-byte AFI, 1-byte reserved, 1-byte SAFI).
pnt/length define the exact logical message bounds, so end is one-past-the-last-valid-byte.
bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int (line 65) returns nonzero for any out-of-range AFI/SAFI, keeping afc_recv/afc/afc_nego indices in bounds; the validating helper is outside the shown code.
limitations: Log sink arguments are static format strings plus peer->host (operator-configured) and bounded numeric bytes; no log/format-string injection is confirmed.
The out-of-bounds read may remain inside the surrounding packet buffer allocation in some layouts, but it exceeds the logical message bounds and is still an OOB read per the analysis rules.
Array writes at lines 88-96 would be OOB only if the unshown AFI/SAFI mapping helper fails its contract; not confirmable from the shown code.
No command, SQL, crypto, or file-handling sinks exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: extract_archive_thread accepts attacker-controlled archive metadata without validating symlink targets or resolving links: it creates symlinks with arbitrary targets (line 220) and then opens/writes regular files (lines 202, 206-207) at paths that are only lexically sanitized (line 45). A two-entry archive — symlink 'evil' -> attacker directory, then regular file 'evil/pwned' — writes file contents outside the extraction destination, enabling arbitrary file write/overwrite within the extracting user's privileges (CWE-59, link following).

evidence.reason: Sink: creates a symlink whose target is the attacker-controlled archive_entry_symlink (taint from archive metadata at entry read) with no validation at all. The only upstream guard, _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe at line 45, sanitizes the entry's own name ('evil') lexically and imposes no constraint on the link target, so an archive entry named 'evil' can install destination/evil pointing to /tmp (or /home/user/.ssh).

evidence.snippet: ostream = (GOutputStream *) g_file_replace (file, NULL, FALSE, G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION, cancellable, &load_data->error);
evidence.reason: Sink: opens/truncates the destination of 'file', which for a subsequent entry named 'evil/pwned' resolves to destination/evil/pwned. The line-45 guard admits 'evil/pwned' (relative, no '..'), but the parent directory resolves through the line-220 symlink to the attacker-chosen /tmp, so the file is created outside the extraction destination; the guard covers only the lexical name, not the link-resolved location.

Sink: writes the attacker-chosen archive payload bytes into the stream opened at line 202, completing the arbitrary file write at the symlink-resolved path (e.g., /tmp/pwned) outside the extraction root.

assumptions: _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe (line 45) performs lexical sanitization only: it returns NULL for absolute/escaping names and admits clean relative names, but cannot resolve symlinks; junk_paths is off so multi-component relative paths like 'evil/pwned' are preserved.

GIO's local-file implementation of g_file_replace resolves symlinked parent directories (temp file + rename in the target's directory), so destination/evil/pwned resolves through the attacker symlink.
The extracting process runs with the unprivileged user's rights, so 'arbitrary write' is bounded by those privileges.
limitations: Direct path traversal ('../', absolute paths) is not confirmed because the implementation of _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe is outside the shown code; if it strips to a basename only (junk_paths mode), the symlink write-through requires junk_paths disabled (the default pass-through mode assumed here).
Hardlink creation (line 154) is confined lexically to the destination; an escape would require an unconfirmed helper bypass and is not claimed.
Unbounded g_strdup/g_strconcat of attacker-sized names (lines 44, 141) is a single-shot allocation with no demonstrated failing allocation and no compounding loop, so no DoS finding.
g_object_unref(NULL) at line 95 is a GLib no-op; no reachable NULL dereference exists in the shown code.
No format-string, command, SQL, log-injection, weak-crypto, or ReDoS sinks exist in this function.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in ReadCINImage's raster loop: the per-row read length (line 378) is derived from the attacker-controlled channel bits_per_pixel (image->depth, line 344) via GetBytesPerRow, while the destination pixels buffer (line 385) is sized for the fixed 32-bit quantums set at line 375 (≈ columns×3×4 bytes) and nothing bounds length against that capacity before ReadBlobStream (line 394) writes length bytes; the only file-size guard at line 352 and the post-write count guard at line 395 do not cover this, so depth>32 with a sufficiently large file overflows the heap.

evidence.reason: length is attacker-controlled end-to-end: bits_per_pixel (byte 0..255 read at line 136) is assigned to image->depth at line 344 with no clamp, and length=GetBytesPerRow(image->columns,3,image->depth,MagickTrue) at line 378 grows with depth, while the pixels buffer obtained at line 385 is sized for the fixed 32-bit quantum set at line 375 (≈ columns×3×4 bytes, un-padded after SetQuantumPad(...,0) at line 384). Guard 352 (columns*rows/8 ≤ GetBlobSize) constrains neither depth nor per-row length, and guard 395 (count==length) passes exactly when the full length-byte write occurs, i.e., precisely the overflow condition. Concrete witness: bits_per_pixel=255, pixels_per_line=100, lines_per_image=1, number_channels=3, file ≥ header+9568 bytes → length=(100*3*255/8+31)&~31=9568 written into a ≈1200-byte buffer (~8368-byte heap overwrite); even with a 4-channel extent (16×columns) depth=64 (24×columns) still overflows.

assumptions: GetQuantumPixels/SetQuantumPad size the pixels buffer from the fixed 32-bit quantum configured at line 375 (≈ columns×number_channels×4 bytes, un-padded after SetQuantumPad(image,quantum_info,0) at line 384) and do not rescale it to the attacker-derived length; no such rescale appears in the shown code.
ReadBlobStream copies the bytes it reads from the file into the caller buffer, and the attacker supplies enough file data for a full length-byte read, so the write size equals length.
limitations: The finding relies on the QuantumInfo extent formula; if an unseen helper resized the buffer to length, the overflow would not occur — but the shown code contains no such protection, and with depth=64 even a 4-channel 32-bit extent (16×columns) is smaller than length (24×columns), so the overflow is robust across plausible extent formulas.

The seek loop at line 354 can read up to image_offset≈4G bytes byte-by-byte; it is bounded by file size (EOF break at line 360 and throw at line 363) and is only an I/O/CPU cost, not a memory-safety finding.
The user-data allocation at line 335 is bounded by the file-size check at line 333 and its failure is handled at line 337; it is a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
File-derived strings stored via SetImageProperty may contain control characters, but no log/header/command/SQL injection sink exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in do_arg_all(): the file-opening loop (line 198) is bounded by count, which is clamped to the initial ARGCOUNT snapshot (lines 180-181), and dereferences AARGLIST(alist)[i] at line 254 without re-checking the current alist->al_ga.ga_len. Autocommands run inside the loop (do_ecmd/win_split/win_close) can shrink the arglist, so i can exceed ga_len and read past the ga_data allocation.

evidence.reason: i at this sink is constrained only by count, clamped at lines 180-181 to opened_len (the initial ARGCOUNT), never by the current alist->al_ga.ga_len; the only arglist-size guard, line 86, protects the earlier window-matching loop, not this one. Concrete failure: with args 'a b', :all, and a BufReadPost autocommand that shrinks the arglist (e.g. :argdel) during the first do_ecmd, ga_len becomes 1 while i reaches 1 (or 0 with ga_len 0), so AARGLIST(alist)[i] reads past the end of the heap ga_data array, causing an out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: ARGCOUNT is the length of the global argument list and, in the common case alist == &global_alist, ga_len == ARGCOUNT at entry; ARGCOUNT is read once into opened_len.
As stated by the in-code comments (lines 49-51 and 178-179), autocommands can change the argument-list size while arglist_locked is TRUE; a shrinking change is required to trigger the OOB read.
limitations: If the target build's arglist lock blocks every size-changing command (e.g. :argdel/:argadd) while do_arg_all runs, the shrinking path is unreachable and the OOB read cannot occur; the snippet itself never re-validates the size.

The read requires the user to run :all/:tab drop in a session where an autocommand shortens the arglist; no command/SQL/format-string injection, weak-crypto, or authz issues are present in this function.

assumptions: MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is the declared dimension of the MngInfo exists/frozen/invisible/x_off/y_off/object_clip arrays (valid indices 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1), corroborated by the shown loops at lines 114 and 326 and the CLIP/MOVE guards that reject i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS.
Line numbers were counted from the first line of the provided snippet (no source file path was supplied).
limitations: MAGN magnification computes (png_uint_32)((image->columns-2)*magn_mx); 32-bit truncation could desynchronize the pixel-write loops from large_image->columns, but requires an embedded PNG layer wider than ~65539 px, a bound not established in the shown code, so it is not confirmed.

TERM/FRAM handlers read a few bytes past the logical chunk length (e.g. mng_get_long(&p[2]) at line 343 with length < 6) but stay inside the length+MagickPathExtent allocation; only uninitialized heap bytes are consumed, with no shown security impact.
A chunk truncated by EOF leaves the allocated tail uninitialized; downstream handlers may consume those bytes with no shown memory-safety or confidentiality impact.
MNG LOOP/ENDL use a raw 32-bit iteration count without the PNG_UINT_31_MAX cap applied to TERM, allowing a multi-billion-pass re-read of the enclosed data — a bounded, volume-scaled DoS concern only.
object_id values 257..65535 are clamped to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS and hit the same OOB index as the confirmed witness 256.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability is confirmable in the shown do_cmdline() code. All memory operations are bounded by explicit guards or documented ownership contracts: lines_ga reads at lines 220-221, 454, and 492 are protected by current_line < ga_len (line 177) / ga_len > current_line (line 449) / ga_len > 0 (line 489); cmdline_copy is always an owned fgetline/strsave allocation (lines 255, 290, 298) so VIM_CLEAR/free at 181, 388, 569 and STRMOVE at 402 stay in bounds; fgetline and vim_strsave NULL results are checked (255, 291); recursion is bounded at max(200, p_mfd) (lines 53-57). No injection, crypto, file, or authz sink exists in the shown code.

assumptions: FEAT_EVAL builds are assumed (code under #ifdef FEAT_EVAL).
fgetline returns a newly allocated, NUL-terminated line or NULL (per comment at line 171 and NULL-check at 255).
STRMOVE has memmove semantics, making the overlapping tail move at 402 safe when both operands are in the same buffer.
do_one_cmd maintains the documented contract (lines 366-369): returns NULL or a pointer inside the buffer now referenced by *cmdlinep, and writes buffer replacement back through the pointer argument.
lines_ga is a garray of owned wcmd_T entries; free_cmdlines/ga_clear own them.
get_loop_line()/store_loop_line() keep lines_ga.ga_len and cmd_loop_cookie.current_line synchronized.
limitations: STRMOVE at line 402 depends on the do_one_cmd in-buffer return contract; the shown code contains no in-line bounds assertion for that pointer, and a concrete failing witness cannot be constructed from the shown code alone.
msg_verbose_cmd at line 364 receives attacker/script-controlled cmdline_copy, but the actual log write/escaping occurs in an unseen helper, so log injection cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

Recursion guard (lines 53-57) permits up to max(200, p_mfd) nested do_cmdline frames; stack-exhaustion DoS would require unseen recursive callers (:execute, function calls) and attacker control of 'maxfuncdepth', so it is not a confirmed finding.
Indexing of cstack arrays (cs_pending/cs_flags/cs_line, e.g. lines 508, 512) assumes do_one_cmd()/rewind_conditionals() keep cs_idx within [0, CSIDX_MAX]; that invariant is enforced in unseen code.
Main-loop non-termination would require fgetline to never return NULL (caller-provided callback), which is outside the shown code.
In-place '%'/'#' expansion and line-continuation appends happen inside unseen do_one_cmd; their internal bounds are not verifiable here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The dangerous-looking operations are all guarded: the ut32 truncation when accumulating total_slide_infos is caught by the overflow check at line 18 (boundary value 2^32-1 + 1 rejected), the infos[] writes at lines 60-63 are tightly bounded by the line-29 allocation because k increments at most once per (i, j) pair summing to total_slide_infos, inner reads are bounds-checked by rz_buf_fread_at with break on short read, the memcpy at line 82 and the maps[1] read at lines 98-99 are within allocation/guard bounds, and all allocations and prev_info dereferences are null-guarded. Remaining concerns (maps array length invariant, ut64 wraparound flows into the unseen get_rebase_info, struct/format size consistency) are not confirmable within the shown code.

assumptions: cache, cache->hdr, cache->buf and cache->hdr_offset are non-NULL and hdr_offset has at least n_hdr entries (parser invariant).
cache->maps has at least mappingCount entries (parser invariant) in the rizin dyldcache loader.
rz_buf_read_le32_at / rz_buf_fread_at are bounds-checked buffered reads that return failure/short counts on out-of-range offsets.
The format string "6lii" decodes exactly sizeof(cache_mapping_slide) bytes, so the local 'entry' write at line 55 is sized correctly.
RZ_NEWS0 maps to calloc, which fails (returns NULL) on overflow/oversize, and all such failures are explicitly handled.
get_rebase_info handles its offset/size arguments without memory-safety failure (code not shown).
limitations: cache->maps[1] (lines 98-99) is safe only if the unseen parser guarantees len(maps) >= mappingCount; no concrete witness within the shown code can violate both the guard and that invariant, so this stays a limitation.

ut64 wraparound in slide_infos_offset += hdr_offset (line 48), infos[k].end = start + entry.size (line 61), and entry.slideInfoOffset + hdr_offset (line 63) could produce wrapped values, but they only feed the bounds-checked read at line 55 and the unshown caller get_rebase_info; no memory operation in the shown code indexes with these values.

A file-controlled n_slide_infos[i] up to 2^32-1 can request a very large allocation at line 29; failure is checked, and the fill loop breaks on the first failed read, so this is DoS-hardening only, not a confirmed finding.
Potential stack overflow of 'entry' from a format/struct size mismatch at line 55 is unverifiable from the shown code and presumed consistent.
NULL or otherwise invalid cache/cache->hdr values could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller.

verdict.summary: cp_create allows an attacker-controlled maxrlvls encoder option (line 166) to bound the loop at line 282, which writes prcwidthexpns[rlvlno] and prcheightexpns[rlvlno] (lines 283-284) past the fixed-size member arrays of the heap-allocated jpc_enc_cp_t. No upper-bound check exists before the write; the only maxrlvls validation (line 376, maxrlvls < 1) runs afterward and admits the triggering value (e.g., maxrlvls=100), yielding a heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: rlvlno is bounded only by tccp->maxrlvls, which is set directly from attacker-controlled optstr at line 166 (case OPT_MAXRLVLS: tccp->maxrlvls = atoi(jas_tvparser_getval(tvp))) with no range check. For a witness value maxrlvls=100, indices 0..99 are written into the fixed-size prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns member arrays, overflowing at index >= JPC_MAXRLVLS (33). The only maxrlvls guard in the shown code is the later lower-bound test at line 376 (cp->tccp.maxrlvls < 1), which runs after the loop and admits 100, so the sink is unprotected.

assumptions: prcwidthexpns and prcheightexpns are fixed-size member arrays of jpc_enc_tccp_t embedded in the heap-allocated jpc_enc_cp_t (line 28), so indices beyond the array length are out-of-bounds heap writes.
optstr originates from user/attacker-supplied encoder options passed by the caller (command-line or configuration string).
jas_tvparser_next returns 0 while a tag=value token is available, so an optstr containing maxrlvls=100 reaches line 166.
limitations: Unsigned wraparound in cp->imgareatlx *= hsteplcm (line 234), cp->imgareatly *= vsteplcm (line 242), and numtiles = numhtiles * numvtiles (line 317) could corrupt tile math, but no memory operation in the shown code consumes those values, so no concrete failure is demonstrated.

A long ilyrrates list can force an allocation at line 321 before the numlyrs > 16384 cap at line 370; the size scales with the input string and no out-of-bounds access is shown, so this is a DoS-only concern, not a confirmed finding.
Option values containing newlines could inject extra lines into jas_eprintf output (e.g., lines 147, 205, 214), but no log/security boundary is established in the shown code.
atoi on huge option strings can be undefined (overflow); in practice it clamps to INT_MAX, which merely amplifies the confirmed maxrlvls overflow.

verdict.summary: In the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write path, the caller-supplied block length data->block[0] is never validated and is stored into the u8 dma_size (line 119); block[0]=255 wraps dma_size to 0 so the memcpy length at line 124 becomes SIZE_MAX, and any block[0] in 33..254 copies 33..254 bytes, giving a reachable kernel out-of-bounds write/read (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: dma_size is declared u8 (line 8) and assigned dma_size = data->block[0] + 1 (line 119) with int arithmetic narrowed to u8, so block[0]=255 yields dma_size=0 and the length argument dma_size - 1 evaluates to -1 (int) then SIZE_MAX as size_t; block[0] in 33..254 yields 33..254-byte copies. data->block[0] is the attacker-controllable SMBus block-length byte and is not constrained on this path — the only length guards (lines 138-139 for BLOCK_PROC_CALL, lines 153-157 for I2C_BLOCK_DATA) do not apply to the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write case (lines 115-124) — so the untrusted value reaches this memcpy and over-reads past the 34-byte block union member and over-writes beyond the DMA buffer, a confirmed out-of-bounds write/read.

assumptions: I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX is 32 and the uapi i2c_smbus_data block member holds I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX+2 bytes.
data->block[0] is the SMBus block-length byte supplied by the caller (e.g., via the I2C_SMBUS ioctl path or kernel i2c_smbus_* callers).
dma_size = data->block[0] + 1 is computed in int and then narrowed to u8 because dma_size is declared u8.
limitations: The copy is in-bounds for block[0] <= 32 (indices 1..32 of the 34-byte block buffer), so any upstream caller that always clamps data->block[0] to I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX would neutralize the trigger; no such clamp exists anywhere in the shown code.

The exact size of priv->buffer (the DMA buffer backing dma_buffer) is not declared in the shown code; the block[0]=255 wrap witness is decisive regardless of that size because the copy length is SIZE_MAX.
ismt_process_desc (line 236) and the dma_map_single/dma_unmap_single implementations are outside the shown code and were not analyzed.

verdict.summary: The XM loader writes sample structures through the cumulative index `smp[g+s]` in the version 0x102/0x103 instrument-header loop without any `MP_MAXSAMPLES` bound (the only such checks are in the later sample-data loops), so a crafted file with many instruments/samples performs an out-of-bounds write (e.g., 128 instruments × 96 samples reaches index ~12192). Independently, the per-note sample map bytes `nbu[sc]` (raw file bytes, 0..255) are used unchecked to index the MP_MAXINSSAMPS-element `smpReloc` array at lines 229/596, giving an out-of-bounds read (e.g., nbu[0]=0xFB reads smpReloc[251]). Other concerns (pattern decompression reads past `patdata`, `len+1` wrap in the MODPLUG text block, negative-length instrument reads, header-size underflow allocations) are noted as limitations because their write/alloc primitives or failure modes live outside the shown code.

evidence.reason: File-controlled `insnum` (line 51, capped at MP_MAXINS) and per-instrument `numSamples` (lines 85-88, capped at MP_MAXINSSAMPS) accumulate into `s` (line 247) and `g`, and the write `smp[g+s]` executes before any MP_MAXSAMPLES bound on this ver=0x102/0x103 path; the only MP_MAXSAMPLES checks are in the later load loops (lines 629/677), which cannot undo these writes. Witness: ver=0x102, insnum=128, every instrument numSamples=96 → indices ≈12192..12288 against an array of MP_MAXSAMPLES (≤255). Guard at line 86 covers only the per-instrument count, not the cumulative index, so an attacker-controlled file drives an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

`nbu` is copied verbatim from attacker-controlled file bytes (line 112, memcpy of MP_MAXINSSAMPS bytes into the instrument header buffer), and `nbu[sc]` (a byte, range 0..255) indexes the MP_MAXINSSAMPS-element stack array `smpReloc`. The only nearby guard (line 86) bounds `numSamples`, not the sample-map byte values, so e.g. `nbu[0]=0xFB` indexes `smpReloc[251]` beyond the array's 96 entries — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the read value then selects `instr[y].snum[sc]` at lines 229-232, and the identical unchecked pattern exists at line 596 for ver=0x104.

assumptions: MP_MAXSAMPLES is a fixed module-table bound smaller than MP_MAXINS × MP_MAXINSSAMPS (e.g., 255 vs 128×96); the loader's own check `if (s>=MP_MAXSAMPLES) return MP_OUT_OF_MEMORY;` at lines 629/677 confirms MP_MAXSAMPLES is the intended size of `module->smp`.
MP_MAXINSSAMPS (the XM per-instrument sample map size, ≤96) is smaller than 256, so raw file bytes in `nbu` can always exceed the `smpReloc` array extent.
`module->smp` is a fixed table (`TXMSample smp[MP_MAXSAMPLES]`) allocated by the framework, and `module->cleanUp()`/caller guarantees the struct pointers are valid (checked at line 17).
limitations: Pattern decompression reads `buffer[pc]`/`memcpy(slot,buffer+pc,5)` (lines 308-343) past the `patdata`-sized heap buffer when `patdata` is smaller than the parsed `rows*channum` cells (witness: patdata=1, first byte 0xFF reads buffer[1..5]); same CWE-125 class as the secondary finding, omitted from the verdict for focus.

MODPLUG text block: `len=0xFFFFFFFF` wraps `len+1` to 0 (lines 778-779) and `f.read(module->message, 1, len)` (line 783) would write up to the remaining file size into a tiny buffer; the write primitive and allocation semantics live in unseen `allocateSongMessage`/`f.read`.

`f.read(insData, 1, instr[y].size - 33)` (lines 107, 461) is reached with negative 32-bit counts for instrument sizes 30-32 (or negative sizes), turning the length into a huge unsigned value; actual write behavior depends on the unseen `f.read` implementation.

`header->hdrsize -= 4` (line 36) can underflow to ~0xFFFFFFFC, forcing an ~4GB allocation at line 42 followed by an unchecked `memset` at line 43 — a DoS/NULL-deref only if the massive allocation fails, and allocation success would make it benign, so it is not counted as a finding.
ModPlug stereo conversion `sample[i + samplen]` (lines 708, 724) assumes `loadModuleSample` allocated exactly `oldSize` samples; buffer sizing is delegated to unseen code.

verdict.summary: decode_errcode_attr derives value.slen from the attacker-controlled STUN attribute length via 'attr->hdr.length - 4' (line 19) with no guard that length >= 4; a length of 0 underflows to 65532 and is passed to pj_strdup (line 22), causing an out-of-bounds read from buf+8 and an attacker-sized allocation. Line 15 additionally reads buf[6]/buf[7] with no length check.

evidence.reason: attr->hdr.length (from attacker-controlled buf bytes via GETATTRHDR, line 13) is subtracted without a '>= 4' check at line 19, so length=0 wraps value.slen to 65532; pj_strdup then copies that attacker-controlled byte count from value.ptr = buf+8 (line 18), reading far past the STUN message (CWE-190 root cause producing a CWE-125 out-of-bounds read).

buf[6] and buf[7] are read with no check on attr->hdr.length; an ERROR-CODE attribute with length field 0 ending the receive buffer leaves only 4 bytes valid, so both reads are out of bounds (CWE-125), the same missing-length-check flaw.

assumptions: GETATTRHDR reads the standard 4-byte STUN attribute header so that attr->hdr.length is the 16-bit value at buf[2..3], ATTR_HDR_LEN == 4, and length arithmetic is unsigned.
pj_strdup allocates and copies value.slen bytes from value.ptr.
buf points to raw attribute data from an untrusted STUN packet, with only the 4-byte header guaranteed by the unseen caller.
limitations: Caller-side STUN message validation is not shown; if an unseen caller rejected length < 4 before calling this function the underflow would be unreachable, but the shown code imposes no such check and msghdr (the natural bound source) is deliberately unused.
The OOB read at line 15 is definitely outside the attribute value for length < 2 and fully out-of-bounds when the truncated attribute is the last bytes of the receive buffer.
pj_strdup's destination allocation and any write-side impact depend on its unseen implementation; the bounded-read and oversized-allocation consequences are confirmed from the shown length flow.

verdict.summary: OS command injection: attacker-controlled title, description, and feed_title are concatenated unquoted into a shell command line and executed via /bin/sh -c (utils::run_program, line 31) or run_interactively (line 22). Only the URL field receives shell-quote escaping (line 12); the other three fields pass shell metacharacters (e.g. $(...) or ;) unchanged.

evidence.snippet:
std::string cmdline = strprintf::fmt("%s '%s' %s %s %s",
		                                       bookmark_cmd,
		                                       utils::replace_all(url,"'", "%27"),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(title)),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(description)),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(feed_title)));
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled title/description/feed_title (function parameters supplied from feed content) are substituted into the bare %s slots. stfl::quote is an STFL-escaper and quote_empty only adds '' for empties, so shell metacharacters survive. A title of "$(touch /tmp/pwned)" reaches cmdline byte-for-byte in an unquoted position; only the url slot (line 12, inside the format's literal single quotes) is shell-escaped, and no guard constrains the other three fields.

cmdline (built at lines 10-15 with unconstrinated attacker content) is passed as the argument to /bin/sh -c via my_argv[2] and executed by utils::run_program at line 31. The guard at line 9 (bookmark_cmd.length() > 0) only checks that a command is configured and does not restrict the payload; the witness title="$(touch /tmp/pwned)" is executed as a command substitution. The same cmdline reaches the exec sink utils::run_interactively at line 22 in the interactive branch.

assumptions: title, description, and feed_title originate from feed/item content published by an untrusted feed owner, i.e., attacker-controlled.
stfl::quote escapes characters for the STFL form-language context (e.g. double quotes/backslashes) and does not neutralize shell syntax; quote_empty only maps empty strings to ''.
bookmark-cmd is operator configuration, not attacker-controlled; the finding requires it to be non-empty, which is the feature's normal configuration (line 9).
limitations: Log injection is possible at line 17 (attacker newlines/metacharacters inside cmdline are written to the DEBUG log), but it is a minor integrity concern and is not counted as a separate CWE.
The URL field's ' -> %27 replacement is protective only for that slot and inside its quote context; it does not sanitize the other fields and produces URL mojibake (correctness, not security).

Helper implementations (stfl::quote, quote_empty, utils::run_program/run_interactively internals) are outside the shown code; the analysis relies on their documented STFL/shell-execution semantics, and the code's own explicit single-quote escaping of only url corroborates that the other fields are not shell-escaped.

verdict.summary: cookedprint() shows no confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All attacker-influenced data reaching memory or output sinks is gated: the LF/OC cases write only fixed indices or use snprintf with sizeof(b) (lines 76-91); the RF fallback requires strlen(value) <= 4 before output (line 65-66); the raw-output block caps copies at MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN via atoascii into 2* sized buffers before the single-byte append at bv[len+1] (lines 117-128); decoder success flags gate decoded values. The only remaining risks depend on unseen callee contracts (decodearr/outputarr discipline on lfparr[8], atoascii honoring its len cap and NUL-terminating), which are out of scope for this snippet.

assumptions: MAXVARLEN and MAXVALLEN are >= 1 so that the 2* sized buffers can hold the capped copy plus the appended output_raw byte and NUL.
nextvar() advances length/data and NUL-terminates name/value so the while loop terminates and strlen(value) is bounded by the packet buffer.
decodeuint/decodets/decodenetnum/decodearr only report success when they fully initialized their out-parameters.
atoascii honors its length argument and NUL-terminates its output; decodearr fills at most the 8 elements of lfparr and sets narr consistently (standard NTP ntpq semantics).
limitations: AR case: a write past lfparr[8] or an inconsistent narr would occur inside decodearr/outputarr, which are not part of the shown code; not confirmable here.

The safety of bv[len] = output_raw; bv[len+1] = '\0' depends on atoascii capping at MAXVALLEN chars; if the callee ignored its len parameter and wrote sizeof(bv)-1 chars, strlen(bv) could reach 2*MAXVALLEN-1 and bv[len+1] would be out of bounds. No evidence in the shown code supports that callee behavior.

Newline/control characters in name or value reaching fprintf(stderr, ...) (line 111) could forge console output, but stderr is not a persistent security log and newline survival depends on nextvar's unseen separator handling.
OC case: snprintf(b, 12, "%03lo", uval) silently truncates very large octal output; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: A failed privilege drop is not fatal: if setresuid()/setuid() (lines 6/8) returns -1 with any errno other than EAGAIN, or with EAGAIN on builds without EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE, control falls through and lines 25-26 unconditionally record euid/egid as dropped while the kernel still holds the elevated IDs. A user forcing setuid EAGAIN by exhausting the real user's RLIMIT_NPROC before exec'ing a setuid-root shell leaves the shell running as root but internally believing privileges were dropped (CWE-270); the setresgid failure at lines 19-23 is likewise only reported, never handled.

evidence.reason: When setresuid()/setuid() at lines 6/8 fails, the only abort is line 15, which requires errno == EAGAIN AND the EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE compile flag; every other failure (EPERM, EINVAL, ENOMEM, ENOSYS, and EAGAIN without the flag) reaches lines 25-26, which unconditionally overwrite the cached identity with the drop targets while the kernel effective uid/gid are unchanged (e.g., still 0 for a setuid-root shell). Concrete witness: the invoking user creates RLIMIT_NPROC+1 processes and execs the setuid-root shell, forcing setresuid at line 6 to fail with EAGAIN; on a build without EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE the function returns with euid still 0 and current_user.euid claiming non-root, so the shell executes user commands as root while internal state says the drop succeeded.

assumptions: current_user.{uid,euid,gid,egid} are populated from getuid/geteuid/getgid/getegid at shell startup and therefore reflect actual process identity.
The failure path of the privilege drop is attacker-influencable because the invoking user controls the process limit (RLIMIT_NPROC) checked by setuid on Linux.
sys_error is a printf-family function; its format argument at lines 12 and 23 is a fixed gettext literal, so no format-string injection exists.
limitations: The unhandled setresgid/setgid failure (lines 19-23) is part of the same CWE-270 finding and was folded into it, not counted as a separate CWE.
setuid-before-setgid ordering was not confirmed exploitable on Linux because an unprivileged process may still adopt its own real gid, so the target gid (the real gid) is always adoptable.

The absence of setgroups()/supplementary-group clearing was not treated as a finding: for a setuid-root binary invoked by an unprivileged user, supplementary groups derive from the invoking real uid and do not grant extra privilege.

The bug's exploitability depends on build configuration (EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE defined or not) and on the shell actually being deployed setuid-root, which is why confidence is 0.7 rather than higher.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled STUN ERROR-CODE attribute length (attr->hdr.length from GETATTRHDR, line 13) flows into value.slen = length - 4 (line 19) and then into pj_strdup (line 25) without any upper-bound check against the actual buffer size; msghdr is discarded (line 9). The only guard (lines 21-22) clamps negative values only, so a header length of 0xFFFF yields slen = 65531 and an out-of-bounds heap read of up to 65531 bytes from buf+8 (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: value.slen is derived at line 19 from attr->hdr.length, which is read at line 13 from attacker-controlled STUN message bytes (range 0..65535); value.ptr points to buf+8 (line 18). The guard at lines 21-22 only replaces slen<0 with 0 and admits slen up to 65531, so an attacker setting the 16-bit length field to 0xFFFF makes pj_strdup copy 65531 bytes from buf+8 regardless of how few bytes actually follow, reading past the end of the buffer (out-of-bounds heap read) when the received message is shorter than 4 + length bytes. No upper-bound check against the real buffer size exists in the shown code, and msghdr is unused (line 9).

assumptions: GETATTRHDR (line 13) reads the 16-bit attribute length field from the attacker-controlled buffer at buf[2..3], giving attr->hdr.length the full range 0..65535.
buf points to the start of a STUN ERROR-CODE attribute within a network-received message, and no buffer-size parameter is passed to this function.
ATTR_HDR_LEN is 4, so value.ptr (line 18) is buf+8 and the copy span is [buf+8, buf+4+attr->hdr.length).
limitations: If the unseen calling message parser pre-validates attr->hdr.length against the remaining message bytes before dispatching here, the overflow would be unreachable in the full library; the shown function nevertheless contains no such protection and discards msghdr.
The exact size of the buffer behind buf is not visible in the shown code; the over-read is relative to a buffer shorter than 4 + attr->hdr.length bytes.

The fixed-offset reads at buf[6]/buf[7] (line 15) and the GETATTRHDR 4-byte read (line 13) also lack length checks, but only bite if buf has fewer than 8/4 bytes respectively; they share the same root cause and are not reported as a separate finding.
Because pj_strdup allocates slen+1 bytes for the destination, the out-of-bounds access is a source over-read (CWE-125), not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).
pij_strdup allocation failure (64 KB cap from a 16-bit length) could only cause a single-shot DoS without attacker-controlled volume and is not treated as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in the CoRRE subrect decode loop: the size check at line 19 multiplies the network-controlled CARD32 hdr.nSubrects by (4 + BPP/8) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so values such as 0x20000001 wrap the product to 8 and pass the RFB_BUFFER_SIZE guard; ReadFromRFBServer then reads only 8 bytes while the loop at line 24 iterates 0x20000001 times, reading 8 bytes per iteration past the end of client->buffer (starting at iteration ~513 for a 4096-byte buffer) at the accesses on lines 25-30.

evidence.reason: hdr.nSubrects is attacker-controlled network data (lines 9-12) used as the loop bound with no cap. With BPP=32 each iteration consumes 8 bytes, so the true requirement is nSubrects*8; the only guard, line 19, computes that product in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, and for nSubrects=0x20000001 the product wraps to 8, passing the '> RFB_BUFFER_SIZE' check. ReadFromRFBServer then loads only 8 bytes, but the loop runs 0x20000001 times and ptr advances 8 bytes per iteration, so the reads at lines 25-30 cross the end of the RFB_BUFFER_SIZE-byte buffer (at iteration ~513 for a 4096-byte buffer) — a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read whose garbage values flow into GotFillRect at line 32.

assumptions: BPP is 32 in the vulnerable build (BPP/8 = 4, 8 bytes per subrect); for smaller BPP (e.g. BPP=8, 5 bytes per subrect) the same overflow exists at a different threshold (nSubrects >= 0x33333334).

client->buffer is a heap allocation of exactly RFB_BUFFER_SIZE bytes, a small compile-time constant (typically 4096); the exact value only changes the iteration at which the out-of-bounds read starts, not the reachability of the overflow.
limitations: The integer overflow does not cause an out-of-bounds write into client->buffer because ReadFromRFBServer copies exactly the wrapped (small) length; the demonstrated damage is limited to the out-of-bounds read and downstream use of out-of-bounds bytes.
GotFillRect's implementation is not shown, so the exact effect of the garbage rectangle values (clipping vs. further memory effects) is not assessed; the confirmed primitive is the OOB read itself.
NULL client/buffer/GotFillRect supplied by an unseen caller is out of scope, since the shown code does not itself produce NULL.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The attacker-controlled huff_rec_count is bounded to [2, HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT] by the guards at lines 10 and 15 before it sizes the malloc at line 30 or bounds the loop at line 37; the loop index i is strictly < huff_rec_count - 1, so it never exceeds the last valid index of the count-1 element symbols array; all curr dereferences are NULL-guarded (lines 15, 38); and the only use of the possibly-wrapping huff_rec_index addition (line 8) is a lookup whose NULL result is checked at line 15.

assumptions: HUFF_RECORD_MAXCNT is a modest compile-time constant (e.g., 256), so (huff_rec_count - 1) * sizeof(*huffcdic->symbols) at line 30 cannot overflow size_t.
sizeof(*huffcdic->symbols) is a pointer-sized type, and the underlying types of curr->size, huffcdic->index_read, and huffcdic->index_count are size_t so the %zu conversions in debug_print are valid.
mobi_get_record_by_seqnumber returns NULL for any sequence number outside the record list, so an out-of-range or wrapped huff_rec_index (line 8) cannot select an invalid pointer.
mobi_parse_huff and mobi_parse_cdic honor their own buffer bounds and return MOBI_SUCCESS only after fully parsing their input.
limitations: Any memory-safety defect residing inside mobi_parse_huff (line 23) or mobi_parse_cdic (line 42) is out of scope: those write operations are absent from the shown code.

A wraparound of *huff_rec_index + offset (line 8) could select a different in-range record than intended; this is a robustness/correctness concern, as no memory operation in the shown code is indexed by the wrapped value.

If a pointed-to header field or record size were a non-size_t type, the %zu conversions at lines 20 and 50 would be undefined varargs behavior, but the format strings are literal and the arguments are numeric, so no injection is possible; the types cannot be verified from the shown code.
A single bounded allocation per parse at line 30 cannot be scaled by attacker-controlled volume, so allocation-failure or memory-exhaustion DoS is not compounded and is not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds heap read in jp2_decode: when a BPCC box declares fewer components than the codestream, the mismatch is only warned about (lines 172-175) and the !samedtype loop indexes bpcs[i] up to image_numcmpts-1 instead of bpcc.numcmpts-1, reading past the file-controlled bpcs buffer (line 182).

evidence.reason: bpcs[] has length = bpcc.numcmpts, taken from the attacker-controlled BPCC box by jp2_box_get (lines 63-115); the loop at lines 179-185 is bounded only by JAS_CAST(jas_uint, jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image)), the attacker-controlled codestream component count, and the only count-mismatch check (lines 172-175) prints a warning and does not exit or bound i. Witness: BPCC box with numcmpts=1 plus a codestream with 3 components of differing bit depths (samedtype=false via lines 149-153) makes i=1 and i=2 index bpcs beyond its 1-element heap allocation at this line, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: jp2_box_get allocates bpcc.bpcs with exactly bpcc.numcmpts entries and cmap.ents with exactly cmap.numchans entries (parser not shown).
jas_image_numcmpts() returns a non-negative component count from the decoded codestream.
limitations: NULL dereference of lutents after the unchecked jas_alloc2 at line 274 requires an allocator failure, is OOM-dependent, and is DoS-only; not considered a confirmed finding.
Line 268 takes &dec->cdef->data.cdef when dec->cdef may be NULL, but the value is unused at runtime (referenced only inside #if 0 blocks), so no dereference occurs.
32-bit overflow of i * pclrd->numchans at line 276 would need numlutents*numchans beyond what the parse-time lutdata allocation could satisfy.
Calls such as jas_image_setcmpttype and jas_image_depalettize may have their own internal bounds checks or faults, but those operations are not in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable in the shown cookedprint body. Every memory write located in the shown code is protected by an identifiable guard: b[0..1] is guarded by the uval > 3 check (line 73), the OC formatting uses snprintf with sizeof(b) (line 91), and the raw-output append at lines 122-123 writes into bv[2*MAXVALLEN] after atoascii is requested to copy at most MAXVALLEN bytes (line 119), so no concrete attacker value can be shown to drive len out of bounds. All other dangerous operations (nextvar, decodets/decodenetnum/decodeuint/decodearr, atoascii, output/outputarr) execute in unseen helpers; per scope rules a finding requires the dangerous operation itself in the shown code.

assumptions: MAXVARLEN and MAXVALLEN are positive compile-time constants with MAXVALLEN >= 2, so bv (2*MAXVALLEN) has headroom beyond the MAXVALLEN copy cap.

Helper contracts hold: nextvar NUL-terminates name/value and terminates; atoascii copies at most its size argument and NUL-terminates; decodearr writes at most 8 entries into lfparr; statustoa/prettydate/nntohost/stoa/refnumtoa/tstflags return valid strings.
data and length are only consumed by nextvar in the shown code, so their bounds are enforced only by that unseen parser.
limitations: The append at lines 122-123 (bv[len] = output_raw; bv[len+1] = '\0') is guarded only by output_raw != '*' and has no explicit len < sizeof(bv)-1 check; its safety rests on the unseen atoascii respecting the MAXVALLEN cap into the 2*MAXVALLEN buffer. No witness value producing len == 2*MAXVALLEN-1 is demonstrable in the shown code, so this fails part 2 confirmation.
decodearr fills the 8-element lfparr (line 97) and outputarr reads narr entries (line 100); any overflow/over-read would occur inside those unseen helpers.

The default-case fprintf(stderr, ...) at lines 111-112 writes attacker-influenced name/value (potentially containing newlines) unneutralized, but stderr is a diagnostic stream rather than a security-relevant log sink, so impact is not demonstrable.
statustoa (line 28) could in principle return NULL and be passed to %s, but the NULL-producing path is in the unseen helper, not the shown code.
length is declared int (line 3) and forwarded by pointer to nextvar (line 31); any negative-length or bounds handling is inside the unseen parser.
Silent truncation by snprintf at line 91 is a robustness note only and has no security impact.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled input reaches any security-relevant sink. The inputs are trusted process-identity globals (current_user.*) and OS return values (setuid/setgid, errno). The log sink at lines 8 and 15 uses constant format strings with numeric arguments only, so no injection is possible. The only weakness is that a setuid/setgid failure other than EAGAIN (or EAGAIN in builds without EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) causes the function to continue and update current_user.euid/egid while the OS effective IDs remain elevated; that trigger is OS-environment data, not attacker-controlled in the shown code, and the EAGAIN case is explicitly handled, so it is a defensive-hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: current_user.uid/euid/gid/egid are populated by the shell at startup from getuid()/geteuid()/getgid()/getegid() before disable_priv_mode() is called, so they are trusted OS identity values.
EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is an optional compile-time macro; without it, even the EAGAIN failure path falls through.
sys_error is a varargs error logger accepting a format string and arguments.
limitations: If setuid() fails with errno other than EAGAIN (or with EAGAIN when EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is not defined), lines 13-18 still execute: setgid() is attempted and current_user.euid/egid are overwritten at lines 17-18 even though the OS effective IDs were not changed. This is an improper privilege-drop failure-handling concern (CWE-269 class), but the trigger is OS-generated errno, not attacker-controlled input in the shown code, so it fails the taint requirement and is not confirmed.
The %d conversion at lines 8 and 15 with uid_t/gid_t arguments (typically unsigned) is a variadic type mismatch, but it has no value change or security impact on the target ABIs.
The _() format strings are compile-time constants in the shown code; locale-derived text is not attacker-controlled through any code shown here.
Reachability of the failure path additionally requires an initial state where euid != uid (or egid != gid), which is implied by the function's purpose but not established by the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: handle_returned_header passes a non-NUL-terminated, network-derived header buffer to sscanf with an unbounded %u conversion. After the trailing CRLF is skipped as whitespace, sscanf reads past ptr[len] (out-of-bounds heap read), potentially crashing the process or disclosing adjacent memory. The CRLF check at line 18 only guards indices len-2/len-1 and does not bound the scan.

evidence.reason:
Attack-controlled header bytes (libcurl header callback data, not NUL-terminated) reach the sscanf sink at line 21 via input = ptr + url->timelimit_header_len (line 19). A header whose value region is whitespace-only (or empty) and ends in CRLF passes the guards at lines 14 and 18, but %u treats  and 
 as skippable whitespace and continues reading at ptr[len] and beyond until it finds a non-whitespace byte or a stray NUL, causing an out-of-bounds read that can cross a page boundary and crash the process (CWE-125). The guard at line 18 covers only the len-2/len-1 index accesses and does not bound the scan.

assumptions: libcurl's CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION delivers exactly len bytes of header data that is not NUL-terminated, matching the documented callback contract and the code's own exact-length arithmetic.
stream/auth_user and the config-derived url fields are supplied by trusted framework code; a NULL there is not produced anywhere in the shown code.
url->auth_header / url->timelimit_header are non-empty configured strings with lengths matching the bytes sent by the auth backend.
limitations: time(NULL) + limit (line 22) accepts limit up to UINT_MAX (~136 years), and overflows signed time_t on 32-bit platforms; treated as a connection-lifetime logic concern, not a memory-safety or authorization break in the shown semantics, so no CWE is attached.
size * nmemb (line 4) could in theory wrap, but curl derives both operands from a real allocation the attacker cannot size independently, so no attacker-reachable overflow is shown.
NULL dereferences of auth_user->client / auth->state (lines 5, 8–9) would require an out-of-scope caller to pass invalid state; the shown code never produces NULL on any path.
client->authenticated = 1 (line 12) is correct given a securely random configured auth_header token; any bypass would stem from weak configuration, not from this comparison logic.

verdict.summary: ismt_access trusts attacker-controlled data->block[0] without a length clamp in the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA (write) and I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL paths. On block[0]=255 the u8 assignment dma_size = data->block[0] + 1 wraps to 0, so the memcpy at line 124 computes dma_size - 1 = -1 and converts it to SIZE_MAX, yielding an unbounded out-of-bounds write through dma_buffer plus an out-of-bounds read of the 34-byte i2c_smbus_data union (block[0]=34 already reads one byte past it). Line 145 uses block[0] directly as the copy length. Both copies execute before the dma_size != 0 mapping guards, and the clamp at lines 149-154 covers only I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA.

evidence.reason: Sink for the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write path. Attacker-controlled data->block[0] (u8, 0..255, from the i2c-dev SMBus ioctl union) is used unchecked: line 119 computes dma_size = data->block[0] + 1 as int and narrows to u8, so block[0]=255 wraps dma_size to 0; the third argument dma_size - 1 is then int -1, converted to SIZE_MAX. The copy reads past the 34-byte union i2c_smbus_data.block (indices 0..33; block[0]=34 already reads block[34]) and writes past every finite priv->buffer/dma_buffer allocation. The clamps at lines 149-154 guard only I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA, and the dma_size != 0 guard at line 190 executes after this statement, so no shown check constrains this copy.

Sink for the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL path. Attacker-controlled data->block[0] (0..255) is the memcpy length with no bound check; block[0]=34 already reads block[34], one byte past the 34-byte i2c_smbus_data union, and block[0]=255 copies 255 bytes from data->block while dma_size (line 138) maps only 32 bytes, so the write overruns the DMA-mapped region and the copy source overruns the union (CWE-125 confirmed by the fixed union size; CWE-787 via the line-124 SIZE_MAX variant of the same flaw).

assumptions: data points to a kernel union i2c_smbus_data whose block[] field is I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX + 2 = 34 bytes, per the I2C ABI referenced by the shown use of I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX.

ismt_access is registered as adapter->algo->smbus_xfer, so the I2C core dispatches i2c_smbus_xfer to it directly without the block-length validation that exists only in the emulated fallback; user space supplies the union contents (including block[0]) via the i2c-dev SMBus ioctl.
dma_size arithmetic follows C integer promotions: u8 promotes to int, so dma_size - 1 with dma_size == 0 is int -1, then converts to SIZE_MAX as the memcpy size_t argument.
limitations: The write-side overflow of priv->buffer cannot be measured from the shown code because priv->buffer's capacity is not shown; the line-124 SIZE_MAX copy is nevertheless a confirmed OOB write because it exceeds any finite allocation, and the line-145 write demonstrably overruns the 32-byte DMA mapping.

If an unseen caller always clamped block[0] before calling smbus_xfer the flaw would be unreachable; the shown code itself contains no such clamp for the BLOCK_DATA-write and BLOCK_PROC_CALL paths, and its I2C_BLOCK_DATA clamp shows the intended check that is missing there.
The wr_len_cmd truncation at line 140 (256 into an 8-bit field) is a descriptor inconsistency without independent memory-safety impact and was not counted as a separate finding.
All non-blocking paths (BYTE, BYTE_DATA, WORD_DATA, PROC_CALL, BLOCK_DATA read, and the clamped I2C_BLOCK_DATA) use fixed sizes and were walked and found safe.

verdict.summary: The backtracking regexp matcher performs catastrophic (exponential-time) backtracking for nested unbounded quantifiers such as \([a-z]\+\)\+Q — the exact pattern named in the code comment at lines 24-25 — when matched against attacker-controlled buffer/file text. case BRACE_SIMPLE/STAR/PLUS (905-983) runs regrepeat (946) and pushes RS_STAR_LONG retry states (968-975), and case RS_STAR_LONG backs the input up one character and re-tries in a loop (1368-1425). The only guards are fast_breakcheck() (interactive Ctrl-C only, line 26), a FEAT_RELTIME timeout that applies only when the caller passes tm (line 47), and a p_mmp cap on regstack memory (958-962) that does not bound iteration count, enabling CPU DoS (CWE-1333).

evidence.reason: Unbounded quantifier sink: for the STAR/PLUS op of a nested pattern such as \(a\+\)\+Q, regrepeat greedily consumes up to rst.maxval repetitions of rex.input (taint source: the matched buffer/file text). Every tail failure re-enters the RS_STAR_LONG retry state pushed at line 968 and re-runs this greedy scan; the only guards (got_int at 947 and the p_mmp stack-size cap at 958-962) do not bound the number of retries, so total work is exponential in the input length.

Catastrophic-backtracking sink: with pattern \(a\+\)\+Q and input of n 'a's (no 'Q'), each failed tail match makes RS_STAR_LONG back the input up one character (MB_PTR_BACK, line 1397) and re-try the whole nested body, enumerating all 2^(n-1) partitions of the input — the concrete witness is input length n=40, giving ~5.5e11 regrepeat/match iterations. The per-state retry is bounded only by --rst->count (1377), and nothing in the shown code bounds the number of outer iterations: fast_breakcheck() (1394, also 26) requires an interactive Ctrl-C, the FEAT_RELTIME timeout (47-57) is active only when the caller passes tm != NULL, and the p_mmp cap (958-962) limits regstack memory, not iteration count, so the DoS is not prevented.

assumptions: Inputs to regmatch() are the compiled regexp program (scan) and the global match state rex, whose rex.input/rex.line point into the NUL-terminated buffer/file text being matched, as set up by bt_regexec_both().
Line numbers are relative to the start of the provided snippet (line 1 = 'regmatch(').
Subexpression/brace array subscripts (no = op - MOPEN/MCLOSE/ZOPEN/ZCLOSE/BACKREF/BRACE_COMPLEX) are confined to 0..9 by the case labels, so those indexes cannot exceed NSUBEXP/10.
Buffer lines are NUL-terminated; NUL-bounded reads (cstrncmp at 462/726/746/790, STRLEN-based advances at 479/768/794) therefore stay inside the line allocation.
limitations: MULTIBYTECODE byte loops (516-541) were examined for OOB/infinite-loop behavior: reads are NUL-bounded and utf_ptr2len()/mb_ptr2len() return >= 1 for non-NUL positions, so no concrete failing witness was found.

BACKREF computes len = rex.reg_endpos[no].col - rex.reg_startpos[no].col (744-745), which could be negative in principle, but the shown engine records MCLOSE positions only after MOPEN on the same forward pass (input never moves backward during a pass), keeping same-line end >= start; no failing witness could be shown.

Potential NULL from reg_getline() in the BEHIND2 walk (1288-1293) is guarded by the previous-line reachability checks (1271-1276) and by the current-line invariant; no NULL-producing path is demonstrable in the shown code.
RE_VCOL/RE_COL fall back to 'curwin' when rex.reg_win is NULL (193-195); this is a correctness concern, not a memory-safety issue.

BRACE_COMPLEX pushes (857/876/893) skip the p_mmp check used at 958-962, but ga_grow() fails gracefully and stack depth is bounded by the repeat count (<= MAX_LIMIT), so no attacker-scalable memory exhaustion is demonstrated.

Pattern provenance for the ReDoS finding: in many Vim flows the pattern is user/plugin-supplied (trusted); the finding relies on the matched text (buffer/file content) being attacker-controlled while a nested-quantifier pattern (e.g., \(a\+\)\+Q) is applied, reachable via interactive search/substitute and runtime patterns applied to file contents.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in the libcurl header callback: ptr is treated as if it contained at least auth_header_len / timelimit_header_len bytes and as a NUL-terminated string, but the delivered length bytes = size*nmemb (L4) is never validated against these read lengths and is only used as the return value (L31). A short header fragment (e.g. 4 bytes when auth_header_len is 18) or a matched 22-byte 'icecast-auth-message: ' prefix without an in-fragment NUL causes strncasecmp/sscanf/'%s' to read past the presented buffer (L11, L13, L16, L22), enabling crash (DoS) or memory disclosure.

evidence.reason: Reads up to auth_header_len bytes from the header fragment ptr, which libcurl presents as exactly bytes = size * nmemb (L4) bytes with no guaranteed terminator. No check such as bytes >= url->auth_header_len precedes the read; a delivered fragment shorter than auth_header_len (e.g. 4-byte 'User' fragment against an 18-byte configured prefix) makes strncasecmp read past the presented region (OOB read, CWE-125).

Parses starting at offset timelimit_header_len inside the fragment without verifying bytes >= timelimit_header_len or a terminator; %u continues scanning digits beyond the fragment when the delivered chunk ends early, reading past the presented buffer, and the unbounded value can wrap or, on format mismatch, force limit=0 (immediate disconnect at L17).

After the 22-byte prefix match at L19 (which itself over-reads a fragment shorter than 22 bytes), %s reads from ptr+22 until a NUL byte with no bound by bytes; a matched chunk that is not NUL-terminated inside the presented region makes the read continue past the buffer until a NUL is found elsewhere in memory — an unbounded OOB read (CWE-125) with crash/information-disclosure impact; the write into errormsg is correctly capped.

assumptions: stream points to a valid auth_client, and client->auth/auth->state are non-NULL as maintained by the unseen libcurl/icecast caller; the shown code checks only client (L7).

libcurl's header callback presents exactly bytes = size * nmemb bytes and does not guarantee NUL termination of that region; fragments in a single callback invocation can be shorter than a configured header-name length.
auth_header/auth_header_len and timelimit_header/timelimit_header_len are admin-configured with positive lengths.
limitations: NULL dereference of client->auth or auth->state (L9-L10) is not a finding: the shown code contains no NULL-producing path; a malformed auth_client could only be supplied by an unseen caller.
bytes = size * nmemb (L4) multiplication overflow would require an impractical >4 GB fragment on 32-bit size_t; no security impact shown.

discon_time = time(NULL) + limit (L17) with unbounded %u can overflow 32-bit time_t or cause immediate expiry when '%u\r\n' fails on a fragment boundary; demoted to a DoS-only limitation requirding control of the auth-server reply.

client->authenticated = 1 (L12) on any prefix match, and unconditional match if a configured header length were 0, depend on admin configuration invariants (auth-server protocol and non-empty header strings) not shown or attacker-controlled here.

Whether the over-read crosses an allocation boundary or lands inside libcurl's larger internal buffer affects crash/leak weaponization, but the API-contract OOB read relative to the presented bytes is confirmed by the shown code.

verdict.summary: Unsigned underflow in the status-buffer length arithmetic lets pcl_status_read compute a huge count and copy from outside pcs->status.buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: count is computed at lines 3-4 as min(max_data, write_pos - read_pos) with no guard that read_pos <= write_pos; because both fields are uint, read_pos > write_pos makes the subtraction wrap to a huge value and count becomes max_data. The guard `if (count)` at line 6 only rejects zero, so the witness read_pos=1, write_pos=0, max_data=256 yields count=256 and memcpy reads 255 bytes past a 256-byte pcs->status.buffer; read_pos then wraps at line 8. The offsets derive from the PCL status subsystem fed by file-controlled status data, making the sink reachable with file-chosen state.

assumptions: pcs->status.buffer is a fixed-size heap allocation (exact size not present in this fragment).
Semantics assumed: a producer appends at write_pos and the consumer advances read_pos, so a well-formed state has read_pos <= write_pos.
