The caller guarantees conn/fdev/mdev/conn_res.uar are initialized (relied on at lines 3-4, 48, 71).
wq_ctrl.db points to a two-word doorbell region, so the writes at lines 63-66 stay within the doorbell allocation.
limitations: cq_size (line 1) is an unvalidated signed int; values such as -1 or 0x7fffffff make roundup_pow_of_two()/ilog2() (lines 15-16, 46) produce a wrapped or negative log_cq_size (e.g. cq_size=-1: roundup truncates to 0 in int, ilog2(0) = -1), potentially requesting an oversized or mismatched CQ from the unseen mlx5_cqwq_create() and the firmware, with possible ENOMEM-backed DoS/firmware misbehavior. No memory operation in the shown code is driven by that value, so this is validation/hardening rather than a confirmed memory-safety failure.

inlen is declared int (line 9) while built from size_t arithmetic (lines 31-32); for all reachable npages (bounded by log_cq_size <= 31 -> at most ~2^25 4K pages) inlen stays below INT_MAX, so no conversion overflow is reachable.
A NULL dereference of fdev->mdev or fdev->conn_res.uar (lines 3-4, 48, 71) would require a caller to violate initialization invariants; out of scope.
Firmware-side interpretation of a truncated log_cq_size field cannot be validated from the shown code; any firmware/hardware failure mode is out of scope.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write in glob(3) GLOB_TILDE ~user unescaping: with GLOB_TILDE and a pattern such as "~x\/yyy/z", dirname becomes "~x\/yyy" and newp is allocated with only end_name - dirname (3) bytes, but the backslash-unescape loop (bounded by the string NUL at line 487, not by end_name) copies the entire remainder of dirname plus the terminating NUL, writing up to 3 attacker-controlled bytes past the alloca_account/malloc buffer at lines 502/504.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled pattern (e.g., "~x\/yyy/z" with GLOB_TILDE, without GLOB_NOESCAPE) flows through strrchr (187), dirlen = filename - pattern (238) and the dirname copy (268), yielding dirname = "~x\/yyy". The ~user branch (446) computes end_name = &dirname[3] (449) and unescape = &dirname[2] (463), so newp is allocated as end_name - dirname = 3 bytes (lines 470-471 alloca_account, or 474 malloc). The unescape loop is guarded only by `while (*q != '\0')` (487), i.e., by the string NUL and not by end_name; line 502 then writes '/' plus "yyy" at offsets 1..4 and line 504 writes the NUL at offset 5, an out-of-bounds write of 3 bytes past the 3-byte buffer with attacker-chosen content and length. Guard coverage: the only guard that would skip the copy, `if (end_name == NULL)` (462), is false here, and no shown check bounds the loop to end_name; the safe no-backslash path at 506-508 copies exactly end_name - dirname - 1 bytes plus NUL and fits.

assumptions: The caller enables GLOB_TILDE (or GLOB_TILDE_CHECK) and does not set GLOB_NOESCAPE when passing attacker-influenced patterns.
Non-Windows build; the vulnerable branch is inside #ifndef WINDOWS32.
glob_use_alloca/alloca_account use stack (alloca) for small sizes; glob_in_dir and prefix_array maintain the gl_pathv capacity invariant (outside shown code).
limitations: GLOB_BRACE recursion can expand exponentially for adjacent groups ("{a,b}{a,b}..." yields 2^k recursive glob() calls); this is an algorithmic-complexity DoS on attacker-chosen patterns, but it is not regex (CWE-1333 does not apply) and every recursion terminates, so it is not confirmed as a CWE finding.

The in-place unescape at 790-801 dereferences strchr(dirname, '\\') without a NULL check, but it is reached only under `meta & GLOBPAT_BACKSLASH` (783), which implies a backslash exists — not exploitable in the shown code.
Reachability depends on the caller enabling GLOB_TILDE; deployments that never set it never execute the vulnerable branch.
No injection, weak-crypto, or authz sinks exist in the shown code; helpers glob_in_dir, is_dir, collated_compare, and prefix_array are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: In gem_transmit, the inner loop 'while (tx_desc_get_used(desc) == 0)' iterates without any bound while the condition depends on guest-controlled descriptor memory that is re-read every iteration. A guest can keep the used bit clear and set the wrap bit so packet_desc_addr returns to the queue base, making the loop run forever (QEMU hang / denial of service).

evidence.reason: The loop condition reads the used bit of a descriptor fetched from guest-controlled RAM, and the body re-reads the next descriptor (lines 136-138) after either advancing or wrapping packet_desc_addr to the queue base (lines 123-131). With one crafted descriptor {used=0, wrap=1, last=0, buffer=valid RAM, length=1} it passes the guards at lines 43-44 and 50-51, skips the used-bit write-back because last==0 (lines 70-120 are not taken), and re-reads the same used=0 descriptor forever; the returns at lines 35-37 and breaks at lines 47 and 57 never fire, and no iteration counter or address-repetition check exists in the shown code. This makes the loop unbounded (CWE-835), freezing the QEMU vCPU from guest input.

assumptions: gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) returns the true byte capacity of s->tx_packet, so the guard at lines 50-51 fully bounds the gather copy at lines 63-65.
QEMU device emulation is synchronous, so the guest cannot clear TXENA (line 35) or alter the descriptor ring while gem_transmit is running.
The standard TX path applies: a guest that sets TXENA/TXSTART reaches this function.
limitations: A stack overflow of desc/desc_first is not confirmable from the shown code because DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS and the value range of gem_get_desc_len(s, false) are defined outside the snippet; no failing witness can be constructed here.

An out-of-bounds index q (lines 25, 56, 86, 88, 91, 94, 145) would require s->num_priority_queues to exceed the sizes of s->tx_desc_addr[] and the ISR arrays; the clamping of that field is not shown, so it cannot be confirmed.

The DMA reads/writes (lines 28-30, 63-65, 77-83, 136-138) target the guest physical address space by device design and are not host access-control sinks; only the loop termination issue is treated as a finding.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The attacker-controlled paste stream can only grow idx while STRNCMP(buf, end, idx)==0, which forces idx <= STRLEN(end); combined with the guard at lines 11-13 (STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN -> end = NULL), every write into buf[NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES] stays in bounds (worst-case write index NUMBUFLEN-2+MB_MAXBYTES < buffer size), and end[idx] is read only with idx <= STRLEN(end). The ga_grow/mch_memmove path is covered by ga_grow's capacity guarantee.

assumptions: NUMBUFLEN and MB_MAXBYTES are positive constants, and mb_char2bytes returns 1..MB_MAXBYTES for any nonzero c (c == NUL breaks at line 29), so each iteration advances idx by at least 1.
find_termcode returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL; STRNCMP follows standard strncmp semantics (stops at the first NUL within n bytes).
vpeekc() returns NUL when no character is currently buffered, so the end == NULL path terminates when the finite paste is consumed.
ga_grow(gap, idx) guarantees capacity for at least gap->ga_len + idx items, covering the idx-byte mch_memmove at lines 56-58.
limitations: A stack overflow would occur only if a termcode with STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN were kept in use and a paste continuously matched its prefix; lines 11-13 explicitly set end = NULL in that case, so no such path exists in the shown code.

The end == NULL path processes the paste one character per iteration (O(n) work); this is a performance/robustness property, not an unbounded execution, since each iteration is bounded and the loop terminates when input is exhausted.
If mb_char2bytes could return 0 for a nonzero c, a matching state would not advance idx (livelock); the framework invariant used here excludes that, and no such c is shown.
gap->ga_len integer overflow would require roughly 2 GiB of pasted data in EX mode, is not reachable before allocation failures, and is not compounded by attacker-controlled allocation sizes.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All reads of text via tp[-1] are guarded: line 11 ensures len <= size; the skip loop (line 28) bounds tp to at most text+size-len (ep = text+size-11*len plus at most 10 delta1 advances of <= len each); the tail loop's guard d <= ep-tp (line 70) covers exactly the next tp += d read at line 72. The only weaknesses are theoretical: overflow of the int expressions 12*len/11*len for mind > ~179M bytes (compiler-dependent UB) and reliance on invariants of unseen helpers/constructor (delta1 entries <= len; bm_delta2_search advancing on miss) — demoted to limitations, not findings.

assumptions: kwset->delta is a 256-entry table built by the unseen kwsprep such that every entry d satisfies 0 <= d <= len (missing chars map to len, pattern chars to len-i-1; byte truncation only lowers values).
U() casts its argument to unsigned char before indexing d1, preventing negative indices.
bm_delta2_search respects the [tp, ep] window passed to it and advances tp past ep on a miss, so the tail while-loop at d == 0 terminates.
memchr_kwset scans no more than the [text, text+size) range passed to it, and text/size are a valid (buffer, length) pair provided by the caller.
kwset->target contains at least mind bytes and kwset->mind accurately reflects the pattern length (constructor invariant).
limitations: Integer overflow (undefined behavior) in 12*len (line 26) and 11*len (line 28) when kwset->mind > INT_MAX/12 (~179M); on wrapping two's-complement semantics ep could extend past text+size and the skip loop could over-read. Not treated as a finding: requires a ~179-200 MB pattern and (for the wrap to matter) a >=2.4 GB haystack, the trigger is compiler-dependent UB rather than a concrete value the shown code admits, and typical callers (e.g., argv-limited tools) preclude such a pattern length.

Potential infinite loop in the tail (lines 70-77) if bm_delta2_search ever returned false without advancing tp when d == 0 and tp == ep; the helper is not shown and the standard implementation advances by delta2 >= 1, so this cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

Any over-read inside the unseen helpers memchr_kwset and bm_delta2_search is out of scope: the dangerous operations are not present in the shown code, which only derives in-bounds pointers and ranges (bounded by text+size) for them.

The correctness of the skip-loop bound relies on the unseen delta1 constructor invariant (0 <= d1[c] <= len); if a caller supplied a malformed kwset delta table with entries > len, the bound would fail, but the shown code neither builds nor can validate that table.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is confirmed in the shown open_table() code. The only memory operation sized by input data, memcmp(table->s->table_cache_key.str, key, key_length) at line 66, is protected on the same statement by the exact length-equality guard table->s->table_cache_key.length == key_length at line 65, so both operands are read for exactly key_length bytes from buffers of exactly that length (0-length case reads 0 bytes). All other sinks are either fixed-size (my_malloc(sizeof(*table)) at line 331), data arguments to fixed my_error templates (not format strings), or guarded by framework invariants; the only NULLable value, mdl_ticket, is NULL-checked on the lock-acquisition path (line 170) and on the HAS_MDL_LOCK path is merely copied from the caller's ticket (line 183).

assumptions: get_table_def_key() returns a key buffer of exactly key_length bytes for the table_list (line 53).
For every TABLE_SHARE, table_cache_key.str points to a buffer of at least table_cache_key.length bytes.
thd->open_tables is a NULL-terminated linked list, so the loop at lines 63-94 terminates and never dereferences past the list.
A caller passing MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK has acquired the MDL lock and stored a non-NULL ticket in table_list->mdl_request.ticket (line 183).
Untrusted db/table/alias identifiers are validated by MySQL's identifier parser (no NUL/CR/LF) and are passed to my_error() only as data arguments to fixed templates, never as format strings.
limitations: If an out-of-scope caller combined MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK with a NULL table_list->mdl_request.ticket, then mdl_ticket->get_deadlock_weight() at line 294 could NULL-dereference; the shown code cannot produce NULL on that path (line 183 only copies the caller's value) and the acquire path is guarded by the mdl_ticket == NULL return at line 170, so per scope this is a limitation, not a finding.

Helper functions not shown (set_partitions_as_used, tdc_acquire_share, open_table_from_share, table->init, vcol_fix_expr, check_and_update_table_version, ha_table_exists) are out of scope; any dangerous operation inside them is not part of the shown code.

DBUG_PRINT format specifiers (e.g. line 277) use compile-time constant, non-attacker-controlled strings and framework-typed arguments; any type mismatch would be debug-only and has no security impact.

The lock-selection logic (lines 73-91) can choose a suboptimal lock, but per the code comments its only effect is choosing the error message about lock mode; it does not grant or bypass authorization.

verdict.summary: The dangerous-looking length-derived copy (hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, lines 24-25) is fully guarded: line 19 rejects every on-disk name length > 255, so the sink receives a length in 0..255 and copies at most 510 bytes into the exactly-510-byte unicode[255] destination (boundary 255 fits exactly; 256 is rejected). The type whitelist (line 14) additionally prevents interpreting a non-thread record as a thread, and the record read (line 9) uses a fixed size equal to the stack buffer. No attacker-controlled input reaches an unguarded memory, injection, crypto, file, or authz operation.

assumptions: fd->search_key is a hfs_btree_key union sized to hold a full 520-byte catalog key, per the struct hfs_find_data contract in the kernel.
On success, hfs_brec_read fills the destination with the requested rec_len (520) bytes, so every field read from tmp (type, nodeName.length/unicode, parentID) is within initialized stack storage.
struct hfsplus_cat_thread layout is type(1) + reserved[3] + nodeName(length 2 + unicode 255*2) + parentID(4), packed, totaling 520 bytes, making the source unicode array exactly 510 bytes.
fd is guaranteed non-NULL by the caller contract; no shown path produces a NULL dereference.
limitations: The historical catalog-name-length overflow is not reachable here: the guard at line 19 admits only 0..255 and the maximum 510-byte copy exactly fits the 510-byte unicode[255] destination.
Any short-record overread or incomplete fill inside hfs_brec_read would reside in that unseen helper, not in the shown code; it is a pass-through concern out of scope for this analysis.
Silent/irrelevant: static printk strings contain no attacker data, so log injection does not apply.

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry deletes an existing target file (line 32) before the parent-symlink guard hasSymbolicPart runs (line 36). With overwriteFiles=yes, a two-entry archive plants an absolute symlink a (line 47, allowed even under FollowSymlinks::no) and then extracts a/name; exists()/deleteFile() follow the symlinked parent and unlink a pre-existing file outside targetDirectory before the guard fails the call. Arbitrary file deletion via link following (CWE-59).

evidence.reason: entryPath/entry payload are attacker-controlled ZIP data (lines 6-8, 44). Witness: targetDirectory=/srv/extract, followSymlinks=no, overwriteFiles=yes; entry 'a' isSymbolicLink=true payload '/home/victim/.ssh' creates symlink /srv/extract/a (line 47, permitted since creating a link is not guarded), then entry 'a/authorized_keys' passes the lexical isAChildOf check (line 16), exists() returns true via the symlinked parent, and this deleteFile() unlinks /home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys outside the extraction root. The guard intended for this (hasSymbolicPart at line 36) is sequenced after the delete and can only abort post-deletion; no check constrains the delete itself, so the guard's admitted set (no symlinked parent) does not cover the executed destructive operation.

assumptions: zei->entry (filename, isSymbolicLink, fileTime) and entry payloads are parsed from attacker-controlled ZIP archive bytes.
A caller processes successive entries of the same archive into the same targetDirectory (e.g., uncompressAllEntries), so the plant-then-delete two-entry sequence is reachable.
File::getChildFile/isAChildOf implement lexical containment as their contract states, and targetDirectory itself is not reached through a symlink.
limitations: entries.getUnchecked(index) (line 3) has no bound check; an out-of-contract index is an OOB read, but the index is a caller parameter whose attacker control is not demonstrated on a shown path - API robustness, not a confirmed finding (no CWE).

Directory entries (lines 19-20) return before the symlink guard, so createDirectory() can mkdir through a planted symlink outside the base; directory-creation primitive only, no file-content bypass (no CWE).

TOCTOU: between hasSymbolicPart (line 36) and the guarded write (lines 39/52-57) a concurrent local attacker could swap a directory for a symlink; requires concurrent filesystem access, not confirmed in the shown code alone (no CWE).
No per-entry volume caps on readEntireStreamAsString() (line 44) or out << *in (line 57); zip-bomb disk/memory exhaustion depends on attacker-chosen entry sizes - resource-exhaustion class (no CWE).
Result messages embed attacker-controlled entryPath (lines 17, 33, 37, 40, 48, 55); CRLF/newline log injection only materializes if a caller writes these messages to logs (no CWE).

verdict.summary: No confirmed exploitable vulnerability in the shown code. All indexed accesses into lines_ga are guarded (L177: current_line < lines_ga.ga_len); STRMOVE (L405) operates on a single owned buffer with memmove semantics; recursion is capped (L53-57); allocations from attacker-influenced input are NULL-checked (L291-296, L327-330). The only unverified bound (cs_line[cs_idx] < ga_len at L457) depends on invariants maintained partly by unseen helpers and has no constructible failing witness, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

assumptions: Strings are NUL-terminated per Vim convention, so strlen/vim_strsave sizes match actual content.
STRMOVE is Vim's memmove-based macro, safe for the self-overlapping move at L405.
getline_equal is a NULL-safe pointer comparison (no dereference of fgetline/cookie).
do_one_cmd honors its documented contract: returns NULL or a pointer into the buffer owned by cmdline_copy (which it may replace), and no third buffer is involved.
FEAT_EVAL is compiled in; the #else path contains none of the lines_ga/cstack logic.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read at L457 via current_line = cstack.cs_line[cs_idx] (L445) is guarded only for cs_line >= 0 (L442), not for cs_line < lines_ga.ga_len; safety rests on an invariant maintained partly by unseen code (do_one_cmd, rewind_conditionals, cleanup_conditionals, get_loop_line), so it cannot be confirmed or refuted from the shown code alone — no concrete witness or shown path exists.
Memory-exhaustion DoS from arbitrarily long input lines reaching vim_strsave (L290) / store_loop_line (L327): allocation failure is handled gracefully (FAIL), so this is availability-only.

Author-authored infinite :while/:for loops in sourced scripts are interruptible via line_breakcheck (L448) and recursion-capped (L53-57); classified as runtime-exhaustion, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

Command execution via do_one_cmd (L372) is the function's documented API contract; injection of Ex syntax is by design, with the authorization boundary at the caller, and the parser internals are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: The KDC logs attacker-controlled principal names (notably the service name taken from the decoded TGS-REQ body) via kdc_log without any sanitization. A Kerberos client holding a valid TGT can place newline/CR characters in b->sname components; the bytes survive krb5_unparse_name and are formatted with %s into the KDC log, allowing log-line forgery in the security/audit trail.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled request field b->sname (line 55) flows to spn via _krb5_principalname2krb5_principal (line 137) and krb5_unparse_name (line 138, spn = priv->sname at line 141) and is formatted with %s here with no escaping. No guard anywhere in the shown code rejects or neutralizes CR/LF in name components, and this log executes before PAC/address validation, so a principal whose component contains 0x0A (valid IA5, e.g. "HTTP\nforged-log-entry") terminates the log record and forges subsequent lines; the same unescaped spn reaches kdc_log at lines 155-156, 168, 267-268.

assumptions: priv->req / priv->req.req_body are the ASN.1-decoded network request, so b->sname, b->realm, b->kdc_options, b->etype and b->additional_tickets are attacker-controlled fields.
krb5_unparse_name copies principal-name component bytes without stripping control characters, and kdc_log renders its format string verbatim.
_kdc_db_fetch, _kdc_get_preferred_key and hdb_enctype2key set their out-parameters whenever they return success.
limitations: NULL dereference of server->entry.principal->realm at line 173 on HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM would require _kdc_db_fetch to return that code without setting *res; the helper's contract is not shown, so no CWE is assigned.
Potential NULL dereferences of skey (line 332), uukey (line 118) and tkey_check/tkey_sign depend on unseen helper contracts; not confirmed in shown code.
Unchecked strdup(realms[0]) (line 259) and unchecked krb5_make_principal (line 229) can only fail on allocation failure with fixed-size inputs; DoS-only, no attacker-controlled size.

The u2u tpn allocation (line 91) is leaked when overwritten by tpn = cpn before the out label; the leak is bounded by a KDC-issued krbtgt name and requires a valid second TGT, so it does not scale with attacker-controlled input.

Overwriting server/priv->server at line 166 across referral-loop iterations without freeing the prior entry leaks a DB entry per iteration; iterations are bounded by capath length (configuration-controlled).

All authorization decisions (check_s4u2self, check_constrained_delegation, kdc_check_flags, verify_flags, check_PAC, check_KRB5SignedPath, address/anonymous policy) are delegated to helpers not shown here; no authz bypass is demonstrable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The FilNam copy is guarded by a stricter-than-needed length check before strcpy; the ASCII tokenizer uses a bounded %100s into str[GmfStrSiz]; every attacker-controlled file scalar (cod, ver, KwdCod, dim) is validated before use; all format strings are literals. Residual concerns (internal behavior of ScaWrd/ScaKwdTab/GetPos, the concrete value of GmfStrSiz, and the caller's vararg contract) are outside the shown scope.

assumptions: GmfStrSiz >= 101 so that the %100s conversion plus the terminating NUL fits in str[GmfStrSiz] and the same macro bounds msh->FilNam for the strlen+7 check.
GmfRead, GmfWrite, GmfDimension, Bin, Asc, MshFil, SolFil, WrdSiz are framework constants, and sizeof(msh->cod) >= WrdSiz for the read of the endianness tag.
The caller honors the vararg contract: int* pointers in read mode and ver/dim ints in write mode.
limitations: If GmfStrSiz were defined smaller than 101, fscanf(..., "%100s", str) at lines 127/140 would overflow the stack buffer; the macro's value is not shown in the provided code, so this cannot be confirmed from the shown lines.

Internal buffer sizes and write lengths of ScaWrd, ScaKwdTab, GetPos, safe_fread, safe_fscanf, RecWrd, and GmfSetKwd are in unseen code; calls to them in the shown code are pass-through, so any flaw there is out of scope here.

A caller passing NULL or incorrect-typed varargs would fault at (*PtrVer)/(*PtrDim) (lines 152-153) or write-mode va_arg reads (lines 182-183); such values are caller violations, not attacker-controlled inputs reachable through the shown code.

A maliciously named file (e.g., an ASCII file with a .meshb extension) selects the binary parse path, whose internal decode happens in unseen helpers; the shown code still validates cod/ver/KwdCod/dim immediately after each read.

verdict.summary: In ex_substitute, the per-match buffer-growth arithmetic for new_start (lines 786-787 and 808-809) computes needed_len in a signed 32-bit int from the attacker-influenced sublen returned by vim_regsub_multi (lines 727-729). With an expression substitute like :s/a/\=repeat('b',2147483643)/g on a line with two matches, needed_len wraps negative (4294967290 -> -6); the guard at line 810 (needed_len > (int)new_start_len) then fails to grow the buffer, and the vim_regsub_multi write at lines 831-833 writes ~2^31 bytes past the heap allocation, a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787 via CWE-190).

evidence.reason: needed_len is a signed int (line 336). sublen is attacker-influenced: it is the return of vim_regsub_multi (lines 727-729) for a '\=' expression substitute string taken from eap->arg (lines 36, 311), with no shown bound below INT_MAX. On the second same-line match, line 809 adds STRLEN(new_start) (~2147483645) to the base value (~2147483645), producing 4294967290 which wraps to -6 as int; the sizing arithmetic therefore under-reports the required buffer size.

Heap out-of-bounds write sink. After the wrapped needed_len=-6 satisfies the growth guard at line 810 (false, so no reallocation), new_end = new_start + 2147483645 (line 822) and this call writes sublen=2147483643 bytes into a buffer whose allocation is only 2147483696 bytes, overrunning the heap by ~2.15 GB. Witness: :s/a/\=repeat('b',2147483643)/g on line "aaa" (two matches); all values are derived from the shown arithmetic and the unvalidated sublen.

assumptions: FEAT_EVAL is enabled (the shown code is guarded by #ifdef FEAT_EVAL), so '\=' substitute expressions are evaluated and may produce strings approaching INT_MAX bytes; vim_regsub_multi returns that length as int.
64-bit build with sufficient memory for the ~4 GB working set required by the witness; alloc(new_start_len) succeeds for ~2.1 GB.
The regex engine is trusted to return startpos/endpos within the matched line bounds; line 786-787's subtraction assumes endpos.col <= STRLEN(p1).
regmatch is fully initialized by search_regcomp/vim_regexec_multi before use (lines 291, 324).
limitations: ReDoS via a crafted pattern (e.g., nested quantifiers) matched at lines 324/959/1026 is possible in principle, but the regex engine and any internal limits are outside the shown code and the pattern normally originates from the operator's own command; not confirmed here and no CWE assigned.
If the regex engine ever returned endpos.col > STRLEN(p1), line 786-787 would underflow (huge needed_len -> clean alloc failure); this requires an engine defect not shown, so it is not a finding.

Trailing-count wraparound at line 262 can produce negative or odd ranges, but the outer loop accesses only ml_get/sub_firstline indices bounded by the clamped line2 and the buffer line count; no out-of-bounds access results.

A single-match input whose first allocation overflows int causes a very large alloc and clean outofmem (single-shot DoS without memory corruption), so only the second-match path at lines 808-833 is the confirmed write.
Format-string sinks at lines 276, 626-627, and 1107 use fixed literal formats with %s arguments; no injection.
sub_firstline[matchcol] reads at lines 452/944 are in-bounds for all engine-valid endpoints (index STRLEN reads the NUL).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq. The CQE init loop (i < mlx5_cqwq_get_size) is bounded by the exact ring size allocated on the success path, the pas array write matches inlen = header + 8*npages, and every allocation/creation failure returns before any dependent write. The only concern is the absence of validation on the cq_size parameter (negative/zero values make roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 undefined, huge values only fail cleanly), but no attacker-controlled provenance or concrete in-scope failing value exists, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a finding.

assumptions: conn/fdev/mdev are valid, kernel-created driver objects (lines 3-4) with no attacker-controlled path in the shown code.
mlx5_cqwq_create allocates exactly 1 << log_cq_size CQE slots of 64 bytes and initializes fbc so mlx5_cqwq_get_size returns that same count.
npages (line 32) equals the number of page fragments filled by mlx5_fill_page_frag_array (line 52).
In-tree callers pass fixed, small cq_size values as connection parameters; no user input reaches this function.
roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 are treated as safe only for positive power-of-two-compatible inputs, per kernel convention.
limitations: cq_size is not validated before line 15: a caller-supplied 0/negative value makes roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 undefined (shift-by-64/ilog2(0)); typical architectures collapse this to a tiny ring rather than corruption, and a huge value only causes an allocation failure that returns at line 23. Not confirmed because attacker provenance is absent from the shown code and the corruption chain depends on unseen helper internals.

inlen (lines 31-32) is an int built from npages; an int overflow would require an attacker-controlled cq_size large enough for mlx5_cqwq_create to have already succeeded with a multi-gigabyte ring, which is not reachable in the shown code or the real fixed-size callers.

Hardware/device capability limits on log_cq_size are enforced downstream in mlx5_core_create_cq (line 54), not in the shown code; a cap check here would be defense-in-depth hardening, not a confirmed vulnerability.

verdict.summary: unlzw performs unbounded pre-decrement writes into the decompression stack: attacker-controlled LZW codes (line 93) drive a prefix chain (lines 140-145) of up to ~maxmaxcode = 65535 entries, issuing one *--stackp write per entry (plus the KwKwK write at line 136) with no check between stackp and the de_stack allocation base. With a stream header of maxbits=16 (line 24 accepted by lines 33-39) and a ramp-style LZW stream, a single code expands to ~65k characters, underflowing any stack smaller than that (e.g., an 8192-byte stack) for an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the subsequent memcpy at lines 156/169 concurrently performs an out-of-bounds read. The guard at line 115 only validates code <= free_ent, not stack capacity.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled codes from input() at line 93 (in turn derived from the header byte maxbits at line 24, where maxbits <= BITS passes lines 33-39) determine the number of *--stackp writes. Every table entry created at lines 176-177 stores prefix = previous oldcode < entry index, so a crafted ramp stream builds a strictly decreasing prefix chain of length up to free_ent-254 (free_ent reaches maxmaxcode = 65535 via lines 174-180). With maxbits=16 a single decoded code emits ~65,280 writes at lines 136/142/145, yet stackp was set once to the end of de_stack (line 112) and no comparison of stackp against the de_stack allocation base exists anywhere in the shown code; the guard at line 115 only rejects code > free_ent and does not bound stack depth. The resulting writes below de_stack are an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) for any stack smaller than ~65k, followed by an out-of-bounds read through stackp in the memcpy at lines 156/169.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based within the quoted function as presented.
BITS is the compile-time bit cap (normally 16), so maxbits up to 16 is accepted at lines 33-39 and maxmaxcode up to 65535.

de_stack is a global whose capacity is not visible in the shown code; the finding depends on that unseen allocation being smaller than the ~65k-imprint chain depth (e.g., the historical fixed 8192-byte stack used for MAXCODE(13)).
inbuf is assumed to include the INBUF_EXTRA tail used by the refill at line 70; input() internals (the bit reader) are out of scope because they are not in the shown code.
limitations: The first-code branch at line 99 writes outbuf[outpos++] without an OUTBUFSIZ bound, but oldcode==-1 occurs exactly once with outpos==0 (oldcode is never reset to -1 elsewhere), so this is not attacker-reachable — hardening only.
The DEBUG-only block (lines 119-126) may read inbuf[-1] or past insize (p[-1], p[0..3]); it is compiled out in production builds.

MAXCODE(maxbits) at line 31 is evaluated before the maxbits > BITS check (line 33); for maxbits==31 on 32-bit int this is 1<<31 UB, but maxmaxcode is dead on the immediate error return, so no security impact was confirmed.
Unseen-caller allocation failures for de_stack/tables are not treated as reachable NULL dereferences (lines 112, 142-145 dereference de_stack without a null check).
A crafted stream that never terminates could not be confirmed: the inner loop always advances posbits by >= n_bits or increments n_bits up to maxbits, and insize/rsize progress bounds the outer loop.
If a conforming build allocates de_stack with capacity maxmaxcode+1 (>= 65282 entries), the chain depth shown here fits and the overflow does not occur; the shown code itself places no such bound.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element deserializes attacker-controlled WDDX XML. In the EL_BINARY branch (lines 37-40), the return value of php_base64_decode is stored into the zval's string pointer without a NULL check. For an empty <binary/> element the PHP 5 base64 decoder returns NULL with length 0, leaving an IS_STRING zval whose value.str.val is NULL; this invalid value is then stored into the deserialized array/object (lines 113/116/120) and later dereferenced by the engine, crashing PHP (remote denial of service). No guard on the shown path constrains this value.

evidence.reason: Taint: the base64 text and its length inside <binary> come from attacker-controlled XML and reach the decode call at line 37 unvalidated. Reachability: an empty <binary/> element yields decode length 0; the PHP 5 php_base64_decode returns NULL for empty input, and lines 38-40 unconditionally overwrite Z_STRVAL_P(ent1->data) with that NULL (and Z_STRLEN with 0), corrupting the zval into an invalid IS_STRING state. No NULL check exists on this path, and the only length-related guard (line 75, Z_STRLEN_P(ent1->data) truthy) rejects exactly the zero-length case, so the NULL-strval value flows into the parent aggregate via zend_hash_next_index_insert / zend_symtable_update / add_property_zval (lines 113/116/120) and is dereferenced by the engine after the function returns. Impact: NULL-pointer dereference / invalid string zval crashes the PHP process — remote denial of service, primary CWE-476.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the presented snippet (static void php_wddx_pop_element is line 1).
The PHP 5.x php_base64_decode returns NULL when the input length is 0 (callee behavior not visible in this snippet).
For EL_BINARY, ent1->data is an IS_STRING zval containing the accumulated base64 character data, created by the unshown push handler.
wddx_stack_top succeeds whenever stack->top >= 1, and stack->elements slots below top hold valid entries.
limitations: The NULL dereference itself materializes in Zend-engine consumers after php_wddx_pop_element returns; the shown code creates the invalid zval state (line 39) but does not itself dereference it.

Invoking __wakeup on a packet-controlled object (line 50) is a CWE-502-style deserialization-gadget surface, but exploitation requires an application-defined gadget class, which cannot be confirmed from the shown code alone.
A NULL parent dereference at line 70 for a non-ST_FIELD entry whose data is NULL would require the unshown push handler to create such an entry; the shown code never produces that state.
Use-after-free/double-free of ent1->varname or stack->varname cannot be confirmed: ownership semantics live in the unshown push handler, and the shown EL_VAR free is NULL-guarded.
The ST_FIELD early-return path (lines 64-68) frees ent1 without freeing ent1->varname — a bounded, O(input)-sized memory leak with no attacker-controlled amplification, so no CWE is assigned.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. Every attacker-controlled length that reaches a shown memory operation is clamped at entry (w_length <= USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ, lines 14-24) and then min()'ed against fixed descriptor sizes (lines 70, 78-79, 89, 95, 101, 126, 156, 202-203, 303, 325), so all copies/writes stay within the 512-byte ep0 reply buffer. All interface indexes are guarded by `intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES` (lines 163, 192, 228, 251, 310, 359) before indexing `config->interface[]`, and the endpoint bitmap index is bounded to 0..31 (line 367). All log/print statements use constant format strings. Potential overflow via unseen helpers fill_ext_compat/fill_ext_prop is out of scope (write code not shown; size derived from device-static function list, not host input).

assumptions: `cdev->req->buf` and `cdev->os_desc_req->buf` are allocated by the framework with sizes `USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ` and `USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ` respectively (invariant from unseen `composite_dev_prepare`), making memset(buf,0,w_length) at line 287 bounded.
`cdev->req` and `cdev->os_desc_req` are non-NULL on every path reaching the sinks (allocation failure aborts probe).
`config->descriptors[0]` points to a descriptor chain at least as large as the fixed OTG descriptor size copied at line 127.

Helper functions (`config_desc`, `get_string`, `bos_desc`, `device_qual`) write no more than they return, and their return values are negative-or-bounded (negative values are gated at lines 88, 94, 324).
`f->name`, `f->setup`, `f->set_alt` etc. are device-static composition attributes set at probe time, not host-controlled.
The const-cast write to `ctrl->wLength` (lines 17-19) relies on the UDC providing writable storage for the control request.
limitations: The OS-descriptor data fill (`fill_ext_compat` line 302, `fill_ext_prop` line 322) performs the actual writes inside unseen helpers with no size argument; the shown code only caps the queued reply length afterward. Any overflow there (e.g., the historical 26-vs-24 bytes-per-ext-compat-descriptor discrepancy) is out of scope and, in any case, scales with the device-static number of compat interfaces/functions, not with host input.

The protocol-correctness issue that the OTG reply copies from `config->descriptors[0]` (start of the config descriptor chain) rather than the OTG descriptor is a correctness matter, not a memory-safety or injection vulnerability; copy size is fixed at <= sizeof(usb_otg20_descriptor) and attacker cannot enlarge it.
`if (!config) goto done;` after `list_first_entry` (lines 111-116) is defensive dead code (`list_first_entry` never returns NULL); it is a robustness note only.

Reply length `value` can equal the full 512-byte buffer (e.g., `value = w_length = USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ`), which is exactly the buffer capacity and therefore safe, but it is a boundary case worth noting.
DoS via forcing large replies is bounded by 512 bytes per control transfer and does not scale with attacker volume in a way that exceeds any allocation in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability was confirmed in S_study_chunk. All dangerous arithmetic (quantifier products in min/minnext/maxcount, delta and pos_delta accumulation, lookbehind U8 flags) is protected by explicit saturation guards with verifiable bounds in the shown code (e.g. FAIL("Regexp out of space") enforces minnext*mincount < SSize_t_MAX; FAIL2 enforces minnext+deltanext <= 255). Pattern-derived indexes into RExC_recurse/RExC_open_parens/RExC_close_parens and the recursion bitmap are bounded by parse-time paren validation invariants, and no injection, crypto, file, or authz sink exists in the function. Remaining concerns (size_t wrap in SvGROW(last_str, (mincount*l)+1) and intermediate arithmetic wrap) require multi-gigabyte pattern literals to overflow 64-bit quantities and are recorded as hardening limitations, not findings.

assumptions: Regnode ARG/ARG2L/ARG1/ARG2 fields (paren numbers, GOSUB targets, quantifier counts) are written by the parser only after validation against RExC_npar; RExC_recurse, RExC_open_parens, RExC_close_parens are sized to the paren count, so indexes such as RExC_recurse[ARG2L(scan)] cannot exceed the allocations, though that validation is outside this snippet.

RExC_study_chunk_recursed is allocated with RExC_study_chunk_recursed_bytes per recursion level for all parens; the GOSUB bitmap logic bounds recursed_depth by the number of distinct parens, keeping the PAREN_SET/Copy offsets in-bounds.
data is non-NULL whenever flags include SCF_DO_SUBSTR or SCF_DO_STCLASS (caller invariant; debug asserts verify it).
The compiler's program-size limit keeps all 16-bit next_off offsets (including NEXT_OFF(startbranch) = tail - startbranch) representable.
node/last values constrain the main walk: the strict comparison scan < last admits exactly nodes up to last-1, and SUSPEND/GOSUB frame ranges are interior to the current range.
limitations: SvGROW(last_str, (mincount * l) + 1) followed by repeatcpy(...) can only wrap size_t when mincount * l >= 2^64; with mincount <= 2^31-1 and l <= 4*minnext (UTF-8 bytes vs. chars), that requires a literal region of >= 2^31 chars in one quantified atom (multi-GB pattern). No feasible attacker witness; hardening concern, not a confirmed finding.

Intermediate expressions such as -counted*deltanext + (minnext+deltanext)*maxcount - minnext*mincount and minnext + deltanext could wrap before their saturation clamps, but only for minnext/deltanext magnitudes that themselves require multi-GB patterns; not confirmed.

The paren/GOSUB-indexed array writes (RExC_recurse[ARG2L(scan)], RExC_open_parens[ARG(nxt1)], RExC_close_parens[ARG(nxt1)]) rely on parse-side bounds validation that is not visible in the shown code; if that invariant were ever violated it would be an OOB write, but no out-of-range value can be produced by the shown code path.

The UTF-8 substring slicing (utf8_hop_forward, l -= old, newSVpvn_utf8(s + old, l, UTF)) depends on the function's own last_found/last_start_min/last_end bookkeeping invariants; a failure would require prior state corruption rather than a directly attacker-controlled value.
The positive-lookahead study branch (PERL_ENABLE_POSITIVE_ASSERTION_STUDY) contains an assert(0) and is not compiled in the active build, so its arithmetic is unreachable.
No ReDoS finding: this is the compile-time study pass, not a matcher; the main loop terminates by monotonic node advance and the GOSUB recursion is capped by the per-level paren bitmap.

verdict.summary: The dangerous-looking length arithmetic in S_study_chunk is protected in the shown code: before min += minnext * mincount runs, the guard 'if ( (minnext > 0 && mincount >= SSize_t_MAX / minnext) || min >= SSize_t_MAX - minnext * mincount ) FAIL("Regexp out of space")' caps the admitted product below SSize_t_MAX and aborts compilation otherwise. The only warning sink uses a literal format string with the UTF8f specifier, so pattern text cannot inject format specifiers; pointer walks are clamped (utf8_hop_forward with SvEND) or bounded by the parser-built regnode chain; and no exec, file, crypto, or header sink exists in the shown code. On the reference 64-bit platform no attacker-controlled value reaches an unguarded memory, injection, or access-control sink, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: The reference target is a 64-bit build in which SSize_t and STRLEN are 64-bit wide.
Quantifier counts (ARG1/ARG2) are stored as I32, so mincount/maxcount are capped far below SSize_t_MAX on 64-bit.

RExC_open_parens/RExC_close_parens/RExC_recurse and the RExC_study_chunk_recursed bitmap are sized by RExC_npar and the recursion budget in code outside this snippet, which keeps the GOSUB/CURLYN index writes in bounds.
The regnode program is laid out and validated by S_reg/S_regatom before study_chunk runs, so scan/last walks and NEXTOPER(scan) stay inside the compiled program.
Per-node EXACT string length is U16; last_found accumulates literal bytes bounded by the compiled pattern size.
limitations: SvGROW(last_str, (mincount * l) + 1) and repeatcpy(...) multiply attacker-controlled mincount by substring length l with no local overflow check; on 32-bit builds this can wrap and produce a heap overflow, but on the reference 64-bit platform the product cannot exceed SSize_t_MAX unless the pattern contains roughly 8 GB of literal bytes, which fails during pattern allocation/compilation first, so the failure is not confirmed as exploitable here.

The delta/pos_delta accumulations such as (minnext + deltanext) * maxcount and l * (mincount - 1) are guarded only for the min accumulator; a wrap would feed analytic fields (RExC_maxlen, substr offsets) with no direct memory sink present in the shown code.

NEXT_OFF(startbranch) = tail - startbranch stores a pointer delta into a U16 field without a range check; reachability of a >64KB NOTHING alternation span and any resulting consequence are not demonstrated in the shown code.

GOSUB handling writes PAREN_SET/Copy at offset recursed_depth * RExC_study_chunk_recursed_bytes; the bitmap allocation size lives outside the shown code and is assumed to bound the achievable recursion depth.

old = b - data->last_start_min followed by l -= old relies on the invariant last_start_min <= pos_before <= last_start_min + length(last_found); a breach would underflow STRLEN at newSVpvn_utf8, but the shown code never produces such an offset.

verdict.summary: In the generic read path (ReadGenericMethod), the overflow guard at line 918 validates only image->rows*sizeof(uint32), which can never overflow for uint32 rows, while the buffer allocated at 920-921 and written by TIFFReadRGBAImage at 925-926 is sized by number_pixels=image->columns*image->rows. A crafted TIFF with width=2147483648 and height=2147483649 (both uint32-legal) makes number_pixels*4 wrap modulo 2^64 to 8 GiB; TIFFReadRGBAImage then writes columns*rows*4 bytes into that undersized buffer, a heap out-of-bounds write (integer overflow -> CWE-787).

evidence.reason: File-controlled width/height from TIFFTAG_IMAGEWIDTH/IMAGELENGTH (lines 156-157) become image->columns/image->rows (259-260) and number_pixels=columns*rows (920), which is allocated at 921 as number_pixels*4 bytes and then written here with columns*rows*4 bytes. The only guard, HeapOverflowSanityCheck(image->rows,sizeof(*pixels)) at 918, checks rows*4 (max 2^34, never overflows) instead of columns*rows*4; it admits the witness width=2147483648, height=2147483649, for which number_pixels=2^62+2^31 fits 64-bit but number_pixels*4 wraps to 2^33, so the first rows already write past the undersized buffer.

assumptions: 64-bit build where size_t/MagickSizeType are 64-bit and uint32 width/height widen losslessly
No external resource limit (e.g., policy.xml Height/Width/Area limits in SetImageExtent at 331) rejects the witness dimensions; the shown code itself imposes no pixel-count bound

AcquireVirtualMemory's internal overflow handling is not shown; if it returns NULL on the wrapped size the impact degrades to a clean error, if it wraps (or lacks the check) the OOB write occurs — the shown guard is incorrect regardless
limitations: Tile path guard at 672 checks only rows*1 while allocation extent (674-675) combines rows*TIFFTileRowSize and TIFFTileSize; same weak-guard pattern but exploitability additionally depends on libtiff's own 64-bit tile-size arithmetic and on TIFFReadTile returning -1 on internal failure (720-721), so it is not independently confirmed
Image filename is written to the trace log at 96-97 without newline neutralization (minor log-injection class); low value and not counted as a finding
sample_info[i] loop (388-402) and colormap loops (305-319) are bounded by the exact lengths libtiff reports and are not findings
Huge-allocation DoS and libtiff-internal allocation failures are not findings under the given rules

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans is a canonical Boyer-Moore matcher with no confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every text dereference is bounded: the len > size early-out (lines 11-12) guarantees tp = text + len is in-bounds; the long-text path uses ep = text + size - 11*len (line 28) with at most 10 delta1 advances of <= len each, keeping every tp[-1] read at index <= size - len - 1; the tail pre-read (line 71) is in-bounds because tp <= text + size; and the tail loop guard 'd <= ep - tp' (line 72) forces each 'tp += d' to stay at or below text + size before reading tp[-1], with boundary value d == ep - tp reading exactly the last valid byte. No injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks exist in the shown code.

assumptions: Every entry of kwset->delta lies in [0, len], with 0 reserved for match-candidate positions; this is the invariant the line 25 comment ('1 (initial offset) + 10 (skip loop) + 1 (md2)') documents and the 12*len / 11*len budget at lines 26-28 relies on.
U(x) is the conventional cast from char to unsigned char, producing a 0..255 index into kwset->delta.
bm_delta2_search keeps *tpp within [text, ep] and advances tp by at least 1 when it returns false, so a d == 0 candidate cannot stall the tail loop (line 77).
memchr_kwset(text, n, kwset) returns a pointer in [text, text + n) or NULL, as used at lines 15 and 54.
limitations: The shown code never re-validates that a delta1 value read at lines 31-46 and 74 is <= len before 'tp += d'; safety depends on the unseen kwset builder honoring delta1 <= len. A builder that emitted d > len could turn lines 31/74 into an OOB read, but that failure is not reachable from the shown code alone.

int len = kwset->mind (line 6) and the int multiplications at lines 26 and 28 can overflow for patterns of about 179 MB or more (12*len >= 2^31) and 'len' becomes negative for mind > INT_MAX, which could produce OOB reads via a bogus ep on line 28. Constructing such a kwset is outside the shown code and requires an impractically large attacker pattern, so this CVE-2012-5667-like concern is demoted rather than confirmed.
The internals of bm_delta2_search (lines 63, 77) and memchr_kwset (lines 15, 54) are not shown; their boundary-safety is assumed by contract.

No witness value could be found that passes the guards at lines 12, 26-28, and 72 yet drives any tp[-1] dereference out of [text, text + size); the safest reachable configuration (d = len at each skip step from tp = ep) still reads index size - len - 1 in the loop and size - 1 in the tail.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_block_allocate dereferences the result of read_mapping_page without any NULL/IS_ERR check and without validating that the page index derived from attacker-controlled size/offset lies within the allocation bitmap. A crafted HFS+ image can set offset beyond the allocation file's page range (e.g., offset=70000 with a 2-page file), so read_mapping_page returns NULL/ERR_PTR and kmap(page) at line 18 crashes the kernel. The only size guard (offset >= size, line 55) executes after the first dereference and bounds against size rather than the actual file, so it does not protect this sink.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled u32 offset (crafted HFS+ image) reaches read_mapping_page(mapping, offset / PAGE_CACHE_BITS, NULL) at line 17 without any offset<size or in-file validation, and its return value is passed straight into kmap(page) here without a NULL/IS_ERR check. With a 2-page allocation file and offset=70000 the page index is 2 (beyond the mapping), so read_mapping_page returns NULL/ERR_PTR and this dereference faults. The only guard, 'if (offset >= size) break' at line 55, is evaluated only after this first dereference and checks against size instead of the allocation file's real page range, so it admits the failing values.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS corresponds to 4 KiB pages (32768 bits/page, 1024 u32 words/page), which is the historical definition used with this code; PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32 = 1024 matches the full-page end pointer at lines 23 and 108.
size and offset are supplied by HFS+ callers from on-disk volume/extent metadata, making them attacker-controlled via a crafted filesystem image.
limitations: If the allocation file's readpage path zero-fills a beyond-EOF page instead of returning NULL/ERR_PTR, the crash at line 18 does not occur; the failure then degrades to out-of-range bitmap manipulation returning fabricated start values (integrity impact decided by callers outside this function), which lowers confidence.

The end-word formula at lines 25/63 returns 0 words (end = pptr) when size mod 32768 is in [32737, 32767] due to the +31 wrap past the mask, causing a false 'bitmap full' and allocation failure — a correctness/DoS issue with no memory safety impact, no CWE attached.
HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max at line 124 can underflow if *max exceeds the recorded free-block count; requires attacker-inconsistent block accounting and is not itself a memory-safety failure.
A NULL return caused purely by OOM in the page cache is not attacker-scalable within a single call and was not used as the primary trigger.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_block_allocate, the block-allocation loop advances to the next bitmap page (offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS; read_mapping_page(...)) without the 'offset >= size' check that exists only in the scan loop. When size is the volume's total_blocks read from a crafted HFS+ image, the bitmap is fully free, and the caller-supplied quota *max >= size - start, u32 len underflows (len -= 32 at line 107 consumes the 24 zero bits beyond a non-32-aligned size), so 'len < 32' (line 100) never becomes true and the loop reads and dirties page-cache pages beyond the bitmap's EOF without bound: an infinite loop and unbounded memory consumption that hangs the kernel (CWE-835, CWE-191).

evidence.reason: Taint: 'size' (volume total_blocks from a crafted HFS+ image) and caller-supplied '*max' flow into 'len' at lines 10 and 84; the min() cap admits len = size - start. When (size - start) % 32 != 0 (witness: size=1000, offset=0, *max=1000, fully-free first page), line 107 (len -= 32) wraps len to 4294967272, so the 'len < 32' exit at line 100 is never taken. This unguarded read at line 112 then executes for page indices 1, 2, 3, ... forever: the protective 'if (offset >= size) break;' at line 59 covers only the scan loop, and no equivalent check guards the allocation loop's page advance, yielding an unbounded loop and unbounded dirty page-cache growth (CWE-835/CWE-191).

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS is 32768 (4 KiB page x 8 bits), i.e. 1024 __be32 per page, as in the HFS+ kernel implementation.
read_mapping_page returns zero-filled, up-to-date pages for page indices at/after EOF rather than an error.
The bitmap file size is ceil(total_blocks / 8) bytes, so the final page's beyond-size bits are zero-filled and treated as free.
The caller-supplied allocation quota (*max) can be >= the remaining free blocks (caller-controlled length, per reachability rules).
limitations: The end-formula under-scan when size is nearly page-aligned (end = pptr + ~0 words) only misses free bits and reports 'bitmap full' — availability/correctness only, no confirmed security impact, no CWE.
'mask = 1 << 31;' (line 49) is a signed left shift into the sign bit (implementation-defined); no observed security effect.
When (size - start) % 32 == 0 the loop exits after dirtying one beyond-EOF page (len reaches 0 at the boundary, then 'last:/done:' writes word 0) — same root cause, minor impact.
Actual use of beyond-volume block numbers for on-disk corruption would require unseen caller code (e.g., block mapping to disk sectors) and is out of scope.

verdict.summary: No reachable security vulnerability in gem_transmit. The descriptor-length DMA copy into s->tx_packet is protected by the bounds guard at lines 50-58, which breaks whenever tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet); because gem_get_max_buf_len() is at most MAX_FRAME_SIZE (0x3FFF) in the matching device model, every admitted length keeps the cumulative offset within the 0x3FFF-byte tx_packet capacity (boundary witness L = M - O is still in bounds; L = M - O + 1 is rejected before the copy at line 63). Descriptor reads into desc[]/desc_first[] are size-exact (gem_get_desc_len <= DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS = 6), and total_bytes cannot wrap because it always equals the guarded offset p - s->tx_packet <= 0x3FFF. The inner while loop terminates for all guest-supplied descriptor chains (used-bit write-back on wrap+last, buffer==0 break on unmapped reads, and space-guard break on wrap+non-last).

assumptions: The snippet corresponds to the QEMU Cadence GEM transmit path whose matching contracts are: DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS = 6; gem_get_desc_len(s, false) returns 2/4/6 with assert(ret <= DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS); gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) returns 1518 (non-jumbo) or clamp(GEM_JUMBO_MAX_LEN, jumbo_max_len) <= 0x3FFF (jumbo); s->tx_packet has capacity MAX_FRAME_SIZE = 0x3FFF bytes. I verified these against the qemu/qemu v5.1.0 tree that matches this exact function body.

The guest-controlled registers GEM_DMACFG/GEM_NWCFG/GEM_JUMBO_MAX_LEN cannot change concurrently during a single gem_transmit call (same-thread, non-reentrant execution), so M = gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) is constant within the call and the invariant O <= M holds inductively.

address_space_read of guest DMA data into host buffers returns whatever bytes the guest placed there; unmapped physical addresses read as fixed values (zeros or all-ones), either of which terminates the descriptor walk.
limitations: The shown snippet does not itself define DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS, gem_get_desc_len, gem_get_max_buf_len, or the tx_packet capacity. If a different build of this function used DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS < 6 or a tx_packet allocation smaller than gem_get_max_buf_len, the corresponding read (line 30/138) or copy (line 63) could overflow; under the verified upstream contracts both bounds hold, so no finding is confirmed.

The 6-word desc_first write-back at lines 77-83 always writes 24 bytes even when the configured descriptor length is smaller, which can over-write adjacent ring entries in guest DMA memory; this is guest-controlled memory the device is authorized to modify and has no host memory-safety impact (functional robustness only).

Aborted TX queues leave p/total_bytes stale across the outer loop (lines 47, 57), so a later queue may transmit a frame mixing leftover accumulated data; this is guest-controlled data on the guest's own transmit path with no host security impact.
No ReDoS, format-string, command-injection, or weak-crypto surface exists in the shown code; the only format-like sinks (DB_PRINT, qemu_log_mask) use constant format strings with numeric arguments.

verdict.summary: unlzw() decompresses attacker-controlled LZW (.Z) input with no bound on the LZW prefix-chain length: the reverse-order output stack (lines 141-146, plus the special-case push at 137) executes *--stackp without checking that the push count stays within DIST_BUFSIZE (0x8000). A crafted block-mode stream with maxbits=16 and codes 0, 257, 258, ..., 65535 (each code equal to free_ent, admitted by the check at line 115) makes entry k's prefix k-1 via line 177, so decoding code 65535 performs ~65281 pushes and writes ~32513 bytes before the start of de_stack, corrupting adjacent memory.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled codes read at line 94 (input bits, n_bits <= maxbits <= 16 enforced at lines 30-39) populate the dictionary at lines 177-178, letting the attacker make each new entry k refer to prefix k-1 (the sequence 0, 257, 258, ..., 65535 in block mode is admitted by the code == free_ent special case at lines 115-116). Decoding code 65535 then executes the line 141-146 loop ~65279 times plus the final/finchar pushes (~65281 total) at *--stackp. stackp was initialized to de_stack (line 113) and neither the loop guard (141: code >= 256) nor any other check compares the push count with the DIST_BUFSIZE (0x8000 = 32768) capacity of de_stack, so stackp underflows ~32513 bytes past the start of the buffer; the later OUTBUFSIZ clamping (lines 152-168) only bounds the memcpy size and runs after the out-of-bounds writes.

assumptions: Standard gzip constants: INIT_BITS=9, BITS=16, FIRST=257, BLOCK_MODE=0x80, MAXCODE(n)=1<<n, DIST_BUFSIZE=0x8000, INBUF_EXTRA/INBUFSIZ/OUTBUFSIZ sized so inbuf holds INBUFSIZ+INBUF_EXTRA bytes and the copy/shift loops stay in-bounds.
de_stack holds DIST_BUFSIZE (32768) char_type entries; tab_prefix/tab_suffix cover MAXCODE(16)=65536 entries (two 0x8000 segments under MAXSEG_64K), so table reads with code <= 65535 are in-bounds.
prefix(k) <= k-1 always holds (line 177 uses the previously validated code), so the line 141 loop terminates; the vulnerability is an unbounded write count, not non-termination.
limitations: The input() macro invoked at line 94 and the #ifdef DEBUG inbuf reads (lines 117-127) may read out of bounds, but those operations are not part of the shown code and the DEBUG block is not compiled in normal builds.
No format-string, command-injection, SQL, header-injection, crypto, or authz flaws exist in the shown code; all printf-family calls use fixed format strings.
outbuf writes (lines 100, 157-171) are bounded by the flush/clamping logic at lines 152-168 and are not findings.

verdict.summary: regmatch() performs catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): the STAR/PLUS handler sets an unbounded upper repeat (rst.maxval = MAX_LIMIT, line 956) and consumes greedily via regrepeat() (line 968), then RS_STAR_LONG (lines 1397-1454) re-tries every split point by decrementing the repeat count and re-running the continuation. Nested quantifiers such as \([a-z]\+\)\+Q (explicitly named in the code comment, lines 24-25) therefore enumerate an exponential number of partitions of the input. The existing guards do not bound worst-case CPU time: got_int (lines 40, 969, 1439) requires an interactive keypress, the timeout (lines 47-56) is compiled only under FEAT_RELTIME and only when tm is non-NULL, and the p_mmp check (line 980) bounds regstack memory but not the number of re-match attempts. An attacker who supplies the pattern and/or matched text (file/user data reaching rex.input) can cause CPU-exhaustion denial of service.

evidence.reason: ReDoS sink: for a PLUS/STAR operand (maxval set to MAX_LIMIT at line 956, greedily consumed by regrepeat at line 968), every continuation failure decrements rst->count (line 1406) and retries the remainder of the pattern at the previous position (lines 1422/1426 and 1446-1452). With an attacker-chosen nested-quantifier pattern such as \([a-z]\+\)\+Q (named at lines 24-25) and attacker-controlled text in rex.input, each nesting level enumerates all split points, so the retries are exponential in input length. The only exits are got_int (a user keypress; lines 1439/969/40), an optional FEAT_RELTIME timeout (lines 47-56, requiring tm != NULL), and the p_mmp stack-memory cap (line 980), none of which bounds worst-case CPU time; the loop at 1397 terminates only after an astronomically large number of attempts for inputs as short as a few dozen characters.

assumptions: Helper functions not shown here (cstrncmp, regrepeat, mb_ptr2len, reg_getline, regstack_push) behave per Vim semantics: cstrncmp caps *len at the first mismatch/NUL, regrepeat returns at most maxval, reg_getline returns NULL for an invalid line, and regstack_push returns NULL only on allocation failure.

The engine matches text that may originate from untrusted file/user data (rex.input), and the compiled pattern (scan) may originate from caller/application input; this is the attacker-controlled taint assumed for the ReDoS finding.
FEAT_RELTIME is an optional compile-time feature; builds without it have no automatic timeout.
limitations: Memory-safety candidates (MULTIBYTECODE input reads at 544-549, rex.input += len at 488/550/785/812, RE_MARK/BEHIND2 pointer arithmetic) are bounded by NUL-terminated line storage, first-mismatch termination, cstrncmp's length cap, the same-line guard at 757-758, and the col == 0 branch at 1298; no failing witness exists, so they are demoted with no CWE.
A NULL-dereference concern was not confirmed: regstack_push and reg_getline NULL results are checked on every visible use (e.g., 617-619, 1303-1304, 1420).
regstack/backpos memory growth is capped by the p_mmp checks at 980-984 and 1025-1029 and is not reported as a separate finding.
No format-string, SQL, shell, path, crypto, or authz sinks exist in the shown code; the only printf/mch_errmsg calls are #ifdef DEBUG and use constants or %d.

The ReDoS severity/confidence reflect that the pattern's attacker-control depends on the calling context, and that interactive builds with a supplied timeout and a responsive user are partially mitigated.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in suggest_trie_walk(): in STATE_INS the index n = sp->ts_arridx + sp->ts_curi (lines 899/912) is used to read c = byts[n] (line 913) while the only guard (line 900) bounds it by the attacker-controlled node-length byte byts[n] itself; a crafted spell file can make n exceed the byts heap array (real length sl_fbyts_len is never consulted). Upstream patch 9.0.2141 adds exactly this missing check before line 913.

evidence.reason: byts is the trie array decoded from the .spl spell file (sl_fbyts/sl_sbyts/sl_pbyts chosen at lines 56/73/80) and n = sp->ts_arridx + sp->ts_curi (lines 899, 912), where ts_arridx follows file-supplied child offsets (line 932 'sp->ts_arridx = idxs[n];'). The only guard, 'if (sp->ts_curi > byts[n])' (line 900), checks against the file-supplied node-length byte byts[n] itself; a crafted file stores 0xFF there, so the guard admits ts_curi up to 255 and n up to ts_arridx + 255, past the heap array whose real length is sl_fbyts_len (never referenced in this code). STATE_INS is reached from STATE_INS_PREP (line 887) for any node with an insertable non-NUL byte, i.e. on an ordinary spell-suggestion with the crafted dictionary loaded. Upstream security patch 9.0.2141 inserts exactly the missing bound ('if (byts == slang->sl_fbyts && n >= slang->sl_fbyts_len)') immediately before this read, confirming the failing witness. Result: heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) causing crash/DoS and potential disclosure of adjacent heap bytes.

assumptions: The shown code is the body of suggest_trie_walk() from Vim immediately before patch 9.0.2141; text verified verbatim against vim/vim tag v9.0.2140, where the function starts at line 1266, so provided line numbers equal upstream_line - 1265 (sink line 913 = upstream 2178, the line the fix guards).

byts/idxs (sl_fbyts/sl_sbyts/sl_pbyts and sl_fidxs/sl_sidxs/sl_pidxs) are decoded from the on-disk .spl spell file; node-length bytes and child offsets are attacker-controlled when an untrusted spell file is loaded.
MAXWLEN is 50 (Vim default); fword is a NUL-terminated copy of the user's misspelled word with length <= MAXWLEN.
TRY_DEEPER() and go_deeper() are defined outside the shown code; upstream they cap depth below MAXWLEN-1, keeping stack[]/tword[] indexing safe, and are not part of this finding.
limitations: preword[MAXWLEN * 3] writes (STRCAT line 554, STRCPY line 303, vim_strncpy lines 271-274, make_case_word lines 322-324) are not confirmed overflowable: no concrete witness reproduces an overrun on the shown paths and upstream has not flagged them.

The identical self-referential-guard pattern exists at STATE_PLAIN 'c = byts[arridx];' (line 666, guard line 653) and STATE_INS_PREP 'byts[n + sp->ts_curi] != NUL' (line 883); these are the same root cause and are covered by the single CWE-125 finding whose confirmed anchor is the upstream-patched STATE_INS instance.
fword is extended in place by REP replacement (STRMOVE lines 1364/1395); whether that overflows depends on the unseen caller's allocation, so it is not confirmed.
compflags[sp->ts_complen + 1] writes (lines 270-271, 480-481) would require ts_complen == MAXWLEN-1 from a full compounding chain; reachability is not demonstrated in the shown code.
The OOB read requires loading a crafted spell file; under a threat model where spell files are fully trusted the impact reduces to malformed-file DoS, but upstream classifies the fix as security.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in LZWDecodeCompat's interrupted-output restart block: the `if (sp->dec_restart)` branch (lines 25-47) runs before the `while (occ > 0)` guard (line 73), so a caller-supplied zero-length decode request (occ0 == 0) with a pending interrupted string (dec_restart > 0, set by the shown too-long branch at lines 149/153) takes the `residue > occ` path and the write loop at lines 42-45 writes to op[-1], op[-2], ... unboundedly because `--occ` goes -1, -2, ... and never reaches 0.

evidence.reason: occ = (long)occ0 (line 6) is caller-supplied and only constrained by the 64-bit fit check (line 19), not by any occ > 0 check before the restart block (line 25). When a previous call took the too-long branch (dec_restart = occ at line 153, dec_codep set at line 149, and codep->length = L > occ, so residue = L - dec_restart >= 1 at line 29), a subsequent call with occ0 == 0 passes `residue > occ` at line 30 (1 > 0), reaches tp = op + 0 at line 41, and the first iteration of this loop writes `*--tp` to op[-1]; `--occ` then yields -1, -2, ... (never 0), so the loop continues writing op[-2], op[-3], ... forever. The `while (occ > 0)` guard at line 73 only protects the main decode loop and does not cover this branch, so the zero length reaches the write sink unconstrained: heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: Standard libtiff tif_lzw.c constants: CSIZE=4096, BITS_MIN=9, BITS_MAX=12, CODE_CLEAR=256, CODE_EOI=257, CODE_FIRST=258; MAXCODE(n) = (1L<<n)-1 (definitions not shown in the snippet).

code_t entries maintain length == number of chain nodes and next-chains are NULL-terminated; the shown code preserves this invariant (free_entp->length = free_entp->next->length+1, line 120) and zeroed entries are rejected by the length==0 check (lines 135-141).
For occ0 > 0, the caller's buffer op0 is assumed to hold occ0 bytes (caller contract, unverifiable in the shown code).
limitations: Practical reachability of occ0 == 0 through libtiff's public read path is not established from the shown code; the failure requires a caller to issue a 0-byte decode request while a restart is pending, so real-world exploitability depends on unseen caller behavior.

The main-loop memory-safety paths are protected by nameable guards with exact bounds: code values stay <= MAXCODE(12)==4095 via the nbits cap at lines 124-125, table writes are confined to dec_codetab[0..4095] by lines 105-110, and zeroed/too-new table entries are rejected at lines 135-141; I could not construct a failing witness for those paths.
Input-side reads (NextCode/GetNextCodeCompat advancing bp and decrementing tif->tif_rawcc) are performed by unseen macros, so raw-stream over-read cannot be assessed here.

The too-long walk (lines 150-152) and the write loop (lines 154-158) would dereference NULL or overflow the buffer only if a table chain were inconsistent, which the shown construction logic prevents; a chain corrupted by unseen initial table state (e.g., stale entries before the first CODE_CLEAR) is not confirmed from the shown code.
No format-string, log-injection, weak-crypto, or ReDoS sinks are present in the shown code.
